The appellant showed no misreading of evidence, perversity, legal or procedural error, or injustice.
Subject matter varied: criminal convictions on eyewitness and medical evidence, specific performance, title and possession, benami holdings, adoption, tenancy, maintenance, and damages.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 136 of the Constitution of India
Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure
Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Section 6(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963
Sections 323 and 447 of the Indian Penal Code, and Section 162(2) of the Gujarat Panchayats Act
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 25 members the Court left the concurrent findings undisturbed and dismissed or affirmed the decision below. This was in about 8 criminal appeals and 17 civil or other appeals.
variations: The exceptions are stated differently: error of law; manifest error or unreasonableness; perversity or no evidence; exceptional circumstances; grave injustice; and procedural or natural-justice violation.
Several members cite earlier authorities, such as Meenakshi Mills, Narayan Gosavi, Bibhabati and Babu v. Dy. Director, while others cite none.
Some members add case-specific reasons: the finding was not challenged below, the fabrication allegation was unproved, or the defence was an afterthought.
Some members treat the finding as a pure question of fact. One notes that construing a document raises a question of law and that adverse possession is a mixed question.

legal_question: When does an earlier decision, order or proceeding fail to operate as res judicata, constructive res judicata or issue estoppel in a later proceeding?

predicates.prior_decision_or_proceeding_relied_on_a: A party invokes an earlier judgment, order or proceeding as precluding the later case by res judicata, constructive res judicata or issue estoppel.
predicates.matter_in_later_proceeding_not_directly_: The issue that arises in the later proceeding was not raised, framed, heard or expressly decided in the earlier proceeding, either directly or constructively.
predicates.prior_proceeding_lacked_final_merits_adj: The earlier proceeding ended without a final decision on the merits between the same parties (for example dismissal for default or non-prosecution, dismissal on a technical ground, an ex parte or summary order, a remand leaving the issue open, or no contest between the parties).
predicates.prior_case_concerned_different_property_: The earlier case concerned different land or property, different parties, or a distinct cause of action, including one arising under a later law, or rested on materially different facts or law.
predicates.prior_decision_on_pure_question_of_law_o: The earlier decision determined only a pure question of law, including a question of a court's jurisdiction.
predicates.later_proceeding_concerns_different_caus: The later proceeding involves a different cause of action and property, or a challenge to jurisdiction that an earlier ruling or estoppel cannot confer.
predicates.res_judicata_does_not_bar_later_proceedi: The earlier decision or proceeding does not preclude the later claim, issue or objection.

definition: Res judicata and its extensions (constructive res judicata, issue estoppel) apply only where the same matter was directly and substantially in issue and was heard and finally decided between the same parties or those claiming under them. They do not apply where the earlier case involved different property, parties, issues or cause of action, ended without a final merits decision, or decided only a pure question of law or jurisdiction.
exceptions_or_limits: The bar applies where all Section 11 requirements are met: same parties, same matter directly and substantially in issue, a final decision, and a competent court.

The plea must ordinarily be pleaded and proved, with the earlier pleadings, issues and judgment produced; it may be waived, and an unpleaded plea is allowed only where the facts were considered and the other side could rebut it.
Summary tenancy proceedings fall outside Section 11 unless the statute expressly extends res judicata to them.
A decision on a pure question of law is not binding in a later proceeding on a different cause of action; it may remain binding where the cause of action and property are the same.
A decision made in ignorance of controlling law may be per incuriam on the omitted issue.

common_material_facts: An earlier suit, writ, appeal or execution proceeding is invoked as a bar to a later proceeding.
The earlier case concerned different land or property, different parties, or a different issue or cause of action.
The earlier case ended in dismissal for default, dismissal on a technical ground, an ex parte or summary order, or a remand, with no final merits decision.
The issue now raised was never framed or decided earlier, for example title, interpretation, possession or tenancy status.
The doctrine is invoked in land ceiling, tenancy and eviction, land acquisition and title disputes.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including Explanation IV on constructive res judicata
Section 115 of the Evidence Act (estoppel)
Article 141 of the Constitution (precedent distinguished from res judicata)
Right to Information Act, 2005
Land ceiling, tenancy, rent control and land grabbing statutes
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 25 members hold that the res judicata or estoppel bar does not apply and the later proceeding may continue. The reasons are mainly no identity of issue, property or parties (about 11), no final merits adjudication (about 9), and pure law or jurisdiction, procedural or pleading defects (about 5).
variations: Some members turn on non-identity of property, parties or cause of action; others on the absence of a final decision.
Some members rest on pleading and proof failures, such as an unpleaded plea or missing earlier records.
Some members rest on the nature of the earlier forum or decision: a summary tribunal, an ex parte order, a pure question of law, a jurisdictional ruling, or a per incuriam decision.
One member applies issue estoppel in a criminal context, where an acquittal did not decide the disputed fact.
One member separates res judicata from the binding force of precedent.

legal_question: When does a landlord seeking eviction from rented premises for own or family occupation or business use establish a genuine (bona fide) requirement, and what must the landlord prove, including the absence of other suitable accommodation and the link between the claimed user and the landlord's own use?

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and landlord_claims_own_or_close_family_use and need_is_genuine_present_and_not_pretext_on_the_evidence and (not other_reasonably_suitable_accommodation_of_landlords_own_available or landlord_explains_unsuitability_of_alternative) and (use_is_landlords_own_or_closely_connected_family_use)

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The case is a proceeding by a landlord to evict a tenant under a state rent-control or accommodation-control statute.
predicates.landlord_claims_own_or_close_family_use: The landlord seeks possession for personal residence or own business, or for a family member or closely connected person whose use can be treated as the landlord's own.
predicates.need_is_genuine_present_and_not_pretext_: The evidence, objectively assessed, shows a sincere, honest, present and reasonable need rather than a mere wish, whim, fanciful desire or ruse, and the landlord bears the burden of proving it.
predicates.other_reasonably_suitable_accommodation_: The landlord owns or occupies other reasonably suitable accommodation (residential or non-residential, as relevant) in the same town that could meet the need; rented premises do not count.
predicates.landlord_explains_unsuitability_of_alter: The landlord shows that any other accommodation of the landlord's own is unsuitable or insufficient for the claimed need.
predicates.use_is_landlords_own_or_closely_connecte: The intended use is the landlord's own occupation or business, or that of a family member or dependent whose use is in substance the landlord's own requirement, as opposed to a separate or distinct business of another person.
predicates.landlord_requirement_is_bona_fide_and_ev: The court holds the landlord's requirement bona fide and the statutory ground for eviction made out.

definition: A landlord succeeds on a personal-need eviction ground only if the landlord proves, on the evidence and objectively, a genuine, present and reasonable need for own or closely connected family occupation or business, and that no other reasonably suitable accommodation of the landlord's own is available. Bare assertion, a pretext, undisclosed or unexplained suitable alternatives, or a need that is not the landlord's own defeat the claim.
exceptions_or_limits: A bare assertion of need, without evidence of genuineness, does not discharge the landlord's burden.

Where the non-residential ground requires absence of other suitable accommodation, the landlord's own available and suitable space, including space acquired during the proceeding, defeats the claim unless unsuitability is shown; rented premises are not the landlord's own accommodation.
Being a partner in a firm does not by itself make the partnership's business the landlord's own business; the landlord must prove own business occupation.
Ownership (including undivided co-ownership) may be a statutory prerequisite under some Acts, and the landlord must establish it where required.
Where concurrent findings of bona fide need are supported by evidence and not perverse, the Supreme Court generally does not interfere.
The precise statutory wording differs by State Act, so the specific provision governs details such as family-member use or presumptions of bona fides.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns a pleading rule (no need to specify the precise nature of the intended business) rather than proof of genuineness or alternative accommodation.
Concerns ownership of the premises as a precondition to the own-business ground, not bona fides of need.
Concerns whether an undivided co-owner counts as an owner, a status question rather than bona fides of need.
Concerns whether a mixed business and residence requirement bars eviction under the statutory scheme, a separate statutory-construction point.

common_material_facts: Landlord seeks possession of residential or non-residential premises for own occupation, own business, or a son's or family member's business.
Trial and appellate courts and the High Court have made findings on genuineness of need that the Supreme Court is asked to review.
Tenant points to alternative accommodation owned or available to the landlord, or alleges pretext.
Landlord's evidence of need (health, inadequate space, inadequate income, business plans) is tested against cross-examination.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 12(1)(f) and Section 23-A(b), Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961
Section 13(3)(a) and 13(3)(a)(ii), East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949
Section 21(1)(h), Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961
Section 10(3)(a)(iii) and 10(3)(e), Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
Section 11(3), Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965
Section 11(1)(h), Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966
Section 13(1)(f), West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956
Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Dr. Mahesh Chand Gupta (1999) 6 SCC 222 (frequently relied on)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 21 covered members, about 15 uphold or establish bona fide need and eviction, usually where evidence supports a sincere need and there is no suitable owned alternative. About 6 reject the claim or require stricter proof, for bare assertion, a suitable available alternative, or lack of proof of own business occupation.
variations: Some members treat the need of a son or family member as the landlord's own, while others require proof that the business is the landlord's own, as in the partnership cases.
Courts defer to the landlord's choice of business and premises once genuineness is established, but scrutinise alternative accommodation, including space acquired during the litigation.
Several decisions turn on deference to concurrent findings of fact rather than fresh assessment.
Statutory wording differs: some Acts presume bona fides in special procedures, and some use 'reasonable and bona fide' while others use 'requires'.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) bona fide need established or defeated on evidence, including pretext and concurrent findings (residential and business); (b) availability of other suitable owned accommodation for non-residential business need; (c) scope of 'own use' or 'own business' for family members and partnerships; and (d) threshold or procedural issues (ownership or co-ownership, pleading of the business, mixed residential and business requirement).

legal_question: Can a party raise for the first time on appeal (including in the Supreme Court or a second appeal) a contention that depends on disputed or uninvestigated facts, or on a mixed question of law and fact, when it was not pleaded or argued in the courts below?

rule.if: appellate_proceeding and contention_raised_for_first_time_on_appeal and contention_not_pleaded_or_urged_in_courts_below and (contention_requires_factual_investigation_or_evidence or contention_is_mixed_question_of_law_and_fact or contention_inconsistent_with_case_below)

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The matter is before an appellate court, whether a first, second, further or final appeal, special leave appeal, or an appeal from a writ decision.
predicates.contention_raised_for_first_time_on_appe: The party advances the contention for the first time at the appellate stage.
predicates.contention_not_pleaded_or_urged_in_court: The contention was not set out in the pleadings, framed as an issue, or argued before the trial court, the lower appellate court or the High Court, as applicable.
predicates.contention_requires_factual_investigatio: Deciding the contention needs evidence, findings of fact or factual inquiry that the record does not supply, or the opposing party had no opportunity to meet it.
predicates.contention_is_mixed_question_of_law_and_: The contention is not a pure question of law, because it combines legal and factual elements.
predicates.contention_inconsistent_with_case_below: The contention contradicts the position the party took in its pleadings or throughout the proceedings below.
predicates.appellate_court_declines_to_entertain_ne: The appellate court refuses to consider the new contention, usually without deciding its merits.

definition: An appellate court, particularly the final court, will not entertain a contention raised for the first time on appeal when it was not pleaded or argued below and its determination needs factual investigation, involves a mixed question of law and fact, or contradicts the party's earlier case.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule concerns factual and mixed questions; a pure question of law arising on the existing record is not shown by the members to be barred.
The refusal is discretionary and procedural. The court usually does not decide the merits and may leave the point open, for example for later proceedings or for determination on relevant materials.
Where the record already contains the necessary facts and the opposing party suffers no prejudice, the members do not decide whether the point could be heard.

If a party disputes the High Court's recorded account of the arguments, it must seek correction from that court. Affidavits filed in the Supreme Court cannot establish that the point was raised below.

outlier_members.reason: The Court expressed no opinion on the limitation plea and left it to be decided on relevant materials. It did not clearly refuse to entertain the plea, although the plea was raised for the first time on appeal and the facts were undetermined.

common_material_facts: The appellant or respondent advances a new factual or mixed ground at the appellate stage that was not in the written statement, the issues or the arguments below.
Deciding the ground would need evidence or findings on disputed facts that the record lacks.
The opposing party had no chance to lead evidence on the point.
Some members involve a new theory inconsistent with the pleaded or earlier case.
Subject areas include tenancy and eviction, land acquisition, tax assessment, limitation and property title.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 136 of the Constitution (special leave jurisdiction)
Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, ss. 209, 210, 18 and 6 (cited but not decided)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, s. 48(3) (left undecided)
Land acquisition ss. 4 and 6 (delay point left undecided)
Limitation Act, 1963 (referred to but not decided)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 24 of the 25 members the court declined to entertain the new contention. In one (508683_2) it left the limitation point open for decision on relevant materials. Merits were generally not decided.
variations: Some members rely on the need for evidence or investigation, others on the mixed nature of the question, and others on inconsistency with the pleaded case.
Some members rely mainly on the absence of a pleading or issue (1880271_3, 739777_2, 870347_3) without stressing the factual character of the point.
Some members refuse a bare factual ground not raised below without further qualification (1479356_4, 1458435_3).
In some members the Court expressly left the underlying legal question open (475851_3, 1315480_4), or noted that the point could be raised in later proceedings (1297238_2).
1408610_5 and 727486_1 turn on the High Court's recorded order, which was treated as conclusive of what was argued below.

legal_question: Can a criminal conviction be sustained when the prosecution's key evidence (eyewitness, sole-witness, dying declaration, approver or confession evidence) is materially unreliable because of contradictions, improvements, interest or hostility, conflict with medical or other evidence, or investigative lapses, and there is no reliable independent corroboration to leave guilt proved beyond reasonable doubt?

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and prosecution_case_rests_on_key_evidence and key_evidence_materially_unreliable and not reliable_independent_corroboration_available

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The matter is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction recorded by the courts below.
predicates.prosecution_case_rests_on_key_evidence: The prosecution's proof of the accused's guilt depends mainly on a particular body of evidence, such as eyewitness or sole-witness testimony, a dying declaration, an approver's testimony, or retracted confessions.
predicates.key_evidence_materially_unreliable: The key evidence is shown to be untrustworthy on the record, through material contradictions or improvements, interest or enmity of the witnesses, unnatural conduct, unexplained delay, conflict with medical or other evidence, or disproof of the circumstances in which it was given.
predicates.reliable_independent_corroboration_avail: Other reliable and independent evidence (witnesses, medical, recovery or circumstantial) connects the accused to the crime and supports the key evidence.
predicates.conviction_set_aside_and_accused_acquitt: The appellate court sets aside the conviction and sentence and acquits the accused, giving the benefit of reasonable doubt because guilt was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.

definition: Guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt on cogent, reliable and trustworthy evidence. Where the evidence the prosecution relies on is materially unreliable on the record, and no reliable independent corroboration connects the accused to the offence, the conviction is unsafe and is set aside with the benefit of doubt to the accused.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the evidence, though from related, interested or single witnesses, is scrutinised with care and found convincing, reliable and corroborated; such testimony is not inadmissible or insufficient in itself.
Where truth and falsehood in the evidence can be separated, the reliable part may still support conviction. Where they are inextricably mixed, it cannot.

An accused's admission, such as presence acknowledged in a statement under Section 313, can lend assurance only to reliable prosecution evidence and only if the exculpatory part is disproved. It cannot alone sustain conviction.
Unexplained investigative lapses, such as late forwarding of the report to the Magistrate, are weighed as part of the cumulative assessment and are not usually decisive alone.
In an appeal against acquittal, the same unreliability supports affirming the acquittal rather than setting aside a conviction, with stricter scrutiny in capital cases.
Persons whose participation is separately and reliably proved, for example by their own admission of presence, may be treated differently from co-accused.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the evidentiary limits of an accused's statement under Section 313 (an inculpatory admission cannot alone sustain conviction), not the general unreliability of the prosecution's key witnesses. It is related but narrower, and no outcome of acquittal is stated.

common_material_facts: Reliance on a sole or a few interested, related or inimical eyewitnesses.
Material contradictions, omissions or improvements between the first report or police statements and the trial testimony.
Conflict between the eyewitness account and the medical or ballistic evidence.
Material or independent witnesses available but not examined.
Unnatural conduct of witnesses or doubt about whether they were present at the scene.
Unexplained delay in the report, the special report or the examination of witnesses, and other investigative gaps.
Failed corroboration: recoveries disbelieved, dying declaration or confession doubtful, approver untrustworthy, handwriting opinion inconclusive.
Pre-existing enmity, factional or property disputes between the parties.
statutes_and_provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure ss. 157, 161, 288, 313
Arms Act ss. 25, 27
Constitution Art. 136
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Almost all the covered members (about 22 of 24) end in setting aside the conviction and acquitting or giving the benefit of doubt. Two are state appeals against acquittal in which the acquittal or the setting aside of convictions is left undisturbed on the same unreliability reasoning. The one outlier holds that an admission in an accused's statement cannot alone sustain conviction.
variations: The defect lies in different kinds of evidence: eyewitnesses, a dying declaration, an approver, handwriting opinion, retracted confessions, or police witnesses.
Some decisions rest on a single decisive flaw. Many rest on a cumulative assessment of several doubts: motive, delay, unnatural conduct and medical conflict.

A few cite authorities (Balaka Singh on separating truth from falsehood; Ramnaresh and Satish on sole-witness and last-seen evidence; Magan Bihari Lal on handwriting experts; Nishi Kant Jha on Section 313). Most cite none.
Procedural posture varies: most are appeals against conviction; two are state appeals against acquittal, where the acquittal is upheld.
Some decisions stress investigative or trial unfairness. Others stress only the witness's credibility.

legal_question: In an eviction claim by a landlord for personal residential or business occupation under a rent control statute, when do the landlord's other accommodation, personal circumstances, or evidentiary gaps defeat or fail to defeat the bona fide and reasonable requirement for the premises?

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_claim_for_landlord_own_requirement and genuine_need_established_on_evidence and not (alternative_accommodation_is_owned_available_and_reasonably_suitable_for_the_proven_need) and not (landlord_has_actual_vacant_suitable_alternative_or_existing_accommodation_meeting_household_needs)

predicates.rent_control_eviction_claim_for_landlord: The landlord seeks possession of tenanted premises under a rent control statute on the ground of reasonable and bona fide need for own (or a dependant's or beneficiary's) residence or business.
predicates.genuine_need_established_on_evidence: The landlord's need is a genuine, objective need and not a mere whim or desire, and is shown by the evidence or by non-perverse findings of the courts below. Dire necessity is not required.
predicates.alternative_accommodation_is_owned_avail: Other accommodation exists that belongs to the landlord, is actually available (vacant or recoverable) and is reasonably suitable in size, location and character for the specific need claimed.
predicates.landlord_has_actual_vacant_suitable_alte: The landlord already has vacant, suitable premises, or existing occupied accommodation that is sufficient to meet the household's or business's needs, so the claimed need is not genuine or reasonable.
predicates.bona_fide_requirement_sustained_and_evic: The court holds the landlord's requirement to be bona fide and reasonable, and the alleged circumstance (other premises, rented residence, planned alterations, lack of experience, wealth, non-examination of a witness, different use by the tenant) does not defeat the eviction claim.

definition: A landlord's bona fide and reasonable need for premises is not defeated by circumstances that do not actually give the landlord suitable accommodation of the landlord's own. Such circumstances include rented, unavailable, licensed, jointly owned or unsuitable alternatives, a relative's house, planned repairs, lack of business experience, wealth, or non-examination of the intended user. It is defeated where the landlord has owned, available and reasonably suitable alternative accommodation, or existing space that already meets the real needs.
exceptions_or_limits: The need must still be genuine and reasonable, not a mere desire. The landlord bears the burden of proving it, and mere availability of the landlord's choice is not enough if the evidence shows no real need.

Where the landlord owns other premises that are vacant or available and reasonably suitable for the claimed use, or existing accommodation already sufficient for the household, the claim fails (e.g. the tax consultancy office case and the case of the landlord with a substantial ground and first floor).
Statutory provisos, such as vacating another building without sufficient cause, can bar the claim if the tenant pleads and proves them.
Some statutes require the alternative to be the landlord's own and in the landlord's occupation, or require an entitlement to possession. Rented or merely tolerated accommodation then does not count.
Summary or leave-to-defend proceedings require a prima facie triable issue. A tenant's bare allegation of other premises, without disputing the intended use, does not raise one.
Findings of fact on need and suitability are generally not reopened absent perversity.

common_material_facts: Landlord seeks eviction for own residence or business, or for a family member's business, under a state rent control Act.
Tenant points to other premises of the landlord (rented, licensed, jointly owned, tenanted, remote or unsuitable) to defeat the claim.
Tenant relies on peripheral points such as lack of business experience, wealth, non-examination of the intended user, continued employment, or planned repairs or alterations.
Lower courts made concurrent findings of bona fide need, which the Supreme Court generally respected.
statutes_and_provisions: M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961, s. 12(1)(f) and s. 23-A(b)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, s. 13(1)(g), 13(1)(hh), 13(1)(a) and s. 17
Kerala Buildings (Lease & Rent Control) Act, 1965, s. 11(3)
Karnataka Rent Control Act, 1961, s. 21(1)(h)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, s. 13(1)(ff)
Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, s. 14(3)(a)(i) and its provisos
Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, s. 14(1)(e)
Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973, s. 13
J&K Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966, s. 11(1)(h)
Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951, s. 8(3)(a)(ii)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 23 of 25 members the landlord's bona fide requirement is upheld or the tenant's objection is rejected, because the alternative or other circumstance was unsuitable, unavailable, not the landlord's own, or legally irrelevant. In about 2 members (the tax consultancy office case and the case of the landlord with substantial existing floors) the claim fails because suitable or sufficient accommodation already existed.
variations: Some members turn on the alternative's ownership or legal entitlement (rented shop, licensee-occupied bungalow, spouse's co-owned property), others on suitability (farmhouse, thirteenth-floor flat, first-floor space).
Some members address evidentiary issues (non-examination of the intended user, the landlord not testifying, prior experience, preparations) rather than alternative accommodation.
Some members address statutory structure, such as own occupation versus demolition and rebuilding, different use by the tenant, or the vacated-building proviso.
The presumption of bona fides and landlord-as-best-judge reasoning appear in some members but are tempered by the requirement of genuine need in others.
The leave-to-defend member turns on the summary procedure's triable-issue standard.

split_suggestion: The cluster could be split into (a) alternative or other accommodation as a bar (ownership, availability, suitability, sufficiency, proviso on vacating), and (b) other objections to bona fide need (lack of experience, non-examination of witnesses, wealth, planned alterations, different use by the tenant, presumption of need, summary leave to defend).

legal_question: Does a procedural defect, irregularity or omission in the investigation, the framing of the charge, or the examination of the accused invalidate a criminal trial or conviction, or is relief available only where the accused shows prejudice or a failure of justice?

rule.if: criminal_proceeding_challenged_for_procedural_defect and (investigation_irregularity or charge_defect_or_omission or accused_examination_defect or document_supply_or_other_trial_procedure_irregularity) and not prejudice_or_failure_of_justice_shown and (evidence_otherwise_establishes_prosecution_case or accused_understood_case_and_had_opportunity_to_defend)

predicates.criminal_proceeding_challenged_for_proce: The accused (or the High Court, in an acquittal) relies on a procedural defect or irregularity in a criminal case as a ground to set aside the conviction, invalidate the trial or acquit.
predicates.investigation_irregularity: The investigation was defective, irregular, incomplete or conducted without proper authority or compliance with procedure.
predicates.charge_defect_or_omission: The charge was defective, omitted a specific offence, section or individual act, or was not altered or added to, although the evidence disclosed the offence.
predicates.accused_examination_defect: The accused's examination (Section 342 of the 1898 Code or Section 313 CrPC) omitted a circumstance, or was cursory, general or limited.
predicates.document_supply_or_other_trial_procedure: There was an irregularity such as failure to supply statements or documents to the accused, or a variation in a local inspection.
predicates.prejudice_or_failure_of_justice_shown: The accused established that the defect caused actual or likely prejudice, misled him, or occasioned a failure of justice or miscarriage of justice.
predicates.evidence_otherwise_establishes_prosecuti: Reliable evidence, independently assessed and unaffected by the defect, proves the foundation of the prosecution case.
predicates.accused_understood_case_and_had_opportun: The accused knew the case he had to meet and had a fair opportunity to explain the evidence and defend himself despite the defect.
predicates.trial_and_conviction_not_invalidated_by_: The defect is treated as a curable irregularity; the trial is not vitiated and the conviction is not set aside (or acquittal is not justified) on that ground alone.

definition: A procedural irregularity in investigation, charge, examination of the accused or trial documentation does not by itself vitiate a trial, set aside a conviction or justify acquittal. The accused must show prejudice or failure of justice, and courts assess the evidence independently of the defect. Where prejudice is shown, as where material circumstances were never put to the accused, the conviction may be set aside or the unput material excluded.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the defect actually prejudices the accused or occasions a failure of justice, the trial or conviction may be set aside or proceedings reopened (e.g. an empty-formality Section 313 examination that left the conviction resting on circumstances never put to the accused).
Circumstances not put to the accused ordinarily must be excluded from consideration even where the trial is not vitiated.
Deliberate dishonesty or abuse of position by the investigating officer, or a defect going to the root of the prosecution case, may justify an adverse inference or affect the outcome.
Courts must still scrutinise the evidence carefully where the investigation is defective; the defect is not simply ignored.
Where the missing charge or provision relates to facts the accused was not told of or could not defend, conviction for the uncharged offence is not safe.

outlier_members.reason: Applies the same prejudice test but reaches the opposite outcome: the Section 313 omission caused prejudice and the conviction was set aside. It is the counter-example that marks the limit of the rule and is not covered by the rule's outcome.

common_material_facts: The accused alleged an irregularity in the investigation (missing forensic reports, diary or report-recording disputes, unauthorised investigator, unsupplied statements).
The accused's examination under Section 342/313 omitted a circumstance or was cursory, and the objection was often raised for the first time on appeal.
The charge omitted a specific offence, section or individual act, but the facts were disclosed in evidence or put to the accused.
Reliable eyewitness, medical or documentary evidence independently proved the case.
No prejudice was identified or explained by the accused.
statutes_and_provisions: CrPC 1898 s.342 / CrPC 1973 s.313 (examination of the accused)
CrPC 1898 ss.161, 162, 173(4), 207A(3), 537, 535 (statements, supply of documents, curable irregularity)
CrPC ss.215, 216, 217, 221, 385(2), 386, 464, 465 (charges and their defects)
CrPC s.310 (local inspection)
CrPC ss.154, 155 and Chapter XII (investigation and registration)
Prevention of Corruption Act s.5A
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About 24 of 25 members hold that the irregularity does not vitiate the trial or conviction, or justify acquittal, because no prejudice or failure of justice was shown or reliable evidence independently proved the case. One member (1445922_1) sets aside the conviction because of proven prejudice.
variations: Investigation-defect cases (the largest group) focus on independent scrutiny of reliable evidence and the rule against acquitting solely for a defective investigation. Examination and charge cases focus on whether the accused understood the case and could defend it.
Some members place the burden on the accused to show prejudice. Others say the court must itself be satisfied that there was no prejudice.
Some members add that dishonest or oblique-motive investigation, or a defect striking at the root of the case, would change the result.
One member holds that a trial court may add or alter charges and was wrong to refuse to convict for lack of a charge.
One member treats a corrected provision of conviction as causing no prejudice.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) investigation defects and acquittal or conviction (101241441_4, 1042486_3, 118703205_1, 1604625_3, 1820883_4, 249515_2, 406413_2, 603545_2, 617176_4, 79334985_3); (b) Section 342/313 examination omissions, with 1445922_1 as the prejudice counter-example (1046645_2, 1253073_5, 144689_2, 1689237_2, 198357_3, 969015_3, 1445922_1); (c) charge defects and omitted or altered charges (1250057_5, 1863698_1, 48110962_1, 79786_1, 37441_4); (d) supply of documents and other trial irregularities (1300725_1, 1830078_1, 146499_1).

legal_question: When may a court rely on testimony that is inherently suspect or partial (an approver's or accomplice's evidence, a retracted confession, a hostile witness's evidence, or the evidence of an interested or sole witness) to convict an accused, and what scrutiny and corroboration does it require?

predicates.criminal_case_turns_on_suspect_or_partia: The prosecution case depends on evidence of a kind needing caution: approver or accomplice testimony, a retracted confession, a hostile witness, an interested or related witness, or a sole eyewitness.
predicates.testimony_or_relied_on_portion_found_rel: The court has scrutinised the evidence, and for hostile or inconsistent witnesses the specific portion relied on, and found it credible and dependable (for an approver, not inherently improbable and not false; for a confession, voluntary and true).
predicates.independent_evidence_corroborates_materi: Other independent evidence (witnesses, recoveries, medical or documentary evidence, circumstances) confirms the crime-implicating parts of the account in material particulars, and for an approver or confession, as to each accused, though not every detail.
predicates.testimony_may_be_relied_on_to_support_co: The court may act on the testimony, or the dependable portion of it, to sustain a conviction.

definition: Evidence from an approver, accomplice, retracted confessor, hostile witness, interested or related witness, or sole imperfect witness is not excluded as such. The court may rely on it, or on its dependable portions, if it is reliable after careful scrutiny and, as a rule of prudence, corroborated in material particulars connecting the accused with the crime. Without such corroboration, a conviction resting on untrustworthy evidence cannot safely stand.
exceptions_or_limits: Corroboration is a rule of prudence, not of law; under s.133 a conviction on uncorroborated accomplice evidence is not illegal, and in exceptional cases trustworthy approver evidence may be acted on without corroboration.
Where the approver is untrustworthy (for example has retracted, has bad character, or is contradicted) and there is no safe material corroboration, the conviction cannot be sustained.
Where a sole witness is neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable, or the testimony has material improvements and lacks material corroboration, conviction on it is unsafe.
Corroboration must confirm the crime-implicating part of the account and connect each accused, not merely collateral matters; it need not prove every circumstance or suffice alone to convict.

A hostile witness's evidence is not rejected en bloc; the court must assess it as a whole, cautiously, and ordinarily seek corroboration. Declaring a witness hostile does not itself exclude the evidence.
Acquittal of co-accused on doubt does not by itself discredit a witness's evidence against another accused.

common_material_facts: Prosecution relied on an approver or accomplice who participated in the crime, with corroboration from eyewitnesses, recoveries, medical or documentary evidence
Witnesses declared hostile whose testimony partly supported the prosecution (presence of accused, injuries, circumstances)
Interested, related or inimical witnesses, or a sole eyewitness, whose evidence was scrutinised with care
Retracted confessions generally corroborated by other evidence
Co-accused acquitted while others were convicted on the same witnesses
statutes_and_provisions: Evidence Act s.133
Evidence Act s.114 illustration (b)
Evidence Act s.154
IPC s.302
IPC s.161 with Prevention of Corruption Act s.5(2)
TADA s.15
CrPC s.161
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Reliance on the evidence is usually permitted: about 21 of 25 members uphold reliance on the evidence or its dependable portions, with corroboration found. Two members (534807_1, 535683_1) refuse to sustain conviction for lack of material corroboration. One (1499233_2) finds the hostile testimony did not support the prosecution on its facts.
variations: Approver cases apply a two-stage test (reliability first, then corroboration, per Sarwan Singh and Lachhi Ram) and often require corroboration as to each accused.
Hostile-witness cases split between those that stress corroboration and those that only require that the portion be reliable and relevant.
Confession cases require voluntariness and truth, with general corroboration sufficing.
Interested-witness and sole-witness cases apply greater caution without a bar on reliance.
Some members cite no authority; others cite long lists of precedents.

split_suggestion: The shared theme is that suspect testimony may be used if reliable and corroborated. If a finer split is wanted, separate into (a) approver, accomplice and retracted-confession corroboration (1174300_2, 1199934_1, 1270588_1, 144689_6, 1593993_1, 289786_1, 406616_3, 534807_1, 63794871_1, 63794871_2, 67600325_1); (b) hostile-witness reliance (1292925_2, 1499233_2, 1558160_3, 157802562_1, 193811258_1, 448685_2, 53756698_2, 746119_2, 969015_2); (c) interested, related or sole witness evidence (141841_1, 149668700_1, 535683_1, 617002_1, 746119_1).

legal_question: When a claimant seeks higher compensation for compulsorily acquired land, must the claimant prove with admissible, comparable evidence that the award is inadequate, and is enhancement refused where that proof is missing?

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and claimant_seeks_enhanced_compensation and (not claimant_proves_award_inadequate_with_admissible_evidence or claimant_fails_to_show_comparator_similarity_or_substantiate_claimed_potential or no_material_supports_value_above_that_already_fixed)

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The case is a reference or appeal about the amount of compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.claimant_seeks_enhanced_compensation: The landowner or claimant asks for compensation above the amount already awarded or fixed.
predicates.claimant_proves_award_inadequate_with_ad: The claimant has produced and proved relevant, admissible evidence (for example proved comparable sales, or similar land shown to have comparable nature and potentiality) showing that the existing award is inadequate and what higher value is justified.
predicates.claimant_fails_to_show_comparator_simila: The claimant relies on other sales, awards, or an asserted special potential or use, but does not establish that the comparator land is similar in location, nature, size and potentiality, or does not substantiate the claimed potential.
predicates.no_material_supports_value_above_that_al: The record contains no material supporting a market value higher than the value already determined by the lower or reviewing court.
predicates.enhancement_denied_and_existing_compensa: The court refuses further enhancement and leaves the existing compensation determination undisturbed.

definition: A claimant seeking more compensation for acquired land must prove inadequacy with admissible evidence, such as proved comparable sales or awards for similar land, or substantiated potential. Where the claimant relies on unproved, dissimilar, or unsupported comparators or claims, or offers no material above the value already fixed, enhancement is refused.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the claimant proves comparability and inadequacy, the burden shifts to the acquiring authority and enhancement may be granted or upheld (e.g. 1121206_3, 1922921_2).

Awards for other acquisitions are evidence, not a conclusive bar or entitlement; they carry weight only where comparability is shown. Comparable awards for the same notification or period may fix the rate.
A reference court cannot award more than the claim made in response to the notice, and market value is fixed as of the notification date, not by the amount claimed.
Genuine, proximate comparable sales may still be adjusted downward for disadvantages of the acquired land, such as location, access, nature or size.

outlier_members.reason: The enhancement was upheld because comparable sale and award evidence and potentiality were proved. This is the converse of the denial rule.
The award was upheld on proved assessment and transaction evidence. It is a positive evidence-supported outcome.
The court fixed the rate by same-period comparable awards and enhanced it. It concerns choosing between comparators, not a denial for lack of proof.
An agreed-compensation award for the same notification must be considered as evidence. It does not concern the claimant's burden.
A reduction from a comparable sale value was justified by dissimilarities. This is a valuation-adjustment point.
Concerns res judicata and the evidentiary value of other acquisition awards, not the burden of proving enhancement.
Same res judicata / evidence-not-bar point as 118999760_1.
Concerns the statutory cap on awards above the amount claimed (s.25(1)).
Holds that market value is fixed at the notification date and is not set by the claimed amount.
Holds that an agreement on price between interested parties does not control the statutory valuation.
An unreasoned change in compensation under the Telegraph Act is set aside and remitted.
Arbitration patent-illegality issue about relying on a comparator without a fair opportunity to respond.
Fraud and a repeated claim after prior vesting and compensation proceedings.
Rejects restitutive compensation as the measure of compensation.

common_material_facts: Claimants relied on sale deeds, awards or judgments for land in other or adjoining villages, or on small plots, without proving similarity in location, nature, size or potential.
Claimants produced no witnesses, no site plan, or no independent proof of the sales mentioned in the Collector's award.
Claimed special potential or use (e.g. a cinema site, or value after development) was unsupported or disbelieved.
A lower court or the High Court had already raised or assessed the value, and no further material was shown.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act 1894 ss. 4(1), 11, 18, 23, 25, 54
Hyderabad Land Acquisition Act
Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 ss. 18, 24, 28, 31, 34 (outlier)
Indian Telegraph Act 1885 ss. 10(d), 16(3) (outlier)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 11 covered members, all refuse or do not grant enhancement, or require the court to determine value afresh on proved evidence. Of the 14 outliers, about 5 uphold or fix compensation on proved comparable evidence, and the rest turn on distinct procedural or doctrinal points.
variations: Some members stress the burden of proof on the claimant under s.18; others stress comparability of land; others stress the absence of any further material.
Where comparable same-notification or same-period determinations exist, courts adopt them instead of the claimant's figure (1647526_1, 149594337_1).
Where evidence is adequate, the burden shifts to the State and enhancement may be upheld or reduced after adjustment.

split_suggestion: Split into: (1) claimant's burden and comparability or potential proof for enhancement (the covered group); (2) the evidentiary weight of other awards and res judicata (118999760_1, 618705_1, 199320363_2, 149594337_1); (3) evidence-supported or adjusted valuation outcomes (1121206_3, 1922921_2, 265971_1); (4) statutory limits and valuation basis (1328520_2, 1733049_2, 1534105_1, 727486_2); (5) distinct issues: Telegraph Act reasons (1541957_3), arbitration (173753317_3), and fraud and repeat claims (25681951_4).

legal_question: When will an appellate court, especially the Supreme Court, decline to disturb a lower court's or tribunal's valuation or compensation award for acquired land or property, and when will it intervene?

rule.if: appeal_challenges_valuation_or_compensation_award and lower_forum_assessed_valuation_on_evidence_and_relevant_factors and not error_of_principle_shown and not important_evidence_overlooked_or_misapplied

predicates.appeal_challenges_valuation_or_compensat: The appeal or special-leave petition challenges the valuation or the quantum of compensation fixed for acquired land, structures or other property by a lower court or tribunal.
predicates.lower_forum_assessed_valuation_on_eviden: The lower court or tribunal fixed the valuation on the evidence before it (such as comparable sales, awards, location, potential or inspection) and considered the relevant valuation factors, or its assessment was within a reasonable range.
predicates.error_of_principle_shown: The appellant has shown that the lower forum applied a wrong legal principle in valuing the property, or that the assessment shows gross injustice or discrimination.
predicates.important_evidence_overlooked_or_misappl: The lower forum overlooked, ignored or misapplied important evidence or a material valuation point that affects the valuation.
predicates.appellate_court_does_not_disturb_valuati: The appellate court leaves the valuation or compensation award undisturbed and dismisses the challenge.

definition: An appellate court will not interfere with a valuation or compensation award for acquired land or property if the lower forum assessed it on the evidence, considered the relevant valuation factors, and the challenger shows no error of principle and no overlooked or misapplied important evidence. Where such an error or oversight is shown, the court may correct the award.
exceptions_or_limits: Interference is warranted where a wrong principle was applied or an important valuation point or evidence was overlooked or misapplied (as in the member where the award was modified).

Where the appellate court has been confined by statute to specified grounds of appeal, interference is limited to those grounds, such as an error of law, a failure to decide a material issue or a substantial procedural defect.
Non-interference rests on the challenger's failure to prove error or undervaluation; the burden lies on the party challenging the award.
Where a party seeks enhancement but has filed no cross-appeal or cross-objection, the court may leave a reasonable valuation as it is.
Some members leave open other questions, such as retrospective enhanced solatium or interest, through a liberty to seek review.

outlier_members.reason: The Supreme Court intervened and modified the award because material valuation points were overlooked or misapplied. This is the counter-case that defines the limit of the non-interference rule, not an instance of it.

common_material_facts: The High Court or reference court fixed market value using comparable sales, earlier awards, location, potential and development costs.
The challenger, whether the State or the landowners, pointed to no error of principle and no overlooked evidence.
Small-plot sales or unsupported oral evidence were discounted by the lower forum.
Some members concern structures such as houses, wells, shops or buildings, and some concern non-acquisition valuations such as wealth tax or property tax.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, s. 4(1) (valuation date), s. 18 (reference), s. 23 (factors for market value), s. 54 (appeal)
Article 136 of the Constitution (special leave)
Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911, s. 77A (limited grounds of appeal)
Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 (retrospectivity left undecided in one member)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 24 of 25 members the valuation or compensation award was left undisturbed and the appeal dismissed. In 1 member (455042_2) the award was corrected because of an overlooked or misapplied valuation point.
variations: Some members state the test in full (error of principle or important evidence overlooked, citing Dollar Company, Thakur Kanta Prasad Singh, the Privy Council cases and others), while others give only a bare 'no reason to interfere'.
Several members concern structures or buildings rather than land.
One member tolerates a valuation the Court considered apparently high because it was affirmed and the claimant had produced evidence.
One member bases non-interference on the absence of a cross-appeal, and another on the statutory limits on appeal.
One member allows a later sale to guide valuation where no evidence shows that market rates fluctuated.

legal_question: Once possession of land has been taken under an acquisition (or the statutory vesting event has occurred) and the land has vested absolutely in the State free from encumbrances, can that vesting be undone by withdrawal, release, lapse for delayed award, later legislation or later orders, or by the former owner's claim to restoration?

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and possession_taken_and_land_vested_in_state_free_of_encumbrances and (acquisition_withdrawal_or_release_sought or lapse_for_delayed_award_claimed or later_law_or_order_invoked_to_divest or restoration_to_former_owner_claimed)

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The dispute arises from a compulsory acquisition (or an analogous statutory acquisition or vesting scheme) of land.
predicates.possession_taken_and_land_vested_in_stat: The State took possession in a manner recognised by law (including by panchnama or memorandum, or before the award under the urgency power), or the statutory vesting event occurred, so the land vested absolutely in the State free from encumbrances.
predicates.acquisition_withdrawal_or_release_sought: The Government or a claimant seeks to withdraw from, cancel, de-notify or release the land from the acquisition after vesting.
predicates.lapse_for_delayed_award_claimed: It is claimed that the acquisition has lapsed because no award was made within the prescribed period.
predicates.later_law_or_order_invoked_to_divest: A later statute, transitional provision, amendment or court order is invoked to divest or revest the land, or to treat the completed acquisition as undone.
predicates.restoration_to_former_owner_claimed: The former owner claims return, reconveyance or restoration of possession, for example because the land is unused, the purpose is complete, compensation was not paid, or the acquisition was set aside.
predicates.vesting_not_undone_and_land_stays_with_s: The vesting stands: the State keeps the land, the acquisition cannot be withdrawn or lapse, and the land does not revert to the former owner.

definition: When possession has been taken and the land has vested absolutely in the State free from encumbrances, that vesting is complete and cannot be reversed. Section 48 withdrawal, Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, Section 11-A lapse, later legislation or transitional provisions, later court orders, or non-use of the land do not restore the land to the former owner, unless the statute itself provides a revesting mechanism.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule applies only where possession was actually and validly taken (or the statutory vesting event occurred). Possession must be actual, though a panchnama or memorandum can suffice depending on the nature of the land.
Where acquisition is still pending and vesting has not occurred, Section 11-A lapse or the effect of scheme lapse may apply and depends on the statutory scheme.
A statute may expressly provide for revesting or divesting, such as Section 37(3) of the Bangalore Development Authority Act.
A court may set aside an acquisition without restoring possession, and the State may proceed afresh.
Vesting does not extinguish the owner's right to compensation. The remedies for unpaid compensation lie in payment and interest provisions.
Some members decide only whether a High Court should interfere at a belated stage, or whether a fresh acquisition can cover land already vested.
In the repeal-legislation member, the Court did not decide whether possession must always be physical.

common_material_facts: Possession was taken (often under the urgency power, Section 17) and the land was handed to a development authority or other body.
An award was made or compensation paid, or an award was delayed beyond the Section 11-A period.
A former owner or the Government later sought withdrawal, release, de-notification, restoration or lapse.
A later statute, transitional provision (Section 24 of the 2013 Act) or earlier court order was invoked to undo the vesting.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 16, 17(1), 17(4), 11-A, 48, 5A, 31, 34
General Clauses Act, 1897, Section 21
Section 24 of the 2013 Act
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 10(3), and Repeal Act, 1999
Bangalore Development Authority Act, Sections 27, 36, 37
Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, Section 52(4)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, Section 4
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 25 members, vesting after possession is held irreversible. The acquisition does not lapse, withdrawal or release is refused, the land is not restored or revested, and later proceedings or laws do not divest the State.
variations: The context varies: withdrawal or release (about 7), lapse for delayed award (about 6), later law or transitional provision (about 5), restoration for non-use (1), fresh acquisition of vested land (1), and a High Court's belated interference (1).
Some members rely on Satendra Prasad Jain and Avinash Sharma, while others cite no authority.
Several members extend the principle by analogy from the 1894 Act to the ceiling statute and state urban-improvement statutes.
The manner of taking possession is itself contested in some members (actual possession, panchnama).

legal_question: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, when is a member of an unlawful assembly vicariously liable for an offence committed by another member, and what must the prosecution prove about membership, common object and the connection of the offence to that object or to the members' knowledge, without proof of a personal overt act?

rule.if: unlawful_assembly_prosecution and assembly_of_five_or_more_with_unlawful_common_object_proved and accused_proved_to_be_member_sharing_common_object_when_offence_committed and not accused_merely_present_or_passive_onlooker and (offence_committed_in_prosecution_of_common_object or members_knew_offence_likely_in_prosecution_of_common_object)

predicates.unlawful_assembly_prosecution: The prosecution seeks to hold the accused liable for an offence committed by a member of a group, relying on the unlawful-assembly provisions (Sections 141 and 149 IPC).
predicates.assembly_of_five_or_more_with_unlawful_c: Reliable evidence shows an assembly of five or more persons with a common object of a kind specified in Section 141 IPC. The object may be inferred from conduct, weapons and circumstances, need not follow prior concert, and may form at the scene.
predicates.accused_proved_to_be_member_sharing_comm: The evidence establishes that the accused joined or remained in the assembly, understood its unlawful character and shared its common object, and had not left it before the offence was committed.
predicates.accused_merely_present_or_passive_onlook: The accused was only present in or near the group, as an innocent or passive bystander, without sharing its common object.
predicates.offence_committed_in_prosecution_of_comm: The offence was committed by a member to further the assembly's common object.
predicates.members_knew_offence_likely_in_prosecuti: The circumstances (weapons carried, conduct, nature of the attack) show that members knew the offence was likely, not merely possible, to be committed in prosecution of the common object.
predicates.accused_vicariously_liable_for_the_offen: The accused may be held liable for the offence, with the aid of Section 149, even though no individual overt act is proved against them.

definition: Under Section 149 IPC, a proven member of an unlawful assembly of five or more who shares its common object is liable for an offence committed by another member if it was committed in prosecution of that object, or if members knew it was likely to be committed in prosecuting it. No personal overt act need be proved, but mere presence is not enough and the common object, membership at the time of the offence and the link to the offence must be established.
exceptions_or_limits: Mere presence in a group, or being a passive or innocent spectator, does not establish membership or a shared common object.
The prosecution must prove the specified common object; if it is not proved, an assembly-based conviction cannot stand.
A person who left the assembly before the offence was committed, or where the evidence does not exclude that the offence occurred after departure, is not liable.
Separate or stray assaults in a large crowd are not imputed to all members unless they were in prosecution of the common object or members knew they were likely.
For the second limb, knowledge that the offence was likely must be shown; awareness of a mere possibility is insufficient.
The assessment is fact-specific, based on the quality of eyewitness, medical and recovery evidence. Absence of weapon recovery from a particular accused is not fatal.

common_material_facts: A group of five or more, usually armed with deadly weapons, attacked a rival party, often in a land, water, crop or other dispute or an enmity.
One or more deaths or grievous injuries resulted, and not every accused was shown to have inflicted the fatal or any injury.
Eyewitness testimony corroborated by medical and recovery evidence was used to infer the common object from conduct, weapons and circumstances.
The common object sometimes formed at the scene, or the original object (for example to beat or to enforce a right) escalated to killing.
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 141 and 142 IPC (unlawful assembly and membership)
Section 149 IPC (both limbs: in prosecution of the common object, and known to be likely)
Sections 147 and 148 IPC (rioting and armed rioting)
Sections 302, 307, 323, 324, 326, 364 and 201 IPC read with Section 149
Section 34 IPC (contrasted)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 21 of 25 members liability was upheld or restored (convictions confirmed or acquittals reversed) on proof of membership and shared object without a personal overt act. In about 4 (1383333_1, 100576613_3, 1944328_1, 1879133_5) liability was refused for lack of proof of common object or membership at the time of the offence, or because a separate assault was not linked to the common object.
variations: Some members rely on the first limb (offence in prosecution of the object) and others on the second (members knew it was likely).
The common object was inferred from weapons and conduct, sometimes formed spontaneously, and sometimes escalated from an original object of beating to killing.
Procedural postures vary: appeals against conviction, State appeals against acquittal, and a review of the overt-act requirement from Baladin.
Some members only apply Sections 147/148 (armed rioting) without needing Section 149.
Cases of non-liability turn on different defects: no proven common object, mere presence, departure before the offence, or a separate assault outside the common object.

legal_question: Is a civil court's jurisdiction under Section 9 CPC excluded, expressly or by necessary implication, where a special land-related statute assigns the matter in dispute (or a question on which the relief depends) to a designated authority, revenue court or special forum and provides finality or remedies there?

rule.if: civil_suit_filed and dispute_or_decisive_question_concerns_land_or_land_related_rights and special_statute_assigns_that_matter_to_designated_authority_or_forum and (statute_expressly_bars_civil_courts or statutory_scheme_is_complete_with_finality_or_remedies) and relief_sought_requires_deciding_the_assigned_matter

predicates.civil_suit_filed: The proceeding was instituted as an ordinary suit in a civil court.
predicates.dispute_or_decisive_question_concerns_la: The dispute, or a question that must be decided to grant the relief, concerns land, tenure, land acquisition, land ceiling, land grants, office emoluments, evacuee property or similar land-related rights.
predicates.special_statute_assigns_that_matter_to_d: A special statute entrusts the determination of that matter (for example tenure status, vesting, acquisition validity, evacuee status, or ryot status) to a revenue court, settlement officer, collector, custodian, special court or other designated authority.
predicates.statute_expressly_bars_civil_courts: The statute contains an express provision excluding civil-court jurisdiction over the matter.
predicates.statutory_scheme_is_complete_with_finali: The statute is a complete code that makes the authority's decisions final and/or provides appeals, references or other adequate remedies, so that exclusion arises by necessary implication.
predicates.relief_sought_requires_deciding_the_assi: On the substance of the claim, not merely its form or framing, granting the relief sought would require the civil court to decide the matter assigned to the special authority or to displace its decision.
predicates.civil_court_lacks_jurisdiction_and_suit_: The civil court cannot entertain or decide the suit, or the relevant part of it. The plaint may be returned or the suit dismissed, and the remedy lies before the statutory forum or, where applicable, under Article 226 or 136.

definition: Where a special land statute entrusts a matter to a designated authority or revenue court, and either expressly bars civil courts or is a complete scheme with finality and remedies, a civil court cannot entertain a suit whose real substance requires deciding that matter. The court looks to the substance of the claim, not its framing, and the aggrieved party must use the statutory forum or constitutional remedies.
exceptions_or_limits: Exclusion of civil jurisdiction is not readily inferred. It requires an express bar or a complete statutory scheme with adequate remedies.
A civil court may retain jurisdiction where statutory requirements are not followed or fundamental principles of judicial procedure are breached (noted in the ceiling-surplus member).
Constitutional jurisdiction under Articles 226 and 136 is not displaced, and acquisition validity challenges may go to the High Court.

A decree passed by a court without jurisdiction is a nullity and can be challenged whenever relied upon. A mere error by the statutory authority within its jurisdiction, such as a wrong classification of premises, is not a nullity and is corrected by the statutory appeal.
A recorded tenure-holder whose title is not under cloud may be treated differently from a claimant who first needs a revenue-court declaration.
Where the question assigned to the authority is not actually in issue, as in a suit for an injunction over a street where the panchayat's ownership is not denied, the bar may not apply.

outlier_members.reason: The bar arises from a sovereign or political reservation of jagir succession under a covenant, not from a statutory revenue or land-scheme forum. It shares the outcome but rests on a different basis, an implied bar, and it is a partial fit.

common_material_facts: A civil suit seeks a declaration, possession or an injunction over land, but the real question is one assigned to a special authority (tenure or ryot status, vesting, acquisition validity, evacuee status, ceiling surplus, village common land status).
The statute provides appeals, references or finality of the authority's orders.
The plaintiff framed the suit to avoid the bar, for example by omitting a direct challenge to the acquisition or by seeking only an injunction.
Earlier or parallel statutory or constitutional proceedings were often pursued.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 9 CPC; Order VII Rule 11(d)
Land Acquisition Act 1894, ss. 4, 6, 9, 11, 16, 18 and others; Articles 226 and 136
Delhi Land Reforms Act 1954, s. 185 and Sch. I
Madras Estates Abolition Act 1948, s. 56; Madras Estates Land Act 1908, s. 189
Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act 1961, ss. 11-13
Administration of Evacuee Property Act 1950, ss. 4, 28, 46
Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act 1876, s. 4
Rajasthan Tenancy Act, ss. 207 and 256
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act 1972, ss. 18 and 26
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act 1953, s. 57B
Andhra Pradesh Land Grabbing (Prohibition) Act 1982, ss. 8 and 15
Haryana Public Premises Act 1972, ss. 5, 9, 15
Patels and Patwaris Law 1900, s. 20; Berar Land Revenue Code, s. 192
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Almost all members (about 24 of 25) hold the civil court has no jurisdiction or the suit is not maintainable. The plaint is returned, the suit is dismissed, or a remand is set aside, and the party is left to the statutory forum or writ remedy.
variations: The bar is sometimes express (the Punjab, Delhi, Madras, evacuee, Bombay and West Bengal statutes) and sometimes implied from a complete code (land acquisition, ceiling).
Some members bar the suit entirely, while others bar only the part that requires deciding the assigned question.
Acquisition cases point the aggrieved party to Article 226.
Some members add res judicata or nullity reasoning, or the conduct of the plaintiff (delay, unused remedies).
One member (930951_1) treats a wrong classification as an error within jurisdiction, to be corrected on statutory appeal.

legal_question: Can a party raise in the Supreme Court (or a higher court in the hierarchy) a plea, contention or objection that was not raised, pleaded, pursued or tried in the courts below, or was abandoned there?

rule.if: appeal_before_higher_court and contention_not_raised_or_abandoned_in_courts_below and (contention_depends_on_unpleaded_facts_or_evidence_or_is_mixed_question_of_fact_and_law or contention_is_new_independent_ground_or_raises_new_case) and not exceptional_circumstances_justifying_new_plea

predicates.appeal_before_higher_court: The contention is sought to be raised in a further appeal, special leave appeal, reference or revision before a court higher than the one(s) where the matter was first litigated, typically the Supreme Court.
predicates.contention_not_raised_or_abandoned_in_co: The contention was not raised, pleaded, argued or pursued before the lower courts, tribunals or authorities (or the High Court), or was available there and abandoned, or was decided against the party and not challenged in the intermediate appeal.
predicates.contention_depends_on_unpleaded_facts_or: Deciding the contention would require facts not pleaded, evidence, findings, an issue to be framed, or an inquiry or remand, because it is a mixed question of fact and law.
predicates.contention_is_new_independent_ground_or_: The contention is a distinct legal, statutory, constitutional or jurisdictional ground or a new case that the lower courts had no occasion to consider.
predicates.exceptional_circumstances_justifying_new: There are exceptional or cogent grounds, such as a pure question of law needing no further facts, that justify departing from the usual practice.
predicates.court_declines_to_entertain_new_contenti: The court refuses to consider the new contention and decides the appeal without examining its merits.

definition: A court of final appeal will ordinarily refuse to entertain a contention not raised, pleaded or pursued in the courts below, or abandoned there. This applies especially where the contention depends on facts or evidence, is a mixed question of fact and law, or is a new independent ground, unless exceptional circumstances justify it.
exceptions_or_limits: The practice is discretionary ("may decline"), not an absolute bar.
The Court may depart from it in exceptional circumstances or on cogent grounds; several members stress the absence of such grounds.

The bar is strongest for mixed questions of fact and law or pleas lacking a pleaded factual foundation; some members apply it to any contention not raised below, and one notes it may apply even if no fresh findings of fact are needed.
A pure question of law needing no new facts is not clearly covered by the stricter members' reasoning (this limit is inferred, not stated by them).
The rule operates at each appellate level, so the High Court may likewise refuse a new request in revision or reference.

common_material_facts: The point was raised for the first time before the Supreme Court (or in revision or before the High Court) and was absent from pleadings, issues or arguments below.
Many points were mixed questions of fact and law, such as limitation, res judicata, submission to jurisdiction, a later will and premature demands, or lacked a pleaded factual foundation.
Some points were available below but abandoned, or decided against the party and not challenged in the intermediate appeal.
Some were new legal, statutory, constitutional or jurisdictional grounds, such as the validity of a provision, a notice or the High Court's revisional jurisdiction.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 115 CPC (revisional jurisdiction)
Section 12(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rents Control Act, 1947
Section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Jayarama Reddy v. Revenue Divisional Officer (abandoned contention)
Baldevdas Shivlal v. Filmistan Distributors and other revision cases (mentioned, not applied)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 25 members the court declined to entertain the new contention and decided without examining its merits; none allowed it.
variations: Some members rest on the mixed fact-and-law character or lack of pleaded facts; others simply on the point not having been raised below.
Some involve abandonment or failure to challenge in the intermediate appeal rather than a point never raised.
One member weighs consequences such as remand, delay and the parties' position.
Most cite no authority, treating the rule as settled practice.
Some arise from references or revisions in the High Court rather than the Supreme Court.

legal_question: Can a criminal conviction (or a reversal of an acquittal into a conviction) be sustained where the prosecution evidence, whether direct or circumstantial, leaves reasonable doubt about the accused's participation or responsibility?

predicates.criminal_appeal_concerning_conviction_or: The matter is a criminal appeal against a conviction, or against the reversal or upholding of an acquittal, in which the sufficiency of the evidence is in issue.
predicates.prosecution_bears_burden_of_proof_beyond: The prosecution must establish the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt on its own evidence, not on weaknesses in the defence.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_unreliable_or_insuf: The prosecution evidence is unreliable, contradictory, inconsistent with medical or forensic evidence, or insufficient; or, in a circumstantial case, the circumstances do not form a complete chain; or the evidence does not identify or connect the accused to the offence.
predicates.prosecution_has_proved_guilt_beyond_reas: The admissible and reliable evidence, taken as a whole, proves the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
predicates.conviction_cannot_stand_and_accused_gets: The conviction is set aside (or the acquittal is upheld or restored) and the accused is acquitted on the benefit of reasonable doubt.

definition: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt through reliable evidence that connects the accused to the offence. Where the evidence is unreliable, inconsistent with the medical or forensic evidence, fails to identify the accused, or leaves a circumstantial chain incomplete, suspicion cannot replace proof and the accused gets the benefit of doubt.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule applies only if the prosecution has not proved guilt beyond reasonable doubt; reliable evidence or a complete, conclusive chain of circumstances supports conviction.

In appeals against acquittal, the appellate court should not interfere where the trial court's view of the evidence is reasonably possible. Several members apply this to restore or confirm the acquittal.
A plausible defence need not itself be proved; it is enough that it creates doubt. A false or unproved defence cannot substitute for prosecution proof.
Absence of proven motive is not by itself fatal, and motive alone cannot complete a chain of circumstances. Recovery under Section 27 of the Evidence Act is not conclusive by itself.
A member decided on its own facts (age of the accused, a plausible private-defence account, or exclusion of inadmissible material) turns on those facts, not on a separate rule.

common_material_facts: Eyewitness testimony that is contradictory, improved, coached, or from witnesses who could not observe or who did not implicate the accused.
Medical or forensic evidence that conflicts with the prosecution account, or no weapon recovered or linked (ballistics, wound type).
Circumstantial cases with weak links: disbelieved extra-judicial confession, doubtful recovery, speculative motive, no exclusive possession, no last-seen proof.
Unexplained or suppressed injuries on the accused and a plausible private-defence or alternative account.
Convictions by courts below or on reversal of acquittal, set aside in the Supreme Court.
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Penal Code Sections 302, 304, 304-B, 498-A, 307, 34, 109, 201
Code of Criminal Procedure Sections 378, 313, 342
Evidence Act Section 27
Arms Act Section 25(c); Indian Arms Act Section 27
Article 227 of the Constitution (in two members)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Convictions are set aside and the accused acquitted on the benefit of doubt in about 22 of 25 members. In about 3 (the abetment, forgery and trial-court acquittal matters) the acquittal is upheld or restored. One member rejects a request to convict for exceeding private defence.
variations: Direct-evidence cases turn on witness reliability, identification and medical consistency; circumstantial cases turn on the completeness of the chain (Sharad Birdhichand Sarda test).

Some members restore or uphold an acquittal, applying the limited scope of interference in appeals against acquittal (Chandrappa, Sheo Swarup), while others set aside convictions affirmed by the courts below.
Some rely on a plausible defence and unexplained accused injuries; others rest only on absence of identification or weapon link.
Most cite no earlier cases; a few cite Sharad Birdhichand Sarda, Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade, Sunil Kundu, Latesh, Chandrappa and Sheo Swarup.

legal_question: Is a later suit or proceeding barred by an earlier one, whether under the rule against splitting claims (Order II Rule 2 CPC), res judicata, or a related procedural bar, when the two arise from distinct causes of action and the later claim or relief was not available or not decided in the earlier proceeding?

predicates.later_proceeding_follows_earlier_proceed: A later suit, petition or claim is brought between the same parties (or those claiming under them) after an earlier proceeding that is said to bar it.
