predicates.open_continuous_exclusive_possession_for: The claimant has proved actual, open, peaceful, continuous, exclusive and uninterrupted possession (nec vi, nec clam, nec precario), adequate in continuity, publicity and extent, for the full limitation period.
predicates.adverse_starting_point_and_animus_proved: The claimant has pleaded and proved when the possession became adverse and that the claimant had a positive intention to possess adversely to, and dispossess, the true owner (animus possidendi), not merely an intention to possess.
predicates.possession_began_permissively_or_under_d: The claimant's possession began with the owner's permission (as licensee, tenant, mortgagee, share-cropper or lessee), in a non-owner capacity, or under a derivative title from a person who could not convey good title.
predicates.hostile_conversion_known_to_owner_proved: The claimant has proved by cogent evidence that the permissive or derivative possession became hostile, with a disclaimer of the earlier title and a hostile assertion brought to the owner's knowledge, and the time and manner of that change.
predicates.adverse_possession_title_not_established: The claimant has not acquired title by adverse possession and the plea fails.

definition: A party claiming title by adverse possession must plead and prove, by clear and cogent evidence, possession that is open, continuous, exclusive and hostile to the true owner, with hostile intent and a identifiable starting point, for the limitation period. Mere long possession, permissive or derivative possession, or denial of the owner's title does not suffice unless it is shown to have become hostile to the owner's knowledge.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the claimant proves open, continuous and hostile possession beyond the limitation period, title by prescription is acquired; the owner's specific knowledge need not be shown unless ouster is pleaded (one member, 865312_2).
One member (159174_2) only states the pleading and proof requirements and leaves the merits open on remand; it does not decide the claim failed.
Concurrent findings of fact against the claimant are binding in second appeal absent an error of law (117835723_2, 177016396_3).
Claims against public or State property call for particular seriousness and circumspection (771263_3, 1742737_3).
The requirement of an admitted owner's title or a disclaimer of derivative title is stressed in some members; it is not a separate condition in all.

outlier_members.reason: Reaches the opposite outcome: title by adverse possession was acquired because possession was open, continuous and hostile beyond the limitation period; it addresses whether the owner's specific knowledge is required.

common_material_facts: Claimant relies on long possession without proving hostility, a starting date or animus
Possession began permissively (tenant, licensee, mortgagee, share-cropper, lessee) or under a derivative title
Claim made against the State or public land
Documents supporting entry (sale deed, agreement, records) unproved or unreliable
Claimant denies the owner's title or claims inconsistent title and adverse possession together
Concurrent findings of the lower courts against the claimant
statutes_and_provisions: Limitation Act 1963, Articles 64 and 65
Limitation Act 1963, Section 27
Limitation Act 1908, Articles 142 and 144 (contrasted)
Section 100 CPC
Registration Act 1908, Section 47

Cases cited: S.M. Karim v. Bibi Sakina; Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India; T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa; P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma; Saroop Singh v. Banto; P. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy; Thakur Kishan Singh v. Arvind Kumar
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: The adverse possession claim fails in about 23 of 25 members; one member (865312_2) finds title acquired, and one (159174_2) states the requirements and leaves the merits on remand.
variations: Some members stress pleading requirements (when possession became adverse); others stress evidentiary failure.
Permissive possession cases (licensee, tenant, mortgagee, share-cropper) require proof of a hostile conversion known to the owner.
Derivative-title purchasers against the State must disclaim their title and bring a hostile claim to the State's knowledge.
Some members treat claiming own title together with adverse possession as inconsistent unless the earlier title is renounced.
Some members add that denying the true owner's title defeats the plea.
865312_2 holds that the owner's specific knowledge is not required.

legal_question: Is a property-acquisition or estate-reform law protected from challenge under Part III fundamental rights (Articles 14, 19, 31) by Articles 31(4), 31A or 31B, and where do those protections stop?

predicates.constitutional_challenge_based_on_fundam: The law or provision is challenged as void for inconsistency with fundamental rights, such as Articles 14, 19 or 31, including grounds like no compensation, no public purpose or unreasonable restriction.
predicates.law_provides_for_acquisition_extinguishm: The law provides for State acquisition of an estate or of rights in an estate, or for extinguishing or modifying such rights, so that it changes proprietary or land-tenure rights rather than merely suspending management or moving property between family members.
predicates.law_is_specifically_listed_in_constituti: The law is specifically named in the Ninth Schedule and so attracts Article 31B independently of Article 31A.
predicates.law_falls_within_estate_definition_or_is: The land is an estate, including its local equivalent under the existing land-tenure law and regardless of the label used, or alternatively the law is scheduled. Scheduled laws are protected even if the land is not an estate.
predicates.challenged_provision_is_the_law_or_integ: The challenged provision, power or consequential notification is the protected law itself or an ancillary and integral part of its machinery.
predicates.challenge_under_part_iii_fails: The law or provision cannot be held void on the asserted fundamental-rights ground.

definition: A law acquiring, extinguishing or modifying rights in an estate (including its local equivalent), or a law specifically listed in the Ninth Schedule, cannot be invalidated on Part III grounds such as Articles 14, 19 and 31. This covers lack of compensation or public purpose and extends to integral ancillary provisions. The protection is independent for scheduled laws, even over non-estate land.
exceptions_or_limits: Article 31A does not protect a law that merely suspends management, or transfers property between family members, without acquiring, extinguishing or modifying estate or land-tenure rights.

A law that does not fall within Article 31A or 31B or the other protective provisions remains subject to fundamental-rights review. This includes general property-deprivation laws and compulsory acquisition outside the protected categories.

Laws for State acquisition or requisition are not tested under Article 19(1)(f) and 19(5) because of the separation made in Article 31(2) as amended. This is not a general immunity from other fundamental-rights review.
A law transferring management and property without compulsory acquisition does not violate Article 31 if made under a valid law.
Fraud-on-the-Constitution claims fail where the prior measures predate the Constitution and no connection to the acquisition is shown.
A notification consequential to a valid statute is not invalid merely because it is an executive act.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns whether a constitutional protection for local special property rights bars a parliamentary recovery law. This is not an estate-acquisition protection question.
The opposite outcome: the protection does not apply to a family-property transfer that leaves land-tenure relations unchanged. It is used here as a limit on the rule.
Holds that a property-deprivation law remains subject to fundamental-rights review. It is a limit on the rule, not an application of it.
Holds that acquisition laws are not exempt from fundamental-rights review where no protective article applies. It is a limit on the rule.
Suspension of management is outside Article 31A. It is a limit on the rule.
Concerns Article 31(1) and (2) and a transfer of association property under a valid law, with no estate protection involved.
Concerns pre-existing general land-acquisition remedies, not the scope of Part III protection.
A fraud-on-the-Constitution claim, a distinct sub-issue.
A fraud-on-the-Constitution claim, a distinct sub-issue.

common_material_facts: Zamindari, jagir or estate abolition and land reform statutes challenged under Articles 14, 19 and 31
Dispute over whether the land counts as an estate or its local equivalent
Statutes listed in the Ninth Schedule where some land was conceded not to be an estate
Ancillary powers such as annulment of transfers made to defeat the law
Allegations of no compensation, no public purpose or fraud on the Constitution
statutes_and_provisions: Article 31A and Article 31A(2)(a) and (b)
Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule
Articles 14, 19(1)(f) and 19(5)
Constitution (Fourth and Seventh) Amendment Acts
Entries 18 and 36 of List II
Entry 42 of List III
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About 16 members uphold the protected law or provision against Part III challenge. About 5 to 6 members set limits where the protection does not apply, such as suspension of management, family transfers and general deprivation. About 3 members are fraud or ancillary issues that were rejected.
variations: Article 31A protection depends on a substantive change in estate or tenure rights. Article 31B protection depends only on listing in the Ninth Schedule.
Some members treat lack of compensation or public purpose as no ground to strike down a protected law.
Some members stress that acquisition laws not covered by these provisions are still reviewable under fundamental rights.
In one member, Justices Imam and Sarkar dissented and read the protection more broadly.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) scope of Article 31A protection for estate acquisition, including integral provisions, compensation and public purpose; (b) independent Article 31B/Ninth Schedule protection; (c) limits where the protections do not apply, covering general deprivation and acquisition review, suspension of management and family transfers; (d) fraud-on-the-Constitution and other peripheral issues.

legal_question: When a party who won below (or who did not appeal) is respondent in an appeal, may it support the decree on grounds or findings decided against it without filing its own appeal or cross-objection, and when must it appeal or cross-object?

rule.if: respondent_in_appeal and respondent_has_decree_or_order_in_its_favour and respondent_seeks_only_to_support_that_decree_or_order and not respondent_seeks_to_alter_decree_or_obtain_greater_relief and not support_would_mutilate_or_destroy_decree

predicates.respondent_in_appeal: The party relying on the ground is a respondent in an appeal, revision or special-leave appeal brought by another party.
predicates.respondent_has_decree_or_order_in_its_fa: The respondent obtained the substantive disposition it wanted below, such as dismissal of the suit or petition, even though some finding or ground went against it.
predicates.respondent_seeks_only_to_support_that_de: The respondent invokes a ground, alternative ground or challenge to an adverse finding only to uphold the decree or order already in its favour.
predicates.respondent_seeks_to_alter_decree_or_obta: The respondent asks the appellate court to vary the decree, grant additional or greater relief, or change a part of the decree adverse to it, such as a costs order or an unconditional decree in place of a conditional one.
predicates.support_would_mutilate_or_destroy_decree: Relying on the ground would undo or cut down the decree under appeal instead of merely upholding it.
predicates.respondent_may_rely_on_ground_or_challen: The respondent may urge the ground, or contest the adverse finding, in support of the decree without filing a separate appeal or cross-objection.

definition: A respondent who already holds a favourable decree or order may defend it on any available ground, including one decided against it below, without a cross-objection. A respondent who wants the decree altered or wants greater relief must file its own appeal or cross-objection.
exceptions_or_limits: Relief beyond the decree needs an appeal or cross-objection. Examples are an unconditional decree in place of a conditional one, a change to a costs order, and possession against appellants (7053_1, 1932437_1, 37505817_7, 776356_8, 236915_1).
A cross-objection may be used against the appellant for relief that could have been sought by separate appeal (236915_1).

In an appeal by special leave under Article 136, Order 41 Rule 22 does not apply of its own force and cross-objections are not maintainable. A respondent aggrieved by an adverse part of the decision must seek leave independently and in time. Supporting a favourable order on an alternative ground rests on general principles, not on Order 41 Rule 22 (1766860_3, 1766860_4, 41340819_3).
Some members stress that the ground must have been raised below and that the opponent must not be surprised (1527823_2, 1614716_3).

One member holds that an adverse finding cannot be challenged without a cross-objection (905254_3). It is best read as a case where the challenge went beyond merely supporting the decree, and it is in tension with the other members.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns an appellate court admitting a new pure question of law on admitted facts, not the respondent's right to support a decree.
Concerns a late pure question of law on undisputed facts where there is no prejudice.
Concerns a pure question of law raised for the first time on second appeal.
Concerns an additional appeal ground on a pure question of law raised at the argument stage.
Concerns a new contention on document construction that needs no factual evidence.
Concerns a new question of law, turning on construction or undisputed facts, raised in a court of last resort.
Concerns an appellate court deciding the legal character of an offence from proved facts.
Concerns a pure question of law raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
Concerns waiver by non-argument of a preserved ground, raised by an appellant.
Concerns a pleaded but unanswered ground relied on by the appellant after the lower court did not consider it.

common_material_facts: The respondent won below but an adverse finding or rejected ground was recorded against it.
The respondent did not file a cross-objection or separate appeal.
The respondent sometimes sought additional relief, such as a costs variation or an unconditional decree, rather than only support for the decree.
The appeal was sometimes by special leave under Article 136.
statutes_and_provisions: Order XLI Rule 22 CPC
Order XLI Rule 33 CPC
Sections 2(2), 96 and 100 CPC
Article 136 and Article 142 of the Constitution
Section 116C of the Representation of the People Act, 1951
Order XIX Rule 4 of the Supreme Court Rules
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 15 covered members, about 9 allow a respondent to support its favourable decree on an adverse or alternative ground without a cross-objection. About 6 deny relief that would alter the decree (costs, greater relief, reversing an unappealed finding, cross-objection in an Article 136 appeal), or deny a challenge to an adverse finding without a cross-objection.
variations: Order 41 Rule 22 applies directly in ordinary appeals but only by analogy or general principle in Article 136 appeals.
Some members stress the absence of surprise or prejudice.
Some members distinguish a challenge to a finding from a challenge to the decree.
905254_3 states more strictly that a cross-objection is needed to challenge an adverse finding.

split_suggestion: Split into two clusters. (1) Respondent's right to support a decree versus the need for cross-objection or appeal, which is the covered group, with the Article 136 cross-objection members as a sub-group. (2) Raising a new or late ground on appeal, especially a pure question of law on admitted facts, which is the outlier group: 1029214_3, 1497995_1, 155267_5, 1752222_1, 180317_1, 1999892_4, 3824_3, 8752021_4, 1732914_5 and 485924_3. 41340819_3 belongs to both.

legal_question: Once land or a proprietary or intermediary interest in it has vested in the State (by completed acquisition or by land-reform, ceiling or surplus legislation), can the former owner or proprietor recover possession, restitution, reconveyance or related relief, or does the vesting bar the claim?

predicates.claim_by_former_owner_or_proprietor_for_: The claimant, a former owner, proprietor, intermediary or decree-holder claiming through such rights, seeks possession, execution of a possession decree, restitution, reconveyance, an injunction, eviction of tenants, challenge to changed use, or compensation for the period after vesting.
predicates.land_or_proprietary_interest_validly_ves: By a completed acquisition (award and possession under the Land Acquisition Act, vesting free from encumbrances) or by land-reform, abolition, ceiling or surplus legislation, the land or the claimant's proprietary or intermediary interest has vested in the State or its nominee, and the claimant's former interest has ceased.
predicates.statutory_saving_or_statutory_reconveyan: The claimant falls within a statutory saving (such as actual khas or home-farm possession at vesting, or a subsisting qualifying mortgage), or the conditions of a statutory reconveyance or return provision are met (for example a determination by the competent authority that the land is no longer required, with the land still vested in the government).
predicates.former_owner_claim_fails_and_relief_deni: The court refuses the claimed relief, so the former owner gets no possession, restitution, reconveyance, injunction, execution or post-vesting compensation, and is left only with any statutory compensation.

definition: Once land or a proprietary interest has validly vested in the State, whether through completed acquisition or through land-reform, ceiling or surplus legislation, the former owner cannot recover possession, restitution, reconveyance or related relief. This holds even if the land is unused, put to another public purpose, or not yet used, unless a statutory saving or a statutory reconveyance condition is satisfied.
exceptions_or_limits: Interests expressly saved by the statute, such as khas or home-farm land in actual possession at vesting or land under a subsisting qualifying mortgage, are not extinguished.

Statutory reconveyance or patta provisions (for example s.48-B LA Act, s.54-A of the Telangana Land Revenue Act) apply only where the competent authority determines the land is no longer required and the land remains vested in the government. A staff or engineer's letter, or a non-statutory instruction without competent relinquishment, is insufficient.
Vesting must be valid and complete. Vesting must be established (possession taken or the statutory vesting date passed) before the bar operates.
Rights to statutory compensation for the pre-vesting period survive; only recovery of land or post-vesting benefits is barred.
Some members leave open the State's own decision on how to use the land, or any rights under other provisions (for example s.18 UP ZA&LR Act).
Under land-reform statutes, the possession remedy lies only with the statutorily recognised classes (Bhumidar, Asami, Gaon Sabha), not with a former proprietor as such.

common_material_facts: Land was acquired, with award and possession taken, or an estate or proprietary interest was vested in the State by land-reform, abolition, ceiling or surplus legislation.
The former owner, proprietor or decree-holder sought possession, restoration, restitution, reconveyance, injunction or execution after vesting.
Acquired land was unused, surplus, diverted to another public purpose or transferred to another agency.
The claimant was not in actual possession at vesting, or no saving provision applied.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act 1894 s.16 (vesting free from encumbrances), s.48-B, ss.40 and 44-B
Bihar Land Reforms Act 1950 ss.3, 4, 6
UP Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act ss.4, 6
MP Abolition of Proprietary Rights Act 1950 ss.3, 4
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act ss.9(1)(i), 10A
Delhi Land Reforms Act 1954
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act 1953
Himachal Pradesh Village Common Lands Vesting and Utilization Act s.3
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act 1999
Telangana Land Revenue Act s.54-A
CPC s.144
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 25 members deny the former owner's claim: possession, restitution, reconveyance, injunction, execution or post-vesting compensation is refused. A few add that statutory return or saving provisions were not triggered on the facts.
variations: Acquisition-law cases (about 10) turn on s.16 vesting and reject restitution for non-use or changed use. Land-reform cases (about 12) turn on statutory vesting of proprietary rights and bar possession decrees, suits or execution.
Some members involve procedural or collateral consequences, such as mesne profits, restitution under s.144 CPC, recurring compensation, easements, or repeal of the ceiling law.
Some members turn on the failure of a statutory or non-statutory return mechanism (competent authority determination, relinquishment, transfer to another agency).
Surplus-land cases bar owners from using tenant-eviction rights or claiming restoration for non-use.
Saving-provision cases (khas or home-farm possession) are decided on whether the claimant was in actual possession at vesting.

legal_question: When does a tenant's payment, tender or deposit of rent (including a deposit in court or with a rent authority, or a late payment) satisfy the statutory requirement so as to protect the tenant from eviction for rent default?

rule.if: rent_default_eviction_proceeding and tenant_paid_or_deposited_rent and (deposit_in_statutory_manner_and_time or (court_deposit_conditions_met and deposit_available_to_landlord_or_landlord_informed) or court_validly_extended_time)

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: The landlord seeks eviction on the ground of non-payment or arrears of rent under a rent-control statute.
predicates.tenant_paid_or_deposited_rent: The tenant paid, tendered or deposited the arrears (with interest and costs where the statute requires them), or the rent due for the relevant period.
predicates.deposit_in_statutory_manner_and_time: The payment or deposit was made by the time (for example, by the first hearing or within the prescribed period) and in the manner the statute prescribes.
predicates.court_deposit_conditions_met: The statutory preconditions for depositing rent in court are satisfied, for example a landlord's refusal of a valid tender, an unanswered request for bank details, or a bona fide dispute over who is entitled to the rent. The conditions are read liberally and, where the statute provides alternative routes, as alternatives.
predicates.deposit_available_to_landlord_or_landlor: The deposit is in the custody of the court or authority hearing the matter, or otherwise at the landlord's disposal without hindrance, and the landlord was informed of it.
predicates.court_validly_extended_time: The statute empowers the court to extend time and the court did so, and the tenant paid or deposited within the extended time.
predicates.payment_or_deposit_treated_as_rent_paid_: The deposit or payment is deemed payment to the landlord and the tenant cannot be evicted on the rent-default ground.

definition: Under rent-control statutes, which are construed liberally in favour of tenants, a tenant's deposit or late payment counts as payment and protects against eviction for default only if it meets the statute's conditions. Those conditions cover time, manner, the circumstances justifying a court deposit, availability to the landlord and any valid extension. A deposit that does not meet the statutory conditions, or a late payment without a court-granted extension, leaves the tenant in default.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the statute allows only a limited extension of time and mandates striking out the defence on default, the court cannot condone a late deposit (Rajasthan scheme).

A direct court deposit made without satisfying the statutory preconditions (a returned money order, a request for bank details, or a bona fide dispute over who is entitled to the rent) is not treated as payment.
A late payment does not protect the tenant unless the court exercises its discretion to extend time; extension is not automatic.
A deposit in a different court in unrelated proceedings, or a partial tender, may not qualify.
Where a statute makes a particular deposit method ineffective (for example, a treasury deposit) and prescribes another, the deposit does not cure the default.
The outcome depends on the particular statute's wording, and the members cover several state enactments.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the independent continuing obligation to pay or deposit rent during the proceeding when the dispute is only about whether rent was paid, not whether a deposit counts as payment.
It concerns the duty to deposit rent during a suit despite denying title, under Order XV Rule 5 CPC, not the effect of a deposit made.
It concerns whether a revenue officer has discretion or a duty to grant time to a cultivating tenant, a different statutory discretion question.
It concerns the officer's discretion to allow time to a cultivating tenant who made no deposit, not whether a deposit counts as payment.
It gives time to complete the deposit to avert execution and leaves security adjustment open, without deciding whether a deposit counts as payment.

common_material_facts: The landlord sued for eviction on the ground of rent arrears or default under a state rent-control Act.
The tenant deposited rent in court or with a rent authority, or paid late, often after the landlord refused a tender or amid a dispute over who was entitled to the rent.
The deposit was made by or around the first hearing and was available to the landlord, who was informed of it.
Some tenants made late deposits and sought condonation or extension of time.
statutes_and_provisions: Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act 1961, ss. 12(3), 13(1), 13(5), 13(6)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act 1949, s. 13(2)(i) proviso
Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act 1934, s. 31
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act 1950, ss. 13(4), 13(5), 19-A(3), 19-A(4)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act 1955, ss. 13(1)(i), 21, 22
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act 1947, ss. 3(1)(a), 7-C
Bihar Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act 1947, s. 11(1)(d)
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act 1965, s. 11(2)(c)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 15 of the 20 covered members, the deposit or payment is treated as valid payment and the tenant is protected from eviction. Examples are deposits available to the landlord at the first hearing, deposits after refusal or a bona fide dispute, and payment within a court-extended time. In about 5 (803896_2, 769814_1, 781949_1, 973429_1 and, in part, 1612858_1, which was remanded), non-compliant, late or unextended deposits leave the tenant in default.
variations: Courts read the deposit provisions liberally and purposively in the tenant's favour, but strictly where the statute's conditions are mandatory and the consequence is stated.
Some statutes empower courts to extend time (Madhya Pradesh), while others limit or deny that power (Rajasthan).
Earlier contrary decisions were overruled or distinguished (Vidya Prachar Trust, Mehnga Singh, Jagdish Kapoor).
Some members concern the sequence of tender routes, and others concern deemed payment of deposits made amid a bona fide dispute over who is entitled to the rent.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) validity of a deposit as payment, covering the manner and conditions for court deposit and availability to the landlord; (b) the court's power to extend time or condone late deposits; and (c) the continuing duty to deposit and the officer's discretion to grant time, which includes the outliers 1308176_2, 145937302_1, 625438_2, 1688111_2 and 823717_2.

legal_question: When can a criminal conviction resting on circumstantial evidence be sustained, and when must it be set aside, in light of the requirement that the proved circumstances form a complete chain consistent only with guilt and excluding every reasonable hypothesis of innocence?

predicates.case_rests_on_circumstantial_evidence: The prosecution case depends on circumstantial evidence, with no direct eyewitness evidence establishing guilt.
predicates.each_incriminating_circumstance_fully_es: Every circumstance relied upon to infer guilt has been proved by reliable evidence beyond reasonable doubt, not merely suspected.
predicates.circumstances_form_complete_chain_consis: Taken cumulatively, the proved circumstances form an unbroken chain, without material gaps, that is conclusive and consistent only with the accused's guilt.
predicates.no_reasonable_hypothesis_of_innocence_re: The proved circumstances exclude every reasonable hypothesis consistent with the accused's innocence, including another culprit, accident or suicide.
predicates.conviction_can_be_sustained: The conviction may be upheld because guilt is proved beyond reasonable doubt; if the conditions are not met, the conviction cannot stand and the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt.

definition: A conviction based on circumstantial evidence is sustainable only if every incriminating circumstance is fully proved and together they form a complete chain pointing only to the accused's guilt and excluding every reasonable hypothesis of innocence. If a material circumstance is unproved, the chain has a gap, or a reasonable innocent explanation remains, the conviction cannot stand, because suspicion, however strong, is no substitute for proof.
exceptions_or_limits: Whether the chain is complete depends on the facts of each case; there is no fixed list of circumstances.
The innocent hypothesis that defeats a conviction must be reasonable, not extravagant or fanciful.
A false defence or the accused's silence cannot fill gaps in the prosecution case; the burden stays on the prosecution.

Where the facts are especially within the accused's knowledge, as with an inmate of the home last seen with the deceased, failure to give a reasonable explanation can be an additional incriminating circumstance, but only alongside an established chain (Section 106 Evidence Act).
Absconding or post-crime conduct is not conclusive alone but may add weight when considered with other established circumstances.
A co-accused's confession is not substantive evidence and may only lend assurance to other independently proved circumstances.
Where two views are possible, the view favouring innocence must be preferred.

common_material_facts: No eyewitness; the prosecution relies on motive, last-seen evidence, recoveries, medical or forensic evidence and the accused's conduct.

Convictions were upheld where several independent circumstances converged, such as motive, opportunity or exclusive access, recoveries at the accused's instance, flight or absence after the crime, and no or a false explanation.

Convictions were set aside where the key circumstances were unproved, witnesses were unreliable or unexamined, last-seen evidence stood alone, the medical evidence was inconclusive, or an alternative suspect or cause such as suicide or an unknown vehicle remained.
Deaths in the accused's home, or the accused being last seen with the deceased, recur as a basis for requiring an explanation.
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Penal Code Sections 302, 34, 201, 396/109, 364
Evidence Act Sections 3, 14, 27, 106
Code of Criminal Procedure Section 313
Hanumant Govind Nargundkar v. State of M.P. (the tests for circumstantial evidence)
Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (the five golden principles)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About 16 of 25 uphold the conviction because a complete chain was proved. About 9 set the conviction aside and acquit, or give the benefit of doubt, because the chain was incomplete or an innocent hypothesis remained: 1499233_1, 1594055_1, 1770950_2, 196830604_1, 471083_2, 599539_1, 774794_1, 797943_2 and 89820566_2.
variations: Some judgments cite long lines of authority (Hanumant, Sharad Birdhichand Sarda, Hukam Singh); others apply the standard with no citation.
Several upheld cases add Section 106 (burden to explain facts within the accused's knowledge), Section 27 disclosure-led recoveries or a co-accused's confession as assurance.
Some upheld cases (e.g. 786487_2, 928028_6, 433507_1, 969015_1) stress cumulative force rather than reciting the chain test, and 969015_1 treats a case with hostile eyewitnesses as circumstantial.
Some acquittals rest on evidentiary failures (unreliable witnesses, uncompared thumb impression, unidentified clothing), others on inconclusive medical evidence or an unexcluded alternative cause.

legal_question: Is a compulsory acquisition that was made for a public purpose invalidated by a collateral, prior, subsequent or extraneous circumstance, such as a later diversion or release of the land, an earlier abandoned or alternative proceeding, the owner's existing or intended use, a plan or land-use mismatch, a failed negotiation, or a procedural or record irregularity, when no defect in the statutory acquisition process or the public purpose itself is shown?

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and acquisition_for_public_purpose and challenge_rests_on_collateral_or_extraneous_circumstance and not statutory_defect_or_improper_motive_shown

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The acquisition, or a notification, declaration or award under it, is challenged as invalid or as mala fide.
predicates.acquisition_for_public_purpose: The acquisition was made, and found by the court, to be for a genuine public purpose and was valid when made.
predicates.challenge_rests_on_collateral_or_extrane: The challenge relies on something other than a defect in the acquisition's statutory procedure or purpose. Examples are a later diversion or release of the land, an earlier abandoned acquisition or requisition, the owner's existing or intended use, a mismatch with the development plan, a land-use permission or official representation, a failed purchase negotiation, a title dispute, the exclusion of other land, the timing of an advance payment, a lack of mutation or registration, or the quashing of the acquisition for other owners.
predicates.statutory_defect_or_improper_motive_show: The record establishes a breach of a mandatory statutory requirement, a purpose that is actually private or no purpose at all, or specific facts showing mala fides or colourable exercise of power.
predicates.acquisition_not_invalidated_by_the_circu: The acquisition remains valid and effective despite the circumstance relied on; any remedy lies elsewhere, for example against the later unlawful act, or in the statutory objection or planning process.

definition: A land acquisition that is valid when made for a public purpose is not rendered invalid by collateral or later events. Examples are later diversion or unlawful release of the land, a prior abandoned proceeding, the owner's existing or intended use, plan or permission mismatches, failed negotiations, or record irregularities. Such events do not invalidate it unless a statutory defect, a sham purpose or specifically established mala fides is shown.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the stated purpose is actually private or is no purpose at all, or where the power is exercised mala fide or colourably on established facts.
A mandatory statutory requirement that was breached in the acquisition process itself is not covered.
The later act may itself be unlawful and be quashed or remedied separately, for example an abusive release or a diversion to an extraneous purpose.
Where the record lacks the evidence needed to show a bar, the court simply holds that the bar is not established.
Where an acquisition is quashed only at the instance of some owners, its effect on other owners depends on the scope of the challenge and the relief actually sought.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns whether a municipal master plan is valid for applying the urban land ceiling law, where the designation requirement is directory. It is not about the validity of a land acquisition.
It concerns the validity of a requisition order for a permanent public purpose, not the validity of an acquisition against a collateral circumstance.
It concerns the constitutional validity of using the notification date for compensation valuation, a different legal point from the validity of the acquisition itself.
It concerns the constitutional validity of a law validating successive acquisitions, tested against the compensation guarantee, rather than a collateral challenge to a particular acquisition.

common_material_facts: The acquisition was for a stated public purpose, such as planned development, a market, a road, a railway facility or an industrial estate.

The landowner relied on a prior, parallel or subsequent event: an abandoned acquisition, a requisition, a later transfer, diversion or release of the land, a change of public use, an existing or intended use, a land-use permission or plan mismatch, or a failed negotiation.
Allegations of mala fides were unsupported by specific facts.
The statutory objection or hearing process was available or had been followed.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894: ss. 3(f), 4, 5A, 6, 12(3), 16, 48 and Part VI
Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966: ss. 126 and 128
Delhi Development Act, 1957: ss. 12, 15
Bombay Land Requisition Act
U.P. Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973: s. 13
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 21 of the 25 members the challenge failed and the acquisition was held valid or not shown to be invalid. The court sometimes preserved separate remedies, as with the quashing of an abusive release. The 4 outliers address master-plan validity, requisition, and compensation valuation.
variations: Some members rest on binding precedent, such as Gulam Mustafa, Vinod Oil and Meera Sahni, while others reason directly from the statute.
One member (1325151_3) rests on an evidentiary gap rather than a positive holding.
One member (187587126_2) goes further and quashes the later abusive release while upholding the acquisition.
Some members add a condition: the later use must be connected to the original purpose (149826_3), or planning approval must still be obtained (869849_2).
Mala fides claims fail for want of specific facts (1196905_3, 588752_2, 727486_7).

split_suggestion: Treat the 21 covered members as one group on collateral or subsequent events not invalidating a valid acquisition. Split off the compensation and valuation members (661580_3, 270610_3) as constitutional challenges to compensation. Split off the master-plan member (1258228_4) and the requisition-purpose member (400997_1) as separate issues. Optionally subdivide the covered group into (a) later diversion or release, (b) prior or parallel proceedings, (c) plan, use or permission mismatches, (d) mala fides, and (e) procedural or record irregularities.

legal_question: Can a party obtain, at the appellate or later stage, relief, a finding or a remand that depends on a claim that was never pleaded or relief that was never sought, or on evidence that was available but not adduced below, when no recognised ground (amendment, prevention despite due diligence, or need for the court to pronounce judgment) is shown?

predicates.outcome_depends_on_matter_outside_the_ca: The relief, finding, enhancement or remand sought or granted rests on something that was not part of the case as pleaded and evidenced in the proceedings below.
predicates.matter_is_unpleaded_claim_or_unrequested: The matter is a factual or legal ground, claim or relief that was not pleaded or prayed for, and the pleadings were not amended to include it. Examples are unclaimed damages or mesne profits, an unpleaded alternative theory, and a new case supplied by the court.
predicates.matter_is_evidence_not_adduced_or_not_on: The matter is evidence, such as documents, another case's judgment or award, or a new factual foundation, that was available but not produced or proved in the courts below, or is not part of the record. A remand to supply such evidence also falls here.
predicates.no_recognised_ground_to_permit_it: None of the recognised grounds is shown. The party was not prevented from presenting the matter despite due diligence. The trial court did not wrongly refuse it. The appellate court does not need it to pronounce judgment. No amendment or application to admit it was made or allowed. No satisfactory explanation is given for the omission.
predicates.court_must_decline_to_consider_or_sustai: The court refuses to admit or consider the evidence, claim or judgment, refuses the remand, or sets aside the decree or relief that rested on the unpleaded or unproved matter.

definition: A court decides a dispute on the case pleaded and the evidence led in the proceedings below. On appeal it will not grant unpleaded or unrequested relief, and it will not admit or remand for evidence that was available but not produced, unless a recognised ground such as prevention despite due diligence, need for the evidence to pronounce judgment, or a proper amendment is shown.
exceptions_or_limits: Additional evidence may be admitted under Order XLI Rule 27 CPC only on the specified grounds: wrongful refusal by the trial court, unavailability despite due diligence, or the appellate court's need for it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. Reasons must be recorded.
A claim may be raised if the pleadings are amended or if the opposing party had notice and an opportunity to meet it.
A remand may be justified where the party was misled or denied an opportunity to present its case; the members refusing remand turn on the absence of that.
Refusing unclaimed damages or mesne profits does not decide whether the party is otherwise entitled to them or whether a separate proceeding lies.
Several members rest on case-specific circumstances, such as disputed genuineness of documents, a late stage after the hearing concluded, or irrelevance to the controversy actually litigated.

common_material_facts: A party tries on appeal, or the lower or appellate court itself, goes beyond the pleaded and proved case.
Documents, judgments or awards from other proceedings are relied on without being brought on record or admitted as additional evidence.
Evidence was available or obtainable earlier, and no explanation was given for not producing it.
Relief such as possession, injunction, damages, mesne profits or allotment was granted or sought although it was never prayed for, and court fees were sometimes unpaid.
Alternative factual theories (riparian rights, adverse possession, destitution, improvements, a Will, a government letter) were raised without pleading or evidence.
Land acquisition compensation appeals and eviction cases recur.
statutes_and_provisions: Order XLI Rule 27 CPC (additional evidence), sometimes read with Section 151 CPC
Order II Rules 2 and 4 and Order XX Rule 12 CPC
Order XVII Rule 3 CPC, and Sections 100 and 101 CPC on second appeals
Section 68 of the Evidence Act
Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act
Section 20 of the Indian Forest Act
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 25 members the court refused the additional evidence, remand, new claim or unpleaded relief, or set aside the decree or relief that rested on it. About 13 concern additional evidence or remand, and about 12 concern unpleaded or unrequested relief or claims.
variations: One subgroup applies Order XLI Rule 27 to additional evidence or remand: unavailability, due diligence, lateness, and lacuna-filling.
A second subgroup applies the pleading rule that relief must be founded on the pleaded case, with or without evidence.
Some members rest on a lack of factual foundation or trial issues rather than on an express rule.
Authorities range from detailed case citations to none at all.
Members differ on whether the defect is lack of pleading, lack of evidence, or both.

legal_question: Is a civil court's jurisdiction (or a later civil suit) barred by a special tenancy, revenue, rent-control or similar statute or forum, or by that forum's earlier decision, where the forum was not empowered to decide the matter or grant the relief claimed?

predicates.civil_claim_before_civil_court: The claim before the civil court (for example title, possession, injunction, recovery of land or debt, execution of a decree, or a declaration) is an ordinary civil claim, and any earlier special-forum decision relied on as a bar concerned a different or merely incidental issue.
predicates.special_forum_empowered_to_decide_the_ma: The special forum (revenue court, rent authority, tribunal, settlement or patta authority) is statutorily empowered to decide the very matter in dispute, or to grant the relief claimed, and not merely to decide it incidentally or summarily.
predicates.statute_expressly_or_impliedly_bars_civi: The governing statute, by express words or necessary implication (for example a complete scheme with its own remedy), excludes civil-court jurisdiction over the matter in dispute.
predicates.civil_court_not_barred_from_adjudicating: The civil court has jurisdiction to hear and decide the claim, and no earlier special-forum decision bars it by res judicata.

definition: Civil courts have general jurisdiction under section 9 CPC, and ouster is not readily inferred. A civil claim is not barred, either by a special statute or by res judicata from an earlier special-forum decision, unless the special forum was actually empowered to decide that matter and grant that relief, or the statute expressly or impliedly excludes the civil court. Incidental or summary findings, or findings made without competence, do not oust the civil court.
exceptions_or_limits: The civil court is barred where the statute makes the special forum competent for the very dispute (for example a rent authority empowered to decide the lawfulness of a sub-tenancy within the prescribed period, or a revenue court assigned landlord-tenant disputes).
A prior ejectment decree does not restore civil jurisdiction where the special authority is still empowered to decide the timely dispute.
The ouster must be established by the party asserting it and is strictly construed; the substance of the claim, not its form, governs.

Res judicata is excluded only where the earlier forum lacked competence to try the later suit, or decided the issue only incidentally; a matter directly and finally decided by a competent forum is not covered by this rule.

outlier_members.reason: Opposite outcome: the statute assigns landlord-tenant disputes to the revenue court, which excludes the civil court.
Opposite outcome: the rent authority was empowered to decide the sub-tenancy dispute within the period, so the civil court lacked jurisdiction.
Opposite outcome: a prior ejectment decree did not restore civil jurisdiction over a dispute the rent authority could decide.
Concerns the statutory conditions for transferring a possession suit under the cultivating tenants' protection law, not the jurisdictional bar or res judicata question.
Concerns the interaction of a pending civil suit with a Section 145 CrPC possession proceeding, which is a criminal-procedure question.
Concerns the discretionary return of a plaint under section 23 of the Small Cause Courts Act, which is a different procedural question.

common_material_facts: A civil suit for title, possession, injunction, recovery of land or debt, or execution, faces an objection based on a special tenancy, revenue, rent-control or wakf statute.
The special authority's earlier order or remit was limited, summary or incidental, or concerned a different issue (for example rent fixation, a patta, or a revenue ejectment).
The statute contains no express bar, or the bar covers only specified matters.
The special forum could not grant the relief sought (for example an injunction or a declaration of title).
statutes_and_provisions: Section 9 CPC
Section 11 CPC and Explanation VIII
Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act ss. 3, 5
Bihar Land Reforms Act ss. 6, 35
Rajasthan Tenancy Act ss. 207, 256
Rajasthan Wakf Act ss. 6, 7, 85
MP Accommodation Control Act ss. 15, 16, 45
MP Land Revenue Code ss. 250, 257
Tamil Nadu Estates Abolition Act ss. 11, 64-C
Punjab Tenancy Act s. 77(3)
Agra Tenancy Act ss. 227, 230, 271
Delhi Land Revenue Act s. 83
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 19 of the 25 members the civil court's jurisdiction is upheld, or the earlier special-forum decision is held not to be res judicata. In about 3 members the civil court is barred because the special forum was empowered to decide the dispute. The remaining 3 raise procedural questions of a different kind.
variations: Some members concern jurisdiction at the threshold (ouster). Others concern res judicata of an earlier special-forum finding.

The reasons for non-exclusion differ: the forum could not decide title; the finding was incidental; the forum lacked competence; there was no express or implied bar; the claim was commercial or collateral; or the suit pre-dated the Act.
The cases that bar the civil court turn on the statute expressly empowering the special authority to decide the specific dispute within a time limit.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) ouster of civil jurisdiction by special statutes (including the three members where the civil court is barred), and (b) res judicata effect of earlier special-forum decisions (1161744_1, 1636196_1, 1983017_1, 796787_2, 978541_4). Move the CrPC s.145, plaint-return and transfer-requirement members to separate clusters.

legal_question: When a party to a pending appeal dies and the legal representatives are not substituted within the prescribed time, does the appeal abate, and if so, does the abatement extend only to the deceased party's interest or to the whole appeal?

rule.if: appeal_pending and party_to_appeal_dies and legal_representatives_not_substituted_in_time and abatement_not_set_aside

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal (first or second, including an execution appeal) was pending when the party died.
predicates.party_to_appeal_dies: An appellant or respondent in the appeal died while the appeal was pending, and the right to sue or appeal, or the liability, survives.
predicates.legal_representatives_not_substituted_in: No application to bring the deceased party's legal representatives on record was made within the prescribed limitation period.
predicates.abatement_not_set_aside: The abatement has not been set aside and the delay has not been condoned.
predicates.appeal_abates_as_to_deceased_party_and_d: The appeal abates automatically, without any order, as to the deceased party. The decree under challenge becomes final between the deceased party and the opposing party and cannot be directly or indirectly modified. The rest of the appeal also abates only if the decree or interest is joint and inseverable, or if allowing the appeal would produce a decree inconsistent with the final one. Otherwise it continues as to independent, severable interests.

definition: Where a party to a pending appeal dies and no timely substitution is made, the appeal abates automatically as to that party and the decree becomes final against that party's side. Abatement extends to the whole appeal only where the decree or interest is joint and indivisible, or success for the survivors would produce contradictory decrees, or effective relief cannot be granted without the deceased party. Where interests are separate and severable, the appeal continues as to the others.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the interests of the other parties or properties are independent and severable, the appeal survives as to them and abates only as to the deceased party's interest.
Survivorship under Order XXII Rule 2 saves the appeal only where the right to sue or appeal actually survives to the remaining parties, which was not shown for a claimed joint Hindu family.
Order XLI Rule 4 (appeal by one party on a common ground) and Order XLI Rule 33 (wide appellate power) do not revive an abated appeal or allow relief affecting the deceased party's final decree.
Abatement can be set aside under Order XXII Rule 9, and condonation of delay is possible.

Where the estate of a deceased respondent is unrepresented and the right to continue survives, the court must first determine and bring the representatives on record. A judgment given otherwise is a nullity.
Substitution in later proceedings in the suit (such as final decree proceedings) does not retroactively save an appeal already filed in which no timely substitution was made.
If the appeal abates without a merits adjudication, no decree on the merits arises and no second appeal lies against the purported decree.
Where the deceased was a tenant in a rent-eviction appeal, the tenant's own comparative-hardship question no longer arises.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns only a tenant's comparative-hardship question under a rent control statute becoming moot on the tenant's death. It does not address substitution or abatement.

common_material_facts: A party (appellant or respondent) died while the appeal was pending.
Legal representatives were not brought on record within the prescribed time, and the delay was often not condoned.
The question was whether abatement as to the deceased extended to co-appellants or co-respondents.
The decree was joint, the property was held jointly or was unpartitioned, or the cause of action was common.
The surviving parties sought to continue the appeal under Order XLI Rule 4 or Rule 33 or by survivorship.
statutes_and_provisions: Code of Civil Procedure Order XXII Rules 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9 and 11
Code of Civil Procedure Order XLI Rules 4 and 33
Code of Civil Procedure Order I Rule 9
Code of Civil Procedure Section 2(2), Section 2(11), Section 11 and Section 100
State of Punjab v. Nathu Ram, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 636, and the cases following it
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 20 of 25 members, the appeal abates as to the deceased party and the decree becomes final against that party. In about 10 of these, the whole appeal fails because the decree is joint or indivisible or inconsistent decrees would result. In about 3, the appeal continues as to independent or severable property. Two members hold that a judgment given after abatement or without representation of the estate is a nullity.
variations: Abatement is limited to the deceased party's property or interest where interests are independent or severable (1275064_3, 35788_4, 1329149_2).

Abatement extends to the whole appeal where the decree is joint or indivisible or success would produce inconsistent decrees (1980657_2, 62991042_1, 67957702_2, 849004_1, 823328_1, 344463_1, 72077064_4, 27271392_4).
Some members state the bare rule of automatic abatement without discussing extent (156119044_1, 1884217_2, 473980_2, 310733_1, 926555_4).
Some members address the consequences of abatement, namely nullity of a later decree or the non-existence of a decree (156119044_3, 785816_1, 1123714_1).
Some members reject attempts to avoid abatement through Order XLI Rules 4 and 33, survivorship, or substitution in other proceedings (1627364_1, 1627364_2, 1627364_3, 72077064_2, 1539480_2).

legal_question: When a party to a pending appeal dies (or is wrongly named as a party) and the legal representatives are not substituted, wholly or in part, or in time, does the appeal abate entirely, or does it survive in whole or in part?

rule.if: appeal_pending and party_died_or_not_properly_party and (deceased_party_estate_or_interest_otherwise_represented_on_record or deceased_party_unnecessary_or_formal_or_no_relief_sought_against_deceased or surviving_parties_interests_independent_or_decree_divisible_without_inconsistent_decrees or right_to_sue_survives_or_proceeding_is_representative) and not fraud_or_collusion_or_unfair_trial

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal (or similar proceeding on appeal) is pending before the court.
predicates.party_died_or_not_properly_party: A party to the appeal (appellant, respondent, plaintiff or claimant) died during the appeal, or a person already dead was named as a party, and legal representatives were not substituted, or were only partly substituted, or not substituted in time.
predicates.deceased_party_estate_or_interest_otherw: The deceased party's estate or interest is already represented by another legal representative, a transferee, or a co-party on record, or the appellant diligently and bona fide brought the known representatives on record in time.
predicates.deceased_party_unnecessary_or_formal_or_: The deceased party was only a proforma, formal or unnecessary party, or no relief was sought against that party, and the controversy can be decided without that party.
predicates.surviving_parties_interests_independent_: The surviving parties have separate or independent interests, or the decree is divisible, so relief to them can be granted without contradictory or unenforceable decrees.
predicates.right_to_sue_survives_or_proceeding_is_r: The right to sue or appeal survives to or against the remaining parties, or the proceeding was brought in a representative capacity, or the deceased's interest was merely managerial.
predicates.fraud_or_collusion_or_unfair_trial: There is fraud or collusion, or the proceeding was not a fair or real trial, or an omitted heir has a special defence that could not be tried.
predicates.appeal_does_not_abate_in_its_entirety_an: The appeal does not abate as a whole and may continue, at least for or against the surviving or represented parties; any abatement is confined to the deceased party's own separate interest.

definition: The death of a party to an appeal, or a failure to substitute legal representatives, does not automatically abate the whole appeal. The appeal continues where the estate is sufficiently represented, the deceased was unnecessary or formal, the right to sue survives, or the decree is divisible so that no inconsistent decrees result. Abatement is confined to the deceased party's own separate interest.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the decree is joint and indivisible and no legal representative of the deceased party remains on record, abatement may defeat the whole appeal because inconsistent or contradictory decrees could result (Nathu Ram, Ram Sarup, Rameshwar Prasad were distinguished on this basis).
Abatement still operates against the deceased party's own separate interest. Unexplained inordinate delay in substitution need not be condoned.
Representation of an estate by the heirs on record fails where there is fraud or collusion, no fair or real trial, or an omitted heir has a special defence that could not be tried.
In an appeal against the deceased respondent, abatement can still occur as to that respondent. The appellate court must then decide whether the appeal can proceed against the survivors.
Legal representatives may raise only defences appropriate to their representative character, not defences personal to the deceased, though they may assert independent title in their own right.
A party that knowingly allows an appeal to proceed on the merits without objecting to abatement cannot raise abatement later.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the scope of defences available to substituted representatives in an eviction appeal, not whether the appeal abates.
Turns on the specific text of s. 431 CrPC 1898 for appeals against acquittal and the complainant's death, which is a criminal-procedure point distinct from civil Order XXII abatement.
Holds that an earlier abatement made the decree final for one parcel and was unaffected by a later consolidation abatement. It does not decide whether the appeal survives abatement.

common_material_facts: A party (appellant, respondent, plaintiff or claimant) dies during the pending appeal and some or all legal representatives are not substituted in time.
Other legal representatives, transferees or co-parties remain on record and arguably represent the estate.
The deceased was a formal or proforma party, or no relief was sought against the deceased.
Several parties hold separate shares or independent interests, so a divisible decree is possible.
The objection that the appeal has abated is raised late or after merits participation.
statutes_and_provisions: Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Order XXII Rules 2, 3, 4, 10, 10A and 11
Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Order XLI Rule 4
Code of Civil Procedure 1908, Order XXX Rules 1 and 4
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, ss. 417 and 431
Land Acquisition Act 1894, ss. 11, 18, 30, 31
Supreme Court Rules, Order XVI Rule 12(a)
Bihar Consolidation of Holdings and Prevention of Fragmentation Act 1956, s. 4(1)(c)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 20 of the 25 members the appeal was held not to have abated in its entirety, or to continue against or for the surviving or represented parties. Abatement was confined to the deceased party's own interest in 2 or 3. The remainder concern related points, namely the scope of defences, a criminal-appeal statute, and finality of an earlier abatement.
variations: Some members rely on the estate being represented by other heirs, absent fraud or collusion (Daya Ram line). Others rely on the deceased being a proforma or unnecessary party.
Some rest on divisibility or independence of interests and the absence of inconsistent decrees (Nathu Ram test).
Some turn on the nature of the proceeding: representative or public suits, managerial interests, firm and partner suits, or transferees on record.
Procedural variants: timely application after learning of the death (Order 22 R.10A), late objections that are waived, and remand allowing representatives to be added.
One member refuses to condone an unexplained delay of over 25 years, so abatement applies to the deceased's own property; another treats the omitted representative as capable of being added.

split_suggestion: Keep the main group on partial or no abatement of civil appeals after a party's death. Move 1205820_4 (defences of legal representatives), 1743339_2 (criminal appeal against acquittal under CrPC s. 431) and 237512_2 (finality after earlier abatement and consolidation) into separate clusters. Optionally subdivide the main group into (a) estate sufficiently represented, (b) deceased formal or unnecessary party, and (c) divisible decree or independent interests.

legal_question: Is a law included in the Ninth Schedule protected by Article 31B from invalidation on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges, fundamental rights in Part III (including the property guarantee carried over from the former constitutional order), and does that protection extend to earlier amendments and operate retrospectively?

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_law: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of an enactment or its provisions, or of action taken under it.
predicates.law_included_in_ninth_schedule: The enactment or the specific provision challenged has been included in the Ninth Schedule (protective schedule), including by listing the principal Act by title with amendments made before listing, and whether the inclusion came before or after any judgment or challenge.
predicates.challenge_based_on_part_three_rights: The challenge alleges inconsistency with, or taking away or abridgment of, rights in Part III (for example Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31, or the second proviso to Article 31A(1)), including a right derived from the former Section 299 property guarantee carried into Part III.
predicates.challenge_barred_by_article_31b_protecti: The challenge cannot invalidate the law, which is not void and is not deemed ever to have been void on the asserted Part III ground.

definition: A law or provision placed in the Ninth Schedule is protected by Article 31B from invalidation on the ground that it violates Part III rights. This applies to pre-constitutional and post-constitutional laws, to earlier amendments of a listed Act, and retrospectively even where a court had already held the provisions invalid, so the Court rejects the challenge without deciding its merits.
exceptions_or_limits: Protection does not reach grounds other than Part III inconsistency; legislative competence remains open to review.
For additions made after 24 April 1973, protection depends on the amending Act not damaging or destroying the basic structure (Waman Rao); on the facts of 818638_2 this did not change the result.
An amending Act that is not itself in the Schedule must rely on other protection such as Article 31A.
A law with no Ninth Schedule protection remains open to challenge, as in the distinction drawn from N.B. Jeejeebhoy.

Pre-constitutional laws not in the Schedule remain subject to Article 13(1) review for inconsistency with fundamental rights. That review operates prospectively and does not revive rights extinguished before the Constitution (49064693_4, 618203_3, 944747_2).

outlier_members.reason: Concerns Article 13(1) review of a pre-constitutional law not shown to be in the Ninth Schedule; it holds the law remains reviewable, not that it is protected.
Concerns non-retrospectivity of fundamental rights for a valid pre-constitutional scheme; it does not involve Article 31B or the Ninth Schedule.

common_material_facts: Land-reform, land-ceiling, tenancy or estate-abolition laws included in the Ninth Schedule
Challenges under Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31 or 31A
Inclusion in the Schedule sometimes came after a High Court judgment or after the challenged action or amendment
Pre-constitutional acquisition laws challenged on the Section 299 Government of India Act 1935 property guarantee
statutes_and_provisions: Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule
Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31, 31A (including its second proviso)
Article 13(1) and 13(2), Article 368, Article 372
Section 299(2) Government of India Act 1935
Constitution (First, Fourth and Seventeenth) Amendment Acts
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About 23 of 25 members hold the Article 31B immunity defeats the Part III challenge, usually without reaching the merits. The other two (49064693_4, 944747_2) are pre-constitutional-law cases outside the schedule and are treated as outliers.
variations: Protection applied retrospectively after a contrary court judgment (1085960_1, 417020_6, 83318_1, 818638_2)
Extension to the former Section 299 property guarantee (112183713_1, 1854392_1, 594226_1, 83318_1)
Extension to amendments made before the parent Act was listed (1913480_1, 418360_1)
The prospective effect of the Golaknath ruling did not unsettle earlier schedule protection (1070043_1, 120358_3)
Dual protection under Articles 31A and 31B (1614622_2)
Post-1973 additions are subject to the basic-structure test (818638_2)
Some members decide only the schedule point and leave other grounds undecided (1752505_9, 596010_3)

legal_question: Can a court decide an issue or grant relief on a ground that was not specifically pleaded or framed as an issue, where the parties understood the matter was in dispute, had an opportunity to lead evidence on it, and suffered no prejudice or surprise?

rule.if: civil_or_quasi_civil_proceeding and matter_not_specifically_pleaded_or_framed_as_issue and (parties_knew_matter_was_in_issue or necessary_facts_on_record) and (evidence_led_or_opportunity_to_present_evidence_or_fully_argued_without_objection) and no_prejudice_or_surprise_to_opposing_party

predicates.civil_or_quasi_civil_proceeding: The matter is a civil suit, appeal, rent or eviction proceeding, or writ proceeding in which pleadings and issues ordinarily define the case.
predicates.matter_not_specifically_pleaded_or_frame: The ground, plea or issue the court is asked to decide was omitted from the pleadings, vaguely or incompletely pleaded, or not framed as a separate issue.
predicates.parties_knew_matter_was_in_issue: Both sides understood, during the trial or hearing, that the matter was disputed and part of the case to be met.
predicates.necessary_facts_on_record: The facts needed to decide the matter are already before the court.
predicates.evidence_led_or_opportunity_to_present_e: The parties led evidence on the matter, or had a real opportunity to do so, or the matter was fully argued without objection.
predicates.no_prejudice_or_surprise_to_opposing_par: The opposing party was not taken by surprise, was not denied an opportunity to meet the point, and suffered no prejudice or injustice.
predicates.court_may_decide_matter_despite_pleading: The omission or deficiency is treated as a curable irregularity, so the court may decide the issue or grant relief on it, and the trial is not vitiated and no remand is required.

definition: Relief should ordinarily rest on the pleadings and framed issues. But a defect in pleading or in the framing of issues is not fatal where the substance of the matter was understood and litigated by both sides, evidence was led or could have been led, and no prejudice or surprise resulted.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not allow a materially different or new case that was never pleaded, was not in substance covered by the issues, and was not knowingly tried (the Trojan & Co. line). One member refused to consider unpleaded conditional-consent letters because the plaint was never amended and the matter was neither tried nor proved.
Prejudice or surprise to the opposing party defeats the rule, for example where the party was denied a chance to lead evidence or to meet the case.
Where a claim is not admitted or relied on by the opponent, mere notice from the pleadings is not enough; the matter must actually have been tried or fully argued.
An appellate court should remand only where a retrial is necessary or a party was denied the opportunity to lead necessary evidence. Remand is not routine and should not be used to fill lacunae.

outlier_members.reason: It states the converse limit: unpleaded material facts cannot support relief when the case was not tried and no amendment was made. It is the boundary of the rule rather than an application of it.
It concerns refusal of remand under Order XLI Rules 23, 23A and 24 where the record is sufficient. It does not involve an unpleaded issue.
It concerns refusal of remand in an appeal from a criminal quashing order where the record is sufficient. It does not involve an unpleaded issue.

common_material_facts: No specific pleading or framed issue on the point, or the pleading was vague.
Both parties knew the point was disputed and led evidence on it, or argued it fully without objection.
The opposing party did not object at trial and claimed no prejudice or surprise.

Recurring contexts include ejectment where tenancy failed but permissive possession was proved, benami and title disputes, rent-control cases on undisclosed other accommodation, specific performance cases on readiness and willingness, and res judicata and lis pendens pleas.
statutes_and_provisions: Order XIV Rule 1 CPC (framing of issues)
Order XLI Rules 23, 23A and 24 CPC (remand and final determination on appeal)
Section 16(c) Specific Relief Act, 1963
Section 14(1)(e) Delhi Rent Control Act (other suitable accommodation)
Article 226 and Article 136 of the Constitution
Section 65 Indian Contract Act
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About 22 of 25 members hold the pleading or issue defect curable and allow the court to decide the point or grant relief. One member (20473749_1) refuses relief on a wholly unpleaded and untried case. Two members (112876941_2, 47961553_3) concern remand and are tangential.
variations: The principal authorities cited include Bhagwati Prasad v. Chandramaul, Nagubai Ammal, Kunju Kesavan, Nedunuri Kameswaramma and Rani Chandra Kunwar. Some members cite no authority.
The proof of no prejudice differs: evidence actually led, opportunity to lead it, full argument without objection, or admission of the alternative case by the opponent.
Some members concern a missing framed issue, others a missing or vague pleading, and one a wording defect in the plaint (the term ouster).
Several members apply the principle to decline remand and let the appellate court decide on the existing record.

legal_question: When is a landlord seeking possession of let premises required to give a separate notice terminating the tenancy (under s.106 of the Transfer of Property Act or the lease), and when is that notice dispensed with because the lease has already ended or a special statutory eviction regime applies?

rule.if: eviction_proceeding and not specific_notice_required_by_rent_statute and not statute_merely_adds_restrictions_preserving_contractual_notice and (lease_determined_by_efflux_of_time_without_lessor_assent_to_holding_over or (statutory_eviction_ground_established and statute_provides_complete_special_eviction_procedure) or public_premises_special_regime_applies)

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The landlord or lessor is seeking possession or ejectment of the occupant through a suit or statutory application.
predicates.specific_notice_required_by_rent_statute: The applicable rent or eviction statute itself prescribes a notice that must be given before eviction.
predicates.statute_merely_adds_restrictions_preserv: The statute only restricts the landlord's right to evict, adding to the landlord's burden without displacing contractual rights, so a notice requirement in the lease still applies.
predicates.lease_determined_by_efflux_of_time_witho: A fixed-term lease has expired by lapse of its term, and the lessor did not expressly or impliedly assent to the occupant's continued possession.
predicates.statutory_eviction_ground_established: The landlord has proved a ground for eviction that the rent-control statute itself recognises.
predicates.statute_provides_complete_special_evicti: The statute lays down a self-contained special procedure for eviction that displaces the ordinary procedure under general property law.
predicates.public_premises_special_regime_applies: The premises are covered by special public-premises eviction legislation that has its own notice procedure and prevails over the general law.
predicates.separate_termination_notice_not_required: The landlord need not give a separate notice to quit or terminate the tenancy under the general property law or the lease before obtaining eviction.

definition: A separate notice terminating the tenancy is not needed where the lease has already ended by efflux of time without the lessor's assent to holding over, where a statutory eviction ground is proved under a complete special eviction code, or where special public-premises law governs. It is still needed where the rent statute itself requires notice, or where the statute only restricts eviction and leaves a contractual notice clause intact, or where the contractual tenancy is still subsisting and has not been validly terminated.
exceptions_or_limits: A notice that the rent-control statute itself prescribes must still be given.

Where the statute only adds restrictions on eviction (for example the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, as construed), a contractual notice requirement in the lease is not displaced and non-compliance defeats the suit.

A landlord cannot treat a tenant as a statutory tenant, so as to dispense with notice, unless the contractual tenancy has first been validly terminated by notice or another mode under s.111 of the Transfer of Property Act.
Where a notice is dispensed with because the lease has expired, the lessor must not have assented to the occupant's continued possession, since holding over with assent requires a fresh termination.
For a forfeiture under a lease made before the amended written-notice requirement took effect, filing the suit sufficed to show the lessor's intention, so no prior written notice was needed.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns whether written consent to sublet survives the end of the contractual term, not notice to terminate.
Concerns the timing of subletting relative to the commencement or retrospective extension of a rent-control statute.
Concerns the tenant-by-sufferance status and the s.4B protection under the Bombay Tenancy Act, not a notice requirement.
Concerns whether a pre-statute subletting that continues supports eviction.
Concerns whether a statutory tenant can sublet and whether the subtenant gets a direct tenancy.
Concerns the transitional enforcement of a permission under a successor rent-control law.
Concerns the saving of a subletting ground on repeal of a rent-control Act.
Concerns when a lawful subtenant becomes the landlord's direct tenant under the Bombay Act.
Concerns the relationship between contractual subletting authority and a statutory validation provision.
Concerns whether a subletting made with written consent becomes unauthorised after the contractual tenancy ends.
Concerns lawful possession for cinema licensing, not notice before eviction.
Concerns the saving of accrued eviction rights on repeal of a rent-control law; only a side point touches notice.
Concerns a procedural bar on raising an untried claim on appeal.

common_material_facts: A landlord seeks eviction under a rent-control or special statute, or by a general-law suit, and the tenant objects that no notice to quit or terminating notice was given.
The lease has expired by efflux of time, or the tenant is a statutory tenant after the contractual term.
The statute provides eviction grounds and a special procedure.
statutes_and_provisions: Transfer of Property Act 1882, ss.106, 107, 111 (including 111(a), 111(g), 111(h)) and 116

Rent-control statutes with their own eviction grounds and procedure, including the Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act 1960 (s.10), the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act 1960 (s.10(2)(ii)(a)), the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act (s.3) and the Saurashtra Rent Control Act 1951 (ss.13(1)(e) and 15)
Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act 1949, s.3
Public-premises eviction legislation
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About 10 of 12 covered members hold that no separate notice is required: the lease had expired, a statutory ground was proved under a complete code, or special law governed. About 2 hold that notice or valid termination was still required: the contractual notice clause under the Calcutta Thika Act, and the unterminated contractual tenancy where statutory-tenant status was claimed.
variations: Some members rest on expiry of the lease by efflux of time, others on the statute being a complete code, and others on the special nature of the premises.
The courts split on whether a rent statute displaces contractual notice clauses: the U.P. Act did, while the Calcutta Thika Act did not.
One member holds that filing the suit itself operates as notice to quit.
One member treats the pre-amendment forfeiture rule, under which suit filing sufficed as an expression of intention.
