predicates.compensation_not_illusory: The compensation is a real, positive amount and is not nominal, arbitrary, or confiscatory.
predicates.compensation_challenge_fails_and_adequac: The challenge to the law on compensation grounds fails, and the court will not examine whether the amount is adequate.

definition: Where an acquisition law is protected by a constitutional saving provision, or where it specifies relevant, non-arbitrary principles tied to the property's value near acquisition and the compensation is not illusory, a compensation challenge fails and adequacy is not justiciable. Courts review only whether the compensation is illusory or the principles are irrelevant to the property or its value, and a law whose principles are irrelevant or illusory, or which gives no adequate standard, is invalid.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the law is not protected, the court may examine whether the principles are irrelevant to the property or its value at or about acquisition, or whether the compensation is illusory. A law failing that test is invalid (machinery valuation at historical cost or tax written-down value; omission of goodwill and unit valuation for a going concern; no standard for cash or substitute property).

Protection applies only where its specific conditions are met, such as a pending bill reserved for and assented to by the President, a pre-Constitution law certified within the allowed period, or agrarian-reform legislation.
Inadequate compensation is distinct from illusory or no compensation; a positive, though substantially lower, amount is not illusory.

One member holds that the adequacy of the principles is justiciable under the earlier text of Article 31(2) because the compensation must be a just equivalent. Another reads the amended Article 31(2) as barring review for inadequacy but still allowing review of illusory compensation or irrelevant principles.
Colourable legislation concerns legislative competence and does not support a challenge to the amount of compensation.

outlier_members.reason: Upholds a lease-determination law on legislative competence under Entry 18 and compliance with Article 31(2). Compensation adequacy was not contested, so it does not address the reviewability of adequacy.

Concerns whether prior government approval of an acquisition award has adequate guiding standards under the Land Acquisition Act. It is an excessive-delegation point, not a compensation-validity challenge.

common_material_facts: Challenges to acquisition, estate-abolition or nationalisation laws alleging inadequate or illusory compensation.
Laws protected by the pending-bill and presidential-assent clause, the agrarian-reform saving article, the Ninth Schedule article, or pre-Constitution certification.
Statutory valuation formulae (net income or net assets, market value at a fixed date, asset-minus-liability valuation of undertakings).
Machinery valued at historical cost or tax written-down value.
Compensation providing a positive amount or a market-value floor, with a court reference or appeal available.
statutes_and_provisions: Constitution Article 31(2), as it stood originally and as amended by the Fourth Amendment
Article 31(4) and 31(6)
Articles 31-A and 31-B and the Ninth Schedule
Article 14
Entry 42 of List III and Entry 18 of List II
Section 299 of the Government of India Act, 1935
Land Acquisition Act, 1894, sections 23-26
Twenty-fifth Amendment
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Most members (about 15 of 22) reject the compensation challenge, either because a saving provision bars it (about 8) or because the principles are relevant and the compensation is not illusory (about 7). Three members (the machinery valuation cases, the undertaking valuation case and the no-standard case) strike the law down because the principles were irrelevant or inadequate. Two others are outliers on other points.
variations: Some members rest on a threshold constitutional bar and never reach the merits; others review the principles for relevance.

Reasoning differs between the pre-Fourth Amendment view (compensation as a just equivalent, with principles reviewable) and the post-amendment view (adequacy non-justiciable, but illusory or irrelevant principles reviewable).
A challenged law may be saved by judicial-review safeguards in its own machinery, such as an inquiry, civil-court appeals or a market-value floor.
The Twenty-fifth Amendment is read down so that the amount must be non-arbitrary and rationally related to the property.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) cases barred by a constitutional saving provision (1105428_4, 112183713_2, 217259_5, 45759_3, 527065_3, 624810_1, 629631_2); (b) cases reviewing the relevance of valuation principles, which uphold or strike down the law (1293816_3, 1634289_2, 35092845_1, 602096_1, 513801_7, 673450_2, 451064_2, 1890860_3, 257876_3, 1983545_2, 815666_2, 909940_4, 86636408_2); and (c) the outliers on competence and delegation (147362898_6, 1637345_2).

legal_question: When does one co-sharer, co-heir or co-owner's exclusive possession of jointly held property become adverse to the other co-sharers so as to oust them and extinguish their title or share, and on whom does the burden of proving this lie?

rule.if: co_sharer_adverse_possession_claim and possession_by_one_co_sharer and not (hostile_title_openly_asserted_and_denial_known_to_other_co_sharer and exclusive_possession_and_enjoyment_to_their_exclusion and hostile_possession_continued_for_statutory_period)

predicates.co_sharer_adverse_possession_claim: One co-sharer, co-heir, co-owner or coparcener pleads ouster or title by adverse possession against another co-sharer of the same property.
predicates.possession_by_one_co_sharer: The property is in the possession of one co-sharer, which in law is ordinarily possession on behalf of all co-sharers.
predicates.hostile_title_openly_asserted_and_denial: The possessing co-sharer clearly and unequivocally denied the other co-sharers' title by an open assertion of hostile or exclusive title, and that denial was brought to the other co-sharers' knowledge.
predicates.exclusive_possession_and_enjoyment_to_th: The possessing co-sharer held and enjoyed the property exclusively, with the other co-sharers excluded, including from participation in income or profits.
predicates.hostile_possession_continued_for_statuto: The hostile and exclusive possession, from an identifiable point at which it became adverse, continued uninterrupted for the full limitation period.
predicates.ouster_not_established_and_other_co_shar: The claimant fails to prove ouster or adverse possession, and the other co-sharers' title or share is not extinguished or barred.

definition: Possession by one co-sharer is presumed to be possession for all. It becomes adverse to the others only if the possessor proves an open, unequivocal assertion of hostile title brought to the others' knowledge, together with exclusive possession and enjoyment for the full statutory period. Long or sole possession, non-participation in profits, mutation, or a failure to demand a share does not suffice, and the burden lies on the party claiming ouster.
exceptions_or_limits: Where ouster is clearly proved, with an open hostile denial known to the other co-sharer, exclusive possession, and the full statutory period, title by adverse possession is perfected against the co-sharer (1183383_2).

Once adverse possession has matured through ouster, a mere later assertion of joint title by the dispossessed co-sharer does not interrupt it unless he effectively re-enters or resumes possession, the possessor acknowledges his title, or exclusive possession ends (227646_2). Conversely, acts of possession by the title holder during the period can break the continuity or exclusiveness of the claimed adverse possession (1794534_2).

Adverse possession must be properly pleaded, including when and how possession became hostile. A vague plea fails (1419648_2, 304121_2, 408373_5). A claimant who earlier asserted co-ownership must show when possession turned hostile.
Limitation does not run before the claimant takes actual possession under a hostile claim. Prior possession by a receiver cannot be counted (1498182_3).
Possession under an arrangement between co-sharers, or permissive possession, is not adverse (1489900_3, 197296101_1).
A purchaser from a co-sharer steps into the vendor's shoes, and a co-sharer who cannot prove ouster cannot obtain an injunction against the purchaser (188937220_2).

outlier_members.reason: Mainly a procedural limitation point: a plea abandoned at an intermediate appeal cannot be re-agitated, and the suit was within time. It also notes that adverse possession must be pleaded with when it began, so it overlaps only partly with the co-sharer ouster rule.

common_material_facts: Co-heirs or co-sharers in inherited or joint property, with one in sole possession and managing or enjoying it
Reliance on mutation, municipal or revenue records, tax payment, or long possession as proof of ouster
Claimant had received some income, maintenance or a share, or had not demanded a share, or lived elsewhere
Adverse possession pleaded without stating when possession became hostile
Partition or injunction suits where limitation by adverse possession is raised as a defence
statutes_and_provisions: Article 65 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963 (cited in 477485_2)
Limitation Act, 1963, referred to generally (1310876_1)

Most members cite no statutory provision and rely on case law: P. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy, Mohammad Baqar v. Naim-un-Nisa Bibi, Vidya Devi v. Prem Prakash, T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa, Karbalai Begum v. Mohd. Sayeed
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 19 of 22 members, ouster or adverse possession fails and the other co-sharer's title or share survives. Only 1183383_2 and 227646_2 uphold adverse possession on proved ouster. 1498182_1 states the test for ouster without deciding whether it was met, and 1794534_2 holds that adverse possession was interrupted.
variations: Some members stress pleading and burden defects (1419648_2, 304121_2, 408373_5). Others turn on the factual absence of a known hostile denial.
Mutation is treated as insufficient unless it clearly denies the other's title (1183383_2, 197296101_1, 477485_2).
Participation in income or payment of maintenance negates ouster (1266860_3, 519788_1, 3074_1).
3074_1 treats the possessing co-sharer as a constructive trustee.
1498182_3 turns on insufficient duration of actual possession, excluding the receiver's earlier period.
227646_2 and 1794534_2 concern interruption of already-claimed adverse possession.
8882900_4 holds that a plea of ouster against one co-owner only, while recognising other co-owners, fails.
1458435_4 notes the absence of any adverse possession plea.

legal_question: When, and subject to what safeguards, may a court (especially an appellate or revisional court) take account of events or changes in law that occur after the litigation began or after the decision under review, and mould or deny relief accordingly?

predicates.proceeding_pending_before_court_includin: The litigation is still pending before the court (trial, first appeal, revision, review or special leave appeal), and the decision under review has not become final.
predicates.subsequent_event_or_change_in_law_occurr: A factual event or a legislative or legal change occurred after the proceeding began or after the decision under review.
predicates.subsequent_event_material_to_entitlement: The event or change materially bears on whether the party is entitled to relief, makes the original relief inappropriate, or affects how relief should be shaped.
predicates.subsequent_event_brought_to_court_prompt: The event was brought to the court's attention diligently and by a procedurally proper route, such as an affidavit, an application for additional evidence, an amendment of pleadings or a commissioner's report.
predicates.opposing_party_has_fair_opportunity_to_r: The other side had notice of the event and a real opportunity to answer or contest it, including by additional pleadings or evidence where needed.
predicates.court_may_take_cautious_cognizance_of_su: The court may, and in appropriate cases must, take account of the subsequent event and grant, deny or adjust relief in light of it.

definition: Although rights are ordinarily judged as at the start of litigation, a court, including an appellate or revisional court, may cautiously consider material subsequent events or changes in law that bear on entitlement to relief or its moulding. It may do so where the event is promptly and properly brought before it and the opposing side has a fair chance to respond. Where the event is a disputed fact, it should ordinarily be introduced by amendment, and an amended plea cannot be decided without giving the other side a chance to contest it.
exceptions_or_limits: The power is exercised cautiously and is not available where the event is raised belatedly or without proper procedure, causes unfair surprise, or is used to delay or harass.
A disputed factual event that is not pleaded, or that is raised only in an affidavit without seeking amendment or any change in relief, will not be considered to impair the decree.
An amendment allowed on account of a subsequent event or change in law cannot be given effect without giving the opposing party an opportunity to file a response and contest the amended plea.

The event must actually be material; it should make the original relief inappropriate, shorten litigation, or be necessary for complete justice. Events that do not undermine the established claim do not defeat it.
A commissioner's report may establish the existing condition of premises but not who caused it.
Where the law has changed before decision, the court applies the current law, and hearing arguments on its effect on an existing issue does not raise a new question.
Contrary legal or equitable circumstances may displace the power.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the procedural requirement that a permitted amendment must be contested before it is decided, not the court's power to consider subsequent events. It is related only as a fairness safeguard and is covered in the limits.

common_material_facts: A rent-control or eviction proceeding was pending in appeal, revision or special leave when something changed.
The change was a fact (death, vacancy, acquisition of other premises, building reaching an age threshold, grant of probate, damage to premises) or an amendment or repeal of legislation.
The event was raised by affidavit, application, amendment or commissioner's report, and the other side was or was not given a chance to answer.
The decision under review was not yet final.
statutes_and_provisions: Order 41 Rule 27 CPC
Order 6 Rule 17 CPC
Section 96 CPC
Section 15(5) East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act
Section 10(3)(iii) Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960
Article 136 of the Constitution
Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. Motor & General Traders
Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 17 of 21 members, the court held that it could or must consider the subsequent event or change in law and mould relief, subject to fairness. In about 3 (1003235_3, 315007_2, 343975_3) the subsequent event was found not to defeat the claim, or not considered for want of proper procedure, or the amended plea was not enforced for lack of opportunity to respond.
variations: Some members concern changes in law, applied as the current law (1201636_6, 1550631_3, 804743_4, 1567371_2), while others concern factual events.
Some allow amendment of pleadings in appeal to raise a new plea or a fresh cause of action (1719442_2, 1966491_1, 1567371_2).
Procedural vehicles differ: affidavit, additional evidence, local commissioner, public documents, or amendment.
The effect of the event varies: it may defeat the claim (1465665_1, 498278_2, 1800832_1), reinforce it (1003235_3), or only mould the relief (42266022_2, 1732740_2).
Some members state the power as discretionary ('may') and others as obligatory in appropriate cases ('must').

legal_question: Does a limited or restricted interest held by a Hindu woman in property that she possessed when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 commenced, and that rests on a pre-existing right such as maintenance, become absolute ownership under Section 14(1) rather than remaining restricted under Section 14(2)?

predicates.female_hindu_possessed_property_when_suc: The Hindu woman possessed the property (actually or constructively) when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force, or was placed in possession of it under a later grant in lieu of maintenance.
predicates.property_held_under_preexisting_right_in: The woman's interest rests on a right that existed before the instrument, decree, will, award or compromise, such as a right to maintenance, a Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act interest, or a share in joint property. Property allotted in lieu of or in satisfaction of that right qualifies.
predicates.grant_created_new_title_for_first_time_w: The instrument, decree, will, award or gift gave the woman a restricted estate as a fresh, independent title, with no pre-existing right behind it (the Section 14(2) exception).
predicates.limited_interest_enlarged_into_absolute_: The woman's limited or restricted interest became full and absolute ownership under Section 14(1). Restrictions on alienation and reversionary or remainder clauses in the instrument do not defeat this, and she may alienate or bequeath the property.

definition: Where a Hindu woman possessed property when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 took effect and held it under a pre-existing right (especially a right to maintenance), Section 14(1) and its Explanation enlarge her limited interest into absolute ownership. Section 14(2) applies only to a restricted grant made for the first time without any pre-existing right, so restrictions in the instrument or any remainder do not prevail.
exceptions_or_limits: Section 14(2) preserves the restriction where the instrument, decree, will or award creates a new and independent title for the first time without a pre-existing right.
Enlargement needs some existing ownership interest or lawful vestige of title; mere possession without title is not enough.
Enlargement extends only to the property the woman actually held or possessed under the pre-existing right (for example the first floor only, not the whole house).
Where a document defers absolute enjoyment until a future event, the document's own terms govern, and an interest that never vested is not enlarged (the case of a daughter who died before the widow).
A woman who has validly given up her rights, for example by compromise, cannot claim the enlarged interest in what she surrendered.
Where the grant is in lieu of maintenance, an express statement of that purpose is not required; the purpose may be inferred from the circumstances.

outlier_members.reason: This turns on construction of a family settlement and when an absolute interest vested in a daughter who died before the widow. It does not apply Section 14(1) enlargement of a woman's limited estate.

This concerns recording a widow as absolute owner and bhumidar under the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act and the Hindu Succession Act. It states no pre-existing-right analysis and cites no authority, so it is only loosely related.

common_material_facts: A widow or other Hindu woman held property under a will, compromise decree, partition award or family settlement that gave her a limited or life interest, often with a bar on alienation and a reversion or remainder.
The property was given in lieu of or in recognition of a pre-existing right to maintenance, or of a statutory share under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937.
She was in possession when the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force, or was placed in possession under a later compromise.
She sold, gifted, leased or bequeathed the property, and reversioners or remaindermen challenged her authority.
statutes_and_provisions: Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 14(1) and its Explanation
Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 14(2)
Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 30 (testamentary disposition)
Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, Section 3
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Sections 19(1)(a), 21(vi), 22(2)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 19 of 21 members the limited interest was held enlarged into absolute ownership under Section 14(1), Section 14(2) was held inapplicable, and the reversioner's or remainderman's claim failed. The usual authority is V. Tulasamma v. V. Sesha Reddi. The two outliers decide other points.
variations: The source of the pre-existing right varies: maintenance from the husband or joint family, a Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act interest, a widowed daughter's maintenance against her father's estate, or a right of residence.
The instrument varies: will, compromise decree, partition award, family settlement, execution compromise or an informal entrustment by the husband.
Timing varies: most grants pre-date the 1956 Act, but one compromise post-dated it and was still held to confer absolute ownership on a woman placed in possession.
Possession varies: actual, constructive, or a retained right to possession.
One member limited the enlargement to the portion actually held, and one held that a surrender of rights by compromise defeated her claim to those rights.
In some members the Court treated the instrument as merely recognising an existing right, so Section 14(2) was not reached.

split_suggestion: Keep the 19 Section 14(1) enlargement members together. Remove 251681_1 (construction of a family settlement and vesting of an interest) and 579492_1 (recording a widow as bhumidar under the land-reform and succession laws) as separate issues.

legal_question: When is a preliminary land-acquisition notification (and the related declaration) sufficient, or invalid for vagueness or inadequate notice? Specifically, does it adequately indicate the public purpose and identify the land so that interested persons can understand the proposal and object, without having to state further matters such as the executing instrumentality or the company route, or to give individual notice?

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and public_purpose_adequately_indicated and land_reasonably_identifiable and statutory_publication_made and no_substantial_prejudice_to_objectors

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges a land-acquisition notification, declaration or proceeding on the ground of vagueness, insufficient description or inadequate notice.
predicates.public_purpose_adequately_indicated: The notification states the public purpose, or the purpose can be gathered from the statute and proceedings, in terms understandable in context (for example, naming the scheme or project). Any omission is limited to details such as the executing instrumentality, the government-or-company route, or the methods of execution.
predicates.land_reasonably_identifiable: The notification, by its own description or by a referenced plan or details available for inspection, identifies the land proposed to be acquired well enough for owners to know their land is affected.
predicates.statutory_publication_made: The publication and public notice required by the statute (Gazette and local public notice) were given, and no rule requires special individual notice.
predicates.no_substantial_prejudice_to_objectors: The objectors understood the proposal and could object, or did object in detail, and show no real prejudice from the wording or the absence of individual notice.
predicates.notification_sufficient_and_not_invalid_: The notification and the proceedings following it are not invalid on the ground of vagueness, insufficient description or lack of individual notice.

definition: A land-acquisition notification is valid if it states or makes ascertainable an understandable public purpose, identifies the land with reasonable precision (including through an available plan), and the required public notice was given. It is not invalidated by omitting the executing instrumentality, the company route or individual notice, or by a theoretical ambiguity that caused no substantial prejudice to objectors.
exceptions_or_limits: The notification is invalid or inadequate if the purpose is so vague that it does not convey what the land will be used for (for example, a bare 'residential' purpose with no beneficiaries or particulars).
The notification is inadequate if the land cannot be located from the notice and no plan is available, and the objection inquiry has not been dispensed with.

Sufficiency is judged on the facts and context. The court asks whether objectors were really prejudiced, and a complaint about description raised only outside the statutory objection period may be rejected.

The omission of an express public-purpose statement is excused only where the purpose can be gathered from the statute and proceedings, as in company acquisitions where the statutory inquiry and government satisfaction are still to follow.
A purely nominal government contribution, or a stated public purpose, does not itself cure a colourable exercise of power.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns whether failure to serve the later notice inviting compensation claims invalidates the award (directory versus mandatory), not the sufficiency of the preliminary notification.
Concerns curable irregularity in service of notices under ss. 9 and 10 and the validity of the award, not the description of purpose or land in the s. 4 notification.
Mainly concerns colourable exercise of power (nominal government contribution and consideration of the objections report). The land-description point is incidental.
Concerns which notice fixes the date for valuing compensation when an earlier notice was defective, not the validity of a notification.
An income-tax exemption case on whether charitable objects are too vague. It is unrelated to land acquisition.

common_material_facts: The notification stated a public purpose, often by naming the scheme or project (housing scheme, diamond park, industrial area, fire station, temple access).
The land was identified by survey numbers or area, or by reference to a plan available for inspection.
Objectors filed detailed objections or otherwise understood the proposal, and showed no prejudice.
The Gazette and local public notice were given, but no individual notice was sent to some interested persons.
The notification omitted the executing instrumentality or whether the land would pass to a company.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act 1894, ss. 4(1), 4(2), 5A, 6, 17(4)
Land Acquisition Act 1894, ss. 39–41 and s. 3 (company acquisitions and the meaning of public purpose)
Rule 30-B of the Gujarat Land Acquisition Rules, and rules under s. 55
Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act 1966, s. 28
National Highways Act 1956, ss. 3A and 3C
U.P. Land Acquisition (Rehabilitation of Refugees) Act 1948, s. 7(1)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 14 of the 16 covered members the notification was upheld against the vagueness or inadequate-notice challenge. Two members (766732_2 on a vague purpose, 1141333_1 on an unidentifiable land description) found the notification inadequate.
variations: Some members concern the purpose description (1045847_3, 348205_6, 588752_1, 766732_2). Others concern identification of the land (1141333_1, 1653066_3, 98737584_2). Others concern whether individual notice was required (1451241_5, 1708491_1).
Some members hold that omitting the instrumentality or company route is immaterial (1003330_4, 1927389_2, 490012_6).
463201_1 excuses even the lack of an express public-purpose statement in a company acquisition.
Courts rely on the objectors' own conduct (detailed objections, acknowledging the purpose, late complaints) to show absence of prejudice, in several members.
Where vagueness was upheld, the defect was that owners could not tell what the land was for or whether their land was affected.

split_suggestion: Keep the core group on the sufficiency of s. 4 notifications. Within it, one could separate (a) purpose-description cases, (b) land-identification cases, and (c) individual-notice and omitted-instrumentality cases. Move the post-notification notice and award cases (287512_1, 546084_5) to a separate cluster, and the remaining outliers 745737_1 (colourable exercise), 858290_1 (valuation date) and 885614_2 (income tax) to their own clusters.

legal_question: When a landlord sues for eviction on a ground created by rent-control legislation, can the tenant rely on general property-law protections, such as relief against forfeiture or a default right to sublet, to defeat or soften the statutory eviction regime?

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and eviction_sought_on_statutory_ground and tenant_invokes_general_property_law_protection and not rent_statute_itself_provides_the_relief

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The landlord seeks eviction of a tenant in a proceeding governed by a rent-control or tenancy statute.
predicates.eviction_sought_on_statutory_ground: The landlord relies on a ground for eviction created by the rent-control statute, such as rent default or unauthorised subletting. The landlord does not rely on forfeiture of the lease under an express re-entry condition.
predicates.tenant_invokes_general_property_law_prot: The tenant relies on a protection from general property law, such as relief against forfeiture under section 114 of the Transfer of Property Act or the default right to sublet under section 108(j), to resist eviction.
predicates.rent_statute_itself_provides_the_relief: The rent-control statute itself contains a provision granting the relief or protection claimed, or incorporates it in modified form, and the tenant satisfies that provision.
predicates.general_property_law_protection_unavaila: The tenant cannot claim the general property-law protection. The case is decided only under the conditions and relief the rent-control statute provides.

definition: Where eviction is sought on a ground created by rent-control legislation, the statute is a self-contained regime. A statutory ground such as rent default does not forfeit the lease or alter the nature of the tenancy, so the tenant cannot add relief against forfeiture or a default right to sublet. The tenant gets only the relief the statute itself gives.
exceptions_or_limits: The tenant can still claim any relief the rent-control statute itself provides, for example a statutory provision allowing the tenant to remedy a breach, or the statutory payment conditions that incorporate the equity of section 114.

Relief against forfeiture under the Transfer of Property Act remains a question only where the suit is actually based on forfeiture of the lease under an express re-entry condition, rather than on a statutory ground.
A lease grant of a subletting right, or the landlord's consent, defeats the unauthorised-subletting ground.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the mandatory eviction decree under section 12(3)(a) of the Bombay Act and the relationship between clauses (a) and (b). It is adjacent to the group but does not decide displacement of general property law.

Concerns whether eviction is mandatory under the Delhi rent-control provisos once a statutory ground is established and no relief is available. This is a different point from displacement of general property law.
Subtenant's acquisition of direct tenancy under the West Bengal Act, and the effect of the savings clause on a pending suit. It belongs to the subtenant-protection group.
A statutory tenant cannot confer direct-tenancy rights on a subtenant. It belongs to the subtenant-protection group.
A subtenant's direct-tenancy rights are not defeated by a lease prohibition on subletting. It belongs to the subtenant-protection group.
Subtenant protection depends on the subletting predating a statutory cutoff. It belongs to the subtenant-protection group.
Subtenant protection depends on the subletting predating a statutory cutoff. It belongs to the subtenant-protection group.
A subtenancy created before the rent-control law came into force is not illegal subletting. It belongs to the subtenant-protection group.
A subtenant is bound by an eviction decree unless statutory protection applies. It belongs to the subtenant-protection group.
Statutory protection of a tenant against its own landlord does not bar eviction by an upstream landlord. It belongs to the subtenant-protection group.
A subtenant cannot be evicted alone when the head tenant is not ordered evicted. It belongs to the subtenant-protection group.
Statutory purchase of land by a tenant under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act and the effect of a pending eviction application. It belongs to a tenancy-purchase group.
Maintainability of eviction applications filed after the statutory purchase date under the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act. It belongs to the tenancy-purchase group.
Postponed statutory purchase where an eviction order has become final. It belongs to the tenancy-purchase group.
A procedural point on the effect of abandoning one ground in an eviction petition covering the entire premises. It is unrelated to the other members.

common_material_facts: The landlord sues for eviction under a state rent-control Act, usually for arrears of rent after a demand notice.
The tenant invokes section 114 (or sections 111(g) or 108(j)) of the Transfer of Property Act, often after paying or tendering arrears during the suit.
The suit rests on the statutory default or subletting ground, not on an express re-entry clause in the lease.
statutes_and_provisions: Transfer of Property Act, 1882: sections 106, 108(j), 111(g), 114
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947: sections 12(2), 12(3)(a), 12(3)(b)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1955: section 4(a)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act: section 3
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965: section 11(4)(i)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all six covered members, the general property-law protection is held unavailable or displaced and the case is decided under the rent statute. Five concern relief against forfeiture and one concerns the default right to sublet.
variations: Some members say the statutory ground never amounts to a forfeiture, so section 114 is not triggered. Others say section 114 is displaced or incorporated in modified form by the statute, so there is no double protection.
One member (969019_1) applies the displacement principle to the default right to sublet, not to forfeiture relief.
The statutory provisions differ across States.

split_suggestion: Split into four groups. (1) Rent-control statutory eviction versus general property law (forfeiture relief, default subletting right): 1028604_5, 1128683_3, 1128683_6, 1644282_2, 688127_2, 969019_1. 1128683_1 and 691833_2 sit with this group as 'mandatory eviction once the statutory ground is made out'. (2) Subtenant protection and direct-tenancy rights under rent statutes: 105509416_1, 123771_4, 707409_3, 1345779_2, 320208_2, 1663425_4, 311833_2, 260033_5, 1783260_2. (3) Statutory tenant purchase under the Bombay Tenancy Act: 1168625_1, 1168625_2, 1168625_3. (4) Procedural effect of abandoning a ground in an eviction petition: 809534_1.

legal_question: When the original document is not produced, on what conditions may secondary evidence of its contents be admitted, and what must the offering party show first?

rule.if: secondary_evidence_offered and original_not_produced and nonproduction_accounted_for_on_permitted_ground and factual_foundation_established and copy_shown_to_be_true_copy

predicates.secondary_evidence_offered: A party tenders a copy, certified copy, photocopy or similar secondary evidence to prove the contents of a document.
predicates.original_not_produced: The original document is not produced before the court.
predicates.nonproduction_accounted_for_on_permitted: The non-production of the original is explained by a ground the Evidence Act recognises, such as the opponent failing to produce it after notice, loss or destruction not caused by the offering party's default, or the original being held by a person who cannot be compelled to produce it.
predicates.factual_foundation_established: The offering party has laid a factual basis, by pleadings or evidence, for why the original is unavailable, for example by showing the search made, the custodian's evidence, or the notice given.
predicates.copy_shown_to_be_true_copy: The copy is a certified copy entitled to a presumption of correctness, or its correctness is otherwise proved or not disputed, so that it is a reliable reproduction of the original.
predicates.secondary_evidence_admissible: The court may receive the secondary evidence of the document's contents, subject to the document still being proved in accordance with law.

definition: Secondary evidence of a document is admissible only if the original is not produced, the non-production is accounted for on a ground the Evidence Act permits, a factual foundation is laid, and the copy is shown to be a true one. A bare copy, or a certified copy tendered without any explanation for the original's absence, is not enough. Where the foundation is incomplete or has not been examined, the party may be given the chance to lay it.
exceptions_or_limits: If the non-production of the original is unexplained or the loss is not satisfactorily proved, the secondary evidence is inadmissible (1462464_1, 516830_6, 799228_3, 993476_1).

An ordinary, uncertified copy needs proof of correctness. A certified copy does not by itself dispense with an explanation for the original's absence where the document is private (1599568_3, 993476_1).
Where an opponent holds the original and fails to produce it after notice, any secondary evidence is admissible even if a certified copy could also be given in evidence (1444483_1).
Where the original's availability has not been examined, the court should give the party an opportunity to lay the foundation rather than exclude the copy outright (1587936_3).
A separate application to lead secondary evidence is not required if the foundation is laid in the pleadings or evidence (9381542_2).
Admission of secondary evidence does not prove the document. Its genuineness and contents must still be established at trial (155718210_2, 42995449_2).

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the effect of allowing additional evidence under Order XLI Rule 27 CPC, which does not dispense with proof. It does not concern the conditions for secondary evidence.
Admission of a signature or document does not prove its contents, which is a separate probative-value question from secondary-evidence admissibility.
Permission to lead secondary evidence does not prove the document. This is the proof-versus-admission theme.
Admissibility is distinct from proof of contents, in the context of an unregistered agreement.
Identifying a signature is not an admission of execution of the document.
Admitting a signature is not admitting execution, which requires assent to terms understood by the signer (Registration Act).
Failure to file a replication is not an admission of facts pleaded in the written statement. This is a pleadings question.
Admission of secondary evidence does not prove the document. This is the proof-versus-admission theme.
Failure to produce rebuttal evidence is not an admission of a document or its contents. This is an admissions question.

common_material_facts: A party relies on a copy, photocopy or certified copy of an important instrument such as a will, sale deed, power of attorney or lease because the original is not produced.
The original is said to be lost, held by the opponent or an official custodian, or previously produced in other proceedings.
Notice to produce the original was given, or searches of custodian records were made.
The opponent denies execution or the correctness of the copy.
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Evidence Act 1872, s. 63 (kinds of secondary evidence)
Indian Evidence Act 1872, s. 64 (documents to be proved by primary evidence)
Indian Evidence Act 1872, s. 65(a), (c), (f) (cases in which secondary evidence is admissible)
Indian Evidence Act 1872, s. 66 (notice to produce)
Indian Evidence Act 1872, s. 79 (presumption of correctness of certified copies)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 12 covered members, about 7 admit or allow the party to lead secondary evidence: 1444483_1, 155718210_1, 1587936_3 (opportunity to lay the foundation), 42995449_1, 889011_1, 9381542_2 and 96039159_3. About 5 exclude it for lack of foundation or proof of loss: 1462464_1, 1599568_3, 516830_6, 799228_3 and 993476_1.
variations: The ground differs: opponent's failure to produce after notice (s. 65(a)), loss or destruction (s. 65(c)), or a certified copy permitted by law (s. 65(f)).
Some members treat the foundation as necessary and already satisfied. Others find it missing, and one directs that the party be given an opportunity to prove it.

The treatment of certified versus ordinary copies varies. Certified copies carry a presumption of correctness, but a certified copy of a private document still requires an explanation for the original's absence.
Several members add that admitting secondary evidence does not itself prove the document.

split_suggestion: Split into two clusters. (1) Conditions for admitting secondary evidence and the need for a foundation for non-production of the original (the 12 covered members). (2) Admission, admissibility or receipt of a document or signature does not prove its contents or execution, or amount to an admission (106296126_2, 1462464_2, 155718210_2, 156545202_3, 232698_3, 36451884_2, 366892_2, 42995449_2, 61939581_2).

legal_question: Does the acquittal of some co-accused, or the rejection of part of a witness's evidence, require the court to acquit the remaining accused or reject the rest of the evidence, where the evidence against the remaining accused is credible and can be separated from the rejected part?

rule.if: multi_accused_criminal_case and (some_coaccused_acquitted or part_of_witness_evidence_rejected) and evidence_against_remaining_accused_credible and evidence_against_remaining_accused_separable_or_independently_supported

predicates.multi_accused_criminal_case: Several persons were tried or appealed together for the same criminal occurrence, with the prosecution relying on common witnesses or common evidence.
predicates.some_coaccused_acquitted: One or more co-accused were acquitted, or given the benefit of doubt, in the same occurrence.
predicates.part_of_witness_evidence_rejected: The court declined to rely on a part of a witness's or approver's account, for example for want of corroboration, contradictions, or omitted names, without finding the whole account false.
predicates.evidence_against_remaining_accused_credi: The evidence against the remaining accused is cogent, consistent and accepted as reliable, for example eyewitness evidence with medical or other corroboration.
predicates.evidence_against_remaining_accused_separ: The reasons for the acquittal or rejection do not apply to the remaining accused, and truth can be separated from falsehood without reconstructing an entirely new case.
predicates.acquittal_or_partial_rejection_does_not_: The acquittal of co-accused or rejection of part of the evidence does not automatically require acquittal of the others or disbelief of the witnesses. Each accused's liability is decided on the evidence against that accused.

definition: The maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is a rule of caution, not a rule of law. Acquitting some accused, or rejecting part of a witness's evidence, does not automatically require acquitting the others. A court must assess the evidence against each accused separately and may convict where the credible evidence is separable or independently corroborated.
exceptions_or_limits: If truth and falsehood are so intermingled that they cannot be separated without reconstructing an entirely new case, the evidence must be discarded as a whole.
The remaining evidence may need closer scrutiny, and the court must be satisfied it is safe to rely on it.
Where the infirmities that led to the acquittal also affect the evidence against the remaining accused, they may be entitled to the same benefit.

Where individual participation or a shared object or common intention is not proved, an accused is acquitted even if others are convicted (the acquittals of some accused were retained in 1807108_1 and 833642_5).
Vicarious liability under Sections 34 or 149 IPC requires proof of its conditions.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns rejecting a self-defence account and upholding concurrent findings on eyewitness evidence, not the effect of acquittals of co-accused or partial rejection of testimony.
It concerns whether an identification parade is dispensable when witnesses knew the accused beforehand, which is a different evidentiary point.
It concerns the effect of defects in an identification parade on identification supported by direct observation, which is a different evidentiary point.
It concerns an unreliable declaration by an injured witness being unable to displace independent eyewitness evidence. It does not concern acquittal of co-accused.

common_material_facts: Several accused were tried for one occurrence, and some were acquitted or given the benefit of doubt while others were convicted.
The same eyewitnesses named both acquitted and convicted accused.
Acquittals rested on grounds specific to the acquitted accused, such as contradictions about their roles, lack of corroboration, doubtful identification, or names missing from a declaration.
The evidence against the convicted accused was corroborated by medical or other independent evidence.
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 34, 148, 149 and 302 of the Indian Penal Code
Section 114 illustration (b) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus
Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab [1957] SCR 953
Nisar Alli v. State of UP, AIR 1957 SC 366 and related cases cited in 29943_2 and 817642_2
Jainul Haque v. State of Bihar, AIR 1974 SC 45
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 15 of the 17 covered members, the Court held that the acquittal of some accused, or rejection of part of a witness's evidence, did not discredit the evidence against the others, and the convictions stood. In 1807108_1 and 833642_5 (appeals against acquittal), acquittals were reversed for accused whose participation was proved and retained for those not sufficiently linked.
variations: Some members apply the rule to ordinary eyewitnesses (the majority). Two apply it to an approver's uncorroborated segment (1199934_2, 67600325_2).
Some members rely on the falsus in uno maxim with precedents (29943_2, 817642_2). Others state the principle without citing authority.
1807108_1 and 833642_5 arise from appeals against acquittal and turn on proof of shared object or common intention.
295629_3 deals with defending an independent witness's presence and omitted names rather than acquittal as such.
1574135_1 states the general principle of individual liability, with Sections 34 and 149 as exceptions.

split_suggestion: The core group covers acquittal of co-accused not compelling acquittal of others, together with the approver-segment and witness-credibility variants. The four outliers on identification parades, self-defence and the injured witness's declaration (1426762_1, 144689_9, 1463693_5, 1807187_7) could form a separate cluster on evaluating eyewitness and identification evidence. The appeals against acquittal (1807108_1, 833642_5) could also be separated as a group on reversing acquittals for proven participants.

legal_question: When a purchaser under a sale agreement fails to pay or complete by the agreed time, or fails to plead and prove continuing readiness and willingness to perform, is specific performance of the agreement refused?

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and (purchaser_failed_essential_payment_or_completion_when_due or readiness_and_willingness_not_pleaded_or_proved) and not default_caused_or_excused_by_seller

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant seeks specific performance of an agreement, usually a sale of immovable property.
predicates.purchaser_failed_essential_payment_or_co: The purchaser did not pay the balance or an essential part payment, or did not complete the transaction, within the agreed period. Time was essential by express terms or surrounding circumstances, or the purchaser's conduct otherwise showed a failure to perform an essential term.
predicates.readiness_and_willingness_not_pleaded_or: The claimant did not aver readiness and willingness to perform their part, or failed to prove it continuously from the contract through the hearing. Examples are disclaiming the contract, seeking a refund, imposing unfounded conditions on payment, lacking funds, or giving no explanation for long delay.
predicates.default_caused_or_excused_by_seller: The seller caused the delay or default, or the parties varied or waived the obligation, or the seller insisted on performance in a manner the contract did not require.
predicates.specific_performance_denied: The court refuses the discretionary relief of specific performance, or treats the suit as lacking a cause of action.

definition: A purchaser who misses an essential payment or completion deadline, or who does not plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform, is not entitled to specific performance. This holds unless the seller caused or excused the default.
exceptions_or_limits: Readiness and willingness are assessed from the claimant's overall conduct and the other side's conduct. A buyer who tenders payment in the manner the contract requires, while the seller insists on a different manner, is ready and willing, and the seller is in breach.

For immovable property, time is not ordinarily of the essence. A missed deadline defeats relief only where express terms, a commercial context or the surrounding circumstances show that time was essential, or where readiness and willingness are otherwise unproved.
The purchaser's conditions on payment defeat readiness only if the agreement did not make them conditions precedent.
Specific performance is discretionary, so unexplained delay or inequitable conduct can also justify refusal.
Separate consequences, such as forfeiture of earnest money or voidness of auction sales, turn on contract terms or statutory rules, not on this rule.

outlier_members.reason: Same readiness-and-willingness inquiry but the opposite outcome: the buyer offered payment as the contract required and the seller was in breach. It supplies the limit on the rule.
Concerns forfeiture of a payment that functioned as earnest money after purchaser default, not specific performance.
Concerns the seller's right to forfeit earnest money under a clear forfeiture term, not specific performance.
Concerns identifying which party breached a sale contract, not the grant or refusal of specific performance.
Statutory auction under a revenue recovery law: late payment of the balance makes confirmation illegal.
Auction under municipal rules: late balance payment makes the sale void, so no interest passes.
Revenue auction: mandatory payment deadline, and late payment renders the sale void.
Auction allotment cancelled for non-payment of the premium, plus the lack of a registered lease; this is a title and registration issue.
Auction cancellation and forfeiture are invalid without the notice the rules require, so the outcome favours the purchaser.
Mainly a forfeiture-of-earnest-money holding, though it also applies the readiness and willingness test. It is covered above for that part but sits close to the forfeiture group.

common_material_facts: Purchaser did not pay the balance or a key instalment within the agreed or auction period.
Contract stated that time was essential, or the circumstances (commercial deal, seller's urgent need for cash) made it so.
Purchaser's notices, correspondence or conduct showed lack of funds, requests for more time, or conditions on payment not found in the contract.
Claimant failed to plead or prove readiness and willingness, or delayed suing without explanation.
Seller remained willing to perform, or the contract gave a right to cancel or forfeit.
statutes_and_provisions: Specific Relief Act 1963, s.16(c) and s.20
Specific Relief Act 1963, s.9
Indian Contract Act 1872, s.55 and s.51
Limitation Act 1963, Art. 54
Code of Civil Procedure, O.21 rr.84-86, and Forms 47 and 48
Revenue and municipal auction statutes and rules
Transfer of Property Act 1882, s.55(6)(b)
Registration Act, s.17
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About 12 of the 21 members deny specific performance, or find no cause of action, because the purchaser defaulted on time or failed to show readiness and willingness. Around 3 uphold forfeiture of earnest money or find purchaser breach. Around 4 treat late balance payment at an auction as voiding or cancelling the sale. One protects a ready and willing buyer against a seller in breach, and one requires notice before cancellation.
variations: Some decisions rest on time being essential under s.55 of the Contract Act, others on s.16(c) readiness and willingness, and some on both.
Some add equitable or discretionary factors under s.20, such as unexplained delay, seller's urgent need or prolonged unpaid occupation.
The forfeiture decisions depend on a clear contractual term and on characterising the payment as earnest money.
The auction decisions apply mandatory statutory deadlines under which late payment is fatal, with no discretion to extend.
One decision requires notice as a condition precedent to cancellation of an auction.

split_suggestion: Split into: (1) specific performance denied for purchaser default or lack of readiness and willingness, with the buyer-ready counterexample 38912453_3; (2) forfeiture of earnest money or advance on purchaser default (16443_1, 59682311_1, 1897611_4, 584252_1); (3) statutory auction sales and non-payment of the balance (1777534_2, 1930357_3, 379060_1, 622430_1, 186498_3).

legal_question: Where a tenant's interest derives only from a mortgagee, can the tenant resist the mortgagor's or owner's claim for possession after redemption, or claim rent-control or occupancy protection against them?

rule.if: tenancy_derived_from_mortgagee and mortgagee_interest_ended_by_redemption_or_extinguishment and not lease_binds_mortgagor_by_authorisation_prudence_or_concurrence and not statute_confers_independent_right_on_tenant

predicates.tenancy_derived_from_mortgagee: The occupant's tenancy or possession was created by a mortgagee in possession, not by the owner or mortgagor.
predicates.mortgagee_interest_ended_by_redemption_o: The mortgage has been redeemed, or the mortgagee's interest has otherwise been extinguished (for example by payment, deposit or sale to satisfy the debt), and the owner or purchaser seeks possession.
predicates.lease_binds_mortgagor_by_authorisation_p: The lease binds the mortgagor after redemption because the mortgage deed clearly authorised a tenancy continuing beyond redemption, or the lease was an act of prudent management, or the mortgagor approved, concurred in or recreated the tenancy.
predicates.statute_confers_independent_right_on_ten: A tenancy, land-reform or rent statute gives the tenant a right to remain or a protected status against the mortgagor, such as an enlargement of tenant rights or a deemed-tenant or bhumidhar provision whose conditions are met.
predicates.tenant_cannot_resist_possession_or_claim: The tenant's rights end with the mortgagee's interest; the tenant must yield possession and cannot rely on rent-control or statutory occupancy protection against the mortgagor or owner.

definition: A tenant who holds only through a mortgagee has rights co-terminous with the mortgagee's interest. After redemption or extinguishment of the mortgage, the tenant must yield possession and has no rent-control or occupancy protection against the mortgagor. The exceptions are a lease that binds the mortgagor (by clear authorisation, prudent management or concurrence) and an independent statutory right.
exceptions_or_limits: The tenancy binds the mortgagor if the deed clearly and unequivocally authorises a tenancy beyond redemption, if the lease was an act of prudent management, or if the mortgagor approved, concurred in or recreated it.

A statute may enlarge the tenant's rights or give deemed-tenant or bhumidhar status (see 224976_2 and 273305_1). Rent-control and occupancy statutes that presuppose a landlord-tenant relationship, or a holding under a proprietor or tenure-holder, do not help a tenant who holds through a mortgagee.
Prudent-management protection under s.76(a) of the Transfer of Property Act has seldom been extended to urban property.
A mortgagee's own possession after redemption is a separate question and is not governed by this rule.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns whether a mortgagee himself is a deemed tenant under the Kerala Land Reforms Act, not a tenant inducted by a mortgagee.
Concerns a permanent occupancy right under the Madras Estates Land Act for a lessee of land that was not an estate. No mortgage is involved.
Concerns the mortgagee's own lack of a right to retain possession after redemption, not a tenant claiming through the mortgagee.
Concerns the khas possession saving under the Bihar Land Reforms Act and vesting, not the tenant's right against the mortgagor.
Concerns whether post-redemption possession is adverse to the owner (limitation principle), not whether a mortgagee's tenancy survives.
Reaches the opposite outcome: a tenant inducted by a mortgagee can be a deemed tenant under the Bombay Tenancy Act. It is a statutory enlargement example.
Reaches the opposite outcome: the tenant, not the owner, gets bhumidhar status and compensation under the Delhi Land Reforms Act. It is a statutory enlargement example.

common_material_facts: A mortgagee in possession let or settled the property with a tenant during the mortgage.
The mortgage was later redeemed, or the mortgagee's interest was extinguished, and the owner or mortgagor sought possession.
The mortgage deed did not clearly authorise a tenancy continuing beyond redemption, or required return of possession.
The mortgagor did not concur in the tenancy, and the letting was found not to be prudent management.
The tenant invoked rent-control or occupancy legislation.
statutes_and_provisions: Transfer of Property Act 1882, ss. 60, 76(a), 76(e), 98, 111(c)
Bihar Tenancy Act, ss. 5(2), 5(3), 20, 21
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act 1961
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act 1947, s. 12
Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act 1965, ss. 2(3), 2(6), 11(1)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act 1949
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 13 of 20 members the tenant claiming through the mortgagee loses. The tenancy ends with the mortgage, and rent-control or occupancy protection is unavailable against the mortgagor. The remaining 7 are outliers, including 2 that reach the opposite result through statutory enlargement.
variations: Some members rest on lack of prudent management, others on the deed's terms, lack of mortgagor concurrence, or an anomalous mortgage under s.98.
Some reject rent-control protection because no landlord-tenant relationship exists with the mortgagor. Others reject occupancy rights because a mortgagee is not a proprietor or tenure-holder.
One member treats the tenant's rights as co-terminous with the mortgagee's, so the tenant need not be joined in execution.
Statutory regimes differ, so some tenants (Bombay, Delhi) obtain protection that the cases in the core group deny.

split_suggestion: Keep the 13 covered members as the core group on the effect of redemption on tenancies created by a mortgagee. Move 224976_2 and 273305_1 to a separate cluster on statutory deemed-tenant or bhumidhar rights of tenants of mortgagees. Move 1937186_1 and 1937186_2 to a cluster on adverse possession and khas possession after redemption. Move 1134025_2 and 1431341_2 to a cluster on statutory tenancy status of mortgagees or lessees. Treat 1556670_2 separately as a mortgagee's retention of possession after redemption.

legal_question: When can the Government validly invoke the urgency power under Section 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 to dispense with the Section 5A objection inquiry, and what effect do administrative delay, 'likely to be needed' wording and similar features have on that power?

predicates.land_acquisition_urgency_challenge: The acquisition is challenged on the ground that the urgency power under Section 17(4) was wrongly used to dispense with the Section 5A objection inquiry.
predicates.government_satisfied_immediate_possessio: The Government formed the opinion that immediate possession is needed and that the urgency is such that the objection inquiry itself must be omitted, not merely that the acquisition is urgent.
predicates.relevant_material_shows_genuine_urgency_: The record or surrounding circumstances (for example the nature of the public purpose, court directions, congestion, housing need or an injunction) show real urgency that the time needed for an inquiry would defeat or prejudice.
predicates.mala_fide_or_colourable_exercise_or_no_a: The challenger has shown bad faith, a colourable exercise of power, failure to apply the mind, or a total absence of relevant material behind the urgency decision.
predicates.dispensing_with_section_5A_inquiry_is_va: The direction dispensing with the Section 5A inquiry is lawful and is not set aside.

definition: The urgency power under Section 17(4) is a matter of the Government's subjective satisfaction, and it is upheld where the public purpose and surrounding material show real urgency that makes omitting the Section 5A inquiry necessary. It is invalid where no genuine urgency is shown, where the authority did not consider whether the inquiry itself had to be omitted, or where urgency merely covers the authorities' own laxity. Administrative delay or 'likely to be needed' wording alone does not defeat the power.
exceptions_or_limits: The power is invalid where there is no real urgency, for example where a long-dormant process is suddenly treated as urgent or the authorities had ample time and their own delay created the 'urgency' (as in 354241_2 and 1704181_1).

Urgency in acquiring the land is not enough. The authority must consider whether the urgency requires dispensing with the inquiry, and formulaic recitals without supporting circumstances may be rebutted (202223_3).
The Government's subjective satisfaction is open to challenge for mala fides, colourable exercise, non-application of mind or total want of material.

Delay alone does not negate urgency, but it can be weighed with other material, and where the delay is pure laxity and no immediate-possession need or supporting material exists, the dispensation fails (1704181_1).

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the sequence and timing of Gazette, newspaper and local-notice publication in an urgent acquisition, not whether urgency justifies omitting the inquiry.
Concerns whether the preliminary notification and the final declaration may be published in the same Gazette issue under urgency. This is a procedural-sequencing question.
Concerns the same-day issue of notification and declaration under urgency. This is a procedural-sequencing question.
Holds that the amended Section 17(4) bars a same-day declaration. This is a statutory-construction question about sequencing, and it reaches the opposite result to the same-day members.
Concerns whether a Master Plan green or agricultural designation bars acquisition for a public purpose. It does not concern urgency or the Section 5A inquiry.

common_material_facts: The State invoked Section 17(1)/(4) and directed that the Section 5A inquiry would not apply.
The public purpose was housing, a market yard, sewage treatment, relocation of a depot or retention of a public office facility.
Challengers pointed to administrative delay before or after the notification, or to wording such as 'likely to be needed'.
Some cases involved a lack of supporting material or an allegation of mala fides.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 4, 5A, 6, 17(1), 17(2)(b) and 17(4)
Punjab amendments to the Act (housing for the poor)
Section 114, illustration (e), Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (presumption of regularity)
Articles 14 and 19 (354241_2)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 12 of the 15 covered members the dispensation was upheld, because genuine urgency was supported by material and delay or wording alone did not defeat it. In about 3 (1704181_1, 202223_3, 354241_2) it was held unjustified for want of real urgency or of consideration of the need to omit the inquiry.
variations: Courts uphold the dispensation for housing, market-yard and public-health purposes, and treat delay as not fatal absent mala fides.
The authority's own laxity or a revived dormant process defeats urgency (1704181_1, 354241_2).
A formulaic recital without circumstances showing why the inquiry must be omitted is insufficient (202223_3).

Some members add side points: a reasoned order is not required (853296_4), 'likely to be needed' wording is not decisive (640323_1, 853296_5), and unlawful occupation by the authority does not bar emergency acquisition (308632_4).

split_suggestion: Split into (1) the core group on the substantive validity of the Section 17(4) urgency dispensation (the covered members); (2) a procedural-sequencing group on timing and same-day publication of the Section 4 notification and Section 6 declaration (129507_1, 1536600_6, 561928_1, 747330_1), noting that 747330_1 reflects the amended text and reaches the opposite result to the earlier same-day cases; and (3) a separate issue on planning designation not barring acquisition (640323_2).

legal_question: Under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, when is a purchaser under an agreement to sell entitled to specific performance, and what must the purchaser plead and prove to show continuous readiness and willingness (financial capacity and conduct)?

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and valid_enforceable_contract_proved and readiness_and_willingness_pleaded and purchaser_proved_financial_capacity_by_competent_evidence and purchaser_conduct_shows_continuous_willingness and not equitable_ground_for_refusal

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell or purchase property.
predicates.valid_enforceable_contract_proved: The plaintiff has proved a concluded, valid and enforceable agreement on sufficiently certain terms.
predicates.readiness_and_willingness_pleaded: The plaintiff has averred, at least in substance, that the plaintiff was and remains ready and willing to perform the essential terms the plaintiff must perform.
predicates.purchaser_proved_financial_capacity_by_c: The purchaser has shown, through competent evidence, the ability to pay or raise the balance consideration when performance was due. Possessing the cash, tendering it or depositing it in court is not required unless the court directs it. Where the purchaser did not testify, an agent with personal knowledge must supply the evidence.
predicates.purchaser_conduct_shows_continuous_willi: The purchaser's conduct and the surrounding circumstances show continuing willingness to perform from the contract date to the hearing. Examples are timely demands or tenders, no abandonment of the contract, prompt suit, and no unexplained default or delay. Terms that the seller prevented or waived do not count against the purchaser.
predicates.equitable_ground_for_refusal: A recognised ground under the court's discretion justifies refusing relief, such as inordinate delay or conduct that would give the plaintiff an unfair advantage over the defendant.
predicates.specific_performance_may_be_granted: The court may grant a decree for specific performance, in the exercise of sound judicial discretion.

definition: A purchaser obtains specific performance only if there is a proved, enforceable contract and the purchaser pleads and proves continuous readiness (financial capacity) and willingness (conduct) to perform the essential terms. If that proof fails, relief is refused, and even where it is made out the court retains discretion under Section 20.
exceptions_or_limits: Actual tender or deposit of the balance price is not required unless the court directs it. A deposit made years after the due date does not prove readiness at the time performance was due.
Terms whose performance was prevented or waived by the seller need not be shown as performed. Seller evasion or refusal of tender supports readiness.

Readiness and willingness cannot be proved by a bare plaint assertion. The purchaser's own testimony is ordinarily needed, and an agent without personal knowledge cannot prove the purchaser's state of mind or capacity, except in a recognised exception where the agent exclusively manages the principal's affairs.
Even where readiness is shown, specific performance is discretionary. It may be refused for inordinate delay or an unfair advantage to the purchaser, and possession does not prevent refusal.
Absence of a concluded contract with certain terms and consensus ad idem defeats the claim regardless of readiness.
Section 16(c) applies in the form it took before the 2018 amendment in several members.

outlier_members.reason: Turns on whether a valid, enforceable contract with certain material terms and consensus ad idem existed, not on the purchaser's readiness and willingness.

Turns mainly on proof of a concluded agreement, where an earlier agreement was not produced and the High Court relied on criminal findings, and on the proper exercise of Section 20 discretion. Readiness is mentioned only as a general requirement.

common_material_facts: Agreement to sell immovable property, with earnest money or part payment made by the purchaser.
Dispute over whether the purchaser had the funds or could raise them when performance was due.
Purchaser's conduct: demands, notices, tender, delay, or late or no deposit of the balance.
Purchaser did not testify, or relied on an agent or power-of-attorney holder lacking personal knowledge.
Seller evasion, refusal of tender, or denial of the agreement.
statutes_and_provisions: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 16(c), and Section 16(1)(c) and 16(b) in some members
Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 20 (discretion)
Specific Relief Act, 1963, Sections 9, 10 and 28
Order III Rules 1 and 2, Code of Civil Procedure (agent's evidence)
Article 54, Limitation Act
Cases cited include N.P. Thirugnanam, Syed Dastagir, Sukhbir Singh, A. Kanthamani, Jamsetji Chinoy, Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani and Vidhyadhar
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 18 covered members, about 9 uphold or grant specific performance because readiness and willingness were proved or established by conduct (1090967_2, 1108197_3, 118013356_4, 118013356_5, 121624333_2, 129719559_1, 159016305_2, 75469_2, 94543326_2). About 9 deny it because capacity or willingness was not proved, whether through no proof of funds, delay, or no competent testimony (1284248_3, 1284248_4, 163454049_1, 169428_2, 182262198_1, 1897611_1, 56652468_1, 763653_1, 84039101_1).
variations: Some members find readiness from conduct and the seller's evasion or refusal of tender. Others find a failure from lack of financial proof or delay.
Some members hold that deposit or cash in hand is unnecessary. Others treat a late deposit or a failure to comply with a deposit direction as evidence against the purchaser.
Some members focus on the evidentiary route, namely that the purchaser must personally testify and an agent cannot substitute.
Delay and unfair advantage under Section 20 operate as a separate equitable ground for refusal in one member.
Two members turn on the existence or certainty of the contract itself.

split_suggestion: Keep the 18 members on readiness and willingness together. If finer granularity is wanted, split them into (a) financial capacity and proof of funds, (b) conduct, delay and prevention by the seller, and (c) competent evidence by a principal versus an agent. Move 1643796_1 and 137193261_1 to a separate cluster on the existence and certainty of a valid, enforceable contract.

legal_question: When may a court allow amendment of a pleading (especially a written statement) under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, notwithstanding delay, an alternative or inconsistent plea, an explained admission or a possible limitation bar, and what conditions such as absence of serious prejudice or costs govern the exercise of that discretion?

predicates.pleading_amendment_application_in_civil_: A party has applied to amend a plaint or written statement in a pending civil proceeding (including appeal) under Order VI Rule 17 CPC.
predicates.amendment_is_needed_to_determine_real_co: The proposed amendment elaborates, clarifies, explains or adds an alternative defence or particulars, or brings a subsequent event before the court, so that it assists in deciding the real dispute or avoids multiplicity of proceedings.
predicates.amendment_withdraws_admission_or_displac: The amendment wholly withdraws a clear admission that conferred a right on the opponent, or takes away a right accrued to the opponent, or substitutes a distinct cause of action or case.
predicates.amendment_causes_serious_or_irretrievabl: The amendment would cause the opponent serious injustice or irreparable prejudice which cannot be remedied by costs or other terms.
predicates.amendment_may_be_allowed_despite_delay_o: The court may (and ordinarily should) allow the amendment, notwithstanding delay, an inconsistent or alternative plea, an explained admission, or a disputed limitation question, subject to costs or other conditions.

definition: Under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, courts liberally allow amendments, particularly of written statements, that are needed to decide the real controversy. Delay, an alternative plea, an explanation of an admission, or a disputed limitation bar does not by itself prevent amendment, provided there is no wholesale withdrawal of an admission, no new cause of action, and no serious prejudice or loss of an accrued right that costs cannot cure.
exceptions_or_limits: An admission cannot be wholly withdrawn if that would prejudice a right it conferred on the opponent; it may only be explained or clarified.
Amendment will not be allowed to substitute a distinct cause of action or case, or to introduce new facts that defeat an accrued right.
Alternative pleas must not be mutually destructive or contradictory of the existing defence in a way that causes irremediable injustice.
Where the amendment is sought after trial commenced, the due-diligence proviso to Order VI Rule 17 applies, though it may be relaxed to correct a description of the property.
Delay and limitation are relevant to discretion but do not remove the power to amend; a disputed limitation bar is left to be decided as an issue.
Where prejudice or delay can be compensated, the amendment is typically conditioned on costs or payment of arrears.
Condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act is a separate inquiry turning on the acceptability of the explanation and the absence of mala fides.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act in restoring a dismissed proceeding, not amendment of pleadings under Order VI Rule 17. It shares only the theme that length of delay is not decisive.

common_material_facts: A defendant seeks to amend a written statement to elaborate, add an alternative defence, or explain an admission.
The application is made after delay, sometimes years later or at the appellate stage.
The opposing party is not shown to suffer serious prejudice, or the prejudice can be met by costs.
A limitation bar is alleged against the amended claim or defence but is genuinely disputed.
Subsequent events or corrections of property description need to be brought before the court.
statutes_and_provisions: Order VI Rule 17 CPC
Section 115 CPC (revisional jurisdiction)
Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963
Section 60(b) of the Indian Easements Act, 1882
Article 136 of the Constitution
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Amendment allowed in about 16 of 19 members, often with costs or other conditions. In two members (123653482_2, 123653482_3) the court partly refused the amendment to the extent it withdrew admissions, while permitting explanation or clarification. In 1243128_2 the matter was remitted for fresh consideration with the discretion affirmed.
variations: Several members allow the amendment subject to costs or payment of licence-fee arrears.
Some turn on explaining an admission, while others turn on elaborating an existing defence with no admission involved.
Limitation-related members allow the amendment and leave the limitation plea to be tried as an issue.
The subsequent-event members (132651_3, 441001_6) allow late amendments to avoid fresh litigation.
449254_1 addresses the post-commencement due-diligence proviso and allows the correction of a property description with costs.
307092_2 notes that the High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 but the Supreme Court declined to interfere.

split_suggestion: Treat 1240908_1 (condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act) separately from the amendment-of-pleadings members.

legal_question: Is a court or rent controller bound to strike out a tenant's defence automatically whenever the tenant fails to pay or deposit rent as ordered in an eviction proceeding, or does it have discretion to retain the defence and condone the default, and when should that discretion be exercised for or against the tenant?

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding is a landlord's eviction suit or application before a court or rent controller under a rent-control or comparable provision, based wholly or partly on non-payment of rent.
predicates.rent_payment_or_deposit_order_made: The court or controller has directed the tenant to pay or deposit arrears and/or future rent, and the governing provision attaches the sanction of striking out the defence to non-compliance.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_comply_with_order: The tenant did not pay or deposit rent in full or on time as directed.
predicates.striking_out_defence_is_discretionary_an: Striking out the defence is a penal, exceptional power to be exercised on the circumstances of the case, not a mechanical consequence of every default (even where the statute says 'shall'), and the discretion not to strike out includes power to condone the default or extend the time for payment or deposit.

definition: Where a tenant fails to comply with an order to pay or deposit rent in an eviction proceeding, the power to strike out the defence is discretionary and penal, not automatic. The court or controller must consider the circumstances and may condone the delay or extend time.
