It may strike out the defence where the default is deliberate, contumacious, repeated or unexplained, and should not do so where the delay is properly explained, technical, in good faith, or the arrears have been paid.
exceptions_or_limits: Discretion is typically exercised against the tenant where the default is wilful, deliberate, contumacious, grossly negligent, repeated or unexplained; no condonation is available without justifiable reasons showing circumstances beyond the tenant's control.

Later or extra payments do not necessarily cure earlier violations of a payment schedule absent an acceptable explanation for the delay, and payments toward arrears cannot be credited to future rent (one separate opinion).
A defence cannot be struck for non-compliance with a direction that never legally existed (e.g. an interpolated order) or where a standard-rent dispute and interim-rent request remain undecided.
Where the payment direction was made outside the statutory compensation procedure, the automatic-dismissal consequence of that procedure does not apply.
Statutory classifications that treat tenants defaulting on admitted rent after a court order differently from those disputing the tenancy do not violate Article 14.
Under some provisions, protection against eviction still depends on substantial compliance with the deposit requirements, so condonation is needed to retain it.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the Madras City Tenants' Protection Act and whether an equitable superstructure-payment direction triggers automatic dismissal of an ejectment suit, not striking out a defence for rent default.
Concerns an Article 14 equality challenge to a procedure for striking out a defence, not the scope of discretion on default.
Turns on the invalidity of an interpolated, non-existent deposit order and the pending standard-rent determination; it is not about discretion in the face of real non-compliance.

common_material_facts: Eviction suit or application based on rent default in which the tenant was directed to pay arrears and/or deposit future rent monthly.
Tenant paid or deposited late, or only partly, and the landlord applied to strike out the defence.
Lower courts or the High Court often treated striking out as mandatory or automatic.
Explanations offered included good-faith payment through an advocate, a compromise between the parties, a mistaken belief that a son had deposited, and technical delays.
statutes_and_provisions: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act 1952, s. 13(5)
Order XV Rule 5 CPC (as amended in U.P.)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act 1956, s. 17(3)
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act 1947, s. 11A, and 1982 Act, s. 13
s. 148 CPC
Article 14 of the Constitution
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 14 of 17 covered members the court holds that striking out is discretionary and that the defence is retained or the delay condoned, or remands for that discretion to be exercised. In 3 members (125378456_3, 145937302_2, 175560689_2) the strike-out or denial of protection is upheld because the default was deliberate, repeated or unexplained.
variations: Some provisions use 'may' (Delhi, CPC O. XV r. 5) and others 'shall' read as directory (West Bengal, Bihar 1947); Bihar 1982 s. 13 is read as requiring striking out only where the delay is unexplained.
Hem Chand's denial of power to extend time is held not to survive Shyamcharan Sharma and Ram Murti, with some members stressing that the Controller must still apply its mind.
The tests for striking out vary in wording: wilful, deliberate, contumacious, negligent, gross neglect, volitional non-performance, or lack of an acceptable explanation.
A timely representation is considered under O. XV r. 5(2), but its absence does not remove discretion.
In the split decision in 125378456, the two judges differed on whether the tenant's payments showed contumacy.

split_suggestion: Keep the 17 members on discretion to strike out the defence for rent default as the core group. Within it, separate (a) members on the existence of discretion and power to condone or extend time from (b) members on how the discretion is applied against the tenant. Move 1051548_1 (Madras tenants' protection and superstructure compensation), 1401686_2 (Article 14 classification) and 1954254_2 (interpolated order and standard-rent dispute) into separate clusters.

legal_question: When a Hindu woman holds property under a will or other instrument that expressly gives her only a restricted (for example lifetime) interest, does Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 enlarge that interest into absolute ownership, or does the Section 14(2) exception keep it restricted?

predicates.female_hindu_holds_interest_under_instru: The woman's interest in the property derives from a will, gift, settlement, award, decree or similar instrument.
predicates.instrument_prescribes_restricted_estate: The instrument expressly limits the woman's interest, for example to her lifetime, with restraints on alienation or a gift-over of the property to others after her death.
predicates.instrument_recognises_preexisting_right: The instrument gives the property in recognition or satisfaction of a right the woman already had, such as a right to maintenance, or a share or title she already held, rather than creating a new title for the first time.
predicates.interest_not_enlarged_to_absolute_owners: The Section 14(2) exception applies, so the interest stays a restricted estate. The woman does not become an absolute owner, and any transfer by her cannot pass more than her limited interest.

definition: Section 14(1) enlarges a Hindu woman's limited interest into full ownership only where she holds it under some pre-existing right. Where a will or other instrument creates a new, expressly restricted estate for her, Section 14(2) applies and the restriction stands, so she cannot pass absolute title to others.
exceptions_or_limits: If the instrument merely recognises or gives effect to a pre-existing right, such as a maintenance right, and the woman possesses the property, Section 14(2) does not apply and the interest is enlarged under Section 14(1). The cluster shows this in 1436076_2, 253723_2 and 1905495_2.

Enlargement under Section 14(1) needs possession at commencement of the Act under some vestige of claim, right or title. Bare possession, trespass, or non-possession at commencement does not produce full ownership.
A bare right to maintenance, with no charge or other right in the testator's separate property, is not a pre-existing right in that property (1468380_1).
Whether an instrument creates a restricted estate depends on reading it as a whole. Differently worded instruments should not be construed by analogy.
A stranger legatee remains bound by the restrictions in the instrument.

outlier_members.reason: Same legal question but opposite outcome. The grant recognised a pre-existing maintenance right, so the exception did not apply and full ownership resulted. It marks the limit of the main rule.
Same legal question but opposite outcome. The instrument recognised a pre-existing maintenance right, so Section 14(2) did not block enlargement.

Concerns whether enlarging a pre-existing restricted interest is retrospective. It is not, where the woman had a pre-existing right and possessed the property. This is the opposite-outcome side and a different question.
Concerns a female alienee of a widow's pre-Act transfer who was not herself a limited owner. The issue is the scope of Section 14(1), not a restricted instrument under Section 14(2).
Concerns a widow who was not in possession at commencement of the Act. It is a possession requirement under Section 14(1), not the Section 14(2) instrument exception.
Concerns possession without any title at commencement. It is a possession-without-title issue under Section 14(1).
Concerns possession not resting on any claim or title. It is a possession-without-title issue under Section 14(1).
Concerns the nature of a widow's estate in property allotted on partition under Benares Mitakshara law. It does not turn on Section 14.
Concerns construing a will to decide whether the widow takes an ordinary life estate or a Hindu widow's estate. It is a will-construction question and does not turn on Section 14.
Concerns the statutory definition of 'stridhana land' under a land-ceiling law. It is unrelated to Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act.

common_material_facts: A will or other instrument (settlement deed, award) gave a Hindu woman, usually a widow or daughter, only a life or restricted interest.
The instrument often barred alienation or provided that the property would pass to named others after her death.
The woman, or someone claiming through her by sale or her own will, asserted that Section 14(1) made her an absolute owner.
The property was often the grantor's self-acquired or separate property, and the grant was made for the first time without satisfying any pre-existing right.
statutes_and_provisions: Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 14(1) and its Explanation
Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 14(2)
Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 30 (testamentary disposition)
Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 4
V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy
Mst. Karmi v. Amru
Sadhu Singh v. Gurdwara Sahib Narike
Jagan Singh v. Dhanwanti
Navneet Lal v. Gokul
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 10 covered members, all hold that the restricted interest is not enlarged and the appeal against the restriction fails or is dismissed. Three further members (1436076_2, 253723_2, 1905495_2) reach the opposite result because a pre-existing right such as maintenance was recognised.
variations: Some members apply Section 14(2) simply because the interest was created by an instrument (498814_4, 998337_1, 83295596_2), while others analyse whether a pre-existing right existed (993554_1, 36104522_1, 45144990_1).
The instruments differ: wills (most members), a settlement deed (1095112_1), a registered award (993554_1) and an oral testamentary disposition (83295596_2).

Some members involve a maintenance provision in the instrument, but the property itself was not given in lieu of maintenance (45144990_1, 36104522_1). Others involve a bare maintenance right with no charge on the property (1468380_1).
Some wills took effect after the Act's commencement (1468380_1, 1622720_1). Others were made before it (177773737_1, a 1944 will).

split_suggestion: Split into three groups. (1) Restricted estate created by an instrument and not enlarged under Section 14(2): the covered members. (2) Pre-existing right or maintenance right recognised, so Section 14(1) enlarges the interest: 1436076_2, 253723_2 and 1905495_2. (3) Possession-without-title and non-possession cases under Section 14(1): 1184690_1, 281123_1, 543934_2 and 7582149_1. Treat 1294884_1, 1622258_1 and 717074_1 as separate topics: the nature of a widow's estate on partition, will construction, and land-ceiling stridhana.

legal_question: When may an appellate court (including the Supreme Court) set aside an acquittal, or uphold a conviction entered on reversal of an acquittal, because the acquittal rested on wrongly rejected, ignored or unsound assessment of credible prosecution evidence?

rule.if: appeal_concerns_acquittal_or_its_reversal and prosecution_evidence_is_credible_and_corroborated and acquittal_rested_on_ignored_or_unsound_grounds and evidence_establishes_guilt_beyond_reasonable_doubt and not evidence_reasonably_supports_two_views

predicates.appeal_concerns_acquittal_or_its_reversa: The appeal is against an acquittal, or challenges a conviction that a higher court entered by reversing an acquittal.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_is_credible_and_cor: The court finds the main prosecution evidence (typically eyewitness testimony, or demand and acceptance evidence in corruption cases) reliable and supported by surrounding material such as a prompt report, medical or ballistic evidence, recoveries, motive or the accused's failure to rebut a presumption.
predicates.acquittal_rested_on_ignored_or_unsound_g: The acquitting court ignored material evidence or relied on perverse, speculative, technical or peripheral grounds such as minor discrepancies, investigative lapses or unsupported defence explanations.
predicates.evidence_establishes_guilt_beyond_reason: On the record as a whole, the prosecution has proved the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
predicates.evidence_reasonably_supports_two_views: The evidence reasonably permits both a view of guilt and a view of innocence, so the acquittal view is plausible.
predicates.acquittal_is_set_aside_and_conviction_is: The acquittal is set aside and the trial court's conviction is restored, or the conviction entered on reversal of the acquittal is upheld.

definition: Appellate courts ordinarily do not disturb an acquittal where two reasonable views are possible. They will set it aside, or uphold a conviction entered on reversal, where the acquittal rested on ignored evidence or perverse, peripheral or speculative grounds and the credible, corroborated evidence establishes guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the evidence reasonably permits two views, or the trial court's view is at least as acceptable as the reversing court's view, the acquittal stands and a conviction entered on reversal is set aside (as in 1330888_1).
Where the cumulative evidence establishes guilt only against some accused, the acquittal is set aside only as to those accused and left undisturbed for the others (as in 41408_6 and 853471_6).
Interested or injured eyewitness testimony needs assurance from surrounding circumstances or other evidence, as a matter of caution.
In corruption cases, guilt rests on proof of demand and acceptance and on an unrebutted statutory presumption.

Discrepancies on collateral events, investigative omissions or delay do not defeat reliable testimony on the core act, but fundamental conflicts with medical evidence or genuine unreliability of the witnesses can.

outlier_members.reason: Opposite outcome: the Supreme Court set aside a conviction entered on reversal of an acquittal because the trial court's view was at least as acceptable. It is the counter-limit to the rule, not an instance of it.

This appeal reversed a High Court's reduction or reversal of trial convictions, not an acquittal. The High Court omitted material evidence on possession. It supports restoring the trial court's decision but is a distinct fact pattern.

common_material_facts: Credible eyewitnesses, often injured or independent, identified the accused as assailants.
A prompt first information report named the accused.
Medical, ballistic or recovery evidence corroborated the eyewitness account.
The acquitting court relied on minor discrepancies, investigative defects, delay or speculative inferences, or ignored material evidence.
Motive or hostility evidence was considered alongside other circumstances.
In the corruption cases, demand, acceptance and recovery of marked money were proved and the presumption was not rebutted.
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Penal Code ss. 302, 34, 149, 147, 148, 307, 323, 304 Part I and II, 299, 447
Code of Criminal Procedure s. 379 with the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act s. 2(a)
Arms Act s. 27
Evidence Act s. 3
Prevention of Corruption Act presumption (s. 20)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 17 of 20 members the acquittal was set aside, or the conviction entered on reversal was upheld, and the trial court's conviction was restored or maintained. One member (1330888_1) went the other way and set aside a conviction entered on reversal. One member (1634747_3) restored trial convictions after a High Court reversal that was not an acquittal.
variations: Some appeals were State appeals against acquittal. Others were accused's appeals against convictions entered by the High Court on reversal of an acquittal.
Some members rest on the two-views test or perversity. Others simply find the acquittal grounds unsustainable.
Some members rely on cumulative circumstances (motive, recoveries, flight) and convict only some of the accused.
Corruption cases turn on demand, acceptance and an unrebutted presumption instead of eyewitness evidence.
Only a few members cite precedents (State of Andhra Pradesh v. K. Narasimhachary; Narendra Champaklal Trivedi; Madan Mohan Lal Verma; C.M. Girish Babu; Sher Singh and others). Most cite none.

legal_question: Where a land ceiling law makes a statutorily defined family the unit for applying the ceiling, must land held by each family member (including separated minor sons and spouses holding separately) be aggregated into the family's holding, and is that family-unit approach constitutionally valid?

rule.if: land_ceiling_law_uses_family_unit and family_defined_by_statutory_relationships and family_member_holds_land and not constitutional_protection_defeated_by_challenge

predicates.land_ceiling_law_uses_family_unit: The applicable agricultural or urban land ceiling statute treats a defined family unit, not each individual member, as the unit for applying the ceiling.
predicates.family_defined_by_statutory_relationship: The statute defines the family by listed relationships (for example a person, spouse and minor children) and not by joint title, joint holding or a Hindu joint family.
predicates.family_member_holds_land: A person who falls within the statutory family holds land, jointly or separately. This includes a minor son holding after partition, a spouse holding separate or stridhan property, and an adult son treated as a separate unit within an aggregate limit.
predicates.constitutional_protection_defeated_by_ch: A constitutional challenge to the family-unit definition or aggregation succeeds, for example because the law is arbitrary under Article 14 or falls outside the protection of Article 31A or 31B.
predicates.family_unit_aggregation_applies_and_is_u: The land of all family members is pooled into the family's holding for applying the ceiling, and the family-unit definition and aggregation are not invalidated on the constitutional grounds raised.

definition: Where a land ceiling statute makes a relationship-based family the ceiling unit, all land held by its members, jointly or separately, is aggregated in the family's holding. That holds even where a minor son has separated by partition or a spouse holds land as separate property. Such a family-unit scheme is not invalid under Article 14 and is protected by Articles 31A and 31B when it is agrarian reform legislation.
exceptions_or_limits: The outcome depends on the particular statute's definition of family and its aggregation clause. Where the statute does not bring a member's separate or self-acquired property into the unit, that property may be excluded (75868557_1, under a differently construed Maharashtra Act).
Transfers made before the statutory cutoff are outside the Act, so land transferred before the cutoff is not aggregated merely because of family relationship.
Adult sons are treated as separate units in some statutes, subject to an aggregate limit on the family and those units (171991274_1).
Aggregation does not extinguish separate ownership. It only determines the ceiling.

Constitutional protection under Articles 31A and 31B applies only to qualifying agrarian reform laws. For urban ceiling laws the Article 14 validity rests on the definition not being arbitrary and not inevitably concentrating wealth.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns an urban ceiling and incomplete land acquisition, where title stays with the declarants. It does not concern family-unit aggregation.
It concerns the same land counting in the holdings of both transferor and transferee under the definition of 'holding'. It does not concern family-unit aggregation.
It concerns post-cutoff transfers disregarded unless they fall within a proviso exception. This is a transfer-evasion issue, not family aggregation.
It concerns post-cutoff involuntary transfers (auction sale) and the burden of proving the proviso exception. This is a transfer issue, not family aggregation.

It reaches the opposite result, excluding the land, because the transfers were made before the cutoff and the statute did not reach a member's separate property. It is better treated as a limit on the rule or grouped with the transfer cases.
It concerns the Article 14 validity of the rule on legitimacy of children of void marriages. It has nothing to do with land ceilings.

common_material_facts: A ceiling statute defines a family unit as a person, spouse and minor children.
Minor sons hold land separately after a partition made before the appointed day.
A wife holds land in her own name as separate or stridhan property.
Landholders challenge the family-unit definition under Article 14 or Article 31A, or on the ground that adult children and joint families are excluded.
The ceiling law is an agrarian reform measure, often placed in the Ninth Schedule.
statutes_and_provisions: Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act 1973, ss 3(f), 3(o), 4, 5
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act 1961, s 4(1) and Explanation
Gujarat Agricultural Land Ceiling Act, s 6(2)
Constitution of India, Arts 14, 19, 31, 31A (including its second proviso), 31B, 39(b)-(c), 367
General Clauses Act 1897, s 3(42)
Sections 2(10), 4(1)-(4) and 7(1) Explanation IV of a ceiling statute defining the family by relationship
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 14 covered members the family-unit scheme prevailed. Six applied the statute to aggregate separated minor sons' land or a wife's separate land. Eight rejected constitutional challenges under Article 14 or the second proviso to Article 31A, largely relying on Articles 31A and 31B.
variations: The statutory-interpretation members aggregate land on the text of the family and unit provisions. The constitutional members rest on Article 14 reasonableness, Article 31A or 31B, or the second proviso to Article 31A.
Some members (693176_2, 766077_2) apply an Article 14 arbitrariness analysis to an urban ceiling law. Others (712047_3, 799151_2, 981808_3) rely mainly on Article 31A or 31B protection.
Some statutes treat adult sons as separate units within an aggregate limit. Others exclude major sons from the family altogether.
A contrary Maharashtra Act result (75868557_1) arose from a pre-cutoff transfer and the absence of any pleading of collusion.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) the family-unit aggregation and constitutional validity group (the 14 covered members), possibly subdivided into statutory construction and constitutional challenge; (b) transfers and the cutoff date (1647440_1, 910696_1, 75868557_1, 1293282_4); (c) urban ceiling and incomplete acquisition (1154981_3); and (d) legitimacy of children of void marriages (391843_3), which belongs to family law.

legal_question: What must the statutory objection-and-hearing procedure before a compulsory land acquisition (chiefly Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894) provide, and what follows when the procedure is or is not complied with?

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and statutory_objection_procedure_applies and not objection_procedure_validly_dispensed_with and affected_person_filed_objections

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns a compulsory acquisition of land under a statute that provides a procedure for objections.
predicates.statutory_objection_procedure_applies: The governing statute gives affected persons a right to object and be heard before the acquisition is finalised (for example Section 5A or an analogous provision).
predicates.objection_procedure_validly_dispensed_wi: The government has validly dispensed with the objection procedure under an urgency provision.
predicates.affected_person_filed_objections: An interested or affected person filed objections to the proposed acquisition within the time allowed.
predicates.authority_must_give_effective_hearing_an: The designated authority must give the objector a real opportunity to be heard, objectively consider the objections and report, and the government must independently apply its mind before the declaration. Substantial failure to do so vitiates the acquisition, while an opportunity that was actually afforded and not availed of does not.

definition: Where a statute gives landowners a right to object before acquisition and the procedure has not been validly dispensed with, the designated authority (usually the Collector) must give a genuine opportunity to be heard and objectively consider the objections. The government must then independently apply its mind to the objections and the report. Denial of the hearing or mechanical or unproven consideration invalidates the acquisition, but an opportunity that was offered and not used, or whose objections were in fact heard and considered, satisfies the requirement.
exceptions_or_limits: The objection procedure may be validly dispensed with under urgency provisions, but the court may still examine whether a bona fide opinion on urgency was formed and may require the State to respond and produce its records.
No violation arises where the objector was notified of a hearing and chose not to appear or to press for a hearing, or could not prove attendance.
A hearing by the government cannot substitute for the hearing the Collector must give.

A defect in the notification, or the lack of a fresh inquiry after an erratum, does not invalidate the acquisition where the owners knew the relevant purpose or participated in the inquiry and suffered no prejudice.
The conclusiveness of the declaration as to need and public purpose does not bar judicial review of the decision-making process, jurisdictional defects or colourable exercise of power.
Rules letting the land-requiring department present its views in the objection inquiry are consistent with the statutory procedure.
Where the State is challenged and fails to produce its records or file a proper affidavit, it cannot show that the objections were considered.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns a hearing for an affected owner in building-control (Cantonments Act) proceedings under Article 14 audi alteram partem, not an acquisition objection procedure.
Concerns the hearing of a third-party assignee in a revision under the Urban Land Ceiling Act, not objections to acquisition.
Concerns a no-prejudice omission in a scheme notification under the City of Mysore Improvement Act; it overlaps with the objection theme but is a distinct point.
Concerns the validity of a rule giving the requiring department a say in the inquiry, not the objector's hearing.

common_material_facts: Landowners filed written objections to a proposed acquisition under Section 5A or an analogous provision.
The Collector or designated officer heard, or failed to hear, the objectors and reported to the government.
The government made a declaration under Section 6 after considering, or without independently considering, the report.
The State's records or affidavits were sometimes missing or deficient.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 4, 5A, 6 and 17
Article 300A and Article 226 of the Constitution
Railways Act, 1989, Section 20D
Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, Section 52(3)
City of Mysore Improvement Act, 1903, Sections 16 and 17
Article 14 (audi alteram partem)
Cantonments Act, 1924, Sections 52 and 185
Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 34
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 15 covered members, about 6 invalidated or found the acquisition unsupported for denial of hearing, non-consideration or non-production of records, and about 3 required fuller scrutiny or preserved judicial review. About 6 upheld the acquisition because the hearing was offered, taken up or not proved to be denied, or because the defect caused no prejudice.
variations: Some members treat the hearing as a mandatory substantive right strictly construed, while others find it satisfied where the objector chose not to appear or could not prove attendance.
Some members concern the Collector's duty (hearing, reasoned disposal), others the government's independent application of mind, and others the burden on the State to produce records.
Some members address the scope of judicial review despite statutory conclusiveness, rather than the hearing itself.
Statutory frameworks vary between the central 1894 Act and state or special statutes.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) a core group on the content and breach of the Section 5A hearing and consideration requirement (hearing denied, mechanical consideration, missing records, versus hearing given or not availed); (b) judicial review notwithstanding conclusive declarations or urgency dispensation; and (c) the non-acquisition natural-justice cases (building control, urban land ceiling) and the procedural-validity cases (erratum, scheme omission, department rule).

legal_question: Is an acquisition law, or an acquisition made under it, unconstitutional or invalid merely because it omits compensation, solatium, interest or rehabilitation that another scheme provides or that the challenger says is required?

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_law and challenge_based_on_omitted_compensation_component and law_within_legislative_competence and (law_protected_by_constitutional_shield or distinct_self_contained_scheme_with_rational_basis_or_public_interest or no_constitutional_or_statutory_requirement_for_omitted_component)

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: The challenge attacks the validity of a compulsory acquisition law, or an acquisition under it, on constitutional grounds.
predicates.challenge_based_on_omitted_compensation_: The challenge rests on the law's omission of compensation, or of an addition such as solatium, interest or rehabilitation, or on an implied compensation duty said to arise from the legislative entries.
predicates.law_within_legislative_competence: The enacting legislature had competence over the subject of acquisition, and the challenge does not show the law to be outside that field.
predicates.law_protected_by_constitutional_shield: The law is protected from Part III or Article 31(2) challenge by a constitutional provision such as Article 31(4), 31-A, 31-B, the Ninth Schedule, or the evacuee-property exception in Article 31(5)(b)(iii).
predicates.distinct_self_contained_scheme_with_rati: The law is a separate, self-contained acquisition or compensation scheme whose differences from the general acquisition law rest on an intelligible differentia, or on public interest, and the compensation it provides is not illusory.
predicates.no_constitutional_or_statutory_requireme: Neither the Constitution nor the governing statute makes the omitted component a condition of valid acquisition, and the law otherwise provides reasonable compensation.
predicates.omission_does_not_invalidate_acquisition: The omission of the compensation component does not make the law or the acquisition unconstitutional or invalid, and the challenge fails.

definition: A challenge to an acquisition law for omitting compensation, solatium, interest or rehabilitation fails where the law is within competence and either a constitutional shield protects it, or it is a distinct scheme with a rational or public-interest basis, or no legal requirement mandates the omitted component. The Court does not read compensation or its additions into legislative entries or into a separate statutory scheme.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply if the law lacks legislative competence.
The rule does not apply if the compensation provided is illusory or unreal; the town-planning member left this open by noting it was not shown.
A law that is not protected by a constitutional shield and does not form a distinct scheme with a rational basis is not saved by this rule.
Where a statute incorporates the general Land Acquisition Act compensation scheme, the omission may be treated differently, as the Nagpur Improvement Trust line is distinguished on this ground.

Where no agreement exists under an evacuee-property law, the law's own compensation provision may make compensation unclaimable. That is a statutory consequence and not a constitutional ground of invalidity.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the statutory meaning of 'injurious affection' and the appealability of a town-planning compensation decision, not a constitutional challenge to omitted compensation.
It concerns an Article 14 classification in a redetermination remedy, not omitted compensation components, though it shares the reasonable-classification reasoning.
It concerns the colorable legislation doctrine (competence versus motive) and an earlier compensated-acquisition proposal, not an omitted compensation component directly.
It concerns whether a 'nationalization' label takes a measure outside legislative competence over acquisition, and does not address compensation.

common_material_facts: The challenger relied on the omission of compensation, solatium, interest or rehabilitation, often by comparison with the general Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
The law was a special or self-contained scheme (slum clearance, town planning, requisition, evacuee property, inam or estate abolition).
The law was protected by Article 31(4), 31-A or 31-B or by the Ninth Schedule, or had received the President's assent.
Legislative entries on acquisition were said to imply a compensation duty.
statutes_and_provisions: Articles 14, 31(2), 31(4), 31(5)(b)(iii), 31-A, 31-B, 294(b) and 300-A of the Constitution
Entry 36 of List II and entry 42 of List III of the Seventh Schedule
Ninth Schedule and the Seventeenth Amendment
Land Acquisition Act, 1894, ss. 23(2) and 28
Defence of India Act, 1971, ss. 30-31
Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1951, ss. 12-13
Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: The challenge fails in all 15 covered members; the omission of compensation or an addition does not by itself invalidate the law. About 7 rest on constitutional protections (Article 31-A, the Ninth Schedule, Article 31(4)). About 5 rest on distinct schemes, reasonable classification or public interest. About 3 hold that the legislative entries or Article 300-A impose no compensation or rehabilitation duty.
variations: Some members rest on constitutional immunity, others on Article 14 reasonable classification and the public-interest rationale of Prakash Amichand Shah.
Some members address legislative competence and implied duties from entries, others the substantive adequacy of compensation.
Rehabilitation is treated as a non-required component under Article 300-A, whereas the others concern solatium, interest or compensation.
In the evacuee-property case, compensation is unavailable for want of an agreement, with the Article 31(2) challenge excluded by the constitutional exception.

split_suggestion: Separate the covered members into (a) challenges barred by constitutional protections (Article 31-A, 31-B, the Ninth Schedule, Article 31(4), the evacuee-property exception) together with the no-implied-compensation-duty competence cases, and (b) Article 14 and reasonableness challenges to special schemes on solatium, interest or rehabilitation. Treat the four outliers as separate issues: statutory meaning of injurious affection, redetermination classification, colorable legislation, and the nationalization label.

legal_question: Does a land-related law, tax, compensation scheme or State action in acquisition, release or withdrawal violate the equality guarantee of Article 14 when it treats similarly situated persons or properties differently (or dissimilar ones alike) without an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the object of the law?

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_land_related_law_or_state_action and (similarly_situated_persons_or_properties_treated_differently or dissimilar_persons_or_properties_treated_alike) and not (classification_rests_on_intelligible_differentia_with_rational_nexus_to_object) and no_valid_justification_shown_by_state

predicates.equality_challenge_to_land_related_law_o: The challenge is under Article 14 to a statute, rule, tax, assessment, compensation provision, or an executive act concerning acquisition, release, withdrawal, ceiling or assessment of land or buildings.
predicates.similarly_situated_persons_or_properties: Owners, creditors, factories, parcels or other subjects that are alike in relation to the law's object receive different treatment, such as different compensation, selection for acquisition, exemption, release, or procedure.
predicates.dissimilar_persons_or_properties_treated: Materially different properties or persons (for example, buildings or land differing in use, quality, productivity or location) are subjected to the same uniform tax, assessment or standard without rational classification.
predicates.classification_rests_on_intelligible_dif: The classification is founded on an intelligible differentia distinguishing those included from those excluded, and that differentia bears a rational relation to the object the law seeks to achieve.
predicates.no_valid_justification_shown_by_state: The State has not explained or shown, in the law or surrounding circumstances, a valid basis for the differential or uniform treatment; the presumption of constitutionality does not supply an undisclosed basis.
predicates.measure_violates_article_14_and_is_inval: The law or action is held to violate Article 14 and is struck down, quashed or declared void, in whole or to the extent of the discriminatory provision (subject to severability), or equal treatment is directed.

definition: Under Article 14, a land-related law or State action is invalid if it treats similarly situated owners, parcels, properties or groups differently, or treats materially dissimilar ones alike, without an intelligible differentia that is rationally related to the law's object and without any justification from the State. Where the discrimination is in executive action (selective acquisition, release or withdrawal), the State must treat comparable owners consistently or the action is set aside.
exceptions_or_limits: Valid classification: differential treatment is upheld where it rests on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the object; fiscal laws allow the legislature wider latitude in classification.
The presumption of constitutionality cannot supply a basis that does not appear in the law or surrounding circumstances.

Where the discriminatory provisions are integral to the scheme and cannot be severed, the wider law or chapter falls (at least as applied to the affected lands); otherwise invalidity may be confined to the offending provision.

Negative equality: a person cannot claim repetition of an unlawful benefit given to others; the equality claim in withdrawal or release cases succeeds only where the comparators were lawfully treated and the State alleges no illegality.
No equality claim arises where the acquisition and vesting predated the Constitution.
Separate opinion in one member (progressive compensation) treated ability to bear loss as a relevant basis and would have upheld the rates.
Some members also rest on additional grounds (the former Article 19(1)(f), absence of hearing); these are not necessary for the core Article 14 rule.

common_material_facts: Landowners or properties alike in relation to the law's object receive different compensation, assessment, selection, exemption or release.
The State offers no explanation, or an explanation unrelated to the law's objective, for the differential treatment.
Special or modified acquisition regimes give lower compensation or fewer rights than the ordinary acquisition law for the same public purpose.
Uniform tax or assessment bases (floor area, flat minimum rates) are applied to materially dissimilar buildings or land.
Artificial family definitions or progressive compensation slabs produce unequal burdens among similarly placed landholders.
Executive release or withdrawal from acquisition is granted to some owners but denied or arbitrarily given to comparable ones.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 14 of the Constitution
Article 19(1)(f) (as it then stood)
Articles 13(2), 265 and 31-A
Land Acquisition Act, 1894, sections 23(2) and 48
U.P. Nagar Mahapalika Adhiniyam, 1959
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 19 members the challenged law or State action was held to violate Article 14 and was struck down, quashed or declared void (in whole or as applied to the affected lands), or equal treatment was directed (for example, same withdrawal treatment, statutory solatium).
variations: Legislative classification challenges (tax, assessment, ceiling, compensation, creditor exclusions, regional or scheduled-factory classification) versus executive-action challenges (selective acquisition, release or withdrawal).

Some cases involve over-inclusion (dissimilar items treated alike, as in floor-area tax and assessment schemes) while others involve under-inclusion or differential treatment of like items (compensation differences, exemptions).
Remedies differ: striking down a provision, invalidating a whole chapter or law as applied, quashing rules, granting solatium, or directing the State to give comparable treatment.
Some members add Article 19(1)(f) or absence of hearing, and one rests on a regional classification whose procedure defeats the stated object.
Severability reasoning appears where discriminatory provisions are integral to the scheme.
One member notes a dissent on whether progressive compensation rates are discriminatory.

legal_question: When can an accused who pleads private defence (of person or property) establish that right, given who was the aggressor, whether there was a reasonable apprehension of danger, the weapons carried, the injuries on each side, and the credibility of the defence account?

rule.if: criminal_case_with_private_defence_plea and not accused_proved_or_made_probable_reasonable_apprehension_of_danger_justifying_force_used and (accused_found_to_be_aggressors_or_initiated_attack or defence_account_improbable_or_unsupported_by_evidence or injuries_on_accused_alone_without_corroborating_circumstances or force_used_deadly_and_disproportionate_to_threat_posed_by_unarmed_opponents)

predicates.criminal_case_with_private_defence_plea: The accused in a criminal trial or appeal claims that their violent act was justified by the right of private defence of person or property.
predicates.accused_proved_or_made_probable_reasonab: On the evidence and surrounding circumstances (including by relying on prosecution evidence), the accused has shown it probable that they faced a reasonable apprehension of danger, such as death or grievous hurt where death was caused, that justified the force used.
predicates.accused_found_to_be_aggressors_or_initia: The courts found on the evidence that the accused, often armed and prepared, started the confrontation or attack rather than responding to an attack by the other side.
predicates.defence_account_improbable_or_unsupporte: The accused's version of the incident (for example that the other side attacked first or was armed) is implausible, speculative, contradicted by eyewitness or physical evidence, or lacks any supporting material, including about how the accused were injured.
predicates.injuries_on_accused_alone_without_corrob: The only basis for the plea is injuries on the accused or their associates, and these were simple, unexplained as to cause or timing, or not linked to an attack by the victim, so the circumstances do not make the defence probable.
predicates.force_used_deadly_and_disproportionate_t: The accused used lethal or grievous force, such as firearms or edged weapons, against opponents who were unarmed, fleeing, trespassing without a threat to life, or otherwise posed no threat of death or grievous hurt.
predicates.private_defence_not_established_and_plea: The right of private defence is held not established, or exceeded, and the plea is rejected, so the conviction is upheld or sustained to that extent.

definition: A plea of private defence fails where the accused do not show, on the evidence and circumstances, a reasonable apprehension of danger justifying the force used. This typically happens where the accused were the aggressors, their account is improbable or unsupported, injuries alone are relied on, or deadly force was used against unarmed opponents posing no serious threat.
exceptions_or_limits: The accused need only make the plea probable on a balance of probabilities and may rely on prosecution evidence or circumstances without examining defence witnesses; if that standard is met, the plea can succeed.

Injuries on the accused do not by themselves establish private defence, but they can matter when the surrounding circumstances (nature, timing, cause, who was the aggressor) corroborate the defence account.

Where an accused in possession of property faces a trespasser, force to remove the trespasser is allowed, but causing death is not justified against ordinary criminal trespass without apprehension of death or grievous hurt; the right is then exceeded rather than wholly absent.
Where there is a concurrent factual finding by the courts below that the claimants were the aggressors, the Supreme Court will not ordinarily disturb it.
Failure to raise the plea expressly in a Section 313 CrPC statement does not bar the court from considering it on the surrounding circumstances.

common_material_facts: Accused arrived armed (firearms, lathis, spears, knives) against unarmed or less-armed opponents, often in land or property disputes.
Accused relied on injuries to themselves or associates, which were simple, superficial, unexplained or not linked to the victim's attack.
Eyewitness, medical or physical evidence (blood, absence of weapons at the scene, injury patterns) contradicted the defence version.
Concurrent findings of the trial court and High Court rejecting the plea.
Deadly force used where no reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt existed.
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Penal Code Sections 96-106, especially 96, 97, 99, 100, 102, 103, 104, 105
IPC Section 441 (criminal trespass)
IPC Sections 302 and 304(1)
CrPC Section 313
Section 117 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1939 (revenue entry presumption)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 19 members the private-defence plea (or the related claim that the complainant side was the aggressor) was rejected or held exceeded, and convictions were upheld or maintained. One member (1736620_1) found a right to remove a trespasser but held it exceeded, and one (1355674_2) found the accused were aggressors, so the opponents' counter-force was justified.
variations: Some members decide on who was the aggressor, others on lack of reasonable apprehension, and others on the weight of injuries.
Burden of proof (balance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt) is stated expressly only in a few members; others apply it implicitly.
Only a few members cite authority (Laxman Sahu, Vidhya Singh, Deo Narain, Rajinder and others); most apply the facts without citing cases.
Property-defence members add the limits from Sections 99, 103 and 441; person-defence members focus on apprehension of death or grievous hurt under Section 100.
1736620_1 ends in the right being exceeded (a reduced offence) rather than wholly unavailable.

legal_question: When a landlord or authority proceeds for eviction on a particular statutory ground or under a special statutory procedure, is it excused from satisfying a further prerequisite or protection (such as prior permission, a comparative-hardship inquiry, independent proof of title, a rehousing duty or tenant-protection law) because that requirement is not part of the invoked ground or is displaced by the invoked scheme?

rule.if: eviction_proceeding_under_statutory_scheme and invoked_ground_conditions_established and additional_requirement_invoked_by_opponent and (requirement_not_part_of_invoked_ground or invoked_scheme_overrides_requirement)

predicates.eviction_proceeding_under_statutory_sche: The case is an eviction or recovery-of-possession proceeding (or its execution) under a rent-control, accommodation-control or public-premises statute.
predicates.invoked_ground_conditions_established: The conditions the statute itself prescribes for the ground or special procedure actually invoked (for example bona fide need, a listed ground, the prescribed certificate, or public premises with an unauthorised occupant) have been pleaded and proved, or are otherwise satisfied.
predicates.additional_requirement_invoked_by_oppone: The tenant or occupant relies on a further requirement or protection, such as prior permission, a comparative-hardship inquiry, independent proof of ownership, a pleading requirement, residential-only letting, a rehousing duty, or protection under another tenancy law.
predicates.requirement_not_part_of_invoked_ground: On the statutory text and structure, the further requirement does not form part of the invoked ground. It may be expressly excepted for that ground, apply only to a different ground, arise only at a later stage, or be answered by estoppel or by a finding that the ground rests in substance on another basis.
predicates.invoked_scheme_overrides_requirement: The invoked special or later statutory scheme, by a non obstante clause, its purpose and policy, or its later and more specific character, prevails over the inconsistent requirement or protection in the other law.
predicates.additional_requirement_need_not_be_satis: The landlord or authority may obtain or execute eviction without complying with the further requirement, and the opponent's objection based on it fails.

definition: Where eviction is sought on a statutory ground or special procedure whose own conditions are met, a further requirement or protection drawn from another provision or statute need not be satisfied if it is not part of that ground, is expressly excepted, or is displaced by the invoked scheme's overriding or later special character.
exceptions_or_limits: The invoked ground's own conditions must still be proved, for example bona fide need (a service certificate does not itself prove it), a listed ground, or the statutory ownership period.
Estoppel against denying title does not apply where the tenant shows attornment to a paramount title holder or the landlord's subsequent loss of title.
Overriding effect applies only to the extent of actual inconsistency, and conflicts between non obstante clauses are resolved by language, purpose and policy.

Statutory restrictions that are part of the invoked ground itself still apply. An example is the statutory postponement of executing a residential-need eviction order, which operates automatically by law, even if the order does not recite it.
Where the order is truly based on the ground that carries the extra duty (for example solely on reconstruction), that duty is not displaced.

outlier_members.reason: It holds that a statutory restriction on executing an eviction order applies automatically without being recited. This concerns the effect of the order, not the removal of a prerequisite to eviction, and it points the opposite way from the rest of the cluster.

common_material_facts: A landlord or public authority seeks eviction on a specific statutory ground such as bona fide need, wilful non-payment, unlawful subletting, material alteration, or unauthorised occupation of public premises.
The tenant or occupant invokes an extra hurdle: prior slum-area or District Magistrate permission, comparative hardship, proof of title, a rehousing duty, or rent-control protection.
The invoked scheme has a non obstante clause, is later or more specific in time, or is expressly excepted from the hurdle.
statutes_and_provisions: Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act 1956, ss. 19 and 39
Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act 1971, including s. 15
U.P. Cantonments (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act 1952, s. 14(1)
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act 1947, s. 3(1)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act 1947, ss. 13(1)(g), 13(2), 13A-1
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act 1961, ss. 12(1)(f), 12(1)(h), 18
Karnataka Rent Control Act 1961, s. 21(4)
East Punjab Urban Land Restriction Act 1949, s. 13-B
Evidence Act 1872, s. 116
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 18 covered members the landlord or authority prevails because the extra requirement is held inapplicable or displaced. About 6 members resolve a conflict with slum-area permission, 2 resolve a conflict with rent-control protection in favour of public premises, 2 or 3 address the District Magistrate's permission, 3 address comparative hardship, 2 address title and estoppel, and 2 address reconstruction.
variations: Some members rest on overriding or later special legislation (slum permission, public premises). Others rest on a plain reading of the ground's text (alternative grounds, listed exceptions, hardship considered only at a later stage). Others rest on evidentiary estoppel under s. 116.
Some members free the landlord from a duty. Others free the landlord from a tenant's defence or protection (public premises over rent control).
The reconstruction members turn on the substance or principal basis of the order, or on the tenant disclaiming the reconstruction ground below.
One member (1319723_2) goes the other way: a statutory limitation operates by law without being recited.

split_suggestion: If a tighter rule is needed, split into: (1) overriding special or later law over slum-area permission or tenant-protection law (1220782_2, 1575265_1, 768853_1, 823591_1, 6571_2, 6571_3, 453977_4); (2) permission exempted for listed or independent grounds (1664566_2, 1821913_2, 1073776_1); (3) comparative hardship not required (1053321_4, 1094547_4, 829250_2); (4) title, ownership and estoppel (109405390_1, 1254746_1); (5) the ground's own scope, covering reconstruction versus personal need and mixed use (1002519_1, 152387_2, 1187427_2). Place 1319723_2 separately.

legal_question: When may a court permit amendment of a pleading in a pending civil proceeding under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, in particular where the amendment supplies particulars, adds or alters relief, or is sought after limitation has expired, without changing the nature of the suit or causing irremediable prejudice?

rule.if: pleading_amendment_application_in_pending_civil_proceeding and amendment_necessary_to_determine_real_controversy and not amendment_changes_nature_of_suit_or_substitutes_new_cause_of_action and not opposing_party_suffers_irremediable_prejudice_beyond_costs and (amendment_stage_is_pretrial or due_diligence_shown_or_amendment_is_formal_on_pleaded_facts)

predicates.pleading_amendment_application_in_pendin: A party has applied to amend a plaint or other pleading in a civil suit or proceeding that is still pending.
predicates.amendment_necessary_to_determine_real_co: The proposed amendment helps decide the real questions in controversy between the parties, for example by supplying particulars, completing or correcting the relief, or covering related events or disputes already in issue.
predicates.amendment_changes_nature_of_suit_or_subs: The amendment would change the basic nature or subject matter of the suit or replace the existing cause of action with a distinct one.
predicates.opposing_party_suffers_irremediable_prej: The amendment would cause the other side injury that cannot be compensated by costs, such as taking away an accrued right or defence, or leaving the other side unable to meet the amended case.
predicates.amendment_stage_is_pretrial: The application was made before the trial began.
predicates.due_diligence_shown_or_amendment_is_form: If the trial has begun, the party shows that the matter could not have been raised earlier despite due diligence, or the amendment only formalises relief on facts already pleaded and tried.
predicates.amendment_should_be_allowed_on_terms: The court should permit the amendment, usually subject to costs and to giving the opponent an opportunity to respond, for example by an additional written statement.

definition: Under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, courts take a liberal approach and allow amendments that are needed to decide the real controversy, provided they do not change the nature of the suit or introduce a new cause of action and do not cause prejudice that costs cannot cure. Expiry of limitation, delay, or a resulting change in forum or valuation does not by itself bar the amendment; these are factors in the court's discretion, and a disputed limitation question can be left for trial.
exceptions_or_limits: Amendment is refused where it introduces a new or different cause of action or changes the basic nature of the suit.
Amendment is refused where it sets up a fresh time-barred claim and deprives the opponent of a defence or accrued right that costs cannot compensate.

Where the application is made after trial has commenced, the proviso requires that the matter could not have been raised earlier despite due diligence, unless the amendment is purely formal on facts already pleaded and tried.
Amendment is not a matter of right; the court has discretion and does not decide the merits of the amended claim at the amendment stage.
Amendment should not be allowed where it withdraws an admission that gave the other side a right.

outlier_members.reason: This concerns whether an appellate court should remand after a formal amendment, not whether the amendment should be allowed. It is related but separate.

common_material_facts: A plaintiff seeks to add or alter relief, such as declaration, possession, redemption, damages or a formal declaration, in a pending suit.
The facts supporting the amendment are already pleaded, or the amendment only supplies particulars or corrects wording.
Lower courts refused the amendment on grounds of limitation, change in the nature of the suit, or delay, and the Supreme Court reversed them.
The application was often made before trial, and the defendant could file an additional written statement.
Allowing the amendment would avoid a separate suit or multiplicity of proceedings.
statutes_and_provisions: Order VI Rule 17 CPC
Order VI Rule 2 CPC
Order I Rule 1 CPC
Section 16(c) Specific Relief Act, 1963
Order XXI Rules 97, 99 and 103 CPC
Section 39 U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972

Leading cases: Pirgonda Hongonda Patil v. Kalgonda Shidgonda Patil; L.J. Leach v. Jardine Skinner; Charan Das v. Amir Khan; A.K. Gupta v. Damodar Valley Corp.; B.K.N. Pillai v. P. Pillai; Pankaja v. Yellappa; Revajeetu Builders
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 18 of 19 members the amendment is allowed, often subject to costs and a chance for the opponent to respond, and orders refusing it are set aside. The remaining member sets aside an unnecessary remand after a formal amendment.
variations: Some members involve limitation expiry (1294056_1, 1100890_1), where limitation is treated as a discretionary factor. Others leave a disputed limitation issue for trial (301256_1, 79183688_1).
Some amendments are made before trial (1033493_1, 104860043_1, 79183688_1), while others are allowed after evidence has been led, as formal relief on pleaded and tried facts (533346_2, 74585509_2).
The amendment types vary: particulars, new relief such as declaration, possession or redemption, valuation correction, enhanced damages, correction of wording, and events during the suit.
Reasoning varies between a general liberal approach and a specific finding of no new cause of action (104860043_2, 1732740_3).

split_suggestion: Optionally, treat 1533893_5 (remand after a formal amendment) separately, and treat the limitation-specific members (104860043_2, 1732740_3, 301256_1) as a sub-cluster on limitation and new cause of action.

legal_question: When is a land-reform or resource-distribution law (or the constitutional amendment protecting it) immune from challenge under the equality, freedom and property provisions of the Constitution, and what connection to agrarian reform or to distribution of material resources for the common good is needed for that immunity?

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_law_or_amend: The validity of a land-related statute, rule or constitutional amendment is challenged as violating equality, freedom, property rights or the basic structure.
predicates.law_forms_part_of_agrarian_reform_or_giv: The measure, judged by substance and dominant purpose, is agrarian reform (for example land ceilings, surplus-land redistribution, tenancy reform, common-purpose reservation, vesting of estates or grants) or gives effect to distributing the community's material resources for the common good.
predicates.required_nexus_or_dominant_purpose_shown: The law has a real, not fanciful, connection to the agrarian-reform or common-good distribution objective, and any ancillary provisions merely support that dominant purpose; a broad view of 'distribution' (allocation, allotment, apportionment) is taken.
predicates.applicable_protective_provision_conditio: The formal conditions of the relevant protective provision are satisfied (for example presidential assent where required, the subject matter falling within the protected category such as an estate, jagir or inam, or the law being a protected amendment), and no express declaration is needed where the law's contents show the policy.
predicates.law_is_protected_from_fundamental_rights: The law cannot be successfully challenged under the covered fundamental rights (equality, freedom, property/compensation), and it does not damage the basic structure.

definition: A law that is genuinely part of agrarian reform, or gives effect to the distribution of community material resources for the common good, is shielded from equality, freedom and property challenges (and does not offend the basic structure) once the required nexus and the formal conditions of the protective provision are met. The shield does not extend to acquisitions unconnected with agrarian reform.
exceptions_or_limits: Protection for estate-acquisition laws applies only where the measure is connected with agrarian reform; a bare transfer of rights or acquisition for unrelated purposes such as general housing schemes is not protected.
A merely fanciful connection to agrarian-reform or rural-welfare purposes is insufficient; land used for unrelated purposes may be restrained.
Where the protective provision requires presidential assent, it must have been obtained.

Laws outside the protected categories remain subject to ordinary constitutional requirements, for example public purpose and compensation for acquisition of State-owned property, and statutory safeguards in emergency acquisition (on which the judges differed and the matter was referred to a larger Bench).
Challenges to the protective constitutional provision itself are tested only against the basic structure, and the right to property is not a basic feature.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns whether Article 300A requires compliance with statutory advance-payment safeguards in emergency acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act. It is not about the agrarian-reform shield, and the judges split and referred the matter.
Concerns whether State-owned property is protected by the Article 31(2) acquisition requirements of public purpose and compensation. It is not about agrarian-reform or common-good immunity.

common_material_facts: Land ceilings, surplus-land acquisition and redistribution to landless tillers or agriculturists
Vesting of estates, jagirs, inams, janmam rights or forests in the State as part of land reform
Consolidation or village-planning reservation of land for common purposes without compensation
Petitioners invoking Articles 14, 19 and 31 or the basic structure against the reform
Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule or enacted with presidential assent
statutes_and_provisions: Article 31A (including 31A(1)(a) and 31A(2)(a))
Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule
Article 31C
Article 39(b) and 39(c)
Articles 14, 19(1)(f), 31 and 300A
Article 368 and Article 13(2)
Entry 18 of List II and Entry 42 of List III
Ranjit Singh, Kochuni, Kesavananda Bharati, Waman Rao, Minerva Mills and Sanjeev Coke
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About 15 of 17 covered members uphold the law or amendment as protected agrarian reform or common-good distribution and reject the challenge. 1634289_1 holds that a housing-acquisition law unconnected with agrarian reform is not protected. 1576124_2 is a definitional step holding that a jagir or inam grant is an estate. Two outliers on acquisition safeguards are excluded.
variations: Some members rely on Article 31A (agrarian reform and estates), others on Article 31C read with Article 39(b) (nexus to distribution of material resources), and others on the basic-structure limit on amendments.
Some members treat the protection as depending on dominant purpose, with ancillary measures not defeating it; others require a close nexus to the common good.
Protection extends beyond land redistribution to common rural purposes, forests, mineral resources, housing sites and amenities.
Presidential assent is stressed in some members but not in others.
One member (1634289_1) shows the limit: no agrarian-reform connection means no protection.

split_suggestion: Keep a core group on agrarian-reform and common-good protection under Articles 31A and 31C. Optionally separate the basic-structure amendment cases (799151_1, 1515136_4, 553582_1) and the estate-definition cases (1576124_2, 1576124_3). Move 56073873_7 and 603736_4 to a separate cluster on constitutional safeguards for compulsory acquisition and deprivation of property.

legal_question: In a summary eviction proceeding where the tenant must obtain leave to contest or defend, when must the Controller or court grant leave, and when may it refuse leave?

predicates.summary_eviction_leave_stage: The landlord seeks possession through a special or summary rent-control procedure in which the tenant must apply, usually by affidavit, for leave to contest or defend.
predicates.tenant_affidavit_discloses_facts_that_if: The tenant's application or affidavit states facts, as opposed to proof, which if accepted at trial could defeat a ground the landlord must establish, such as bona fide need, absence of alternative accommodation, ownership or landlord status, the existence of a tenancy, or the purpose of letting. These facts raise a genuine triable issue.
predicates.defence_is_bare_vague_sham_or_outside_st: The tenant's defence consists of bare or unsupported assertions, is illusory, frivolous or contradicted by the tenant's own sworn position, or rests on matters that cannot defeat the statutory ground for recovery.
predicates.leave_to_contest_must_be_granted: The Controller or court must give the tenant leave to contest or defend, and the dispute is then decided after the tenant is allowed to contest and prove the defence. Leave may be conditional, for example on depositing arrears of rent.

definition: In summary eviction proceedings, leave to contest must be granted where the tenant's affidavit discloses facts which, if proved, could disentitle the landlord from possession and which raise a genuine triable issue. The leave stage concerns disclosure, not proof, so the Controller must not decide disputed facts on affidavits. Leave may be refused where the defence is bare, vague, sham, estopped or irrelevant to the statutory grounds.
exceptions_or_limits: Leave is not granted on mere assertion. Unsupported allegations about alternative accommodation, or grounds outside the matters the landlord must establish, do not suffice.
A defence contradicted by the tenant's own sworn acknowledgment, or found sham, illusory or moonshine, does not raise a triable issue.
Where the special provision confines the inquiry to specific statutory grounds (for example section 14A or section 13-B), only facts negating those grounds count.
The test is not the Order XXXVII CPC 'substantial defence' test. It is narrower and focused on disclosure of facts that could disentitle the landlord.
Leave may be made conditional on depositing arrears and continuing to pay rent.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns judgment on admissions under Order XII Rule 6 CPC in an ordinary eviction suit, not leave to contest under a special rent-control procedure. It is analogous (no summary decree where a root-level defence is disputed) but rests on a different provision.
Concerns judgment on admissions under Order XII Rule 6 CPC in a possession suit where a sale-agreement defence needs evidence. It is a different procedural route from leave to contest.
A civil injunction suit between a father-in-law and daughter-in-law, decided under Order XII Rule 6 CPC. It is not a landlord-tenant leave-to-contest case.

Concerns the burden on a tenant to plead and prove circumstances against eviction once a statutory ground is established, where the Rent Controller has discretion under section 13(2). It is not a leave-stage question.
Concerns proof of alternative accommodation and the rejection of judicial notice in a comparative-hardship assessment. It is not a leave-to-contest question.
Concerns whether a revision against refusal of leave should be heard on its merits rather than dismissed for delay or procedural reasons. It does not decide the test for granting leave.

common_material_facts: The landlord seeks summary eviction, most often for bona fide personal or residential need.
The tenant files an affidavit seeking leave to contest or defend.
The tenant disputes need, alternative accommodation, ownership or landlord status, the existence of a tenancy, or the purpose of letting.
The Controller refused leave after deciding disputed facts on affidavits, or on vague or unsupported assertions.
statutes_and_provisions: Delhi Rent Control Act 1958, sections 14(1)(e), 14A, 25B(4), 25B(5) and related sub-sections
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act 1949, sections 13-B, 18-A(4) and 18-A(5)
Bihar Buildings (Lease Rent and Eviction) Control Act 1982, section 14(4) and (5)
Order XXXVII CPC, rejected as an analogue
Order XII Rule 6 CPC (outlier members)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 13 covered members, leave was granted or held required in about 9 (1025530_1, 1187427_4 as the test, 1323229_1, 1331869_1, 1331869_5, 158079666_1, 1594520_1, 370236_1, 378172_1; 1977447_2 states the same test). Leave was refused or the refusal upheld in 3 where the defence was vague, sham or irrelevant (1020200_2, 141468481_2, 171435_2). The remaining member (1977447_2) states the test and confines it to the statutory grounds.
variations: Some members stress that the Controller must not weigh disputed facts at the leave stage. Others stress that unsupported or sham defences may be rejected.
The grounds raised vary: alternative accommodation, bona fide need, landlord status or title, the tenancy relationship, mixed-purpose letting, and a sale agreement.
Some members cite earlier cases (Santosh Kumar, Charan Das Duggal, Mangat Ram). Others cite none.
Leave is sometimes conditional on depositing arrears (158079666_1).
Under the NRI-specific provision, the inquiry is confined to the matters the landlord must prove under that section.

split_suggestion: Keep the 13 leave-to-contest members as the core cluster. Move the three Order XII Rule 6 judgment-on-admission members (109034285_1, 94788381_1, 62368827_2) into a separate cluster on summary decrees on admissions where a material defence is disputed. Treat 1178802_3 and 562631_3 (burden of proof on discretion or hardship) and 1872012_2 (revision procedure) as separate singletons.

legal_question: Does a person who qualifies as a tenant under a protective tenancy or rent-control statute keep tenant status and protection against eviction after a general-law event (expiry of a fixed term, termination, an eviction decree, absence of an allotment order, or the lessor's death), so that eviction is possible only on a statutory ground and through the prescribed process?

rule.if: statutory_tenancy_regime_applies and occupant_within_statutory_tenant_definition and general_law_event_would_otherwise_end_tenancy and not (statutory_eviction_ground_established or tenancy_ended_by_prescribed_statutory_process) and not statute_expressly_excludes_occupant

predicates.statutory_tenancy_regime_applies: A protective land-tenancy or rent-control statute governs the premises or land and restricts eviction of tenants.
predicates.occupant_within_statutory_tenant_definit: The occupant falls within the statute's definition of tenant, for example because the definition includes a person continuing in possession after termination, a person from whom rent is payable, or a cultivating tenant.
predicates.general_law_event_would_otherwise_end_te: A general-law event has occurred that would end or defeat the tenancy outside the statute, such as expiry of a fixed term, notice of termination, an eviction decree, a lease made without an allotment order, a lessor's death, or letting out of structures on the land.
predicates.statutory_eviction_ground_established: The landlord has proved one of the grounds on which the statute permits eviction.
predicates.tenancy_ended_by_prescribed_statutory_pr: The tenancy has been ended by a lawful eviction, relinquishment, or termination carried out in the manner the statute prescribes (for example the designated revenue authority or required permission or notice).
predicates.statute_expressly_excludes_occupant: The statutory definition or a provision expressly excludes the occupant, for example a person against whom an eviction decree has already been made.
predicates.tenant_status_and_statutory_protection_c: The occupant remains a tenant with the statute's protection, and the landlord can recover possession only on a statutory ground through the prescribed procedure.

definition: Where a protective tenancy statute defines tenant to cover a person who continues in possession, or otherwise covers the occupant, the end of the contractual or general-law tenancy does not remove tenant status. The tenant stays protected and can be evicted only on the statute's grounds and by its procedure, and a civil claim or decree resting only on expiry, termination or a similar event fails.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule yields where the statute expressly excludes the occupant, for example a person already subject to an eviction decree under that Act's own definition.
It does not apply once a statutory eviction ground is proved or the tenancy is ended by the prescribed process, such as court eviction or relinquishment.

Protection depends on the particular statute's wording, so the same facts can give different results under different statutes. The Karnataka land-reform member shows that continued tenancy can also trigger statutory consequences adverse to the tenant, here a company's prohibition on holding agricultural land.
A statute that expressly restricts succession or imposes qualifications can limit the protection passing to heirs. Prospective amendments do not divest rights vested before they took effect.
One member (107607168_1) expressed its view in conflict with an earlier decision and referred the point to a larger Bench, so the point is not settled.

outlier_members.reason: The issue is the temporal operation of a prospective amendment on vested succession rights, not whether tenant protection survives termination.
The issue is whether ordinary agricultural tenancy rights are heritable under personal law. No termination or holding-over is involved.
The issue is whether ordinary tenancy rights are heritable under personal law in the absence of a special statutory rule. No termination or holding-over is involved.
The issue is heirs acquiring a non-residential tenancy under a statutory definition that includes heirs. It concerns succession, not survival of protection after termination.
The issue is the timing of the continuous-tenancy period needed to exercise a statutory right to purchase proprietary rights.

common_material_facts: A tenant stayed in possession after a lease expired, a tenancy was terminated, or an eviction decree was passed.
The landlord sought possession by a civil suit, execution, or ejectment without a statutory ground or the prescribed procedure.
The statutory definition of tenant included a person continuing in possession or a person paying rent.
Some tenants died and their heirs claimed continued protection.
The lease was made without an allotment order, or the lessor was a life-estate holder who died.
statutes_and_provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act 1953, ss 2(6), 9, 14-A, with Punjab Tenancy Act 1887, ss 4(5), 40
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act 1949, ss 2(i), 13(1)
Delhi Rent Control Act 1958, ss 2(1)(ii), 14
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act 1950, ss 3(vii), 13(1)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act 1961, ss 2(i), 14
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act 1947, ss 2(g), 3(1)
Karnataka Land Reforms Act, ss 5, 6, 79-B
Himachal Pradesh Abolition of Big Landed Estates and Land Reforms Act, s 11(1)
Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act 1955, ss 2(aa), 3
Non-agricultural Urban Areas Tenancy Act 1955, s 5(1)(a)
Transfer of Property Act 1882, ss 106, 116
Rent Act s 21(1) and s 3(r) (statute not named in the member)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 13 of the 14 covered members, the tenant or heirs were held to retain tenant status and protection, and eviction, execution or the civil suit failed or was barred. The exception is the Karnataka company, where continued tenancy led to a statutory vesting in the State. The outliers mostly concern heritability or timing and also favour the tenant or heirs.
variations: The trigger differs: expiry of a fixed term, notice of termination, an eviction decree or compromise, no allotment order, the lessor's death, or letting out of structures.
Some members are agricultural land-tenancy cases and others are urban rent-control cases.
Several members extend the protection to heirs, with commercial and residential premises treated differently where the statute restricts residential succession.
A later-applicable rent restriction was held to bar execution of an earlier decree, but a statute that expressly excludes decree-affected persons ends the protection.
The reasoning rests on beneficial construction of the statute, on the statutory definition of tenant, or on holding-over under s 116 TPA.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) survival of tenant status and protection after expiry, termination, decree or lack of allotment, which is the core group; (b) heritability and succession to tenancy (1327310_1, 1887042_1, 1584099_1, 1327310_2, 158115_1, 1464257_3, 390420_3); and (c) statutory rights and conditions of tenants such as purchase of proprietary rights, notice at the agricultural year end, and non-forfeiture on letting out (165933_2, 1323567_1, 1385220_2, 1879186_2).

legal_question: Does an existing tenancy or subordinate interest continue despite an intervening event (partial acquisition of the reversion, merger of interests, statutory abolition or vesting, a termination notice or pending possession proceeding, a third-party title suit, or wrongful dispossession) that does not satisfy the legally prescribed requirements for ending it?
