rule.if: existing_tenancy_or_subordinate_interest and intervening_event_occurred and not event_satisfies_legal_requirements_for_termination and not clear_intention_or_express_statutory_provision_ending_interest

predicates.existing_tenancy_or_subordinate_interest: A valid tenancy, lease or subordinate interest (such as a raiyati interest) existed when the intervening event occurred.
predicates.intervening_event_occurred: An event occurred that is said to end the tenancy: a partial acquisition of the reversion or a unity of holding, abolition or vesting of the landlord's interest, a termination notice or pending possession or ejectment proceeding, a suit by a superior claimant, a change in the landlord's identity, or wrongful dispossession.
predicates.event_satisfies_legal_requirements_for_t: The event meets the conditions the governing law sets for ending a tenancy, such as vesting of the lessor's and lessee's interests in the whole property in one person at the same time and in the same right, an order or decree of the competent authority, or the commencement of a provision extinguishing the relationship.
predicates.clear_intention_or_express_statutory_pro: The parties' clear intention to merge or end the interest is shown, or a statutory provision already in force expressly extinguishes the landlord-tenant relationship.
predicates.tenancy_or_subordinate_interest_continue: The tenancy or subordinate interest remains subsisting, with the tenant's rights and obligations (including statutory purchase, pre-emption or rent-control rights and duties) unaffected by the event.

definition: An existing tenancy or subordinate interest is not ended by a partial acquisition of the reversion, a unity of holding of non-higher/lower interests, abolition or vesting, a termination notice or pending proceeding, a third-party title suit, or wrongful dispossession, unless the legally prescribed mode of termination is completed or a clear intention or an operative statutory provision ends it. The tenant's statutory rights and obligations therefore continue.
exceptions_or_limits: Merger does end a lease where the lessor's and lessee's interests in the whole property vest simultaneously in one person in the same right with no intervening or outstanding interest.
A subordinate interest can merge where a clear intention to merge is shown, apart from statute.
Where a statutory provision extinguishing the landlord-tenant relationship has come into force, or an eviction order or decree has been validly made before the relevant date, the relationship ends.

The conclusions depend on the particular statute in each case (for example the Transfer of Property Act s.111(d), the Hyderabad and Bombay tenancy and abolition statutes, and the Punjab, Pepsu and Tamil Nadu statutes) and should not be extended beyond the provisions considered.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns whether a nontransferability condition on a regrant bars a tenant's purchase right under s.32G(6). That is a statutory limit on a condition, not the continuation of a tenancy after an intervening event.

It concerns the scope of a special recovery remedy that applies only to tenancies created on or after a cutoff date. It is an applicability question under s.39, not termination or continuation of a tenancy.

It concerns whether a registered covenant to demolish and surrender falls within a statutory exception to a tenant's purchase right. That is a question of contractual override of statutory protection, not termination by an intervening event.

common_material_facts: A landlord-tenant relationship or subordinate holding existed before the event said to end it.
The tenant or occupant acquired only some co-owners' or part of the landlord's interest, or held a lease and a mortgage in different capacities.
Abolition, vesting or acquisition of the landlord's estate was said to terminate existing tenancies.
A notice, a pending ejectment or possession application, or a superior-title suit was filed, but no final order ended the tenancy.
The party seeking a termination had an interest in asserting merger or extinction.
statutes_and_provisions: Transfer of Property Act 1882, ss.105, 109, 111(d), 44, 58 and 101
Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act 1950, ss.32(2) and 44(1)
Hyderabad Abolition of Inams Act 1954, ss.3 and 33
Hyderabad Abolition of Inams and Cash Grants Act 1954, s.6(1)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act 1948, ss.32, 32-O and 32G
Bombay Merged Territories Miscellaneous Alienations Abolition Act 1955, ss.4-9 and 28
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act 1953, ss.9, 14-A and 18
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act 1955, ss.4, 7 and 7A
Great Eastern Hotel (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act 1980, ss.4(1) and 4(2)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act 1960, s.2(6)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 16 covered members the tenancy or subordinate interest was held to continue, so the tenant kept eviction protection, purchase or pre-emption rights, or rent-control obligations. About 7 of these turn on the Transfer of Property Act merger doctrine (partial reversion, lease and mortgage), about 7 on abolition, vesting, notice or pending proceedings, and 2 on a raiyati interest not merging.
variations: Some members apply statutory merger under s.111(d) of the Transfer of Property Act, while others apply the general doctrine of merger by intention (raiyati interest) or state-specific abolition and tenancy statutes.

Some members protect the tenant's continuing rights, such as purchase or pre-emption, while others confirm the tenant's continuing duties, such as rent deposit or delivery of possession at the end of the tenancy.
A few members turn on the timing of commencement of provisions or on whether an order was passed before a cutoff date.
In the lease-and-mortgage members the reason is that neither is a higher or lower estate than the other, rather than partial acquisition of the reversion.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) merger cases (108721012_1, 500624_1, 628977_2, 362062_1, 601351_1, 876929_2, 1578099_1, 1578099_2); (b) continuation of tenancy after abolition, vesting, acquisition, notice or pending proceedings (1126588_3, 1295163_1, 1295163_2, 1295956_1, 1338325_1, 32246_1, 628271_3, 739777_1); and (c) statutory limits on tenant protection or remedies (1295163_3, 1377832_3, 493375_1).

legal_question: Does an entry in revenue, mutation, settlement or similar fiscal records (including occupancy entries, pattas and municipal tax entries) establish or transfer title to immovable property, or is it only evidence of possession or liability to pay revenue?

predicates.title_to_immovable_property_in_dispute: Ownership or title to land or other immovable property is contested in the proceeding.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_revenue_or_fiscal_rec: The claimant relies on a revenue record, mutation entry, record-of-rights entry, occupant entry, settlement patta, municipal tax entry or similar fiscal record as proof of ownership.
predicates.independent_title_established_by_valid_i: The claimant has proved title through a valid transfer instrument, such as a registered deed, or other cogent evidence independent of the fiscal entry.
predicates.entry_does_not_establish_or_transfer_tit: The entry neither creates, transfers nor extinguishes title and has no presumptive value as to title; it may at most support a rebuttable inference of possession or show who is liable for revenue or tax.

definition: Revenue, mutation, settlement, patta and municipal tax entries are fiscal or administrative records; they do not create, transfer or extinguish title. They may support a rebuttable presumption of possession or show liability for revenue, but title must be proved by independent evidence.
exceptions_or_limits: Revenue entries may carry evidentiary value, even strong prima facie value, and a rebuttable presumption of possession, but they are not conclusive of title.
Where there is no or very little proof of ownership, lawful possession may support a rebuttable presumption of title; this does not arise where the facts disclose a competing title.
Long-standing entries and tax payments may be considered with other evidence, and entries made after a dispute arose carry little weight.
Non-production of revenue records does not defeat title where the missing records do not affect title.
A statutory scheme may make a revenue authority's determination final on matters entrusted to it, but only within that scheme.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the effect of non-production of revenue records on established title, not whether a revenue entry proves title. It is related but is a different point.

common_material_facts: A party relies on a mutation, occupancy, record-of-rights, patta or tax entry to claim ownership.
No registered or valid transfer instrument, or no other independent evidence of title, was produced.
Entries were often made after the dispute arose or during pending litigation, or recorded only occupancy or possession.
Competing title, often the Government's, or an unproved gift, sale or heirship was in issue.
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Evidence Act, 1872, ss. 35, 110 and 114
Madras Minor Inams (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1963, ss. 3, 8, 11, 12, 43 and 46
Land Registration Act, 1876 (Register D)
Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 6
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, s. 145
Indian Penal Code, 1860, ss. 154 and 158
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 17 of 18 members the Court held that the entry did not establish or transfer title, usually allowing it as evidence of possession or revenue liability. One member (162171512_5) is an outlier. In most members the claim failed or the lower court's reliance on the entry was reversed.
variations: Mutation entries are described as fiscal enquiries with no presumptive value, while record-of-rights entries and Register D entries are admissible and may carry a rebuttable presumption, in some cases strong prima facie evidence.
Some members hold the entry supports a presumption of possession; others hold it wholly inconsequential, as where a forest-transfer record or unproved instrument was involved.
Patta and settlement cases turn on the limited scope of the statutory process; municipal tax records turn on the governing scheme.
One member finds title follows possession for open land; another finds the possession presumption displaced by proof of the Government's title.
Some members cite Sawarni, Balwant Singh and Nirman Singh; others state the principle without citing authority.

legal_question: When does an amendment apply to proceedings that were pending when it took effect, or to claims and events that arose before it, rather than operating only prospectively?

rule.if: amendment_in_force_and_relevant_to_dispute and (transitional_or_express_provision_covers_the_proceeding or amendment_is_procedural_without_affecting_vested_substantive_rights or amendment_is_clarificatory_or_declaratory_of_existing_law or retrospective_intent_clearly_inferred_from_language_and_connected_provisions) and not exclusion_or_saving_for_the_proceeding_applies

predicates.amendment_in_force_and_relevant_to_dispu: The amending provision has come into force and bears on the issue the court must decide in the proceeding or claim.
predicates.transitional_or_express_provision_covers: The amending Act, through a transitional clause, a retrospectivity or deeming clause, or a pending-proceedings clause, expressly extends the amendment to this kind of proceeding. It may do so by reference to a cut-off date or to the stage reached, for example whether an award had been made or the proceeding began after a given date.
predicates.amendment_is_procedural_without_affectin: The amendment governs only procedure, evidence or method, such as the mode of recovery, valuation method or res judicata, and does not create, alter or take away substantive rights or liabilities.
predicates.amendment_is_clarificatory_or_declarator: The amendment merely clarifies, declares or cures doubt or conflict about what the earlier law already meant, rather than changing it prejudicially.
predicates.retrospective_intent_clearly_inferred_fr: Although retrospectivity is not stated for this provision, the language, context and linked provisions show unequivocally that the legislature intended it to operate retrospectively.
predicates.exclusion_or_saving_for_the_proceeding_a: The amending Act expressly excludes the provision from the general rule for pending proceedings, or contains a saving that protects this proceeding.
predicates.amendment_applies_to_the_pending_or_earl: The amended law governs the pending proceeding or the earlier-arising claim, or a later proceeding or award that relies on earlier facts, to the extent the amendment covers it.

definition: An amendment governs a pending proceeding, or a claim that arose before it, where the legislature has said so expressly or by transitional provision, where it is purely procedural, where it only clarifies existing law, or where retrospective intent is clearly implied. A substantive amendment without such indications operates only prospectively, although it can still apply to acts such as awards made after commencement in proceedings that began earlier.
exceptions_or_limits: A substantive provision that creates or alters rights is prospective unless the statutory language or necessary intendment shows retrospective intent, as for the redetermination remedy and the additional-amount provision.
An amendment that is prospective does not reopen concluded awards or decisions made before commencement. It can apply to a later award or decision made in a proceeding pending at commencement.

Transitional provisions apply only to the categories and cut-off dates they specify, for example proceedings pending on the bill's introduction with no Collector's award by then, or proceedings commenced after a stated date.

An express exclusion or saving for pending proceedings displaces the general rule that procedural amendments apply to them. Absent express words, no saving for pending litigation will be implied in an expressly retrospective amendment.
An express retrospective amendment is applied according to its plain terms, even if the legislature enacted it on a mistaken assumption about the law.

common_material_facts: A proceeding (suit, appeal, acquisition, reference or assessment) was pending, or a claim had arisen, when the amending law took effect.
The amending Act contained a transitional clause, a pending-proceedings clause or a deeming-retrospectivity clause.
The amendment was described as procedural, evidentiary, clarificatory or declaratory.
In land acquisition cases, the Collector's or court's award date, the date possession was taken and a statutory cut-off date determined whether the benefit applied.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 23(1-A), 28-A, 18 and 3(d)
Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984, Section 30(1)(a) and (b)
Code of Civil Procedure Amendment Act, 1976, Section 97(3)
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, Section 48
Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966
Income Tax Act, 1961, Sections 22 and 27(iii), (iiia), (iiib)
Land Acquisition (Andhra Pradesh Amendment and Validation) Act, 1983, Sections 1(3) and 2
Gujarat Amendment Act, 1965, Sections 7 and 18 (Sections 43C and 88(1)(b) of the tenancy law)
Pre-emption law amendment of 1964 (Section 15(2)(b)) and Section 31 of the 1960 amendment
Tenure and land-reform amendment provisions, including Sections 4 and 7 and Sections 157(1)(a) and 21(h)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 19 members the amendment was held to apply to the pending proceeding or earlier-arising claim, or to the later award or proceeding at issue. About 8 rest on transitional or express retrospective language, about 4 on the procedural character of the change, about 4 on a clarificatory or declaratory character, and 1 on inference from connected provisions. One member (1806862_3) applies the amendment only prospectively, but still allows it to operate on awards made after commencement in references pending at commencement.
variations: Some members rest on express statutory text, such as Section 97(3), Section 30(1) and the deeming clauses. Others rest on judicial characterisation of the amendment as procedural or clarificatory.

Land acquisition members turn on how the transitional cut-off interacts with the award date: no award by the cut-off, a proceeding commenced after the cut-off, a reference court award after commencement, or a court award made before commencement.
Some members extend the amendment to proceedings initiated after commencement as well as pending ones (the evacuee property recovery and fresh-declaration acquisition members).
The redetermination member shows the limit: a substantive remedy is prospective and does not reopen concluded awards.
One member infers retrospectivity for a linked provision so that another provision's express retrospectivity is not neutralised.

split_suggestion: The members share one theme, the temporal reach of amendments to pending or earlier matters. If a finer split is wanted, divide them into (a) the Land Acquisition Act Section 23(1-A) and Section 28-A transitional-provision members (1296921_3, 1698351_1, 1806862_3, 183116_1, 183116_2, 812937_3, 845127_1), (b) procedural-amendment members (1315480_1, 1401686_3, 1463870_2, 1842039_2), and (c) clarificatory or express-retrospectivity members (1338345_4, 147362898_4, 1658374_1, 21176_1, 242594_2, 289533_1, 518414_2, 82667_2).

legal_question: Does an earlier proceeding that ended without a reasoned decision on the merits (a non-speaking or in limine dismissal, refusal of special leave, withdrawal, or dismissal for laches or alternative remedy) bar a later proceeding on the same matter through res judicata, merger or precedent?

rule.if: later_proceeding_raised and earlier_proceeding_ended_without_merits_determination and not earlier_issue_decided_on_merits_by_speaking_order and not earlier_findings_relevant_to_later_claim

predicates.later_proceeding_raised: A later writ, suit, review, appeal or special leave proceeding has been brought on the same matter, or on a related issue, that was before an earlier forum.
predicates.earlier_proceeding_ended_without_merits_: The earlier proceeding was dismissed in limine or by a non-speaking order, was withdrawn, was dismissed for laches or an available alternative remedy, or was a special leave petition refused without granting leave or giving reasons. It may also have been one in which the relevant issue was never raised or decided.
predicates.earlier_issue_decided_on_merits_by_speak: The earlier forum finally decided the relevant issue on the merits by a reasoned or speaking order.
predicates.earlier_findings_relevant_to_later_claim: Facts found in the earlier proceeding are themselves relevant to the later claim.
predicates.earlier_disposal_does_not_bar_later_proc: The earlier disposal does not operate as res judicata, merger, declared law or an otherwise binding bar, and the later proceeding may be considered on its merits.

definition: A prior disposal that did not decide the relevant issue on the merits by a reasoned order does not bar a later proceeding. This covers non-speaking or in limine dismissals, withdrawals, dismissals for laches or alternative remedy, and refusals of special leave. Such a disposal creates no res judicata, no merger of the challenged order, and no precedent. The later forum may still examine the matter, and review remains open.
exceptions_or_limits: A matter decided on the merits by a speaking order in an earlier writ or other proceeding may operate as res judicata.
Facts found by the earlier court may remain relevant and bind or influence the later proceeding, as in the laches and alternative-remedy dismissal context.
The Supreme Court's Article 136 jurisdiction is discretionary, so whether it entertains a later appeal can still depend on the circumstances, for example manifest injustice or case progress.
Where an effective statutory or appellate remedy is available and unused, the court may still dismiss a writ and leave that remedy open.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns dismissal of a writ because a first appeal is available. It does not concern the effect of an earlier non-merits disposal, and its outcome is that the writ is dismissed.
It concerns parallel pending proceedings and a writ for implementing court directions. It is not about the preclusive effect of an earlier non-merits disposal.
It concerns failure to pursue an intra-court (Letters Patent) appeal before special leave, which is a discretionary maintainability question and not preclusion.
Same as 1690960_2: failure to pursue an intermediate appeal is no automatic bar to special leave.
It is a preliminary objection about an unpursued judicial-assignment concern, which is unrelated to prior disposals.
It concerns maintainability of an appeal against a review dismissal when the underlying appeal order was not separately challenged. It is not about the effect of an earlier non-merits dismissal.

common_material_facts: An earlier writ petition or special leave petition was dismissed in limine, by a non-speaking order, or by withdrawal.
A later suit, writ, review or appeal was then filed, and the opposing party pleaded res judicata, merger or an implied affirmation of the decision.
The earlier forum did not give reasons or decide the merits, or the later issue had not been raised earlier.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 136 of the Constitution
Article 141 of the Constitution
Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution
Section 11 CPC
Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC
Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala (2000) 6 SCC 359
Daryao v. State of U.P.
Workmen of Cochin Port Trust v. Board of Trustees of the Cochin Port Trust
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 13 covered members the earlier non-merits or non-speaking disposal was held not to bar the later proceeding. Eight of these concern special leave dismissals, and the remainder concern writ dismissals. Of the six outliers, five reject a procedural objection to maintainability and one (87147211_1) dismisses a writ because a first appeal was available.
variations: Some members concern refusal of special leave (no merger, no declared law, review remains open). Others concern writ dismissals (no res judicata for a later writ or suit).
Some members add a relevance exception for findings of fact in the earlier proceeding (414792_2).
One member rests on the Supreme Court's wide Article 136 discretion to remedy manifest injustice and not on the absence of a merits ruling (607622_2).
In 1612492_1 the later claim was also distinct, because compensation relief had not been sought earlier.

split_suggestion: Keep the 13 covered members as the core group on the preclusive effect of non-merits dismissals. This group could be split into (a) refusal of special leave (merger, precedent and review) and (b) writ dismissals (res judicata). Treat 1690960_2 and 707752_1 as a separate group on unpursued intermediate appeals before special leave. Treat 1407555_3, 87147211_1, 1459209_1 and 953085_2 as separate procedural and maintainability issues.

legal_question: Does delay at some stage of a criminal case (in reporting, forwarding the report to a magistrate, recording statements, collecting evidence, investigating or disposing of an appeal) by itself undermine the prosecution or require quashing or acquittal, or must it be assessed in light of its explanation, the circumstances and any prejudice or indication of fabrication?

rule.if: criminal_proceeding_involving_delay and not delay_shown_to_have_caused_prejudice_or_fabrication_or_discredited_prosecution_evidence and (delay_explained_by_circumstances or other_credible_evidence_supports_prosecution_case or no_independent_ground_for_quashing_or_discharge)

predicates.criminal_proceeding_involving_delay: The case is a criminal investigation, trial, quashing petition or appeal in which a delay is alleged, whether in lodging or forwarding a report, recording a statement, collecting evidence, investigating, or deciding the case.
predicates.delay_shown_to_have_caused_prejudice_or_: The record shows that the delay caused the accused real prejudice, indicates fabrication or ante-timing, or discredits the informant or witnesses.
predicates.delay_explained_by_circumstances: The delay is reasonably explained by the facts, such as injuries and medical needs, fear or threats, distance, weather, other investigative duties, or practical difficulties.
predicates.other_credible_evidence_supports_prosecu: Credible evidence, such as reliable eyewitness testimony, prompt identification, a promptly recorded report or supporting documents, supports the prosecution account despite the delay.
predicates.no_independent_ground_for_quashing_or_di: There is no separate legal ground for quashing or discharge, such as a legal bar, allegations disclosing no offence, manifest failure of proof, or grave prejudice from unreasonable investigative delay.
predicates.delay_alone_does_not_undermine_prosecuti: The delay by itself does not make the prosecution case doubtful or the evidence unreliable, and does not justify quashing, discharge or exoneration; the court assesses it on the circumstances.

definition: Delay at any stage of a criminal case is not by itself fatal to the prosecution and does not by itself justify quashing or exoneration. The court assesses its length, cause and effect on the case, and the delay matters only if it is unexplained and coupled with prejudice, fabrication, discredited witnesses or another independent ground.
exceptions_or_limits: Unreasonable and substantial investigative delay from indolence or inefficiency that causes grave prejudice may justify quashing under the inherent power; there is no fixed time limit.
Delay that is unexplained and accompanied by indications of fabrication, ante-timing or a discredited informant can justify an adverse inference.
Delay in sending the report to the magistrate under section 157 is improper, but it matters only if it is shown to have prejudiced the accused or to indicate infirmity in the investigation.
Explanation is assessed realistically on the circumstances; there is no mathematical rule, and a witness's reaction or silence cannot be judged by a fixed standard of natural conduct.
Delay in disposing of an appeal does not by itself lead to exoneration because limitation law does not apply to criminal proceedings.

common_material_facts: Reports were delayed by hours to days after violent offences, often involving injured victims who needed medical care.
Special or occurrence reports reached the magistrate late, but the first information report was recorded promptly.
Witness statements or evidence collection were delayed because of fear, injuries or other investigative tasks.
The defence alleged ante-timing or fabrication without evidence, and showed no prejudice.
Some members involve prolonged investigation or appeal delay, where the accused sought quashing or exoneration.
statutes_and_provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, section 561-A
Code of Criminal Procedure, section 482
Code of Criminal Procedure, section 157
Code of Criminal Procedure, section 159
Constitution of India, article 21
Limitation Act, 1963 (inapplicable to criminal proceedings)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 18 members, the delay alone did not defeat the prosecution or justify quashing or exoneration. About 12 turned on the delay being explained, 4 on the absence of prejudice or fabrication, and 2 on the absence of an independent legal ground. One (1642644_1) states the case-specific assessment test.
variations: Reporting delays (about 8 members) turn on explanation by injury, fear, distance or weather.
Magistrate-forwarding delays (about 5 members) turn on a prompt first information report, an explanation and no prejudice.
Witness-statement and evidence-collection delays (about 3 members) are excused by explanation and reliability.
Investigation and appeal delays (about 3 members) rest on the absence of grave prejudice or an independent legal ground, and the Limitation Act's inapplicability for appeals.
Some members need an affirmative explanation, while others need only the absence of prejudice or evidence of fabrication.

split_suggestion: Not necessary, but the cluster could be split into (a) delay in reporting or forwarding the first information report, statements and evidence, which turns on explanation, fabrication and prejudice; and (b) delay in investigation or appeal disposal, which turns on the quashing standard, grave prejudice, and limitation law not applying.

legal_question: Where a party seeks to avoid or displace a decree, compromise, instrument, will or apparent ownership by alleging fraud, coercion, undue influence, benami or a different real transaction, must that party plead the material particulars and prove the allegation, failing which the challenge fails?

rule.if: challenge_to_decree_instrument_will_or_apparent_title and challenger_alleges_vitiating_ground_or_different_real_transaction and (particulars_not_pleaded or allegation_not_proved_by_definite_evidence) and not burden_shifted_to_beneficiary

predicates.challenge_to_decree_instrument_will_or_a: The proceeding seeks to set aside or deny effect to a consent decree, final judgment, compromise, registered or written instrument, will, or the apparent ownership of property.
predicates.challenger_alleges_vitiating_ground_or_d: The challenger alleges fraud, coercion, undue influence, forgery, benami ownership, non-receipt of recited consideration, or that the document does not record the real transaction.
predicates.particulars_not_pleaded: The pleadings state only general or vague allegations without the material particulars (nature, manner, circumstances, advantage obtained) or without separately pleading the specific ground.
predicates.allegation_not_proved_by_definite_eviden: The challenger did not discharge the burden of proving the allegation by definite, cogent evidence (for example the source of purchase money in a benami claim), and contemporaneous records or conduct support the apparent position.
predicates.burden_shifted_to_beneficiary: The challenger established a dominating position and an unconscionable transaction so that the burden moved to the beneficiary to show free consent, and the beneficiary did not discharge it.
predicates.challenge_fails_and_apparent_transaction: The challenge is rejected and the decree, compromise, instrument, will or apparent title remains effective.

definition: A party who alleges fraud, coercion, undue influence, forgery, benami ownership or a different real transaction bears the burden of pleading the particulars and proving the allegation by definite evidence. If this is not done, the challenge fails and the apparent transaction or title stands, unless a dominating position and an unconscionable transaction shift the burden to the beneficiary.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the challenger shows that the beneficiary was in a position to dominate the other's will and the transaction is unconscionable, the burden shifts to the beneficiary to prove absence of undue influence, and failure results in the transaction being set aside (156545202_2).
A will propounder must still dispel suspicious circumstances that independently raise doubt, and must prove due execution and, where disputed, the testator's majority.
A voidable instrument obtained by fraud is not void ab initio and must be set aside in order to be avoided.
Mere relationship or old age alone does not establish undue influence.
Courts cannot construct an unpleaded case of undue influence from vague allegations or the opponent's pleading.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the burden on the will's proponent to prove the testator's majority, not a challenger's burden to plead and prove a vitiating ground. It supports the general allocation of burdens but sits on the opposite side of the rule.

common_material_facts: Challenge to a consent decree, compromise, registered deed, gift, will or apparent title based on fraud, coercion, undue influence or benami
Vague or general pleadings lacking particulars of the alleged influence, threat or fraud
Documents acknowledged or registered, with contemporaneous records or later conduct supporting the apparent transaction
In the benami cases, a claim that property bought in another's name was a ruler's or spouse's, with no reliable proof of the source of purchase money
Oral evidence that was unsupported or unreliable
statutes_and_provisions: Order VI Rule 4 CPC (and Rule 2)
Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC
Section 16 Indian Contract Act, 1872
Sections 91, 92 and 106 Evidence Act, 1872
Section 68 Evidence Act and Section 63 Indian Succession Act
Sections 30 and 31 Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Jaydayal Poddar v. Bibi Hazra (benami)
Bishundeo Narain v. Seogeni Rai
Ladli Prasad Jaiswal v. Karnal Distillery
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 16 of 17 covered members the challenger fails for want of particulars or proof, so the decree, instrument, will or apparent title stands. One member (156545202_2) goes the other way because the burden shifted to the beneficiary after domination and unconscionability were shown. Several members (246887_1, 64921_2) hold that a court cannot grant relief on an unpleaded undue influence case.
variations: Benami cases (168653623_2, 168653623_4, 583554_3, 385942_1) turn on the source of purchase money and contemporaneous conduct, with the State-ownership records adding weight in three.
1827303_2 allocates the burden to the party alleging that the written instrument does not record the real transaction.
Will cases address forgery, coercion or undue influence, and the propounder's own duties vary.
156545202_2 is the only case where the challenger succeeds.

split_suggestion: If a tighter grouping is wanted, split into (a) pleading-particulars and proof of fraud, coercion or undue influence (1049099_2, 246887_1, 64921_2, 684433_4, 256224_2, 16848121_1, 59167167_3, 156545202_2); (b) will-challenge burden (1626809_3, 208164_2, 646144_2, 802307_5); and (c) benami and recital-of-transaction burden (168653623_2, 168653623_4, 583554_3, 385942_1, 1827303_2, 719370_3).

legal_question: When a tenant has paid, tendered or remitted the arrears in the manner or within the time the statute, the court or the landlord's accepted practice allows, can the landlord still obtain eviction for rent default?

rule.if: rent_default_eviction_proceeding and tenant_cured_or_met_payment_requirement_in_permitted_manner and not statute_makes_past_default_independently_sufficient and not independent_eviction_ground_established

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: The landlord seeks eviction under a rent-control or tenancy statute on a ground of non-payment, wilful default, habitual arrears or irregular payment of rent.
predicates.tenant_cured_or_met_payment_requirement_: The tenant paid, tendered or remitted the arrears (for example by money order, within the notice or grace period, or as the court determined within the time it fixed). Alternatively, the landlord had long accepted delayed or lump-sum payments without objection or warning, or the tenant paid with reasonable punctuality. Alternatively, all arrears had been paid and accepted before the proceeding was filed, or the tenant is otherwise entitled to statutory relief.
predicates.statute_makes_past_default_independently: The governing statute, as construed, makes failure to pay within the notice period a complete ground for eviction even if the arrears are later paid.
predicates.independent_eviction_ground_established: The landlord has separately established another statutory ground for eviction, such as irregular payment without sufficient cause, that is not displaced by the cure of the arrears.
predicates.tenant_not_evictable_for_rent_default: The tenant cannot be evicted, or the proceeding is treated as if no default was committed, on the rent-default ground.

definition: Rent-control statutes protect a tenant from eviction for rent default where the tenant has paid, tendered or remitted the arrears as the statute or court allows, or where the landlord's long unprotested acceptance of irregular payments shows there is no habitual or wilful default. The protection does not apply where the statute makes failure to pay within the notice period a complete ground for eviction, or where a separate eviction ground is established.
exceptions_or_limits: The outcome depends on the wording of the particular statute. Under the Madhya Pradesh Act of 1955, failure to pay within the notice period suffices even if the arrears were paid before suit.
Cure of arrears does not bar eviction on a separate, independently established ground, such as irregular payment without sufficient cause.

Reasonable punctuality is required. Persistent payment at irregular intervals may still fail the requirement, and acceptance of late rent under protest with a warning does not imply agreement to a changed payment practice.

Statutory protection that depends on a court-determined payment requires compliance within the time the court fixes. A prior protection counts as used only where possession was actually withheld because of the tenant's compliance, not where the landlord merely withdrew the earlier proceeding.
Repeat protection can be lost if later defaults reach the statutory threshold, for example four months' default within twelve months, or if the later default is knowing and wilful.

outlier_members.reason: The landlord succeeds. Under the Madhya Pradesh Act of 1955, failure to pay within the notice period is a complete ground even though the arrears were later paid and accepted before suit. This is the 'statute makes past default sufficient' exception to the rule.

Timely payment of arrears did not prevent eviction because a separate ground (irregular payment without sufficient cause) was established. This is the independent-ground limit to the rule, not an application of it.

common_material_facts: Tenant paid, tendered or remitted arrears, for example by money order or bank draft, within a notice, grace or court-fixed period
Landlord had long accepted lump-sum or delayed rent without objection or warning
No arrears were outstanding when the eviction proceeding was filed
Amended statutory provisions let tenants cure arrears by paying an amount determined by the court in pending suits
Landlord refused or did not encash a timely remittance or tender
statutes_and_provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act 1947, ss. 12(1), 12(2), 12(3)(a) and 12(3)(b)
Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act 1960, s. 10(2)(i)
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act 1947, ss. 11(1)(d) and 13(1)
C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order 1949, cl. 13(3)(ii)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rents and Eviction) Act, ss. 13-A and 13(6)
West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act 1956, ss. 17(2A), 17(3) and 17(4), and the 1967 Amendment Ordinance
Delhi Rent Control Act 1958, ss. 14(2), 15(1) and 15(6)
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act 1948, ss. 25(1) and 25(2)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act 1955, s. 4(a)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 16 of 18 members the tenant is protected from eviction for rent default, or is held entitled to claim statutory relief. Two members go the other way: one where the statute makes failure to pay within the notice period sufficient, and one where an independent ground was established.
variations: Some members turn on statutory cure mechanisms: money-order remittance, court-determined payment, instalment relief and one-time protection. Others turn on the landlord's conduct in accepting late rent, which negates habitual or wilful default.
Several members apply protective or liberal construction to remedial amendments, for example by extending the application period to tenants who lacked notice of the suit or to pending appeals.
Members differ on whether past default is extinguished by payment before filing. The Tamil Nadu and Bombay Tenancy members say it is, but the Madhya Pradesh s. 4(a) member says it is not.

A few members concern procedural entitlement to claim relief, such as maintainability of an instalment application or availability of the one-time protection, rather than a merits finding of no default.

split_suggestion: Split into: (a) cure by payment, remittance or tender within a statutory, notice or court-fixed period (1045299_1, 153124_1, 969224_2, 969224_3, 769101_1, 1719372_4, 936128_1); (b) landlord acquiescence in irregular payments negating habitual or wilful default (1371446_1, 1427154_2, 1761668_1, 1789087_1); (c) procedural eligibility for statutory relief (1857401_1, 1857401_2, 282348_1, 282348_2, 617845_1); (d) cases where cure does not defeat eviction (1028604_3, 18725_2).

legal_question: When may compensation for acquired land be fixed by reference to a prior or final award or valuation for comparable land acquired for the same purpose, under the same notification, or nearby, and when must parity be refused because the lands are not shown to be comparable?

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The case is a reference, appeal or other proceeding to determine or enhance compensation for land acquired under a land acquisition statute.
predicates.comparable_land_prior_award_or_valuation: There is an earlier award, judgment or valuation (typically final or unappealed) fixing compensation for other land acquired for the same purpose, under the same notification, or nearby.
predicates.lands_shown_similar_in_nature_quality_an: The evidence or the courts' findings show that the acquired land and the comparator land are similar in nature, quality, potentiality, area and situation, so that they are comparable.
predicates.no_material_difference_proved: Neither the claimant nor the acquiring authority has proved any material difference (in advantages, features, distance, timing or value) that would justify distinguishing the lands.
predicates.compensation_determined_in_parity_with_c: Compensation is fixed at the same rate as, or consistently with, the comparator land's award or valuation.

definition: Where land acquired for the same purpose, under the same notification, or nearby is shown to be similar to land for which a final or unchallenged award or valuation exists, and no material difference is proved, courts fix compensation at the same rate to ensure consistency and avoid discrimination. Parity is not available merely because the lands lie in the same village or notification, or are contiguous, without proof of comparable advantages and features.
exceptions_or_limits: Parity is refused where the claimant does not prove that the land has the same advantages, features or value as the comparator; being in the same village or under the same notification, or contiguity alone, is not enough.

A prior award need not be followed where a material difference in location, quality, potentiality or acquisition timing is shown; distance or area alone does not justify reduction unless it reflects a proved difference in quality or potentiality.
Timing differences alone do not justify enhancement over a uniform rate where no sufficient basis to distinguish the lands is shown.
A prior award may serve as a valuation basis mainly where it has become final or unappealed and other direct evidence such as sale instances is absent, or is used alongside other evidence.
Collector's awards are admissible and useful only where the land is comparable and reasonably proximate.
The burden of proving market value and comparability lies on the claimant.
Courts may depart from a strict lower-value finding and apply a common rate in the circumstances (e.g. later acquisition), as in two members.

common_material_facts: Land acquired for the same purpose or under the same notification, in the same or a neighbouring village
An earlier award or High Court decision for comparable land that had become final or was not appealed by the State
Claimants or the State sought to distinguish lands on distance, timing, area or classification
Little or no sale-instance evidence, or sale instances used alongside the prior award
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, s.4 / s.4(1) (notification)
Land Acquisition Act, 1894, s.18 (reference)
Land Acquisition Act, 1894, s.23 / s.23(1) (market value)
Jammu and Kashmir Land Acquisition Act, s.4(1)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 16 of 18 members, compensation was aligned with the comparable award, or the High Court's parity-based determination was upheld. Two members (1334507_1 and 1733049_1) refused enhancement or parity because no basis for distinction was shown or comparability was not proved. Several enhanced compensation to the comparator rate; 48799_1 reduced compensation to the earlier rate.
variations: Direction of adjustment: some enhance to the higher comparator rate (160641463_1, 80221_1, 871763_3), others reduce to an earlier rate (48799_1), others uphold the existing figure.
Basis of comparability: same notification, same purpose, adjacency or proximity, or equal value.
1733049_1 rejects the 'village as one unit' approach and requires proof of comparability.
1647526_2 and 1101281_4 apply a common rate even though the farther land was found to have a lower value.
17773545_1 adjusts the rate for different acquisition dates, rather than applying a strict parity.
Comparator evidence ranges from a final award to Collector's awards, used with or without sale instances.

legal_question: When does a homicide conviction fall short of murder under Section 302 IPC and become culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 304 Part I or Part II) because the circumstances do not establish the intention required for murder?

predicates.homicide_conviction_under_appeal: The conviction for causing death (usually under Section 302 IPC) is under challenge in a criminal appeal, or a lower court's reduction of it is challenged.
predicates.fatal_injury_caused_by_accused: The evidence shows that the accused caused or participated in causing the injury or injuries that resulted in death.
predicates.murder_intent_or_ordinary_course_suffici: Taking together the weapon, force, body part struck, number of blows, suddenness of the quarrel, premeditation, provocation and conduct after the assault, the prosecution has proved an intention to cause death, or an intention to inflict an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, and no Section 300 exception applies.
predicates.offence_is_culpable_homicide_not_amounti: The offence is culpable homicide not amounting to murder, punishable under Section 304 Part I (intention to cause the injury or an injury likely to cause death) or Part II (knowledge only).

definition: Where the whole circumstances (weapon, force, body part, single or few blows, sudden quarrel without premeditation, absence of animosity, stopping of the attack, uncertain attribution of the fatal injury) do not establish an intention to kill or to cause an injury sufficient in the ordinary course to cause death, a murder conviction is reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Part I applies where the injury was intended and likely to cause death, and Part II where there was only knowledge that death was likely. A single blow does not by itself decide the matter.
exceptions_or_limits: Murder is upheld where the circumstances show an intention to cause death or an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, for example a dangerous weapon used with great force on a vital part of an unarmed victim, with no sudden fight or provocation (1173740_4).
A single blow does not automatically reduce the offence; intention is inferred from all the circumstances.

Where the evidence does not attribute the fatal injury to a particular accused, liability may fall further, to grievous hurt (Section 325) or hurt (Section 324), rather than culpable homicide (1603327_1, 1944328_5).
Whether Part I or Part II applies depends on whether the accused intended the injury likely to cause death or had only knowledge that death was likely.
A common-intention conviction under Section 34 may stand without a specific charge if no prejudice results, but participation and common intention must be proved.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns attribution of the fatal injury. The accused was moved from Section 304 Part II to grievous hurt under Section 325 because the evidence did not link his blow to the fatal injury, not because intent was lacking.

The accused were convicted of a lesser assault (Sections 324/34, knife injury to the informant) in place of a murder-related conviction, because murder liability was not shown. This is not a reduction to culpable homicide.

common_material_facts: Sudden quarrel or altercation without premeditation, often over land, a boundary, a wall or a trivial matter
Single or few blows, often to the head or abdomen, with a stick, knife, yoke or agricultural implement
Assault stopped once the victim fell or someone intervened
No prior animosity, or accused also injured, or firing out of fear or anger without a deliberate aim
Medical or attribution evidence not establishing ordinary-course sufficiency of the injury to cause death
Several accused acting with common intention under Section 34
statutes_and_provisions: IPC Sections 299, 300 (clause thirdly, Exception 4), 302
IPC Section 304 Part I and Part II
IPC Section 34 (also 109, 149)
IPC Sections 324, 325, 307
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Murder convictions are reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder in about 14 of 18 members (roughly 7 under Part I and 6 under Part II, with the rest unspecified or maintained). One member upholds murder. Two members reduce to hurt or grievous hurt because the fatal injury was not attributed to the accused.
variations: Part I applies where the injury was intended and likely to cause death; Part II applies where only knowledge was present.
Some members reduce the conviction themselves, while others uphold a High Court reduction (131010_1, 189893384_1, 1931444_3).
Some rely on Virsa Singh, Rayavarapu Punnayya or Exception 4, while many cite no authority.
Some reductions come with sentence consequences, such as release on time already served.
1221178_2 and 1279400_5 reduce the conviction with only a general reference to the circumstances.

split_suggestion: Keep the core group (murder reduced to Section 304 Part I or II for lack of proved murderous intention) together. Consider sub-splitting into Part I (intended likely-fatal injury) and Part II (knowledge only). Move 1603327_1 and 1944328_5 to a separate cluster on reduction to hurt or grievous hurt where the fatal injury is not attributable. Treat 1173740_4 as the contrasting case where murder is upheld.

legal_question: Can a party challenge an earlier interlocutory order (including a non-terminating remand order or other intermediate ruling) in an appeal from the final decree, order or judgment, even if no appeal lay from it or an available appeal was not taken when it was made?

predicates.appeal_from_final_decision_in_same_proce: The party is appealing from the final decree, order or judgment in the same suit or proceeding in which the earlier order was made (including after remand).
predicates.earlier_order_interlocutory_not_finally_: The earlier order (such as a remand order, an order on an interim application, or a provisional-rent order) did not finally terminate the proceedings or finally dispose of the matter separately.
predicates.party_challenges_earlier_order_in_final_: The appellant expressly challenges the correctness of the earlier interlocutory order in the appeal from the final decision.
predicates.statute_expressly_bars_challenge: A statutory provision (for example the restriction in section 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure for an appealable remand order) expressly bars challenge to the earlier order in the later appeal.
predicates.earlier_interlocutory_order_may_be_chall: The appellate court may examine the correctness of the earlier interlocutory order in the appeal from the final decision, and the failure to appeal it earlier is no bar.

definition: A non-terminating interlocutory order may be challenged in an appeal from the final decision in the same proceeding, whether no appeal lay from it or an available appeal was not taken, unless a statute expressly bars the challenge. Such orders are not treated as finally closing the issue, although they may bind the lower courts until set aside.
exceptions_or_limits: A statutory bar such as section 105(2) CPC for an appealable remand order, or an analogous provision, may preclude the challenge; the rent statute in one member contained no such bar.
The principle does not apply to earlier decisions that effectively terminated the earlier proceedings, which were distinguished in one member.
The earlier determination continues to bind the trial court and later benches until set aside in the higher appeal.

The challenge may be premature or infructuous where no final decree has been passed against the appellant, or where later proceedings have overtaken the order, or where the merits were also decided against the appellant.
Where an appeal lay and the matter was separately and finally disposed of, the challenge may be unavailable (the members do not decide this).

outlier_members.reason: Concerns whether a separate statutory remedy for setting aside eviction decrees displaces a pending appeal; it is not about challenging an interlocutory order in a final appeal.
Concerns whether deciding the merits appeal renders a challenge to a delay-condonation order infructuous; it is a different mootness point.
Concerns the forum choice (same court or appeal) against a temporary injunction order, not deferred challenge in a final appeal.
Concerns a remittal challenge becoming infructuous and declining a direct eviction order while a rent appeal is pending.
Concerns delay condonation being academic when the appeal was also decided on its merits.

common_material_facts: An interlocutory or remand order was made earlier in the suit or proceeding and was not appealed, or no appeal lay from it.
The proceedings continued (often after remand) to a final decree or order.
The aggrieved party renewed the challenge to the earlier order in the appeal from the final decision.
Lower courts or the High Court sometimes treated the earlier order as unchallengeable or as no longer pending.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 105(1) and 105(2) Code of Civil Procedure
Section 97 and section 11 CPC
Section 39 Arbitration Act
Section 15(1)(b) East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949
Section 9 and 9A Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act
Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi, [1960] 3 S.C.R. 590 (relied on repeatedly)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 13 of the 18 members the challenge to the earlier interlocutory order was permitted in the appeal from the final decision, sometimes leading to the subsequent proceedings being set aside. One of these (1909386_5) held the challenge premature. The other five members deal with related but distinct points (mootness, forum choice, displacement of remedies).
variations: Some members rest on section 105 CPC; others rest on Satyadhyan Ghosal or on general principles where the statute (rent or arbitration law) has no bar.
Some orders were not appealable at all, while others were appealable but not appealed.
1675460_3 adds that the earlier determination binds the courts below but remains open to challenge in the Supreme Court.
231666_2 concerns defending a favourable judgment by contesting an adverse ruling within the same proceeding.
1909386_5 held the limitation challenge premature because no final decree had been passed, leaving it open for the future.
1553975_3 holds that an interlocutory order permitting evidence does not foreclose the appellate tribunal from deciding legal maintainability.

split_suggestion: Keep the 13 covered members as the core group on challenging interlocutory orders in a final appeal. Split off 1994192_1, 730740_4 and 5341205_3 as a separate group on mootness or academic challenges. Treat 1567371_6 (additional statutory remedy does not displace a pending appeal) and 442524_1 (forum choice against a temporary injunction) as separate singletons.

legal_question: When a male Hindu coparcener dies after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 commenced, leaving a Class I female heir, does his interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property devolve by succession rather than survivorship, how is it quantified, and what do the heirs take?

predicates.male_hindu_died_after_succession_act_com: The male Hindu coparcener died after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
predicates.deceased_held_interest_in_mitakshara_cop: At death the deceased had an undivided interest in Mitakshara coparcenary or joint family property, with no prior partition separating his share.
predicates.class_i_female_heir_survived: The deceased left a female relative specified in Class I of the Schedule, such as a widow or daughter.
predicates.no_testamentary_disposition_of_interest: The deceased made no will disposing of his coparcenary interest.
predicates.interest_devolves_by_succession_not_surv: The deceased's interest is calculated as the share he would have received on a partition immediately before his death and passes by intestate succession, not survivorship. The heirs take it individually as tenants in common, and a female heir who would have received a share on the notional partition takes it in addition to her share as heir.

definition: Under the proviso and Explanation 1 to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, a deceased coparcener's interest passes by succession, not survivorship, when a Class I female heir survives him. The interest is fixed by a notional partition immediately before death, and the fiction is carried through fully. A female entitled to a share on that partition therefore receives it in addition to her share as an heir. The heirs hold their inherited shares individually, not as joint family property.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule applies only where the deceased still held an undivided coparcenary interest. If an earlier partition made the share separate property, devolution is by ordinary intestate succession under Sections 8 to 10 and, for a female's property, Sections 15 and 16.

The rule applies to a death after commencement of the 1956 Act. Deaths under the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 are governed by a different statutory scheme, under which the widow's share is fixed at the date partition is claimed.
A testamentary disposition of the interest displaces intestate devolution.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns Section 15(2)(b) and Section 16 Rule 3, the devolution of a widow's property inherited from her husband. It does not concern coparcenary property.
Concerns Section 15(2)(b) and Section 16 Rule 3, identifying the husband's heirs by class (Class II over agnates). It does not concern coparcenary property.
Governed by the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, as extended to Bihar. It holds that a widow's partition claim defines her interest, which devolves to her husband's heirs.
Concerns a widow sharing hereditary shebaitship with a son under the 1937 Act (Dayabhaga).
Concerns the 1937 Act and a widow's unquantified share until partition.
Concerns a widow's right to a share and to maintain a partition suit under the 1937 Act and the Bihar extension.
Concerns whether a widow under the 1937 Act holds a coparcenary interest, in an estate duty setting.
Concerns the liability of a widow's coparcenary interest to estate duty under the Estate Duty Act, 1953.
Concerns the 1937 Act and the date at which the widow's share is assessed (when partition is claimed).
Concerns intestate succession to separate property after an earlier division (Sections 8 to 10, 15 and 16), not Section 6 devolution of a coparcenary interest.
Concerns the widow of a predeceased son as a Class I heir sharing by branch under Sections 8 to 10, in a will-construction setting. It does not involve a coparcenary interest.

common_material_facts: A male Hindu died leaving a widow and children, including daughters, as Class I heirs.
The dispute arose in a partition or inheritance suit over joint family property.
There was no will, and no earlier partition separated the deceased's share, except in the cases involving separate property.
The shares were computed by a notional partition and then by succession.
statutes_and_provisions: Hindu Succession Act, 1956, s. 6, its proviso and Explanation 1
Hindu Succession Act, 1956, ss. 4(b), 8, 9, 10, 15, 16, 19 and 30
Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, ss. 3(2) and 3(3)
Estate Duty Act, 1953, ss. 7 and 39
Mysore Hindu Law Women's Rights Act, 1933
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Across the 7 covered members, the interest devolves by succession, not survivorship. It is quantified by a notional partition, and the female heir takes both her partition share and her share as heir. The 11 outliers apply the 1937 Act, Sections 15 and 16, or ordinary intestacy, and mostly confirm a widow's entitlement to a share.
variations: Some members compute exact fractions, such as 7/24 for a widow or 38.1% after successive devolution, and others state only the principle.
128638041_1 emphasises that heirs hold as tenants in common, not as an HUF.
186220869_1 involves an earlier partition that made the share separate, so the 'coparcenary interest' element is weaker there.
The outliers split into three groups: the 1937 Act (widow's interest and its timing), Sections 15 and 16 (female intestate succession), and general Sections 8 to 10 intestacy.

split_suggestion: Split into four clusters: (1) Section 6 proviso and notional partition after 1956 (the covered members); (2) the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 widow's interest (1627271_1, 34963020_1, 401087_3, 694388_3, 5232_1, 5232_2, 1652416_1), with the estate duty and shebaitship cases as sub-groups; (3) Sections 15(2)(b) and 16 devolution of a widow's property inherited from her husband (1066523_2, 1357931_2); (4) general Sections 8 to 10 intestate distribution of separate property (70913397_2, 1923018_3).

legal_question: When an appellate decree is compared as a whole with the trial court's decision as a whole, does it count as a decree of affirmance, and which kinds of variation (merits, interest, costs, concession or consent, favourable or unfavourable to the would-be appellant) change that character?

rule.if: civil_decree_appeal and appellate_decree_compared_as_whole_with_trial_decision and appellate_court_adjudicated_variation_on_merits and not variation_only_as_to_costs and not variation_due_to_concession_consent_or_withdrawal

predicates.civil_decree_appeal: The case concerns an appellate decree in a civil appeal whose character (affirmance or variation) must be determined, for example for a certificate to appeal further under Article 133(1) of the Constitution.
predicates.appellate_decree_compared_as_whole_with_: The appellate decree is compared in its entirety with the trial court's decision in its entirety, not part by part or only as to the portion challenged in the further appeal.
predicates.appellate_court_adjudicated_variation_on: The appellate court, by its own adjudication on the merits, changed the trial court's decision. This includes a change in an award of interest that forms part of the dispute between the parties, whatever the extent of the change and whether or not it favours the party seeking further appeal.
predicates.variation_only_as_to_costs: The only difference between the appellate decree and the trial decision is in the order as to costs, which is a matter of the court's discretion under section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
predicates.variation_due_to_concession_consent_or_w: The change arose from a party's concession, the parties' consent, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter, not from the appellate court's adjudication on the merits.
predicates.appellate_decree_not_one_of_affirmance: The appellate decree is a decree of variation, not a decree affirming the decision below.

definition: An appellate decree is not one of affirmance if, compared as a whole with the trial court's decision as a whole, the appellate court varied that decision by adjudication on the merits. This holds whether the variation is large or small and whether or not it favours the party seeking further appeal. Variations that are only as to costs, or that result from concession, consent or withdrawal, do not change an otherwise affirming decree.
exceptions_or_limits: A variation confined to costs does not prevent the appellate decree from being one of affirmance.

A variation resulting from concession, consent of the parties, or withdrawal of part of the subject matter does not alter the decree's character, because it is not an appellate adjudication on the merits.
A variation in an award of interest counts as a merits variation only where the interest forms part of the dispute between the parties.
The valuation condition for a further appeal under Article 133(1)(a) is an independent requirement and does not control how the affirmance test is construed.
The rule is stated for the affirmance test under Article 133(1) of the Constitution. It does not address merger or the running of limitation for execution.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the doctrine of merger: the trial decree merges into the appellate decree, which becomes the operative decree for execution. It does not concern the affirmance test.
Concerns merger and the operative decree under the debt-relief law, where the appellate preliminary decree supersedes the trial decree. It is not about affirmance.
Concerns merger and the starting point of limitation for execution under Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
Concerns merger of a specific performance decree into the appellate decree for execution purposes.
Concerns execution limitation under Article 136 and the effect of a later appeal dismissed as time-barred. It is a merger and limitation issue.
Concerns merger of a trial judgment into the appellate judgment to fix the scope of an earlier suit.
Concerns whether an appeal in a collateral proceeding gives a fresh starting point for execution limitation under Article 182 of the Limitation Act, 1908.
Concerns whether a decree in a separate proceeding on a third party's title restarts execution limitation under Article 182. It is a limitation issue, not affirmance.

common_material_facts: A trial decree was appealed and the appellate court decided the appeal.

In the affirmance group, the appellate court partly reversed the trial court (for example, holding some alienations non-binding and granting partition, or setting aside ejectment and reducing a money award), and the beneficiary then sought a certificate to appeal further.
In the merger and limitation groups, the question was which decree is operative or enforceable, and when limitation for execution begins.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 133(1) of the Constitution (decree affirming the decision below; valuation condition)
Sections 34 and 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure (interest and costs)
Article 136 and former Article 182 of the Limitation Act (execution limitation)
Order 41 Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 10 covered members, 6 hold that a merits variation (including a variation in interest forming part of the dispute) makes the decree one of variation, whether or not it favours the intending appellant. 4 hold that costs-only variations or concession, consent or withdrawal variations leave an affirming decree unchanged, or that the valuation condition does not control the test. Of the 8 outliers, 6 apply merger so that the appellate decree is the operative decree (limitation or execution runs from it), and 2 hold that collateral proceedings do not restart limitation.
variations: 136976989 and 1758207 are two reports of the same decision and overlap almost completely.
60827_2 applies the same whole-versus-whole comparison to an ejectment and money decree.
Some members state the converse (the decree stays affirmance), while others state the main rule (not affirmance).
The valuation member (1758207_5) addresses a separate eligibility condition, not the affirmance test itself.

split_suggestion: Split into three clusters: (1) the affirmance test under Article 133(1): 136976989_1-4, 1758207_1-5, 60827_2; (2) the doctrine of merger and the operative decree, including limitation running from the appellate decree: 1192149_1, 1313128_1, 1463985_1, 147061017_1, 1480964_2, 1644933_1; (3) collateral proceedings not restarting execution limitation under Article 182: 1264696_2, 349715_1.

legal_question: When an acquisition is governed by a special, self-contained statute (or a special scheme that declares itself exclusive), can provisions of the general land-acquisition law (time limits, lapse, procedures, redetermination, or the general acquisition power itself) be applied to it?

predicates.acquisition_governed_by_special_statute: The acquisition is carried out, or is required to be carried out, under a special statute (planned development, town improvement, industrial areas, planning, requisition or welfare-scheme law) rather than only under the general acquisition law.
predicates.special_statute_covers_the_matter_or_is_: The special statute is a self-contained code that has its own provisions on the stage or matter in dispute (for example notification, declaration, vesting, lapse, compensation or award), or it expressly makes its own procedure the only way to acquire land for its purpose.
predicates.general_law_provision_adopted_by_express: The special statute expressly incorporates, or by necessary implication adopts, the particular general-law provision (including a later amendment) that a party seeks to apply, and applying it is compatible with the special scheme.
predicates.general_law_provision_does_not_apply_to_: The general-law provision (a deadline, lapse consequence, procedural step, redetermination route, or the general acquisition power) cannot be applied to the acquisition. An acquisition attempted under the general law for the special purpose, bypassing the special procedure, is invalid.

definition: Where a special, self-contained statute provides its own acquisition scheme, or makes its procedure exclusive for a stated purpose, the general acquisition law's provisions do not apply unless the special statute adopts them expressly or by necessary implication. This holds for general-law deadlines, lapse, procedures and remedies. Later amendments to a law that was merely incorporated are not imported. The State also cannot use the general acquisition power to bypass the special procedure.
exceptions_or_limits: General-law provisions apply where the special statute expressly incorporates them, or adopts them by necessary implication (for example substantive compensation principles). Such provisions apply only so far as they are applicable and compatible with the special scheme.
A statute that is merely supplemental to the general law and not a self-contained code (the Mariyappa line) does not exclude the general law's provisions.

A special procedure applies only when the special body exercises its own acquisition power. Where the government acquires under the general law without the board using its own power, the special procedure does not apply, even if the acquisition serves the board's purpose.

outlier_members.reason: It is the converse situation. The special board procedure was held inapplicable because the government acquired under the general law and the board did not exercise its own power. It is best treated as a limit on the rule rather than an application of it.
It concerns a purpose-limitation direction on the use of acquired land. It does not address the relationship between special and general acquisition law.

It concerns the scope of a statutory exception for land taken for acquisition versus requisition under the estates acquisition law. It does not involve displacement or incorporation of the general acquisition law.

common_material_facts: A special statute (development authority, town improvement, industrial areas, planning, requisition or welfare-scheme law) has its own acquisition, vesting, lapse or compensation provisions.
A landowner relies on a general-law time limit (Section 6, Section 11A or the 2013 Act's lapse provision), a procedure (Section 5A) or a remedy (Section 28A) to invalidate the acquisition.
The special statute applies the general law only 'so far as applicable', or incorporates it at a point in time that predates the later amendment.
In some cases land vests on publication of the final declaration independently of an award.
In others, the State invokes the general acquisition law for a purpose covered by a special scheme that makes its own procedure exclusive.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 5A, 6, 11A, 16, 23 and 28A
Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976, Sections 15-19, 27 and 36
Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, Sections 28(4) and 28(5)
Kanpur Urban Area Development Act, Sections 71 and 114
Punjab Regional and Town Planning and Development Act, 1995, Sections 14, 42 and 56
Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, Section 24(2)
West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, Section 3
Constitution of India, Article 254
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 14 of 17 members the general-law provision was held inapplicable to the special acquisition. Deadlines, lapse and procedures were not imported, and general-law proceedings were quashed where a special scheme was exclusive. Three members are outliers, one of which is the converse case.
variations: Some members rest on the special statute being a self-contained code (Munithimmaiah, Offshore Holdings, Girnar Traders).
Some rest on the incorporation versus reference distinction (M.V. Narasimhan, Jainul Islam), under which later amendments are not imported.
Some rest on an express exclusivity clause that displaces the general law for a stated purpose.
In the vesting cases, vesting on the final declaration meant no lapse for want of an award.
In 812937_2, substantive compensation principles were applied by necessary implication while the procedural award deadline was not.
802392_4 applies the same logic to the State's general power of eminent domain.

split_suggestion: Keep the 14 covered members together as the main group. If a finer split is wanted, separate (a) the 'incorporation versus reference / later amendment not imported' and 'self-contained code, no general-law deadlines' members from (b) the 'exclusive special scheme bars use of the general law or general power' members (1000425_5, 1159928_5, 802392_4). Treat 1312879_1 as a counter-limit, and move 1524072_8 and 919234_2 to separate clusters (post-acquisition purpose limitation; scope of the requisition versus acquisition exception).

legal_question: When is a person who, by representation, conduct, acquiescence or acceptance of benefits, led another to act on an apparent state of title to property estopped from later challenging the resulting transfer, division or settlement, and when is a transferee denied the corresponding protection of the ostensible-owner rule?

predicates.property_title_challenge: A party seeks to challenge or deny title under a property transfer, division, settlement or order.
predicates.challenger_by_representation_conduct_acq: The challenger, by an express representation, by conduct or silence amounting to acquiescence, or by knowingly accepting consideration or benefits (including claiming through someone who did so), caused or permitted the other party to believe in the apparent ownership, division or arrangement.
predicates.other_party_relied_and_acted_to_detrimen: The other party (purchaser, co-claimant or similar) relied on that belief, changed position or acted on it, and would suffer detriment if the challenge were allowed.
predicates.challenger_estopped_from_denying_apparen: The challenger is barred from denying the represented facts or from impeaching the transfer, division or settlement.

definition: A person who represents, or by conduct, silence or acceptance of benefits permits others to believe, that property is owned by or validly allotted to another, and who thereby induces reliance to their detriment, is estopped from later denying that position or challenging the resulting transfer or arrangement. Estoppel can bind those claiming through that person, even in a later capacity such as reversioner, whereas a transferee relying on ostensible ownership gets protection only if the true owner's consent, reliance, reasonable care and good faith are shown.
exceptions_or_limits: Estoppel needs a representation of existing fact (not mere law), reliance and detriment; reliance on the transferor's own title rather than on any representation by the true owner gives no estoppel or ostensible-owner protection.

Ostensible-owner protection (s.41 TPA) requires the true owner's express or implied consent, reasonable care by the transferee to ascertain authority, and good faith; the transferee bears the burden of proof. Mere management of common property or a record entry does not show consent.
A transferee who knew of the transferor's defective or disputed title, or who could readily have discovered lack of authority, cannot claim protection.
A transferee of a transfer meant to defeat creditors must prove good faith once the transferor's fraudulent intent is shown (s.53 TPA).
Estoppel does not extend to persons who did not make the representation or take the benefit (e.g. minors), or to claimants with independent title or no proven benefit.
No estoppel where a statutory bar exists, and a mere admission does not itself create title.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the good-faith exception to a fraudulent transfer against creditors under s.53 TPA, not estoppel by the challenger; it supports only the limit that good faith must be proved.
Applies s.41 TPA and denies protection for lack of owner consent and reasonable enquiry. It is the converse, transferee-protection side of the point.
Denies s.41 protection because the transferee knew the title was defective; this is a transferee good-faith issue, not estoppel against a challenger.
Denies s.41 protection because there was no representation by the true owner and the purchaser relied on the transferor's title; a transferee-side limit.
Denies s.41 protection because reasonable care would have shown the agent's lack of sale power; a transferee-side limit.

common_material_facts: The challenger consented to, acquiesced in, or accepted consideration or benefits from a sale, division, award or family settlement.
The other party relied on the apparent ownership or arrangement and changed position (paid advance, paid liabilities, bought property, gave up part of the estate).
Successors or reversioners claimed through, or in the same position as, the person who had accepted the benefit.
In the transferee-protection cases, the purchaser knew or could easily have found that the transferor's title or authority was defective.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 41, Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Section 53(1), Transfer of Property Act, 1882
