Section 115, Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Section 116, Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Section 3, Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937
Kanhai Lal v. Brij Lal (1919) 45 I.A. 118
Ramgouda Annagouda v. Bhausaheb
Ramcoomar v. Macqueen
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of 17 members, 12 find the challenger estopped (some also hold a successor or reversioner bound), and 5 deny the transferee ostensible-owner or good-faith protection for want of consent, reasonable care or good faith.
variations: Estoppel arises from different sources: acceptance of consideration, acceptance of an award or family settlement, express oral representation, silence or delay, or support of an order in earlier litigation.
Some members concern the true owner's estoppel against challenging a transfer, others the transferee's own entitlement to protection.
Reversioner cases turn on whether the claimant took only through the estopped predecessor or personally benefited, as opposed to holding independent title.
Estoppel was limited to the representing party's own share and did not bind minors.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) estoppel against a challenger by representation, acquiescence or acceptance of benefits, including reversioner and family-settlement cases (12 members), and (b) the transferee-side requirements for s.41 ostensible-owner or s.53 good-faith protection (1642365_3, 51976_2, 844274_6, 90856652_2, 148755915_3).

legal_question: When is a bona fide arrangement among family members or near relations, made to settle existing or possible property disputes or to preserve family harmony, valid and binding on its parties even though a recipient lacks an established legal title or the parties have no conflicting legal claims?

rule.if: family_arrangement_challenged and parties_are_family_members_or_near_relations_with_relationship_or_possible_claim and bona_fide_and_fair_arrangement and (existing_or_possible_dispute_settled or family_peace_or_harmony_purpose) and not fraud_coercion_or_undue_influence_proved

predicates.family_arrangement_challenged: A party or other person challenges the validity or binding effect of an agreement or settlement said to be a family arrangement.
predicates.parties_are_family_members_or_near_relat: The participants are family members or near relations, and each has at least a relationship plus a possible, apparent or assumed claim to the property. An established legal title or right of succession is not required.
predicates.bona_fide_and_fair_arrangement: The arrangement was made honestly and voluntarily, on terms that are fair and equitable in the circumstances. Where relevant, the family's needs and the interests of minors were considered.
predicates.existing_or_possible_dispute_settled: Read as a whole, the arrangement settles actual or apprehended disputes or competing claims among the family members. The disputes need not be legal claims, need not cover every item, and need not pit every participant against every other.
predicates.family_peace_or_harmony_purpose: The arrangement was made to preserve family harmony or prevent future disputes, even without conflicting legal claims.
predicates.fraud_coercion_or_undue_influence_proved: The challenger has pleaded and proved fraud, coercion, undue influence or similar vitiating circumstances.
predicates.family_arrangement_binding: The arrangement is upheld as a valid family arrangement and binds the parties, who may not repudiate it. A party who takes a benefit under it, or an allotted share under it, is held to it.

definition: A bona fide, fair and voluntary arrangement among family members or near relations that settles actual or possible disputes, or preserves family harmony, is upheld and binds the parties. This holds even if some recipient had no enforceable antecedent title or there were no conflicting legal claims, unless fraud, coercion or undue influence is proved.
exceptions_or_limits: The arrangement must be bona fide, voluntary and fair; fraud, coercion or undue influence must be clearly pleaded and proved to defeat it.
A draft or tentative proposal that was not accepted or concluded is not a binding arrangement.
Validity is judged on the facts and understanding existing when the arrangement was made, not on a later change in the law or judicial interpretation.
Acceptance of benefits and long acting on the arrangement strengthen its enforceability and bar repudiation.

A statutory restriction on transfer, such as the Court of Wards restriction, does not invalidate a bona fide family settlement, which is not a transfer or alienation. The members note the ward authority's knowledge and acceptance of payment as relevant.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the Registration Act s.17(2)(vi) exception for pre-amendment compromise decrees covering property outside the suit, not family-arrangement validity.
Registration question: a consent decree acknowledging a pre-existing family-settlement right over suit property needs no registration.
Registration question: a family settlement on antecedent titles does not need registration because it creates no interest for the first time.
Registration question: a compromise decree on suit property, with no collusion alleged, needs no registration.
Registration question: a family composition deed incorporated into a decree needs no registration.
Registration and admissibility of a decree recognising a pre-existing family-arrangement right, relied on in a pre-emption suit.
Registration Act s.17(1) and s.17(2)(vi) scope for court decrees and orders.
Evidence law: admissibility of a prior judgment under s.13 of the Evidence Act as a transaction asserting a right, not an admission.
Evidence law: a judgment not inter partes is admissible under s.13 as evidence of assertion or recognition of a property right.
Evidence law: relevance of a prior judgment on the same will under ss.11, 13 and 35 of the Evidence Act.

common_material_facts: Close relatives settle competing or apprehended claims to family or ancestral property.
The settlement is found bona fide and fair; allegations of fraud or undue influence are unproved.
The parties acted on the arrangement or accepted benefits under it.
The recipient's title is doubtful or absent, or the claims are possible rather than established.
Many members involve a later challenge to a document or decree arising from a family settlement.
statutes_and_provisions: Registration Act 1908 s.17(1)(b),(c), s.17(2)(i), s.17(2)(vi)
Evidence Act 1872 ss.11, 13, 21, 35
U.P. Court of Wards Act 1912 s.37(a)
Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act 1929
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 18 members, 8 uphold a bona fide family arrangement as binding. 7 hold that a decree or family settlement needs no registration, and 3 admit a prior judgment as relevant evidence. In nearly all, the challenge to the arrangement, decree or document failed.
variations: The family-arrangement members differ on what dispute suffices: actual competing claims, possible claims, or only a harmony purpose.
Some members involve a statutory bar (the Court of Wards restriction) or a later change in law.

The registration members concern a different question: whether an arrangement or decree needs registration, depending on whether it creates a right for the first time and whether it covers property outside the suit.
The evidence members concern relevance and admissibility of earlier judgments under the Evidence Act, not the validity of family arrangements.

split_suggestion: Split into three clusters. (1) Validity and binding effect of bona fide family arrangements: 1412888_2, 1649431_1, 1794534_1, 1846187_1, 1847257_4, 20394_2, 271205_1, 271205_4. (2) Registration Act s.17 exemptions for decrees, compromise decrees and family settlements: 136109_1, 180951885_1, 1946998_3, 199732092_1, 386828_3, 935946_1, 935946_2. (3) Evidentiary relevance of prior judgments under Evidence Act s.13 and related sections: 150069_3, 1880790_1, 428148_2.

legal_question: Can a writ challenge to land-acquisition notifications or proceedings be rejected for delay and laches when it is brought after an unreasonable, unexplained lapse of time, although the grounds were available earlier and the acquisition has advanced in the meantime?

rule.if: acquisition_challenge_writ and substantial_or_unreasonable_delay and grounds_available_earlier and not delay_satisfactorily_explained

predicates.acquisition_challenge_writ: The petitioner challenges land-acquisition notifications, declarations or proceedings (or a ground within them) by way of a writ petition.
predicates.substantial_or_unreasonable_delay: The challenge was filed after a substantial, unreasonable lapse of time from the notification or declaration, typically after the acquisition process had advanced (award made, possession taken, or award imminent).
predicates.grounds_available_earlier: The grounds now raised were available to the challenger when the notification or declaration was published, or at an earlier stage such as the objection inquiry.
predicates.delay_satisfactorily_explained: The challenger has given an adequate and credible explanation for the delay.
predicates.challenge_barred_by_laches: The challenge is rejected, or not entertained, on the ground of delay and laches.

definition: A challenge to land-acquisition notifications or proceedings must be brought within a reasonable time. If the challenger waits unreasonably, without adequate explanation, until the acquisition has advanced, and raises grounds that were available earlier, the court may reject it for laches without reaching the merits.
exceptions_or_limits: Delay may be excused where it is adequately explained. In 874426_3 the delay did not validate a notification that failed a mandatory statutory requirement, and the owner's explanation was considered.
Reasonableness of the delay is assessed in light of what was done in the interval in reliance on the notifications, such as the award, possession, expenditure and third-party rights.
Permission to bring a fresh challenge does not itself remove the laches bar (80086234_1).
Delay caused by the challenger's own litigation and interim orders cannot be used to argue that the public purpose has lapsed, absent evidence that the purpose is exhausted (1398535_3).
Constructive res judicata bars a ground omitted from an earlier proceeding on the same acquisition (876879_1). This is a related but distinct bar.
The court may reject the challenge without deciding whether the issuing authority was in fact authorised (1568935_5).

outlier_members.reason: Reaches the opposite outcome: the delay was explained and a notification violating its governing statute was not validated by delay. It marks a limit on the rule.
Rests on constructive res judicata under section 11 CPC for a ground omitted from an earlier writ, not on laches from delay.
Concerns whether delay caused by the challenger shows that the public purpose has ceased, not whether the challenge is barred by laches.
Concerns a representative challenge to village land management, not an acquisition. It is rejected as not bona fide and delayed because the challengers accepted benefits.

common_material_facts: Writ petitions were filed years after the notification or declaration, often when the award was imminent or made, or after possession was taken.
The grounds raised (vague public purpose, procedural defects, authority, private-company procedure) were available when the notification was published.
No timely objection was filed, or no explanation for the delay was offered.
The State had acted on the notifications, with awards, possession, compensation or expenditure on the public purpose.
statutes_and_provisions: Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution
Sections 4, 5A, 6 and 9 of the Land Acquisition Act and the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953
Section 15 of the Delhi Development Act
Section 11 CPC (constructive res judicata)
Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, [1975] 1 SCR 802, and the cases it discusses (Tilokchand Motichand, Rabindranath Bose)
Indrapuri Griha Nirman Sahakari Samiti, Larsen & Toubro, and Swaika Properties
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About 13 of 17 members reject the delayed challenge for laches or delay, mostly following Aflatoon. One holds that delay does not validate a statutorily defective notification, one applies constructive res judicata, one rejects a delay-based public-purpose argument, and one rejects a non-acquisition representative challenge.
variations: Some members stress completion of the acquisition and State expenditure, others the challenger's acquiescence, acceptance of compensation or failure to object.
Some decline to decide the merits at all, for example the authority question or the inquiry-hearing non-compliance.
The delay ranged from about four years to about seventeen years.
One member excuses delay because it was explained and the statutory defect was fundamental.

split_suggestion: Keep the core group of delay and laches bars to acquisition challenges. Separate 876879_1 (constructive res judicata), 1398535_3 (public-purpose survival), 874426_3 (delay explained, defective notification) and 217758_4 (non-acquisition representative challenge).

legal_question: Does an amendment that alters substantive rights, or that enlarges jurisdiction over or removes the finality of an existing decision, apply to proceedings already pending or decided before it took effect when it does not expressly or by necessary implication say so?

rule.if: amendment_affects_substantive_rights_or_finality and proceeding_or_decision_predates_amendment and not express_retroactive_intent and not necessary_implication_of_retroactivity

predicates.amendment_affects_substantive_rights_or_: The amendment changes substantive rights or obligations, narrows or creates a ground of relief, ousts or enlarges jurisdiction over an existing decision, or removes the finality of a decision. It is not merely procedural or clarificatory.
predicates.proceeding_or_decision_predates_amendmen: The suit, application, appeal, decree or final decision in question began or was made before the amendment took effect, and the amendment is invoked to alter its outcome.
predicates.express_retroactive_intent: The amendment's text expressly states that it applies retrospectively or to pending proceedings or past decisions.
predicates.necessary_implication_of_retroactivity: The amendment's language, scheme or context leaves no sensible reading other than that it applies to pending proceedings or past decisions. A beneficial purpose, or the mere fact of substitution, does not supply this.
predicates.amendment_operates_prospectively_and_pri: The amendment applies only from its commencement. The pending proceeding, earlier decree or vested right is decided under the law in force when the proceeding began or the decision was made.

definition: A statutory amendment that affects substantive rights, or enlarges jurisdiction over or undoes the finality of an existing decision, is presumed prospective. It does not govern proceedings already pending, or decisions already made, unless it expressly or by necessary implication says so. A beneficial purpose, the label 'substituted', or a claim that it is declaratory does not change this where the earlier text was clear and the amendment does not clarify any doubt.
exceptions_or_limits: Retrospective effect applies where the legislature expressly provides for it or it follows by necessary implication.
Declaratory or explanatory amendments that remove a real doubt or supply an obvious omission may operate retrospectively. The substance of the amendment, not its label, decides this.
Purely procedural changes that do not affect vested rights generally apply to pending proceedings.
A requirement that governs only future enforcement, without disturbing past acts or existing rights, can apply to a pending proceeding without being retrospective (see 673187_2).
Benevolent construction helps only where the text is ambiguous. It cannot add words to a plain provision.
Even where a statute has some retrospective operation, it should not be read to interfere with vested rights beyond what its plain words require.

outlier_members.reason: It holds that a new permission requirement governing future enforcement can apply to a pending eviction proceeding without being retrospective. This is a limit on the presumption, not an application of it.
It concerns the construction of a decree-conformity clause that refers to a specific earlier 'said Act'. It does not address whether a substantive amendment applies to pending matters.

common_material_facts: A suit, appeal, execution application or decree was initiated or decided before the amendment took effect.
The amendment contained no express retrospective language.
The amendment altered substantive rights, such as eviction grounds, pre-emption, compensation, jurisdiction or the finality of decisions.
The party seeking the benefit of the amendment argued that it was beneficial, that it was a substitution, or that it was declaratory.
statutes_and_provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, s. 13(3)(a)(iii)
Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, ss. 24 and 25, and the Bihar Land Reforms (Validation and Amendment) Act, 1974, ss. 1(2) and 6
Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, ss. 9-A and 64-A(2)
Andhra Pradesh Tenancy Laws (Amendment) Act, 1979, s. 93, and Limitation Act, s. 5
Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, s. 19, as amended in 1964
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, s. 29(2), and Gujarat Act 18 of 1965
Punjab Pre-emption Act, including s. 31 and the substituted pre-emption provision
Agricultural leases legislation of 1951, as amended in 1953, ss. 16, 16A and 16B
Code of Civil Procedure, s. 115
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 15 of 17 members the amendment was held prospective and the earlier law governed the pending proceeding or earlier decision. One member (673187_2) applied a new enforcement requirement to a pending proceeding as not truly retrospective. One member (82667_3) construed a decree-conformity clause narrowly.
variations: Some members concern pending proceedings (suits, appeals, execution). Others concern decisions that had already become final (527336_1, 663930_1, 1322950_4, 1461370_3).

Some members add rules on specific arguments: beneficial construction (1701224_3), substitution or declaratory character (1701224_4, 661966_3), and an amendment that expressly adds a power to condone delay (1406099_2).
Jurisdictional amendments were tested by the requirement of express words or necessary implication to oust civil-court jurisdiction (660623_1).
In 1916007_1 the court also considered that applying the amendment could leave a decree-holder without a remedy.
The authorities cited vary: Garikapati Veeraya, Hitendra Thakur and Moti Ram for pre-emption and compensation; Keshavlal Jethalal Shah for final decisions and declaratory enactments.

split_suggestion: Keep the 15 covered members together as the presumption of prospectivity for substantive amendments. Move 673187_2 to a separate group on procedural or enforcement requirements that apply to pending proceedings. Move 82667_3 to a group on the construction of cross-referencing clauses in amending enactments.

legal_question: Under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, can statutory interest or the additional amount under s.23(1-A) be awarded for a period before publication of the preliminary (s.4(1)) notification because possession was taken earlier, or is the owner confined to other remedies such as rent or damages?

predicates.land_acquisition_act_1894_compensation_p: The claim for compensation, interest or an additional amount arises under acquisition proceedings governed by the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
predicates.possession_taken_before_preliminary_noti: The State or its agency took possession of the land before the preliminary notification under s.4(1) was published.
predicates.statutory_interest_or_additional_amount_: The claimant seeks statutory interest (ss.28/34) or the additional amount (s.23(1-A)), or interest at a rate or for a period beyond the statute, for the time before the s.4(1) notification.
predicates.urgency_provision_possession_under_valid: Possession was taken under the s.16/s.17 urgency provisions following a s.4(1) notification, so the possession is treated as lawfully taken under the Act.
predicates.statutory_interest_and_additional_amount: Statutory interest and the s.23(1-A) additional amount run only from publication of the s.4(1) notification, not from the earlier possession. The owner may instead seek rent or damages for the earlier use and occupation, and courts cannot add equitable interest outside the statute.

definition: The 1894 Act is a self-contained code. Possession taken before the s.4(1) notification is outside the Act and does not trigger statutory interest or the s.23(1-A) additional amount for the earlier period. Those run from publication of the notification. The owner keeps title and may claim rent or damages for the earlier occupation.
exceptions_or_limits: The owner may separately seek rent or damages for pre-notification use and occupation, and the Collector may determine the amount.
Where possession is taken under the urgency provisions after a valid notification, compensation and interest may be payable from that possession.
The Act's interest scheme cannot be supplemented by equitable or common-law interest at a higher rate or for a longer period.
The rule is limited to the 1894 Act. Where another law or the general law on compulsory taking applies, interest from possession may be available, subject to any clear statutory exclusion.
If the factual basis for pre-notification possession (for example, alleged submergence) is disputed, it must first be established, and the Collector may be directed to examine it.

outlier_members.reason: Awards the s.23(1-A) additional amount from pre-notification possession. This is the Gadag-type view that other members in the cluster (190336_2, 522924_1) reject or overrule.
Concerns only the factual question of whether possession preceded the award. It does not address pre-notification possession.
Concerns interest under ss.31 and 34 where compensation is not paid or deposited before possession, which is a different point.
Concerns whether the interest claim is enforceable against the State and the Collector's liability, which is a different point.

Concerns interest from possession under a state statute that applied s.23(1) of the 1894 Act, based on the general rule that taking possession implies interest. It does not concern pre-notification possession under the 1894 Act.
Concerns interest on unpaid requisition compensation for the period of deprivation, absent clear statutory exclusion. It is a different statutory context.
Concerns equitable interest under the Interest Act, 1839 for deprivation under a failed exchange arrangement. It is not an acquisition-statute case.
Concerns additional interest for non-payment of advance compensation in an emergency acquisition. It is not about pre-notification possession, and the judges were referred to a larger Bench.
Concerns the valuation date for compensation after breach of the advance-payment condition, and the judges were referred to a larger Bench. It is a different point.

common_material_facts: Possession was taken (often by submergence or for a project) before the s.4(1) notification.
The notification and award followed later.
The lower courts or the Collector had awarded interest or the additional amount from the earlier possession date.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, ss.4(1), 17, 23(1-A), 28, 34, 48
Special Tehsildar v. M.A. Jabbar (followed)
Assistant Commissioner, Gadag v. Mathapathi Basavannewwa (disapproved)
R.L. Jain v. DDA and Lila Ghosh v. State of West Bengal
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 8 of the covered members, awards of statutory interest or the additional amount for the pre-notification period were set aside or denied. Where possession was pre-notification, owners were sometimes pointed to rent or damages (3 members). The members outside the covered group, such as 382270_1, took the contrary approach on the additional amount.
variations: Some members concern interest under ss.28/34, others the additional amount under s.23(1-A).
One member (177401_1) bars equitable interest on top of the statutory scheme rather than addressing pre-notification possession directly.
Some members add the rent or damages remedy, including a direction to the Collector to determine it, while others only deny interest.
The urgency-provision exception is noted in some members but was not applied on the facts.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) pre-notification possession under the 1894 Act: statutory interest and s.23(1-A) additional amount denied, rent or damages available (covered members plus 382270_1 as the overruled contrary view); (b) interest from possession on general principles outside the 1894 Act's statutory interest scheme (1890797_5, 1927634_1, 751356_4); (c) non-payment or deposit of compensation and advance payment under ss.17, 31 and 34 (1696931_1, 1696931_2, 56073873_4, 56073873_6); (d) 117687_3 as a fact-specific interest commencement issue.

legal_question: When should the Supreme Court set aside or commute a death sentence for murder and substitute life imprisonment, because the case is not a rarest-of-rare case and the circumstances of the crime and the offender do not show that life imprisonment is inadequate?

rule.if: appeal_against_death_sentence and murder_conviction_sustained and (not rarest_of_rare_threshold_met) and (mitigating_or_non_aggravated_circumstances_present or aggravating_basis_not_proved)

predicates.appeal_against_death_sentence: The Supreme Court is hearing an appeal or review against a death sentence imposed or confirmed by a lower court.
predicates.murder_conviction_sustained: The conviction for murder is upheld, or the court is considering sentence for a proven murder.
predicates.rarest_of_rare_threshold_met: On the whole of the circumstances of the crime and the offender, the case is one of the rarest of rare cases in which life imprisonment is inadequate and the alternative is unquestionably foreclosed.
predicates.mitigating_or_non_aggravated_circumstanc: The record shows mitigating or non-aggravating features, such as no premeditation or planning, a triggering dispute or provocation, impulsive or unplanned conduct, no extreme brutality, no personal gain, reform prospects, no continuing threat, delay, or offender-specific mitigation.
predicates.aggravating_basis_not_proved: The aggravating basis relied on by the courts below is not established on the evidence, for example the manner of killing, extreme brutality, rape, the offender's individual role, or a property motive.
predicates.death_sentence_replaced_with_life_impris: The death sentence is set aside or commuted and imprisonment for life is imposed, the murder conviction usually remaining.

definition: Life imprisonment is the norm for murder and death is an exception reserved for the rarest of rare cases. Where the circumstances of the crime and the offender, weighed with mitigation, do not show that life imprisonment is inadequate, or the aggravating basis relied on is not proved, the Supreme Court commutes the death sentence to life imprisonment while upholding the conviction.
exceptions_or_limits: Death may still be imposed where the crime is extremely brutal, grotesque, diabolical, revolting or dastardly and the alternative of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed.
Circumstantial evidence alone is not an absolute bar to death, but it weighs against it.
The assessment is case-specific; the gravity of the crime alone does not dispense with weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
Some courts add that life means imprisonment for natural life or bar release for a minimum period; this is not the general result.
A few members rest on fact-specific factors, such as delay, the weapon used, or the hesitancy of the court, rather than a fully articulated rarest-of-rare analysis.

common_material_facts: A murder conviction upheld, with a death sentence imposed or confirmed by the courts below
Crime arising from a family, land, property or water dispute, often with prior quarrels or provocation
Absence of premeditation or planning, or of extreme brutality or cruelty
Offender-specific mitigation, such as no habitual criminality, reform prospects, age, long custody, serious injuries to the offender, or delay in proceedings
Weak or unproved aggravating bases, such as rape not proved, unclear manner of killing, or unreliable evidence of individual role
statutes_and_provisions: Section 302 IPC
Section 354(3) CrPC (special reasons for death)
Sections 360 and 361 CrPC
Section 57 IPC (life imprisonment and release)
Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab
Machhi Singh v. State of Punjab
Ediga Anamma v. State of Andhra Pradesh
Rajendra Prasad
Bishnu Deo Shaw
Sahdeo v. State of U.P.
Dudh Nath Pandey v. State of U.P.
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 17 members set aside or commuted the death sentence and imposed life imprisonment, upholding the murder conviction (one also set aside a rape finding, one directed imprisonment for natural life, and one restricted release for a minimum term).
variations: Several members apply the express rarest-of-rare test with Bachan Singh and Machhi Singh, while others give brief fact-based reasoning with no authority cited.
Mitigation varies: lack of premeditation, provocation, intoxication, family or property dispute, age and custody, reform prospects, delay, or the weapon used.
Some members turn on evidentiary weakness (circumstantial evidence, unreliable accomplice evidence, unproved rape, unknown manner of killing) rather than on mitigation.
Some members commute despite acknowledging gravity (gruesome killings, planned or cold-blooded murder, depraved motive) because of the irreversibility of death or the possibility of reform.
Some members add conditions on the life sentence, such as natural-life imprisonment or a minimum term before release.

legal_question: When a competent legislature retrospectively validates earlier acts (acquisitions, vestings, evictions) that were defective or made under a repealed or invalid law, does the validation sustain those acts against challenges based on the cured defect, such as a missing procedural step, a prior court order, a repealed law, or discrimination between procedures?

predicates.validating_law_enacted_by_competent_legi: The validating enactment was passed by a legislature with legislative power over the subject matter (and any required assent was obtained).
predicates.validating_law_operates_retrospectively_: The enactment expressly or by necessary implication applies to past actions, deems them valid or taken under it, or applies notwithstanding other laws or court judgments, decrees or orders.
predicates.past_action_within_scope_of_validating_l: The challenged earlier action falls within the category the validating law covers and meets any substantive conditions it sets (for example, the public-purpose conditions, or that the action would have been proper under the earlier law).
predicates.validating_law_removes_or_overrides_the_: The validating law cures, deems away, or overrides the defect relied on by the challenger: a missing or irregular procedural step, a repealed or invalid earlier law, a prior judgment setting the action aside, or a choice between competing procedures.
predicates.independent_constitutional_violation_in_: The validating law itself infringes a constitutional limit, such as a fundamental right or Article 14 discrimination that the validation does not remove. Constitutional objections stay open even where a validating law bars other grounds.
predicates.past_action_is_sustained_and_not_open_to: The earlier action is treated as valid, and the challenge fails to the extent it rests on the defect the validating law cured.

definition: A competent legislature may retrospectively validate earlier actions, including by deeming missing steps taken, overriding court orders, or making one of two competing procedures the only applicable one. Challenges to such actions based on the cured defect then fail, provided the actions meet the validating law's own conditions and the law does not itself violate the Constitution.
exceptions_or_limits: Validation operates only on actions within the validating law's scope and satisfying its substantive conditions, for example the public-purpose conditions, or consistency with the later law.

Constitutional and fundamental-rights objections, and challenges expressly preserved under the governing acquisition law, remain available. Clauses barring challenges on any other ground are read down accordingly.
The legislature must have competence over the subject, and any required assent must have been obtained.

Where a court order is overridden, the validating law must expressly operate notwithstanding court judgments, and the acquisition must be complete (for example, the land vested in the Government) and meet the law's conditions.
Validation does not discriminate where earlier and later acts must satisfy the same substantive conditions.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns whether lawful cancellation of a quasi-permanent evacuee allotment breaches the property right. This is not about retrospective validation.
Concerns whether a quasi-permanent allotment is constitutionally protected property under Articles 19(1)(f), 31(1) and 31(2). This is not about validation.
Concerns whether cancellation of an allotment under statutory power is deprivation without authority of law. This is not about validation.
Concerns whether an allotment is property protected by Article 19(1)(f). This is not about validation.
Concerns whether cancellation under the allotment's own statutory power violates Article 31(1). This is not about validation.
Concerns whether cancellation of an allotment is an acquisition or requisitioning under Article 31(2). This is not about validation.
Concerns whether deprivation under a valid parliamentary law satisfies Article 31(1). It is only loosely related to 82588_3 on authority of law and does not involve retrospective validation.

common_material_facts: An earlier acquisition, vesting or eviction action was alleged to be defective: a missing notice, an invalid or repealed enactment, a procedure choice held discriminatory, or a prior court order setting it aside.
A later enactment deemed the earlier actions valid or taken under it, retrospectively and often notwithstanding court judgments.
Legislative competence over the subject was undisputed or established.
Challengers invoked Article 14, Article 31(1) or non-compliance with the displaced law.
statutes_and_provisions: Administration of Evacuee Property Act 1950, s. 8(2), 8(2A)
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act 1957, s. 28(3), 28(3A), and the 1969 Amendment Act, s. 3
Bangalore Acquisition of Lands (Validation) Act 1962, s. 2(1)(a), 2(2)
Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act 1971, ss. 15 and 20, and the 1958 Act, s. 5
Articles 14 and 31(1) of the Constitution
Land Acquisition Act 1894
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 10 covered members the validation was upheld and the earlier action sustained or the challenge rejected. The Article 14 and Article 31(1) challenges failed, and defects in procedure or in the earlier law were cured.
variations: Some members cure a missing procedural step by a deeming fiction (866209_1, 1098092_1).
Some override a prior court judgment (1521043_4).
Some remove discrimination between competing procedures (215754_1, 958208_2).
Some address the Article 31(1) 'authority of law' point (82588_3).
Some address the scope of retrospective operation (82588_1, 270610_2).
958208_1 preserves constitutional and statutory objections despite a bar on other grounds.
1521043_3 turns on equal substantive conditions for earlier and later acquisitions.

split_suggestion: Split into (1) retrospective validating legislation (the 10 covered members, which could be further divided into validation curing procedural defects or court orders and validation answering Article 14 or Article 31(1) challenges); and (2) constitutional treatment of quasi-permanent evacuee allotments and their cancellation under Articles 19(1)(f), 31(1) and 31(2) (1665121_4, 1882779_1, 1882779_2, 1988725_1, 1988725_2, 1988725_3). 232712_2 (deprivation under a valid law) could sit with group 2 or with the Article 31(1) members of group 1.

legal_question: Is a land acquisition proceeding invalid merely because a prescribed form, express recital, prior scheme or plan, prior permission or earlier-sequenced inquiry was omitted, when the governing statute does not require it at that stage?

predicates.acquisition_proceeding_challenged: The validity of a land acquisition notification, declaration, award or related proceeding is challenged.
predicates.challenge_based_on_omitted_formality_rec: The challenge rests on the absence of a prescribed form, an express recital or statement, a prior scheme or development plan, a prior permission, or an earlier-sequenced inquiry.
predicates.governing_statute_does_not_require_it_at: The governing statute, expressly or by necessary implication, does not make the omitted item a prerequisite at the stage when the challenged step was taken. This includes cases where the work is done by the government rather than by a trust or authority that must first frame a scheme, and where the notification does not state that it is for executing a formal scheme.
predicates.substantive_statutory_conditions_satisfi: The substantive conditions the statute does impose are met, for example the government's actual satisfaction, a genuine basis for urgency where urgency is invoked, and any required inquiry before the final declaration.
predicates.acquisition_not_invalid_on_that_ground: The acquisition or proceeding is not invalidated by the omission relied on, although it may still be challenged on other grounds.

definition: An acquisition proceeding is not invalidated by the absence of a prescribed form, express recital, prior scheme or plan, prior permission or earlier inquiry, where the governing statute does not require that item at that stage and its real substantive conditions are met. Substance prevails over form, and acquisition may precede development planning.
exceptions_or_limits: A scheme is mandatory where the trust or authority itself undertakes the work, or where the notification expressly states that the land is acquired to execute a formal scheme prepared under the statute.

Substantive conditions remain open to challenge. The government must actually be satisfied, and urgency must be genuinely justified on the circumstances and records. A notification can be invalid for lack of genuine urgency even if it need not recite the urgency.

Inquiries that the statute or rules make a precondition of the final declaration, such as the company-acquisition inquiry, must still precede that declaration, even if not the preliminary notification.
Later development must still comply with the applicable approval and sanction requirements, and a scheme should exist before developed sites are disposed of.

A planning-law notice lapses or releases land only where the land is specifically designated for compulsory acquisition in the plans and acquisition has not already proceeded under the acquisition law.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the positive scope of a statutory urgency power over land that is neither waste nor arable. It does not concern the effect of an omitted form, recital, scheme or prerequisite.

common_material_facts: Owners or appellants challenged an acquisition for lack of a scheme, master plan, development-area declaration, prior permission, prescribed form or express recital.
The acquisition was for planned development, urban improvement or housing, or by a company.
The government or acquiring authority had issued the notification or declaration and the substantive statutory steps were otherwise followed.
The High Court had often invalidated the acquisition on the formal ground, and the Supreme Court reversed.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963, Rule 4
Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, ss. 2(1)(vi), 29, 52, 72
Delhi Development Act, 1957, ss. 12, 15, 55
Tamil Nadu Housing Board Act, ss. 35, 36, 37-56, 70
U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Adhiniyam, 1965 and U.P. (Regulation of Building Operations) Act, 1958, s. 6
Land Acquisition (U.P. Amendment) Act, 1954 (s. 17(1-A))
Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953, s. 17(4)
Constitution of India, Arts. 215 and 299
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 16 covered members the omission was held not to invalidate the acquisition. About 6 concern the absence of a prior scheme or plan, about 6 the absence of a form or recital, and the rest sequencing, permission or planning-notice objections.
variations: Some members concern the content of notifications (urgency, waste or arable land, satisfaction). Others concern prerequisite schemes or plans, and others the sequencing of inquiries or permissions.
The scheme cases turn on who undertakes the work (trust or government) and on whether the notification invokes a formal scheme.
One member (the urgency recital) is accompanied by the caveat that genuine urgency must still be shown.
The consent-award and award-in-substance members rely on substance over form rather than on statutory silence.
The planning-notice member rests on the land not being designated for compulsory acquisition, rather than on an omitted formality.

split_suggestion: Optionally split into (a) no prior scheme or development plan required for acquisition (1539693_1, 1568935_4, 1883818_2, 284811_6, 488907_1, 63447541_2, 234754_1, 1809461_4); and (b) no prescribed form or recital required in notifications, declarations and awards (1407555_2, 1514028_1, 1527139_3, 1704181_2, 351816_1, 37963_2, 469498_3, 303393_1). Treat 18928039_1 separately as a question of the scope of the urgency possession power.

legal_question: When is a suit confined to a bare declaration or a bare injunction not maintainable because the plaintiff omitted available further relief (such as possession) or a declaration of title, and when is that omission excused?

rule.if: ((declaratory_suit_only and further_relief_against_defendant_available and further_relief_omitted) or (bare_injunction_suit and genuine_title_dispute_or_cloud and title_requires_full_adjudication and declaration_not_sought)) and not (further_relief_unavailable_against_defendant or title_already_finally_adjudicated)

predicates.declaratory_suit_only: The plaintiff sues only for a declaration (of title, ownership or invalidity), with at most incidental relief.
predicates.further_relief_against_defendant_availab: The plaintiff, being out of possession or facing a defendant in possession, is able to seek a further consequential relief against the defendant, such as recovery of possession or setting aside an order.
predicates.further_relief_omitted: The plaintiff did not claim that available further or consequential relief.
predicates.bare_injunction_suit: The suit seeks only an injunction (usually to protect possession) and does not seek a declaration of title.
predicates.genuine_title_dispute_or_cloud: The defendant raises a real, substantiated dispute over the plaintiff's title that casts a cloud on it, including on a vacant site where possession depends on title.
predicates.title_requires_full_adjudication: Deciding title involves complicated questions of fact or law, or the title issue was not properly pleaded and raised, so a full trial in a comprehensive suit is needed.
predicates.declaration_not_sought: The plaintiff did not seek a declaration of title in the suit.
predicates.further_relief_unavailable_against_defen: The defendant is not in possession and cannot deliver possession, for example because the property is in custody of the law, so no further relief lies against the defendant.
predicates.title_already_finally_adjudicated: The plaintiff's title has already been finally decided in proceedings binding on the opposing party, so res judicata applies.
predicates.limited_relief_suit_not_maintainable: The suit, as framed, cannot be maintained or the declaration or injunction cannot be granted, and the plaintiff must seek the fuller relief.

definition: A plaintiff who sues only for a declaration, while omitting further relief such as possession that is available against the defendant, cannot obtain the declaration. A plaintiff who sues only for an injunction, when the defendant raises a genuine and complex dispute over title, must seek a declaration of title in a comprehensive suit. The omission is excused where no further relief lies against the defendant, as with property in custody of the law, or where title has already been finally adjudicated.
exceptions_or_limits: Further relief means relief against the defendant. If the defendant is not in possession and cannot deliver possession (for example, property attached and in judicial custody with the custodian not a party), a declaration may be sought without claiming possession.
Where property is attached and held in custody of the law, a party may seek determination of its entitlement to possession without a separate prayer for recovery of possession.
A court may decide a simple, straightforward title issue in an injunction suit if the necessary pleadings and an appropriate issue exist; this is an exception.
A dispute over title does not in every case require a declaration. It does only where the defendant raises a genuine dispute that clouds the plaintiff's title.
Where title has already been finally adjudicated and binds the parties, a separate declaration is not required before suing for possession (1257214_1).

outlier_members.reason: It turns on res judicata making a separate declaration unnecessary before a possession suit. It is only a related limit, not part of the main rule.
It concerns the need for a finding on actual or constructive possession within the limitation period (Article 142) and remand. It does not concern the form of relief.
It concerns whether specific performance can be claimed in the alternative to rescission of the same contract.
It concerns election between rescission and specific performance when no cause of action for specific performance is pleaded.
It concerns limiting a decree to possession where no finding of the plaintiff's possession was made, a remedial modification only.
It concerns the duty to decide disputed title and the burden of proving it in a title-based suit, not the maintainability of a limited-relief suit.
It concerns whether an injunction suit based on continuing possession can be treated as a summary possession suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

common_material_facts: The plaintiff is out of possession, or the defendant disputes title and possession, and the plaintiff sues for a bare declaration or a bare injunction.
Possession or a declaration of title was available but not claimed.
The disputed property is often a vacant site where possession follows title.
The defendant raises a substantiated cloud on title, such as competing deeds or acquisition proceedings.
In the exception cases the property is attached and in judicial custody and no party is in possession.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (proviso)
Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act (1877 Act)
Section 146(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure
Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) 4 SCC 594
Jharkhand State Housing Board v. Didar Singh (2019) 17 SCC 692
Ram Saran v. Ganga Devi, AIR 1972 SC 2685
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 10 covered members, 8 hold the declaration-only or bare-injunction suit not maintainable, or relegate the parties to a comprehensive title or declaratory suit. 2 (1699330_1 and 337165_3) hold that possession need not be claimed because the property is in custody of the law.
variations: Some members rest on the declaration proviso (Sections 34 and 42). Others rest on the Anathula Sudhakar line for bare injunctions.
In 190311198_1 the plaintiff had already amended the pleadings to seek a declaration, so the remand was left undisturbed.
In 540361_3 the court refused to decide title because it was complex and not properly pleaded or raised.
710942_4 applies the bar to a declaration challenging an order, where setting aside the order was the omitted relief, rather than to possession.
The custody-of-law cases show that omitting possession is not fatal when no relief can be had against the defendant.

split_suggestion: Split into: (a) declaration-only suits barred for omitting further relief, with the custody-of-law exceptions (123401091_1, 61939581_5, 1683926_1, 710942_4, 1699330_1, 337165_3); (b) bare-injunction suits where title is genuinely disputed and a declaration is needed (124421981_1, 190311198_1, 41602852_1, 540361_3); (c) title and possession proof and remand issues (826407_1, 826407_2, 1388988_2, 50400_2, 1257214_1); (d) rescission versus specific performance (1554781_1, 1554781_3).

legal_question: When may a higher court (second appellate, revisional, writ or special-leave court) interfere with concurrent or supported findings of fact by rent or eviction fact-finding authorities on matters such as the landlord's bona fide need, comparative hardship, acquiescence or fair rent?

predicates.challenge_to_findings_of_fact_in_rent_or: The appeal, revision or special-leave petition attacks factual findings (for example bona fide need, comparative hardship, acquiescence, or fair rent) made in rent control or eviction proceedings.
predicates.findings_made_by_fact_finding_authoritie: The trial court, rent controller, prescribed authority or first appellate court made the finding, and it was either concurrently affirmed by the other courts or authorities or rests on evidence on the record.
predicates.finding_shown_to_be_perverse_or_legally_: The challenger has shown that the finding is perverse, or that the law was misinterpreted or misapplied, or that there was another legal infirmity.
predicates.other_sufficient_ground_for_interference: The challenger has shown some other appropriate or acceptable ground for the higher court to disturb the finding, for example the finding was never properly considered or displaced by the reviewing court.
predicates.factual_findings_left_undisturbed: The higher court declines to reappraise the evidence or disturb the factual findings, and they stand.

definition: Where fact-finding authorities have made findings in rent or eviction matters, particularly concurrent findings on bona fide need, comparative hardship or similar issues, and those findings are supported by evidence, a higher court exercising second-appeal, revisional, writ or special-leave jurisdiction will not disturb them unless the challenger shows perversity, legal error or another sufficient ground.
exceptions_or_limits: Interference is permitted where the finding is perverse or the law has been misinterpreted or misapplied.
Interference is permitted where an appropriate or acceptable ground is shown; mere possibility of a competing view on the record is not enough.
Revisional power under some rent statutes is wider than under Section 115 CPC but does not make the High Court a second court of first appeal.
A tenant pleading greater hardship must show that alternative accommodation is unavailable.
An issue finally decided between the same parties in earlier certificate proceedings cannot be reopened, and evidence directed only at it does not justify remand.

outlier_members.reason: Turns on finality and bar on relitigating a partition issue decided in earlier certificate proceedings, not on the limits of interference with factual findings.

Concerns whether a revisional authority may remand to admit evidence on a finally decided partition issue; it rests on the same finality bar, though it also treats the concurrent need finding as not open to reopening.

common_material_facts: Landlord sought eviction or release of premises on bona fide personal or family need, often with a comparative hardship comparison.
Trial and first appellate authorities made findings that the High Court affirmed or that the higher court was asked to disturb.
The challenger did not demonstrate perversity, legal error or other ground for interference.
Some findings were corroborated by a commissioner's inspection or local commission report.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 100 and Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Section 50 of the Mysore Rent Control Act, 1961
Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Sections 4(2)(a) and 4(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949
Sections 88-C and 33-B of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 14 core members the higher court left the factual findings undisturbed. Of these, about 11 were findings for the landlord on need or hardship, one was a finding against the landlord (1761668_2), one on fair rent and one on acquiescence. The two outliers also kept the concurrent findings intact, on the ground of finality.
variations: The standard is stated differently: perversity or legal error (special leave, second appeal), no sufficient or acceptable ground, or no reason to disregard.
Some members rely on specific supporting evidence such as a commissioner's report, the absence of tenant evidence on alternative accommodation, or the testimony of one landlord.
Some members cite precedent (Bega Begum, Vinod Kumar Arora, Dhanpal Chettiar); many cite none.
In one member the writ court had not displaced the hardship finding, so it stood.
Findings concerned different subject matter: need, hardship, acquiescence, or fair rent.

split_suggestion: Optionally separate the two Bombay Tenancy members (1717694_2, 1717694_3), which turn on finality of the earlier certificate proceedings and the bar on relitigating the partition issue, from the rest, which concern restraint in disturbing findings of fact.

legal_question: When the law changes while an appeal or other proceeding is pending, must the appellate court decide it under the changed law, or does the earlier law (or a vested right) continue to govern?

rule.if: proceeding_pending_when_law_changed and later_law_applies_to_pending_proceedings_expressly_or_by_necessary_implication and later_law_is_valid and not saving_provision_preserves_the_right

predicates.proceeding_pending_when_law_changed: An appeal (including a further appeal or a leave petition treated as a pending appeal) or other proceeding was still pending, and the decree under challenge had not become final and effective, when the later law came into force.
predicates.later_law_applies_to_pending_proceedings: The later law, by its express words, by clear intendment, or by deeming and retroactive language, covers suits, appeals or proceedings already pending, or removes the legal basis of the decree or judgment under challenge.
predicates.later_law_is_valid: The later law is constitutionally valid and does more than simply declare a judgment ineffective while leaving its legal basis unchanged.
predicates.saving_provision_preserves_the_right: A saving provision, which the later law left unchanged, or an equivalent expression of intent preserves the accrued or vested right or the pre-existing transaction in issue.
predicates.appellate_court_decides_pending_matter_u: The appellate court must apply the later law as it stands, even where that sets aside a decree, removes a remedy, or affects rights obtained at first instance, and must dispose of the appeal accordingly.

definition: An appeal is a continuation or rehearing of the suit. Where a valid later law expressly or by necessary implication covers pending proceedings, or removes the basis of the decree, the appellate court must decide the appeal under the changed law, even if that defeats rights obtained at first instance. Without such retroactive intent, or where a saving provision applies, the earlier law and vested rights continue to govern.
exceptions_or_limits: If the later law shows no express or necessarily implied retroactive intent, a right fixed by the decree or acquired under the law in force when the suit began is not impaired, and the appellate court does not apply the amendment (1913453_1, 661966_1).
A saving provision that the later law leaves unchanged keeps the pre-existing alienation or right protected, so the appeal remains maintainable (1475334_3).
A change in the law does not reopen a decree that has become final and has been effectively executed (717095_2).
A legislature may remove the basis of a judgment retrospectively, but it may not simply declare a judgment ineffective while leaving its legal basis intact (1835110_2, 522381_2).
Whether a petition for special leave counts as a pending appeal depends on the challenge having been filed before the law changed, not on leave being granted (803866_2).

outlier_members.reason: It decides only that a statutory review procedure does not restrict an appellate court's power to decide a pending appeal under a retrospective amendment. It does not decide which law governs the pending appeal, though it is consistent with the rule.

common_material_facts: A decree or judgment was under appeal, or a remedy application was pending, when an amendment, repeal or new enactment came into force.
The amendment either expressly covered pending suits and appeals (often by barring decrees inconsistent with the amended law) or was silent on retrospectivity.
Pre-emption suits under the Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913 and its 1960 amendment or the 1973 Repeal Act recur frequently.
Tenancy and ejectment remedies omitted by amendment, including section 28 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, recur.
Retrospective deeming provisions removed the basis of earlier High Court compensation judgments.
statutes_and_provisions: Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, section 31, as amended by Punjab Act 10 of 1960
Punjab Pre-emption (Repeal) Act, 1973, section 3
Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, section 28, and the Amendment Act, 1953, section 1(2)
Bengal General Clauses Act, section 8
Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, section 4
Article 136 of the Constitution
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, section 88(1)(d)
Punjab Customs (Power to Contest) Act, 1920, section 4
Order 20 Rule 14 CPC
Punjab Relief of Indebtedness Act, sections 5 and 6, and Usurious Loans Act, section 3
United Provinces Agricultural Income-tax (Amendment) Act, 1956, section 11
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 12 of 17 members the changed law was applied in the pending appeal. This usually meant setting aside the decree, dismissing the suit, or denying the omitted remedy. In 3 members (1475334_3, 1913453_1, 661966_1) the earlier law or a vested right prevailed because the amendment lacked retroactive intent or a saving provision applied. The remaining members deal with ancillary points: pendency of a leave petition, the review procedure, and the law in force at judgment.
variations: Some members rely on the principle that an appeal is a rehearing or continuation of the suit, so the appellate decree replaces the trial decree.
Others turn on the express wording of the amendment, such as 'no decree inconsistent with the amended law' or 'applies to pending proceedings'.
Some members apply the law as it stands at the date of judgment, while the vested-right members protect rights fixed by the law in force when the suit began.
The deeming-fiction members rest on carrying the fiction to its logical conclusion, subject to the limit on legislative reversal of judgments.
1658374_2 treats abatement of a pending suit on appeal and leaves open the effect of possession delivered earlier.

legal_question: When a landlord seeks eviction for rent default under a state rent-control statute, what must a tenant pay or tender, when, and how regularly, to obtain or keep the statutory protection from eviction, and what happens if the tenant falls short?

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: The landlord seeks eviction or possession (in a suit, application, appeal or revision) on the ground of rent default or arrears under a rent-control statute.
predicates.tenant_seeks_statutory_payment_based_pro: The tenant relies on a statutory provision that bars or avoids eviction (or permits a revision or appeal) if the tenant pays, tenders or deposits the rent due.
predicates.tenant_fully_complied_with_statutory_pay: The tenant paid or tendered unconditionally the entire amount the statute requires (rent including time-barred rent, permitted increases, interest, and costs if directed) by the first hearing, deadline or date fixed by the court, and continued paying regularly and punctually until final decision.
predicates.tenant_not_entitled_to_statutory_protect: The tenant cannot claim the statutory protection from eviction, and the eviction or possession decree follows, or the revision is not maintainable.

definition: Statutory protection from eviction for rent default is conditional on strict compliance with the statute's payment requirements. The tenant must pay or tender the full amount due (including time-barred rent, and costs if directed) unconditionally by the prescribed time and then pay regularly until final decision. Shortfall, lateness, irregular payment, or unpaid costs defeats the protection. Courts have no discretion to excuse non-compliance.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the tenant genuinely disputes the rent rate or amount, the outcome depends on the statutory mechanism. Under the Bombay Act the tenant must apply to the court within one month of the demand notice. Under the East Punjab Act the Controller must first provisionally assess the amount before the tender is due, and must then finally adjudicate the dispute.

Interim rent is not standard rent. Costs are payable only if the court directs them. An appellate court that enhances standard rent may fix a date for paying the difference, and the absence of such a date is a technical error.

The time for a deposit may be fixed by a specific statutory trigger, such as knowledge of the pending suit under Section 39 of the U.P. Act. The tenant's own delay in seeking other information does not extend it.
Where the tenant complies fully, the protection applies. Under the East Punjab Act, compliance with the provisional assessment does not end the case, because the dispute is still finally adjudicated.
The rent-control revision requirement to deposit arrears on filing is subject to the statutory summary procedure where the amount is actually disputed.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the Controller's duty to provisionally assess disputed arrears before the tenant's tender is due. It is a procedural duty of the adjudicator, not a consequence of the tenant's non-compliance.
Concerns the Controller's duty to finally adjudicate the dispute after the tenant tenders the provisionally assessed amount. It is a different legal point from the tenant's loss of protection.

common_material_facts: Landlord sues for eviction or possession on the ground of rent arrears or default.
Tenant deposits or pays only part of the amount due, deposits late, or pays irregularly during the suit or appeal.
Tenant omits a component of the amount due, such as time-barred rent, suit costs or rent accrued during the proceeding.
Tenant disputes the rent amount but does not take the prescribed step within the notice period.
statutes_and_provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, ss. 11(3), 12(1), 12(3)(a), 12(3)(b) and Explanation
U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, ss. 20(2)(a), 20(4), 39
Karnataka Rent Control Act, s. 29(1), (3), (4)
Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, s. 14(2)(i) third proviso
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, s. 13(2)(i) and proviso
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 13 of the 16 members, the tenant is denied protection or relief for incomplete, late, conditional or irregular payment, and the eviction decree is upheld or restored. The remaining members are procedural: they require the Controller to assess disputed arrears provisionally and then adjudicate them (2), or set out the conditions on which a tenant qualifies for protection (1).
variations: The defect differs: arrears not deposited by the first hearing, irregular monthly payments, unpaid costs, omitted time-barred rent, a late dispute over standard rent, a late deposit measured from knowledge of the suit, or no deposit on filing a revision.
Some members define what counts as the amount due, such as time-barred rent or rent accrued during the proceeding, and some define the standard of regularity.
The East Punjab members adopt a tenant-protective construction requiring provisional assessment, while the others stress strict compliance.
One member (1802788_3) states the positive conditions for qualifying for protection and treats a missing payment date as a technical error.

split_suggestion: Separate the two East Punjab Controller-assessment members (868147_2, 868147_3) into their own cluster on the adjudicator's duty to assess and adjudicate disputed arrears. Optionally, subdivide the rest into (a) the amount due and its components (time-barred rent, accrued rent, costs), (b) timing and regularity of payment, and (c) disputed-rent procedure within the notice period.

legal_question: Can a writ or public interest petition be dismissed or relief refused on the ground of delay and laches where the challenge is brought after substantial, unexplained delay, particularly after the impugned action has become final (for example, award made, possession taken, refund accepted)?

predicates.writ_or_public_interest_challenge_to_sta: The petitioner invokes writ jurisdiction (or files a public interest petition) to challenge an acquisition, allotment, cancellation, administrative decision or similar state action.
predicates.challenge_filed_after_substantial_delay: The petition was filed after a long period (years, or long after the award, possession, cancellation or order) when it could have been brought earlier.
predicates.adequate_explanation_for_delay: The petitioner has given a plausible, substantiated reason for the delay.
predicates.court_may_refuse_relief_or_dismiss_for_d: The court may, in its discretion, dismiss the petition or refuse relief because of delay and laches, without deciding the merits.

definition: Relief under Article 226 (or in a public interest petition) is discretionary, and a court may dismiss a challenge brought after substantial, unexplained delay. This applies with particular force where the impugned action has become final, for example an acquisition award made and possession taken, a refund accepted without protest, or the petitioner participated in earlier proceedings and did not pursue remedies.
exceptions_or_limits: Whether delay warrants dismissal depends on the facts of each case; the delay must be unexplained or the explanation unsubstantiated or implausible.
The discretion is strongest where an acquisition award has been made and possession taken, and courts are loath to quash acquisition proceedings at that stage.
Dismissal for laches does not decide the merits of the underlying challenge.

Some members rest on additional factors, such as acceptance of a refund, missed conditional restoration deadlines, a prior dismissed writ, Order II Rule 2 CPC, or non-joinder of affected parties. These reinforce the denial but are not always necessary.
Where the claimant relies on an earlier decision, it does not help if its facts are materially different.

common_material_facts: Land acquisition challenged by writ after the award was made and possession taken (about 7 members)
Delay of years, from about 17 months to 17 years, with no or an inadequate explanation
Allottee accepted a refund after lease cancellation and did not challenge the cancellation for years (4 members)
Petitioner knew of or participated in the earlier proceedings but did not pursue remedies
Earlier or related proceedings had been lost or had become final
statutes_and_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution
Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (one member)
Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (vesting; one member)

Cases cited: Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development Investment Co.; C. Padma v. Deputy Secretary, Tamil Nadu; State of Rajasthan v. D.R. Laxmi; Municipal Council, Ahmednagar v. Shah Hyder Beig; Larsen & Toubro v. State of Gujarat; Shivgonda Anna Patil; Swaika Properties
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 16 members deny relief or dismiss the petition for delay and laches, or reverse a High Court order that had granted relief or interfered with a dismissal. Several were decided without reaching the merits.
variations: Acquisition cases (about 7) stress that finality of the award and possession bars the challenge; lease-restoration cases stress acceptance of the refund, acquiescence and missed deadlines.
Some members add a second ground: a prior dismissed writ, omission of a claim from an earlier petition (Order II Rule 2), or failure to join affected landholders.
One member is a public interest petition against an allotment, and one is a ryotwari patta claim, where no finality event is involved and delay alone suffices.
162629_1 and 63062099_1 rest on delay alone, with no or little authority cited; others rely on a line of Supreme Court acquisition-delay precedents.

legal_question: When may a court draw an adverse inference against a party (or the prosecution) from the non-production of evidence, the non-examination of a witness, or a party's failure to testify or explain, and what limits apply to that inference?

rule.if: proceeding_before_court and evidence_or_witness_or_explanation_within_party_power_and_relevant_to_issue and party_withheld_or_failed_to_produce_or_testify_or_explain and no_reasonable_explanation_given and not (other_reliable_evidence_already_establishes_point_or_opposing_party_failed_to_use_available_production_procedure)

predicates.proceeding_before_court: The matter is a civil, criminal, execution or appellate proceeding before a court in which evidence is being assessed.
predicates.evidence_or_witness_or_explanation_withi: The document, record, witness, own testimony or explanation was within the party's power or possession, or the party was the one required to give it, and is relevant or material to a disputed issue.
predicates.party_withheld_or_failed_to_produce_or_t: The party (or the prosecution) did not produce the document or record, did not examine the witness, did not enter the witness box, or did not explain incriminating circumstances.
predicates.no_reasonable_explanation_given: No adequate explanation was offered for the non-production, non-examination, non-appearance or silence.
predicates.other_reliable_evidence_already_establis: Other reliable evidence on the record already establishes the point in issue, or the opposing party did not seek production through the available procedure and no production order was disobeyed.
predicates.court_may_draw_adverse_inference_against: The court is entitled, as a matter of discretion, to infer that the withheld evidence or unexplained matter would be unfavourable to the party withholding it.

definition: A court may, in its discretion, infer that withheld evidence, an unexamined witness, a party's unexplained absence from the witness box, or an unexplained incriminating circumstance is unfavourable to the party responsible, where the material was within that party's reach, relevant, and unexplained. The inference is not automatic: it is not justified where other reliable evidence already establishes the point or the opposing party did not use the available production procedure, and it must be weighed with the rest of the evidence.
exceptions_or_limits: The inference is discretionary, not automatic (Section 114(g) Evidence Act); the court must consider relevance, burden of proof, diligence of the opposing party and any explanation.
No adverse inference where other reliable or unimpeachable evidence already establishes the point in issue.

Non-examination of a witness is not fatal in itself; the prosecution need not multiply witnesses, and the inference arises mainly where the witness is essential or independent and the existing evidence is infirm or needs corroboration.
A party's failure to testify is only one circumstance and cannot replace consideration of the other oral and documentary evidence.
Where the opposing party made no attempt at discovery, inspection or production and no court order was disobeyed, an inference against the holder of the records may be unjustified.
A court's direction to produce records, especially with a warning of consequences, strengthens the inference when the authority defaults.

common_material_facts: A party or the prosecution failed to produce a document, account book or official record within its possession or control.
A party did not enter the witness box or submit to cross-examination without explanation.
Available material or independent prosecution witnesses were not examined and no explanation was given.
An accused gave no explanation for incriminating circumstances put to him.
A court had directed production of records and the authority defaulted, sometimes after a warning.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 114, Illustration (g), Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Section 313 Code of Criminal Procedure
Order XI CPC (discovery and inspection)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 13 of 16 members an adverse inference was drawn, permitted or held available (civil non-production or non-testimony, criminal non-examination, authority default after a court direction, accused's silence). In about 3 members (61939581_1, 852133_1, 958443_2) the inference was refused or qualified because other evidence existed or the opposing party had not used the available procedure.
variations: Subject: the prosecution's failure to examine witnesses, an accused's silence under Section 313, civil parties' non-testimony, documents or accounts withheld, and public authorities' default on production orders.

Some members treat the inference as arising from the withholding alone (even without a demand for production or a burden of proof on the party), while others require diligence by the opposing party and use of discovery procedure.
Some members allow the inference only if no other evidence exists on the point; others allow it alongside other evidence but require that evidence to be weighed too.

The consequence differs: reduction of a claim, rejection of a defence, an inferred fact (for example disclosure of a pending suit), weakening of the prosecution case, or a remand for fuller assessment of the evidence.
In 1780305_5 the point is prospective: production is directed, and the inference or another order is reserved for later withholding.

legal_question: When can promissory estoppel be invoked against a public authority or the government, and in particular does it fail where the promise is contrary to law, beyond the authority's or officer's power, or not clearly made and relied on?

predicates.promissory_estoppel_claim_against_public: A party seeks to hold a public authority or the government to a promise or representation by invoking promissory or equitable estoppel.
predicates.promise_contrary_to_law_or_beyond_author: Performing the promise would violate a statute, statutory rule, mandatory statutory procedure or sanctioned plan, or the promise exceeded the authority's legal power, or the officer who made it had no authority to bind the body.
predicates.no_clear_specific_representation_or_no_d: The claimant cannot show a clear and specific representation intended to be acted on, or cannot show that it acted on it and materially changed its position to its detriment.
predicates.public_interest_justifies_withdrawal: A supervening public interest or special consideration affecting the State's general interest requires or supports the authority's departure from the promise.
predicates.public_interest_established_by_material: The authority has placed relevant material or evidence before the court showing that enforcing the promise would actually prejudice the public interest.
predicates.promissory_estoppel_does_not_bind_public: The doctrine does not prevent the public authority from withdrawing the promise or acting according to law, and cannot be used to compel performance.

definition: Promissory estoppel can bind a public authority to a clear, authorised promise that the promisee has acted on to its detriment. It cannot compel performance of a promise that is contrary to law, beyond the authority's power or made by an officer without authority. It also fails where there was no specific representation or no detrimental reliance, and it yields to a public interest that the authority proves with material.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the promise is within the authority's legal power, is clear and unequivocal, and the promisee has relied on it and changed position to its prejudice, the authority is bound and cannot withdraw arbitrarily (1635654_2, 1902038_7, 1936933_3).
A public interest defence must be supported by material evidence under a rigorous standard; a bare assertion of public interest or possible revenue loss does not displace estoppel (74190276_6).
Estoppel does not prevent an authority from discharging statutory or legislative duties.
Where the authority has statutory power to grant the promised benefit, the ultra vires bar does not apply (1271427_2 distinguishing Nestle).

outlier_members.reason: Reaches the opposite outcome: the authority is bound because the promise was lawful, clear and relied on. It is the counter-condition to the rule, not an instance of it.
Holds the government bound by an authorised representation that was relied on. It states the limit (no validation of ultra vires acts) but its outcome is the opposite of the rule.
Holds estoppel was not displaced because the authority gave no material proof of public harm. It supports the public-interest limb of the rule but yields a binding outcome.

common_material_facts: A public body, municipality, development authority or government department made a promise, permission, exemption or contractual term on which a private party relied.
The promise conflicted with a statute, development control rule, sanctioned plan or mandatory procedure, or was made by an officer or body without power.
The authority later withdrew, refused to honour or changed the position.
In several cases the claimant could not prove a specific assurance or a detrimental change of position.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 115, Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Sections 31(6), 37(2) and 159, Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966
Section 70(2)(c), Punjab Municipal Act, 1911
Article 162 and Article 299(1), Constitution of India
Sections 10, 25, 63, 65 and 70, Indian Contract Act, 1872
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 13 of 16 members, estoppel failed against the public authority, mainly because the promise was ultra vires or contrary to statute (about 8), the representation or reliance was missing (about 4), or public interest or sovereign function applied.
