definition: An instrument that required registration but is unregistered, or that is chargeable but insufficiently stamped, cannot be used to prove the transaction it itself effects. Secondary or oral evidence of its contents is barred likewise. Only a genuinely collateral use remains: for non-registration this is, for example, severance of status or the character of possession. For non-stamping, even a collateral use is barred until the instrument is impounded and the duty and penalty are paid.
exceptions_or_limits: Non-registration: under the proviso to s.49 of the Registration Act, the instrument may be used for a collateral purpose, such as showing severance of joint status, intention to divide, or the nature of possession. It cannot prove title, allotment of specific properties, or division by metes and bounds.
A document that only records severance of status or defines shares, without allotting specific property, is not compulsorily registrable and is admissible to prove the severance.

Non-stamping: s.35 of the Stamp Act bars admission for any purpose, including a collateral one, until the instrument is impounded and the deficient duty and penalty are paid. Even then, proof and relevance remain necessary.

Section 36 of the Stamp Act protects only an original instrument already admitted without objection and judicially determined to be admissible. It does not validate secondary evidence or a merely tentative marking.

The substance and recitals of the document, not its label or the tendering party's pleadings, decide whether it is registrable. A memorandum of an earlier completed partition differs from an instrument that itself effects the division.

The collateral-purpose proviso does not let a party prove the very transaction the instrument creates. Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act is unavailable where there is no transfer or part performance.
Under s.91 of the Evidence Act, oral evidence cannot supplement or replace a document intended to be the sole evidence of the transaction where that document is itself unusable.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the court's mandatory duty under s.33 of the Stamp Act to impound an insufficiently stamped instrument, not the admissibility of the instrument for a particular purpose.
It concerns a registering officer's mandatory duty under s.33(1) of the Stamp Act to impound an instrument presented for registration, not evidentiary admissibility.

common_material_facts: An unregistered and/or insufficiently stamped written instrument is tendered in a civil proceeding.
Most members are partition or family-arrangement disputes in which an unregistered writing allocates specific immovable properties.
The tendering party offers the instrument, or oral or secondary evidence of it, for a primary or alternatively a 'collateral' purpose.
The objection is based on ss.17(1)(b) and 49 of the Registration Act or ss.33, 35 and 36 of the Stamp Act.
statutes_and_provisions: Registration Act, 1908, ss.17(1)(b) and 49 (proviso)
Indian Stamp Act, 1899, ss.2(14), 33, 35 and 36
Indian Evidence Act, 1872, ss.59-65 and 91
Transfer of Property Act, 1882, s.53A
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About 8 of 13 covered members hold the instrument inadmissible to prove the primary transaction (partition by allotment or the instrument's contents). About 5 allow a limited or collateral use, usually proof of severance of status or the nature of possession. Where stamp duty is deficient, that use is allowed only after impounding and payment of duty and penalty. Two further members, treated as outliers, hold that impounding is mandatory.
variations: Defect type: registration-only defects allow collateral use, while stamp defects bar all uses until cured.
Form of evidence: some members deal with the document itself, others with secondary or oral evidence (ss.91 and 63-65 of the Evidence Act, or s.35 of the Stamp Act).
Nature of the document: allotment of specific property makes it registrable, while a bare record of severance does not.
Some members are non-partition disputes (a mortgage suit, a suit to recover consideration, an impounding duty on a sale deed).

split_suggestion: Split into (a) admissibility of unregistered partition or family-arrangement instruments, covering primary versus collateral use under the Registration Act (1173284_1, 1173284_4, 164917823_1, 164917823_2, 1946998_2, 1979172_1, 403856_5, 59829381_1, 59829381_2, 725442_3); (b) the Stamp Act bar on admitting insufficiently stamped instruments for any purpose, including secondary evidence (1142196_1, 1729274_1, 333037_2); and (c) the mandatory duty to impound under s.33 (1729274_2, 856631_3, 333037_2).

legal_question: Does the enacting legislature (State or Parliament) have legislative competence under the Seventh Schedule entries, read broadly, to enact a law on land, land tenure, landlord-tenant relations, agrarian reform, agricultural debt relief, town planning or acquisition of property?

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge: The validity of the law is challenged on the ground that the enacting legislature lacked legislative power over its subject matter.
predicates.enacting_legislature_is_state_or_parliam: The law was enacted by the State Legislature or by Parliament, the body to which the relevant entry is said to be assigned.
predicates.law_in_pith_and_substance_concerns_subje: Looking at its pith and substance, object, scheme and effect, the law falls within an entry assigned to that legislature (for example land, land tenures, landlord-tenant relations, rent, agricultural debt, land revenue, state-vested land, or acquisition and requisitioning of property in the Concurrent List).
predicates.entry_read_broadly_to_include_ancillary_: The relevant entry is given a wide and liberal construction that covers ancillary and subsidiary matters fairly comprehended by its terms, and no narrower reading is required by its wording or another part of the Constitution.
predicates.enacting_legislature_has_legislative_com: The enacting legislature had legislative competence to enact the law, so the competence challenge fails.

definition: A law is within the competence of the State Legislature or Parliament if, in pith and substance, it falls within a Seventh Schedule entry assigned to that legislature. Entries are construed broadly to include ancillary matters, so land reform, tenancy, agricultural debt relief, planning and acquisition laws are upheld against competence challenges.
exceptions_or_limits: Competence is separate from other constitutional limits, such as Article 31(2) on compensation and public purpose, or fundamental rights. Those limits were not displaced by the competence holdings.

House and building tenancies were held to fall under Concurrent List fields (transfer of property, contracts, civil procedure), not the State List land entry (1802623_1). The correct entry must therefore be identified.
Where acquisition is not directly covered by the land entry, competence rests on the Concurrent List acquisition entry read with the land entry (1878241_2).
Where a law's dominant purpose falls under a different subject, such as public order, competence depends on the pith and substance, and here that was acquisition (52822922_1).
Protection of acquisition as agrarian reform under Article 31A (913722_2) is a separate question from legislative competence.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns whether acquisition and retention of surplus land is protected under Article 31A as agrarian reform, not which legislature has competence under the Seventh Schedule.

common_material_facts: A law was challenged as beyond the enacting legislature's legislative competence.
Most laws concerned land: tenure reform, ceilings and surplus-land acquisition, tenancy and rent, jagir resumption, and town planning.
Some laws concerned acquisition of property, including State-owned coal land acquired by Parliament and the acquisition of rights by statute after communal violence.
Some laws gave agriculturists debt relief or rent-arrears relief.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 246 and Article 246(3)
Entry 18, List II (land, tenures, landlord-tenant, rent)
Entry 30, List II (agricultural indebtedness)
Entry 45, List II (land revenue)
Entry 35, List II (state-vested land)
Entry 36, List II (acquisition)
Entries 64 and 65, List II
Entry 42, List III (acquisition and requisitioning of property)
Entry 20, List III (economic and social planning)
Entries 52 and 54, List I
Articles 31(2), 31A, 39, 294 and 298
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Competence upheld in 14 of 15 members, in each case on a broad construction of the relevant entry. The remaining member (913722_2) was decided on Article 31A protection rather than competence.
variations: Some members rely on a single entry (for example Entry 18 or Entry 30 of List II). Others combine entries, such as the land entry with Entry 42 of List III.
Most members involve State legislatures. Two (52822922_1 and 603736_3) uphold Parliament's competence under the concurrent acquisition entry, and 603736_3 extends this to State-owned property.
Some members decide on the pith and substance doctrine (1802623_1, 52822922_1). Others rely only on broad construction of the entry.
Some members rely on no earlier authority (for example 1395543_3), while others cite long lines of cases such as Atiqa Begum, Navinchandra Mafatlal and Megh Raj.

legal_question: Does a written family arrangement, partition record or arbitration award need compulsory registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 when it only records a completed arrangement, sets terms for future division, or creates a right to later documents, rather than itself creating, declaring, assigning, limiting or extinguishing rights in immovable property in the present?

predicates.document_relates_to_family_or_partition_: The document is a family arrangement, settlement, partition record, memorandum or arbitration award dealing with rights in immovable property.
predicates.document_itself_creates_declares_assigns: The document by its own operation creates, declares, assigns, limits or extinguishes a present right or interest in immovable property, so that it is the source or title document of that right.
predicates.document_records_completed_prior_arrange: The document only records or acknowledges an arrangement, settlement or partition that was already completed, orally or otherwise, before the document was made, for evidence, record or information.
predicates.document_only_provides_for_future_divisi: The document only fixes terms for a possible future partition, or only gives a right to obtain a later instrument that will itself create or transfer rights (Section 17(2)(v)).
predicates.document_only_preserves_existing_interes: The document only preserves existing securities or interests, declares a pre-existing interest, or makes relinquishment conditional on payment, without itself creating or extinguishing the interest.
predicates.document_not_compulsorily_registrable_an: The document does not require compulsory registration under Section 17, so lack of registration does not bar its admission, its use as corroborative evidence of the arrangement and the parties' conduct, or its being made a rule of court or decree. It cannot, however, be used to prove a property transaction that itself required registration.

definition: Under Section 17(1)(b) and 17(2)(v) of the Registration Act, a family arrangement, partition memorandum or arbitration award needs registration only if it itself creates or extinguishes present rights in immovable property. A writing that merely records an already completed (often oral) arrangement, sets terms for future partition, preserves existing interests, or only gives a right to later documents is not compulsorily registrable and can be received as evidence of the arrangement and conduct.
exceptions_or_limits: Registration is required where the document itself effects the partition or allotment, or embodies the bargain as the operative instrument of title. Section 49 then bars it as evidence of the transaction, and Section 91 of the Evidence Act bars secondary evidence.

Even where an unregistered record is admitted, it cannot be used to prove a transaction affecting immovable property that itself required a registered instrument. It serves only as a corroborative or collateral record.
Whether a document needs registration depends on what it purports to do, not on its label (memorandum, award, list).
Stamp duty treatment depends separately on whether the writing is a mere memorandum of an existing arrangement.
A document that itself allots specific immovable property or divides it by metes and bounds in the present is registrable.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the validity of an oral family arrangement and whether a family member's consent had to be recorded. It does not address Section 17 registration, though it is from the same dispute as 818453_4.

common_material_facts: A family partition or arrangement was reached orally, or completed, before the writing was made.
The writing recites or records the arrangement for record, remembrance or information of a court or authority.
The writing was unregistered and was challenged as inadmissible or unenforceable for want of registration.
Arbitration awards that declare pre-existing shares, preserve securities, make relinquishment conditional on payment, or direct later documents.
Parties' conduct, such as separate possession, mutation, payment and signatures, supported the prior arrangement.
statutes_and_provisions: Registration Act 1908 s.17(1)(b)
Registration Act 1908 s.17(1)(c)
Registration Act 1908 s.17(2)(v)
Registration Act 1908 s.49
Evidence Act 1872 s.91
Code of Civil Procedure 1908 Order 13 Rules 3 and 4
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 14 of 15 members the document was held not compulsorily registrable and could be admitted, relied on, or made a rule of court or decree. The remaining member (818453_2) is an outlier on family-arrangement validity. In several members the use of the unregistered document is limited to corroboration and cannot prove a transaction affecting the property.
variations: Some documents record a completed past arrangement (the majority).
Some only provide for future partition or later documents (1649431_2, 167236031_1, 977039_1) and rely on s.17(2)(v) or the present-versus-future distinction.
Some awards declare a pre-existing interest or preserve existing security (1817558_1, 793151_1, 81682_1).
Admissibility is qualified in 161176425_1, 163599410_1 and 169349322_3, which allow only corroborative use. 1946998_1 allows the writing to prove the partition.
Procedural settings vary: mutation, evidence marking, partition appeal, and award enforcement or rule of court.

legal_question: Does the death of a party or landholder, before or after a proceeding, order or determination is made, abate or invalidate that proceeding, order or determination, or does it continue or stand against the legal representatives or heirs?

rule.if: party_or_holder_died and (proceeding_pending_at_death or order_or_determination_already_made_or_reserved) and not statute_makes_death_terminate_proceeding and (legal_representatives_available_or_liability_attached_to_holding_or_order_independent_of_deceased)

predicates.party_or_holder_died: A party to the proceeding, or the landholder whose holding is in issue, has died.
predicates.proceeding_pending_at_death: A proceeding (suit, appeal, execution or ceiling proceeding) was pending, or not yet completed, when the death occurred.
predicates.order_or_determination_already_made_or_r: The order or determination had already been made, signed, finalised, or had its hearing concluded with judgment reserved, before or around the death.
predicates.statute_makes_death_terminate_proceeding: A statute or procedural rule expressly provides that the death ends, abates or invalidates the proceeding in the circumstances.
predicates.legal_representatives_available_or_liabi: Legal representatives are on record or can be brought on record, or the liability attaches to the holding as on a reference date, or the order operates independently of the deceased person.
predicates.death_does_not_abate_or_invalidate_proce: The proceeding does not abate and the order or determination is not void. The proceeding continues, or the order or liability stands, against the legal representatives or the estate.

definition: Absent a statutory provision to the contrary, a party's or holder's death does not by itself abate a pending proceeding, nullify an order or judgment, or extinguish a liability attached to a holding. The proceeding continues, or the order or determination stands, with the legal representatives or heirs standing in the deceased's place. Death also does not reopen a final determination or disturb completed allotments.
exceptions_or_limits: Where a statute or rule expressly provides for abatement or termination on death, the outcome may differ. Ordinary abatement rules do not apply to execution proceedings, but a court may dismiss for default, not as abated, if a deceased judgment debtor's representatives are not brought on record within a reasonable time fixed by the court.

In ceiling cases the surplus is fixed by the deceased holder's holding on the appointed or imposition date. The heirs cannot claim separate ceilings as independent holders, and they take only the residual land after the surplus is surrendered.
A person who is brought on record after bona fide inquiry represents the whole estate only in the absence of fraud or collusion.
Where the order is an administrative order, only the deceased person's name as a person to be served needs correction. This holds where the order affects the premises independently of that person.

Where the order was reserved, or written and signed before death, pronouncement after death is valid. The cases concern pronouncement after the hearing or after signing, not the position where death occurs earlier in the proceeding.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns survival of accrued State rights and landholder liabilities after repeal of the ceiling law under a General Clauses Act saving provision. It does not concern death of a party.

Concerns whether a final surplus determination can be reopened under a later law because family circumstances or ceiling limits changed. It does not concern death, although it shares the finality and reference-date logic.

common_material_facts: A party, decree holder, defendant or landholder died while a proceeding was pending, after the hearing was reserved, or after a determination or order was made.
Legal representatives or heirs were brought on record, only some of them were brought on record, or they were not formally identified.

In ceiling cases, the holder held land above the ceiling on the appointed or imposition date and died before the surplus was declared. The heirs claimed separate holdings or sought to drop the proceedings.
In final-determination cases, the surplus had been determined and allotments completed before the death or before the later reassessment.
statutes_and_provisions: Code of Civil Procedure Order XXII Rules 4, 6 and 12
Uttar Pradesh Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, ss. 5, 9, 10, and rule 19 of the 1961 Rules
Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, ss. 3, 4, 8, 10, 12, 18–21; Maharashtra Act 21 of 1975, s. 5
Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, s. 32-FF (and the provision referred to as s. 33-FF)
Haryana Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972, ss. 7, 9, 33(2)(ii)
Reduction Act, ss. 3(1) and 3(2)
Section 18 (Controller's execution proceedings treated as before a civil court)
Requisition provisions, ss. 6(4)(a) and 13
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 13 covered members, death did not abate or nullify the proceeding, order or determination. The proceeding continued with the legal representatives, or the order, determination or allotment stood. This covers about 5 civil-procedure abatement cases, 5 ceiling cases where the liability relates back to the reference date, 2 final-determination or allotment cases, and 1 administrative order case.
variations: Some members apply the Code of Civil Procedure abatement rules. Others rest on the scheme of a ceiling statute, and one on the administrative character of the order.
In the ceiling cases, death before declaration leaves the liability fixed as on the reference date. In the Pepsu cases, death after a final determination or completed allotment cannot reopen it.
Some cases keep the proceeding alive with legal representatives on record or added late. Others hold the order valid even though its pronouncement or addressee post-dates the death.
One member (1794547_3) is about construing a later amendment as declaratory, not about death directly.

split_suggestion: Split into three sub-clusters: (a) civil-procedure abatement and substitution (1243915_2, 1430046_2, 1528864_2, 169428_1, 1932635_5, and the administrative order case 188115_4); (b) ceiling cases where death before declaration leaves the liability fixed as on the reference date (1205287_2, 1745408_1, 1794547_2, 1794547_3, 572071_3); (c) finality of surplus determinations and completed allotments (1917260_1, 1917260_2, 27271392_2). The repeal and saving case 1763928_2 should sit with finality or accrued-rights issues, not with death.

legal_question: When may a court condone delay in filing an appeal or other proceeding (including delay in filing required documents or accompanying applications), and when will a higher court interfere with the lower court's exercise of discretion on condonation?

rule.if: (delayed_filing_of_appeal_or_proceeding and condonation_sought) and (sufficient_cause_shown_for_delay or court_permitted_later_filing_or_defect_is_curable) and not (delay_explanation_arose_only_after_limitation_expired)

predicates.delayed_filing_of_appeal_or_proceeding: An appeal, petition or application was filed after the prescribed limitation period or after a time allowed by the court.
predicates.condonation_sought: The party asked the court to condone the delay, or the court is asked to consider condonation or enlargement of time.
predicates.sufficient_cause_shown_for_delay: The party gave a satisfactory, rational explanation showing it was prevented from filing in time by a cause that existed before limitation expired, and not by negligence, inaction or lack of bona fides.
predicates.court_permitted_later_filing_or_defect_i: The court had allowed a required document to be filed later and it was filed promptly, or the defect (such as omitting a delay application at presentation) was cured before the appeal was rejected.
predicates.delay_explanation_arose_only_after_limit: The only explanation offered is an event arising after limitation had expired, with no pre-expiry obstacle to timely filing.
predicates.delay_may_be_condoned_in_the_courts_disc: The court may, and in suitable cases should, condone the delay and consider the matter on its merits rather than dismiss it as time-barred.

definition: Delay may be condoned in the court's judicial discretion where the party shows sufficient cause that arose before limitation expired, or where the court permitted later filing or the defect was curable. Delay is not condoned where the explanation is inadequate, reflects negligence, or arises only after limitation expired. Appellate courts generally do not disturb a discretionary decision on condonation unless it was improperly exercised.
exceptions_or_limits: Delay is not condoned where the explanation is inadequate, such as bare illness for a very long delay, or where negligence, inaction or lack of bona fides is shown.
A cause arising only after limitation expired cannot explain why the appeal was not filed in time, though it may explain further delay after that point.
A higher court will interfere with a condonation decision only if the discretion was exercised improperly or the governing principles were disregarded.
Where the court dismisses a time-barred appeal without considering its power to enlarge time or to consider a later delay application, the dismissal may be set aside and the matter remitted.
Some members condoned delay without stating any test, so they carry little precedential weight.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns whether a time-barred appeal disposed of on a preliminary ground without a merits hearing remains an appeal (relevant to res judicata and similar consequences), not whether delay should be condoned.

common_material_facts: Appeals or petitions filed after the limitation period, with an application to condone delay.
Explanations offered: official or agency inaction, illness, disturbances, tampered certified copies, or a later change of view.
Certified copy or delay application not filed with the appeal at presentation but filed later.
Lower court dismissed the appeal as time-barred without considering its power to condone or enlarge time.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 5, Limitation Act, 1963
Article 114, Limitation Act
Section 148, Code of Civil Procedure
Order 41 Rule 3A and Order 42 Rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure
Section 24, Recovery of Debts due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Delay was condoned or the condonation upheld in about 9 of 13 covered members, including the curable-defect and Section 148 remand cases. It was refused in about 3 of 13 (1471225_2, 1830120_1, 95455039_1) where the cause arose after expiry or was inadequate. One member (876341_4) declined to reverse a writ court's decision for delay alone.
variations: Some members decide on the strength of the explanation (sufficient cause). Others turn on procedural curability (Order 41 Rule 3A) or on the court's power to enlarge time under Section 148.
Some members concern a higher court's reluctance to disturb discretionary condonation, and one concerns delay in a writ petition (laches) rather than limitation.
Some members, such as 11649885_2 and 1052096_1, give little or no reasoning.
The refusal cases differ in reason: a post-expiry cause in two, and a weak explanation (illness) for very long delay in one.

split_suggestion: Split into: (a) the substantive sufficient-cause standard under Section 5 (grant and refusal); (b) procedural curability and enlargement of time (Order 41 Rule 3A, Section 148); (c) appellate deference to discretionary condonation or delay decisions (605621_5, 845683_2, 876341_4, 122795087_3). Move 1489516_1 to a separate cluster on the nature of a time-barred appeal.

legal_question: Does a highest bidder at a public auction or tender acquire any vested right to the property, or does a concluded sale or contract arise, before the competent authority accepts or confirms the bid, communicates that acceptance, and completes the steps the auction terms or statute require (such as full payment and a sale certificate)?

rule.if: public_auction_or_tender_sale and highest_bid_made_or_deposit_paid and (acceptance_or_confirmation_required_by_terms_or_statute and not acceptance_or_confirmation_given_and_communicated)

predicates.public_auction_or_tender_sale: The property or licence was offered through a public auction, tender or statutory sale procedure.
predicates.highest_bid_made_or_deposit_paid: The claimant made the highest bid or offer and may have paid earnest money or an initial or part deposit.
predicates.acceptance_or_confirmation_required_by_t: The auction conditions, tender terms or governing rules make the bid provisional, or reserve final acceptance, confirmation or approval to a competent authority.
predicates.acceptance_or_confirmation_given_and_com: The competent authority actually accepted or confirmed the bid and the acceptance was communicated to the bidder, for example by an allotment or confirmation letter.
predicates.no_concluded_sale_or_vested_right_in_bid: No concluded contract or completed sale arose, and the bidder has no vested or enforceable right to the property, to specific performance, to allotment, or to declaratory relief. The bidder also bears no liability for any resale deficiency.

definition: Where the auction terms or governing rules make a bid provisional or reserve final acceptance to a competent authority, the highest bidder has no vested right and no concluded contract arises until the bid is accepted or confirmed and the acceptance is communicated. Where the rules or terms also require full payment and a sale certificate, the sale is not complete until those steps are done. A deposit or highest bid alone does not change this, and courts cannot compel allotment or completion.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule applies only where acceptance, confirmation or approval is required by the auction terms, tender terms or statute. Where acceptance is not reserved, the bidder's rights depend on the conditions of the auction.
The authority may reject even the highest bid only for good reasons and without arbitrariness or favouritism. The bidder keeps a right to fair and equal treatment in the evaluation of bids.
Once confirmation is given and communicated, a contract may arise. A statutory sale scheme may still require full payment and a sale certificate before the sale is complete or ownership passes.
Approval of a bid may create a binding contract without transferring the property, where the terms make full payment and a sale certificate the condition for transfer.

outlier_members.reason: This issue is procedural: whether substantial questions of law arise in a second appeal. It depends on the no-right conclusion but is not itself a rule on auction bids.

common_material_facts: The claimant made the highest bid at a public auction or tender and often paid earnest money or an initial deposit.
The auction terms made acceptance provisional or reserved confirmation to a named authority.
The authority did not confirm or accept the bid, rejected or cancelled it, or did not communicate acceptance.
No allotment letter, confirmation letter or sale certificate was issued.
The bidder sought to compel the sale or allotment, or claimed a legal right or protection based on the bid.
statutes_and_provisions: Rule 8(1)(h), Chapter III, Punjab Package Deal Properties (Disposal) Rules, 1976
Regulation 6(2), Haryana Urban Development (Disposal of Land and Buildings) Regulations, 1978
Rule 4(3) and proviso, Nagpur Improvement Trust Land Disposal Rules, 1955
Clause 33 of the auction conditions and clauses 16 and 21 of Rule 5.34 (resale and confirmation by the Chief Commissioner)
Rules 8 and 9, Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002
Section 34, Specific Relief Act, 1963
Sections 3 and 4, Indian Contract Act, 1872
Sections 20 and 29, Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954, and rule 90 of its rules
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 13 of 14 members, the Court held that no vested right or concluded contract arose before acceptance, confirmation or communication, or before full payment and a sale certificate where required. Relief such as specific performance, allotment, declaration, or liability for a resale shortfall was denied. The remaining member (3353753_4) applies the same conclusion to a second-appeal question.
variations: Some members turn on lack of confirmation by a named authority. Others turn on lack of communicated acceptance, and others on unpaid full consideration or no sale certificate.
The relief sought differs: specific performance or transfer, mandatory allotment, a declaration, recovery of a resale deficiency, or protection as a tenant of a transferee.
One member holds that a withdrawn later offer prevented a concluded contract. One holds that a company's board decision did not complete a tender sale without state approval.
Another member (77089_2) acknowledges that approval of a bid may create a binding contract, yet holds that property is not transferred until full payment and a sale certificate.

legal_question: When a claimant invokes the discretionary writ jurisdiction of a constitutional court after substantial delay, can relief be refused for laches, and what circumstances (explanation for the delay, third-party rights, the nature of the interest) decide the point?

rule.if: discretionary_writ_jurisdiction_invoked and substantial_delay_in_approaching_court and not delay_satisfactorily_explained

predicates.discretionary_writ_jurisdiction_invoked: The claimant seeks discretionary public-law relief, such as mandamus or certiorari, from a High Court under Article 226 or in appeal from its decision.
predicates.substantial_delay_in_approaching_court: The claimant approached the court long after the cause of action arose or became known, and the delay was unreasonable or inordinate in the circumstances.
predicates.delay_satisfactorily_explained: The claimant gave a credible and sufficient explanation for the delay. General assertions of representations, or pursuit of remedies that could not give the relief sought, do not count as such an explanation.
predicates.writ_relief_may_be_refused_for_laches: The court may, in its discretion, decline writ relief because of delay and laches. This is a matter of discretion, not an inflexible rule of law.

definition: Writ relief under Article 226 is discretionary. A claimant who comes to court after substantial delay without a satisfactory explanation may be refused relief for laches, particularly where third-party rights have intervened or the State's position has been altered. There is no fixed rule, however, and an adequately explained delay, or one where no third-party rights have crystallised, may be excused. The Supreme Court ordinarily does not disturb a High Court's discretionary decision on delay unless it is arbitrary or improper.
exceptions_or_limits: Delay is not an inflexible bar. Where the delay is reasonably explained and no third-party rights have crystallised, a belated writ may be entertained (1962061_1).
Delay is not decisive where valuable public trust property is at stake and the proposed development has not begun (120571917_3).
The refusal is stronger where third-party rights have intervened and those parties have substantially relied on the impugned action (320843_4, 373267_1).
Repeated representations, or pursuit of remedies that cannot give the relief sought, do not by themselves explain the delay (373267_1, 607622_1).
The delay plea must actually be considered. A High Court that ignores a pleaded delay objection errs (607622_1, 1391679_3). Delay does not automatically defeat the claim (1391679_3).
Even where delay would ordinarily bar relief, relief supported by the respondent's own conduct, such as counsel's invitation to pass the usual order, may be preserved in a limited form (953085_3).
The Supreme Court will not interfere with a High Court's discretionary decision on laches, either way, unless it is arbitrary, improper or based on irrelevant considerations (1505541_2, 1962061_1).

outlier_members.reason: Concerns condonation of delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act for a State revision. The test is sufficient cause, not discretionary laches in a writ.
Concerns condonation of delay in filing a special leave petition under Section 5. A later enhancement of compensation was held not to be sufficient cause.
Concerns condonation of delay under Section 5 for a public authority's appeal. Involvement of public money was held not to be sufficient cause.

common_material_facts: A long gap, from several years to decades, between the cause of action or the impugned decision and the filing.
No explanation, or only a vague one such as general representations or pursuit of the wrong forum.
Intervening third-party rights or changed positions, for example land acquisition, leases, licences and allotments.
Many cases involve land acquisition or State action, and some involve a public authority as the delaying party.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution (discretionary writ jurisdiction)
Article 136 of the Constitution (limited Supreme Court interference with discretion)
Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 (sufficient cause)
Section 36 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950

Authorities cited include Lindsay Petroleum v. Prosper Armstrong, Moon Mills, Balwant Regular Motor Service, Dehri Rohtas Light Railway, Ramchandra Deodhar, Tilokchand Motichand and Rabindra Nath Bose.
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 11 covered members, about 8 refuse or uphold refusal of writ relief for unexplained delay, sometimes coupled with third-party rights. One reaches the same result in principle but preserves a limited relief (953085_3). One remands for consideration of delay (1391679_3). Two decline to treat delay as a bar, on an adequate explanation or the nature of the property (1962061_1, 120571917_3). All three outliers deny condonation under Section 5.
variations: Some members rely only on unexplained delay. Others add intervening third-party rights or changed positions as a strengthening factor.
Some members stress that a High Court must consider delay (607622_1, 1391679_3). Others stress that the Supreme Court defers to the High Court's discretion (1505541_2, 1962061_1).
Two members refuse to treat delay as fatal, based on the explanation given, the absence of third-party rights, or the public trust character of the property.
Three members arise under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, not writ laches.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) writ-jurisdiction laches (the 11 covered members, with 1962061_1 and 120571917_3 as the counter-pattern where delay is excused) and (b) Section 5 Limitation Act condonation of delay, including whether a public authority gets special indulgence (106803917_1, 138947_1, 1471225_3).

legal_question: When does a final decision on an issue in an earlier suit or proceeding, made by a court competent to decide it, bar relitigation of that issue between the same parties or their privies in a later suit or proceeding?

rule.if: later_proceeding_raises_same_issue and issue_directly_and_substantially_decided_in_earlier_proceeding and earlier_decision_final and same_parties_or_privies and deciding_court_competent

predicates.later_proceeding_raises_same_issue: The later suit or proceeding raises the same issue that was decided earlier. Differences in subject matter, additional parties or the material placed before the court do not matter if the issue and the contesting parties are the same.
predicates.issue_directly_and_substantially_decided: The issue was directly and substantially in dispute in the earlier suit or proceeding and was actually heard and decided there.
predicates.earlier_decision_final: The earlier decision was final: it was not appealed or was upheld on appeal, or the proceeding ended with the decision standing.
predicates.same_parties_or_privies: The parties to the later proceeding are the same as in the earlier one, or the claimant litigates under or through a party to the earlier proceeding.
predicates.deciding_court_competent: The court that actually decided the earlier matter had jurisdiction to decide that issue. Where the section 11 'competent to try the later suit' test applies, the court's competence is judged as of the filing of the former suit, or by the court that actually decided it after any transfer. Lack of competence to try the later suit does not defeat the bar under the general principle or Explanation VIII.
predicates.relitigation_barred_by_res_judicata: The earlier decision is conclusive and the issue, or the claim depending on it, cannot be reopened in the later proceeding.

definition: A matter directly and substantially in issue and finally decided between the same parties or their privies by a competent court cannot be reopened in a later suit or proceeding. Competence is judged by the court that actually decided the matter, as of the former suit. A court of limited pecuniary jurisdiction or a special-proceeding court can create the bar even if it could not have tried the later suit.
exceptions_or_limits: The bar does not arise if the earlier court lacked jurisdiction. Decisions beyond a court's jurisdiction cannot operate as res judicata, although a court does not lose jurisdiction merely because its decision may be wrong.

Where the section 11 competence test applies, the former court must have been competent to try the later suit, assessed as of the filing of the former suit. A later rise in property value does not undo this. This requirement does not apply to res judicata under general principles or Explanation VIII.

Interlocutory or intermediate decisions in the same proceeding do not automatically bind later stages. The result depends on the nature of the proceeding, the scope of the enquiry, the procedural provisions and the first court's competence.

If the earlier court disposed of the case on a preliminary point that made decision on the substantive issue unnecessary, the substantive observations may not bind. Where a decision rests on several independently sufficient grounds, each ground binds.
An observation in the earlier judgment that a fresh suit may be filed does not override the binding ratio or remove the bar.

The bar requires an actual decision of the issue between the same parties or those claiming under them. Differences between the suits do not defeat it if the issue and contesting parties are identical.

common_material_facts: An earlier suit or proceeding finally decided an issue, such as title, entitlement, jurisdiction, adoption or enforceability, between the same parties or their privies.
A later suit or proceeding, often for possession or a declaration, raised the same issue again.
The competence of the earlier court was questioned. Examples are a court of limited pecuniary jurisdiction, a special-proceeding judge, a transferred suit, or a later increase in property value.
The earlier decision had become final through non-appeal, dismissal of an appeal, or withdrawal.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 11 CPC
Section 11 Explanation I (former suit defined by decision, not institution)
Section 11 Explanation II (competence irrespective of appeal provisions)
Section 11 Explanation IV (matters that might and ought to have been raised)
Section 11 Explanation VIII (courts of limited jurisdiction)
Section 12 CPC
Order II Rule 2 CPC
Section 80 CPC
Article 299 of the Constitution
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 14 members the res judicata plea was upheld or the principle was applied. In 13 the later claim or issue was barred. In the remaining one (1608703_2) the principle was recognised in principle but made dependent on the nature of the earlier decision and the court's competence.
variations: Competence is tested differently: the court that actually decided the matter versus the court where the suit was first filed (1633194_2, 837833_1); competence at the time of the former suit's filing (1464203_1); competence to decide the issue only (1047975_1, 1481962_3, 1842039_1).
Some members extend the principle beyond section 11 to general principles, to stages of the same proceeding, and to execution or revision proceedings (1481962_3, 1608703_2, 612201_3).
1827303_1 and 553409_1 deal with what counts as a decided issue: a suit dismissed because the claim was satisfied, and findings on alternative grounds.
1633194_3 and 1633194_2 deal with what counts as a former suit: timing of decision versus institution, and separate suits with separate appeals.
1988625_1 holds that an observation permitting a fresh suit does not remove the bar.

split_suggestion: The members share one core rule, but they could be split into two sub-clusters. (a) Competence of the former court: 1047975_1, 1464203_1, 1481962_3, 1633194_2, 1633194_3, 837833_1, 612201_3. (b) Finality, identity of issue and scope of the decided matter: 1379496_1, 1608703_2, 1827303_1, 1842039_1, 1966491_2, 1988625_1, 553409_1.

legal_question: Does a statute that leaves to the executive or an administrative authority the application, extension, enumeration, rate-fixing or implementation of its provisions amount to excessive delegation or abdication of essential legislative function, where the legislature has stated its policy and supplied guidance or safeguards?

rule.if: delegation_challenged_as_excessive and legislature_has_laid_down_policy_and_standards and delegated_task_is_implementation_or_subordinate_detail and delegate_is_guided_or_confined_by_policy_criteria_or_safeguards and not delegate_empowered_to_determine_the_legislative_policy_itself

predicates.delegation_challenged_as_excessive: The validity of a statutory provision is challenged on the ground of excessive delegation or abdication of legislative power.
predicates.legislature_has_laid_down_policy_and_sta: The legislature has expressed its policy and purpose, in the preamble, the operative provisions or the scheme of the Act, with enough clarity to guide the delegate.
predicates.delegated_task_is_implementation_or_subo: The delegated task is subordinate or administrative, such as extending an existing law to areas, selecting from enacted laws, enumerating relations, identifying areas on facts, fixing a rate or limit, assigning executive functions or applying the law to individual cases. It is not the making of essential policy.
predicates.delegate_is_guided_or_confined_by_policy: The delegate's discretion is bounded by statutory purposes, relevant criteria, a maximum or cost-linked limit, a defined set of choices, budget or procedural controls, executive or parliamentary oversight, or binding constitutional principles.
predicates.delegate_empowered_to_determine_the_legi: The delegate is left to decide the substantive policy of the law, or to change the substance of an enactment, rather than implement a policy the legislature has already settled.
predicates.delegation_is_valid_and_not_excessive: The delegation is upheld as valid and as not an abdication or excessive delegation of legislative power.

definition: A legislature may delegate subordinate or implementing tasks to the executive or an administrative body without abdicating its function, so long as it has itself settled the essential policy and the delegate is guided or confined by that policy, relevant criteria or safeguards. Such a delegation is not excessive merely because the statute leaves details, or a maximum, minimum or enumeration, to the delegate.
exceptions_or_limits: The delegation fails if the legislature has not laid down policy and the delegate is left with unguided or uncanalised power.
The delegate must not be able to make substantive changes to the law or its policy; selection among enacted laws or assignment of administrative functions is permissible.
A law is not invalid merely because the delegated discretion might be abused; actual abuse can be challenged separately.
The degree of guidance required varies with context. A broad statement of policy suffices for territories without a legislature, while rate-setting needs purposes, budget or cost links and controls.
Essential legislative functions, including determining policy, cannot be delegated.

common_material_facts: A statute left to the government or an administrative body the extension, application, enumeration, rate-fixing, area identification or reorganisation of functions.
The statute's preamble, purposes or scheme stated a policy, such as anti-evasion, industry development, land reclamation, slum clearance, agrarian reform or tribunal independence.
Safeguards were present in many cases: budget processes, elected or accountable bodies, central government control, laying of rules before Parliament, maximum rates or cost-linked rates.
The delegate selected, applied or implemented rather than changing the substantive law.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 246(4) and section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966
Section 129(b) proviso and sections 95-100, 127, 150, 454-457 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act
Commissioners of Divisions Act, 1957, sections 3(3), 3(4), 6 and 7
Section 2(1) of the Abolition Act
Section 4(1) of the Bhopal Reclamation and Development of Lands (Eradication of Kans) Act, 1954
Section 3 and schedule of the drainage tax statute
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 14 members uphold the delegation as valid and not excessive, because the legislature had stated policy and the delegate was guided or confined.
variations: Some delegations concern geographic extension of laws (1110593_1, 147362898_3), some enumeration or identification (1133248_2, 569143_1), some tax rate-setting (1648125_4, 1829323_1, 298959_3), some administrative reorganisation (284811_1, 490012_1, 336529_3) and others the application of the law to individual cases or the variation of limits (678245_2, 919121_4).

The source of guidance varies: express statutory policy, the preamble, budget and oversight procedures, cost linkage, binding constitutional principles from precedent, or enumerated relevant criteria.

Some members rely on an additional safeguard such as parliamentary review (1297272_2), a legislative power to impose a ceiling (1829323_1) or the delegate's inability to alter substantive law (1110593_1, 284811_1).

Some reasoning rests on the nature of the task, a factual determination unsuitable for legislative definition (569143_1) or the legislature's enactment of the law before the executive selected areas (147362898_3).

legal_question: Is a state law that acquires or vests land, minerals or an undertaking invalid for want of legislative competence or for repugnancy to a central law on a related subject (planning, mining, forests, industry control, electricity or land acquisition), where the two laws have different dominant purposes and can operate together?

predicates.challenge_to_state_law_on_competence_or_: The state law is challenged as beyond legislative competence or as repugnant to a central law (Art. 246/254 or the legislative entries).
predicates.state_law_in_pith_and_substance_within_s: Judged by its substance and operative provisions, the state law is mainly about a matter within the state's legislative power, such as land, acquisition, land reform, planned development or vesting of property.
predicates.acquisition_or_overlap_is_incidental_or_: Any acquisition or effect on the central field is incidental to the state law's main purpose, or the central law deals with a different subject (for example industry regulation, mining regulation, forest management or electricity supply), or it neither acquires the property in question nor prohibits acquisition.
predicates.irreconcilable_conflict_or_exhaustive_ce: The state and central laws cover substantially the same field and are directly and irreconcilably inconsistent so that both cannot be obeyed, or the central law is an exhaustive code that excludes state legislation.
predicates.state_law_is_valid_and_not_repugnant_to_: The state law is within the state legislature's competence and is not invalid for repugnancy, so presidential assent under Art. 254(2) is not needed on that ground.

definition: A state law that in pith and substance falls within a state legislative field, for example land, acquisition, land reform, planned development or vesting of property, is not invalid for lack of competence or for repugnancy merely because it overlaps incidentally with a central law on another subject. It stands where the central law does not cover the same field, is not an exhaustive code, and creates no direct, irreconcilable conflict, so that the two can operate together.
exceptions_or_limits: Repugnancy is made out if the laws occupy the same field and conflict directly and irreconcilably, or if the central law is intended as an exhaustive code.
A declaration of central control over an industry removes state power only to the extent of the field actually occupied by the central legislation.
A law that regulates an activity (for example mining) does not by itself vest ownership in the state; vesting needs an express transfer or acquisition provision.
Where a state law vests mineral ownership, mining rights governed by central law subsist only if the claimant shows they exist and are affected.
Where the central law does not itself address the point, a state law that merely adds a modification mechanism is not repugnant, because both can operate together.
For pre-Constitution state laws, continuation under Art. 372 depends on the law having been valid when enacted and not altered by a competent legislature.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the effect of vesting mineral ownership on subsisting mining leases, not competence or repugnancy. It is a related corollary that keeps rights governed by central law alive.
It concerns whether a central mining regulation law itself vests mineral ownership in the state. It is a statutory-interpretation point, not a state-versus-central competence or repugnancy question.

common_material_facts: A state statute on land acquisition, planned development, land reform, vesting of minerals or acquisition of an undertaking is challenged as repugnant to or encroaching on a central law.
The central law covers a different dominant subject, such as industry control, mining regulation, forests, electricity or general land acquisition.
The central law contemplates or does not prohibit acquisition, or is silent on the point in issue.
Acquisition is incidental to the state law's principal purpose.
statutes_and_provisions: Constitution Arts. 245, 246, 254 and 372
List II Entries 5, 18, 24 and 36
List I Entries 52 and 54
List III Entry 42
Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (ss. 41, 42)
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (ss. 2, 4, 16, 17)
Tea Act
Indian Electricity Act, 1910 and Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 12 of the 14 members the challenge fails and the state law is held valid, with no repugnancy and no need for presidential assent. The other two (1201636_2 and 64111525_2) deal with the effect of vesting on mining rights and with whether a regulatory law vests ownership. They are resolved in favour of subsisting rights and against implied vesting.
variations: Some members rest on the pith-and-substance and incidental-encroachment doctrines to uphold competence; others apply the Art. 254 test of direct, irreconcilable conflict.
Some turn on the central law's silence or its contemplation of state vesting or acquisition; others on the central law not covering the particular company or property.
One member decides competence by the purpose of the acquisition rather than by who holds the property afterwards, under the pre-Seventh Amendment entries.
One member applies Art. 372 continuation to a pre-Constitution law.

split_suggestion: Keep the 12 covered members as the repugnancy/competence group. Move 1201636_2 and 64111525_2 to a separate group on the effect of mineral vesting and regulation on mining and proprietary rights. Optionally separate pure legislative-competence members (567012_3, 815666_1, 1682508_1, 1293816_1) from the Art. 254 repugnancy members.

legal_question: When an accused personally and intentionally inflicts a bodily injury that is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death (or is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death), and death results, is the accused guilty of murder, irrespective of the number of blows, the absence of an intention to cause death, or the absence of shared intention with co-accused?

rule.if: accused_personally_inflicted_injury and injury_caused_death and (injury_sufficient_in_ordinary_course_to_cause_death or injury_so_imminently_dangerous_as_to_probably_cause_death) and intention_to_inflict_that_injury_established_or_inferable and not (right_of_private_defence_available or exception_to_murder_established or intervening_negligent_treatment_caused_death)

predicates.accused_personally_inflicted_injury: The accused's own act, proved by reliable ocular and/or medical evidence, caused the bodily injury in question, so liability does not depend on common intention or other vicarious liability.
predicates.injury_caused_death: The victim died as a result of the injury inflicted by the accused.
predicates.injury_sufficient_in_ordinary_course_to_: The injury, objectively and on the medical and other evidence, was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
predicates.injury_so_imminently_dangerous_as_to_pro: The act was so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death or bodily injury likely to cause death, and the accused knew this (e.g. a deadly weapon on a vital part).
predicates.intention_to_inflict_that_injury_establi: The intention to inflict the particular injury found is proved or can be inferred from the circumstances, such as the weapon, force, body part targeted, manner of attack, and the victim's helplessness; an intention to cause death is not required.
predicates.right_of_private_defence_available: The accused had a right of private defence that covers the act.
predicates.exception_to_murder_established: A statutory exception reducing murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder (e.g. sudden fight in the heat of passion without undue advantage or cruel conduct) is made out on the evidence.
predicates.intervening_negligent_treatment_caused_d: Negligent medical treatment, rather than the injury itself, is shown to have caused the death, breaking the causal connection.
predicates.accused_guilty_of_murder: The accused is guilty of murder (Section 302 IPC read with Section 300), and a murder conviction is sustained, restored or substituted as the case may be.

definition: A person who personally and intentionally inflicts a bodily injury that is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, or that he knows is so imminently dangerous that it will probably cause death, is guilty of murder if death results. This holds even without intent to kill, even for a single blow, and without reliance on common intention, unless private defence, a statutory exception, or a break in causation is shown.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the right of private defence is available, the rule does not apply; the members note that its absence was part of the basis for conviction.

Where an exception to Section 300 (e.g. Exception 4, sudden fight) is established, the offence may be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder. That exception requires absence of premeditation, a sudden fight, heat of passion and no undue advantage or cruel or unusual conduct; absence of premeditation alone is not enough.
A single blow does not by itself rule out murder, but it is assessed with the weapon, body part, force and circumstances.
Where the probability of death is lower than very high, or the injury's nature is not medically established, the offence may be culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
Negligent medical treatment shown to have caused the death would break causation; a mere hypothetical possibility of survival with treatment does not.

One member (1733210_2) upheld a conviction under Section 304 Part I for a fatal act during a sudden fight without premeditation, showing that sudden-fight circumstances can lead to a lesser homicide classification.

outlier_members.reason: It shares the principle that a participant who personally inflicts the fatal wound is individually liable. However, the outcome was a conviction under Section 304 Part I (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) after a sudden fight without premeditation, not murder. It is consistent with the rule's limits but does not support the murder outcome.

common_material_facts: A sharp-edged or pointed weapon (knife, dagger, axe, spear, penknife) was used on a vital part such as the head, neck, chest or abdomen.
Medical evidence identified the injury as sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death and as the cause of death.
Reliable eyewitness evidence attributed the fatal injury to the particular accused.
Often only a single blow or wound was inflicted, or the other accused did not share the intention, so liability under Section 34 or common intention was displaced or unnecessary.
Some attacks were on a fallen or unarmed victim or followed a sudden quarrel.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 299 IPC
Section 300 IPC, clause thirdly and clause fourthly
Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC
Section 302 IPC
Section 304 Part I and Part II IPC
Section 34 IPC
Right of private defence
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 13 of 14 members the accused who personally inflicted the fatal injury was held guilty of murder under Section 302, and a murder conviction was upheld, restored or substituted for a lesser one or for a Section 34 conviction. One member (1733210_2) maintained a Section 304 Part I conviction for a sudden fight.
variations: Some members rest on clause thirdly (intentional injury sufficient to cause death), citing Virsa Singh; one rests on clause fourthly (imminently dangerous act).
Several members convert a Section 302/34 conviction into an individual Section 302 conviction because the direct assailant is identified.
Some members address defences or mitigating arguments: single blow, sudden quarrel or fight, absence of intention to kill, private defence, negligent treatment.
The reasoning on intention ranges from an explicit Virsa Singh analysis to a bare application of Section 302 on medical and ocular evidence.
In one member a state appeal sought to alter the classification from Section 304 Part II to murder.

legal_question: Under rent-control legislation, when the statutory conditions for eviction on the ground of non-payment of rent are satisfied (qualifying arrears, a valid demand notice and failure to pay or cure within the prescribed time), must the court or Controller order eviction, and what makes a demand notice valid?

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and statutory_arrears_conditions_met and valid_demand_notice_served and tenant_failed_to_pay_or_cure_within_statutory_period and not rent_amount_genuinely_disputed

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The landlord seeks eviction or possession on the ground of non-payment of rent under a rent-control statute.
predicates.statutory_arrears_conditions_met: The arrears meet the statute's requirements, for example the minimum period of default and monthly rent, so that the statutory ground is established.
predicates.valid_demand_notice_served: The landlord served a notice that, read in substance and context, demands legally recoverable arrears for the accommodation actually let and satisfies the statute's notice requirements.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_pay_or_cure_within_stat: The tenant did not pay or tender the arrears within the period allowed after the notice, or did not make the full statutory cure at the first hearing where the statute provides for that.
predicates.rent_amount_genuinely_disputed: There is a genuine dispute about the standard rent or permitted increases.
predicates.court_must_order_eviction_without_discre: The court or Controller is bound to pass an eviction decree. The word 'may' gives no discretion to refuse, and payment after the statutory period, such as after suit or before decree, does not prevent eviction.

definition: Where the statutory ground of rent default is made out, with qualifying arrears, a valid demand notice and no payment or cure within the statutory period, and the rent is not genuinely disputed, the court or Controller must order eviction. Statutory 'may' is read as 'shall', and late payment after the deadline, including after suit or before decree, gives no relief. Eviction fails if the notice is not a valid demand or the arrears do not qualify.
exceptions_or_limits: If the notice is not a valid demand (it merely asserts rent is due, or it describes substantially different accommodation from that let), the eviction suit on the rent-default ground fails.
If the tenant is not in qualifying arrears, for example because of payments or deposits, eviction for rent default fails.
Where the statute provides a cure (payment or tender at the first hearing, or regular deposits), a tenant who makes it can avoid eviction; mandatory eviction applies only where the cure is not made.
Where the standard rent or permitted increases are genuinely disputed, the mandatory provision for undisputed arrears does not apply.
A notice is read in substance and context; a description such as 'use and occupation charges' or notices read together can still amount to a valid rent demand.
Amended provisions apply only to suits or proceedings (and terminations) that follow the amendment; a mere right to rely on an earlier statutory provision is not an accrued right.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns whether an amended notice requirement for each rent default applies to a proceeding begun after the amendment (accrued rights and retrospectivity under a tenancy statute). It does not concern the mandatory eviction or demand notice validity point.

common_material_facts: Landlord seeks eviction for non-payment of rent under a state rent-control Act.
Rent is payable monthly and arrears run for at least six months (or four months under the U.P. Act).
A written demand notice was served and the tenant did not pay within the statutory period after it.
Tenant paid or deposited only after the deadline, after suit or before decree, or paid only in part at the first hearing.
Several cases dispute the sufficiency of the demand notice (wording as use and occupation charges, notices read together, wrong accommodation, a bare Section 106 notice).
statutes_and_provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act 1947, ss. 12(1), 12(2), 12(3)(a), 12(3)(b)
Delhi Rent Control Act 1958, s. 14(1)(a), 14(2)
East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act 1949, s. 13(2)(i) and s. 13
Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act 1987, s. 14(2)
U.P. Urban Buildings Act 1972, s. 20(2)(a)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act 1961, s. 12(1)(a)
Transfer of Property Act 1882, s. 106
Article 14 of the Constitution
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About 10 of the 13 covered members hold that eviction must be decreed once the statutory conditions are met ('may' read as 'shall', no relief from forfeiture, late payment irrelevant). Three turn on demand notice validity: two uphold a notice read in context, and the others reject a defective notice or non-qualifying arrears (the U.P. and M.P. cases).
variations: Some members concern the mandatory reading of 'may' (Himachal Pradesh, Bombay), others the content of the demand notice.
Bombay cases address whether payment before decree or after suit saves the tenant after the amendment, distinguishing earlier cases on the former law.
Punjab cases apply the first-hearing cure proviso, with eviction following where the cure is incomplete.

Notice cases split: a notice described as damages for use and occupation or notices read together suffice, while a notice for a substantially different premises or a bare assertion that rent is due does not.
One member's facts (1802788_2) involve a rent dispute, so the stated rule is the principle and the facts fall outside it.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) mandatory eviction when the statutory default conditions are met ('may' means 'shall', no relief for late payment): 1143655_2, 1272131_2, 156898_2, 1587367_2, 1760015_2, 1802788_2, 223749_2, 71219_3, 886958_1; (b) validity and sufficiency of the demand notice or qualifying arrears: 151181_1, 676555_1, 806314_1, 1743111_2; (c) retrospective application of an amended notice requirement: 1797739_1.

legal_question: What limits and standards govern an appellate court's review and reversal of a lower court's findings, particularly an acquittal or findings based on witness credibility, and what must it do before reversing?

rule.if: appellate_court_reviews_lower_court_findings and (finding_is_acquittal or finding_turns_on_witness_credibility_or_perception or concurrent_factual_findings) and not (trial_assessment_materially_erroneous or substantial_compelling_reasons_shown or cogent_reasons_for_departure)

predicates.appellate_court_reviews_lower_court_find: An appellate court is hearing an appeal against the findings or decision of a trial court or lower court.
predicates.finding_is_acquittal: The finding under challenge is an acquittal, so the presumption of innocence and benefit of reasonable doubt are reinforced.
predicates.finding_turns_on_witness_credibility_or_: The finding depends on the credibility or sensory perception of oral witnesses whom the trial judge saw and heard.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: Lower courts have made concurrent adverse factual findings that the appellate court is asked to disturb.
predicates.trial_assessment_materially_erroneous: The trial court's appraisal is perverse, materially irregular, based on inadmissible evidence, a misreading of evidence, a misdirection of law, or conjecture.
predicates.substantial_compelling_reasons_shown: The appellate court has identified substantial and compelling reasons, or a special feature overlooked or sufficient proved improbability, that displace the trial court's view.
predicates.cogent_reasons_for_departure: The appellate court has given cogent reasons, addressing the material circumstances, for departing from the lower court's findings.
predicates.appellate_court_must_give_due_weight_to_: The appellate court must give due weight to the trial court's finding and presumptions in the accused's favour, and reversal without adequate grounds is not sustained.

definition: An appellate court has wide power to reappraise evidence, but when reviewing an acquittal or findings resting on witness credibility or concurrent findings, it must give due weight to the trial court's view. It may reverse only for substantial, cogent reasons such as perversity, material error or an overlooked feature, after actually examining the material evidence, and it may not reverse without them.
exceptions_or_limits: Restraint is a rule of practice, not an absolute bar: the trial court's finding is not infallible and can be displaced by material error, perversity, misreading of evidence or overlooked special features.
Where credibility is not in issue, the appellate court is better placed to draw inferences from proved facts.

In an appeal from conviction, the appellate court must examine the material evidence, especially direct eyewitness testimony, before acquitting. Failure to do so makes the acquittal liable to be set aside and, in some cases, remanded.

In special leave appeals after a reversal of acquittal, the Supreme Court ordinarily examines only enough evidence to test whether the High Court followed the governing approach, and does not reassess the evidence if the principles were applied correctly.
An acquittal not appealed against cannot be set aside, though evidence concerning the acquitted co-accused may be assessed incidentally in the appeal of convicted co-accused.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the duty to examine eyewitness evidence before reversing a conviction (CrPC ss. 385-386), not deference to the trial court's findings.
Same duty as 1292925_1: the appellate court must consider eyewitness testimony before acquitting on appeal from conviction.

The appellate court acquitted without considering the evidence, treating the case as compoundable by compromise; set aside and remanded. This is a duty to decide on the evidence, not trial-court deference.
Concerns the scope of an appeal by convicted co-accused and the finality of an unappealed acquittal of a co-accused, a distinct point.

common_material_facts: A High Court reversed a trial court's decision, either an acquittal or a finding based on oral testimony, and the Supreme Court tested that reversal.
The trial court's finding rested on witness credibility or demeanour (adoption, mortgage attestation, acquittal on unreliable prosecution evidence).
In several members the High Court acquitted or reversed without examining the eyewitness or material evidence.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 136 of the Constitution
Section 100 CPC (contrasted with intra-court appeal power)
Section 68 Indian Evidence Act
Sheo Swarup, Sanwat Singh, Chandrappa, Watt v. Thomas and W.C. Macdonald v. Latimer lines of authority
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 10 covered members, about 6 restored or upheld the trial court's finding because the reversal lacked adequate grounds (127405_1, 151619456_1, 1579663_1, 1946601_3, 454120_1, 1613023_2). Two upheld a reversal of acquittal because the approach was correct (1220660_1, 667950_2), and two state the governing principles or the Supreme Court's limited review (1126312_1, 480287_2). Of the 4 outliers, 3 set aside an acquittal for failure to examine the evidence, and 1 allowed incidental assessment of evidence on an unappealed acquittal.
variations: Criminal appeals against acquittal stress presumption of innocence and preference for the acquittal where two views are reasonable; civil appeals stress the trial judge's advantage in seeing witnesses and the 'special feature or balance of improbability' test.
Some members uphold a reversal because the High Court applied the principles properly, while others set it aside because it did not.
One member concerns a Letters Patent appeal and a Division Bench's restraint towards a Single Judge's findings.
One member concerns the Supreme Court's own scope of review under Article 136.

split_suggestion: Split into: (a) deference to trial court findings on credibility and acquittals (1126312_1, 1220660_1, 127405_1, 667950_2, 480287_2, and the civil credibility cases 151619456_1, 1579663_1, 454120_1, 1946601_3, 1613023_2); (b) the duty to examine the evidence before reversing a conviction (1292925_1, 1820883_1, 1379472_1); (c) the effect of an unappealed co-accused acquittal (884859_1).

legal_question: When is a constitutional challenge to a land acquisition, requisition or land-reform law (on grounds such as violation of property rights, colourable legislation, absence of public purpose, or confiscatory deprivation) rejected?

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_land_law and (law_saved_by_constitutional_protection or law_within_legislative_competence_in_substance) and not law_transgresses_competence_indirectly

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_law: The validity of a law or proceeding on land acquisition, requisition, land reform, or a closely related measure such as a tax feeding into compensation is challenged on constitutional grounds, such as the property guarantee, the compulsory acquisition article, colourable legislation, or fraud on the Constitution.
predicates.law_saved_by_constitutional_protection: The law is shielded from the particular challenge by an express constitutional saving. Examples are the saving of pre-Constitution laws, the bar on questioning the adequacy of compensation, or the special character of non-heritable jagir property that is held only by the State's grace.
predicates.law_within_legislative_competence_in_sub: On examination of its true character, effect and purpose, the law falls within a subject on which the enacting legislature may legislate, such as acquisition, land reform, land tenure or taxation of agricultural income.
predicates.law_transgresses_competence_indirectly: Under the form of a competent subject, the law in substance does something the legislature could not do directly, so it is colourable legislation.
predicates.constitutional_challenge_fails: The court rejects the constitutional challenge on the ground raised and the law or proceeding stands.

definition: Constitutional attacks on land acquisition, requisition and land-reform laws fail where the law is protected by an express constitutional saving, or where in substance it falls within the legislature's competence and does not indirectly do what the legislature cannot do directly. Colourable legislation concerns competence, not motive.
exceptions_or_limits: Even where laws are protected from compensation-based challenges, a challenge that the acquisition lacks a public purpose remains open to judicial review (41868_3).
Subordinate rules or provisions that go beyond the enabling provision can still be ultra vires, even if the parent law is upheld (9285_2: fund assistance extended to persons not affected by the law).
Saving of a pre-Constitution law does not decide whether every company acquisition is for a public purpose (463201_3); it only defeats the challenge under the compulsory acquisition article.

The Court cannot strike down a law merely because the legislature's motive was to reduce compensation or to profit; the test is competence, and a law that actually exceeds that competence is not covered by the rule.

outlier_members.reason: It holds that a public-purpose challenge remains reviewable despite the constitutional protection, so it states a limit on the saving rather than a challenge failing. The Court did not decide the challenge on its merits.

common_material_facts: Challenges to land acquisition, requisition or land-reform statutes by landowners or intermediaries, often by invoking the property guarantee (Art. 19(1)(f)) or Art. 31
Many statutes pre-dated the Constitution, or were protected by Art. 31(4), 31-A, 31-B or Art. 31(5)(a)
Allegations of colourable legislation, such as profit-making by the State, diversion of compensation, or tax raised to reduce compensation
Land-reform schemes transferring land to cultivators or tenants against payment, with compensation fixed by statutory formula
statutes_and_provisions: Constitution Art. 19(1)(f) and 19(5)
Art. 31-A and 31-B
List II entry 36 and entry 46
List III entry 42
Land Acquisition Act, s. 6(3) and Part VII (s. 40)
Bhanji Munji, Lilavati Bai, Babu Barkya Thakur, Gajapati Narayan Deo
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: The challenge is rejected in 13 of 14 members, because of an express constitutional saving or because the law is within legislative competence. One member (41868_3) holds that the public-purpose challenge stays reviewable. One member (9285_2) also strikes down subordinate rules that go beyond the enabling provision.
variations: Some members rest on an express constitutional saving: Art. 31(5)(a) for pre-Constitution laws, or Art. 31(4) for compensation adequacy.
Others turn on the colourable legislation test of competence and substance, rather than on a saving.
Some decisions are thinly reasoned and rely on precedent alone (1451241_1, 463201_4, 879756_3).
1395167_2 rests instead on the special non-heritable character of jagir property.

split_suggestion: Split into three groups. (a) Challenges defeated by an express constitutional saving: Art. 31(5)(a), 31(4), the Bhanji Munji line, and bare rejections (1536600_2, 208309_1, 463201_3, 463201_4, 1451241_1, 879756_3, 1395167_2, 775246_3). (b) Colourable legislation and competence challenges to land-reform and tax measures (696070_2, 775246_1, 919121_5, 9285_2, 45759_4). (c) Scope of judicial review despite protection: public purpose (41868_3).

legal_question: Does a law or grant condition that restricts, regulates or retrospectively affects property rights (by limiting transfers, evictions, rents or recovery of possession) infringe the constitutional property guarantees (Articles 19(1)(f), 31, 31A) when it is a reasonable measure serving a public purpose, or when the claimant's interest was defeasible or merely regulated rather than acquired?
