predicates.act_in_furtherance_of_contract: The transferee did an act in furtherance of the contract that is unequivocally referable to it, rather than a preliminary act or mere retention of possession that is independently justified (for example as tenant or mortgagee).
predicates.transferee_performed_or_willing: The transferee has performed, or is proved to have been continuously ready and willing to perform, his obligations under the contract.
predicates.no_privity_with_transferor: The owner never contracted with the claimant, who claims only through an intermediate purchaser without transferable title.
predicates.opposing_party_is_purchaser_for_value_wi: The party against whom protection is claimed bought the property for consideration without notice of the contract or the part performance.
predicates.part_performance_protection_unavailable: The Section 53A defence fails and the claimant cannot protect possession on the basis of the agreement.

definition: Protection of possession under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act is available only against the transferor or those claiming under the transferor, and only if all requirements are proved: a signed written contract with ascertainable terms, possession in part performance, an act in furtherance, and performance or willingness to perform. It also fails against a purchaser for value without notice. If any element is missing, the protection is unavailable.
exceptions_or_limits: Expiry of limitation for a specific-performance suit does not by itself defeat the defence if all other statutory requirements are met.
A payment may support part performance when considered together with other acts, but it is not automatically part performance.
The protection is only a shield against the transferor or persons claiming under the transferor; it does not confer ownership.

The adverse-possession outcome is a related but separate limb: a person who entered under an agreement and relies on it cannot claim adverse possession unless he disclaims the agreement and proves hostile assertion of title to the owner's knowledge for the full prescriptive period.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the inconsistency between reliance on an agreement and a plea of adverse possession, not the elements of part performance. It is closely related and could form a separate sub-group with 732785_3.
Concerns the inconsistency between a Section 53A possession claim and adverse possession, requiring later hostile assertion; this is a different legal point from the elements of part performance.
Concerns characterisation of a sale with reconveyance and rent note as a usufructuary mortgage under Section 58, not part performance.

common_material_facts: The occupant claims to hold possession under an agreement to sell, often an oral or loosely documented one.
The occupant was already in possession in another capacity (tenant, mortgagee, agent or permissive occupant) before the alleged contract.
The occupant did not show an act in furtherance or readiness and willingness to perform.
The writings relied on were letters or acknowledgments lacking essential terms.
In some cases a subsequent purchaser for value without notice, or an owner with no privity, was the opposing party.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 53A, Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Section 16(c), Specific Relief Act
Section 58(c) and 58(d), Transfer of Property Act
Section 91, Indian Trusts Act
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In the 6 core members the Section 53A defence was rejected and possession or eviction went to the owner or purchaser. Of the 3 outliers, two rejected an adverse possession plea inconsistent with reliance on an agreement, and one held the transaction was not a usufructuary mortgage.
variations: Different elements failed: writing and terms in some, change of possession character and act in furtherance in others, willingness to perform in others, privity or notice in others.
Prior possession as tenant or mortgagee needed something beyond retention of possession.
Procedural contexts varied: eviction, redemption, title and possession suits, and a late amendment of the defence.

split_suggestion: Keep the six Section 53A elements cases together (129022414_1, 1390060_1, 1678794_1, 1719909_2, 1965204_1, 78422638_2). Move 1557321_1 and 732785_3 to a separate group on inconsistency between a part-performance claim and adverse possession. Treat 647998_2 (mortgage characterisation under Section 58) as a separate issue.

legal_question: When an eviction order has been upheld, restored or is under challenge, may the Court exercise its discretion to give the tenant (typically a business tenant) time to vacate or postpone execution of the eviction, and on what conditions?

predicates.eviction_order_upheld_restored_or_in_iss: The eviction order or decree has been upheld, restored or allowed on appeal, or is before the Court in an eviction appeal.
predicates.tenant_in_possession_carrying_on_busines: The tenant remains in possession and has run a business (such as a shop, cloth, hardware or hotel business) in the premises, or has occupied them for a long period.
predicates.tenant_requests_time_or_court_finds_hard: The tenant asked for time to vacate, or the Court finds that immediate eviction or relocation would cause hardship, or the parties agreed to a temporary extension.
predicates.court_imposes_conditions_such_as_underta: The Court makes the extra time conditional on safeguards such as an undertaking to surrender vacant possession, not to create third-party rights or damage the property, payment of rent, arrears or costs, or other terms.
predicates.hardship_justifies_deferral: The Court considers that the circumstances, such as scarcity of alternative accommodation or loss of established goodwill, justify deferral even where no express conditions are stated.
predicates.court_grants_tenant_time_to_vacate_or_de: The Court allows the tenant to remain for a limited period, or postpones execution of the eviction order, leaving the eviction order itself in force.

definition: Even where an eviction order stands or is restored, the Court may use its discretion to give a tenant, usually one with a long-running business or long occupation, a limited period to vacate. The time is granted on hardship, request or agreement, and normally on conditions such as an undertaking to surrender vacant possession, payment of rent, arrears or costs, and no third-party rights or damage.
exceptions_or_limits: The relief is discretionary and temporary; the eviction order remains in force.
The time granted is usually conditional, and failure to file the undertaking or to comply with the conditions ends the protection.
The members cite no statutory provision or earlier case for this relief; it rests on the Court's equitable discretion.
The town-planning scheme case (837893_5) differs in that it orders alternative premises and permits occupation only until they are provided.

outlier_members.reason: It arises under a town planning scheme and orders the provision of a suitable alternative shop, with interim occupation until handover, rather than merely giving time to vacate after an eviction order.

common_material_facts: The tenant carried on a business (cloth, hotel, hardware or general shop) in the premises, often for many years.
The tenant remained in possession after the eviction order was upheld or restored, or while the appeal was decided.
The tenant asked for time to vacate, or the parties agreed to it.
The Court required an undertaking, and sometimes payment of rent, arrears or costs.
statutes_and_provisions: No statutory provision or earlier case is cited in most members; the relief rests on the Court's discretion.
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 9 members the Court granted some accommodation to the tenant. In 8, execution of eviction was postponed or time to vacate was given, usually on an undertaking or other conditions; in 1, alternative premises were ordered.
variations: Some grants rest on hardship and scarcity of accommodation (1308956_2, 529393_2); others rest on the tenant's request alone (562631_4, 78997925_3).
Conditions vary: undertaking only, undertaking plus rent or arrears, costs, safeguards against third-party rights or damage, or reciprocal landlord undertakings (465210_2).
895961_2 rests on the parties' agreement.
837893_5 involves a planning scheme and alternative premises.

legal_question: In a succession dispute between a female heir (daughter or sister) and collateral relatives, where the collaterals rely on an asserted custom excluding the female heir, who bears the burden of proving the custom, and what rule applies if the custom is not proved?

rule.if: succession_dispute_over_inheritance and female_heir_claims_against_collaterals and collateral_relies_on_custom_excluding_female_heir and not asserted_custom_proved_for_the_property_in_question

predicates.succession_dispute_over_inheritance: The case concerns succession to a deceased person's property, where the parties are in Punjab or governed by Punjab customary law and personal law.
predicates.female_heir_claims_against_collaterals: A daughter or sister (or her line) of the deceased claims the property against collateral relatives.
predicates.collateral_relies_on_custom_excluding_fe: The collateral relies on an asserted custom, or a Riwaj-i-am or digest statement, under which the female heir is excluded in favour of collaterals.
predicates.asserted_custom_proved_for_the_property_: The party asserting the custom has proved by evidence, or the custom is entitled to judicial notice, that it excludes the female heir for the kind of property in dispute (for example, non-ancestral property).
predicates.personal_law_or_established_preference_a: Because the exclusionary custom is not established, the parties' personal law or the recognised customary preference for daughters or sisters governs, and the female heir inherits ahead of the collateral relatives.

definition: A custom displacing personal law, or the ordinary preference of daughters and sisters over collaterals, must be proved by the party asserting it. Entries or answers that are general or that relate to ancestral property do not prove an exclusion for non-ancestral property. Where the custom is not proved, the female heir takes in preference to collaterals under personal law or the recognised customary preference.
exceptions_or_limits: If the exclusionary custom is proved for the relevant kind of property, or has been so repeatedly recognised by courts that it can be judicially noticed, it governs instead.
The rule concerns non-ancestral or separate property; Riwaj-i-am entries are ordinarily read as relating to ancestral property unless a clear indication shows otherwise.

Where the applicable custom is proved to favour the daughter's line, that custom governs and a transfer to the daughter's sons may accelerate their succession (a separate point, not common to all members).
Proof of a special or institution-specific custom must be particular and adequate; the proof required for a general, well-recognised custom may be lighter.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the daughter's sons taking in preference to collaterals and acceleration of succession by gift, not the burden of proving a custom excluding a female heir.
It concerns proof of an institution-specific custom for succession to a religious headship (Gurbhai succession), not female heirs against collaterals.

common_material_facts: Dispute over non-ancestral or separate property between a daughter or sister and collateral relatives
Collateral relies on Rattigan's Digest or Riwaj-i-am entries asserting a custom of exclusion
Riwaj-i-am entries found general or related only to ancestral property
Parties are Punjab Hindus or Sikhs to whom Hindu law applies
statutes_and_provisions: Section 5, Punjab Laws Act, 1872
Sections 35, 48 and 57(1), Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Hindu Law of Inheritance (Amendment) Act, 1929
Rattigan's Digest of Customary Law, paras 23 and 24
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In most members the asserted custom is unproved or needs proof, and the daughter or sister succeeds under personal law or the recognised customary preference (about 5 of 9 members). The remaining members state the burden of proof or judicial-notice standard generally (1490310_1, 1888918_1), reject proof of an institutional custom (1859350_2), or favour the daughter's sons (1225694_1).
variations: Some members decide on a custom proved by the female claimant (1490310_3), others on personal law once the custom fails (1490310_4, 1713965_2).
1490310_1 and 1888918_1 state only the burden and proof standards, with no final preference for a female heir.
1814506_3 applies traditional Hindu law with no custom in issue.
38559_1 relies on the Digest's recorded preference and treats the Riwaj-i-am entry as insufficient.

split_suggestion: Split into: (a) female heir versus collateral where the exclusionary custom is unproved (1490310_3, 1490310_4, 1713965_2, 38559_1, 1814506_3); (b) general burden and judicial-notice rules for proving custom (1490310_1, 1888918_1, 1859350_2); (c) the daughter's sons and acceleration point (1225694_1).

legal_question: Is a land acquisition for a project involving a private company or concessionaire treated as a public-purpose acquisition under the ordinary procedure (Part II) rather than an acquisition for a company under Part VII, and how does the source of the compensation (public funds or the company) decide this?

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and acquisition_has_public_purpose_character and private_company_participates_or_benefits and public_funds_bear_wholly_or_partly_the_acquisition_cost and not company_bears_entire_cost_by_original_arrangement

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The validity or procedure of a land acquisition is challenged before the court.
predicates.acquisition_has_public_purpose_character: The acquisition serves a public purpose, for example an integrated public infrastructure or development scheme led or controlled by the State or a public body.
predicates.private_company_participates_or_benefits: A private company, joint venture partner, concessionaire or society takes part in or benefits from the project.
predicates.public_funds_bear_wholly_or_partly_the_a: The compensation or acquisition cost is paid wholly or partly from public revenues or a fund of a State-owned or controlled corporation or authority, as part of the arrangement.
predicates.company_bears_entire_cost_by_original_ar: The company alone bears the whole acquisition cost under the original arrangement, with no public contribution, or only a belated nominal one.
predicates.acquisition_proceeds_as_public_purpose_u: The acquisition is valid as a public-purpose acquisition under Part II, and the company-acquisition procedure under Part VII (Sections 39-41) is not required.

definition: Private participation or benefit does not make a public-purpose acquisition invalid or one 'for a company'. Where public funds bear wholly or partly the acquisition cost, the acquisition may proceed under Part II without the Part VII procedure. Where the company bears the entire cost, the Part VII procedure must be followed.
exceptions_or_limits: If the company bears the entire compensation and there is no public contribution, the company-acquisition procedure (Part VII, Sections 39-41) is required.
A nominal State contribution made belatedly, after the challenges were filed and outside the original arrangement, does not convert a company acquisition into a public-purpose acquisition.
A declaration must identify the acquisition as either for a public purpose or for a company, not both.
Where project assets revert to the public body and the project was conceived independently of the concessionaire, implementation by a private party does not make it an acquisition for a company.
Under the industrial development statute, land away from the main alignment is covered only if it is connected to components of an integrated project within the statutory definitions.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns whether land away from the main road alignment falls within an integrated project and the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act. It does not concern the funding-based choice between Part II and Part VII.

It concerns the validity of a supplementary scheme under the United Provinces Town Improvement Act, 1908, where land is allotted to a private concern. It does not concern the funding-based choice between Part II and Part VII.

common_material_facts: A private company, concessionaire, joint venture partner or cooperative society participates in or benefits from the acquisition.
The source of compensation (public funds, a State corporation, or the company alone) is the decisive fact.
The project is a State-led integrated infrastructure or development scheme.
The State or a public body retains control or ownership of the project assets.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act 1894, Section 3(e) and 3(f)
Land Acquisition Act 1894, Sections 4 and 6, including the second proviso and Explanation 2
Land Acquisition Act 1894, Part II and Part VII, Sections 39-41
Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act 1966, Sections 2(6) and 2(7-a)
United Provinces Town Improvement Act 1908, Sections 24(h) and 32
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 9 issues, 7 turn on the funding question. In 5 of those the acquisition was upheld as a public-purpose acquisition without the Part VII procedure because of public funding or a public character (1313008_1, 1313008_3, 1963266_1, 20367_2, 208309_3). In 2 the company-acquisition procedure was required because the company paid the entire cost (1981888_3, 557996_1). The other 2 members, which are outliers, upheld the acquisition as public-purpose.
variations: Some members rest on public funding (1313008_3, 20367_2, 208309_3), while 1963266_1 relies on asset reversion and the project's independent conception.
1313008_1 rests on the breadth of the definition of public purpose and does not treat the funding source as decisive.
1981888_3 and 557996_1 reach the opposite outcome because the company bears the entire cost. 557996_1 adds that a belated nominal State contribution is insufficient.
Two members apply different statutes (the industrial areas and town improvement Acts) to questions of scope and scheme validity.

split_suggestion: Keep the 7 funding-source and private-participation members together. Split 348205_7 (scope of an integrated project under the industrial areas statute) and 985731_1 (validity of a supplementary scheme under the town improvement statute) into a separate group on public purpose under special statutes. 1313008_1 could also sit in that group, as a general public-purpose holding.

legal_question: Does an earlier decree, order or judgment (especially a consent or compromise decree, or an order that reserves the merits or does not decide the point) bind the parties or later courts, by res judicata, estoppel or precedent, on an issue that the earlier court did not actually adjudicate?

rule.if: later_proceeding_raises_issue and earlier_decree_or_order_exists and not earlier_court_adjudicated_the_issue

predicates.later_proceeding_raises_issue: A later suit, application or case raises a particular issue or point between the parties, or before a court asked to follow the earlier ruling.
predicates.earlier_decree_or_order_exists: There is an earlier decree, consent or compromise decree, order or judgment that is relied on as barring the issue (res judicata or estoppel) or as binding precedent.
predicates.earlier_court_adjudicated_the_issue: The earlier court heard, considered and actually decided the issue as part of its ratio. This is not so where the decree merely records a compromise, the order expressly reserves the merits or only directs a hearing, the point was not argued or considered, or the remarks were unnecessary to the result.
predicates.earlier_decree_or_order_does_not_bind_on: The earlier decree or order creates no bar by res judicata or estoppel, and is not binding precedent, on that issue; the later court may decide it afresh.

definition: A decree or order binds, by res judicata, estoppel or precedent, only on what the earlier court actually decided. Consent or compromise decrees that record the parties' agreement, orders that reserve the merits or merely direct a hearing, and observations on points not argued or not necessary to the decision do not bind on the undecided issue.
exceptions_or_limits: A consent or compromise decree may still create an estoppel by conduct according to its terms, or bar a direct challenge to the compromise as unlawful (Order 23 Rule 3A CPC).
Where the earlier court actually decided the issue and it formed part of the ratio decidendi, the decision binds.
A new statute conferring fresh rights may allow the issue to be raised again, subject to that statute's terms.

Where a party was excluded from the earlier suit by compromise and restitution was finally determined in its favour, it is not bound by that decree. This is a specific application of the principle, not a separate exception.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the pleading and issue-framing rule that a court must not decide a compromise's validity when that challenge was not pleaded. It does not concern the binding effect of an earlier undecided matter.

common_material_facts: An earlier suit or proceeding ended in a compromise or consent decree, or in an order that expressly reserved the merits or only directed a hearing.
The later proceeding raised a distinct issue (title, nature of a lease, scaling down, exemption entitlement, an alternative site) that the earlier court never decided.
A party relied on the earlier decree or order as res judicata, estoppel or precedent.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 11 CPC (res judicata)
Order 23 Rule 3A CPC
Section 144 CPC (restitution)
Article 141 of the Constitution (ratio decidendi and obiter)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 8 covered members the earlier decree or order was held not to bar or bind on the undecided issue, so the later proceeding or court was free to decide it. Roughly 4 turned on res judicata or estoppel from consent decrees and 4 on precedent or binding effect of orders.
variations: Some members concern res judicata or estoppel between parties (consent decrees), others concern precedential force under Article 141 or the ratio/obiter distinction.
Reasons differ: the court did not adjudicate the matter, the order expressly disclaimed the merits or precedential value, the point was not argued, or the observations were unnecessary to the result.
One member turns on exclusion of a party by compromise and final restitution, and another on a statute conferring new rights.

split_suggestion: Optionally split into (a) res judicata and estoppel effect of consent or compromise decrees on undecided issues (134990086_3, 595622_1, 716698_4, 35788_1), and (b) binding precedent effect of orders or observations that reserved or did not decide the point (1703667_4, 327169_2, 662814_2, 869190_6). Treat 1847257_2 (unpleaded challenge to a compromise) separately.

legal_question: Must lands acquired together, in the same village or under the same notification, be given a uniform rate of compensation, or may different rates or belts be fixed where the lands differ materially in location, quality, access, potential or legal restrictions on use?

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The case concerns determination or review of compensation or market value for compulsorily acquired land (including appeals and challenges to the award).
predicates.lands_acquired_together_or_in_same_villa: The lands were acquired in one acquisition, as one block, under the same notification, or lie in the same village.
predicates.lands_differ_materially_in_location_qual: The lands differ materially in location (e.g. road frontage versus interior), soil or category, accessibility, development or building potential, or a legal restriction on use.
predicates.differences_affect_market_value: The differences are such that a willing and prudent purchaser would pay different prices for the lands, as shown by the evidence or record.
predicates.different_compensation_rates_or_belts_ar: The court may fix different rates, categories or belts of compensation for the lands, and need not apply one uniform rate; equality or same-block arguments do not require uniformity.

definition: Lands that are acquired together, form one block, lie in the same village or are covered by the same notification need not receive the same compensation. Where differences in location, quality, access, potential or use restrictions affect market value, the court may classify the lands, or divide them into belts, and fix different rates. A uniform rate applied without regard to such differences is erroneous.
exceptions_or_limits: Classification must rest on evidence or material in the record; a claim for uniform valuation fails absent supporting material, and a classification needs a reasonable basis.
Similarly situated lands with the same advantages and potentialities may still warrant the same compensation.
Where the differences do not affect market value, or the record does not show them, a uniform rate may be appropriate.
A uniform rate or average applied without examining intrinsic evidence of differing prices (e.g. sale deeds) is erroneous.

common_material_facts: Lands acquired in one acquisition, one block, one village or under one notification
Road-abutting land versus interior or rear land
Differences in land quality or category, building potential versus agricultural use, or a use restriction
Claimants argued for a uniform rate on grounds of same block, same purpose, same location or equality
Sale deeds or record evidence showing different prices or the absence of support for uniformity
statutes_and_provisions: Land acquisition compensation and market value provisions (Land Acquisition Act, generally)
Constitutional equality guarantee (Article 14), as argued in one member
Tarlochan Singh v. State of Punjab; Kanwar Singh v. Union of India
Union of India v. Mangatu Ram
Mirza Nausherwan Khan v. Collector
Subh Ram v. State of Haryana
K. Periasami and DDA v. Bali Ram Sharma (as to same compensation for similarly situated lands)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 8 members the claim for a uniform rate was rejected, and different rates, belts or categories were upheld or directed. In 2 members (1771435_1, 845284_2) a uniform rate applied by the High Court was set aside as erroneous.
variations: The basis of differentiation varies: location, road access, land category, building potential, or a legal restriction on use.
Some members uphold belting by lower courts (1227757_1, 979365_1, 737329_2), while others correct a uniform rate (1771435_1, 845284_2).
One member addresses the constitutional equality challenge (1771435_2) and another addresses a restriction on use under the same notification (1659688_4).
Belt distances differ: about 500 yards in one member, 100 yards in another.

legal_question: Where an accused who had a right of private defence (of body or property) causes death but uses force exceeding that right, is the accused liable for culpable homicide not amounting to murder (generally under Section 304) rather than murder, and how does the excess bear on conviction and sentence?

predicates.private_defence_right_available_on_facts: The evidence, on a preponderance of probabilities or as found by the court, shows the accused had an accrued right of private defence of body or property (including of another person) against a real and immediate threat.
predicates.accused_caused_death: The accused's act caused the death of the victim.
predicates.force_used_exceeded_limits_of_private_de: The force used went beyond what was necessary for defence, so that the circumstances did not justify causing death or inflicting that degree of harm.
predicates.accused_liable_for_culpable_homicide_not: The accused is convicted (or the conviction is maintained or substituted) under Section 304 of the Indian Penal Code rather than Section 302.

definition: When an accused kills while exercising a genuine right of private defence of body or property but exceeds its limits, the offence is culpable homicide not amounting to murder, usually under Section 304 Part I, rather than murder. The excess does not erase liability, and the defensive context can also mitigate the sentence.
exceptions_or_limits: If the force is recklessly excessive so that Exception II to Section 300 does not apply, the murder conviction may stand. The defensive circumstances may still be weighed in sentencing, for example by commuting a death sentence (1561519_1).

The defender is not expected to weigh the force with precision in the moment, but the right does not cover force beyond what is necessary, such as continuing an attack after the victim has fallen or a fatal blow where no reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt existed.
Whether the conviction falls under Part I or Part II of Section 304 depends on the intention or knowledge found; one member used Part II (1839895_5) and most used Part I.
Where a conviction for culpable homicide is already in place and the right was exceeded in fear, the excess may only reduce the sentence rather than alter the offence (1931444_4).
The right of private defence must first be established or probable; unexplained injuries on the accused support it, but without a right of private defence the rule does not apply.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns sentencing only: Exception II was held inapplicable because the force was recklessly excessive, the murder conviction stood, and the private defence context led to commutation of the death sentence.
Concerns reduction of sentence for excess of private defence made in fear, with the conviction maintained, rather than reclassification of the offence.

common_material_facts: Deceased attacked the accused or a relative first, or there was a sudden affray or dispute over land or crops.
The accused suffered injuries, sometimes unexplained by the prosecution.
Fatal force was disproportionate, such as a stab to the heart, a spear blow, multiple axe blows, or repeated shots.
Initial conviction was for murder under Section 302, sometimes with Section 34.
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Penal Code Section 300 Exception 2
Indian Penal Code Section 302
Indian Penal Code Section 304 Part I
Indian Penal Code Section 304 Part II
Indian Penal Code Sections 97, 99 and 101
Indian Penal Code Section 34
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 7 of 9 members, excess of private defence led to a murder conviction being altered to, or a conviction being retained as, culpable homicide under Section 304 (mostly Part I). Two members addressed sentence only: one reduced the sentence and one commuted a death sentence.
variations: Sentences ranged from six months to seven years of rigorous imprisonment.
Some members were appeals against murder convictions, one followed a State appeal against acquittal, and two were sentence-only appeals.
Defence of the person of another or of property appeared alongside defence of one's own body.
Reasoning ranged from a probability standard with unexplained injuries (1884217_1) to the Section 99 limit on harm (820403_4, 1839895_5).

legal_question: Can a High Court quash a criminal complaint, FIR, cognizance order or prosecution merely because the same facts also give rise to a civil claim, a pending civil suit, a commercial dispute or arbitration, where the allegations prima facie disclose the ingredients of an offence?

predicates.criminal_proceeding_challenged_for_quash: A complaint, FIR, investigation, cognizance order or charge is under challenge before a court exercising power to quash (for example under Section 482 CrPC or Article 226).
predicates.allegations_taken_at_face_value_prima_fa: Read as a whole and taken at face value, the allegations disclose the ingredients of a criminal offence, leaving their truth to be decided at trial.
predicates.civil_remedy_or_civil_dispute_or_commerc: The same facts also give rise to a civil claim, a pending civil suit, a commercial or contractual dispute, or pending arbitration.
predicates.complaint_shown_frivolous_mala_fide_or_v: The complaint is shown to be frivolous, mala fide, vexatious or oppressive, or the allegations on their face disclose no offence.
predicates.criminal_proceeding_not_to_be_quashed_so: The criminal proceeding cannot be quashed merely because the dispute has a civil, commercial or arbitral aspect, and it must be allowed to proceed according to law.

definition: A civil remedy, a pending civil suit, a commercial character or arbitration does not by itself justify quashing a criminal proceeding. If the allegations, taken at face value, prima facie disclose an offence and the complaint is not shown to be frivolous, mala fide or vexatious, the proceeding must go on and its truth is left to trial.
exceptions_or_limits: Quashing remains available where the allegations, taken at face value and in their entirety, disclose no offence.
Quashing remains available where the complaint is frivolous, vexatious, oppressive or mala fide.
The inherent power may still be used to prevent abuse of process, but not on the sole ground that a civil remedy exists.
A court deciding on quashing must actually examine the complaint's allegations; relying on the civil dispute without doing so makes the quashing order unsustainable.
Disputed questions of fact and defence material generally cannot be the basis for quashing at the initial stage.

common_material_facts: Property or land transactions (gift deed, development agreement, sale agreement, power of attorney, tenancy and possession disputes) alleged to involve fraud, forgery, cheating or breach of trust.
The High Court quashed the criminal process, or in one case refused to quash, because it saw the dispute as civil, or because a civil suit or arbitration was pending.
The complainant's allegations, if taken as true, disclosed offence ingredients, and nothing showed mala fides.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 482 CrPC (inherent power to quash)
Article 226 of the Constitution
State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal guidelines
Trisuns Chemical Industry v. Rajesh Agarwal (arbitration is no substitute for criminal prosecution)
Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd.
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 8 members the criminal proceeding was not quashed on the civil-dispute ground. In 7 the High Court's quashing order was set aside and the proceedings restored or allowed to continue. In 1 (42336483_1) the High Court's refusal to quash was upheld.
variations: Some members involve a pending civil suit, one an arbitration, one a commercial contract and one a mixed civil and criminal dispute.
Procedural stages differ: pre-investigation FIR, cognizance by the Magistrate, framing of charges, and a complaint after remand.
One member (166062129_1) rests on the High Court's failure to assess the complaint's allegations rather than on a finding that offence ingredients exist.
One member (42336483_1) is an appeal against refusal to quash and relies on specific forgery allegations, with disputed facts not a basis for quashing.
Reasoning varies: some stress that the court must not weigh defence material or likelihood of conviction, and others stress that the dispute may carry both civil and criminal liability.

legal_question: When can a writ of mandamus be refused for want of a legally enforceable right in the applicant and a corresponding legal duty in the public authority?

predicates.mandamus_sought: The applicant seeks a writ of mandamus against a public authority or the State.
predicates.applicant_has_subsisting_legally_enforce: The applicant has, on the date of the petition, a present legally protected right that a court can enforce, and the right does not depend on a condition not yet satisfied, such as a court declaration or an unauthorised sanction.
predicates.public_authority_has_corresponding_legal: A statute, rule or other binding law imposes on the authority a mandatory duty to do the act sought, and the authority has failed to perform it, or a demand was made and refused (or was futile).
predicates.mandamus_cannot_issue: The court cannot or should not grant the writ of mandamus.

definition: A writ of mandamus will not issue unless the applicant shows a subsisting, legally enforceable right and a corresponding legal duty on the public authority that has not been performed. Without these, including where the claimed right rests on non-binding arrangements, unmet preconditions or law that has been displaced, the writ is refused.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the authority has a statutory function that it has not yet exercised, a court may at most direct it to decide by a reasoned order. It may not substitute its own decision, for example by directing a licence to be granted or land to be released.
Where a matter has been placed before the competent authority and remains undecided, a direction to decide may be available even though a direction to decide in a particular way is not.
A demand and refusal is ordinarily required, unless a demand would be manifestly futile or an empty formality.
One member (26511_2) expressly left open whether mandamus would be available once the right to possession had been established in a civil court.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the limit on a writ court's power to direct a statutory authority to grant a licence before the authority has decided the application, which is the separation-of-functions point. It does not turn on the applicant's lack of an enforceable right. It overlaps with one strand of 136212417_4.

common_material_facts: The applicant asked a writ court to compel a public authority or the State to act, for example to hand over property, execute a lease, transfer premises, make payments, release land or approve a plan.
The asserted entitlement rested on a non-binding proposal, an unsanctioned contractual term, a right conditioned on a prior court declaration, or a right that no longer subsisted.
No statute or rule was shown to impose the claimed duty.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution (High Court writ power)
Sections 31(6) and 37(2) of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Mandamus was refused or set aside in all 8 members: 7 for lack of an enforceable right or corresponding duty, and 1 because the court cannot perform the authority's statutory function.
variations: Some members stress the dual requirement of a statutory duty and a corresponding right (146451_5, 586046_3, 703650_3).
Others stress only the right (1053043_4, 26511_2) or only breach of a mandatory duty (565554_2).
136212417_4 adds the requirement of demand and refusal and the rule against substituting the court's decision for the authority's.
703650_3 turns on the right ceasing to subsist after a binding Supreme Court decision.
1140708_3 concerns the court's overreach into the authority's decision-making role, not the applicant's right.

legal_question: In a suit for specific performance, how is the plaintiff's readiness and willingness to perform under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 to be established, and is it satisfied by the substance of the pleadings, the evidence and the plaintiff's conduct without any prescribed wording or formula?

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and plaintiff_pleaded_readiness_and_willingness_in_substance and evidence_and_conduct_support_readiness_and_ability and not evidence_shows_inability_or_unwillingness

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff seeks specific performance of a contract, typically an agreement to sell immovable property, so that Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 applies.
predicates.plaintiff_pleaded_readiness_and_willingn: The plaint, read as a whole, conveys in substance that the plaintiff performed or was always ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract, whether or not any particular words or formula are used.
predicates.evidence_and_conduct_support_readiness_a: The evidence and the plaintiff's conduct before and after the suit (for example part payment, demands or notices for performance, deposit of the balance, prompt suit, or means to raise the balance) support readiness and willingness and the ability to perform.
predicates.evidence_shows_inability_or_unwillingnes: The evidence establishes that the plaintiff lacked the means to perform or was unwilling to perform the contract.
predicates.readiness_and_willingness_requirement_is: The plaintiff has satisfied the requirement to aver and prove readiness and willingness to perform their part of the contract.

definition: Readiness and willingness under Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act is a question of fact decided from the substance of the pleadings read as a whole, the evidence and the plaintiff's overall conduct. No prescribed phraseology is needed, and the requirement is met where the pleadings and the evidence together show continuing readiness and ability to perform.
exceptions_or_limits: The plaintiff must still both aver and prove readiness and willingness; failure to do so is fatal to the claim.

Where the pleadings disclose a material factual dispute bearing on readiness and willingness, the court must require proof of the facts and cannot decree specific performance on deemed admissions or the absence of a written statement alone (Order 8 Rules 5(2) and 10 CPC).
Actual tender or deposit of the balance is not essential unless the court directs it, though a deposit is evidence of willingness.

Readiness and willingness must be shown continuously from the date of the contract to the hearing; the plaintiff need not make incessant demands, and need not hold ready money if the means to raise the consideration are shown.
Specific performance remains discretionary relief, to be exercised on sound and reasonable judicial principles.

outlier_members.reason: It does not decide that readiness and willingness is established. It holds that, where pleadings disclose a disputed material fact bearing on readiness, the court must require proof instead of decreeing on deemed admissions. This is a procedural point on proof, not a finding of satisfaction. It is consistent with the main rule and is recorded as a limit.

common_material_facts: Suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell property.
Plaint asserts the plaintiff was always ready and willing, or conveys this in substance, without a prescribed formula.
Plaintiff paid part or most of the consideration, or earnest money.
Plaintiff demanded execution of the sale deed, sent a notice, or made repeated requests.
Plaintiff deposited the balance consideration in court, or showed means to raise it.
Courts below or the High Court had found against the plaintiff on a technical ground, such as missing words or a court-fee delay.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, with Explanations (i) and (ii)
Section 16 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963
Sections 21 and 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963
Order 8 Rules 5(2) and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Section 58 of the Evidence Act
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 7 of 8 members the plaintiff was held ready and willing (or the decree was upheld), and technical objections about wording or delay were rejected. In 1 member the matter required proof of disputed facts before any decree.
variations: Some members rely on the plaint read as a whole (Syed Dastagir, Chandiok, Ardeshir Mama), others on conduct and surrounding circumstances (Venkatesh, Mademsetty Satyanarayana).
The evidence of readiness differs: deposit of the balance, part payments, notices, ability to arrange funds, or prompt suit after learning of a breach.
One member addresses delay within the limitation period and holds that incessant demands are not required.
One member (182831_3) is procedural and concerns proof despite deemed admissions.
One member (634059_2) states the principle without citing earlier authority and frames specific performance as discretionary.

legal_question: Does a tenant's departure from the specific use for which premises were let (an additional or different trade, incidental residential or resting use, a different occupant, or a business in part of a residential building) amount to use for a different purpose that justifies eviction, where the general character of the letting is preserved and the landlord's interest is not prejudiced?

rule.if: eviction_sought_for_change_of_user and tenant_use_differs_from_specific_use_in_letting and general_character_of_letting_preserved and (original_use_continues or new_use_is_same_class_of_use) and use_is_incidental_or_minor_or_of_same_class and no_covenant_prohibiting_the_use and no_prejudice_to_landlord_interest_or_premises

predicates.eviction_sought_for_change_of_user: The landlord seeks eviction on the statutory ground (or under s.108(o) TPA) that the tenant used the premises for a purpose other than that for which they were let.
predicates.tenant_use_differs_from_specific_use_in_: The tenant's actual use departs in some respect from the specific use stated or implied in the letting (e.g., additional or different trade, incidental residence or resting, different occupant, or a business in one room of a residential building).
predicates.general_character_of_letting_preserved: The use remains within the basic class of purpose of the letting (residential, business or trade), and the premises are not converted to a substantially different mode of enjoyment.
predicates.original_use_continues: The tenant continues the original use for which the premises were let, or the premises remain primarily used for the let purpose.
predicates.new_use_is_same_class_of_use: Where the original use has ended, the new use is of the same general class (e.g., one business replaced by another, or residential use by a different occupant).
predicates.use_is_incidental_or_minor_or_of_same_cl: The departure is incidental, occasional, temporary or minor, or is merely a change within the same class of use, and not a substantial change.
predicates.no_covenant_prohibiting_the_use: The lease contains no express covenant or negative stipulation prohibiting the tenant's alternative use.
predicates.no_prejudice_to_landlord_interest_or_pre: The use does not damage or impair the premises, create a nuisance, or otherwise prejudice the landlord's interest.
predicates.change_of_user_ground_not_established: The court holds that the tenant's use does not amount to use for a purpose other than that for which the premises were let, so the change-of-user ground for eviction fails.

definition: A tenant is not liable to eviction for change of user where the use remains within the basic class of purpose of the letting (the original use continues, or the new use is of the same class), the departure is incidental, temporary or minor, there is no prohibitory covenant, and the premises and landlord's interest are not prejudiced.
exceptions_or_limits: Eviction may be justified where the change makes the use alien to the purpose of the letting, such as converting commercial use to manufacturing or residential use, or ceasing the original trade and converting the premises into a residence.
An express negative covenant restricting the use or trade can make the departure actionable.
The outcome depends on the facts: damage, impairment, nuisance or prejudice to the landlord, or a substantial change in the mode of enjoyment, would support eviction.
Statutory wording differs (West Bengal, East Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Haryana, U.P. Acts; s.108(o) TPA), so the test is applied within each statute's framework.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns whether a building remains 'residential' under s.21(1) Explanation (iv) of the U.P. Act (a landlord's bona fide need ground), not a change-of-user eviction ground. It is analogous, since a minor business use does not alter the building's character, but it is a different legal question.

common_material_facts: The tenant's actual use departs partly from the use specified in the letting.

The original or basic use continues alongside the departure (paying guests with family residence, TV sales with repair shop, shoes plus garments, watch shop with resting space, cobbler with incidental residence).
The departure is temporary, incidental or within the same class of use.
There is no express covenant against the use and no shown damage or prejudice to the landlord.
statutes_and_provisions: s.13(1)(h) West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act
s.13(2)(ii)(b) East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949
s.10(2)(ii)(b) and s.21 Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
s.13(2)(ii)(b) Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973
s.108(o) Transfer of Property Act, 1882
s.21(1) Explanation (iv) U.P. Act 13 of 1972
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 9 members the eviction ground or the change of use was not established, and the tenant succeeded. Eight members directly concern change of user; one (819201_1) concerns building character.
variations: Some members rest on continuing the original business (1376714_1, 1604349_1, 1790866_1, 1909184_2), others on the purpose staying within the same class (692129_2, 88513_1).
Some stress absence of prejudice to the landlord or premises (1376714_1, 88513_1), while others stress the absence of a covenant (1604349_1) or landlord's knowledge (1909184_2).
844409_3 gives little reasoning and relies on earlier precedents, and its facts include a swap between workshop and residential use.
692129_2 turns on the purpose of letting being the type of use, not the identity of the occupant.

split_suggestion: Keep the change-of-user members together. Treat 819201_1 (classification of a building as residential or non-residential under the U.P. Act) as a separate issue. Optionally separate the 'same-class substitution' members (692129_2, 88513_1, 844409_3) from the 'additional or incidental use alongside continuing original use' members.

legal_question: Can a court refuse or deny discretionary, equitable or extraordinary relief, without examining the merits, to a litigant who suppresses or misrepresents material facts, orders or proceedings relevant to the relief sought?

predicates.discretionary_or_equitable_relief_sought: The litigant invokes a discretionary, equitable or extraordinary jurisdiction, such as Article 136 special leave, Article 226 or 227 writ jurisdiction, specific performance, or a defendant's plea for discretionary refusal of relief.
predicates.material_fact_known_to_party: The fact, order, document or prior proceeding was within the litigant's knowledge and bears on the relief sought or on the determination of the dispute.
predicates.material_fact_suppressed_or_misrepresent: The litigant withheld, omitted, distorted or misstated the material fact, order, evidence or prior proceeding, including by claiming it was irrelevant, so that the court was not candidly informed.
predicates.court_may_refuse_or_deny_relief_for_want: The court may dismiss the petition, refuse the relief or deny the equitable discretion on the ground of suppression or lack of clean hands, without deciding the merits.

definition: A litigant invoking a court's discretionary, equitable or extraordinary jurisdiction must make full, frank and truthful disclosure of material facts, orders and proceedings. Suppression or misrepresentation of such facts permits the court to refuse relief, often without reaching the merits, because the litigant lacks clean hands.
exceptions_or_limits: The suppressed fact must be material, meaning it bears on the relief sought or the determination of the dispute; immaterial omissions do not justify refusal.
Refusal is discretionary ('may'), not automatic.
The litigant cannot decide relevance for itself; relevance is for the court, so the litigant's own view that the fact is irrelevant does not excuse non-disclosure.

In the specific performance cases, the suppression or misrepresentation by the plaintiff leads to denial of relief, while misrepresentation or withholding of evidence by the defendant prevents the defendant from relying on equitable discretion against specific performance. The direction of the outcome depends on which party suppressed.
Some members also impose costs.

common_material_facts: The litigant omitted interim orders, earlier final orders, prior suits and appeals, or other proceedings bearing on the relief sought.
The litigant concealed or misdescribed facts about property, such as third-party interests, the commercial character of land, or a lease acknowledging vesting.

In the specific performance cases, a party misstated facts or withheld evidence: the plaintiff omitted the refusal of the returned earnest money, and the defendants misdescribed the agent's authority and withheld the original authority document.
The opposing party or the court discovered the suppressed fact.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 136 of the Constitution
Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution
Section 11-A (explanation) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and Section 36 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976
Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963
R v. Kensington Income Tax Commissioners (1917) 1 KB 486 principle
Hari Narain v. Badri Das, AIR 1963 SC 1558
Ramjas Foundation v. Union of India, (2010) 14 SCC 38
K.D. Sharma v. Steel Authority of India Ltd., (2008) 12 SCC 481
Prestige Lights Ltd. v. State Bank of India, (2007) 8 SCC 449
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 8 members refuse relief for suppression: 3 special leave petitions or appeals dismissed, 2 writ matters dismissed without merits, 1 appeal dismissed with costs, 1 specific performance denied to the plaintiff, and 1 defendant barred from invoking equitable discretion against specific performance.
variations: The forum differs: special leave under Article 136, High Court writ jurisdiction, civil suit for specific performance, and an appeal.
The suppressed matter differs: interim orders, a prior final order, a prior suit and appeal, a lease or other document, or misstated facts and withheld evidence.
The authority relied on differs: Kensington, Hari Narain, Ramjas Foundation, the clean-hands principle in Spry's Equitable Remedies, or Rooke's Case on judicial discretion.
Some members add costs or invoke the inherent power to prevent abuse of process.
In the defendant-side specific performance case, the effect is that the defendants cannot resist specific performance on equitable grounds, rather than that relief is denied to them.

legal_question: Is a consent or compromise decree for eviction under rent-control legislation valid and executable, and not a nullity, where the court's satisfaction that a statutory ground for eviction exists can be inferred from the compromise, the pleadings and other material, or from the tenant's express or implied admissions?

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and compromise_or_consent_decree_for_eviction and lawful_compromise_under_order_23_rule_3 and (statutory_ground_for_eviction_shown_by_record_or_inferable or tenant_admitted_statutory_ground_expressly_or_impliedly)

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding is a suit or case for eviction of a tenant governed by a rent-control statute that restricts eviction to specified statutory grounds.
predicates.compromise_or_consent_decree_for_evictio: The eviction decree was passed on the parties' compromise or consent rather than after a contested adjudication.
predicates.lawful_compromise_under_order_23_rule_3: The compromise is lawful and does not violate the rent-control law, so the court may record it and decree it under Order 23 Rule 3 CPC.
predicates.statutory_ground_for_eviction_shown_by_r: The pleadings, evidence, compromise terms and other material before the court disclose, at least prima facie, a ground for eviction permitted by the statute, so the court's satisfaction can be inferred or presumed.
predicates.tenant_admitted_statutory_ground_express: The tenant, in the compromise or pleadings, clearly admitted facts (such as rent arrears, the landlord's bona fide need, or lack of alternative accommodation) constituting a statutory ground, expressly or by necessary implication, or unconditionally withdrew the defences to it.
predicates.compromise_eviction_decree_valid_and_enf: The compromise eviction decree is not a nullity and may be executed, subject to its own terms, such as any agreed time for vacating.

definition: A compromise eviction decree under rent-control law is not void merely for lack of an express finding on the statutory ground. It is valid and executable where the compromise is lawful and the record, including the tenant's express or implied admissions, shows that a statutory ground existed so that the court's satisfaction can be inferred or presumed.
exceptions_or_limits: Consent alone cannot confer power to evict where the statute restricts eviction; if no statutory ground is disclosed by the material or admissions, the decree is a nullity (Bahadur Singh, Kaushalya Devi and Ferozi Lal line, as distinguished by the members).
A compromise that violates the rent-control law is not lawful and must not be recorded.
Enforcement is subject to the compromise's own conditions, such as the agreed period before possession can be recovered.
Where the tenant genuinely disputes the ground or the standard rent and the compromise contains no admission, the inference of satisfaction may not be available.

common_material_facts: Landlord sued for eviction on a statutory ground, such as rent arrears, bona fide personal or business need, or lack of alternative accommodation.
Parties compromised, and the tenant admitted arrears or the claim for ejectment, or withdrew defences.
The decree was later resisted in execution as a nullity for want of a finding or material on the statutory ground.
The tenant often agreed to vacate or pay arrears by a later date and failed to do so.
statutes_and_provisions: Order 23 Rule 3 CPC
Section 58 of the Evidence Act
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, ss. 12(3)(a), 12(3)(b), 13(1)(g), 13(2)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, ss. 12(1)(a), 12(1)(f)
Section 10(1) and 10(3)(a)(i) of the rent-control statute in 1065009_1
K.K. Chari v. R.M. Seshadri; Nagindas Ramdas v. Dalpatram Ichharam; Roshan Lal v. Madan Lal; Nai Bahu v. Lala Ramnarayan
Distinguished: Bahadur Singh v. Muni Subrat Dass; Kaushalya Devi v. K.L. Bansal; Ferozi Lal Jain v. Man Mal
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 8 members uphold the compromise decree as valid and executable, not a nullity, because the court's satisfaction on a statutory ground is inferred or presumed from the material or admissions.
variations: The material supporting the ground differs: tenant's admission of arrears (4 members), landlord's unrebutted evidence and withdrawal of defences (1), pleadings read with the compromise on business need (2), and prima facie pleadings and record (1).
189872_2 states the general duty under Order 23 Rule 3 to record a lawful compromise, rather than applying it to a particular ground.
108728217_1 turns on enforcement after the tenant missed the agreed payment deadline.
96229_2 frames the point as a presumption of satisfaction arising from judicial admissions.

legal_question: Can a person who acquires an interest in the subject property during a pending suit, appeal or proceeding (a transferee pendente lite) be impleaded or substituted and heard to protect that interest, and on what conditions?

rule.if: pending_proceeding_concerning_property and interest_acquired_during_pendency and transferee_seeks_or_has_been_joined and transferee_has_substantial_direct_interest_that_may_be_affected

predicates.pending_proceeding_concerning_property: A suit, appeal, execution proceeding or similar proceeding concerning the property is pending when the transfer or acquisition occurs.
predicates.interest_acquired_during_pendency: The applicant acquired an interest in the disputed property by assignment, sale, creation or devolution after the proceeding began (for example, a court sale or a transfer after the decree while the appeal is pending).
predicates.transferee_seeks_or_has_been_joined: The transferee has applied to be impleaded, substituted or heard, or has already been impleaded, in the pending proceeding.
predicates.transferee_has_substantial_direct_intere: The transferee's interest is real, direct and more than colourable or peripheral, and the outcome of the proceeding may affect it or bind the transferee.
predicates.transferee_may_be_joined_and_heard_to_pr: The court may, and ordinarily should, add or substitute the transferee as a party and hear them to protect the acquired interest, subject to the court's discretion and without deciding the merits of the transfer.

definition: A transferee pendente lite who has a substantial, direct interest in property under litigation, and who will be affected or bound by the outcome, may ordinarily be impleaded or substituted and heard to protect that interest. The power rests on Order I Rule 10, Order XXII Rule 10 and Section 146 of the CPC, read with Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. Joinder is not a matter of absolute right.
exceptions_or_limits: Joinder is discretionary and not an absolute right. The interest must be substantial, direct and more than merely colourable, not peripheral.
Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act leaves the transfer valid but subject to the rights decided in the suit, and the transferee remains bound by the decree.
Joinder or a hearing does not decide the validity of the transfer, the alleged fraud or the transferee's good faith. Those matters may remain open.
Being heard does not entitle the transferee to succeed on the merits. For example, a court-fee objection gives no right to succeed merely because the fee was deficient.
An unimpleaded transferee may appeal only with the appellate court's leave.
The result may differ where the parties' knowledge of a restraint order is undisputed (as the distinction from Surjit Singh suggests).

common_material_facts: Property was transferred or an interest acquired while a suit, appeal or execution proceeding concerning it was pending.
The transferee applied to be impleaded or substituted, or had already been impleaded.
The decree or outcome could affect or bind the transferee's title.
In several members the transferor had ceased to contest or no longer had an interest.
statutes_and_provisions: Order I Rule 10(2) CPC
Order XXII Rule 10 CPC
Section 146 CPC
Section 52 Transfer of Property Act
Order XXIII Rule 1-A CPC
Sections 12(2) and 12(4)(a) Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 8 members the transferee was allowed to be joined or heard: 5 were joined, impleaded or substituted, 1 was permitted to be heard on a withdrawal application, 1 was heard to raise a court-fee objection, and 1 was held entitled to apply and be heard, with leave to appeal.
variations: The procedural vehicle differs: Order I Rule 10, Order XXII Rule 10, Section 146 CPC, or inherent powers.
The stage differs: trial suit, first or second appeal, execution appeal, or a withdrawal application.

Some members treat joinder as a matter of ordinary course (1066164_2, 854247_1). Others make it conditional on a disputed good-faith or restraint-order question, or on a non-colourable claim (1869954_1, 1965204_2).
One member is limited to a right to be heard on withdrawal of the suit (786763_2).
One member is limited to a statutory court-fee objection (91564105_1).
Some members involve a court-sale purchaser or a transferee with notice of a prior agreement (1965204_2, 66021170_2).

legal_question: In a statutory income-tax reference, is the High Court (or the higher court on appeal) confined to answering the referred legal questions on the facts found by the Tribunal, so that it cannot go behind those findings or reassess or investigate facts, unless a question challenging their validity has been properly referred?

predicates.income_tax_reference_proceeding: The court is exercising its advisory jurisdiction on a reference (or an appeal from a reference decision) under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
predicates.tribunal_made_factual_findings: The Tribunal, as the final fact-finding authority, found or affirmed the facts relevant to the referred question.
predicates.referred_question_challenging_validity_o: A question has been properly referred to the court challenging the Tribunal's findings, for example as unsupported by evidence or as raising a point not decided by the Tribunal.
predicates.reference_court_must_decide_on_tribunal_: The court must answer the referred legal question on the facts as found by the Tribunal. It may not reject or reappraise those findings, substitute its own, direct a fresh factual investigation, or decide unreferred issues.

definition: In a reference under the Income-tax Act, 1922, the court acts in an advisory capacity and decides only the referred legal questions on the facts found by the Tribunal. It cannot go behind or reappraise those findings, order fresh fact investigation, or decide unreferred matters, unless the validity of the findings is properly raised by a referred question.
exceptions_or_limits: The Tribunal's findings can be examined if a question challenging them (for example as based on no evidence) has been properly referred.
A supplementary statement of case may be called for if the Tribunal's findings are incomplete and the court cannot answer the referred question.
A court does not err by relying on facts admitted between the parties or already found by the income-tax authorities.
A court need not order a reference where the answer is apparent from the Tribunal's supported findings.
The court may decide only questions referred to it or arising out of the Tribunal's order; arguments not raised before the Tribunal and not referred cannot be decided.

common_material_facts: The Tribunal had made findings of fact on the matter underlying the referred question.
A party, or the High Court itself, sought to reappraise, contradict or supplement those findings, or to raise a new point, in the reference.
No question challenging the findings as unsupported by evidence had been referred.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Section 66(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Section 66A(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 6 of 8 members the court held that the reference court was bound by the Tribunal's findings and set aside or refused any going behind them. In 2 of 8 members (1132580_2 and 1068493_2) the court refused to direct a reference or a fresh investigation. One member (1403810_3) barred decision of an unreferred issue. One member (1448253_1) held that reliance on admitted or found facts does not vitiate the decision.
variations: Some members concern the High Court overreaching by reappraising the evidence or substituting its own findings (1421992_1, 1766505_2, 1866696_2).
Some concern a party's attempt to challenge findings before the higher court (1716978_2) or to seek fresh investigation (1068493_2).
One concerns the scope of questions the court may decide (1403810_3).
One concerns refusal to call for a reference where the answer is apparent (1132580_2).
One is a permissive holding that reliance on admitted facts is not vitiating (1448253_1).

legal_question: When can time spent prosecuting an earlier civil or execution proceeding, diligently and in good faith, be excluded under Section 14 of the Limitation Act when computing limitation for a later suit on the same matter or cause of action?

rule.if: later_proceeding_follows_prior_civil_or_execution_proceeding and prior_and_later_proceedings_same_matter_or_cause_of_action and prior_proceeding_prosecuted_in_good_faith_and_with_due_diligence and prior_court_unable_to_entertain_or_decide_for_jurisdictional_or_like_defect and not prior_proceeding_failed_on_merits

predicates.later_proceeding_follows_prior_civil_or_: The later suit or proceeding was brought after an earlier civil proceeding, including an execution proceeding, had failed or ended.
predicates.prior_and_later_proceedings_same_matter_: The earlier and later proceedings are founded on the same cause of action or concern the same matter in issue.
predicates.prior_proceeding_prosecuted_in_good_fait: The earlier proceeding was prosecuted honestly and diligently, without negligence or want of good faith.
predicates.prior_court_unable_to_entertain_or_decid: The court in the earlier proceeding could not entertain it or decide it on the merits because of a defect of jurisdiction (e.g. pecuniary or subject-matter) or another cause of a like nature, read ejusdem generis. Examples are a wrong procedural forum, a statutory bar, or an inability to determine rights in summary proceedings.
predicates.prior_proceeding_failed_on_merits: The earlier proceeding was decided against the claimant on the merits, or was dismissed as premature by a court able to entertain it, and not because of a preliminary defect.
predicates.time_spent_in_prior_proceeding_excluded_: The time spent in the earlier proceeding is excluded when computing the limitation period for the later suit.

definition: Section 14 of the Limitation Act excludes the time spent prosecuting an earlier civil or execution proceeding in good faith and with due diligence. The earlier proceeding must be on the same cause of action or matter, and must have failed because the court could not entertain it for a jurisdictional defect or a cause of like nature. The exclusion is construed liberally. It is denied where the earlier proceeding failed on the merits, was dismissed as premature by a court able to entertain it, or rested on a different cause of action.
exceptions_or_limits: No exclusion if the earlier court could entertain the proceeding and dismissed it on the merits or as premature.
No exclusion if the later proceeding is founded on a different cause of action or matter in issue.
Good faith and due diligence must be shown, as the conditions in the section are cumulative.
'Other cause of a like nature' is read ejusdem generis with defect of jurisdiction. It must be a preliminary defect that prevents the court from entertaining or deciding the proceeding.

Where the court in fact entertained the proceeding and the litigant was not cautioned about its maintainability, a like-nature defect may still be found if the court could not determine the rights in that proceeding.

common_material_facts: An earlier civil or execution proceeding was prosecuted and failed before the later suit was filed.
The earlier proceeding failed for a defect of forum, procedure, jurisdiction or a statutory bar, or alternatively on the merits or as premature.
Good faith and due diligence in the earlier proceeding were found or assumed.
The later suit rested on the same or a different cause of action.
statutes_and_provisions: Limitation Act, 1908, Section 14(1)
Limitation Act, 1963, Section 14(1) and Explanation (C)
Limitation Act, Article 117 (suit on foreign decree)
Limitation Act, Article 109 (alienation by father)
Limitation Act, Article 11A
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 21 Rules 97–103
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Exclusion was allowed in 6 of 8 members (107557078_2, 1082212_1, 1341810_1, 1795292_2, 307289_1, 437299_4). It was denied in 2 (1475334_2, 750958_1), where the earlier court could entertain the case and the failure was premature or on the merits, or the cause of action differed.
variations: Many members involve failed execution proceedings, while others involve suits filed in a court lacking pecuniary jurisdiction or in a money suit that could not grant the relief.
1341810_1 turns on a liberal reading of 'cause of like nature' and an effective decree later set aside, with a concurring view on a fresh cause of action.
1082212_1 involves a revision where the court could not decide the rights, and distinguishes a case where the litigant was warned that the appeal was not maintainable.
437299_4 involves a statutory obstacle to sale and is reasoned more briefly.
The denial cases differ in their basis: 1475334_2 turns on a premature dismissal and a different cause of action, 750958_1 on a merits failure and a different matter in issue.

legal_question: In a contract for the sale of immovable property, is time presumed not to be of the essence, and what must be shown to displace that presumption or to establish that a party failed to act within a reasonable time?

rule.if: immovable_property_sale_contract and not unmistakable_time_essential_term and not strong_circumstances_showing_time_essential

predicates.immovable_property_sale_contract: The dispute concerns an agreement to sell immovable property (land or buildings).
predicates.unmistakable_time_essential_term: The contract expressly and unequivocally states that time is of the essence, or its terms clearly show that intention.
predicates.strong_circumstances_showing_time_essent: The contract's terms, the nature of the property and the surrounding circumstances are strong enough to show the parties intended time to be essential.
predicates.time_is_not_essential_but_performance_is: Time is not of the essence, and a fixed date, penalty clause or deadline does not alone change that. The party seeking enforcement must still act within a reasonable time judged on all circumstances, and delay alone is not default unless the other side has given notice requiring completion within a reasonable time.

definition: In a contract for the sale of immovable property, time is presumed not to be of the essence. Fixing a period or including a penalty does not displace the presumption; only unequivocal language or sufficiently strong circumstances do. Even where time is not essential, the parties must perform within a reasonable time assessed from the contract and circumstances, and delay alone is not default without a reasonable-time notice.
exceptions_or_limits: The presumption is displaced where the contract uses unequivocal language, or where its terms, the nature of the property and the surrounding circumstances show the parties intended time to be essential (e.g. 1757550_1, where the payment deadline was held essential).
A court should not hold time essential where no party pleaded or argued it and the contract does not unmistakably say so.
Even where time is not essential, a purchaser who delays beyond a reasonable time, judged in context, may be refused specific performance (580446_2).
The notice requirement for converting delay into default applies where time was not originally essential (1160146_2).
945911_4 did not decide whether time was essential on its facts; it only required applying the Constitution Bench test.

common_material_facts: Agreement to sell immovable property with a stipulated completion, payment or performance period
Contract does not expressly state that time is of the essence
Specific performance sought and delay or timing of performance in dispute
Penalty, forfeiture or deadline clauses relied on to argue that time was essential
statutes_and_provisions: Section 55, Contract Act, 1872
Section 20, Specific Relief Act, 1963
Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani
K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan
Gomathinayagam Pillai v. Palaniswami Nadar
Govind Prasad Chaturvedi v. Hari Dutt Shastri
Jamshed Khodaram Irani v. Burjorji Dhunjibhai
Stickney v. Keeble
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Time is held not essential in 4 of 8 issues (1108197_1, 1160146_1, 1884106_2, and the presumption in 945911_4). Time is held essential in 1 (1757550_1). The remaining issues hold that a reasonable-time requirement or notice rule still operates: one finds the buyer acted in time (215897_2), one finds the purchaser's delay unreasonable (580446_2), and one holds delay alone is not default without notice (1160146_2).
variations: Some members decide whether time is essential (1108197_1, 1160146_1, 1757550_1, 1884106_2); others address the consequences of time not being essential (1160146_2, 215897_2, 580446_2).
1757550_1 is the only member finding the presumption displaced, relying on emphatic wording and the sequence of obligations.
215897_2 and 580446_2 apply the reasonable-time standard with opposite results depending on the buyer's promptness.
945911_4 is procedural: it remands the test without ruling on the merits.
1884106_2 adds a pleading point: time cannot be held essential if not pleaded or tried.

legal_question: When does an appellate court sustain a conviction for attempted murder under Section 307 IPC, and when must it reduce or alter the conviction to a lesser offence (such as hurt or grievous hurt by a dangerous weapon) or decline to convict, depending on whether intention or knowledge to cause death is established from the weapon, the injury, the part of the body targeted and the surrounding circumstances?

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_attempted_murder: The matter is an appeal against a conviction (or an acquittal) on a charge of attempt to murder under Section 307 IPC.
predicates.intention_or_knowledge_to_cause_death_es: On all the circumstances (weapon used, manner of use, body part targeted, nature and severity of injuries, motive, credible evidence), the intention or knowledge necessary to constitute murder is established beyond reasonable doubt.
predicates.overt_act_in_execution_of_that_intention: Credible evidence identifies the accused as having committed an act in furtherance of the murderous intention.
predicates.attempted_murder_conviction_upheld: The conviction under Section 307 IPC is sustained, although the sentence may still be reduced.

definition: A Section 307 IPC conviction stands where the intention or knowledge required for murder is inferred from the circumstances (weapon, body part, severity of injury) and an overt act by the identified accused is proved. Where that intention is not established, or the accused is not tied to the grievous injury, the conviction is altered to a lesser offence such as Section 324 or 326 IPC, or an acquittal is not disturbed.
exceptions_or_limits: If death intent is not established but a grievous injury was caused by a dangerous weapon, the conviction is altered to grievous hurt by a dangerous weapon (Section 326 IPC).

If death intent is not established and the injury is simple but the weapon is one likely to cause death, the conviction is altered to hurt by a dangerous weapon (Section 324 IPC). Abetment is likewise reduced where instigation to kill is not established.
If the grievous injury cannot be attributed to the accused, the conviction is limited to simple hurt with a sharp weapon.
If the fight was sudden and reciprocal, the blunt side of the weapon was used and there was no motive, the attempt-to-murder charge fails.
A court may uphold the conviction and still reduce the sentence in the circumstances; the members give little reasoning for such reductions.
A fatal or death-capable injury is not essential for Section 307 IPC; intention is the key requirement.

common_material_facts: Assault with a dangerous or sharp weapon (spear, farasa, pharsi, sharp-edged weapon) on the victim
Appeal against a Section 307 IPC conviction (or acquittal) in which the injury's severity and the weapon are weighed
Medical evidence classifying injuries as simple or grievous
Injured eyewitnesses or the surviving victim identifying the accused
