statutes_and_provisions: Section 307 IPC
Section 324 IPC
Section 326 IPC
Section 109 IPC
Section 34 IPC
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of 8 issues, 3 uphold Section 307 IPC (115651329_1, 273583_3, 531211_5), the last two with a sentence reduction. 4 alter the conviction to a lesser offence (Section 324 or 326 IPC, or abetment thereof) with reduced sentences (1086707_3, _4, _5, 234452_4). 1 leaves an acquittal undisturbed (212245_1).
variations: Upheld cases rely on a vital body part, severe injuries and corroborated injured-witness evidence; the altered cases turn on absence of proven death intent, a simple injury, or non-attribution of the grievous injury.
1086707_5 concerns abetment (Section 109 IPC) and conflicting accounts of whether the instigation was to kill or to assault.
234452_4 turns on failure to attribute the grievous injury to the accused rather than on intention alone.
531211_5 and 273583_3 uphold the conviction but reduce the sentence with little or no stated reasoning.
212245_1 is an appeal against acquittal, resolved by finding no murderous intent.

legal_question: Can a party, by amending its pleading or changing its stand, withdraw or resile from a categorical admission or deliberate election on which the opposing party has relied or which would displace the opposing party's case?

predicates.litigant_made_clear_admission_or_deliber: The party made a categorical admission in a pleading, or a deliberate concession or election communicated in the proceedings.
predicates.litigant_later_seeks_inconsistent_positi: The party later applies to amend its pleading, or argues a position, that retracts or contradicts the earlier admission, concession or election.
predicates.withdrawal_would_displace_opponents_case: Allowing the withdrawal would remove the basis of the opposing party's case or cause prejudice to it that cannot be adequately compensated.
predicates.opponent_relied_on_it_or_benefit_obtaine: The opposing party relied on the admission or concession to its detriment, or the party obtained a procedural or other benefit from the court on the strength of the position it took.
predicates.amendment_merely_explains_or_clarifies_a: The proposed amendment only explains or clarifies the admission, or adds an alternative plea that is not mutually destructive, without erasing the admission.
predicates.litigant_is_held_to_admission_and_withdr: The court refuses the amendment or inconsistent stand and binds the party to its earlier admission, concession or election.

definition: A party is held to a categorical admission, concession or election made in litigation. It cannot withdraw it by amendment or approbate and reprobate where the withdrawal would displace the opponent's case or prejudice the opponent who relied on it, or where the party obtained a benefit on that basis. Explaining or clarifying an admission remains permissible.
exceptions_or_limits: An admission may be explained or clarified, and alternative pleas may be taken if they are not mutually destructive.
Amendments are generally considered liberally under Order VI Rule 17 CPC; the bar applies where the amendment wholly retracts a categorical admission or causes irretrievable prejudice.
Amendments to a written statement are treated more leniently than plaint amendments that substitute the cause of action.
A consequential amendment must answer the opponent's amendment; an unrelated new plea needs an independent amendment application.
The change-of-nature and distinct-cause-of-action ground for refusing amendments (the mortgage challenge case) is distinct from the admission and estoppel ground.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns refusal of an amendment that changes the nature of the suit and adds a distinct cause of action, with no admission or election involved.
It concerns the permissible scope of a consequential amendment responding to an opponent's amendment, not withdrawal of an admission or inconsistent stands.

common_material_facts: A party made a clear admission, concession or election in a pleading or in the proceedings.
The party later sought to amend the pleading or take a contrary stand.
The opposing party had relied on the admission or would lose its case if the admission were withdrawn.
The application often came after a long delay.
statutes_and_provisions: Order VI Rule 17 CPC
Section 58 Evidence Act
Order VIII Rule 5 CPC
Order XII Rule 6 CPC
Order XV Rule 1 CPC
Order VI Rule 7 CPC
Doctrine of election, estoppel, and the rule against approbating and reprobating
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In the six covered members the party was held to its admission, concession or election, and the amendment or inconsistent stand was refused. Modi Spinning is the main authority, and Akshaya Restaurant was treated as per incuriam. The two outliers also end in refusal of the amendment, but on different grounds.
variations: Some members rest on pleading amendment under Order VI Rule 17, others on estoppel or election outside amendment (the licensee and the government concession).
Some stress irretrievable prejudice to the opponent, others stress reliance or benefit obtained.
The plaint amendment case adds a change in the nature of the claim and the time bar.
The authorship challenge to the written statement in one member was rejected on inquiry.

split_suggestion: Keep the six members on admission, concession and election together. Treat 129198577_1 (change in nature of suit and distinct cause of action) and 1381144_7 (scope of consequential amendment) as separate amendment-scope groups. The estoppel members (1124455_3, 1933595_2) could be a sub-cluster apart from the pleading-amendment members.

legal_question: When may the Supreme Court exercise, or decline to exercise, its discretionary appellate jurisdiction under Article 136, including where an appeal comes up on a defective or limited certificate or where an error is found in the decision below?

predicates.supreme_court_appeal_within_article_136_: The matter is before the Supreme Court under its discretionary special-leave or special appellate jurisdiction, including after special leave has been granted.
predicates.circumstances_do_not_warrant_interferenc: On the facts (for example delay, long possession, finality, disproportionate costs, small stakes, or laches), the case does not present exceptional circumstances or grave injustice calling for appellate intervention.
predicates.decision_below_substantially_just: The decision under appeal is eminently just in its result.
predicates.supreme_court_may_decline_interference_e: The Supreme Court may, in its discretion, refuse to interfere and dismiss the appeal or leave the order undisturbed, even if it finds a legal error or doubts the lower court's power.

definition: The Supreme Court's power under Article 136 is discretionary and continues after special leave is granted. It may decline to interfere, even where the decision below is legally erroneous, if the result is just or the circumstances (delay, equities, costs, finality) do not warrant intervention.
exceptions_or_limits: The power is exercised sparingly; intervention is generally warranted where exceptional circumstances and substantial and grave injustice are shown.

A defective certificate (for example, one without reasons, or one that is invalid) does not bar the Court from hearing the matter as a special-leave appeal where the questions or legal errors warrant consideration.
Where a certificate is valid under Article 133, the Court's review is not confined to the questions in the certificate; this concerns the scope of the appeal, not the discretion to decline.
Some members rest on case-specific equities and do not state a general test.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns treating an unreasoned High Court certificate appeal as a special-leave appeal. It is about the route to jurisdiction, not declining interference.
Concerns the scope of review under a valid Article 133 certificate, not the discretion to decline relief.
Concerns whether the Court may fall back on Article 136 after an invalid certificate, and here the Court chose to entertain the matter, not to decline.

common_material_facts: Appeal reached the Supreme Court under Article 136 or a certificate route.
The Court found, or assumed, an error or irregularity in the decision below.
Equitable factors such as delay, long possession, finality of the decree, small amounts or disproportionate costs weighed against interference.
statutes_and_provisions: Constitution of India, Article 136
Constitution of India, Articles 133 and 134(1)(c)
Constitution of India, Article 142
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 6 Rule 17
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of 8 members, 5 decline interference and dismiss the appeal or leave the order undisturbed, despite errors in some; 3 concern certificate-route questions, where the Court retains or extends its jurisdiction (hearing the appeal as special leave, reviewing beyond the certificate questions, or considering Article 136 after an invalid certificate).
variations: Some members decline because the decision below is just, others because of delay or equities, and others because of costs and small stakes.
Some members decline after granting special leave, and others at the stage of the amendment application.
The certificate-based members address the Court's jurisdiction and the scope of the appeal rather than refusal of relief.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) discretionary refusal of relief under Article 136 despite error (1155131_3, 1496338_4, 1939821_2, 326572_2, 477485_4) and (b) certificate-route jurisdiction and scope (1534105_4, 388201_1, 808611_2).

legal_question: Under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, can a court condone a substantial or inordinate delay in filing an appeal, or in applying to substitute legal representatives, when the applicant knew of the adverse decision or the relevant event and the explanation is inadequate, implausible, false, or shows negligence or want of diligence?

rule.if: delay_condonation_sought and substantial_or_inordinate_delay and (applicant_had_knowledge_of_proceedings_or_event or applicant_had_capacity_to_act) and (no_adequate_explanation_for_material_period or explanation_false_or_implausible or applicant_negligent_or_lacked_diligence)

predicates.delay_condonation_sought: The applicant asks the court to excuse a delay in filing an appeal, or in applying to bring legal representatives on record or set aside abatement, under Section 5 of the Limitation Act or an analogous provision.
predicates.substantial_or_inordinate_delay: The delay is long or inordinate, not merely short or technical.
predicates.applicant_had_knowledge_of_proceedings_o: The applicant knew, or on the record had reason to know, of the proceedings, the adverse decision, or the death of a party.
predicates.applicant_had_capacity_to_act: The applicant had the means, institutional legal machinery, counsel or help needed to act on time (for example a legal department, panel lawyers, or an assisting relative).
predicates.no_adequate_explanation_for_material_per: The explanation leaves a material part of the delay unexplained, or relies on routine administrative process or counsel's inaction without showing diligent follow-up.
predicates.explanation_false_or_implausible: The account given for the delay is inconsistent, contradicted by the record, or found untrue.
predicates.applicant_negligent_or_lacked_diligence: The applicant's conduct shows negligence, inaction, lack of bona fides or want of due diligence in pursuing the matter.
predicates.sufficient_cause_not_shown_and_delay_not: The court holds that sufficient cause is not established and refuses to condone the delay; a contrary condonation order is set aside, and the appeal or substitution application fails as time-barred.

definition: Delay is condoned under Section 5 only on sufficient cause. Where the delay is substantial and the applicant, knowing of the decision or event and able to act, offers no adequate explanation, a false or implausible one, or shows negligence, the court refuses condonation. A liberal, justice-oriented approach and latitude for the State do not cure unexplained delay or lack of bona fides, especially where the opposing party's rights have accrued.
exceptions_or_limits: Courts may take a liberal, justice-oriented approach where sufficient cause is actually shown and no negligence, inaction or lack of bona fides is attributable.
Shorter delays are treated more liberally than inordinate ones; there is no hard-and-fast rule and each case turns on its own facts.
Some latitude may be given to the State for its collective decision-making and administrative processes, but not for implausible or false explanations or unexplained gaps.
Condonation cannot rest on equitable grounds, the merits of the appeal, or the imposition of costs alone when no sufficient cause is shown.
Where a substitution application is refused as time-barred, the related application to bring legal representatives on record does not survive.

common_material_facts: Long delay (hundreds to thousands of days) in filing an appeal or in applying for substitution of legal representatives
Applicant, often a State body, statutory authority or university, had knowledge of the proceedings or of the adverse decision or death
Explanation blamed counsel, officials, administrative processes, illness or ignorance, and was gapped, inconsistent or contradicted by the record
Opposing party had acquired rights through the decree or abatement
In several cases a lower court or High Court had condoned the delay and the Supreme Court reversed it
statutes_and_provisions: Section 5, Limitation Act, 1963
Order XXII Rules 3 and 9, CPC (abatement and substitution)
Order 41 Rule 3A, CPC
Order XVI Rule 14, Supreme Court Rules, 1950
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 8 members refuse condonation for want of sufficient cause. In 4 of them (1264971_1, 57092922_1, 912526_1 and, in effect, the appeal-stage reversals) the Supreme Court set aside a High Court condonation order; in the others it upheld a refusal or itself dismissed the application.
variations: Appeals from decrees (second appeal, first appeal, intra-court appeal) versus substitution or abatement applications
Applicants were private parties (heirs, an ex-parte decree defendant) or institutional litigants (statutory authority, university, State officials)
Reasons for refusal vary: false account, inconsistent account, unexplained gap, counsel-blame without follow-up, or unexplained delay after institutional approval
Some members stress the stricter standard for inordinate delay, others the accrued right of the opposing party, and others the want of bona fides
Members differ on whether hardship (poverty, illiteracy, illness) is accepted; here it was insufficient on the facts

legal_question: Where land-ceiling (or similar land-tenure) legislation has been repealed or superseded, does statutory vesting alone, without actual possession having been lawfully taken by the State before the repeal, suffice to defeat the holder's claim or keep the proceedings alive?

predicates.urban_land_ceiling_proceeding_affected_b: The dispute concerns land declared or treated as excess/surplus under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, and the Repeal Act of 1999 had taken effect in the State while the matter was pending or unresolved.
predicates.actual_possession_lawfully_taken_by_stat: Before the repeal took effect, the State or an authorised person actually took possession, by voluntary surrender, peaceful delivery after notice, or forcible taking after notice and non-compliance, as established on the record.
predicates.state_cannot_rely_on_deemed_vesting_and_: Deemed or de jure vesting, notices or later transfer receipts do not preserve the proceedings; they abate and the holder keeps the land under the Repeal Act's saving.

definition: Under the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976 and the Repeal Act, 1999, vesting of excess land under Section 10(3) passes title and de jure possession but not de facto possession. Unless the State proves that possession was actually and lawfully taken before the repeal, pending proceedings abate and the holder keeps the land. Later administrative receipts or omitted-land claims do not cure this.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the record establishes that possession was voluntarily surrendered, peacefully delivered after notice, or forcibly taken after notice before repeal.
The saving proviso to Section 4 of the Repeal Act applies only to proceedings under specified sections concerning land whose possession has been taken by the State or an authorised person.
The State cannot raise a belated jurisdictional objection that the land was State land where the land never vested in the State and the proceedings were initiated on a different footing.
The tenure-abolition decree issue is a separate point: an existing possession decree remains executable unless the statute expressly bars execution, and the holder keeps a conditional regrant right.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the Section 19 State-land exclusion, and whether the State could disregard land-ceiling proceedings on a belated vesting argument. It does not concern possession and repeal.
It concerns the enforceability of a possession decree after abolition of hereditary tenure under a regrant scheme. It is not a land-ceiling or repeal case.

common_material_facts: Land was declared excess or surplus and was treated as vested in the government under Section 10(3).
Notices were issued to surrender possession, but the record showed no actual peaceful or forcible taking of possession.
The Repeal Act of 1999 took effect while proceedings were pending or unresolved.
The State conceded or did not show that it had taken possession, or relied only on later receipts or panchnamas.
statutes_and_provisions: Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976, Sections 8, 9, 10(1), 10(3), 10(5), 10(6) and 19
Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Repeal Act, 1999, Sections 2, 3(1)(a) and 4
State of U.P. v. Hari Ram (2013) 4 SCC 280
Pt. Madan Swaroop Shrotiya Public Charitable Trust v. State of U.P., Ghasitey Lal Sahu, Mukarram Ali Khan and Sulochana Chandrakant Galande
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In six of eight members, the lack of proven actual possession before repeal led to abatement or quashing of the proceedings, or to the holder retaining the land. The other two members turn on different points.
variations: Some members frame the result as the holder retaining the land (115941239_1, 186418602_1). Others frame it as abatement of proceedings (133345714_1, 1902516_1, 408123_2) or quashing of notices (186418602_2).
One member adds that the land was omitted from the statutory statements and notices (115941239_1).
One member holds that a later possession receipt cannot cure the absence of possession before repeal (186418602_2).
Some members rely on Hari Ram, while others rely on the Madan Swaroop line of cases, and one relies on no precedent (1902516_1).

split_suggestion: Keep the six repeal and possession members as one cluster. Move 181804_3 (Section 19 State-land exclusion and belated jurisdictional objection) and 410681_1 (executability of a possession decree after abolition of hereditary tenure) into separate clusters.

legal_question: Does a law governing property, housing, rent or premises violate the Article 14 guarantee of equality merely because it treats different categories of property, premises, tenants or buildings differently, where the categories rest on an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the law's object?

predicates.equality_challenge_to_property_or_housin: The law, whether a pre-emption, rent-control, housing, premises-regulation or housing-levy law, is challenged as violating the constitutional guarantee of equality.
predicates.law_treats_property_or_premises_categori: The law exempts, includes, prices or applies different procedures to different categories of property, premises, buildings or tenants.
predicates.categories_differ_in_use_occupancy_owner: The categories differ in a real and substantial way, such as use, occupancy, ownership, profit motive, age of construction or procedural nature, and that difference bears on the law's purpose.
predicates.classification_has_rational_relation_to_: The differentia has a rational nexus to the object the law seeks to achieve, including a legislature's choice to address a feasible part of a problem.
predicates.challenger_shows_unequal_treatment_of_si: The challenger has established that persons or things similarly situated in relation to the law's purpose are treated unequally, for example because the comparison group is comparable or the criteria differ materially.
predicates.classification_does_not_violate_article_: The classification or differential treatment is upheld as not discriminatory under Article 14.

definition: Differential treatment of categories of property, premises, buildings or tenants does not violate Article 14 where the categories are distinct on an intelligible basis (use, occupancy, ownership, profit motive, construction period or procedure) that rationally relates to the law's object. A challenger must show that similarly situated persons are treated unequally; comparison with a dissimilar group does not suffice.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not protect a classification whose differentia has no rational connection to the law's object.
The challenger can succeed by showing that the comparison group is truly similarly situated, for example comparable tenancies, or that persons in the same class are treated unequally.
In the rent-fixation and pricing members, the result depended on substantially similar criteria or unequal treatment not being shown within the comparable class.
Differences in actual condition or individual benefit within a class do not alone establish discrimination (taxing law member).
Courts give wide latitude to legislatures in fiscal and economic classification and to executives in price fixation, absent patent hostile discrimination.

common_material_facts: A statute classifies or exempts categories of property, premises or buildings, such as agricultural or public-use premises, public housing, newer buildings, owner-occupied or non-residential buildings, or particular projects.
The challenger compares the treated class with a privately held, older, or otherwise differently placed class.
The legislature or authority had a stated purpose, such as housing shortage, building safety, preventing brothels near public places, or reducing housing costs for lower-income groups.
The comparison group differed in profit motive, ownership, occupancy, regulatory regime, or procedure.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 14 of the Constitution
Section 18, Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956 (and sections 3 and 7)
Section 4, Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Section 3-A, Bombay Housing Board Act (1951 amendment)
Urban-property pre-emption law exempting agricultural and public-resort property
Housing-safety levy legislation and rent-fixation provisions for new premises
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 8 members uphold the classification as consistent with Article 14, holding the categories distinct and rationally related to the law's purpose.
variations: Some members apply the classic two-part test of intelligible differentia and rational nexus (1300233_1, 152211_1, 152211_2, 790021_1).
Taxing-law members stress legislative latitude to tax some objects and not others (1728700_2, 1728700_3).
The pricing member relies on executive discretion in price fixation and on defining the comparable class by scheme, area, time and income group (1732064_2).
Some members turn on the challenger's failure of proof, such as no evidence of comparable tenancy or no unequal treatment within the class (152211_1, 1732064_2).
The rent-fixation and procedure members also rely on safeguards or substantial similarity of criteria (790021_1, 1300233_1).

legal_question: Where mining leases are granted under a statutory scheme (the MMDR Act and the Mineral Concession Rules, or equivalent state rules), must the authority decide applications only through the prescribed notification and criteria, so that extra-statutory considerations such as past investment, past State commitments, equity, or applications filed outside the prescribed notice cannot decide the grant?

predicates.mining_lease_grant_governed_by_statutory: The grant of a mining lease is regulated by a statute and rules (such as the MMDR Act and Mineral Concession Rules, or state minor-mineral rules) prescribing the procedure and criteria for selecting applicants.
predicates.authority_relies_on_extra_statutory_basi: The State or authority prefers or recommends an applicant on a ground outside the statutory criteria, such as past investment, captive use, a past State commitment, an applicant category, or equitable considerations, in place of the prescribed factors such as proposed investment.
predicates.application_filed_outside_prescribed_not: The application was filed before the required notification of the area, or under an earlier notice, rather than in response to the notification or fresh notice that the statute or a binding judgment requires.
predicates.extra_statutory_basis_or_non_compliant_a: The preference, recommendation or premature or old application cannot be sustained or considered, and the authority must decide the competing applications through the statutory notification process and criteria.

definition: Where a statute and rules govern the grant of mining leases, the State acts as a statutory delegate and must follow the prescribed notification procedure and criteria. Past investment, past commitments, equity, or applications made outside the required notification cannot displace them, and a recommendation or consideration contrary to the scheme is invalid.
exceptions_or_limits: Past investment and captive consumption were treated as relevant only in the distinct context of a second renewal under Section 8(3), not an initial grant under Section 11.
The first proviso to Section 11(2) applies to virgin areas, not to previously held areas governed by Rules 59 and 60.
A court direction to consider applications 'in accordance with law' does not itself authorise consideration of premature applications unless it expressly so directs.
The rule rests on a statutory scheme that actually governs the grant; where no such scheme applies, the conclusion may differ.

common_material_facts: Competing applications for mining leases over a notified or previously held area
The State or authority preferred applicants on grounds such as existing steel-plant investment, captive use or past commitments
Applications filed before the notification, or under an earlier notice, were sought to be considered
Equitable considerations or prior court directions were invoked to support the non-statutory preference or application
statutes_and_provisions: MMDR Act 1957, Sections 2, 8(3), 11(1)-(5)
Mineral Concession Rules 1960, Rules 35, 59 and 60
UP Minor Minerals (Concession) Rules 1963, Rule 72
Prem Nath Sharma v. State of U.P.; State of Assam v. Om Prakash Mehta; M.A. Tulloch; Kedar Lal v. Hari Lal
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 8 members hold that the statutory scheme controls. The non-statutory preference or recommendation is invalid (1220288_1, _5, _6, _7, 93595604_5), and applications filed outside the notification process are not entertained (1201771_3, 1220288_2, _3).
variations: Some members concern substantive selection criteria (past versus proposed investment, commitments, equity), while others concern procedural timing (premature or old applications).
One member concerns interpreting an earlier court direction, and one is a review proceeding.
One member arises under the UP Minor Minerals Rules, and the others under the MMDR Act and Mineral Concession Rules.

legal_question: Under sections 122 and 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, when is a gift of immovable property complete and valid, and does the donor's retention of possession, use or income during life affect that?

rule.if: gift_governed_by_transfer_of_property_act and immovable_property_gift and gift_formalities_satisfied and donee_accepted_during_donor_lifetime and gift_presently_effective_and_unconditional

predicates.gift_governed_by_transfer_of_property_ac: The validity of the gift is tested under sections 122 and 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, not under personal law or a fiscal statute.
predicates.immovable_property_gift: The subject of the gift is immovable property.
predicates.gift_formalities_satisfied: The gift is made by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses.
predicates.donee_accepted_during_donor_lifetime: The donee accepted the gift, expressly or by inference from conduct and circumstances, while the donor was alive and capable of giving.
predicates.gift_presently_effective_and_uncondition: The deed transfers ownership immediately and absolutely. It is not conditional on future events and is not postponed to take effect only on the donor's death.
predicates.gift_valid_and_complete_regardless_of_do: The gift is valid and complete even if the donor reserved possession, use or income for life, because delivery of possession is not required.

definition: A gift of immovable property made by a registered, signed and attested instrument, accepted by the donee in the donor's lifetime and presently and absolutely transferring ownership, is valid. The donor's reservation of lifetime possession, use or income does not invalidate it. A gift that is conditional, takes effect only on the donor's death, or lacks proved acceptance is incomplete and the donor may cancel it.
exceptions_or_limits: If acceptance is not proved, or the deed is conditional or limited until the donor's death, the gift stays incomplete and the donor can cancel it before death (1593210_1, 173119126_2).
Acceptance has no prescribed mode and may be inferred from delivery of the deed, possession, revenue entries or other conduct (39052800_2).
Gifts under Muhammadan law are governed by personal-law requirements, including delivery of actual or constructive possession, so the no-delivery rule does not apply to them.
Under the Estate Duty Act, 1953, a donor's continued occupation defeats exclusive possession and enjoyment by the donee, whatever the gift's validity under the Transfer of Property Act.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953 and whether the donor was excluded from possession and enjoyment. It is a fiscal question, not gift validity under the Transfer of Property Act.
An oral gift under Mohammedan law, where delivery of actual or constructive possession is essential. This is the opposite of the Transfer of Property Act position.
A gift under Muhammadan law that is incomplete without actual or constructive possession. It is governed by personal law, not sections 122 and 123 of the Transfer of Property Act.

common_material_facts: A gift of immovable property by a deed, with the donor reserving or retaining possession, use or income
Acceptance by the donee, proved or unproved, is the decisive factual issue
Dispute over whether the deed was conditional or postponed to the donor's death
Evidence of possession, rent collection, mutation or tax payment used to show acceptance or delivery
statutes_and_provisions: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, sections 122, 123, 6 and 129
Estate Duty Act, 1953, sections 5 and 10
Mulla's Principles of Mahomedan Law, sections 149, 150 and 152
Tyabji's Muslim Law, section 394
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 5 Transfer of Property Act members, 3 uphold the gift (retained enjoyment does not invalidate a registered, accepted, absolute gift) and 2 hold the gift incomplete and cancellable (conditional or death-postponed, with acceptance unproved). Both Muslim-law members hold the gift not established for want of possession. The estate-duty member finds the property liable because the donor was not excluded.
variations: The Transfer of Property Act requires no delivery of possession, whereas Muslim law requires it.
Retained possession is harmless to validity under the Transfer of Property Act but fatal for estate duty exclusion.
Acceptance is shown by recital in one case, by conduct and revenue records in another, and not proved in another.
Naramadaben is used both to distinguish conditional gifts and to support inference of acceptance.

split_suggestion: Keep the five Transfer of Property Act members (11608427_1, 1593210_1, 173119126_2, 173119126_3, 39052800_2) together. Treat the two Muslim-law possession-delivery members (59167167_2, 96681271_2) as a separate cluster. Treat the estate-duty member (1946226_1) as a separate cluster on exclusion of the donor.

legal_question: When a will describes a first beneficiary as owner (or otherwise appears to give an absolute gift) but, read as a whole, also provides for others to take after that beneficiary's death or restricts the first beneficiary's enjoyment, does the first beneficiary receive only a life estate, with the later gift taking effect?

predicates.will_construction_dispute: The dispute turns on interpreting the dispositions of a will to find the testator's intention.
predicates.first_beneficiary_described_as_owner_or_: The will calls the first beneficiary owner (e.g. malik) or makes a gift in terms that on their own would suggest an absolute estate.
predicates.will_read_as_whole_gives_property_to_oth: Other clauses of the will direct that the property pass to other persons (heirs, named beneficiaries, adopted son, etc.) after the first beneficiary's death or line of descent, or restrict the first beneficiary to lifetime income or bar alienation.
predicates.life_interest_reading_harmonises_disposi: Construing the first beneficiary's interest as a life estate allows every disposition in the will to take effect, or, where clauses are irreconcilable, the later clause prevails.
predicates.first_beneficiary_takes_only_life_estate: The first beneficiary acquires only a life interest and the persons designated to take afterwards receive the remainder as the will provides.

definition: A will is construed as a whole, and an expression of ownership or an apparently absolute gift to a first beneficiary does not confer an absolute estate where other provisions give the property to others after the beneficiary's death or restrict the beneficiary's enjoyment. The life-estate construction is preferred because it gives effect to every disposition, and the later clause prevails where clauses cannot be reconciled.
exceptions_or_limits: Words such as 'malik' or 'naslan bad naslan' ordinarily indicate full proprietary rights; they are displaced only where the will as a whole, its restrictions, or surrounding circumstances show a limited intention.
A restraint on alienation does not by itself cut down an absolute estate; it is relevant only as evidence that a limited estate was intended.
Later-clause priority applies only where the clauses are truly irreconcilable (Succession Act s.88); harmonisation is preferred first.

Two members (the adoption-contingency cases) concern whether an earlier remainder survives a later clause, not whether an owner-described beneficiary takes a life estate; the presumption against intestacy applies only on genuine ambiguity and cannot override plain words.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns whether an earlier remainder disposition survives a later clause under a different adoption contingency, not whether an ownership description is cut down to a life estate. The life estate was undisputed.
Same adoption-contingency issue as 154566_1: the question is whether an earlier remainder disposition remains operative, not whether an apparently absolute gift is cut down to a life estate.

common_material_facts: The will calls the first beneficiary (widow, daughter, wife, etc.) owner or uses language suggesting absolute rights.
Another clause gives the property to heirs, named persons or an adopted son after the first beneficiary's death.
Restrictions on transfer, limitation to income, or contrasting language used for absolute bequests elsewhere in the will.
In the adoption cases, a life tenant's remainder is stated in an earlier paragraph and not repeated in a later clause.
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Succession Act 1925, s.88 (last of irreconcilable clauses prevails)
Indian Succession Act 1865, ss.69, 72, 73, 82, 84 and illustrations
Ramchandra Shenoy v. Hilda Brite
Venkata Narasimha v. Parthasarthy
Re Edwards; Jones v. Jones (presumption against intestacy)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Six of eight members hold that the first beneficiary receives only a life estate and the later beneficiaries take the remainder. The other two hold that an earlier remainder disposition survives a later clause and the adopted son's claim as heir fails.
variations: Some members rely on harmonisation of dispositions, one on the last-clause rule (s.88), one on the 1865 Act sections, and others on general construction principles.
Restraint on alienation is treated as supporting a limited estate in some members and as absent or secondary in others.
The adoption-contingency members apply the presumption against intestacy only narrowly and do not turn on the owner-description point.

split_suggestion: Split into (a) cases where an owner-described or apparently absolute first gift is cut down to a life estate by a gift over (1230342_1, 1275064_2, 1468380_2, 231145_1, 575045_1, 685498_1) and (b) cases where an earlier remainder after a life estate survives a later clause in an adoption contingency (154566_1, 983794_1).

legal_question: When may a court or authority condone a delay (or a failure to meet a procedural time limit) in filing a proceeding, and on what showing of sufficient cause, such as bona fide pursuit of another remedy or an explained delay?

rule.if: late_filing_or_time_limit_exceeded and (sufficient_cause_shown_on_record or bona_fide_pursuit_of_other_remedy or exceptional_circumstances_for_delay) and forum_has_power_to_condone_or_limit_is_directory

predicates.late_filing_or_time_limit_exceeded: The application, petition, revision, review or written statement was filed after the prescribed or ordinary time limit.
predicates.sufficient_cause_shown_on_record: The material before the court, such as an explanation or condonation application showing steps taken, or the surrounding facts, shows sufficient cause for the delay.
predicates.bona_fide_pursuit_of_other_remedy: The party in good faith pursued another remedy in a court or forum (for example review, revision or a High Court proceeding) during the period of delay.
predicates.exceptional_circumstances_for_delay: Exceptional circumstances, supported by sufficient cause, prevented timely filing.
predicates.forum_has_power_to_condone_or_limit_is_d: The court or authority has a statutory or inherent discretion to condone the delay, or the time limit is directory and not an absolute bar.
predicates.delay_may_be_condoned_and_late_filing_ac: The court may condone the delay and treat or accept the late filing as if it were within time.

definition: Where a proceeding or pleading is filed late, the court or authority may condone the delay in its discretion if sufficient cause is shown. Sufficient cause includes bona fide pursuit of another remedy, an explanation of the steps taken, or exceptional circumstances. This holds even without a formal written condonation application, and where the time limit is directory rather than absolute.
exceptions_or_limits: Condonation is discretionary and not available as of right; the authority may require an application or affidavit explaining the delay.
Condonation does not extend the limitation period; it treats the late proceeding as if filed in time.
For written statements under Order VIII Rule 1 CPC, late filing is accepted only in exceptional cases where sufficient cause is shown.
Where the provision gives no power to condone and the limit is mandatory, the rule would not apply. None of the members addresses this.

common_material_facts: A filing was made after the prescribed or ordinary time limit.
The party had pursued another remedy (High Court proceedings, review, revision, enforcement proceedings) in the interim.
The party offered an explanation for the delay, such as steps taken within a department, counsel's advice or unavailability of records.
The party acted promptly once the obstacle was removed.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 5, Limitation Act, 1963
Order VIII Rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure
Rule 54 proviso, Mineral Concession Rules, 1960
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 8 members allow the delay to be condoned or the late filing to be accepted: 3 on written-statement or formal-application points, 3 on bona fide pursuit of another remedy, 1 on an explained delay, and 1 on the nature of condonation.
variations: Written-statement members (2) rest on the time limit being directory and on exceptional circumstances; the others rest on sufficient cause under Section 5 or an equivalent statutory power.
One member holds that no formal written condonation application is mandatory.
One member clarifies that condonation treats the filing as timely rather than extending limitation.
One member (30307115_3) gives no reasoning beyond the pursuit of review.
In one member (93595604_1) the sufficient cause was steps taken at various levels within a Ministry.

legal_question: Can a tax or statutory assessment demand, reassessment or amendment of an assessment list reach a period that ended, or became closed, before the relied-on amendment, power or notification took effect, or does it need express or necessarily implied authority to do so?

predicates.fiscal_demand_or_reassessment_proceeding: The dispute concerns a tax, assessment, contribution demand, or an attempt to amend or reopen an assessment.
predicates.demand_reaches_period_before_operative_a: The demand or reassessment covers a period that ended, or an assessment that was completed or time-barred, before the relied-on amendment, new power or notification took effect or was made.
predicates.statute_authorises_operation_for_that_ea: The governing statute, read in its scheme, expressly or by necessary implication allows the amendment or reassessment to operate on the earlier period. Examples are a retrospective provision, or a power to amend a list 'at any time' for the year it covers, exercised after notice and a hearing and within a reasonable time for property omitted by mistake.
predicates.demand_for_earlier_period_invalid: The demand, amendment or reopening cannot lawfully be enforced for the earlier period and is quashed or refused effect.

definition: A tax or assessment demand cannot rest on an amendment, new reassessment power, notification or late list-alteration to cover a period before it took effect, unless the statute expressly or by necessary implication allows that. Where the scheme permits later amendment of the list for its original year, as with omitted property under the Punjab Municipal Act, the amendment may operate on that earlier year.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the scheme allows an assessment list to be amended 'at any time', an omitted property can be added for the year the list covered. This holds if notice and a hearing are given and the power is exercised within a reasonable time.
Where the scheme makes the official year the unit of taxation and requires the alteration and authentication to occur within that year, a later alteration cannot reach an expired year.
A new reassessment power does not reopen completed assessments, and an amendment does not revive time-barred assessments, unless retrospectivity is express or necessarily implied.
The result turns on the construction of the specific statutory scheme. Different municipal Acts produce different results.

common_material_facts: The State or a municipality sought tax, assessment or contributions for a period preceding the amendment, notification or alteration relied on.
The relied-on amendment or power was not expressly retrospective.
Assessments were already completed, finalised, expired or time-barred.
In the two Punjab Municipal Act cases, property was omitted from a finalised list and the municipality gave notice before amending it.
statutes_and_provisions: Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, ss. 66, 67 and 68A
Maharashtra Municipalities Act, s. 123, and Bombay Municipal Boroughs Act, 1925, s. 82(3)
Andhra Pradesh Non-Agricultural Lands Assessment Act, ss. 2(j) and 12, and Act 28 of 1974
Estate Duty Act, 1953, ss. 56-65 (former s. 62 and substituted s. 59), as amended in 1958
Income Tax Act, 1961, ss. 149 and 150
Aided Schools Act, s. 6, and Punjab Municipal Act, ss. 52 and 59
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 6 of 8 members the demand or reopening for the earlier period was held invalid or unlawful: 1338177_1, 1968670_3, 214272_1, 319428_3, 619140_1 and 944301_5. In 2 of 8 (1233714_1 and 1343356_1, both under the Punjab Municipal Act) the municipality could amend a finalised list for its original year.
variations: The two permissive members rest on a statutory power to amend 'at any time', while the others rest on the absence of retrospective effect or on the structure of the taxing scheme.
1338177_1 turns on the official year being the unit of taxation, which requires authentication within the year. The other municipal members turn on the wording of the Act.
214272_1 and 619140_1 concern reopening completed or time-barred assessments. The rest concern demands for pre-amendment periods or amendments of lists.
1343356_1 adds that the amendment power must be exercised within a reasonable time, a point not decided there.

split_suggestion: The group can be kept as one, with the permissive Punjab Municipal Act list-amendment cases (1233714_1, 1343356_1) as a contrasting sub-group. Alternatively it can be split into: (a) non-retrospective amendments or notifications and pre-amendment demands (1968670_3, 319428_3, 944301_5, 214272_1, 619140_1); (b) amendment of finalised municipal assessment lists (1233714_1, 1343356_1, 1338177_1).

legal_question: When is an alleged adoption, relied on to displace natural succession, proved as a fact and valid, and what evidence (credible giving and taking, consistency, contemporaneous records, absence of suspicion) decides whether the claimant discharges the burden?

predicates.adoption_claimed_in_succession_or_proper: The adoption is asserted in a dispute over succession or property, so that it would displace the natural course of succession.
predicates.claimant_bears_burden_of_proving_fact_an: The party asserting the adoption must prove both that it occurred (factum) and that it was valid.
predicates.actual_giving_and_taking_proved_by_credi: Reliable, consistent and probable evidence (witness testimony, contemporaneous deed or other documents) shows the child was actually given by the natural parent or guardian and received by the adoptive parent.
predicates.unexplained_suspicious_circumstances_or_: The evidence is contradictory or unreliable, contemporaneous records are missing or conflict with the claim, or ceremony witnesses who should have been available are not produced and their absence is unexplained.
predicates.no_additional_rite_required_by_applicabl: No further ceremony (such as datta homam) is shown to be required by the law or custom governing the parties.
predicates.adoption_proved_and_valid: The court holds the adoption established in fact and valid in law.

definition: A person alleging an adoption that would displace natural succession must prove its fact and validity with evidence that is consistent, probable and free from suspicion. Proof of actual giving and taking (with no further rite required by custom or law) establishes the adoption, whereas inconsistent or unreliable evidence, missing or conflicting contemporaneous records, or unexplained absence of witnesses leaves it unproved.
exceptions_or_limits: If the evidence is inconsistent or unreliable, contemporaneous records are missing or contradict the claim, or available ceremony witnesses are unexplainably absent, the adoption is held not established.
A testator's statement of adoption in a will is admissible but not conclusive.
Consent or an executed deed alone does not suffice without actual giving and taking.
An additional ceremony such as datta homam is needed only where the applicable law or custom requires it.
A greater allowance for missing evidence may be made where a very long time has passed since the adoption.
Concurrent findings of fact rejecting the adoption are ordinarily not disturbed.
Where a formal adoption with giving and taking is shown, references to custom do not negate the intent to transfer the child (Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, s. 11(vi)).

common_material_facts: Adoption is pleaded to displace natural succession or alter inheritance of property.
The dispute turns on oral testimony about giving and taking and on contemporaneous documents such as adoption deeds, wills, letters, school records and sale deeds.
Courts examine consistency of witnesses, the availability of ceremony witnesses and any conflicting records.
In the successful claims, a deed executed at the time of the adoption corroborated credible evidence of giving and taking.
statutes_and_provisions: Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, 1956, s. 11(vi) (intent to transfer the child) and s. 4 (overriding effect over custom)
Mulla's Hindu Law, Art. 512 (grave and serious burden)
Case law on the burden of proof and the essentials of giving and taking (Kishori Lal v. Chaltibai, A. Raghavamma v. A. Chenchamma, Lakshman Singh v. Rupkanwar, and others)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of 8 issues, 4 hold the adoption not established or not proved (1301243_1, 1359532_1, 388201_4, 70561952_2) and 4 hold it proved, valid or its transfer intent established (151619456_3, 1579663_3, 723893_1, 839124_1).
variations: Failure cases rest on unreliable or contradictory testimony, missing or conflicting records, or unexplained absence of witnesses; success cases rest on credible proof of giving and taking with a contemporaneous deed.
Two members (151619456_3, 1579663_3) restore the trial court's finding of adoption, emphasising that adoption is proved like any other fact and that no datta homam was required by custom.
839124_1 concerns the statutory intent-to-transfer requirement and the effect of references to custom, not the evidentiary burden.
388201_4 rests on the fixed burden of proof and on deference to concurrent findings.

legal_question: When a claimant succeeds in a suit for possession of immovable property against a defendant who wrongfully occupies it, is the claimant entitled to mesne profits (past and, through an inquiry under Order XX Rule 12, future), and what limits apply to the period recoverable?

predicates.suit_for_possession_of_immovable_propert: The proceeding is a suit (or an appeal from a suit) for recovery of possession of immovable property, with a claim for mesne profits or damages for use and occupation.
predicates.claimant_entitled_to_possession: The claimant has established title or a right to possession and obtains a decree for possession, or would have obtained one but for supervening vesting.
predicates.defendant_wrongfully_in_occupation: The defendant occupied or continued to occupy the property wrongfully, including during the litigation or appeal.
predicates.claimant_entitled_to_mesne_profits_with_: The court may award mesne profits for the period of wrongful occupation and direct an inquiry under Order XX Rule 12 into profits until delivery of possession, subject to the three-year outer limit from the decree, the limitation period, and the date of any vesting in the State.

definition: A claimant who succeeds in a suit for possession against a wrongful occupant is entitled to mesne profits for the period of wrongful occupation. Under Order XX Rule 12, the court may direct an inquiry into future mesne profits until delivery of possession, even without a specific prayer for them. The period is limited by the three-year outer limit from the decree, by limitation, and by any vesting of the land in the State.
exceptions_or_limits: Future mesne profits under Order XX Rule 12(1)(c) run only until the earliest terminating event, including expiry of three years from the decree. A direction expressed as 'until delivery of possession' is construed in conformity with that limit (majority view in 1752222_2).

Where the land vests in the State (for example under land reform legislation), mesne profits are recoverable only up to the vesting date. Recovery also remains subject to limitation, so the pre-suit period is typically capped at three years.
Past (pre-suit) mesne profits must be specifically pleaded, valued and fee-paid. Future mesne profits need not be, and the court may order an inquiry into them in its discretion.
The decree may be conditional on payment of the appropriate court fee or stamp.
The wrongfulness of the occupation is a precondition. Without it, no mesne profits arise.

common_material_facts: Suit for recovery of possession of immovable property combined with a claim for mesne profits or damages for use and occupation
Defendant remained in occupation during the suit or appeal, sometimes under a stay, so the litigation was prolonged
Court directs an inquiry into mesne profits, with the final amount determined later by the trial court
In two members, land vested in the State under land reform legislation, which cut off the period of recovery
statutes_and_provisions: Order XX Rule 12(1)(c) and 12(2), Code of Civil Procedure
Order 7 Rules 1, 2 and 7, Code of Civil Procedure
Section 7(1), Court Fees Act
Section 6, Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 8 members uphold entitlement to mesne profits. About 5 direct an inquiry into future profits or profits from the suit. 2 limit the period because of State vesting. 1 limits the period by the three-year outer limit.
variations: Some members confirm the basic entitlement under Order XX Rule 12 (1419648_4, 1591216_5, 159739558_5).
One member holds that a direction for future profits is subject to the three-year outer limit (1752222_2).
One member allows an inquiry into future profits despite no specific prayer (199284_3).
Two members cut off mesne profits at vesting in the State (213143_3, 466878_2).
One member awards profits from suit filing where no pre-suit profits were claimed, conditional on stamp payment (844377_3).

legal_question: In a criminal trial, what burden does an accused bear when relying on a defence, exception or facts within his special knowledge, and does the accused's failure to prove or explain it relieve the prosecution of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt?

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The matter is a criminal trial or appeal in which the prosecution must prove the charge.
predicates.accused_relies_on_defence_or_exception_o: The accused pleads private defence or another general exception, offers an explanation, or the case involves a fact especially within the accused's knowledge.
predicates.accused_failed_to_prove_or_explain_or_le: The accused offered no explanation, did not raise the defence when questioned, did not call defence evidence, or could not fully prove the defence.
predicates.prosecution_has_proved_guilt_beyond_reas: The prosecution has, on its own evidence, established every element of the offence and every link in the chain beyond reasonable doubt.
predicates.prosecution_burden_remains_and_accused_n: The prosecution's onus to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt never shifts. Any burden on the accused is discharged by showing a probable version (preponderance of probabilities), which may rest on prosecution evidence. The accused's silence, weak defence or failure to produce evidence cannot fill gaps in the prosecution case.

definition: The prosecution must always prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt on its own evidence. An accused relying on private defence or another exception need only make it probable, using evidence from either side, and not prove it beyond reasonable doubt. A weak, false or absent defence, or a failure to explain facts in the accused's knowledge or to call evidence, cannot supply missing proof or serve as an additional link unless the prosecution has first established its case.
exceptions_or_limits: The accused's burden to bring the case within an exception (Evidence Act s.105) is real: where no factual basis is shown on a preponderance of probabilities, as with a fabricated injury or unproduced witnesses, the plea fails.

A false or absent explanation may be used only as an additional link, and only after the prosecution has proved the other links, which must point with reasonable definiteness to guilt and be proximate in time and situation.
Even if an exception is not established, the evidence may still raise a reasonable doubt about an element of the offence.
Section 106 of the Evidence Act does not relieve the prosecution of its burden.

common_material_facts: The accused pleaded private defence or offered an explanation for the incident or for entrusted money.
The accused did not call evidence, did not explain, or did not raise the defence under s.313 CrPC.
The prosecution relied on the weakness or falsity of the defence or on s.106 to fill gaps in its case.
The accused relied on prosecution witnesses, documents or circumstances to support the defence.
statutes_and_provisions: Evidence Act ss. 101, 105, 106, 3 and 5
Code of Criminal Procedure s. 313
Partap v. State of U.P.
Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration
State of U.P. v. Ram Swarup
Harbhajan Singh v. State of Punjab
Sharad Birdhichand Sarda
Sunil Kundu v. State of Jharkhand
Dahyabhai v. State of Gujarat
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 8 members hold that the prosecution's burden is beyond reasonable doubt and never shifts, and that the accused's burden is only a preponderance of probabilities. In 6 of 8, the accused's silence or defence weakness is held not to relieve the prosecution or support an adverse inference. In 1 of 8 (1344060_1), the private-defence plea failed for want of any factual basis.
variations: Some members concern the standard of the accused's burden (1344060_1, 1931444_1, 194959_1, 31903_1).
Others concern the impermissibility of adverse inference or of using s.106 or silence to fill gaps (170282973_2, 194959_2, 95032993_3, 8337733_2).
The outcome for the accused differs: in 1344060_1 the plea failed on the facts, while in 194959_1 and 8337733_2 the accused's version raised doubt and succeeded.
170282973_2 frames the point within circumstantial evidence and the Sharad Sarda 'additional link' test.

legal_question: Do parallel or earlier civil proceedings (suits, decrees, findings) bar, stay, or bind criminal proceedings arising from the same transaction or subject matter, and does the converse hold for criminal findings in civil proceedings?

predicates.civil_and_criminal_proceedings_concern_s: A civil proceeding (suit, recovery decree, probate, specific performance, cheque complaint) and a criminal complaint or investigation arise from the same transaction, document or dispute.
predicates.statute_or_binding_principle_makes_one_p: A statutory provision or legal principle (for example the limited relevance of previous judgments under the Evidence Act) makes the findings of one proceeding final or conclusive in the other.
predicates.civil_proceedings_do_not_bar_stay_or_bin: The civil suit, decree or findings neither bar, oust, quash or automatically stay the criminal proceeding, nor bind the criminal court; the two are decided independently on the evidence adduced in each, applying their different standards of proof.

definition: Civil and criminal proceedings on the same facts are separate and independent. A civil suit, decree or finding does not by itself bar, oust, stay or quash a criminal prosecution or investigation, and findings in one are not binding on the other because the standards of proof differ and each proceeding turns on its own evidence. Criminal findings likewise are not conclusive proof of a fact, such as an agreement, in a civil suit without the civil court's independent finding.
exceptions_or_limits: Whether to stay one proceeding pending the other depends on the facts and circumstances of each case; there is no general bar to simultaneous proceedings, but also no absolute rule against a stay.
A purely contractual breach is not automatically a criminal offence; criminal proceedings need allegations disclosing the ingredients of cheating, fraud or other offence.
Previous judgments may be relevant in limited circumstances under Sections 41 to 43 of the Evidence Act, but that relevance does not make them binding or conclusive.
Different considerations may apply to summary proceedings such as Section 145 CrPC possession proceedings, which were distinguished.
Criminal court findings cannot substitute for the civil court's own assessment, for example of the existence of an agreement for specific performance.

common_material_facts: The same transaction or document (loan scheme, agreement to sell, receipt, will, security cheques) is the subject of both civil and criminal proceedings.
The criminal side alleges forgery, cheating, fraud or breach of trust.
A civil suit, decree or appeal was pending or decided, and a party relied on it to defeat, stay or quash the criminal case (or the reverse).
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Evidence Act, 1872, Sections 13 and 41 to 43
Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
Section 145 CrPC (distinguished)
M.S. Sheriff v. State of Madras
K.G. Premshanker v. Inspector of Police
Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah
R. Venkatkrishnan v. CBI
S.W. Palanitkar v. State of Bihar
Anil Mahajan v. Bhor Industries
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 7 members hold that civil proceedings or findings do not bar, oust, stay or bind criminal proceedings (6 directly, 1 in the converse direction, where criminal findings are not conclusive in a civil suit). Quashing or stay orders resting on the civil case were set aside or held unsustainable.
variations: Direction of non-bindingness: most members concern civil findings not binding criminal courts, while 137193261_2 concerns criminal findings not conclusively proving an agreement in a civil suit.
Procedural posture differs: decrees not overriding a prosecution, quashing of a complaint, stay of an investigation, pending suit and ouster of jurisdiction.
Reasoning differs in detail: some rely on differing standards of proof, some on the independence of the proceedings, and one cites no authority.
Some members add that a civil-law contractual character does not preclude criminal liability if fraud or cheating is alleged.

legal_question: When is a killing committed after a quarrel or fight denied the benefit of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC (sudden fight), so that the offence remains murder, particularly where the accused used a weapon against an unarmed victim or otherwise took undue advantage or acted cruelly or unusually?

rule.if: homicide_conviction_appeal and sudden_fight_exception_claimed and (accused_took_undue_advantage or accused_acted_cruelly_or_unusually or (not sudden_fight_with_deceased) or premeditation_shown) and not all_exception_requirements_established

predicates.homicide_conviction_appeal: The accused is challenging a conviction for murder or homicide and seeks to reduce it to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
predicates.sudden_fight_exception_claimed: The accused invokes Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC (sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel).
predicates.accused_took_undue_advantage: The accused gained an unfair advantage, for example by using a deadly or formidable weapon against an unarmed victim who posed no threat, or by arming himself beforehand.
predicates.accused_acted_cruelly_or_unusually: The manner of the attack was cruel or unusual, for example multiple blows or continued blows on a fallen victim.
predicates.sudden_fight_with_deceased: There was a sudden fight, a mutual transaction with blows exchanged, between the accused and the person killed.
predicates.premeditation_shown: The accused prepared for the confrontation, fetched weapons, or acted on pre-existing malice before the assault.
predicates.all_exception_requirements_established: Every requirement of Exception 4 is met: no premeditation, a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, with the person killed, and no undue advantage or cruel or unusual conduct.
predicates.sudden_fight_exception_unavailable: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC does not apply, and the offence remains murder.

definition: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC applies only if all its requirements are met together: no premeditation, a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel with the person killed, and no undue advantage or cruel or unusual conduct. A sudden quarrel alone is not enough. The exception fails where the accused used a deadly weapon against an unarmed victim, armed himself beforehand, struck repeated blows, or killed someone who was not part of the fight.
exceptions_or_limits: All the conditions of Exception 4 must be present; failure of any one defeats it.
Absence of premeditation and the existence of a sudden quarrel are necessary but not sufficient.
Whether undue advantage was taken depends on the weapons used, the parties' relative ability to defend themselves, and the manner of the attack.
The explanation to Exception 4 makes it immaterial which party provoked the quarrel or struck first, but this does not cure undue advantage or cruelty.
A mutual fight alone is not a sudden fight preceded by a sudden quarrel.

common_material_facts: Accused used a deadly weapon (axe, knife, pharsa, pistol, sharp-edged weapon) against an unarmed victim or victims.
A quarrel or dispute preceded the killing, often over land, boundaries or a personal altercation.
Several members involve repeated blows or blows on a fallen victim, or the accused arming himself before the attack.
Several members involve no real exchange of blows, or a victim who was not part of the fight.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 300 IPC, Exception 4
Section 302 IPC
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 7 members the sudden-fight exception was held inapplicable and the murder conviction was upheld or the offence stayed murder.
variations: Grounds differ: undue advantage (10229171_2, 1113505_2, 446535_2), cruel or unusual conduct (1113505_2, 500779_4), premeditation or fetching weapons (321504_3, 10229171_2), absence of a bilateral fight (1356415_2, 586838_2, 446535_2).
In 500779_4 the cruel or unusual finding came from the trial court even though only a single blow was struck.
In 586838_2 and 1356415_2 the Court stressed that a sudden fight requires mutual blows, not just a sudden quarrel.
In 446535_2 the deceased was an intervener outside the fight.

legal_question: When a court or statutory financial corporation sells (or approves the sale of) a debtor's or company's assets in liquidation or enforcement of security, must the sale process be fair and competitive and secure the best or a reasonable price, and what follows if it is not?

predicates.distressed_asset_sale_by_court_or_financ: The sale is of a company's assets in winding-up (subject to court confirmation or approval) or of a defaulting borrower's assets by a statutory financial corporation enforcing its security.
predicates.sale_process_fair_transparent_and_aimed_: The sale was conducted with adequate publicity, competitive participation, proper valuation or disclosure, and fair opportunity to interested parties (including the debtor), with the objective of securing the best possible price.
predicates.price_reasonable_on_scrutiny: The court (or the corporation) independently examined a reliable valuation and the interests of creditors and was satisfied that the price offered was adequate or reasonable.
predicates.sale_is_invalid_or_confirmation_must_be_: The sale is held invalid, confirmation or approval is refused, or the sale is set aside, usually with a direction to revalue and resell.

definition: A court confirming a liquidation sale, or a financial corporation enforcing security, must itself ensure a fair, publicised, competitive process and a reasonable price based on reliable valuation and regard for creditors and the debtor. A sale lacking this is liable to be refused confirmation or set aside, whereas a sale that followed a fair, transparent process and in which the debtor failed to use an opportunity to better the terms is upheld.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the corporation ran a fair, widely advertised, bona fide process, sought the best price, and the borrower had an opportunity to match or better the offer but failed to do so, the sale remains valid and a writ court should not substitute its commercial judgment (910940_1).
Auction is the preferred method for corporation sales, but tenders and negotiated sales are permissible if justified and accompanied by wide publicity and a genuine search for the best price.
The court's duty to scrutinise price in liquidation sales applies whether or not fraud, irregularity or objections are alleged.
Judicial review of a corporation's sale is limited to statutory violation or unfair or unreasonable conduct.

common_material_facts: Sale of a company's or defaulting borrower's assets in liquidation or under enforcement of security
Inadequate publicity, single or few offers, or higher offers surfacing after the sale
Valuation absent, unreliable or not disclosed to secured creditors; no reserve price
Court confirmed or approved the sale without examining price adequacy or creditor interests
Debtor or secured creditor not given notice or an opportunity to respond or better the offer
statutes_and_provisions: Rule 273, Companies (Court) Rules, 1959
Section 29, State Financial Corporations Act, 1951
Sections 529-A and 536(2), Companies Act, 1956
Section 100, Transfer of Property Act
Article 226 of the Constitution
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Six of seven members set aside or refused to uphold the sale or its confirmation, usually directing revaluation, a reserve price and readvertisement or fresh sale; one (910940_1) upheld a corporation's sale as fair and reversed the High Court's direction to repeat it.
variations: Liquidation-court cases (1032947_1, 20344_1, 519148_1, 643909_4) focus on the court's custodial duty to scrutinise price; financial corporation cases (1390111_1, 494062_3, 910940_1) focus on section 29 duties and fairness to the debtor and other chargeholders.
643909_4 concerns a private sale rather than an auction, and stresses creditor priorities including section 529-A.
910940_1 reaches the opposite outcome because the process was fair and the borrower failed to use its opportunity to purchase or better the offer.
1390111_1 turns also on proceeds not being realised and distributed, and on transfer before bids closed.

legal_question: When may a criminal court, on sentencing or appeal, award compensation to a victim or the victim's dependants under Section 357 CrPC (alone or alongside a reduced sentence), and what must it consider in deciding whether to order it and how much?

predicates.conviction_sustained_or_sentence_under_r: The court is passing sentence after conviction or is hearing an appeal in which the sentence or compensation is open to review.
predicates.victim_or_dependants_suffered_loss_or_in: A person was injured by the offence, or the dependants or family of a deceased victim suffered loss from the offence.
predicates.court_finds_compensation_suitable_having: The court has considered the nature of the crime, the injury or loss, the justness of the claim and other relevant circumstances, and concluded that compensation is an appropriate response.
predicates.offender_has_capacity_to_pay: The court has found or ascertained that the offender can pay the compensation, at least in part, or the offender has offered and is able to pay.
predicates.court_may_order_compensation_to_victim_o: The court may direct payment of compensation (with default consequences such as imprisonment or revival of the original sentence) and may, where circumstances justify, reduce imprisonment to the period already served or set aside the fine, or increase inadequate compensation.

definition: Under Section 357 CrPC, a trial or appellate court may order compensation to a victim or dependants in addition to other sentences. The amount must be reasonable given the nature of the crime, the injury, the justness of the claim and the offender's ability to pay. Where circumstances justify it, such as time already served, the court may reduce imprisonment to the period undergone, with default enforced by imprisonment or revival of the original sentence.
exceptions_or_limits: An order for compensation is ineffective if the offender cannot pay, so capacity to pay must be assessed. Where evidence is lacking, the court may estimate and may hold a summary inquiry.

Reducing imprisonment to the period already served depends on the circumstances, such as custody undergone, prolonged proceedings, absence of antecedents, the gravity of the offence and the motive. It is not automatic.
Where more than one accused is liable, equal contributions are the norm unless their capacities differ considerably. Instalments and a reasonable payment period may be allowed.
Where compensation under Section 357 is insufficient, Section 357-A allows State-funded compensation to make up the shortfall.
The court should not first choose compensation and then set a higher fine; it should assess fine and compensation on the same relevant circumstances.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns adjusting sentence length and setting off time already served. The enhanced fine and compensation are incidental, and no Section 357 principle or capacity-to-pay analysis is applied.

common_material_facts: Victims suffered serious bodily injury (head injury, fracture, deep wounds) or died, leaving dependants who suffered loss.
Offenders had already served part of the sentence, or a long time had passed since the offence.
Offenders had the means to pay or offered to pay.
Default of payment was backed by imprisonment or by revival of the original sentence.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 357(3) CrPC
Section 357(4) CrPC
Section 357 CrPC generally
Section 357-A CrPC
Section 545 of the 1898 Code
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Compensation was ordered or increased in all six covered members. In four of them (115651329_3, 14570141_3, 195057826_2, 329579_3) it came with imprisonment reduced to time served or replaced, and in 212245_3 and 285059_2 compensation was ordered or enhanced alongside the sentence.
variations: Some members reduce custody to time served (115651329_3, 14570141_3, 329579_3).
Others increase compensation on appeal (212245_3).
Others direct that the fine be paid as compensation (285059_2).
Others replace the fine and ordinary imprisonment with compensation (195057826_2).
Capacity to pay was established by finding, by offer, or, in 195057826_2, without detailed evidence.
The cited authorities differ: Hari Singh, Balraj, Palaniappa Gounder, Ankush Shivaji Gaikwad and others. Some members cite none.

split_suggestion: Keep the Section 357 compensation members together. Treat 10229171_6 as a separate sentencing-discretion and set-off issue. Optionally separate the members that reduce custody to time served from those that only fix or increase the amount of compensation.

legal_question: Under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, does a child adopted by a Hindu widow become the adopted child of her deceased husband and his family, so as to claim coparcenary or inheritance rights in his property, and when does the proviso to section 12(c) (no divesting of an estate vested before adoption) bar that claim?

rule.if: valid_adoption_under_1956_act and adoption_made_by_widow and adoptive_widow_belonged_to_deceased_husbands_family and not property_estate_vested_in_another_before_adoption

predicates.valid_adoption_under_1956_act: The adoption was validly made after the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 came into force.
predicates.adoption_made_by_widow: The child was adopted by a Hindu widow after her husband's death.
predicates.adoptive_widow_belonged_to_deceased_husb: The widow, being a married woman, belonged to her deceased husband's family, so the child is absorbed into that family on adoption.
predicates.property_estate_vested_in_another_before: The property in question had already vested as an individual estate in another person before the adoption, so that the adopted child's claim would divest that person. Property merely held by a joint family and passing by survivorship to a sole surviving coparcener does not count as vested for this purpose.
predicates.adopted_child_is_child_of_deceased_husba: The adopted child is treated as the adopted son of the widow and her deceased husband, and may claim coparcenary, partition or succession rights in the husband's family property.

definition: A child adopted by a widow under the 1956 Act is, by sections 11, 12 and 14, absorbed into her deceased husband's family and is treated as his adopted son, with coparcenary or succession rights in that family's property. The proviso to section 12(c) bars the claim only where an individual estate had already vested in another person before the adoption. Joint family property passing by survivorship to a sole surviving coparcener is not such a vested estate.
exceptions_or_limits: Under section 12 proviso (c), an adoption does not divest a person of an estate that had vested in them as an individual estate before the adoption (for example, a widow's absolute property inherited from her husband before she adopted).

Under section 13, an adoptive parent keeps the power to dispose of property, and an agreement to the contrary is effective only if it is admissible. An unregistered covenant requiring registration cannot be admitted in evidence and so does not restrain transfer.
The claim to joint family property depends on the property retaining its joint family character; the result may differ if it has become separate property of an individual.
Nara Hanumantha Rao v. Nara Hanumayya, which took the contrary view, was overruled; its result is explained as consistent with the rule against divesting an already vested estate.

common_material_facts: A man or coparcener died, leaving a widow, and she later adopted a child after the 1956 Act came into force.
The adopted child claimed a share or title in the deceased husband's property or joint family property, often against a surviving brother or reversioner.
The joint family property remained joint after the death of a coparcener, and survivorship was argued to be a vesting.
In two members the property had already vested absolutely in the adopter or the claimant before the adoption.
statutes_and_provisions: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, sections 5, 6, 8, 11, 12 (including proviso (c)), 13 and 14
Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Registration Act, 1908, sections 17(1)(b) and 49
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about five of seven members the adopted child succeeded in becoming the deceased husband's adopted son and a coparcener or claimant.
