Fraud, collusion, material irregularity or illegality in the sale, or a grossly inadequate or throwaway price, can justify setting aside or refusing confirmation.
Before confirmation the court retains a duty to assess adequacy of the price and may accept or reject a bid.
Where the governing rule allows a sale to be set aside only before confirmation, a confirmed sale cannot be set aside under that power, and the remedy lies in the statutory objection process.
Departure from the rule in cases involving material irregularities or peculiar facts does not create a general rule that a later higher offer permits reopening.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns finality after confirmation and a sale certificate in the context of an unchallenged fraud-objection order under Order XXI Rules 92 and 94 CPC. No later higher offer is involved, so it shares only the finality-of-confirmed-sale theme. It could still be covered loosely by the finality limb.

common_material_facts: A sale was held by auction or by acceptance of the highest bid under court or statutory supervision.
A later higher offer, often from a non-participant or unsuccessful bidder, or a later rise in the property's value, was relied on to challenge the sale.
In most members the sale was confirmed, the price paid, and a certificate or deed issued or possession delivered.
No fraud, collusion or irregularity was established in most members.
statutes_and_provisions: Rule 38(6)(a) and 38(7) (recovery rules: setting aside before confirmation; sale certificate conclusive)
Order XXI Rules 92 and 94, Code of Civil Procedure
Navalkha and Sons v. Sri Ramanya Das (1969) 3 SCC 537
Valji Khimji & Co. v. Official Liquidator of Hindustan Nitro Product (Gujarat) Ltd.
S. Soundarajan v. M/s. Roshan & Co., AIR 1951 Mad 986
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 5 of 6 members the sale was upheld or confirmation was not to be refused on the strength of a later higher offer, or the attempt to disturb a confirmed sale failed. In the first member the same principle was stated but the condition of an adequate price was not met.
variations: Some members concern refusal of confirmation before confirmation (Navalkha principle), while others concern setting aside after confirmation.
One member turns on the limits of an authority's statutory power to set aside a sale only before confirmation.
One member turns on the finality of an unchallenged objection order after confirmation, with no higher offer.
In one member a challenge by non-participants after more than two decades was also treated as weak on locus and delay.

split_suggestion: Keep the core group on later higher offers (1032947_4, 182164785_2, 55578845_1, 86762634_1). Treat 116061333_2 and 157385843_2 as a separate group on the finality of confirmed execution sales and the limits of procedural powers after confirmation.

legal_question: When a High Court deals with a reference (a death-sentence confirmation reference, or a reference arising from a judge's disagreement with a jury verdict), must it independently consider the entire evidence and reach its own conclusion, and what follows if it does or does not?

predicates.high_court_dealing_with_statutory_refere: The High Court is deciding a reference under the Code of Criminal Procedure, either for confirmation of a death sentence or following a trial judge's disagreement with a jury verdict, possibly together with an appeal.
predicates.high_court_independently_considered_enti: The High Court examined the whole evidence and material arguments for itself and reached its own conclusion, rather than relying only on a partial objection, a general statement or the lower court's view.
predicates.high_court_failed_statutory_duty_and_its: The High Court's decision is treated as defective for breach of its duty; the Supreme Court sets it aside and remands, or itself examines the record where remand would cause unnecessary hardship.

definition: A High Court deciding a reference, whether for confirmation of a death sentence or from a judge-jury disagreement, must itself consider the entire evidence and all aspects of the case and reach an independent conclusion. If it does so, its review is adequate; if it does not, the decision is defective and is set aside and remanded, or the Supreme Court examines the record itself.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the High Court has in fact examined the evidence, the arguments and the infirmities, its review is adequate and the challenge fails (1048134_2, 1840759_1).
The High Court may dispense with further inquiry or additional evidence where it is not needed to decide guilt or innocence.
Remand is not automatic: the Supreme Court may examine the evidence itself where remand would cause unnecessary hardship, for example long pendency (1586356_5, 1772025_1).
In a jury reference under s.307(3), the jury's view prevails if the evidence can properly support either view, and it may be disregarded only if no reasonable body of men could have reached it.
In an ordinary criminal appeal, the appellate court need not examine the whole record independently; the duty is heightened where a death-sentence reference is before it.

common_material_facts: A trial court imposed death sentences, or a jury returned a majority verdict from which the trial judge disagreed, and the matter went to the High Court on a reference.
The adequacy of the High Court's examination of the evidence was challenged before the Supreme Court.
In several cases the High Court gave only a general statement, ignored defence evidence, or considered only the objection to the jury charge.
statutes_and_provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure ss. 374, 375, 376 (death-sentence confirmation)
Code of Criminal Procedure s. 307(3) (jury reference)
Code of Criminal Procedure s. 423 (appellate powers, as discussed in Bhupendra Singh)
Jumman v. State of Punjab, AIR 1957 SC 469
Bhupendra Singh v. State of Punjab, [1968] 3 SCR 404
Akhlakali Hayatalli v. State of Bombay; Ramanugrah Singh v. The Emperor
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Where the High Court examined the case independently (2 of 6), its review was upheld. Where it did not (4 of 6), the omission was held a breach of duty: 2 jury-reference cases were set aside and remanded, and 2 death-reference cases saw the Supreme Court examine the evidence itself instead of remanding.
variations: Jury-reference cases apply the Akhlakali/Ramanugrah standard of deference to the jury, while death-reference cases stress independent reappraisal as a continuation of the trial.
The remedy differs: remand in the jury-reference cases, but Supreme Court assessment of the record in the death-reference cases, where remand would cause hardship.
Some members concern adequacy of review (outcome favourable to the State), others concern its absence.

legal_question: Can a dispute be referred to arbitration, or an arbitrator's authority extended, only to the parties and disputes covered by the specific arbitration agreement invoked, and what is the effect of a non-signatory or a separate agreement on that scope?

predicates.arbitration_agreement_invoked: A party relies on a particular arbitration clause or agreement to seek reference, appointment of an arbitrator, or to support an award.
predicates.dispute_or_person_outside_scope_of_invok: The dispute arises under a different or future agreement, or a person sought to be bound is not a party to (or claiming under a party to) the invoked arbitration agreement.
predicates.non_party_has_no_relevant_right_or_undis: The only non-signatory involved has no relevant right in the dispute, or has an interest whose extent is undisputed and can be left out of the award, and the other material parties are bound so referral would not split the cause of action or parties.
predicates.arbitration_confined_to_parties_and_disp: The arbitration may proceed only between the parties bound by the invoked agreement and only on disputes within its scope; outside parties or disputes are excluded, not referred, or any award on them is set aside.

definition: An arbitration clause supports reference only for disputes and parties it actually covers; disputes under separate or future agreements and persons not bound by the clause cannot be brought within it, and awards beyond it are liable to be set aside. However, the presence of a non-signatory who has no relevant right or whose share is undisputed does not bar referral between the parties who are bound.
exceptions_or_limits: A non-signatory's presence does not bar referral between bound parties where the non-signatory has no relevant right in the dispute, or has an undisputed share that can be left out of the award, and no bifurcation of cause of action or parties results.
Where the dispute arises under a separate agreement with its own arbitration terms, an arbitrator appointed under another agreement has no authority over it unless it falls within the submission.
Joinder of a non-party in a Section 11 proceeding is impermissible; the non-party should be deleted or expressly excluded while the appointment stays effective for bound parties.

common_material_facts: More than one agreement or contract exists, and the arbitration clause sits in only one of them
A person or entity involved in the dispute is not a party to the invoked arbitration agreement
Arbitration is invoked or an award is rendered on a dispute lying outside the clause's subject matter
statutes_and_provisions: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 7, 8, 11
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, s. 34(2)(a)(iv) and (v)
Arbitration Act, 1940, s. 20
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Four members (106024089_2, 153664247_1, 24736_3, 298157_1) confine arbitration to the parties and disputes covered by the invoked clause, excluding the outside dispute or party. Two members (137915996_2, 1737932_1) permit referral between bound parties despite an absent non-signatory whose interest is absent or undisputed.
variations: Some members concern the scope of the subject matter (separate or future contracts), others concern the identity of parties (non-signatories).
Procedural posture varies: Section 11 appointment, Section 8 or Section 20 referral, Section 34 challenge to an award, and jurisdictional challenge.
Two members are permissive about non-signatories where their interest is undisputed or non-existent, while the others restrict the scope of the clause.
Only some members rely on precedent (Yogi Agarwal, Jagdish Chander, S.N. Prasad, M.R. Engineers, Rahul Yadav); others rest on the facts alone.

split_suggestion: If finer granularity is wanted, split into (a) subject-matter scope: clause does not reach disputes under separate or future agreements (106024089_2, 153664247_1, 24736_3), and (b) non-signatory parties: exclusion of a non-party from arbitration (298157_1) versus referral despite a non-signatory with no relevant or undisputed interest (137915996_2, 1737932_1).

legal_question: When a tax was lawfully levied before a constitutional or statutory transition, does it continue to be valid and collectable under the saving or continuation provisions, and what changes (in amount, governing local law, or later procedural requirements) leave its continuing validity unaffected?

rule.if: continuing_tax_claim_based_on_pre_transition_levy and tax_lawfully_levied_before_transition and same_tax_in_nature_type_and_subject_matter and (only_amount_or_governing_law_or_later_procedural_requirement_changed) and not local_authority_state_changed_since_constitution

predicates.continuing_tax_claim_based_on_pre_transi: The local authority or taxing body claims or collects a tax by relying on a saving or continuation provision for a levy that existed before a constitutional or statutory transition.
predicates.tax_lawfully_levied_before_transition: The tax, or the power to impose it, was validly conferred, assented to and exercised before the transition, and the earlier imposition has not been superseded or modified.
predicates.same_tax_in_nature_type_and_subject_matt: The tax claimed now is of the same nature and type and falls on the same property or subject as the earlier tax, and is consistent with any successor law or the same local purposes.
predicates.only_amount_or_governing_law_or_later_pr: The only differences are a change in the rate or amount, a change in the local statute under which the tax is claimed, or a later procedural requirement for future lawmaking that does not invalidate earlier law.
predicates.local_authority_state_changed_since_cons: The claiming local authority is no longer in the same State in which it was located immediately before the Constitution commenced, so Article 285(2) does not apply.
predicates.pre_transition_tax_continues_valid: The tax is treated as the same tax and remains valid and collectable under the saving or continuation provision.

definition: A tax lawfully imposed before a constitutional or statutory transition continues to be valid under the relevant saving provisions where it remains the same tax in nature, type and subject matter. Changes in amount, in the local law relied on, or later procedural requirements for new legislation do not alter its identity or validity. Under Article 285(2), the continuation of a tax on Union property is lost if the local authority is no longer in the same State.
exceptions_or_limits: For Union property under Article 285(2), continuation is unavailable if the local authority is no longer in the same State in which it was located immediately before the Constitution commenced (a change in State by transfer of the area). Parliament may alter this by law.
A genuinely new tax, as opposed to a continuing one, is not protected (Amravati was distinguished as concerning new taxes).
An earlier resolution continues only where a later resolution did not supersede or modify it and the tax is not inconsistent with the successor statute.
Article 277 and section 143 preserve collection and application only for the same local purposes.

common_material_facts: A local authority levied a tax before a constitutional or statutory transition (1915 Act, 1935 Act, Constitution, successor panchayat statute).
The tax was later challenged after a change in amount, governing law, procedure or territory.
The nature and type of the tax and the subject property were the same before and after.
statutes_and_provisions: Constitution of India Article 285(2)
Constitution of India Articles 277 and 372
Government of India Act, 1935, sections 143 and 292
Government of India Act, 1915, sections 80A(3), 81(1), 81(3) and 84(2)
Scheduled Taxes Rules, rule 5
Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1958, section 186(8)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 5 of 6 members the pre-transition tax was held to continue valid or to remain the same tax. In 1 member (104873780_3) continuation under Article 285(2) was denied because the local authority was in a different State.
variations: Two members (104873780_2, 1812473_2) address the identity of the tax under Article 285(2) despite changes in amount or local law.
104873780_3 turns on the meaning of 'that State' in Article 285(2) and goes against the municipality.
1648637_1 concerns the effect of a later procedural sanction requirement under the 1915 Act.
1648637_3 concerns Article 277 and section 143 saving the levy for the same local purposes.
1114841_2 concerns a successor statute's saving clause and a later resolution that did not supersede the earlier one.

split_suggestion: If a tighter grouping is needed, separate (a) the Article 285(2) Union property members (104873780_2, 104873780_3, 1812473_2), and within them the same-State limit from the tax identity point, from (b) the general local tax saving members (1114841_2, 1648637_1, 1648637_3).

legal_question: Can a person who succeeds to or claims through a party's interest in the subject matter of a pending appeal (by assignment, transfer, devolution or succession) be brought on record to continue or defend the appeal, even where the formal procedure for substitution was not followed or was incorrectly invoked?

predicates.pending_appeal: An appeal is pending when the successor or claimant seeks to participate.
predicates.successor_or_claimant_acquired_party_int: The person claims under or through a party to the appeal, by assignment, transfer, devolution, inheritance or succession to office, to the interest in the subject matter of the dispute.
predicates.claimant_seeks_to_be_brought_on_record: The person has applied, or has been allowed in substance, to be added, impleaded or substituted in the appeal.
predicates.claimant_may_be_added_or_substituted_and: The court may add, implead or substitute the person, who may continue, maintain or defend the appeal. This is subject to leave where required, and a procedural defect, wrong provision or absence of a formal order does not defeat it.

definition: A person who has acquired a party's interest in the subject matter of a pending appeal, whether by assignment, devolution, inheritance or succession, may be added or substituted and may continue or defend the appeal. Section 146, Order 22 Rules 3, 4 and 10, and Order 1 Rule 10 are applied liberally, and technical defects such as a wrong procedure, delay or the lack of a formal order do not defeat this.
exceptions_or_limits: Leave of the court is required under Order 22 Rule 10 to continue proceedings against or by the person acquiring the interest.
Addition may be made subject to the opposing party's right to object to the claimant's standing (109083_2).
Where the claimant disputes another claimant's title, as with the son's alleged will against the widow, the court may admit both and hear them (1879794_3).
The leniency about the wrong procedure was applied where the successor was already on record; it does not mean the correct provision need not be invoked (1400082_2).
The claimant must actually derive the interest from a party; a stranger with no interest in the subject matter is not covered.

common_material_facts: A party to a pending appeal died or transferred their interest in the property or office in dispute.
A successor, assignee or heir sought to be added or substituted.
The formal substitution was missing, late or made under the wrong provision.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 146 CPC
Order 22 Rule 10 CPC
Order 22 Rules 3 and 4 CPC
Order 1 Rule 10 CPC
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 6 members the successor or claimant was allowed to be added or substituted and to continue or defend the appeal. In 3 of these (1400082_2, 1879794_3, 379679_1) procedural irregularity or delay was excused.
variations: Section 146 was relied on in 2 members (109083_2, 1262724_2) for persons claiming under a party.
Order 22 Rule 10 was relied on for devolution of interest in 379679_1 and 785132_4.
Order 22 Rule 4 was relied on for a successor karta in 1400082_2, which also held Rule 10 was not the correct procedure.
1879794_3 cites no authority and rests on the court's discretion, treating the heir as substituted in substance and also substituting the widow.
785132_4 also allows a transferee to be added under Order 1 Rule 10.

legal_question: When a notice or summons is correctly addressed and sent by post (registered post or otherwise) but is returned unclaimed, refused, undelivered or unacknowledged, may service be presumed, and what must the recipient do to rebut that presumption?

rule.if: notice_or_summons_correctly_addressed and sent_by_post_with_proper_dispatch and (returned_unclaimed_or_refused_or_unavailable_or_acknowledgment_not_received) and not recipient_rebutted_presumption_with_evidence

predicates.notice_or_summons_correctly_addressed: The notice or summons was addressed to the recipient's correct or proper address.
predicates.sent_by_post_with_proper_dispatch: The notice or summons was duly sent through the post (typically registered post, prepaid), with dispatch shown by postal records, endorsement or intimation.
predicates.returned_unclaimed_or_refused_or_unavail: The postal article came back unclaimed, refused, undelivered or with an endorsement that the addressee was unavailable, or the acknowledgment was never received.
predicates.recipient_rebutted_presumption_with_evid: The recipient produced convincing evidence, beyond a bare denial, that the address was wrong, the endorsement was incorrect, or the notice was not in fact served.
predicates.service_presumed: The notice or summons is treated as served on the recipient, without need for further proof such as examining the postman.

definition: A notice or summons that is correctly addressed and duly posted, typically by registered post, is presumed served under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act or Section 114 of the Evidence Act even if it is returned unclaimed, refused or unacknowledged. The presumption is rebuttable and not compulsory, and the recipient must rebut it with real evidence rather than a bare denial.
exceptions_or_limits: The presumption is rebuttable and permissive, not mandatory; the court must weigh the evidence.
A bare denial of receipt, or an unsubstantiated challenge to the postal endorsement, does not rebut it.
The presumption depends on correct addressing and proof of proper dispatch; if the address was wrong or dispatch is not shown, it does not arise.
Where the recipient proves the endorsement or address was wrong, service is not presumed.
The treatment of notice averments as part of the pleading applies only where the pleading refers to and relies on the notice.

common_material_facts: Notice or summons sent by registered post to the correct address
Article returned unclaimed, refused, unavailable or acknowledgment not received
Recipient offered no evidence or only a bare denial
Frequently arises in sale-agreement and specific performance disputes
statutes_and_provisions: Section 27, General Clauses Act, 1897
Section 114 (illustration (f)), Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Section 27, Post Office Act
Order 5 Rule 19A (second proviso) and Order 9 Rule 13, Code of Civil Procedure
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Presumption of service upheld in all 6 issues (a remand-style direction to weigh the evidence in light of the presumption in 1); the recipient's failure to rebut was decisive in most.
variations: Return reasons vary: unclaimed after intimation, refusal, unavailability, unacknowledged, or generic undelivered remarks.
Contexts vary: execution of sale deed, ex parte decree setting aside, administrative allotment letter, specific performance suit.
One member stresses that the postman need not be examined; another stresses the presumption is permissive, not inevitable.
One member also treats the notice's averments as part of the pleading when relied on.
Some members cite the General Clauses Act, others the Post Office Act, the Evidence Act or CPC provisions, and one cites no provision.

legal_question: Does a daughter acquire equal coparcenary rights under the amended Hindu Succession Act (or the state amendment) where a partition suit is pending and partition has not been legally completed before the statutory cutoff, so that a preliminary decree or notional partition does not defeat her share?

rule.if: coparcenary_property and daughter_of_coparcener_entitled_under_amended_law and partition_not_legally_completed_before_cutoff and (partition_proceeding_pending_when_amendment_took_effect or only_preliminary_decree_passed)

predicates.coparcenary_property: The property in dispute is joint family coparcenary property.
predicates.daughter_of_coparcener_entitled_under_am: The claimant is a daughter of a coparcener who qualifies for coparcenary status under the amended provision (for example, she was alive when it commenced, and, where a state amendment is relied on, she was unmarried at that time), irrespective of her birth date or whether her father was alive.
predicates.partition_not_legally_completed_before_c: No partition by a duly registered deed or a court (final) decree was effected before the statutory cutoff date; a notional partition or a preliminary decree alone does not count as completed partition.
predicates.partition_proceeding_pending_when_amendm: A partition suit, final-decree proceeding or appeal was pending when the amendment came into force.
predicates.only_preliminary_decree_passed: Only a preliminary decree declaring shares has been passed and no final decree dividing the property by metes and bounds has been made.
predicates.daughter_entitled_to_equal_coparcenary_s: The daughter has the same coparcenary share, rights and liabilities as a son, and the preliminary decree must be varied or the final decree drawn to give effect to it.

definition: A daughter who qualifies under the amended coparcenary law is entitled to a share equal to a son's wherever partition was not legally completed (by registered deed or final court decree) before the cutoff. A pending suit or a preliminary decree, or a notional partition, does not defeat her right, and the shares must be adjusted before the final decree.
exceptions_or_limits: Dispositions, alienations, partitions and testamentary dispositions completed before the statutory cutoff (a registered partition deed or a court decree) remain protected and are not reopened.
The daughter must be a qualifying daughter of a coparcener (alive at commencement under the 2005 amendment; unmarried at commencement under the Karnataka amendment).
The rights operate from the commencement of the amendment; the provision is retroactive, not a reopening of settled transactions.
A notional partition only fixes a deceased coparcener's share and does not end the coparcenary.

outlier_members.reason: It states the saving or limit (earlier completed transactions stay unaffected) rather than the entitlement. It is the complementary boundary of the rule and is captured in exceptions_or_limits.

common_material_facts: Partition suit in which only a preliminary decree had been passed and final-decree proceedings or appeals were pending
Property not divided by metes and bounds or by registered deed before the cutoff
Daughters claiming equal shares with sons in Mitakshara coparcenary property under a beneficial amendment
Daughters born before the amendment, sometimes with the father already dead
statutes_and_provisions: Hindu Succession Act 1956, s. 6(1), 6(3), 6(5) and Explanation (as substituted in 2005)
Section 6A, Hindu Succession (Karnataka Amendment) Act 1990
Articles 14, 15(1), 15(3) of the Constitution
Sections 151, 152, 153 CPC
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Daughters succeed in all 5 substantive members: shares are recognised or the decree amended despite a preliminary decree. The sixth member (67965481_2) confirms that earlier completed transactions are protected.
variations: One member applies the Karnataka state amendment, which requires the daughter to be unmarried, rather than the 2005 central amendment
One member (67965481_1) decides the status-by-birth question and overrules the living-father requirement, while the others address the procedural stage of the suit
One member (67965481_3) addresses the notional partition fiction in addition to preliminary decrees
One member (88759498_2) recites Prakash v. Phulavati but rests on the pending-suit reasoning

legal_question: When an instrument (deed, gift, compromise or award) grants property to a person, especially a Hindu woman, in clear words of full ownership such as 'malik', 'malik mustakil' or 'permanent owner', does the grantee take an absolute estate unless other words or circumstances in the instrument unambiguously qualify the grant?

predicates.instrument_grants_property_to_person: The document under construction (gift deed, compromise deed, award or similar) allots or transfers immovable property to an identified person, including a woman.
predicates.operative_words_convey_full_ownership: The dispositive words of the instrument clearly describe the grantee as full or permanent owner (for example 'malik', 'malik mustakil', 'permanent owner', or 'absolute rights').
predicates.instrument_or_context_unambiguously_qual: Other passages of the instrument, or the surrounding circumstances, clearly and unambiguously cut down the grant, for example to a life estate, a trust, or a non-alienable interest.
predicates.grantee_takes_absolute_estate: The grantee acquires an absolute, heritable and transferable estate in the property.

definition: Where an instrument grants property in clear words of full ownership, the grantee takes an absolute estate. There is no presumption that a Hindu female grantee takes a limited interest. Recitals about maintenance, residence, expected devolution or the presence of a dependant do not cut down the grant unless they do so unambiguously.
exceptions_or_limits: The outcome differs where other words in the instrument or the surrounding circumstances unambiguously qualify or limit the grant, for example by restricting it to a life interest or creating a trust.
A recital of maintenance or residence as the purpose of the grant is treated as motive and does not by itself limit the estate.
Maintenance grants in impartible estates, or in different circumstances, were distinguished and are not governed by this rule.
Where the instrument is not clear, intention is determined from its words read with the surrounding circumstances.

common_material_facts: Property was allotted or gifted to a woman (widow, daughter or wife), or to a recipient under an award, in words of full ownership such as 'malik', 'malik mustakil' or 'permanent owner'.
Other passages or recitals mentioned maintenance or residence, the character of the property, expected devolution, or a dependent son, but did not clearly qualify the operative grant.
The instruments were deeds, compromises or awards that settled family disputes.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 8, Transfer of Property Act (a transfer carries the full interest absent contrary intention)
Ram Gopal v. Nand Lal
Bishunath Prasad Singh v. Chandika Prasad
Tagore v. Tagore
Kollani Koer v. Luchmee Parsad
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 6 members hold that the grantee took an absolute estate, because the clear operative words were not unambiguously qualified.
variations: Four members involve Hindu women grantees (the gift, oral-will deed, compromise and husband's gift cases), while two involve awards where the grantee's sex is not emphasised.
Some members rely on Transfer of Property Act s. 8 and the absence of any presumption of a limited estate for women, while others rely only on plain-meaning construction.
One member (1861085_2) cites no authority and also rejects the argument that a recital about a minor son created a trust.
One member (1141020_1) addresses the maintenance and residence purpose and the absence of express words of alienability.

legal_question: Can a person who improves or spends money on property while knowing they have no title or lawful right to it claim compensation, a proprietary interest or reimbursement for that expenditure from the true owner?

rule.if: occupier_has_no_title_or_lawful_right_to_property and occupier_knew_of_lack_of_title_or_right and occupier_made_improvements_or_expenditure_on_property and not true_owner_consented_to_improvements

predicates.occupier_has_no_title_or_lawful_right_to: The person in possession or occupation had no title to the property and no lawful authority to occupy it (for example, a trespasser, or possession under a void or unauthorised transfer).
predicates.occupier_knew_of_lack_of_title_or_right: The occupier knew, when making the improvements or expenditure, the true state of ownership or that they had no right to occupy.
predicates.occupier_made_improvements_or_expenditur: The occupier made improvements, repairs, reconstruction or planting on the property, or spent money on it.
predicates.true_owner_consented_to_improvements: The true owner consented to or authorised the improvements or expenditure.
predicates.occupier_not_entitled_to_compensation_or: The occupier cannot recover the cost or value of the improvements from the true owner and acquires no proprietary interest through the expenditure.

definition: A person who knowingly improves or spends money on property to which they have no title or lawful right, without the true owner's consent, cannot charge the owner for the improvements or acquire a proprietary interest through them. A good intention to improve does not change this.
exceptions_or_limits: Applies where the improver knew of the lack of title or right; the members do not decide the position of a bona fide improver without knowledge.
Does not apply where the true owner consented to the improvements.

Statutory compensation schemes or equitable claims such as acquiescence were considered and held not to assist the knowing improver on the facts; the members do not exclude them in other circumstances.
One member (compensation for acquisition) concerns refund of money rather than improvements and is only analogous.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns a purchaser without title who withdrew acquisition compensation under an undertaking and must refund it. It does not involve improvements by an occupier, though it shares the theme that a person without title has no right to money attached to the land.

common_material_facts: The claimant occupied or dealt with property without valid title or lawful authority.
The claimant knew the true state of title or that their possession was unauthorised.
The claimant spent money on improvements, repairs, reconstruction or planting.
The owner had not consented to the improvements.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 51, Transfer of Property Act (did not assist the improver)
Sections 5 and 6, Travancore Land Conservancy Act, 1916
Ramsden v. Dyson (distinguished)
Vallabdas Narainji v. Development Officer, Bandra, A.I.R. 1929 P.C. 163
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 5 covered members the knowing improver or occupier was denied compensation or any proprietary interest. The sixth member, on a related theme, also went against the person without title (refund ordered).
variations: Some members treat the claim as one for reimbursement of improvement costs from a co-heir, others as a claim for compensation for trees, others as a claim to ownership through expenditure.
In one member the expenditure was not proved at all, so the statement is partly obiter.
The basis of lack of right differs: knowing possession of co-heirs' property, deliberate trespass on government land, possession under a void agreement, or knowledge of the registered title.
Reasoning ranges from the knowledge of the improver to the unlawfulness of the possession, and in one member to the point that a trespasser cannot be better placed than a lawful tenant.

split_suggestion: Keep the five improvement and expenditure members together. Treat the acquisition compensation refund member (159016305_5) separately, as a restitution issue about a person without title retaining compensation.

legal_question: Can a landlord or claimant succeed on a rent-related claim (past rent, rent arrears, or an eviction ground based on rent default or tenant conduct) or rely on a rent document, where the tenancy, its terms, the rent payable or the supporting evidence has not been established, or where the ground was not pursued on appeal?

predicates.rent_related_claim_or_ground_asserted: A party asserts a claim for past rent, rent arrears, an eviction ground tied to rent default or tenant conduct, or reliance on a rent document.
predicates.tenancy_or_its_terms_or_rent_payable_not: The party asserting the claim has not proved by evidence the tenancy, its terms, the rent rate or amount payable, or the facts alleged (for example, the rent document is too vague to identify the property or the parties, or the allegation of non-use is unsupported).
predicates.ground_not_pursued_on_appeal: The ground relied on was rejected or not pursued or defended in the appellate proceedings, so it is not available to support the decree.
predicates.rent_related_claim_or_ground_fails: The claim, ground or document is rejected or not accepted as establishing the relief or title sought.

definition: A party claiming past rent, arrears, an eviction ground based on rent default or non-use, or title through a rent document must prove the tenancy, its terms, the rent payable and the alleged facts. Where the proof is lacking, or the ground was not pursued on appeal, the claim fails.
exceptions_or_limits: Two members (1286314_2, and in part 1167532_2) also note that under the U.P. rent control legislation a letting without the required permission would be invalid; this is an additional, not a necessary, ground.
The appellate-abandonment strand (1601894_1, 860753_3) depends on the ground not having been pursued or defended on appeal and, in 1601894_1, on a statutory amendment changing the requirements.
The rule concerns failure of proof; it does not apply where the tenancy, its terms and the rent are proved.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the scope of the appeal after a personal-requirement ground was rejected and abandoned following a statutory amendment, not failure to prove tenancy or rent. It fits only the 'ground not pursued on appeal' strand.

common_material_facts: Landlord or plaintiff asserts a tenancy, rent arrears or a rent default without adequate proof
Courts below or the High Court rejected the claim on evidence, and the Supreme Court declined to interfere
Key evidence is missing (rent rate, tenancy terms, identifying details, a witness with knowledge)
Some grounds were not pursued in the appeal
statutes_and_provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 and the preceding Ordinance (permission for letting)
Section 13(1)(ff), West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956
Sections 12(2) and 12(3)(a), Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All six reject or confine the rent-based claim. Four concern unproved tenancy, rent or non-use; one concerns a vague rent note; one concerns a ground abandoned on appeal. The Supreme Court mostly leaves the lower findings undisturbed.
variations: Past rent claims (2 members) turn on an unproved tenancy, with a possible permission defect
Arrears claim fails because the rent rate per tenant is unproved and the landlord did not testify
Rent note fails as proof of title for lack of identifying details and because of the pleadings
Eviction grounds fail through abandonment on appeal or lack of evidence

split_suggestion: Split into (a) failure to prove tenancy, terms, rent or alleged facts (1167532_2, 1286314_2, 1593488_2, 61939581_10, and the non-use part of 860753_3) and (b) grounds not pursued or defended on appeal (1601894_1 and the default part of 860753_3).

legal_question: When a prior decision of the Supreme Court (or of the same court) decides the legal issue now arising, is the later or lower court bound to follow its ratio, even where it is argued that other decisions conflict with it?

rule.if: prior_decision_declares_law_on_issue and prior_decision_governs_issue_before_court and (deciding_court_is_lower_court_or_bound_by_the_prior_decision) and not prior_decision_validly_distinguishable

predicates.prior_decision_declares_law_on_issue: A prior decision of the Supreme Court, or of the same court in the case of the same-court member, deliberately decided the legal issue and declared the principle (ratio decidendi).
predicates.prior_decision_governs_issue_before_cour: The issue in the present case is the same as the one the prior decision decided, in the same or an equivalent statutory setting and on indistinguishable facts and law.
predicates.deciding_court_is_lower_court_or_bound_b: The court now deciding is a subordinate court, such as a High Court or Full Bench, to the court that rendered the prior decision, or is the same court applying its own earlier decision on identical points.
predicates.prior_decision_validly_distinguishable: The prior decision can properly be distinguished on its facts, issue or statutory scheme, or is shown to have been rendered per incuriam or to be overruled. The cited conflicting decisions concern different questions or statutes, or have been considered and distinguished by the prior decision, so they do not count.
predicates.deciding_court_must_follow_prior_decisio: The deciding court is bound to apply the prior decision's ratio and may not take a contrary view, and a conflicting decision or contrary finding must yield or be set aside.

definition: Under Article 141 (and the rule that a court is bound by its own earlier decision on identical facts and law), the ratio of a prior decision that actually decided the issue binds subordinate courts, and the same court in like cases. A lower court cannot depart from it by relying on conflicting lower-court rulings or on Supreme Court decisions that address distinct questions or have been distinguished.
exceptions_or_limits: Only the ratio decidendi binds, read in light of the facts and the issue decided; incidental observations do not.
A decision on a materially different statute or a different question is not binding on the present issue and creates no conflict.

The same-court member rests on identical facts and law; departure remains possible on limited grounds such as per incuriam or the Court's power to reconsider its decisions, which the members discuss but do not apply.
A conflicting earlier High Court decision does not prevail and stands impliedly overruled to the extent of the conflict.

common_material_facts: A lower court or later bench departed from, or was urged to depart from, an earlier binding Supreme Court decision.
A conflicting decision was cited: an earlier High Court ruling, decisions on a different statute, or earlier Supreme Court cases.
The Supreme Court found the cited decisions distinguishable, distinct in issue, or impliedly overruled.
The same statutory scheme or issue was involved in the prior decision and the present case.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 141 of the Constitution of India
Land acquisition and industrial development statutes (solatium, interest, subsequent allottee)
Rent control legislation, including the Karnataka Rent Control Act s. 31
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, paras 98-99
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 6 members hold that the prior decision binds: 5 apply Article 141 to a lower court or later bench, 1 applies same-court precedent on identical facts. The contrary ruling is set aside or treated as not conflicting.
variations: Four members involve High Courts or a Full Bench departing from Supreme Court law, one a two-judge versus three-judge Supreme Court bench, and one the same court's earlier decision.

Some members resolve an apparent conflict by distinguishing the other cases on a different statute or question (1145726_2, 502158_3, 58839229_2); another treats a conflicting High Court decision as impliedly overruled (1481214_1).
One member (1443146_1) concerns a Constitution Bench's directions being treated as non-binding by the High Court.
The same-court member (538289_2) rests on common facts and law across appeals from one judgment rather than on Article 141 hierarchy.

legal_question: When an eviction or ejectment decree has been passed and the occupant stays in possession after it (whether because of a stay pending appeal or delayed execution), must or may the court require payment of mesne profits or compensation for post-decree use and occupation, and is that compensation limited to the contractual rent?

predicates.possession_decree_passed: A court or tribunal has passed a decree or order for ejectment or eviction of the occupant, in favour of the landlord or claimant.
predicates.occupant_remains_in_possession_after_dec: The occupant or tenant continues to hold the property after the decree has been passed.
predicates.possession_not_yet_delivered: Possession has not yet been handed over to the decree-holder.
predicates.execution_stayed_or_delayed: Execution of the decree is stayed pending appeal or is otherwise delayed, so the decree-holder is kept out of possession.
predicates.occupant_liable_to_pay_reasonable_post_d: The court may (and in a plain ejectment decree must) direct the occupant to pay reasonable mesne profits or damages for use and occupation from the decree until possession is delivered. The amount may reflect the market rent and is not capped at the contractual rent.

definition: Once a decree for ejectment or eviction has been passed, an occupant who stays in possession must pay reasonable mesne profits or compensation for use and occupation from the decree until possession is delivered. A decree for ejectment should include such a direction. Where execution is stayed or delayed, the court may impose payment as a condition of the stay or as interim relief. The amount may reflect the market rent and is not capped at the contractual rent.
exceptions_or_limits: The obligation is mandatory only where the decree for ejectment is itself being granted or finalised (two members); during a stay or delay the members describe it as discretionary, as reasonable terms imposed by the court.
The compensation must be reasonable. In one member the tenant did not contend that the amount was grossly excessive.
A stay is discretionary and equitable, not a right, and Order 41 Rule 5(3) considerations (substantial loss, delay, security) apply.
The interim-compensation order in the delayed-execution member did not decide the merits of the occupant's claimed tenancy rights, which were pending in a separate suit.

common_material_facts: A decree or order for ejectment or eviction had been passed in favour of the landlord or claimant.
The occupant or tenant remained in possession after the decree.
Execution was stayed pending appeal or otherwise delayed in four members.
The contractual rent was low compared with the market rent in the stay cases, and the landlord sought compensation for the delay.
statutes_and_provisions: Order XLI Rule 5 and Rule 5(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure
Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Section 38(3) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd. v. Federal Motors (P) Ltd.
Marshall Sons & Co. (I) Ltd. v. Sahi Oretrans (P) Ltd.
State of Maharashtra v. Super Max International Pvt. Ltd.
South Eastern Coalfields Ltd. v. State of M.P.
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All six members award or uphold post-decree compensation for use and occupation. Two (1167532_3, 1286314_3) hold that the ejectment decree must include future mesne profits. Four (1452318_2, 1651002_1, 309033_1, 77210495_3) allow compensation to be imposed during a stay or delay, in three of them at market-based rates exceeding the contractual rent.
variations: Two members concern plain ejectment decrees where the direction for future mesne profits is mandatory; the other four concern stays or delays in execution where the direction is discretionary.
One member (1452318_2) cites no authority. It adds the option of appointing a receiver and orders instalment payment of arrears.
Some members tie the amount expressly to the rate at which the premises could be let (market rent); others use the trial court's assessed monthly rate.
One member (309033_1) makes the compensation a condition of the stay, with deposits held until the appeal is decided.

legal_question: Can solatium (and interest) be denied to owners of compulsorily acquired land merely because the land is acquired under a special or different enactment, for a different public purpose or by a different authority, rather than under the general land-acquisition law?

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_disp: The proceeding concerns the amount or components of compensation payable for land compulsorily acquired.
predicates.special_enactment_excludes_or_omits_sola: The enactment under which the land was acquired (a local, improvement, state or highway-acquisition law) does not provide for, or expressly excludes, solatium or interest that the general land-acquisition law would give.
predicates.owners_similarly_situated_to_those_acqui: The owners are in the same position as owners whose land is, or could be, acquired for the same or a comparable purpose under the general land-acquisition law, which grants solatium and interest.
predicates.difference_based_only_on_enactment_or_pu: The only basis for the difference in compensation is the statute used, the public purpose, or the acquiring authority, not any difference in the owner's right or the land.
predicates.no_rational_basis_for_distinction: The difference has no intelligible differentia rationally related to the object of the legislation. For example, paying solatium would not defeat the aim of the special scheme, or the government was empowered to apply the general provisions.
predicates.exclusion_is_invalid_and_solatium_and_in: The exclusion or omission cannot be relied on to deny the owner, because it violates equal protection or is read down. Solatium (and interest, where the general law gives it) is payable as under the general acquisition law.

definition: Where a special or different enactment would leave owners of acquired land without solatium or interest that owners under the general acquisition law receive, and the only difference is the statute, purpose or authority with no rational basis, the exclusion is invalid under Article 14. Solatium and interest remain payable.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the governing statute is a self-contained compensation scheme that deliberately omits solatium and interest, and no equal-protection invalidity is established or the scheme is distinguishable, solatium and interest are not added (see 1145726_1).
A rational, object-related basis for the distinction would justify different treatment.
Separate compensation for user or easement rights held by others does not justify withholding solatium and interest from owners whose ownership is acquired.

outlier_members.reason: Reaches the opposite outcome. Solatium and interest were denied because the statutory scheme deliberately omitted them. The case followed earlier authority that the statute occupies the field, and no Article 14 challenge to the omission was decided.

common_material_facts: Land acquired under a special, local, improvement or highway enactment that gives no solatium or interest, or gives less than the general Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
Owners under the general law receive solatium (s. 23(2)) and interest (ss. 28, 34).
The government could have acquired the same land under the general law, or could apply its provisions.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 14 of the Constitution
Land Acquisition Act, 1894, ss. 23(2), 28, 34, 3(b), 9, 31(1)
Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, s. 4(3)
Highway-acquisition scheme and its 1997 amendment
Local land development and planning enactments, and improvement legislation
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 5 of 6 members, solatium (and interest) was held payable or the discriminatory exclusion was struck down or held not to justify withholding. In 1 member (1145726_1), the claim was rejected because the statutory scheme deliberately omitted solatium and interest.
variations: Some members rest on constitutional invalidity under Article 14 (337342_2, 92512441_1, 81931_3). Another rests on a statutory power to apply the general law's provisions (260704_4).
One member (92512441_3) answers a narrower argument, that separate user or easement compensation justifies the exclusion.
One member (1145726_1) treats the statutory scheme as exhaustive and denies the claim.

split_suggestion: Keep the Article 14 / equal-treatment members together as the main group. Treat 1145726_1 (statute occupies the field, deliberate omission, no discrimination challenge) as a separate sub-cluster or an exception.

legal_question: Can a court or revenue/execution sale be set aside merely because the price obtained was allegedly inadequate, without proof of fraud or material irregularity in the conduct of the sale causing substantial injury?

rule.if: compulsory_sale_challenged and inadequate_price_alleged and not (fraud_or_material_irregularity_in_sale_proved and substantial_injury_shown)

predicates.compulsory_sale_challenged: The challenge is to a sale held in execution of a court decree or as a revenue sale, i.e. a compulsory sale rather than a private sale.
predicates.inadequate_price_alleged: The challenger alleges that the property fetched less than its true or estimated value.
predicates.fraud_or_material_irregularity_in_sale_p: The challenger has proved fraud, or a material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale.
predicates.substantial_injury_shown: The challenger has shown that the fraud or irregularity caused substantial injury.
predicates.sale_not_set_aside_for_price_inadequacy_: The sale is not set aside or declared void on the ground of alleged inadequacy of price alone.

definition: A compulsory court or revenue sale is not liable to be set aside or declared void merely because the price was allegedly inadequate. The challenger must prove fraud or a material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale, together with substantial injury caused by it (Order XXI Rule 90 CPC), and must also offer evidence of the higher value claimed.
exceptions_or_limits: The sale can still be set aside on independent grounds, such as procedural defects, excessive execution, or proven fraud or material irregularity causing substantial injury (as in 1362442_11).
Inadequacy of price may be relevant evidence where it is tied to proven irregularity or fraud, but it does not suffice by itself.
The challenger bears the burden of proving the higher value, fraud or irregularity, and substantial injury; bare assertions do not suffice.
A challenge brought as an objection under section 47 CPC rather than under Order XXI Rule 90 does not widen the available grounds (1190054_2).

common_material_facts: The judgment-debtor or owner alleges that the property was sold for far less than its worth.
No fraud or material irregularity in publication or conduct of the sale was alleged or proved.
There was no reliable evidence that the property was worth substantially more.
The sale was a court execution or auction sale, or a revenue sale.
statutes_and_provisions: Order XXI Rule 90 CPC (fraud or material irregularity plus substantial injury)
Section 47 CPC
Order XXI Rules 54, 64, 66-68 CPC (proclamation and sale procedure)
Kayjay Industries v. Asnew Drums (court sale is a forced sale)
Saheb Khan v. Mohd. Yousufuddin
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 6 members, inadequacy of price alone did not justify setting aside the sale. In 1362442_11 the sale was nonetheless set aside on other grounds, and in 155745050_2 the executing court's dismissal of the objection was restored.
variations: Some members rest expressly on Order XXI Rule 90's requirement of substantial injury (1190054_2, 1362442_11, 155745050_2); others state the principle without citing a provision (1529365_2, 844274_7).
155745050_2 is a fuller procedural-compliance case, covering notice period, publicity, multiple bidders and disclosed valuations.
1641051_2 turns on an evidentiary failure to prove higher value, and on mortgage encumbrances and the absence of fraud.
844274_7 and 1641051_2 concern revenue sales, while the others concern court execution sales.

legal_question: Can the State take or retain possession of private property, or evict occupants, by executive action without following a procedure authorised by law, and what follows when it does so?

predicates.state_took_or_seeks_possession_of_proper: The State or government has taken, retained, or is trying to obtain possession of private property or premises from an owner or occupant.
predicates.no_lawful_authority_or_prescribed_proces: The possession was taken or sought by executive action, force, or by invoking a power that does not apply to the person or situation, without a legally prescribed acquisition, eviction or possession procedure.
predicates.owner_or_occupant_entitled_to_protection: The affected person is an owner whose title is admitted or not disputed by the State, or an occupant (such as a continuing tenant) whom the invoked power does not cover.
predicates.state_action_is_unlawful_and_possession_: The State's taking, retention or forcible eviction is impermissible; it must proceed through a procedure recognised by law, and the owner must be compensated where property was taken without such process.

definition: The State cannot deprive a person of property or possession except by authority of law and a legally prescribed procedure. A general power to secure possession, a public-purpose claim, or an enforcement power meant for other persons or processes does not justify self-help or forcible eviction. Where property was taken without lawful process, the owner is entitled to lawful acquisition and compensation.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not bar the State from acquiring or recovering possession through a procedure that is authorised by law and followed.
A statutory force power applies only to the class of persons it names, for example non-tenants without written authority. It cannot be used against tenants or others outside that class.

The compensation consequence is stated only for the unlawful-taking and owner-title-conceded members. The eviction members require possession to be obtained in due course of law, without a separate compensation ruling.
The Court did not decide whether the 1976 West Bengal Act applies only to residential premises.

common_material_facts: The State took or kept possession of property by executive action, without acquisition proceedings or a lawful possession process.
The State relied on a statutory power or a public-interest justification that did not fit the situation.
The owner or occupant remained entitled to protection, through admitted title or continuing tenancy.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 300A and former Article 31 of the Constitution
Section 4(8) of the Great Eastern Hotel (Acquisition of Undertaking) Act, 1980
Section 6A of the West Bengal Government Premises (Tenancy Regulation) Act, 1976
Section 47 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 6 members hold the State's action unlawful. Two (the road-taking and the retained-possession cases) direct compensation or lawful acquisition. Four (the hotel-acquisition issues) hold that possession must be obtained in due course of law and that the invoked power or justification does not authorise forcible eviction.
variations: Two members concern uncompensated taking of land and rest on Article 300A and the right to property as a human right.
Four members concern the scope of statutory possession and enforcement powers in a hotel acquisition and eviction dispute.

The reasoning differs: no legal process at all, a power that does not authorise force, a public-interest claim rejected, a power limited to non-tenants, and an inapplicable analogy to Section 47 of the Land Acquisition Act.

split_suggestion: Optionally split into (a) uncompensated taking or retention of land without acquisition under Article 300A (127924004_1, 46771491_2) and (b) limits on statutory possession, enforcement and eviction powers (1338325_2, 1338325_3, 1338325_4, 1338325_6).

legal_question: Does a statutory provision barring courts from questioning orders made under the Act (or excluding civil suits) prevent a court from examining an order that was made without jurisdiction, outside the statute, or in breach of fundamental procedure or natural justice?

rule.if: challenge_to_statutory_order_protected_by_bar and (order_made_without_essential_jurisdictional_prerequisite or order_outside_statutory_scope_or_authority or order_in_breach_of_fundamental_procedure_or_natural_justice) and not authority_properly_exercised_jurisdiction

predicates.challenge_to_statutory_order_protected_b: A court challenge is brought against an order or action under a statute that contains a clause barring or excluding court challenges or civil suits.
predicates.order_made_without_essential_jurisdictio: The authority made the order without a jurisdictional fact or statutory prerequisite on which its power depended (for example a prior requisition or an actual vacancy).
predicates.order_outside_statutory_scope_or_authori: The order or action falls outside the statute or beyond the limited authority conferred on the tribunal or officer, so it is a nullity for jurisdictional error.
predicates.order_in_breach_of_fundamental_procedure: The order was made in violation of fundamental principles of judicial procedure, without relevant evidence, without reasonable opportunity to be heard, or without vital procedural requirements.
predicates.authority_properly_exercised_jurisdictio: The authority acted within its jurisdiction and followed the required procedure, so only the correctness or propriety of the order is in question.
predicates.statutory_bar_does_not_oust_court_review: The statutory bar does not prevent the court from entertaining the challenge and examining the order, which may be set aside or quashed.

definition: A clause barring court challenges protects only orders validly made within the authority's jurisdiction and procedure. Courts may still examine, and set aside, orders made without a jurisdictional prerequisite, outside the statute, or in breach of fundamental procedure or natural justice. They cannot review the propriety of orders made in the proper exercise of jurisdiction.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the authority properly exercised its jurisdiction, the court cannot examine the propriety or merits of the order.

Where a statute provides appellate remedies, the court ordinarily directs the aggrieved person to them, and entertains a suit only if the order is prima facie a nullity, outside the statute, or vital procedures were not followed (demolition context).

Where a statutory bar concerns claims against the Government, it does not apply if the Government is only a formal party and no substantive relief is sought against it; it does apply where the claim cannot be separated from relief against the Government.
Exclusion of civil court jurisdiction is not readily inferred.

common_material_facts: A statute contained a clause barring court challenges to orders made under it, or barring civil suits.
The challenge alleged that the authority lacked a jurisdictional prerequisite (requisition, vacancy), acted outside the statute, or violated procedure or natural justice.
Several cases involved rent control, allotment, rent-fixing or land acquisition orders.
statutes_and_provisions: Assam Land (Requisition and Acquisition) Act, 1948, ss. 3, 4, 11
U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, ss. 7, 7A, 16
Section 8(1) and s. 3(2) of the rent-fixing statute
Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876, s. 4(a)
Code of Civil Procedure, s. 9
Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, ss. 343(4)-(5), 347E
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 6 members the statutory bar was held not to prevent court examination of the challenged order, in 5 because of a jurisdictional defect, outside-statute action or procedural violation, and in 1 because the Government was a formal party. Two members also limit review: no review of propriety where jurisdiction was properly exercised, and a preference for statutory remedies in demolition cases.
variations: The ground of review differs: missing prerequisite (1208823_2, 1212607_2), no evidence and procedural violation (1552948_2), limited tribunal exceeding authority with the Government as a formal party (472343_4), natural justice (80590_2), and jurisdictional error or vital procedure (863497_1).
Some members concern civil suits and others review of orders in other proceedings, such as a reference or the State's revisionary power.
863497_1 conditions entertaining the suit on a prima facie nullity and the availability of statutory appeals; 80590_2 states the limit on review of propriety most clearly.
472343_4 turns partly on the Government's formal-party status rather than only on jurisdictional error.

legal_question: Can the government or a superior executive authority direct a statutory authority (a Collector or development authority) to take a particular action in respect of land that the governing statute commits to that authority, where the direction is unauthorised, bypasses the prescribed procedure, or conflicts with the statute's purposes?

predicates.statutory_authority_vested_with_power_ov: The governing statute or rules assign the decision on transfer, allotment, disposal or reconveyance of the land to a designated statutory authority such as a Collector or development authority.
predicates.government_or_superior_authority_directs: The State Government, a Minister or another superior executive authority directs the statutory authority to take a particular action on an individual matter concerning the land.
predicates.direction_not_authorized_by_statute: No provision of the statute, rules or the Constitution (including a valid government order under Article 166) authorises the direction, or the general supervisory or direction power relied on does not extend to individual matters.
predicates.direction_conflicts_with_statutory_purpo: The directed action is contrary to the purposes of the Act, the development scheme, or the specific conditions and rules governing the power.
predicates.prescribed_statutory_procedure_bypassed: The statutory inquiry, process or conditions prescribed for exercising the power were not followed.
predicates.direction_and_resulting_action_invalid_a: The direction does not bind the statutory authority, and any permission, allotment or transfer made under it is invalid and liable to be set aside.

definition: A statutory power over land must be exercised by the authority named in the statute, in the prescribed manner and for the statute's purposes. A government direction that is unauthorised, bypasses the prescribed procedure or runs contrary to the statute's purposes is not binding, and action taken under it is invalid. General supervisory or direction powers do not let the government usurp the authority's function.
exceptions_or_limits: Government directions are valid where the statute authorises them and they are necessary or expedient for carrying out the Act's purposes (e.g. Section 65 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act).
Where the statute requires prior State approval for disposal, the State may exercise that approval role, but it cannot itself take over the disposal function.
The reconveyance issue rests on the absence of any statutory power to reconvey; it does not turn on a government direction.

outlier_members.reason: This issue concerns the absence of statutory power in a development authority to reconvey acquired land, so a writ cannot compel it. It involves no government direction or usurpation of the authority's function, although it is related in lacking statutory authority.

common_material_facts: Land is vested in, or its disposal is entrusted by statute to, a Collector or development authority.
The State Government, a Minister or the Chief Minister directs a particular transfer, allotment, reconveyance or conversion of the land.
The directed action departs from the statutory scheme, such as an open space or civic amenity site, the prescribed process or the authority's own rules.
The authority often implemented the direction without exercising its own independent judgment.
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 89, 89A and 126 of the Tenancy Act
Sections 15(3), 19(4), 32(5), 38-A and 65 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976
Article 166 of the Constitution
Sections 58, 72 and 73 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, and Rules 3–5 and 19–20 of the 1975 Rules
Section 29(2) of the City of Bangalore Improvement Act, 1945
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 5 of 6 members the government direction and the resulting permission, allotment or transfer were held invalid or not binding. The sixth held that a development authority cannot be compelled to reconvey land because it has no statutory power to do so.
variations: One member relies on the doctrine that a power must be exercised in the prescribed manner (Taylor v. Taylor) and on the limits of Section 126; others rely on Section 65 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act.
One member also tests the direction against Article 166 and the objective validity of public orders.
Some members protect specific public uses (parks, civic amenity sites, roads), while others concern general disposal of authority land or a transfer of agricultural land for industrial use.
One member (1271427_1) is purely about lack of statutory power to reconvey, with no government direction.

split_suggestion: Keep the five members on invalid government directions to statutory authorities together. Treat 1271427_1 (no statutory power to reconvey acquired land) as a separate issue on the limits of a development authority's statutory powers, or pair it with 1271427_5, which arises from the same case.

legal_question: Does a final decision on the merits by a competent court or tribunal, including in a constitutional writ proceeding or quasi-judicial proceeding that is not itself a suit, bar the same parties or their privies from relitigating the same issue or matter in a later proceeding?

rule.if: prior_competent_forum_decision_on_merits and prior_decision_final_not_reversed_or_modified and same_parties_or_privies and same_issue_or_matter_directly_decided and later_proceeding_seeks_to_relitigate

predicates.prior_competent_forum_decision_on_merits: An earlier proceeding (a suit, a writ petition under Article 32 or 226, or a quasi-judicial tribunal proceeding) was decided on the merits by a forum with jurisdiction, after a contest or a fair opportunity to contest.
predicates.prior_decision_final_not_reversed_or_mod: The earlier decision has attained finality and has not been reversed or modified through an appropriate appeal, review or constitutional remedy.
predicates.same_parties_or_privies: The later proceeding is between the same parties as the earlier one, or between persons claiming under them (privies).
predicates.same_issue_or_matter_directly_decided: The issue or matter raised in the later proceeding is the same as one directly and substantially decided in the earlier proceeding (the same facts and the same or similar relief, where relief is relevant).
predicates.later_proceeding_seeks_to_relitigate: The later suit or petition seeks to reopen or re-agitate the issue or matter already decided.
predicates.later_proceeding_barred_by_res_judicata: The later suit or petition is barred, or the decided issue cannot be reopened, under Section 11 CPC or the general principle of res judicata.

definition: Res judicata rests on public policy and finality and is not confined to the technical terms of Section 11 CPC. A final merits decision of a competent court, writ court or quasi-judicial tribunal binds the same parties or their privies on the same issue in later proceedings, unless it has been reversed or modified through an appropriate remedy.
exceptions_or_limits: The earlier forum must have been competent; a judgment of a court lacking inherent jurisdiction is a nullity and creates no bar.
The earlier decision must be on the merits, after a contest or fair opportunity to prove the case, and final; a decision reversed or modified through an appropriate procedure does not bar.
The parties (or privies) and the issue or matter must be the same.
A final finding may be reconsidered by the Court itself in changed circumstances, but cannot be unilaterally displaced by a legislature (as stated in the dam safety member).

common_material_facts: An earlier proceeding (writ petition, suit, constitutional proceeding between States, or quasi-judicial application) was contested and decided on the merits.
A later suit or petition between the same parties raised the same issue, facts or relief.
The earlier decision was final: appeal confirmed, review dismissed, or not reversed or modified.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (including Explanation VIII), treated as non-exhaustive
Articles 32 and 226 of the Constitution of India
Daryao v. State of U.P.
Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Dr. Shree Krishna Sinha
Raj Lakshmi Dasi v. Banamali Sen
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 6 members, the later suit or petition was barred by res judicata or by a principle analogous to it. Of these, 4 involve earlier writ or constitutional proceedings, 1 an earlier civil suit, and 1 a quasi-judicial tribunal decision.
variations: The earlier forum varies: a High Court or Supreme Court writ proceeding, a civil suit, or a quasi-judicial rent-control authority.
The later proceeding varies: a regular suit, a fresh Article 32 petition, or an original suit between States.
Some members apply Section 11 directly, while others apply the general principle that goes beyond Section 11 because the earlier proceeding was not a suit.
In one member, the petition was not pressed in the earlier proceeding after an adverse interpretation of the law, and the decision was still treated as one on the merits.
The dam safety member adds that a final finding may be revisited by the Court in changed circumstances, but not unilaterally displaced by a legislature.

legal_question: On an application to reject a plaint under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (no cause of action, or suit barred by law), what material may the court consider, and does it decide the application on the plaint alone, without the defendant's written statement, defence or evidence?

predicates.application_to_reject_plaint: A party has applied under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint.
predicates.cause_of_action_ground: The application asserts that the plaint discloses no cause of action.
predicates.apparent_legal_bar_ground: The application asserts that the suit appears from the plaint's statements to be barred by law, for example by limitation.
predicates.court_decides_application_on_plaint_aver: The court decides the application only on the plaint's averments, assumed true and read as a whole, together with documents the plaintiff filed with and relied on in the plaint, and disregards the written statement, the defendant's pleas and evidence recorded outside the plaint. It does not defer the decision until the written statement is filed.

definition: When a plaint is challenged under Order VII Rule 11(a) or (d), the court must decide the application from the plaint's averments, read meaningfully and as a whole, together with the documents the plaintiff relies on. The defendant's written statement, disputed merits and evidence outside the plaint are irrelevant, and the application should be decided before the defendant is required to file a written statement. The power may be exercised at any stage before the trial concludes.
exceptions_or_limits: Documents filed with and relied on by the plaintiff as the basis of the plaint (Order VII Rule 14) may be considered as part of the plaint.
The plaint's factual allegations are taken as true, but a sham or illusory cause of action created by clever drafting may still be rejected.
Rejection applies to the plaint as a whole; Order VII Rule 11 does not permit rejecting only part of a plaint or particular reliefs. Improper matter is dealt with under Order VI Rule 16.
Where the plaint as a whole discloses a cause of action and shows no legal bar, the application must be dismissed; where it discloses none or shows a bar, rejection is mandatory.
The decision cannot depend on evidence led in the trial, such as cross-examination answers.

common_material_facts: A defendant or owner applied under Order VII Rule 11 on the grounds of no cause of action and/or a legal bar such as limitation.
The defendant's written statement, defence pleas or evidence outside the plaint was invoked or relied upon by a court or party.
The courts below sometimes erred by looking beyond the plaint, by delaying the decision until the written statement was filed, or by reading the plaint in parts.
statutes_and_provisions: Code of Civil Procedure, Order VII Rule 11(a) and (d)
Order VII Rule 14(1)
Order VI Rule 2
Order VI Rule 16
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all six members the application is decided on the plaint alone. In about four, the court corrects a departure from that approach (a direction to file a written statement first, reliance on cross-examination, a part-wise reading, or reliance on defence material). One affirms rejection based on the plaint and its sale deed. One affirms a remittal after defence material was relied on.
variations: One member allows consideration of documents filed with and relied on in the plaint, such as a sale deed.
One member stresses that the plaint must be read as a whole and that partial rejection is not allowed.
One member concerns the timing of the decision, which must come before the written statement is required.
One member concerns evidence recorded at trial, such as cross-examination, and holds it cannot be used.
Outcomes differ: rejection affirmed, rejection set aside, application dismissed, or remand.

legal_question: Does a statutory power to prohibit, restrict or control exports include the power to canalise export trade through selected agencies and exclude other participants, and is such canalisation, with a preference for a state trading agency and exclusion of new entrants, a reasonable restriction on the right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g) and 19(6)?

predicates.export_control_case: The dispute challenges an export restriction or licensing scheme made under export-control legislation or a delegated order.
predicates.government_has_statutory_power_to_contro: The governing statute empowers the government to prohibit, restrict or otherwise control exports, and the order permits licensing authorities to channel exports through special or specialised agencies or channels.
predicates.export_trade_is_channelled_through_selec: Exports of the commodity are routed through selected agencies or classes of exporters (for example, a state trading corporation and established exporters), so that other persons, such as newcomers, are excluded from direct export.
predicates.canalisation_and_resulting_exclusion_of_: The canalisation provision is within the delegated rule-making power, and the exclusion of some participants is a permissible reasonable restriction in the public interest, provided it rests on a rational basis.

definition: A power to control exports includes the power to canalise exports through selected agencies and to classify and limit who may export. Excluding newcomers and preferring a suitable state agency is a reasonable restriction under Article 19(6) where it has a rational basis in the nature of the trade and public export objectives such as regular, uniform-quality supply and foreign-exchange earnings.
exceptions_or_limits: The reasonableness holding depends on a rational basis for the classification and selection, for example a negligible domestic market, a need for reliable and uniform supply, and an agency suited to those objectives.

Exclusion alone does not show an unlawful restriction, but the challenger may succeed by showing improper inclusion of comparable participants or that the selected agency is unsuitable; none of the members found this shown.
