Article 19(6)(ii) does not itself authorise a state monopoly by administrative action; the restriction must be justified under the general reasonable-restrictions limb.
The reasonableness holding was by majority; Subba Rao J. dissented in one member, finding the effects on excluded mine owners unreasonable.
A selected agency need not have prior expertise in the trade; it is 'special' because it is selected to advance the canalisation purpose.

common_material_facts: Manganese ore exports controlled through quotas and selected categories of exporters under an export control order
Order allowed licensing authorities to channel exports through special or specialised agencies
Negligible domestic market, with the ore produced mainly for export
Newcomers without export performance in specified earlier years were excluded and could sell only to established exporters or the state trading corporation
Government aimed at regular supplies of uniform quality, continuity of trade and foreign-exchange earnings
The appellant did not allege that established exporters were improperly included
statutes_and_provisions: Section 3, Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1947
Clause 6(h), Export Control Order, 1958
Article 19(1)(g)
Article 19(6) (first part) and 19(6)(ii)
Glass Chatons Importers and Users Association v. Union of India
Saghir Ahmad v. State of Uttar Pradesh (referred to)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All six members uphold the scheme. Three (1405373_1, 247451_1, 29862148_1) hold that canalisation is within the statutory power. Three (1405373_2, 247451_2, 29862148_2) hold that exclusion of newcomers and preference for the state trading corporation is not an unreasonable restriction. 247451_2 carried a dissent.
variations: Three members address vires of the statute and order, and three address the Article 19(1)(g) reasonableness of the restriction.
The vires members rely on Glass Chatons; the reasonableness members rely on the rational basis of the classification.
Rules differ in phrasing: some require the full set of factual conditions, while 247451_1 is broader (restricted or channelled exports).
Subba Rao J. dissented on reasonableness in 247451_2.

legal_question: Does property that has the character of Hindu joint-family property lose that character, and become the separate property of one member, merely because the coparcenary is reduced to a sole coparcener or the family status is severed, while the property remains unpartitioned and other family members (such as widows or daughters) have continuing rights?

rule.if: joint_family_property_character_dispute and property_was_joint_family_property and (only_one_coparcener_remains or family_status_severed_without_partition or sole_coparcener_received_property_on_partition) and not property_validly_partitioned_or_separately_acquired

predicates.joint_family_property_character_dispute: The case turns on whether certain property is joint-family property or the separate property of an individual member.
predicates.property_was_joint_family_property: The property was impressed with joint-family (ancestral or coparcenary) character before the event relied on to change its character.
predicates.only_one_coparcener_remains: Through death or partition, the coparcenary has been reduced to a single male coparcener, with female family members (widow, wife or daughters) still part of or having rights in the family.
predicates.family_status_severed_without_partition: A member has declared an intention to sever the joint status, but the property has not been divided by metes and bounds.
predicates.sole_coparcener_received_property_on_par: A coparcener received joint-family property on partition and has no son or other male coparcener, though he has a wife or daughters.
predicates.property_validly_partitioned_or_separate: The property has actually been partitioned among the members, or was the separate property of the holder before it came to him, rather than property already impressed with joint-family character.
predicates.property_retains_joint_family_character: The property remains joint-family property (and the family may be assessed or treated as a joint family) and is not the individual property of the sole or severing member.

definition: Joint-family property does not become the separate property of a single member merely because the coparcenary shrinks to one coparcener or because family status is severed. It retains joint-family character until it is actually partitioned, with the rights of widows, wives, daughters and possible future sons remaining relevant.
exceptions_or_limits: Does not apply to property that was the separate property of the holder before it came to him, rather than already impressed with joint-family character.
Does not apply once the property has been actually partitioned among the members.

The maintenance right of a widow of a predeceased son against the father-in-law's estate is a distinct point and does not itself decide the character of the property; it lasts only while she does not remarry.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns a widow's right to maintenance from her father-in-law's estate while unmarried, not the retention of joint-family character by property.

common_material_facts: Ancestral or joint-family property held by brothers or a father and sons
One coparcener died or the coparcenary was reduced to a sole survivor
A widow, wife or daughters remained in the family, often with a maintenance right
A claim that the property had become the sole coparcener's or a member's personal property
statutes_and_provisions: Wealth Tax Act 1957, sections 3 and 5(1)(ii)
Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act 1956, section 19 (held not to govern in the outlier)
Hindu Women's Right to Property Act 1937, section 3(2) (outlier)
Gowli Buddanna v. CIT, Mysore
Attorney General of Ceylon v. A.R. Arunachalam Chettiar
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 5 covered members the property retained its joint-family character: 3 sole-coparcener cases after a death, 1 sole coparcener after partition, 1 severance without partition. The sixth member is an outlier on widow's maintenance.
variations: The reduction to one coparcener arose from death in some members and from partition in another.
One member concerns severance of status without partition rather than a sole coparcener.
The supporting female-member rights vary: widow's maintenance, or wife and daughters with a possible son born or adopted.
The setting varies between civil property disputes and wealth-tax assessment.

split_suggestion: Treat 1849559_1 (a widow's maintenance right against a father-in-law's estate) as a separate cluster. Keep the other five together as the joint-family-character group.

legal_question: Under the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, is a landlord's eviction suit that requires official permission maintainable, depending on whether the permission was effective when the suit was instituted (or the decree passed) or was revoked or cancelled before or after institution?

predicates.eviction_suit_requiring_permission: The landlord's eviction suit falls in a category for which the statute requires prior official permission to sue.
predicates.permission_cancelled_or_revoked_before_f: The Commissioner or the State Government actually cancelled or revoked the permission before the suit was instituted, leaving no effective permission at filing.
predicates.permission_effective_at_institution: A valid permission was in force when the suit was filed, so the suit was validly instituted.
predicates.restored_permission_effective_before_dec: The original permission, after being revoked, was restored by the State Government setting aside the revocation, and it was effective when the decree was passed.
predicates.suit_is_maintainable_and_later_revocatio: The suit is maintainable, and a later revocation by the State Government does not make it incompetent or the decree unenforceable.

definition: An eviction suit needing statutory permission is maintainable if valid permission existed when it was instituted. A later State Government revocation does not defeat it, because the revisional power is exhausted once the suit is validly instituted. A cancellation or revocation made before filing leaves no valid permission, and the suit is not maintainable. Where the Government sets aside a revocation, the restored permission supports the suit if it is effective when the decree is passed.
exceptions_or_limits: If the Commissioner cancels or the State Government revokes permission before the suit is instituted, the suit lacks valid permission and is not maintainable (404039_1, 404039_2).

The protection applies only to suits validly instituted under permission; a mere pending application for revocation before filing does not by itself defeat the suit, since the actual revocation came only after filing.
Where the Government directs that restored permission takes effect later, maintainability depends on its being effective when the decree is passed (1472953_1).
The rule rests on the absence of statutory language making a validly instituted suit incompetent or a decree inexecutable; it does not cover express statutory provisions to the contrary.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns whether a rent-deposit direction under section 11A of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act survives the setting aside of an ex parte decree. It does not concern permission to sue under the U.P. Act.

common_material_facts: Landlord needs permission from the District Magistrate, the Commissioner or the State Government before suing for eviction.
Permission was granted, often by the Commissioner on revision, and the tenant sought revision or revocation before the State Government.
The timing of the revocation or cancellation relative to the filing of the suit and the passing of the decree is decisive.
A decree was often passed before the State Government's revocation order.
statutes_and_provisions: U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, sections 3(1), 3(3), 3(4), 7-F and 14
Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1947, section 11A (outlier only)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In the 5 covered members, a revocation after valid institution does not defeat the suit (3: 404039_3, 80590_1, and 1472953_1 where permission was restored and effective before decree). A cancellation or revocation before institution leaves the suit without valid permission (2: 404039_1, 404039_2).
variations: 404039_1 concerns cancellation by the Commissioner, while 404039_2 and 404039_3 concern revocation by the State Government.
1472953_1 involves revocation by the Commissioner that was later set aside by the State Government, restoring the permission, rather than a final revocation.

Earlier cases are treated differently: Bhagwan Das v. Paras Nath is followed or distinguished; Bashi Ram v. Mantri Lal is upheld on State Government revocation but disapproved on Commissioner cancellation.

split_suggestion: Remove 197746_3 as a separate issue on rent-deposit directions after an ex parte decree is set aside. The other five can stay together, or be split into 'before-filing revocation (not maintainable)' (404039_1, 404039_2) and 'after-filing or restored permission (maintainable)' (404039_3, 80590_1, 1472953_1).

legal_question: Does a later-enacted law or amendment restricting, invalidating or deeming the effect of transfers apply to a transfer completed before that law took effect, where the law is not expressly retrospective?

predicates.transfer_proceeding_challenging_validity: The proceeding questions the validity, legal effect or tax or ceiling treatment of a transfer, gift or surrender of property under a statutory restriction, ceiling or duty provision.
predicates.transfer_completed_before_later_law_took: The transfer was made and completed before the commencement of the later law, amendment or trigger period relied on to attack it or alter its treatment.
predicates.later_law_not_expressly_retrospective: The later law, amendment or provision does not operate retrospectively by express words or necessary implication, and its operative period or reference excludes the earlier transfer.
predicates.later_law_does_not_apply_to_prior_transf: The later law or amendment does not govern, invalidate or alter the treatment of the earlier transfer, which is judged under the law in force when it was made.

definition: A statute or amendment that restricts, invalidates or deems the effect of transfers operates prospectively unless it says otherwise. It does not reach a transfer completed before it came into force, and that transfer is judged under the law then in force.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the later law is expressly or by necessary implication retrospective.
The earlier transfer must still comply with the law in force when it was made. One member noted that no breach of any other provision then in force had been shown.
Where the earlier regime itself restricts the transfer, for example by a restriction still in force and unperfected title, the transfer may still be affected under that earlier regime.
Some members add that the transfer must be bona fide, or that a statutory reference to a specific earlier law cannot be read as a later one.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns reading down a recovery law so it does not reach transfers outside the restriction or titles already perfected by prescription. The temporal element (title perfected before commencement) overlaps, but the other limbs, expiry of the restriction and no breach, are not about later-law prospectivity.

common_material_facts: The transfer, gift or surrender took place before the commencement of the later statute or amendment.
The later provision either was not retrospective or named a specific earlier law or a later trigger period.
The later law was invoked to cancel, void or re-tax the earlier transfer.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 50-B, Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, and Section 18, A.P. General Clauses Act
Sections 3(2) and 5, Rajasthan Urban Property (Restrictions of Transfers) Act, 1973, and its 1978 repeal; Section 5, Rajasthan Urban Property Ceiling Act, 1972
Section 10 proviso, Estate Duty Act, 1953, as amended by the Finance Act, 1965
Sections 6 and 40, Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings Act, 1973
Section 46, Chota Nagpur Tenancy Act, 1908
Sections 4 and 5 of a land-grant transfer recovery law (outlier)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all five covered members the later provision was held not to apply to the earlier transfer, which survived. The sixth member (outlier) read down a recovery law to protect perfected titles.
variations: Some members turn on a specific statutory reference (the 1961 ceiling law) rather than on general non-retrospectivity.
One member relies on an interpretive refusal to use a later amendment to change the meaning of the earlier provision.
One member adds a bona fide requirement.
One member concerns an earlier restriction law that only deemed the transferor to remain owner and did not void the transfer, and the later ban applied only to post-commencement transfers.

split_suggestion: Keep the five prospectivity members together. Treat 1545120_2's cousin 1545120_5 (reading down a recovery law to protect perfected titles and non-breaching transfers) as a separate group on the scope and constitutional reading-down of transfer-recovery statutes.

legal_question: Does a joint Hindu family member's unilateral declaration of an intention to separate sever joint status only where the intention is clear and unequivocal and has been communicated or made known to the affected co-sharers?

predicates.joint_hindu_family_severance_claim: A party asserts that a member's status in a joint Hindu family (Mitakshara coparcenary) was severed or that a separation or partition occurred.
predicates.unilateral_declaration_of_intention_to_s: A member, acting on his own, expressed in a document (trust deed, will, notice, deed of allotment) or by conduct an intention to hold his share separately.
predicates.declaration_clear_and_unequivocal: The declaration is definite and unambiguous, is not merely conditional or contingent, and does not itself treat the property as remaining joint.
predicates.intention_communicated_or_made_known_to_: The intention reached the knowledge of the co-sharers affected, by a process appropriate to the circumstances. This may be proved by actual notice, by knowledge of the contents, or by inference from the document, surrounding circumstances and subsequent conduct. Formal dispatch or receipt is not essential.
predicates.joint_family_status_severed: The member's status in the joint family stands severed, whether or not the property has been divided by metes and bounds.

definition: A member of a joint Hindu family may sever joint status unilaterally by a definite, unequivocal declaration of an intention to separate. The declaration takes effect only if it is brought to the knowledge of the affected co-sharers. An uncommunicated, conditional or equivocal declaration, including one in a trust deed or will, does not sever status.
exceptions_or_limits: An uncommunicated declaration is only an unexpressed intention and has no effect. Where the declarant dies before the affected member learns of it, no severance occurs.

A declaration that is conditional, or a will that treats the property as joint, directs it to remain joint, or denies that the property is ancestral, does not unequivocally express an intention to separate.
Communication need not take the form of formal dispatch or receipt. Knowledge of the contents is enough, and it may be inferred from the document, surrounding circumstances and subsequent conduct.
Once severance has occurred it cannot be undone by mere withdrawal of the communication, absent reunion.
Mere presence of an affected member's guardian in the house does not establish knowledge of the contents of the declaration.

common_material_facts: A member of a Mitakshara joint family relied on a document (trust deed, will, notice or deed of allotment) as a declaration of an intention to separate.
The dispute was whether the intention was clear and unequivocal and whether it was communicated to or known by the affected co-sharers.
In several members the declaration was conditional or ambiguous, or was not shown to have reached the affected co-sharer.
statutes_and_provisions: Mitakshara Hindu law of partition and severance of status
Girja Bai v. Sadashiv Dhundiraj
A. Raghavamma v. A. Chenchamma
Puttrangamma v. M.S. Ranganna
Suraj Narain v. Iqbal Narain
Bal Krishan v. Ram Krishan
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Severance was held not to have occurred in 4 of 6 members (two trust-deed declarations never communicated, a will whose contents were not shown to have reached the affected member before the testator's death, and a will that was not unequivocal). Severance was held to have occurred in 2 of 6 members (an intercepted notice whose contents were known to the family, and a deed of allotment with exclusive enjoyment and subsequent conduct).
variations: The instrument differed: trust deed, will, notice or allotment deed.

Communication was proved by actual knowledge of the contents despite interception of the notice, or inferred from the deed and subsequent conduct such as exclusive enjoyment, separate revenue records and the family's acquiescence.
One member turned on the lack of an unequivocal declaration in the will's terms, not on communication.
One member (388201_6) rejected the contrary approach in Narayana Rao v. Purushothama Rao and declined to accept it insofar as Indira v. Sivaprasada Rao followed it.

legal_question: Once a compensation determination, payment or related direction in land-acquisition matters has become final or been satisfied at an earlier stage, can it be reopened, recalled or reappropriated in later proceedings (reference, appeal, execution or fresh acquisition proceedings)?

rule.if: land_compensation_matter_in_later_proceeding and earlier_compensation_determination_or_payment_final_or_satisfied and later_proceeding_seeks_to_reopen_or_reallocate_that_earlier_matter and not (earlier_matter_void_for_want_of_jurisdiction or court_expressly_directs_otherwise)

predicates.land_compensation_matter_in_later_procee: The dispute arises in a later stage or proceeding (reference, appeal, execution, fresh determination or later acquisition proceeding) concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.earlier_compensation_determination_or_pa: An earlier award, valuation, court direction or payment or deposit of compensation has attained finality, for example through dismissal of a challenge, non-challenge or acting upon it, or has been satisfied or paid.
predicates.later_proceeding_seeks_to_reopen_or_real: A party seeks to re-agitate, recompute, reappropriate or obtain repeat payment on the earlier final or satisfied matter, as distinct from dealing with a fresh enhancement or component.
predicates.earlier_matter_void_for_want_of_jurisdic: The earlier determination or award is a jurisdictional nullity (not merely erroneous), or the later enhancement or benefit was granted without jurisdiction, so that it can be challenged.
predicates.court_expressly_directs_otherwise: The court expressly directs a different treatment, such as fresh determination of compensation.
predicates.earlier_final_or_satisfied_compensation_: The earlier final or satisfied compensation matter stands and cannot be reopened, reappropriated or paid again in the later proceeding.

definition: Compensation determinations, directions and payments in land acquisition that have become final or been satisfied at an earlier stage bind the parties and cannot be reopened, reappropriated or paid again in later reference, appellate, execution or acquisition proceedings. Only later enhancements or components, or jurisdictionally void orders, can be addressed afresh.
exceptions_or_limits: A jurisdictional nullity, or a benefit or enhancement awarded without jurisdiction, may be challenged in execution (s.47 CPC) or set aside; mere error in exercising jurisdiction cannot be corrected in execution.
An unlawful later enhancement may be set aside even though the original award stays final.

Where the court sets aside decisions and orders fresh determination, it may expressly protect recipients from refund of enhanced amounts already paid; this is a direction protecting payments rather than reopening them.
Each later enhancement is dealt with at its own stage, with interest on the enhanced amount under the statutory scheme.

common_material_facts: An earlier award, valuation, direction or payment had become final or was satisfied.
A later stage (reference, appeal, execution or fresh acquisition proceeding) was invoked to reopen or reallocate it.
The party seeking to reopen had not challenged the earlier decision or had its challenge dismissed.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act 1894 ss. 18, 23, 26, 28, 34, 53, 54
CPC s. 11 (res judicata), s. 47, Order XXI Rule 1
Article 226 of the Constitution
Himachal Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act 1972 s. 11
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: About five of six members hold that the earlier final or satisfied matter cannot be reopened (finality, res judicata, no repeat compensation, no reappropriation). The sixth protects already-paid enhanced compensation from refund on fresh determination.
variations: The basis differs: res judicata and issue estoppel, statutory scheme of successive stages, binding final valuation in execution, extinguishment of rights under ceiling law, or an express direction against refund.
One member allows an unlawful later enhancement to be set aside while keeping the original award final.
One member allows challenge in execution to additional benefits granted without jurisdiction.
The refund member (15173_6) concerns the consequence of setting aside, not finality of the earlier decisions, so it fits the rule only loosely.

split_suggestion: Optionally separate 15173_6 (no refund of enhanced compensation on fresh determination) from the finality and non-reopening members. Keep ceiling-law double compensation (25681951_2) as a sub-group if a narrower rule is needed.

legal_question: Where a construction contract describes time as essential but also provides for extensions of time and/or delay compensation, is the completion period of the essence, and if not, is an employer's rescission for delay without first fixing a further reasonable period wrongful, so that it cannot forfeit the contractor's security deposit?

rule.if: construction_contract_dispute and (contract_allows_extension or contract_provides_delay_compensation) and employer_rescinded_for_delay and employer_fixed_no_further_completion_period

predicates.construction_contract_dispute: The dispute arises out of a construction contract between an employer and a contractor.
predicates.contract_allows_extension: The contract empowers the employer or its engineer to extend the completion period on reasonable grounds.
predicates.contract_provides_delay_compensation: The contract provides for compensation for each day the work remains unfinished after the stipulated completion date.
predicates.employer_rescinded_for_delay: The employer rescinded the contract on the ground that the contractor did not complete the work within the stipulated period.
predicates.employer_fixed_no_further_completion_per: The employer did not give notice fixing a further reasonable period for completion and making time essential for that period before rescinding.
predicates.rescission_wrongful_and_security_forfeit: The rescission is a wrongful breach by the employer, and the employer cannot forfeit the contractor's security deposit on the basis of the contractor's alleged breach, so the deposit must be refunded.

definition: Even if a contract expressly says time is essential, extension and delay-compensation provisions can show that the completion period was not of the essence (or that the time was waived). An employer who rescinds for delay without first fixing a further reasonable period and making time essential for it acts wrongfully, and cannot forfeit the contractor's security deposit, which must be refunded along with any established dues.
exceptions_or_limits: Whether time is of the essence depends on the parties' intention from the contract as a whole; the rule applies only where the other terms displace the express time-essential stipulation or the stipulated time has been waived.
If time remained of the essence and was not waived or displaced, the requirement to fix a further period would not arise.
If the employer validly fixes a further reasonable period, makes time essential for it, and the contractor fails to complete within it, rescission may be justified.
Recovery of unpaid work and damages depends on the amounts being established, as found by the trial court in one member; nominal damages were restored there.

common_material_facts: The contract described time as essential but allowed the engineer to extend the period and provided for compensation for delay.
The contractor was permitted to continue work after the stipulated period expired and sought extensions before it expired.
The employer rescinded without fixing a further period and making time essential.
The employer forfeited the contractor's security deposit on rescission.
statutes_and_provisions: Halsbury's Laws of England, 4th ed., Vol. 4, para. 1179
Lamprell v. Billericay Union; Webb v. Hughes; Charles Rickards Ltd. v. Oppenheim
Clauses 2 and 6 of the contract (extension and delay compensation)
No statutory provision cited
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All six members favour the contractor: in two, time is held not of the essence; in two, rescission is held wrongful and illegal; in two, forfeiture of the security deposit is disallowed and refund ordered (with unpaid balance and nominal damages in one). The cluster contains two duplicated sets of three issues.
variations: The 186692596 set adds an alternative finding of waiver of the stipulated time.
The 1533730 set requires both an extension clause and a delay compensation clause, while the 186692596 set accepts either.
186692596_3 also awards the unpaid balance for completed work and nominal damages, beyond the refund of the deposit.
Members are staged: the first decides whether time is essential, the second whether rescission is wrongful, and the third the consequence for the security deposit.

legal_question: Under Section 3(2)(d) and Explanation (1) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, when is an inam grant of, or relating to, a village an 'estate', and does a grant expressed to be of a named village raise a presumption of estate status, and on whom lies the burden of proving or rebutting it where parts of the village were excluded or separately granted?

rule.if: inam_estate_classification_case and ((grant_expressed_as_named_village and not party_denying_estate_proved_exclusion_exception) or (grant_of_entire_village_proved and government_confirmed_or_recognised_whole_grant))

predicates.inam_estate_classification_case: The dispute turns on whether land held under an inam grant is an 'estate' under Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908 (including for rent reduction or occupancy rights consequences).
predicates.grant_expressed_as_named_village: The grant, as shown by the available records, is expressed to be a grant of a named village.
predicates.party_denying_estate_proved_exclusion_ex: The party contending that the land is not an estate has proved the facts taking the grant outside the definition, for example that the excluded minor inams were created by the grantor contemporaneously with or after the village grant and are not within the stated categories.
predicates.grant_of_entire_village_proved: The evidence establishes that the grant covered the entire village and not merely a substantial part of it.
predicates.government_confirmed_or_recognised_whole: The Government made, confirmed or recognised the grant as extending to the whole village and not to only part of its area.
predicates.land_is_an_estate_under_section_3_2_d: The land or village in question is held to be an 'estate' within the meaning of Section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, so that the consequential legislation (such as rent reduction or estate abolition) applies to it.

definition: An inam village is an estate only if the grant was of the whole village (or expressed as a grant of a named village, which Explanation (1) allows despite excluded lands). Most members hold that a named-village grant raises a rebuttable presumption of estate status, with the burden on the party denying it. One member holds that the Explanation creates no presumption either way, and where the grant was shown to be of less than the whole village, estate status fails.
exceptions_or_limits: The members conflict on whether a named-village grant raises a presumption. 1435737_1 and 872053_2 say it does, with the burden on the challenger. 1479218_2 says the Explanation creates no presumption either way, so the description alone does not establish the excluded lands' prior grant.

Where the claimant must prove estate status and the evidence shows only a substantial part of the village was granted, with no proof the grant was expressed as a named village or that the excluded lands were previously granted or reserved, the land is not an estate (1431341_1).
Where the grant was of less than the entire village and the Government confirmed only part of the area, with the excluded lands treated as separate property, the land is not an estate (795303_3).
Minor inams of immemorial or earlier origin, or created by the grantees, do not show reservation by the grantor and do not defeat estate status (703197_1).
The Explanation operates only if the grant is shown to be of a named village; Explanation (1-A) (1956) confirms that differing confirmation dates, title deeds or grantees do not defeat estate status.

common_material_facts: The original grant deed was unavailable, so the grant's scope was inferred from inam registers and other records.
Minor inams or excluded lands existed within the village, and there was no evidence of when they were created or whether the grantor carved them out.
The dispute arose in the context of rent reduction, occupancy rights or abolition-related estate status.
statutes_and_provisions: Madras Estates Land Act, 1908, s. 3(2)(d) and Explanation (1)
Explanation (1-A), inserted by Act XXXV of 1956
Act 2 of 1945, which added the Explanation and applied it from the 1936 amendment
Madras Estates Rent Reduction Act, 1947
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Estate status was upheld in 3 members (1435737_1, 872053_2, 703197_1). It was denied in 2 (1431341_1, 795303_3) because the grant was not shown to cover the whole village. 1479218_2 held that a named-village grant raises no presumption.
variations: Presumption: 1435737_1 and 872053_2 find a rebuttable presumption, with the burden on the challenger and no need to prove prior exclusion because of the non-obstante clause. 1479218_2 rejects the presumption.
Burden: 1431341_1 puts the burden on the claimant to prove estate status, whereas 1435737_1 and 872053_2 put it on the party denying estate status.

Evidence: 795303_3 turned on the partial confirmation and the zamindar's dealings with the excluded land. 703197_1 turned on the register's treatment of the whole extent, including poramboke, as granted.
1431341_1 records a difference among the judges on whether 'other tenure' is limited by ejusdem generis.

split_suggestion: Optionally split into (a) the presumption/burden question for named-village grants (1435737_1, 872053_2, 1479218_2) and (b) the fact-based question of whether the grant covered the whole village and was confirmed as such (1431341_1, 795303_3, 703197_1).

legal_question: Should a court decline to disturb a long-standing, settled judicial or administrative interpretation of a statute or legal rule when people have arranged their affairs and transactions in reliance on it?

predicates.settled_interpretation_long_standing: A statutory provision or legal rule has been consistently interpreted in the same way, by courts or by long-standing official practice, over a considerable period.
predicates.reliance_on_interpretation_in_transactio: People have entered into transactions, property dealings or titles, or arranged their affairs, in reliance on the established interpretation, or unsettling it would plausibly upset such reliance.
predicates.interpretation_clearly_erroneous_or_comp: The established interpretation is patently or clearly erroneous (for example, contrary to clear statutory language), or there is an exceptional or compelling public-interest reason to depart from it.
predicates.settled_interpretation_should_be_followe: The court should adhere to and apply the established interpretation rather than adopt a different one, leaving any needed correction to the legislature.

definition: Where a statutory provision or rule has been uniformly interpreted over a long period and transactions or property titles rest on it, a court will ordinarily follow and not disturb that interpretation (stare decisis or deference to settled construction), unless it is clearly erroneous or a compelling or exceptional reason requires departure. Any anomalies are left to the legislature.
exceptions_or_limits: Does not apply where the interpretation is patently erroneous or contrary to clear statutory language and no titles or transactions have been founded on it.
Departure is permitted where public interest compels it.
Practice or usage does not bind a court to perpetuate a mistaken interpretation; long-standing practice is mainly an aid where the statute is obscure.
Deference to a High Court's reading of a local statute is ordinary, not absolute, and may serve only as an additional reason supporting the result.
Legislative inaction or amendment of other provisions without change to the relevant one is treated as supporting caution, but is not independently decisive.

common_material_facts: An established interpretation had stood for a long period (decades in some cases).
Property transactions, titles or arrangements were made in reliance on that interpretation.
The challenge asked the court to adopt a different reading of a statute or rule.
Often the legislature amended related provisions without changing the relevant rule.
Several members involve local or State statutes (tenancy, building tax, money-lending, Hindu law alienations).
statutes_and_provisions: Local building-tax statute (High Court interpretation)
Municipal tax provision on tenant-built structures
Money-lending registration requirement
Bihar Tenancy Act and section 117 of the Transfer of Property Act
Local tenancy statute provisions on occupancy holdings
Hindu law rule on alienee's knowledge (Suraj Bunsi Koer)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 6 members leave the established interpretation or rule undisturbed and apply it, citing stare decisis, reliance and the need for certainty.
variations: Source of settled view: High Court decisions (16203461_4, 857581_1, 579475_1, 2376_2), municipal administrative practice (1916580_2), or an old Privy Council-era judicial rule (281138_3).
Strength of reliance on it: it was an additional reason in 16203461_4, but the primary basis in the others.
579475_1 followed the settled view even though its reasoning was open to question, absent a compelling public-interest need.
2376_2 added penal consequences and legislative non-amendment as reasons for caution.
1916580_2 recognised that practice cannot perpetuate a mistaken interpretation.
281138_3 declined to revisit the rule through ancient texts and left anomalies to the legislature.

legal_question: Can a person be held in contempt (or penalised) for non-compliance where the order or legal obligation was unclear, undecided, or never undertaken, and the person acted on a bona fide understanding, so that wilful disobedience is not established?

predicates.contempt_or_penal_proceeding: The proceeding seeks to punish the person, by contempt or by a penalty, for non-compliance with an order or legal obligation.
predicates.alleged_breach_alleged: The applicant or authority alleges failure to comply with a court order, undertaking, or statutory obligation.
predicates.wilful_disobedience_not_established_beyo: The record does not prove deliberate or wilful disobedience to the standard required for contempt, or deliberate or dishonest default in the penalty context.
predicates.order_or_obligation_did_not_clearly_impo: The order did not decide the liability, did not contain the direction alleged, was a consent order without a recorded undertaking, or no undertaking was given, or the legal position was uncertain.
predicates.bona_fide_reasonable_understanding_by_al: The alleged defaulter acted on a genuine and reasonable understanding of the order or law, where competing interpretations were possible or the legal position was uncertain.
predicates.contempt_or_penalty_not_sustained_and_re: Contempt action or penalty is not warranted or is set aside, and any underlying claim may be pursued through execution or other lawful proceedings.

definition: Contempt, a quasi-criminal remedy, or a penalty requires wilful, deliberate non-compliance with a clear order or obligation. Where the order was ambiguous or undecided on the point, no undertaking was actually given, or the person acted on a bona fide reasonable understanding of the order or an uncertain law, the breach is not sustained and the underlying dispute is left to execution or other remedies.
exceptions_or_limits: Does not apply where the order is clear and the disobedience is wilful and proved beyond reasonable doubt.
Does not apply where an undertaking was in fact expressly given to the court, in writing or orally and recorded; its wilful breach can be contempt.
The finding is on wilfulness only and does not decide the underlying liability, which remains open in execution or other proceedings.
The tax-penalty member applies the bona fide belief principle outside contempt, and only where the legal position was genuinely uncertain.

common_material_facts: The alleged breach concerned an order that was ambiguous, did not decide the point, or was a consent order.
No undertaking was recorded in the court.
The alleged contemner acted on a bona fide interpretation of the order.
An alternative remedy such as execution was available.
In the tax case, the law was uncertain and the taxpayer bona fide excluded the disputed amounts.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 129 of the Constitution
Sections 2(b), 12 and 14 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
Code of Civil Procedure execution provisions (consent orders)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 6 members found that the breach or penalty was not sustained: 5 contempt matters were dismissed or the conviction set aside, with disputed claims left to execution or other proceedings, and 1 tax penalty was set aside.
variations: Two members turn on the absence of an undertaking (consent order or undertaking never given).
Three members turn on bona fide or competing interpretations and the doubt benefiting the alleged contemner.
One member concerns property damage, where the evidence was inadequate and the facts complex.
One member concerns a tax penalty rather than contempt, based on bona fide belief amid legal uncertainty.

split_suggestion: If a tighter cluster is wanted: (a) contempt where the order is ambiguous or the interpretation bona fide (18545704_2, 18545704_3, 403270_2); (b) contempt where no undertaking was given (458739_1, 615500_2); (c) tax penalty for bona fide non-inclusion under uncertain law (996616_3).

legal_question: Will the Supreme Court, on appeal, interfere with or accept a procedural-timeliness or alternative-remedy objection (delay, laches, or an available statutory remedy) where the court or authority below exercised its discretion to entertain the proceeding and the objection was not pressed or the delay was explained?

rule.if: appeal_before_supreme_court and procedural_objection_based_on_delay_or_alternative_remedy and (forum_below_exercised_discretion_to_entertain_or_accepted_explanation or objection_not_raised_or_pressed_earlier or no_statutory_limitation_period_applies) and not delay_alone_shown_to_vitiate_the_discretion

predicates.appeal_before_supreme_court: The matter is before the Supreme Court in an appeal or special leave proceeding challenging the decision or the conduct of the proceeding below.
predicates.procedural_objection_based_on_delay_or_a: A party objects that the proceeding should have been rejected because of delay in approaching the forum or because an alternative statutory remedy (such as an appeal) was available.
predicates.forum_below_exercised_discretion_to_ente: The High Court, revisional authority or lower court decided to entertain the delayed proceeding or accepted the explanation for the delay.
predicates.objection_not_raised_or_pressed_earlier: The objector did not raise the objection in the appeal or did not seriously press it before the High Court.
predicates.no_statutory_limitation_period_applies: The governing statute prescribes no limitation period for the proceeding, so timeliness is a matter of reasonableness left to the authority's discretion.
predicates.delay_alone_shown_to_vitiate_the_discret: Delay is the only ground, or is shown to be of such a kind that it by itself requires the discretionary decision to be set aside.
predicates.procedural_objection_not_accepted_and_di: The Supreme Court rejects or declines to entertain the delay or alternative-remedy objection and leaves the discretionary decision to entertain the proceeding undisturbed.

definition: Delay and the availability of an alternative remedy are matters of discretion for the forum below. The Supreme Court will not accept such an objection, or disturb the decision to entertain the proceeding, where the objection was not raised or pressed, the delay was explained and accepted, or no limitation period applies. Delay alone is not enough to set the decision aside.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the Supreme Court itself is asked to condone delay in approaching it, it may refuse condonation if it finds no merit in the explanation (209256_1).

Delay, particularly where third-party interests have intervened, remains relevant to how the discretion is exercised, and the alternative-remedy objection is noted as relevant even if not entertained.
Where no statutory period applies, the authority should normally act only within a reasonable time, and it is for that authority to judge what is reasonable.
The rule concerns non-interference with discretion. It does not hold that delay can never justify dismissal.

outlier_members.reason: The Supreme Court itself refused to condone delay in a special leave petition. This is the opposite posture: it concerns the Court's own condonation power, not deference to a lower forum's discretion to entertain a delayed or alternative-remedy-barred proceeding.

common_material_facts: A proceeding was brought or entertained after substantial delay or despite an available alternative remedy.
The forum below (High Court or revisional authority) chose to entertain the proceeding or accepted the explanation for delay.
The objecting party did not raise or press the objection earlier, or the statute prescribed no limitation period.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution (writ jurisdiction)
Article 136 of the Constitution (special leave jurisdiction)
Section 27, Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 (revision at any time)
Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874 (no limitation period for revision)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 5 of 6 members the Supreme Court rejected the delay or alternative-remedy objection or declined to disturb the discretionary decision to entertain the proceeding. In 1 member it refused to condone the petitioner's own delay.
variations: Some members rest on the objection not being raised or pressed (164655261_2, 1704181_7). Others rest on the absence of a statutory limitation period (405349_3, 472343_3). One rests on deference to High Court discretion (80568_3).
In 80568_3 and 405349_3 the delay was substantial, and the Court still declined to interfere.
209256_1 involves refusal of condonation, not deference to a lower forum.

split_suggestion: Keep the five deference or non-entertainment members together. Treat 209256_1 (condonation of delay in filing a special leave petition) separately, together with other condonation-of-delay cases. Optionally separate the alternative-remedy member (164655261_2) from the delay members.

legal_question: Does a merger covenant recognizing a former ruler's property as private property, or guaranteeing its enjoyment, prevent the State from acquiring that property under a law that treats it as private property, and can a court adjudicate a challenge based on the covenant?

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_law_based_on_me: The acquisition of property is challenged on the ground that it violates a merger covenant or the constitutional assurances (such as Article 362) given to rulers.
predicates.covenant_recognizes_property_as_ruler_pr: The merger covenant or arrangement identified the property as the ruler's private property rather than State property.
predicates.acquisition_law_treats_property_as_priva: The acquisition law acquires the property in its capacity as private property, typically providing compensation on the same basis as for other owners, and does not single out the ruler's personal rights, privileges or dignities.
predicates.covenant_recognition_does_not_bar_acquis: The covenant or Article 362 does not guarantee the property against acquisition, the acquisition does not contravene the asserted guarantee, and the challenge fails.

definition: Where a covenant recognizes property as a ruler's private property and the acquisition law acquires it as private property on the same footing as other private property, the acquisition does not breach the covenant or Article 362. Article 362 does not guarantee perpetual existence of the property or impose an enforceable obligation on the legislature. Where the dispute arises out of the covenant, Article 363 may also bar judicial determination of it.
exceptions_or_limits: The Article 363 bar applies only where the dispute arises out of the covenant (members stress the Government of India being party to it); it is not stated as a general rule for all challenges.
The rule rests on the property being acquired in its recognized capacity as private property; acquisition singling out the ruler's personal rights, privileges or dignities is not covered.
Factual claims such as a privy purse having been fixed in reliance on the property's income fail where unsupported by material.

common_material_facts: A merger covenant recognized specified properties as the ruler's private property.
The acquisition law treated the properties as private property and provided compensation.
Former rulers invoked covenant guarantees or the constitutional assurance on personal rights, privileges and dignities.
In some members, the Government denied that the privy purse had been fixed in reliance on the property's income and no material rebutted the denial.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 362 of the Constitution
Article 363 of the Constitution
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 6 members reject the covenant-based challenge: acquisition as private property did not breach the guarantee. 4 members (217259_9, 45759_6, 511375_7, 629631_7) also invoke the Article 363 bar on adjudicating covenant disputes, and 41868_11 notes limits on judicial intervention.
variations: Some members rest on Article 362 not guaranteeing perpetual existence or not imposing an enforceable obligation, others on Article 363 non-justiciability, and others on acquisition being in the same capacity as other private property.
49043_9 and 511375_7 add the unsupported privy-purse allegation; 511375_7 and 629631_7 stress that compensation recognizes the ruler's ownership.
511375_7 ties Article 363 to the Government of India being a party to the covenant, while others state the bar more generally.

legal_question: When does a Hindu joint family member's separate or self-acquired property lose its separate character and become joint family property by blending, and is physical mixing, joint use or ambiguous dealing enough without a clear intention to abandon separate rights?

predicates.property_was_separate_or_self_acquired_o: The disputed property was originally the separate or self-acquired property of a coparcener or family member (for example, acquired by him, allotted to him, devised to him, or received from a non-ancestor).
predicates.claimant_asserts_blending_into_joint_fam: A party claims that the separate property was thrown into the common stock or blended with joint family property and so became joint family property.
predicates.clear_intention_to_abandon_separate_righ: The party asserting blending has proved, as a fact, that the owner voluntarily placed the property in the common stock with a clear intention to waive or surrender his separate rights. Physical mixing, joint use by family members, use of income to support the family, absence of separate accounts, loose recitals in loan documents, or family-related loans do not by themselves meet this.
predicates.property_retains_separate_character_and_: The property remains the owner's separate property and is not treated as joint family property by blending.

definition: Separate or self-acquired property of a joint family member becomes joint family property by blending only if the owner voluntarily puts it into the common stock with a clearly established intention to abandon his separate rights. Physical mixing, joint use, generous use of income for the family, lack of separate accounts, or ambiguous recitals do not suffice, so absent proof of that intention the property stays separate.
exceptions_or_limits: The outcome is different if the claimant proves a clear, voluntary intention to abandon separate rights; intention is a question of fact.
The burden of proving the intention to abandon lies on the party asserting blending.
Recitals or conduct pointing to family benefit may be relevant, but they are not conclusive where they may be explained otherwise, for example as made to obtain loans.

common_material_facts: Property was originally separate or self-acquired (own business, allotted share, property devised by will, property received under a settlement).
The claimant alleged blending with joint family property, usually in a partition suit or proceeding.
The evidence showed only family use, support from income, absence of separate accounts, loans or ambiguous recitals, and no clear intention to abandon separate rights.
statutes_and_provisions: Hindu law doctrine of blending of separate property with joint family property (case-law based, no statutory provision cited)
Hurpurshad v. Sheo Dyal, 3 I.A. 219
Lal Bahadur v. Kanhaiya Lal, 34 I.A. 65
Lakkireddi Chinna Venkata Reddy v. Lakkireddi Lakshamama
K.V. Narayanan v. K.V. Ranganadhan
G. Narayana Ram v. G. Chamaraju
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 5 members the claim of blending failed because a clear intention to abandon separate rights was not established, and the property remained separate.
variations: One member concerns a business and its proprietorship, while the others concern immovable or inherited property.
One member stresses loan-related recitals of family benefit as insufficient, and another stresses lack of separate accounts and joint use.
In one member the High Court's reversal of concurrent lower-court findings was held unjustified.
In one member the consequence was the widow's entitlement to a fourth share in the separate property.
The principle is stated with reference to differing authorities, and one member cites none.

legal_question: Where property under an agreement of sale (or a decree requiring retransfer) has been transferred to a subsequent transferee, what is the proper form of the decree: must the vendor perform the original contract while the subsequent transferee is directed to join the conveyance only to pass the title held by that transferee?

predicates.specific_performance_or_retransfer_decre: The proceedings seek, or the court is making, a decree for specific performance of a sale agreement, or a decree requiring retransfer of property to the party entitled to it (e.g., on redemption).
predicates.property_transferred_to_subsequent_trans: The vendor (or mortgagee) has transferred the property to a subsequent purchaser or transferee.
predicates.subsequent_transferee_holds_title_needed: The title that must be passed to the plaintiff or entitled claimant to complete the conveyance resides in the subsequent transferee.
predicates.vendor_performs_original_contract_and_su: The decree directs the vendor to perform the original contract and requires the subsequent transferee to join in the conveyance to pass its title, without joining in special covenants between the original parties and without cancelling the later transfer.

definition: In a decree for specific performance (or retransfer) where the property has passed to a subsequent transferee, the vendor is directed to perform the contract, and the subsequent transferee is directed to join in the conveyance only to pass the title vested in it. It does not assume the special covenants of the original contract (Lala Durga Prasad v. Lala Deep Chand). The vendor remains a necessary party because their participation is needed.
exceptions_or_limits: The subsequent transferee joins only to pass title and is not bound by special covenants between the plaintiff and the vendor.
The form of decree does not involve cancelling the later transfer (one member declined the approach that cancelled the later sale).
The vendor's necessity as a party is tied to the vendor having to execute the conveyance and/or to alternative relief being sought against the vendor.
Where the subsequent transferee holds no title needed for the conveyance, the direction to join is not required.
In one member, the direction was also supported by Article 142 of the Constitution to do complete justice.

common_material_facts: Vendor had agreed to sell, or a mortgagee held property, and later transferred it to a subsequent purchaser.
Plaintiff or claimant is entitled to specific performance or retransfer by decree.
Title needed to complete the conveyance resides in the subsequent transferee.
Original contract covenants exist only between the plaintiff and the vendor.
statutes_and_provisions: Lala Durga Prasad v. Lala Deep Chand, [1954] S.C.R. 360 / AIR 1954 SC 75
R. C. Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal, [1971] 2 S.C.R. 573
Section 91 Indian Trusts Act, 1882
Section 3 illustration (g) and Section 27 Specific Relief Act, 1877
Section 40 Transfer of Property Act
Article 142 of the Constitution of India
Kafiladdin v. Samiraddin, A.I.R. 1931 Cal. 67; Potter v. Sanders, 67 E.R. 1057
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members apply the Durga Prasad form of decree: the vendor performs the contract and the subsequent transferee joins in the conveyance to pass title. 4 directly approve directing the transferee to join; 1 holds the vendor a necessary party.
variations: One member concerns party joinder (vendor is a necessary party, partly because of alternative monetary relief) rather than the transferee's direction.
One member involves retransfer on redemption of a mortgage rather than a sale agreement, and also relies on Article 142.
One member discusses statutory provisions and contrasts conflicting High Court approaches, rejecting cancellation of the later transfer.
Several members state the rule only briefly, citing Durga Prasad.

legal_question: Can the agreement that forms criminal conspiracy under Sections 120-A and 120-B IPC be proved by circumstantial evidence (surrounding circumstances and the accused's conduct), and what must those circumstances show?

predicates.prosecution_for_criminal_conspiracy: The accused is prosecuted for criminal conspiracy (Sections 120-A/120-B IPC), alone or with another offence.
predicates.agreement_to_commit_illegal_act_or_act_b: The alleged conspiracy is an agreement between two or more persons to do an illegal act, or a legal act by illegal means.
predicates.proved_circumstances_and_conduct_support: Solidly proved surrounding circumstances and the accused's antecedent, concurrent or subsequent coordinated conduct support an inference of a meeting of minds or prior concert.
predicates.circumstances_not_reasonably_explainable: The proved circumstances are not capable of another reasonable explanation, so the inference rests on more than suspicion or surmise.
predicates.conspiracy_may_be_found_established_by_c: The court may hold criminal conspiracy proved without direct evidence of the agreement, and without proof of an overt act where the agreement is to commit an offence.

definition: Because conspiracies are usually secret, the agreement may be inferred from proved surrounding circumstances and the accused's coordinated conduct before and after the act. The inference must rest on solid facts and exclude other reasonable explanations. Where it does not, as with ambiguous evidence, suspicion or surmise, the charge fails.
exceptions_or_limits: Suspicion, surmise or ambiguous material (for example, unclear communications) cannot support the inference of agreement; the charge fails if the circumstances admit another reasonable explanation.
The accused's knowledge of the unlawful act or means is necessary, although each conspirator need not know every step the others will take.
Where the agreement is to commit an offence, no overt act need be proved; the agreement itself is the offence.

common_material_facts: No direct evidence of an express agreement was available
Coordinated or connected conduct of the accused at multiple stages, before and after the act
Surrounding circumstances such as payments, loan sanctions, altered records, undue haste, preparations or following the victim
In the one acquittal-type member, ambiguous communications could not connect the accused to the plan
statutes_and_provisions: Section 120-A IPC
Section 120-B IPC
Section 107 IPC (abetment by conspiracy distinguished)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 4 of 5 members the court inferred conspiracy from circumstantial evidence and upheld or supported the conviction or finding. In 1 member the evidence was too ambiguous and the conspiracy charge failed.
variations: Some members involve public servants and property or pecuniary benefit; others involve killings.
One member stresses that circumstances must be incapable of another reasonable explanation, and another that the inference must rest on solid facts.
One member notes that overt acts are unnecessary and that the agreement itself is the offence.
The judgment in 836678_3 cites no precedent, while the others rely on Sheetla Sahai, Noor Mohd., V.C. Shukla, K. Narayana Rao, Yash Pal Mittal and similar cases.

legal_question: Does an arbitrator exceed jurisdiction, so that the award (or the offending part) can be set aside, by awarding relief outside the contract, the claim or the reference, or by disregarding contractual terms, formulas or methods that bind the claim?

predicates.award_challenge_proceeding: A court is reviewing an arbitral award on a challenge to set it aside.
predicates.arbitrator_awarded_contrary_to_contract_: The arbitrator awarded a claim or item that the contract excludes, does not provide for, or makes conditional on requirements (such as an architect's certification) that were disregarded.
predicates.arbitrator_departed_from_prescribed_form: The contract or the reference prescribed a specific formula or valuation method for the claim, and the arbitrator used a different one.
predicates.arbitrator_awarded_beyond_claim_or_refer: The arbitrator awarded relief exceeding the amount or rate claimed, relying on an unpleaded change to the claim, or compensated a loss not part of the dispute referred.
predicates.award_or_offending_portion_set_aside_for: The award is invalid, at least to the extent of the excess, for exceeding jurisdiction or for legal misconduct.

definition: An arbitrator's authority comes from the contract, the reference and the claims presented. An award that grants what the contract excludes, ignores a prescribed formula, method or condition, or goes beyond the claim or reference is beyond jurisdiction and invalid, at least to the extent of the excess.
exceptions_or_limits: A mere error in construing the contract or reaching a conclusion is ordinarily within jurisdiction and is not enough to set the award aside.
Where the excess portion can be separated from the matters properly submitted, only that portion is set aside (Section 34(2)(iv) proviso; the awards upheld on other heads in the first member)
Where the agreement does not prescribe the method, departing from a particular method is not excess of jurisdiction.

common_material_facts: Arbitration awards on construction, works or partnership disputes were challenged as going beyond the contract, the claim or the reference
The contract prescribed a price, formula, valuation method or procedural condition that the arbitrator ignored
The award granted more than was claimed or compensated a head of loss not referred
statutes_and_provisions: Arbitration Act, 1940, section 30 (legal misconduct, excess of authority)
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, section 34(2)(iv) and its proviso
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 5 members the award, or the offending portion, was set aside as beyond jurisdiction. In the first member, the labour-escalation award was also set aside and the other set-asides were upheld.
variations: Excess arises from three sources: the contract's terms or formula (1015491_2, 231673_2), the pleaded claim (640382_2), or the reference or submission (676743_1, 899911_1)
Statutory basis differs between the 1940 Act (section 30) and the 1996 Act (section 34(2)(iv))
Some members frame the defect as legal misconduct rather than excess of jurisdiction
Severability of the excess portion is stressed in 676743_1 and 899911_1

legal_question: When is an isolated or one-off purchase (and resale, often after subdivision) of land or property an adventure in the nature of trade, so that the resulting profit is taxable as business income rather than as the gain on an investment?

rule.if: income_tax_classification_dispute and isolated_property_purchase_and_resale and resale_profit_intent_shown_by_total_circumstances and not countervailing_circumstances_rebutting_trading_intent

predicates.income_tax_classification_dispute: The dispute is in an income-tax assessment, reference or appeal on whether profit from a property transaction is business income or something else.
predicates.isolated_property_purchase_and_resale: The taxpayer bought land or other property and resold it, whether in one transaction or a single venture, outside any regular business of dealing in such property.
predicates.resale_profit_intent_shown_by_total_circ: Taken together, the facts show that the property was acquired to resell at a profit rather than to hold as an investment or use. Relevant facts include prompt subdivision or resale, pre-arranged buyers, borrowed or inadequate funds, inability to use the property, no development or use, and organised planning.
predicates.countervailing_circumstances_rebutting_t: Facts that rebut the inference of trading intent, such as a genuine intention to hold as an investment or to use the property for industry, housing or cultivation.
predicates.transaction_is_adventure_in_the_nature_o: The transaction is held to be an adventure in the nature of trade, and the profit or proceeds from it are assessable to tax as business income.

definition: A single purchase and resale of property is an adventure in the nature of trade, and the profit is taxable business income, when the total impression of all circumstances shows the property was acquired to resell at a profit as part of a profit-making scheme. No single test governs, and the inference can be rebutted by facts showing investment or use.
exceptions_or_limits: No abstract formula applies; the total effect of all relevant facts and circumstances decides the question, not a mechanical count of factors.
A land transaction is not presumed to be an adventure in the nature of trade without more.
A sole intention to resell raises a strong but rebuttable presumption, which can be displaced by countervailing circumstances.
On references, the court usually examines only whether the record supports the fact-finder's conclusion, so outcomes depend on the findings of intention.

common_material_facts: A single or isolated acquisition of land or property followed by resale at a profit
Subdivision into plots and prompt sale, often within months (3 of 5 members)
Taxpayer lacked means or intention to cultivate, develop or use the property, or financed the purchase by borrowing
Claimed investment or industrial-use purpose was rejected or not established
statutes_and_provisions: Income-tax Act, 1922, s. 2(4) (definition of business including adventure in the nature of trade)
Income-tax Act, 1922, s. 10
Income-tax Act, 1922, s. 34(1)(a)
Income Tax Act s. 256(1) (reference to High Court)
Hyderabad Income Tax Act (equivalent provisions)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold the transaction to be an adventure in the nature of trade, with the profit taxable as business income.
variations: Some members stress the total-impression test with English authorities (Californian Copper, Martin v. Lowry, Rutledge, Fraser); others decide briefly on the facts without citing cases.
One member treats subdivision, development and sale of plots as dealing with the land as stock-in-trade.
One member relies on a sole resale intention raising a rebuttable presumption.
Another member relies on financing by borrowing and the use of sale proceeds to repay debts.

legal_question: Where a landlord sues (or applies) to recover possession from a tenant, does limitation run from the proved determination or termination of the tenancy under the specific provision for landlord-tenant recovery, so that a filing within the period counted from that point is not time-barred?

rule.if: landlord_seeks_possession_from_tenant and tenancy_determined_or_terminated_and_proved and filed_within_specific_period_counted_from_determination and not time_run_from_earlier_event

predicates.landlord_seeks_possession_from_tenant: The claim is by a landlord (or the landlord's successor) in a suit or application to recover possession of property from a person holding as tenant under a lawful tenancy.
predicates.tenancy_determined_or_terminated_and_pro: The tenancy was ended by notice, expiry of the term or other determination, and that determination is established on the evidence.
predicates.filed_within_specific_period_counted_fro: The suit or application was filed within the period prescribed by the specific provision for landlord-tenant recovery, counted from the determination of the tenancy.
predicates.time_run_from_earlier_event: Limitation is claimed to have started from an earlier event, such as the tenant's breach, an unproved notice, or a transfer by a former manager that was unauthorised, and that earlier start is legally or evidentially established.
predicates.possession_claim_not_barred_by_limitatio: The claim for possession is held to be within time and not barred by limitation.

definition: A landlord's claim for possession against a tenant is governed by the specific limitation provision for recovery from a tenant, and time runs from the proved determination of the tenancy. It is not governed by the residual provision, by the date of the tenant's breach, by an unproved earlier notice, or by the rule for unauthorised transfers by a former manager. A claim filed within that period is not time-barred.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the property is endowment property transferred for valuable consideration by a previous manager, the special rule for successor managers applies regardless of the transferor's representation of ownership (1319210_1).
The starting point must be proved; an unproved termination notice cannot fix an earlier start for limitation.
Statutory tenancy regimes may specify their own period and trigger (for example, two years from termination under the Bombay tenancy statute).
Where the tenancy was not lawfully granted, or forfeiture or breach is the basis of the suit, a different article (forfeiture or breach) may apply.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the special rule for a successor manager recovering endowment property after a previous manager's transfer for valuable consideration. It involves no landlord-tenant recovery and no termination of a tenancy, so it is the converse category that 1038664_4 distinguishes.

common_material_facts: Landlord sues or applies to recover possession from a tenant.
The tenancy ended by notice or expiry before filing.
The filing was within the prescribed period counted from termination.
The opposing side argued for an earlier start of limitation or a shorter or different provision.
statutes_and_provisions: Limitation Act, 1908, Articles 134-B, 139 and 144, and section 28
Limitation Act, 1963, Articles 65, 66 and 67
Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, sections 14(1) and 29(2)
Transfer of Property Act, section 111
Evidence Act, sections 62 and 64
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 4 of 5 members, the landlord's possession claim was held timely because limitation ran from determination of the tenancy. The fifth member applied the special rule for endowment transfers by a previous manager.
variations: One member is governed by a statutory tenancy provision with a two-year period.
One member rejects the residual three-year provision in favour of the twelve-year specific article.
One member turns on the failure to prove an earlier termination notice.
One member contrasts the landlord-tenant article with the previous-manager article.
One member applies the previous-manager article to endowment property irrespective of the transferor's claim of ownership.

split_suggestion: Keep 1038664_4, 203938_1, 224201_1 and 30445757_2 together as the landlord-tenant limitation group. Move 1319210_1 to a separate cluster on the limitation rule for a successor manager's recovery of endowment property, which could also take 1038664_4 as a contrast.

legal_question: Must a person who is not the direct party to an administrative or statutory proceeding, but whose interests (possessory, tenancy, beneficiary or bidder interests) may be adversely affected by its outcome, be given notice and an opportunity to be heard before the decision is made?

predicates.affected_person_has_cognisable_interest_: The person has a sufficient interest in the property or scheme, such as being a beneficiary of an acquisition, a company for whose benefit acquisition is proceeding, a tenant in possession, or a later bidder whose bid was provisionally accepted. This is so even if no full legal title or right has yet accrued.
predicates.decision_in_administrative_or_statutory_: The outcome of the proceeding (for example withdrawal of acquisition, revision of a title order, a town-planning scheme, or restoration of a cancelled sale) may prejudice the person's possession, rights or expectations.
predicates.person_not_given_notice_and_opportunity_: The authority decided the matter without notifying the person or giving a chance to respond.
predicates.no_express_or_necessarily_implied_exclus: The governing statute does not expressly or by necessary implication exclude a hearing for this person.
predicates.person_must_be_given_notice_and_opportun: The person is entitled to notice and a reasonable hearing, and an order passed without it is invalid and liable to be set aside, with the matter reconsidered after a hearing.

definition: Natural justice, or the statute's own hearing requirement, entitles a person with a real interest in the subject matter, such as a beneficiary, a company, a tenant in possession or a provisionally accepted bidder, to notice and a hearing before a decision that may prejudice that interest. An order passed without hearing that person is vitiated and the matter is reconsidered afresh, even if the person has no complete legal right.
exceptions_or_limits: Natural justice is read into a statutory power unless excluded expressly or by necessary implication, and the party asserting an exception bears the burden of proving it.
A mere highest bidder acquires no right in the property until the sale is confirmed and a deed is executed; the entitlement rests on potential prejudice, not on a vested right.

For beneficiaries and companies, the acquisition must have progressed substantially (for example declaration, award, or completion of company-acquisition procedures) before a right to be heard in the withdrawal arises.
In town-planning schemes, a tenant is entitled only if in lease-based possession on the date the scheme is published.
A landowner's position differs from that of a beneficiary, since a landowner has a separate statutory compensation remedy.
In the tenancy revision case the entitlement also depends on the claimant actually being interested, that is, likely to be affected by the decision.

common_material_facts: The authority decided without notifying a person whose possession, tenancy, beneficiary status or bid was affected.
The affected person had an interest short of full title, such as a bid, a beneficiary position or a tenancy.
The decision could prejudice the person's property-related interests.
The proceeding had progressed to a stage that gave the person a concrete stake, such as provisional acceptance, award, agreement or possession.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 39–42, 48(1) and 48(2)
Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963, Rules 3 and 4
Proviso to Section 42, East Punjab Holdings (Consolidation and Prevention of Fragmentation) Act, 1948
Section 105, Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Rule 21(3) and (4), Bombay Town Planning Rules, 1955
General principles of natural justice, as in Col. J.N. Sinha, Olga Tellis and Bombay Salt and Chemical v. Johnson
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 5 members, the person was held entitled to notice and a hearing, and the order or withdrawal passed without it was quashed, set aside or held invalid, usually with remand for fresh consideration after hearing.
variations: The source of the right to be heard differs: general natural justice (bidders, beneficiary), a statutory proviso (Section 42 revision), or statutory scheme and rules (company acquisition, town planning).
The interested persons differ: later bidders, an association beneficiary, a company, tenants, and tenants or sub-tenants in possession on the date of publication.
Some members tie the right to a specific stage or date, such as completed company procedures or possession on publication, while others rest on likely prejudice alone.
The remedy varies between quashing and remand, invalidity of the withdrawal, and a declaration of entitlement to notice.

legal_question: When part of a statute, amendment, lease, or administrative grant is invalid or unauthorized, can that part be severed so the valid remainder stays in force, and what conditions must be met?

predicates.challenged_instrument_contains_invalid_p: The statute, amendment, lease, deed, or order under challenge contains a provision or condition that is invalid, unauthorized, or beyond competence.
predicates.invalid_part_separable_from_valid_remain: The invalid provision is distinct and not inextricably bound up with the valid provisions, so that the legislature or authority would have enacted or granted the valid part without it.
predicates.valid_remainder_complete_and_workable_in: After the invalid part is removed, the remaining provisions form a complete, effective and workable scheme that can operate on its own.
predicates.invalid_part_severed_and_valid_remainder: The invalid part is held inoperative or quashed, and the remaining valid provisions stay valid and enforceable.

definition: An invalid, unauthorized or incompetent portion of a statute, lease, assignment or order does not vitiate the whole if it is separable and the remainder is complete and workable without it. The court strikes out only the defective part and upholds the rest. The test is whether the valid and invalid parts are inextricably mixed, judged by whether the enacting authority would have made the valid part without the invalid.
exceptions_or_limits: If the valid and invalid parts are inextricably mixed, or the invalid part is integral to the transaction, the whole fails.
If the remainder cannot operate independently or would not have been enacted or granted without the invalid part, severance is unavailable.
For a defective amendment cured by a retrospective correction (1038746_3), the original enactment must be independently valid and the correction must precede judicial invalidation.
Where the corrective legislation is relied on, the remainder after correction must itself be complete and workable.

common_material_facts: A discrete invalid provision, clause, proviso or condition sits within an otherwise valid instrument.
