The ordinary bar on separate suits against compromise decrees continues to apply where the compromise was recorded by an ordinary civil court and the challenge is not of the kind described above.

common_material_facts: A decree, compromise or order of a revenue, tenancy or arbitral-related proceeding is attacked as fraudulent or collusive.
A statutory provision is invoked to bar the civil court or a separate suit.
The special forum cannot grant the relief sought or cannot adjudicate fraud effectively.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 9 CPC
Order XXIII Rules 3 and 3A CPC
Section 242 U.P. Tenancy Act, 1939
Sections 331 and 341 and Schedule II, U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act
Sections 85, 85-A and 88-B(1)(d), Maharashtra Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act
Sections 32 and 33, Arbitration Act, 1940
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold that the challenge is not barred at the threshold: suits are maintainable (3), a plaint cannot be rejected on an absolute bar (1), and a writ challenge to a compromise decree is not barred (1).
variations: Three members rest on the special forum's inability to grant the relief or decide the fraud.
One rests on the distinction between attacking the decree and attacking the award.
One rests on reading the bar together with a stay-and-refer provision and an unexamined exemption.
One arises as a writ by a non-party devotee against a compromise involving a statutory board, not a civil suit.

split_suggestion: The shared theme is that fraud challenges survive statutory bars. If a finer split is wanted, separate (a) civil suits where the revenue forum cannot grant relief or decide fraud (128921130_3, 150118615_1, 168358062_2), (b) the arbitration-decree case (470596_1), and (c) the writ challenge to a compromise decree by a non-party devotee (1306104_1).

legal_question: Is a written agreement to sell immovable property (or a consent decree whose terms themselves transfer the property) that provides for or records transfer of possession, without a separate conveyance, chargeable to stamp duty as a conveyance?

predicates.written_instrument_concerning_immovable_: The document in question is a written agreement or decree relating to immovable property.
predicates.instrument_provides_for_sale_or_transfer: The instrument expresses an intention to sell, or itself records or effects a transfer of, the immovable property.
predicates.possession_delivered_or_contemplated_und: The instrument records delivery of possession or contemplates delivery of possession within a stipulated time.
predicates.no_separate_conveyance_required_or_execu: The instrument does not require, and the parties have not executed, a separate conveyance deed.
predicates.statute_deems_such_instrument_a_conveyan: An applicable stamp-law explanation or amendment deems an agreement to sell with possession and no conveyance to be a conveyance.
predicates.instrument_itself_effects_transfer_betwe: The terms of the instrument, such as a consent decree, themselves operate to transfer title between living persons and so fall within the definitions of conveyance and instrument.
predicates.instrument_chargeable_to_stamp_duty_as_c: The instrument is liable to stamp duty at the rate applicable to a conveyance.

definition: Where an agreement to sell immovable property provides for or records delivery of possession without a conveyance being required or executed, the stamp-law explanation deems it a conveyance and it is chargeable with conveyance duty. A consent decree whose terms themselves transfer the property between living parties is likewise chargeable as a conveyance. Such a levy is a duty on the instrument, and an insufficiently stamped instrument is inadmissible in evidence until the deficient duty and penalty are paid.
exceptions_or_limits: The deeming rule for agreements depends on the particular state stamp-law explanation (Bombay or Madhya Pradesh) and on its conditions being met, namely sale intention and possession transferred or contemplated without a conveyance.
Consequences for admissibility apply only where duty is insufficient; the instrument can be admitted on payment of the deficient duty and penalty under Section 35.
A decree that merely creates a charge on property outside the subject matter of the suit is not a decree operating as a conveyance.
Execution of the agreement under a flats-ownership statute does not displace the stamp-duty rule.

common_material_facts: Written agreement to sell immovable property with possession delivered or promised
No separate conveyance executed or contemplated
Dispute over the duty classification of the instrument or its admissibility in evidence
Consent terms recording sale, payment of price and vacant possession (one member)
statutes_and_provisions: Explanation I to Article 25 of Schedule I, Bombay Stamp Act, 1958
Section 32A and Section 3, Bombay Stamp Act, 1958
Entry 44 of List III and Entry 91 of List I, Seventh Schedule
Explanation to Article 23 of Schedule IA, Stamp Act as amended in Madhya Pradesh (1989 and 1990 amendments)
Sections 2(10), 3 and 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899
Sections 2(g) and 2(1) of the Bombay Stamps Act, 1958; Entry 25 of Schedule I
Avinash Kumar Chauhan v. Vijay Krishna Mishra, (2009) 2 SCC 532
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold the instrument chargeable as a conveyance. One upholds the constitutional validity of the levy as a duty on the instrument, and one holds the instrument inadmissible until deficient duty and penalty are paid.
variations: Four members concern deeming provisions for agreements to sell; one concerns a consent decree that itself transfers title, on the basis of the general definitions.
One member addresses constitutional competence, one addresses admissibility under Section 35, and the others address chargeability.
Possession is contemplated in the future in one agreement and already delivered in the others.
The decree member rests on the substance of the document, not a deeming explanation, and the 1985 amendment is treated as made out of abundant caution.

legal_question: Can a landlord-tenant dispute over eviction or recovery of possession be taken out of the jurisdiction of the court or forum designated by law (rent court or civil court) and referred to an arbitrator, or to another non-court forum, because of an arbitration clause or other overriding provision?

predicates.landlord_tenant_possession_or_eviction_d: The dispute is between a landlord (or licensor) and a tenant (or claimed tenant or licensee) over eviction, recovery of possession, or closely related rent or ancillary reliefs.
predicates.statute_reserves_dispute_to_designated_c: A tenancy or rent-control statute covers the premises and gives a designated court or forum exclusive jurisdiction over possession, overriding contrary contracts, with tenant-protection purposes.
predicates.premises_outside_rent_control_so_civil_c: The premises fall outside the rent-control statute through an exclusion, so the Transfer of Property Act governs the rights and the ordinary civil court is the forum.
predicates.arbitration_clause_or_alternative_forum_: A party relies on an arbitration clause in the lease or agreement, or on another statute's overriding provision such as cooperative arbitration, to send the dispute to a forum other than the designated court.
predicates.dispute_not_arbitrable_and_decided_by_de: The arbitration clause or alternative forum is ineffective for the dispute, and the rent court (where the statute covers the premises) or the civil court (where it does not) alone decides it, with no referral to arbitration under Section 8.

definition: A landlord-tenant eviction or possession dispute is not arbitrable. Where a rent-control statute covers the premises, its designated court has exclusive jurisdiction and parties cannot contract out of it. Where the premises are excluded from the statute, the civil court decides the dispute. In either case an arbitration clause (or a competing cooperative-arbitration provision) does not oust that court.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule concerns eviction or possession disputes between landlord and tenant; disputes with no statutory bar to arbitration (e.g., ordinary commercial or finance disputes) were distinguished and remain arbitrable.
Which court is the proper forum (rent court or civil court) depends on whether the rent-control statute applies to the premises.

The cooperative-arbitration member rests on harmonising two overriding provisions by purpose and policy, not on an arbitration clause; the Court left open whether the Registrar is a court under the Rent Act.

common_material_facts: A landlord, licensor or bank claiming to be landlord sought eviction or possession from a tenant, licensee or claimed tenant.
An arbitration clause, or a cooperative-arbitration route, was invoked to take the dispute away from the court.
A rent-control statute applied or was claimed to apply, offering tenant protection and a designated forum.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 28(1), Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Section 91, Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960
Section 6, West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997
Sections 2(3) and 8, Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996
Section 3, Delhi Rent Act, 1955
Transfer of Property Act
Natraj Studios v. Navrang Studios; Booz Allen & Hamilton v. SBI Home Finance
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold that the eviction or possession dispute is decided by the designated court (rent court in 3, civil court in 2) and not by an arbitrator or cooperative forum.
variations: Three members involve premises covered by a rent statute (Bombay, West Bengal) and rely on exclusive statutory jurisdiction and public policy.
One member involves premises excluded from the Delhi Rent Act, so the civil court decides under the Transfer of Property Act.
One member (177237522_1) rests on Natraj Studios and Booz Allen without a specific rent statute.
One member (1985369_3) concerns a clash between the Rent Act and a cooperative statute's overriding clause rather than an arbitration agreement.

legal_question: Can a person enforce in municipal courts, against a successor sovereign that has acquired territory by conquest, cession or otherwise, rights or grants derived from the former sovereign when the successor has not recognized them?

predicates.claim_based_on_right_or_grant_from_forme: The claimant asserts a proprietary or other right, or a grant, that arose under the former sovereign or its laws before the change of sovereignty.
predicates.territory_acquired_by_successor_sovereig: The territory passed to a new sovereign by conquest, cession or similar acquisition, and the claim is made against that new sovereign or its government.
predicates.successor_sovereign_recognized_right: The new sovereign recognized the right expressly or by implication, for example through a regrant, executive action or a statutory saving that covers the right. Recognition must be attributable to the sovereign. Continuing the old laws, a general treaty promise to respect existing rights, or conditional acts of subordinate officers do not suffice.
predicates.claim_not_enforceable_against_successor_: The claimant cannot enforce the right or grant against the successor sovereign in municipal courts.

definition: Rights or grants derived from a former sovereign bind the successor sovereign, and are enforceable in its courts, only if the successor recognized them expressly or by implication. Continuation of the old laws, general promises to respect existing rights, constitutional property protections, or conditional acts of subordinate officers do not amount to recognition.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the successor sovereign has recognized the right expressly or impliedly, or has conferred it by legislation, a regrant or executive action, or a statutory saving provision that covers the right.
Recognition must be attributable to the sovereign. Temporary or conditional permissions by subordinate officials, made subject to the government's eventual decision, are not recognition.

A general treaty or proclamation promising respect for existing rights only means that rights found to exist after investigation will be recognized. The claimant bears the burden of proving recognition.
A constitutional or statutory protection of property protects only rights the claimant already holds against the successor. It does not create or enlarge rights.

common_material_facts: The claimant relied on grants, titles or tenures from a former ruler or sovereign.
The successor government repudiated, rejected or did not accept the claimed rights.
The claimant relied on continuity of the old laws, a treaty promise, or an official's conduct as implied recognition.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 5(1) of the Goa, Daman and Diu (Administration) Act, 1962
Section 4(2) of the Goa, Daman and Diu (Laws) Regulation, 1962
Section 299(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold the claim unenforceable against the successor sovereign for want of recognition. The claimants lost in each.
variations: The territorial change is conquest in some members, cession by treaty in others, and an unspecified assumption of sovereignty in the rest.
The claimed rights vary: mining titles, land grants, sovereign or zamindari rights, and forest rights.
The claimants pointed to different supposed recognitions: continuation of old laws, a treaty's general promise, conditional permissions by forest officials, and a constitutional property clause.
One member is a separate opinion, and another concerns the burden of proof and the absence of possession.

legal_question: When a public authority's deficient service, negligence or misfeasance in a public function injures a consumer or other claimant, can compensation be awarded against the authority, and when must the authority recover it from the officials responsible?

predicates.public_authority_function_or_service_inv: The claim arises from a service or public duty performed by a statutory or public authority, such as housing or construction work, and not from a sovereign function.
predicates.injury_or_loss_established: The claimant's loss, harassment or mental suffering is proved on the material and, where a money amount is awarded, the amount is assessed.
predicates.deficient_service_or_negligent_performan: The authority's service was deficient, or it negligently performed or failed to perform its legal or public duty, and this caused the injury.
predicates.official_conduct_oppressive_capricious_o: The injury was caused by the conduct of responsible officials that was mala fide, oppressive, arbitrary or capricious, found on careful and convincing material.
predicates.public_authority_liable_to_compensate_cl: The authority must pay compensation to the claimant. A consumer forum may award it, including for harassment and mental suffering. Where the injury arose from oppressive, capricious or mala fide official conduct, the authority must recover the amount from the responsible officials, proportionately if there are several.

definition: A public authority is liable to compensate a claimant for established injury caused by deficient service or negligent performance of a public duty. A consumer forum may award this compensation, including for harassment and mental agony. Where the injury results from officials' oppressive, capricious or mala fide conduct, found on convincing material, the authority pays and then recovers the amount from the responsible officials in proportion to their responsibility.
exceptions_or_limits: Sovereign-function immunity does not protect housing, construction and similar services.
Compensation for harassment or mental agony needs a specific finding of misfeasance or oppression, supported by material and convincing circumstances.

Recovery from officials applies only where the injury comes from mala fide, oppressive or capricious conduct and the responsible officials can be identified. Compensation for ordinary loss from the authority's discharge of its duties is borne by the authority itself.
Ordinary commercial-contract damages are distinguished from compensation for mental agony based on administrative-law principles.
No misfeasance was found where the authority promptly corrected its own mistake.

common_material_facts: A development authority or State body failed to perform or complete a public service or work, such as flat possession, construction, or a bundh.
The claimant suffered quantifiable loss and, in the consumer cases, harassment and mental agony.
The findings of negligence or deficiency were established by a forum or court below.
statutes_and_provisions: Consumer Protection Act (compensation power and deficiency in service)
Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta
State of Gujarat v. Memon Mahomed Haji Hasam
Lala Bishambar Nath v. Agra Nagar Mahapalika
Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of U.P. (distinguished)
Donoghue v. Stevenson
Rookes v. Barnard
Cassell & Co. Ltd. v. Broome
Geddis v. Proprietors of Bann Reservoir
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold the public authority liable to compensate. 3 of them (1375046_2, 1682813_1, 1503529_4) rest on the authority's liability alone. 2 (1375046_3, 1682813_3) add that compensation for harassment caused by oppressive or capricious officials must be recovered from those officials.
variations: 1503529_4 is a civil tort suit for negligent public works. The others are consumer-forum proceedings.
1375046_2 and 1682813_1 concern the forum's power to award compensation. 1375046_3 and 1682813_3 concern who ultimately bears it.
Only 1375046_3 and 1682813_3 require identifying the responsible officials and apportioning recovery among them.

split_suggestion: To tighten the cluster, separate (a) the authority's liability and the forum's power to award compensation (1375046_2, 1682813_1, 1503529_4) from (b) recovery of compensation from responsible officials (1375046_3, 1682813_3).

legal_question: Where a male Hindu holds property inherited from paternal ancestors or allotted to him on partition of ancestral property, does the property take or keep coparcenary (ancestral) character as against his male issue, and what follows from that character?

predicates.property_derived_from_paternal_ancestors: The property was inherited by the holder from a paternal ancestor within the recognised degrees, or was allotted to him on a partition of ancestral property.
predicates.holder_has_male_issue_or_a_son_is_later_: The holder has a son or male descendant, including one born after the holder received the property (for example after a partition in which the holder was the sole surviving coparcener).
predicates.succession_or_partition_governed_by_mita: Succession opened or the partition took place under Mitakshara principles, and not after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force so as to displace them.
predicates.property_is_coparcenary_property_as_rega: The property is treated as ancestral or coparcenary as against the holder's male issue, who hold an interest in it by birth. As against other relations it may be the holder's separate property.

definition: Under Mitakshara law, property that a male holder inherited from paternal ancestors, or received on partition of ancestral property, is coparcenary as regards his male issue, who take an interest by birth. If he was a sole coparcener or had no son, it is his separate property until a son is born, and then it becomes coparcenary. For other relations, or where he leaves no male issue, it is treated as his separate property.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the holder leaves no male issue, the property is separate property as against other relations such as collaterals, and a sister may take under a custom favouring her for non-ancestral property (1497910_1, which proceeded on an assumed custom).
The rule does not apply where succession opened after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force; that case (Uttam v. Saubhag Singh) was distinguished in 162171512_1.
While the holder is the sole surviving coparcener with no son, the property is his separate property.

On the holder's death, Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act (and not Section 8) governs the coparcenary interest. Where a Class I female heir survives, the interest devolves by succession and not survivorship (420921_1). The Act is not retrospective, and the 2005 amendment does not apply to succession opened earlier.

common_material_facts: Property derived from paternal ancestors, by inheritance or by allotment on partition.
The holder's male issue claim an interest, or the holder has or had no son.
Succession or partition occurred under Mitakshara law, before or independently of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
statutes_and_provisions: Mitakshara law as stated in Mulla, Principles of Hindu Law
Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Sections 4, 6 and 8
Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, which was held inapplicable in 420921_1
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Four of the five members hold the property coparcenary as against the holder's male issue (162171512_1, 184162387_1, 420921_1, 45150156_1). The fifth (1497910_1) holds the property non-ancestral as against collaterals because there was no male issue, so the sister took it.
variations: 1497910_1 turns on the absence of male issue and a custom ranking the sister against collaterals.
184162387_1 and 420921_1 concern separate property becoming coparcenary on the birth of a son.
162171512_1 and 45150156_1 concern a partition share that remains coparcenary as against the allottee's male descendants.
420921_1 goes on to the devolution of the coparcenary interest under Section 6 when a female Class I heir survives.

legal_question: Can a final land-acquisition compensation award or decree be reopened, whether by redetermination or by a later application for additional statutory benefits, when the applicant has no statutory basis for doing so, such as a prior reference, a missed limitation period, or a request beyond mere correction?

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and compensation_award_or_decree_final and later_application_seeks_redetermination_or_additional_benefits and not application_within_express_statutory_remedy

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The matter concerns compensation determined under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, whether before the Collector, the reference court or a higher court.
predicates.compensation_award_or_decree_final: The compensation award or decree has become final and conclusive, for example because no appeal or special leave was sought in time or the appeal was dismissed.
predicates.later_application_seeks_redetermination_: After finality, a fresh application or petition seeks redetermination of compensation or additional statutory benefits (such as additional amount, solatium or interest) that were not part of the original decision.
predicates.application_within_express_statutory_rem: The application falls within a remedy the Act expressly gives and meets its conditions, such as a section 28A redetermination by a person who did not seek a reference and applied in time, or a correction of a clerical or arithmetic error under section 13-A of the Act or section 152 CPC.
predicates.final_award_cannot_be_reopened_and_resul: The final award or decree cannot be reopened through the later application, and any order granting relief on it is without jurisdiction, void or a nullity.

definition: A final compensation award or decree under the Land Acquisition Act can be reopened only through a remedy the Act expressly provides, such as section 28A redetermination within time by a person who did not seek a reference, or a permitted correction. Applications for redetermination or for additional benefits outside those remedies, whether by a prior reference applicant, out of time, or by inherent power, are without jurisdiction and resulting orders are void.
exceptions_or_limits: Section 28A redetermination is available only to persons who did not seek a section 18 reference and who apply within three months of the reference court's award, excluding the day of the award and the time taken to obtain a copy.
Correction of clerical or arithmetic mistakes under section 13-A of the Act or section 152 CPC remains permissible.
Statutory additions such as those under sections 23(1-A), 23(2) and 28 can be awarded only as part of a valid compensation determination or enhancement, not as an independent entitlement.
Section 151 CPC inherent powers cannot supply jurisdiction to grant fresh substantive relief where the Act defines the court's powers.

common_material_facts: A compensation award or decree had already become final or been made under the Act.
A later application or proceeding sought redetermination or additional statutory benefits.
The application did not fit within an express statutory remedy because of a prior reference, delay, absent jurisdiction, or a request for substantive rather than corrective relief.
Lower authorities or courts had nonetheless granted relief, which was set aside.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, sections 18, 25, 28A (including 28A(1) and 28A(3))
Sections 23(1), 23(1-A), 23(2), 26(2), 28 and 13-A of the Act
Sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold that the reopening or redetermination was impermissible and that the resulting orders were without jurisdiction, void or set aside.
variations: Two members (439812_1, 91449410_1) concern post-decree applications for benefits introduced by amendment, resolved on the limits of inherent and correction powers.
One member (138947_2) turns on the applicant's earlier section 18 reference, which excludes section 28A.
One member (1771435_5) turns on the three-month limitation under section 28A(1).
One member (166471636_3) turns on a redetermination made without jurisdiction, so statutory additions could not be granted independently.

legal_question: What is the effect of a prior magistrate's or administrative authority's order on possession (a summary or non-final determination) on a civil or other competent court's independent adjudication of possession and property rights?

predicates.prior_possession_order_by_magistrate_or_: A magistrate (e.g. under Section 145 CrPC) or an administrative authority has earlier made an order concerning possession of the property.
predicates.order_is_summary_or_not_final_adjudicati: The earlier order was made in a summary inquiry into possession, or is not final and binding on the parties, and did not adjudicate title or civil rights.
predicates.competent_court_adjudicates_possession_o: A civil court or other court competent to decide title or entitlement to possession is deciding the parties' possession or property rights.
predicates.competent_court_may_decide_possession_in: The competent court may reach its own finding on possession and rights, treating the earlier order at most as evidence of what was ordered and of possession at that time, not as binding.

definition: A magistrate's summary possession order, or a non-final administrative order, determines at most possession at a particular time. It confers no title and does not bind a competent court, which may decide possession and entitlement independently, with the earlier order being only evidence. The declaration of possession is also not disregarded merely because of it, and a concluded order is not quashed merely because a civil suit is later filed.
exceptions_or_limits: A concluded, final criminal possession order is not to be quashed merely because the unsuccessful party later files a civil suit; the party must seek relief in the civil court (718309_1).
The prior order is still relevant as evidence of the order made and, between the parties, of possession; it is not wholly irrelevant.
A magistrate's declaration of actual possession, without an order transferring possession, does not deprive the declared party of statutory benefits attached to its possession (1497995_5).
The rule on non-binding effect applies to summary or non-final orders; it does not extend to orders that are final and binding between the parties.

common_material_facts: A magistrate or administrative authority had made an earlier order on possession of disputed property.
A civil suit or civil proceeding about possession or title followed or was pending.
The earlier order was summary or not final, and did not adjudicate title.
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 145(4), 145(6) and 146(1) CrPC
Section 145 CrPC, 1973
Bhinka v. Charan Singh, AIR 1959 SC 960
Jhunamal v. State of M.P., (1988) 4 SCC 452
Anil Behari Ghosh v. Latika Bala Dassi, AIR 1955 SC 566
Ram Sumer Puri Mahant v. State of U.P., [1985] 1 SCC 427
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In about 4 of 5 members, the earlier possession order does not bind the civil or competent court, which may decide possession independently. In 1 member (718309_1), a concluded criminal order is protected from being quashed merely because of a later civil suit. In 1 member (1497995_5), the declared possession is not disregarded because of the magistrate's order.
variations: 337165_1 and 718309_2 stress that a summary inquiry into possession does not bind the court deciding rights.
1575163_2 concerns an administrative (settlement) order that was not final, rather than a criminal order.
718309_1 concerns the procedural point that a concluded criminal order should not be quashed because of a later civil suit, a complement rather than an application of the main rule.
1497995_5 concerns whether a magistrate's declaration of possession, with no transfer order, affects statutory benefits tied to possession.

split_suggestion: Optionally separate 718309_1 (no quashing of concluded criminal orders because of a later civil suit) and 1497995_5 (declared possession not disregarded for statutory benefits) from the core group (337165_1, 718309_2, 1575163_2) on the non-binding effect of summary or non-final possession orders.

legal_question: Does a contractual clause stipulating a sum (damages, penalty or liquidated damages) payable on breach of an agreement to sell bar specific performance, or is it a bar only where the contract makes payment an alternative to performance by giving the defaulting party an option to pay instead of performing?

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The plaintiff seeks specific performance of an agreement (here, an agreement to sell or transfer property).
predicates.contract_names_sum_payable_on_breach: The contract names a sum (called damages, penalty or liquidated damages, possibly with refund of advance) payable if a party breaches.
predicates.contract_gives_defaulting_party_option_t: On a proper construction, the contract makes payment of the named sum an alternative to performance, so the defaulting party may elect to pay instead of performing; the clause does not merely secure performance or provide compensation, and does not make money an exclusive remedy.
predicates.breach_sum_clause_does_not_bar_specific_: The named-sum clause does not prevent the court from decreeing specific performance, subject to the other statutory requirements and the court's discretion.

definition: A sum named in the contract for breach does not by itself bar specific performance. It is a bar only if, on construction, the contract makes payment an alternative to performance by giving the defaulting party an option to pay instead of performing. A clause that merely secures performance is at most evidence on the question of adequacy of damages and does not rebut the presumption in favour of specific performance of immovable property contracts.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the contract gives the defaulting party an option to pay the named sum instead of performing, or makes money the exclusive remedy.
The stipulated sum is evidence on whether damages are an adequate remedy but is not conclusive.

Specific performance remains discretionary and subject to the plaintiff proving the defendant's breach and the plaintiff's readiness and willingness; the court may also consider compensation where it refuses specific performance and compensation was claimed.
The presumption of inadequacy of damages for immovable property can be rebutted by other proof such as fraud, misrepresentation or unfair advantage, which was not established in the members.

common_material_facts: Agreement to sell immovable property contained a clause for damages, penalty or liquidated damages on breach, often with refund of advance
The clause did not give the seller or defaulting party an option to pay the sum instead of conveying the property
Buyer sought specific performance despite the clause and the seller relied on the clause to resist it
statutes_and_provisions: Specific Relief Act, 1963 sections 10, 20, 21, 23
Specific Relief Act, 1877 sections 12, 20, 22
Jammu and Kashmir Specific Relief Act, 1977 (1920 A.D.) section 20
M.L. Devender Singh v. Syed Khaja; Sir Edward Fry's treatise on the distinction between security for performance and an alternative to performance
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold that the stipulated-sum clause does not bar specific performance because it secures performance rather than providing an alternative to it.
variations: Some members rest on statutory text (sections 20/23 and their predecessors), while one rests only on construction of the contract without citing authority.
One member frames the point as the clause being only evidence on the section 12/10 presumption of inadequacy of damages.
One member characterises the clause as a penalty, another as liquidated damages.
One member holds an earlier contrary decision (Dadarao v. Ramrao) per incuriam for ignoring section 23.
One member notes the agreement was silent on specific performance and that compensation is available under section 21 if specific performance is refused.

legal_question: When a will is challenged as suspicious, does a single feature such as exclusion of natural heirs, unequal distribution, or non-registration make it invalid, or must the court assess all surrounding circumstances cumulatively and consider the explanations offered?

predicates.will_validity_contested: The validity or due execution of a will is challenged in court on the ground of suspicious circumstances.
predicates.suspicious_feature_relied_on_is_isolated: The challenger relies on a single feature of the will or its execution (for example exclusion or reduced share of natural heirs, unequal distribution, a difference in registration, or an unusual formality) as the basis for suspicion.
predicates.other_unexplained_suspicious_circumstanc: Other suspicious circumstances surrounding the will remain unexplained to the court's satisfaction, so that cumulatively they raise doubt about execution or the testator's free disposition.
predicates.feature_alone_does_not_make_will_suspici: The single feature, taken alone, does not establish a suspicious circumstance or justify rejecting the will; the court decides on a cumulative assessment of all circumstances.

definition: A will is not rendered suspicious or invalid by any single feature, such as exclusion of natural heirs, unequal distribution of property or a difference in registration. The court must weigh all unusual features cumulatively, and features that are explained or reasonably accounted for do not defeat the will.
exceptions_or_limits: The propounder must still explain genuine suspicious circumstances to the court's satisfaction; if unexplained circumstances remain, the cumulative assessment may lead to rejection of the will.
The rule does not validate a will where the isolated feature is accompanied by other unexplained suspicious circumstances.
Where a feature is relied on, the explanation offered (for example a reason for exclusion or for a registration difference) must be reasonable on the evidence.

common_material_facts: Testator excluded or gave lesser shares to natural heirs such as sons, a wife, or a son and daughters
Reasons for the disposition were apparent or evidenced, such as care by beneficiaries, neglect by the heir, lifetime settlements or gifts, or family acrimony
Other unusual features (registration difference, change of witnesses, missing original, place of execution discrepancy) were explained
The challenged disposition was found natural in context
statutes_and_provisions: H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma (principles on proof of wills)
Ved Mitra Verma v. Dharam Deo Verma
Rabindra Nath Mukherjee v. Panchanan Banerjee
Leela Rajagopal v. Kamala Menon Cocharan (cumulative assessment)
Sections 281 and 282, Indian Succession Act, 1925 (verification in probate petition)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold that the single feature relied on, or the set of features once explained, did not make the will suspicious, so the will was upheld or the finding of suspicion was set aside.
variations: One member is a cumulative assessment of several explained circumstances; the others deal with one specific feature (exclusion of heirs in 3, unequal distribution in 1, non-registration in 1)
Some members rest on authorities and others (335629 issues) cite no authority
Exclusion of heirs is supported by caring beneficiaries, neglect by the heir or lifetime settlement in different members
335629_2 turns on an explanation of why one will was registered and the other was not

legal_question: Does a statutory agricultural land ceiling apply to restrict a person's holding, and make the excess liable to surrender, whenever the holding is found to exceed the permissible limit as defined by the statute, including where the excess arises after commencement or where the ordinary-acre cap is exceeded?

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The case concerns the application of an agricultural land ceiling statute to a person's or family's landholding.
predicates.holding_exceeds_statutory_permissible_li: The person's holding, measured as the statute defines it (including any ordinary-acre cap that applies where standard-acre conversion yields a larger area), exceeds the permissible limit, whether at commencement or by later acquisition, redemption or restoration of possession.
predicates.excess_land_is_liable_to_surrender_under: The ceiling restriction applies and the land above the permissible limit is liable to be surrendered or treated as surplus, even if the holding is below the standard-acre figure or the Act lacks express enforcement machinery.

definition: A land ceiling statute applies on its plain terms whenever a person is found to hold land above the permissible area, whether the excess existed at commencement or arose later. The limit is the one the statute defines, so an ordinary-acre cap applies even if the holding is under the standard-acre figure, and the excess is liable to surrender.
exceptions_or_limits: The permissible area must be computed under the statute's own definition; a holding below the standard-acre figure is not protected where the ordinary-acre ceiling is exceeded.
Specific provisions on particular later acquisitions (e.g. ss. 32-L, 32-M) do not restrict the general ceiling provision.
Absent excess over the permissible limit, the rule does not apply; for acquisitions, the bar operates only where the acquisition would take the total holding above the ceiling.

common_material_facts: Landowner's holding exceeded the statutory permissible area, measured in standard or ordinary acres
Excess arose after commencement of the ceiling provisions, through redemption of a mortgage, restoration of possession, or acquisition
Earlier decisions or claims treated a lower or different limit as applicable
statutes_and_provisions: Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, s. 2(2)/2(3) (permissible area; 30 standard acres or 60 ordinary acres)
Section 32-A, 32-A(1) (continuing ceiling on personal cultivation)
Sections 32-B, 32-L, 32-M
Sections 3, 5 and 9 of a ceiling Act (prohibition, ceiling area, bar on acquisition beyond ceiling)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members apply the ceiling on its plain terms and find the excess liable to surrender or the ceiling applicable: 2 on the continuing operation of s. 32-A, 2 on the ordinary-acre cap, and 1 on the bar on acquisition beyond the ceiling.
variations: Two members concern the continuing, post-commencement operation of s. 32-A.
Two members concern the definition of permissible area, with the ordinary-acre cap overriding the standard-acre figure.
One member concerns the general bar on acquiring land beyond the ceiling.
One member holds that the lack of express machinery does not defeat the plain words of the provision.

legal_question: Can a court (reference court or civil court) determine or enhance compensation for acquired land under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, when no valid reference on compensation has been made to it under Section 18, and can that defect be cured by acquiescence, a later clarification, or an ordinary suit?

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The matter arises under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and concerns the amount of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.no_valid_reference_on_compensation_objec: No valid reference of the compensation objection was made to the court under Section 18. For example, the reference was limited to apportionment, the Collector made no reference, or the claimant had bound himself by a consent award.
predicates.court_or_civil_suit_determines_compensat: A reference court or an ordinary civil court has determined, or enhanced, compensation or awarded statutory benefits such as solatium and interest.
predicates.court_lacks_jurisdiction_to_determine_or: The court had no jurisdiction to decide the compensation, and its determination or enhancement is a nullity and liable to be set aside.

definition: Under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, a court's jurisdiction over compensation arises only from a valid Section 18 reference and is confined to the matters referred. Without a reference on compensation, the court cannot determine or enhance it, nor award statutory benefits that depend on the reference. An ordinary civil suit cannot substitute for the reference, and the defect is not cured by the parties' failure to object or by a later clarification.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule concerns jurisdiction over compensation; a valid reference on compensation confers jurisdiction to determine market value, solatium and interest.

Section 28-A redetermination (1806862_8) is a distinct statutory remedy. It depends on a court's enhancement of compensation for comparable land under the same notification, and not on an award on an unrelated objection.
The jurisdictional defect cannot be waived by acquiescence or by the failure to object before the trial court, so the objection can be raised on appeal.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the scope of Section 28-A redetermination, which requires an award enhancing compensation for comparable land under the same notification. It does not address a court's lack of jurisdiction for want of a valid reference, though it shares the principle that the remedy depends on a reference on compensation.

common_material_facts: Compensation was determined or enhanced by a reference court or civil court although no reference on compensation had been validly made.
The reference was limited to apportionment, or the Collector made no reference, or a consent award existed.
The objection to jurisdiction was raised late, on appeal, or in superior proceedings.
Claimants sought enhancement through a civil suit or through a later clarification of the reference.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 28-A (redetermination)
Section 9, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (impliedly excluded)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 4 of 5 members the court's determination or enhancement of compensation was held to be without jurisdiction and set aside. The fifth member limits Section 28-A redetermination to comparable land whose compensation was enhanced.
variations: The missing reference arose in different ways: a consent award (1549211_3), a reference limited to apportionment (1550957_1, 247119_1), and no reference at all with an ordinary suit instead (1622535_1).
Some members stress that the defect cannot be waived or cured by acquiescence (1550957_1, 247119_1), while others stress that the special procedure impliedly excludes civil suits (1622535_1).
1806862_8 concerns the scope of Section 28-A redetermination and comparability of land, not jurisdiction.

split_suggestion: Keep 1549211_3, 1550957_1, 1622535_1 and 247119_1 together as 'no valid reference means no jurisdiction over compensation'. Treat 1806862_8 separately as a Section 28-A redetermination issue.

legal_question: When will a challenge to a land acquisition fail because of the landowners' own conduct or because a procedural or technical objection (delay, prematurity, non-service, late communication, symbolic possession) is not made out on the facts?

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a land acquisition (by suit, appeal or petition) on a procedural, technical or timing ground.
predicates.procedural_defect_made_out_on_record: The record establishes the asserted defect, for example that notice was not served, possession was only symbolic, a statutory step was not completed before the declaration, or the claimants were guilty of laches.
predicates.challenge_not_sustained_on_that_procedur: The particular objection (non-service, lack of possession, prematurity, late communication or laches) does not defeat the acquisition or the claimants' relief, as the case may be, on that ground.

definition: A land acquisition challenge, or an objection to it, turns on whether the alleged procedural or technical defect is made out on the record and under the statute. Where notice was in fact served, possession was in fact taken, objections were decided before the declaration, or the timing objection is merely technical and unraised, the defect does not invalidate the acquisition or bar the suit; where claimants were diligent, laches does not bar relief.
exceptions_or_limits: The members do not share a single narrow rule; the common thread is that outcomes depend on the facts found and on what the statute actually requires.
The outcome depends on factual findings (service, possession certificates, absence of delay) that must be established on the record.
The prematurity holding is limited to cases where the declaration came before the written statements and prematurity was not raised at trial.
The late-communication holding applies only where the statute does not make communication before the declaration a condition of validity and the objections were in fact decided earlier.
The laches member is the only one where the claimants succeed on the point; the others reject the challenge.

common_material_facts: A challenge to land acquisition rests on an alleged procedural, timing or notice defect.
The record (service reports, possession certificates, orders dated before the declaration, pleadings history) answers the alleged defect.
Lower courts' concurrent findings of fact are not disturbed.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 28(1), Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966
Sections 3C(2) and 3D(1), National Highways Act, 1956
Raghbir Singh Sehrawat v. State of Haryana (distinguished on facts)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 4 of 5 members the procedural or technical objection to the acquisition is rejected. In 1 (laches) the landowners' relief is held not barred. In all 5 the objection or bar fails on the facts or statute.
variations: One member concerns the claimants' own conduct (laches or acquiescence), not a defect in the acquisition process.
One member concerns the maintainability of a suit (prematurity).
Three members concern notice, possession or communication under specific statutes.
Reasoning ranges from statutory interpretation to appreciation of evidence to a discretionary equitable assessment.

split_suggestion: Split into: (a) laches, delay and acquiescence and maintainability or prematurity of suits (1564044_2, 1802930_1); (b) notice, possession and communication defects in the acquisition process (185311903_4, 348205_5, 98737584_1). Group (b) could be split further into factual non-service or possession (185311903_4, 348205_5) and statutory sequencing of objections and declaration (98737584_1).

legal_question: Is the characterization of a transaction as an adventure in the nature of trade (or as investment versus dealing) a mixed question of law and fact that a court can review in a tax reference or appeal, even though the Tribunal's primary findings of fact are accepted?

predicates.tax_proceeding_from_tribunal_decision: The matter is a statutory tax reference (or an appeal arising from one) challenging a Tribunal's decision under the Income-tax Act.
predicates.tribunal_found_primary_facts: The Tribunal has found the primary evidentiary facts of the transaction(s).
predicates.ultimate_characterization_requires_apply: Deciding whether the transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade, or investment as against dealing, requires applying the legal meaning or criteria of trade or business to the found facts.
predicates.characterization_is_a_mixed_question_of_: The characterization is a mixed question of law and fact; the court accepts the primary findings but may examine whether the Tribunal correctly applied the legal principles.

definition: Whether a transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade (or an investment or dealing) is a mixed question of law and fact. The court accepts the Tribunal's primary factual findings but may review in a tax reference whether the legal test was correctly applied to them.
exceptions_or_limits: The court is bound by the Tribunal's primary findings of fact and may not re-appraise the evidence.
Interference with the ultimate conclusion is justified where the Tribunal misdirected itself in law or the inference is not justified in law on the proved facts.
Holding that the question is reviewable does not decide the merits of the classification; in one member the merits were left undecided.

common_material_facts: The Tribunal classified a transaction (property purchase and sale, land sale, or share or asset dealings) as an adventure in the nature of trade or as dealing.
The classification depended on primary facts such as the purpose of acquisition, intended resale, holding period, frequency of transactions, and the circumstances of sale.
The challenge was brought in a reference under section 66(1) of the 1922 Act, or in an appeal arising from such a reference.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 2(4), Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 (definition of business, including an adventure in the nature of trade)
Section 66(1), Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 (reference of questions of law)
G. Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. C.I.T. (relied on in 4 of 5 members)
Sree Meenakshi Mills v. C.I.T.; Oriental Investment Co. v. C.I.T.; Liquidators of Pursa Ltd. v. C.I.T.; Edwards v. Bairstow
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold the characterization to be a mixed question of law and fact open to review in the reference or appeal. In one of them the High Court's refusal to interfere was held wrong.
variations: Some members state the point generally (1575591_1, 1604881_2, 551145_2).
812823_1 applies it to investment versus dealing in shares and the treatment of profits as business profits.
971939_3 adds that review is available where the Tribunal misdirected itself in law, and it held that the High Court wrongly treated the conclusions as pure fact.
551145_2 relies on Meenakshi Mills, Oriental Investment and Edwards v. Bairstow.
1604881_2 arises from a special leave appeal rather than a reference.

legal_question: Where a statute provides a specific remedy or procedure for a claimed right (adjustment or refund of excess rent, or restoration of possession to a tenant), can the party bypass it by relying on an automatic or general-law set-off, or on a summary procedure?

predicates.statute_provides_specific_remedy_or_proc: The governing statute provides a specific remedy, election or procedure (for example adjustment or refund of excess rent, or restoration of possession before the designated authority) for the right the party asserts.
predicates.party_did_not_invoke_or_follow_that_proc: The party did not elect, claim or follow the statutory procedure, including by not specifically claiming adjustment or by not applying to the designated authority within time.
predicates.party_relies_on_automatic_adjustment_gen: The party relies on automatic set-off of excess rent, a general-law set-off, or a summary eviction procedure, instead of the statutory remedy.
predicates.alternative_route_not_available: The automatic set-off, general-law set-off or summary procedure is not allowed, so the defence to eviction fails or the authority lacks jurisdiction.

definition: Where the statute gives a specific remedy or procedure, such as electing and claiming adjustment of excess rent or seeking restoration from the designated authority, a party cannot bypass it through automatic set-off, general-law set-off or a summary procedure. Excess rent therefore does not automatically offset arrears to defeat eviction, and a summary eviction application is not maintainable where the ordinary statutory remedy exists.
exceptions_or_limits: Automatic set-off is not barred where the tenant has an agreement for adjustment or has specifically claimed adjustment (for example by a set-off claim made in accordance with the applicable procedure); the rent cases distinguish decisions involving such an agreement or claim.

Summary eviction under the relevant section remains available where the Act provides no other remedy, or in the other categories it specifies (for example land whose management was assumed, or possession obtained through an invalid transfer).
The rent-arrears members concern rent-control statutes whose adjustment provisions differ; the rule applies only where the statute or general law does not allow automatic adjustment.

common_material_facts: Tenant paid rent above the lawful or fair rent and later fell into arrears, and the landlord sought eviction for default (3 members).
The tenant had not elected adjustment, claimed set-off, or followed the statutory refund procedure.
A tenant sought summary eviction of a landlord holding land after a surrender that lacked statutory formalities, although restoration from the Mamlatdar was available (2 members).
statutes_and_provisions: Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1977, s. 8(2)
West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, s. 7
Tenancy Act ss. 29(1), 70(n), 74 and 84 (including s. 84(c)), as cited in the members
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members reject the shortcut: 3 deny automatic or general-law set-off against rent arrears, and 2 hold the Collector lacks jurisdiction for summary eviction because the tenant has a remedy before the Mamlatdar.
variations: Two members concern eviction for rent default and set-off; two concern the Collector's summary-eviction jurisdiction under a tenancy statute; one concerns a general-law set-off against a special rent statute's refund procedure.
In the Bihar cases the bar is lack of election or claim for adjustment, whereas in the West Bengal case it is non-compliance with the statutory procedure and time limit and lack of foundation.
The Bihar cases distinguish precedents on the basis of an advance payment or an adjustment agreement; the tenancy cases rely on the statute's structure and the appeal under s. 74.

split_suggestion: For a tighter rule, split into (a) excess rent and set-off against arrears in eviction proceedings (150175_2, 510826_1, 800820_2) and (b) the Collector's summary-eviction jurisdiction under s. 84 versus the s. 29(1) remedy (1879419_2, 738221_2).

legal_question: Does a mistake, omission or procedural irregularity in the notification or the steps imposing a municipal or local tax invalidate the levy when the authority had power to levy the tax, the defect is not fundamental, inhabitants were not substantially prejudiced, and the imposition was officially notified?

rule.if: challenge_to_local_tax_levy and authority_has_power_to_levy_the_tax and defect_in_notification_or_imposition_procedure and not defect_is_fundamental and not substantial_prejudice_to_inhabitants

predicates.challenge_to_local_tax_levy: The validity of a tax imposed by a municipality, board or town area authority is challenged on the ground of a defect in the notification or the imposition process.
predicates.authority_has_power_to_levy_the_tax: The taxing authority has statutory power to impose the tax on the subject or service that the levy covers.
predicates.defect_in_notification_or_imposition_pro: There is a mistake, omission or irregularity, such as a wrong clause reference, non-publication of a resolution or modified proposal, or an omitted boundary schedule, in the notification or in the steps leading to the levy.
predicates.defect_is_fundamental: The defect goes to the root of the levy, for example by leaving the taxed subject or area in real doubt or by denying inhabitants a right they had under the Act.
predicates.substantial_prejudice_to_inhabitants: The defect deprived inhabitants of a real opportunity to object or otherwise caused them substantial prejudice.
predicates.defect_does_not_invalidate_tax_levy: The levy remains valid and effective despite the defect, which is treated as a curable irregularity or an inconsequential mistake.

definition: A local tax levy is not invalidated by a non-fundamental mistake or irregularity in the notification or imposition steps if the authority had power to levy the tax, the taxed subject and area are clear, and inhabitants suffered no substantial prejudice. Where the statute makes the official notification conclusive proof of compliance, that provision reinforces this result.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the defect is fundamental or causes substantial prejudice to inhabitants, for example by depriving them of a right to object that they actually had.
The rule does not apply where the authority lacks power to tax the subject. A mistaken clause reference is excused only because the power exists under another clause.
The cure by conclusive-proof provisions depends on an official notification of imposition having actually been issued under the relevant Act.
Where the boundaries or taxed subject are genuinely uncertain, an omission may not be treated as inconsequential.

common_material_facts: The taxing authority had power to impose the tax and had issued a final notification of imposition.
There was a technical defect in the notification or in the preparatory steps, such as a wrong clause reference, unpublished resolution, unpublished modified proposal or omitted boundary schedule.
Inhabitants had notice of, or an opportunity to object to, the proposed levy, and no real prejudice resulted.
The subject and area of the tax were reasonably clear despite the defect.
statutes_and_provisions: U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, s. 128(1)(xi) and (xii)
U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, s. 132(2)
U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, s. 134(2)
U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, s. 135(2) and (3)
U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, s. 94
U.P. Town Area Act, 1914, ss. 39(2), 39(3) and 15B(4)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 5 members the defect was held not to invalidate the tax. It was treated as a mistake, a curable irregularity or an inconsequential omission.
variations: One member turns on the existence of taxing power despite a wrong clause citation, with no procedural cure involved.
Three members rely on the conclusive-proof effect of the notification under s. 135(3) to cure non-fundamental procedural irregularities.
One member concerns a defect in the notification itself (omitted boundary schedule), cured by a later consistent insertion and the existing area designation.
The defects differ: wrong provision cited, non-publication of a modified proposal, non-publication of an imposition resolution, and a missing boundary schedule.

legal_question: Under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, can a claimant seek redetermination of compensation on the strength of a later award or an appellate judgment, or must the application rest on, and be filed within three months of, an award of the reference court of original jurisdiction under Part III?

predicates.land_acquisition_redetermination_claim: The claimant seeks redetermination of land acquisition compensation under Section 28-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
predicates.claim_based_on_appellate_judgment: The claim relies on a judgment of an appellate court (for example, in an appeal under Section 54) rather than on an award of the reference court under Part III.
predicates.later_award_relied_on_after_period_from_: The claimant relies on a later award or decision after the three-month period from the reference court award on which the claim is based has already expired.
predicates.application_filed_after_three_months_fro: The application was filed more than three months (excluding statutory exclusions such as the day of the award and time to obtain a copy) after the reference court award on which it is based.
predicates.redetermination_not_available_and_applic: The redetermination application fails as barred by limitation, or because it lacks a qualifying reference court award as its basis.

definition: A Section 28-A redetermination application must rest on an award of the court of original jurisdiction on a reference under Part III and be made within three months of that award. Appellate judgments and later awards neither qualify as a basis nor revive or restart an expired period.
exceptions_or_limits: Time excluded under Section 28-A(1) (the day of the award and time needed to obtain a copy) is allowed when computing the three months.
The Section 28-A scheme operates prospectively from 24 September 1984, so an earliest award that predated it cannot be revived by later decisions.
Babua Ram and Karnail Singh were overruled insofar as they confined the right to the earliest reference award; the period runs from the reference award on which redetermination is sought.

Where a redetermination order reflected the award in force when it was made and a superior court later reduces compensation, a further redetermination to apply the reduction is not barred by earlier delay (the 192469_2 situation, which concerns a different question).

outlier_members.reason: It concerns whether delay in challenging earlier redetermination orders bars applying a later appellate reduction of compensation, not the basis or limitation for a Section 28-A application.

common_material_facts: Claimants sought redetermination under Section 28-A relying on a later award or an appellate judgment.
A reference court award existed earlier, and the application came after the three-month period from it or relied on an appellate decision.
Claimants usually accepted the Collector's award and did not seek a reference themselves.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Section 28-A(1)
Sections 18, 26(2), 54, 2(d) and 3(d)
Part III and Part VIII of the Act
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 4 of 5 members the redetermination claim was rejected as time-barred or unavailable because it rested on an appellate judgment or a later award. The remaining member allowed a later appellate reduction to be applied despite earlier delay.
variations: Some members stress the limitation period running from the reference award (178452445_1, 1806862_2), others the nature of the qualifying award (179658922_1), and one the prospective operation of the scheme (166471636_1).
166471636_1 followed Babua Ram's earliest-award approach, which 178452445_1 later qualified by holding that the period runs from the reference award on which redetermination is sought.
192469_2 addresses the effect of a later reduction on prior redetermination orders and is not a Section 28-A limitation holding.

split_suggestion: Keep the four members on the basis and limitation of a Section 28-A application together. Move 192469_2 to a separate cluster on the effect of delay and later appellate reduction on existing redetermination orders.

legal_question: Is a person whose right to or interest in property (land, a land grant, an assessment-free holding, or a payment charged on an estate) is extinguished or modified by a jagir or inam abolition statute entitled to compensation under the statute's compensation provisions?

rule.if: compensation_claim_under_abolition_statute and claimant_had_right_or_interest_in_property_before_abolition and abolition_statute_extinguished_or_modified_that_interest and not compensation_otherwise_provided_for_the_change and not interest_was_mere_concession_or_resumable_remuneration_or_personal_liability

predicates.compensation_claim_under_abolition_statu: The claim is made under the compensation provisions of a jagir, inam or similar abolition statute (for example, a provision for jagirdars or for persons other than jagirdars).
predicates.claimant_had_right_or_interest_in_proper: Before abolition the claimant held an established right to or interest in property, such as unbuilt village-site land, a grant of land burdened with service, a right to hold land free of assessment, or a payment charged on the estate.
predicates.abolition_statute_extinguished_or_modifi: The abolition statute vested the property in the State, extinguished the interest, or changed it to the claimant's disadvantage (for example by making assessment-free land assessable).
predicates.compensation_otherwise_provided_for_the_: The statute or another law already provides compensation for the extinguishment or modification (relevant to claims by persons other than jagirdars).
predicates.interest_was_mere_concession_or_resumabl: The interest was only a revocable concession, a resumable grant of profits as remuneration for an office, a mere temporary suspension of revenue, or only the personal liability of the estate holder rather than a charge on the estate; also covers interests within the statute's express exceptions.
predicates.claimant_entitled_to_compensation: The claimant is entitled to claim compensation, with the amount determined in further inquiry.

definition: Where an abolition statute extinguishes or modifies an established right to or interest in property, the holder is entitled to compensation under the statute's compensation provisions, unless compensation is already provided or the interest was a mere concession, resumable remuneration, a temporary suspension or a personal liability, or falls within a statutory exception.
exceptions_or_limits: No entitlement where compensation for the change is otherwise provided under the Act.
A reduced assessment that was only a concession rather than an established right does not qualify.
A grant of land profits as remuneration for an office is resumable and is not compensable in the same way as a grant of land burdened with service.
A payment that is only the personal liability of the estate holder, and not a charge on the estate, is not an interest in property.
A mere temporary suspension of land revenue does not qualify.
A jagirdar's compensation for unbuilt village-site land is subject to the exceptions in section 11(3)(i) to (iii) and requires proof of a right or interest.
The claimant must prove the interest; the quantum is left for further determination.

common_material_facts: Abolition of a jagir or inam estate under a Bombay-area abolition statute affected the claimant's rights in property.
In three members the claimant was not the jagirdar and claimed under the 'person other than a jagirdar' provision (section 14(1)).
In two members the right was to hold land free of assessment under a compromise or consent decree, and the land became assessable after abolition.
The statute provided no other compensation for the change.
The interests were land, village-site land, a land grant burdened with service, or an allowance charged on the estate.
statutes_and_provisions: Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, sections 3, 4, 8, 11(3) and 14(1)
Bombay Bhil Naik Inam Abolition Act, 1955, section 7(1)
Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (as the compensation measure under section 11(3))
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold that the claimant is entitled to compensation, with the amount to be determined later in several of them.
variations: One member concerns a jagirdar's compensation under section 11(3) for land vested in the State; the others concern non-jagirdars under section 14(1) or the analogous section 7(1).
Two members turn on whether assessment-free enjoyment is an interest in property modified by making the land assessable, distinguishing concession cases and Shapurji Jivanji.
One member turns on whether a grant was of land burdened with service (not resumable) or of revenue as remuneration (resumable).
One member turns on whether a cash allowance was a charge on the estate or a personal liability.

legal_question: In an inquiry preceding a land acquisition for a company, must interested landowners be given a reasonable opportunity to be heard, and what is the consequence of an inquiry held without that hearing?

rule.if: company_land_acquisition_proceeding and collector_inquiry_examines_company_negotiation_efforts_or_land_suitability and landowners_are_interested_persons and not landowners_given_reasonable_opportunity_to_be_heard

predicates.company_land_acquisition_proceeding: The acquisition is sought for a company and falls under the company-acquisition provisions (Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act and the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963).
predicates.collector_inquiry_examines_company_negot: The Collector's inquiry required before government consent covers matters such as the company's efforts to buy the land by negotiation at a reasonable price and the suitability and extent of the land.
predicates.landowners_are_interested_persons: The persons claiming a hearing are owners or others interested in the land proposed for acquisition.
predicates.landowners_given_reasonable_opportunity_: The landowners were given a fair chance to be heard and to adduce material in the inquiry to prove or disprove the company's claims.
predicates.inquiry_is_invalid_and_cannot_support_go: The inquiry is defective for breach of natural justice and cannot validly support the government's consent or the acquisition.

definition: Where the Collector's inquiry in a company acquisition looks into matters such as the company's negotiation efforts and the suitability of the land, the interested landowners must be given a reasonable opportunity to be heard and to produce material. An inquiry held without that hearing is invalid and cannot support government consent. A later objection inquiry under section 5-A cannot substitute for it.
exceptions_or_limits: The hearing duty is implied from the nature of the inquiry even where the rules are silent on procedure or the Collector's report is only recommendatory.
The required procedure depends on the circumstances, statutory framework and function performed; a reasonable opportunity, not a formal trial, is what is required.

A section 5-A inquiry cannot be treated as the section 40 inquiry where the state amendment (Gujarat) removed the link between them. A later section 5-A hearing cannot be assumed because section 17 may dispense with it.

A general objection inquiry under section 5-A, where the Collector only recommends and the government decides public purpose, is administrative. In such an inquiry the commissioner may appoint an authorised officer as Collector and consider the report, absent proof of irregularity.

outlier_members.reason: Concerns the administrative character of a section 5A objection inquiry and the commissioner's power to appoint a Collector and consider the report. It does not address a hearing right in a company-acquisition inquiry.
Concerns a corridor notification, where disputed facts on acreage and enforcement were referred to an inquiry committee. It is not a company land acquisition and does not involve the Companies Rules.

common_material_facts: Acquisition sought for a company, with a Collector's inquiry under Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 into negotiation efforts and land suitability
Landowners were not heard or allowed to submit material in that inquiry
The Collector's report was recommendatory, or a section 5-A inquiry was relied on instead
statutes_and_provisions: Rule 4, Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963
Land Acquisition Act, 1894: sections 5A, 17, 39, 40, 41, 55, 23, 24
Gujarat amendment to sections 40 and 41
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In the 3 covered members, landowners were held entitled to a hearing in the company-acquisition inquiry; where it was denied, the inquiry was invalid and could not support the consent (2 members concerned the invalidity of the inquiry, 1 the duty to hear). The 2 outliers involve different points: administrative character of the 5A inquiry, and referral of factual disputes for inquiry.
variations: 1675739_1 grounds the hearing right in implied natural justice and fair play.
830852_1 grounds it in the owners being the persons with whom the company would negotiate.
830852_4 adds that a section 5-A inquiry cannot stand in for the section 40 inquiry after the Gujarat amendment, so consent fails.

split_suggestion: Keep 1675739_1, 830852_1 and 830852_4 together as the hearing right in company-acquisition inquiries. Move 1964341_3 to a group on the administrative nature of section 5A inquiries and delegation to a Collector. Move 59422893_4 to a group on referring disputed facts to an inquiry committee with a hearing.

legal_question: Is a pending application for building plan approval or permission decided under the law in force when the authority decides it (sanction or refusal), or under the law in force when it was filed, where the applicant has no vested right to approval?

predicates.pending_application_for_statutory_permis: An application for a statutory permission, approval or confirmation (typically a building plan or development permission) had been filed and was still undecided.
predicates.no_final_determination_or_sanction_befor: No sanction, permission or final determination had been made on the application before the applicable law, rules or regulations changed.
predicates.changed_law_effective_when_application_i: The amended or replacement law, rules, bye-laws or restrictions had come into force by the time the authority considered, sanctioned or refused the application.
predicates.application_governed_by_law_in_force_at_: The application must be decided under the law in force at the time of decision or sanction, and filing or pendency of the application, or a settled expectation, gives the applicant no vested right to approval or finality under the earlier law.

definition: A pending application for building plan approval or similar statutory permission confers no vested right to be decided under the law prevailing at filing. It is governed by the law in force when the authority decides or sanctions it, including changes that took effect while it was pending. A right to finality or approval arises only when the determination is actually made.
exceptions_or_limits: The change must actually be in force when the decision is made. A merely proposed or unenforced revised plan does not displace the existing law.
The rule applies where no sanction or final determination had been made before the change. A completed determination or an already vested right may stand differently.
A court order permitting an application or asking for its timely consideration does not direct approval and does not freeze the applicable rules.
The authority must still exercise its jurisdiction within a reasonable time.

common_material_facts: An application for building plan approval or permission was pending and undecided.
The governing regulations or law changed between filing and decision.
The applicant claimed entitlement under the earlier law because of filing or settled expectation.
statutes_and_provisions: Cantonments Act, 1924, ss. 181(2), 181A, 186, 283 and the 1988 bye-laws
Section 5-B of the East Punjab Evacuees' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947
Rule 20(3) of the Building Rules
Howrah Municipal Corporation v. Ganges Rope Co. Ltd.
Director of Public Works v. Ho Po Sang
Kuldeep Singh v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi
Usman Gani J. Khatri v. Cantonment Board
State of West Bengal v. Terra Firma Investment and Trading Pvt. Ltd.
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 5 members hold that the pending application confers no vested right and is decided under the law applicable at the time of sanction or consideration. In 4 members the application is a building plan or permission, and in 1 it is an application for confirmation under evacuee property law.
variations: One member (752151_2) concerns finality of a confirmation order under evacuee property legislation, not building plans.
One member (955330_2) adds that a court order to consider an application within a time does not freeze the rules, and that public interest in civic services justifies restrictions.
One member (1737598_2) stresses that a proposed revised plan not yet in force does not apply.
One member (1703667_2) applies the principle to successive bye-laws and building-restriction schemes under the Cantonments Act.

legal_question: What consequential relief should a court mould when land acquisition proceedings are quashed or found vitiated: should the land be restored to the former owners, and should compensation already received be refunded, retained or treated as compensation?

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The case concerns a challenge to the validity of a land acquisition or of later action under it.
predicates.acquisition_proceedings_quashed_or_vitia: The acquisition proceedings, or later releases, transfers or abandonment under them, are held invalid, unlawful or fraudulent.
predicates.court_exercises_remedial_power_to_mould_: The court uses its remedial or equitable powers (for example Article 142 or restitution principles) to decide the consequences of the invalidity.
predicates.court_directs_consequential_relief_on_re: The court orders restoration of the land, retention or refund of compensation, or a structured restitution scheme, depending on the public purpose, whether the project is abandoned, whether restoration is practicable, and third-party and unjust-enrichment concerns.

definition: Once acquisition proceedings are quashed or vitiated, courts decide the consequences case by case. They may restore the land to the owners, with compensation retained or refunded, or they may preserve the acquisition and order structured restitution, depending on whether the project is abandoned, whether restoration is practicable, and the equities of owners, builders and third parties.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the project has been abandoned and the acquisition is invalid, restoration may be ordered without recovery of compensation already paid.
