definition: Where custom, as shown by customary-law records and a settled line of decisions, gives the holder of ancestral agricultural land the power to transfer it for consideration, the existence of sons does not restrict that power. The sale cannot be set aside by sons or reversioners unless it was for an immoral purpose.
exceptions_or_limits: The transfer can be challenged if it was for an immoral purpose (found not to be so in these cases).
The rule rests on the customary law of the relevant area, as proved by customary records and decisions, and applies to transfers for consideration, not gifts or other gratuitous transfers.
A doubtful statement in a customary-law manual or an unfollowed contrary decision does not displace settled customary law.

common_material_facts: Ancestral agricultural land held by Jats in the Rohtak customary area was sold for consideration by the holder.
The holder's sons (and other reversionary heirs) challenged the sale.
Allegations of immoral purpose were rejected by the courts.
Customary records (Riwaj-i-am, Joseph's Manual, Tupper) and many earlier decisions supported the power to transfer.
Budal v. Kirpa Ram took a contrary view but had not been followed.
statutes_and_provisions: Riwaj-i-am for Rohtak District
Joseph's Customary Law Manual
Tupper's Statements of Customary Law
Telu v. Chuni
Pahlad Singh v. Sukhdev Singh
Sheoji v. Fajar Ali Khan
Gujar v. Sham Das (agnatic theory)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 4 members uphold the holder's customary power to transfer ancestral land for consideration; sons do not restrict it and the sale is not set aside absent immoral purpose.
variations: Two members (337537_1, 463019_1) address the general power to transfer and the immoral-purpose limit.
Two members (337537_2, 463019_2) address specifically whether the existence of sons restricts the power, and hold that it does not.
The sons-based members also discuss the agnatic theory and the doubtful statement in Joseph's Manual.

legal_question: When does immovable property acquired by the holder of a customary impartible estate become part of that estate, and what evidence shows the holder's intention to incorporate it?

rule.if: customary_impartible_estate and immovable_property_acquired_by_holder and holder_intended_incorporation and not incorporation_excluded_by_statute_or_custom

predicates.customary_impartible_estate: The estate in dispute is a customary impartible estate, typically ancestral and descending by primogeniture.
predicates.immovable_property_acquired_by_holder: The property in question is immovable property acquired by the holder after the original grant of the estate, whether self-acquired or acquired from estate income.
predicates.holder_intended_incorporation: The holder intended to make the property part of the impartible estate, shown by express declaration or inferred from conduct, treatment, administration and other evidence taken as a whole.
predicates.incorporation_excluded_by_statute_or_cus: A statute or proved custom removes or restricts the holder's power to incorporate acquired property into the estate.
predicates.property_forms_part_of_impartible_estate: The property takes on the estate's incidents, including impartibility and descent by primogeniture, and is not divisible as ordinary family property.

definition: A holder of a customary impartible estate may incorporate acquired immovable property into the estate. The test is the holder's intention, which may be express or inferred from conduct and the evidence as a whole, unless a statute or custom excludes the power. Once incorporated, the property is impartible and not divisible.
exceptions_or_limits: The power can be excluded by statute or by custom.
Intention is decisive. Acquisition from estate income does not by itself make the property part of the estate.
The principle applies to immovable property only. Movable property is impartible only if a family custom to that effect is proved.
Incorporation is decided on the facts of each property.
Where both lower courts have concurrently found incorporation on the evidence, the Supreme Court will not ordinarily disturb that finding.
Under the Madras Impartible Estates Act, 1904, property incorporated before the Act can form part of the scheduled estate, which is not confined to the original grant.

common_material_facts: A customary impartible estate, usually ancestral and descending by primogeniture.
Immovable property acquired after the original grant.
A dispute over whether the property is part of the impartible estate or is divisible or separate property.
Intention shown by conduct, administration or treatment of the property as part of the estate.
statutes_and_provisions: Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Devi, relied on in all four members
Madras Impartible Estates Act, 1904, ss. 2(2), 2(3) and 3
Collector of Madura v. Mootoo Ramalinga Sathupathy, on proven usage
Other Privy Council and Supreme Court authorities cited in one member
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all four members the acquired immovable property was held to be incorporated into, or within, the impartible estate, on the basis of the holder's intention.
variations: One member states the general power of incorporation.
One member applies the intention test to a public market and to leasehold rights administered as estate property, and upholds concurrent findings.
One member addresses lands acquired from estate income and notes that income alone is insufficient.
One member concerns the statutory scheduled estate and incorporation before the enactment.

legal_question: Is the belting method (valuing different belts of a large acquired tract at different rates according to road frontage and location) a permissible and appropriate way to determine market value in compulsory acquisition?

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns determination of market value or compensation for land compulsorily acquired.
predicates.large_acquired_tract: The acquired land is an extensive area, not a tiny plot, so that the value of a small plot is not a fair measure of the whole.
predicates.tract_has_road_frontage_land_and_interio: The acquired tract includes land fronting or abutting a road, which is more valuable or attractive, together with land farther inside the tract or differing in location or features.
predicates.belting_method_is_permissible_and_approp: The court may value the tract in differential belts, with higher rates for roadside frontage and lower rates for land farther from the road, and applying that method is not an error.

definition: Where a large tract is acquired and part of it fronts a road while the rest lies inside or differs in location, the court may use the belting method, valuing frontage land higher than interior land. Frontage is ordinarily more valuable, and the value of a tiny plot is not a proper yardstick for a large acquisition.
exceptions_or_limits: The principle has limitations (the Court noted this in citing the older authorities), and the method depends on local circumstances.
A landowner who shows that the method is improper on the facts may succeed, but failing to object or to show impropriety weakens the challenge.
The method is not suited to small or compact plots without meaningful differences in location or frontage.

common_material_facts: Large or extensive tract acquired
Part of the land abuts or fronts a road and is valued higher than interior land
Landowners either earlier sought the method, did not object, or did not show it was improper
Differences in location or local features among parcels
statutes_and_provisions: Section 23, Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (as modified by the Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911)
Union of India v. Mangatu Ram (1997) 6 SCC 59
Andhra Pradesh Industrial Infrastructure Corporation Ltd. v. G. Mohan Reddy (2010) 15 SCC 412
Mohini Mohan v. Province of Bengal, AIR 1951 Cal. 246
Kunjukrishna v. State, AIR 1953 T.C. 177
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members uphold use of the belting method for a large tract with roadside frontage and reject challenges to it.
variations: One member is urban land under the Calcutta Improvement Act, while the others are general acquisitions.
In one member the owner had earlier sought belting and then objected, and uneven land and a tiny-plot comparison were also considered.
In one member the parties did not challenge the method or the belt depths; in another the owners failed to object before the Collector.

legal_question: Does extracting or removing minerals from the surface of land (not only from beneath it) amount to a mining operation, so that the land used for it is treated as a mine or as comprised in or appurtenant to a mine under the relevant mining statutes?

predicates.mineral_deposits_on_or_in_land: The land holds mineral deposits (including minor minerals such as sand or gravel, or coal), whether on the surface or beneath it.
predicates.activity_extracts_or_removes_minerals_to: The activity on the land consists of excavating, removing or collecting the mineral in order to win or obtain it.
predicates.extraction_is_on_or_beneath_surface: The extraction is carried out on or beneath the earth's surface, so that surface location of the deposit is not a bar.
predicates.activity_is_mining_operation_and_land_is: The activity is a mining operation, and the land used for it (or adjacent land used for the mine's purposes) falls within the statutory definition of a mine or is comprised in or appertains to a mine.

definition: Under the mining statutes, winning minerals by excavating or removing them is a mining operation whether the deposit lies on the surface or underground. Land on which such operations are carried on, or adjacent land used for the mine's purposes, falls within the statutory meaning of a mine or is comprised in or appertains to one.
exceptions_or_limits: Applies only where the activity is aimed at winning or obtaining the mineral; the members do not address incidental surface activity.
Treatment of adjacent land as part of a mine depends on its actual use for the mine's purposes (e.g., stacking and sale of coal), as in the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act definition.
The precise definition of 'mine' depends on the statute in question (Mines Act 1952, MMDR Act 1957, Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act 1973, state minor mineral rules).

common_material_facts: Minerals (sand, gravel, coal) lay on or near the land surface rather than deep underground
Excavation or removal of the mineral was ongoing or proposed
The dispute arose in a collateral setting (estate vesting, civil title, challenge to mining regulation) where mine status mattered
statutes_and_provisions: Section 2(j), Mines Act, 1952
Sections 3(d) and 3(e), Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957
Section 2(h)(iv) and (vi), Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973
Rules 2(5) and 2(7), UP Minor Minerals (Concession) Rules, 1963
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that surface extraction is a mining operation and the land is, or forms part of, a mine.
variations: Two members rely on the MMDR Act definitions of mining operations and minor minerals; one relies on the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act definition of mine.
One member extends to adjacent land used for mine purposes; the others concern the deposit land itself.
Contexts differ: estate vesting/retention, civil title, and challenge to mining regulation.

legal_question: Under Section 340(1) CrPC, when must a court make a complaint about an offence connected with its proceedings, and how is the expediency of an inquiry in the interests of justice assessed?

predicates.court_considers_complaint_under_section_: The court is considering whether to make a criminal complaint under Section 340 CrPC (or its equivalent) about an alleged offence.
predicates.alleged_offence_is_connected_to_a_court_: The alleged offence (such as forged or false documents or declarations) relates to or was committed in or in respect of a proceeding before a court, so that it affects the administration of justice.
predicates.court_complaint_is_discretionary_and_dep: The court is not bound to file a complaint automatically and any preliminary inquiry is optional. The court decides whether further inquiry is expedient in the interests of justice by looking at the offence's effect on the administration of justice, not merely the magnitude of injury to an individual, and without deciding guilt.

definition: A court is not obliged to make a complaint whenever an offence affecting the administration of justice appears. It may hold a limited preliminary inquiry, if it thinks one necessary, not to decide guilt but to decide whether an inquiry is expedient in the interests of justice. That expediency turns on the offence's impact on the administration of justice rather than merely on the harm to an affected person.
exceptions_or_limits: The preliminary inquiry is not a trial and does not determine guilt or innocence; the court should express no view on guilt at this stage.
The offences must fall within the category identified in Section 195(1)(b) CrPC, relating to court proceedings.
The expediency assessment should consider the overall factual matrix and the probable consequences of prosecution.

common_material_facts: Allegedly forged or false documents or declarations were used in judicial proceedings (probate, compensation claim, other litigation).
The court was asked, or itself considered, whether to make a criminal complaint.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 340(1) CrPC
Section 195(1)(b) CrPC
Section 2(g) CrPC
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members treat the complaint as discretionary. Expediency is judged by the impact on the administration of justice rather than by individual injury (2 members expressly), and a preliminary inquiry is optional and limited to expediency (1 member).
variations: One member focuses on the standard for expediency (impact on the administration of justice).
One member focuses on the nature and scope of the preliminary inquiry (optional, not a determination of guilt).
One member focuses on the point that a complaint is not automatic.

legal_question: In a partition suit by a co-owner or co-sharer who is not in actual physical possession, is the claimant treated as in joint possession, so that the suit is maintainable and the lower joint-possession court fee is payable, unless exclusion or ouster is clearly pleaded (and, for maintainability, proved)?

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking partition and separate possession of jointly held property.
predicates.claimant_is_coowner_with_undisputed_shar: The claimant is a co-owner or co-sharer (for example, an heir) with a share in undivided joint property, and the entitlement to a share is not disputed.
predicates.exclusion_or_ouster_clearly_pleaded_and_: The plaint clearly and specifically alleges exclusion or ouster from joint possession and the exclusion or ouster is established. Mere non-receipt of income or lack of actual physical possession does not satisfy this.
predicates.claimant_treated_as_in_joint_possession_: The claimant is regarded in law as in joint possession, may maintain the partition suit even without actual possession, and the lower court fee for a plaintiff in joint possession is payable rather than the market-value fee for an excluded plaintiff.

definition: A co-owner's possession is in law the possession of all co-owners, so a co-sharer seeking partition is treated as in joint possession and may sue even if not in actual possession. Court fee is payable at the joint-possession rate unless the plaint clearly and specifically pleads exclusion or ouster (and, for maintainability, it is proved).
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where exclusion or ouster is clearly and specifically pleaded and proved; the higher market-value fee for an excluded plaintiff then applies and the suit's maintainability may be affected.
Mere non-receipt of income or lack of actual physical possession is not enough to show exclusion.
The rule assumes the plaintiff's share or entitlement is not disputed.
Court-fee questions do not decide the merits (for example, the validity of a will).
The court-fee statutory references are State-specific (Section 37(1) and 37(2)); the equivalent provisions may differ in other States.

common_material_facts: Plaintiff or claimant is a co-sharer or heir in undivided property seeking partition
Possession by the claimant is alleged or pleaded to be joint, or the claimant is alleged to be out of possession
No clear and specific plea of exclusion or ouster was made or proved
statutes_and_provisions: Section 37(1) and 37(2) of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act
Article 17(b) of the Central Court Fees Act (predecessor provision)
Proviso to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members favour the claimant: partition suit maintainable or the lower joint-possession court fee applies (2 on court fee, 1 on maintainability).
variations: Two members concern the court-fee category; one concerns maintainability of the suit by a non-possessing co-sharer.
One member relies on strict construction of fee provisions that restrict access to justice, with doubt resolved in favour of the lower fee.
One member holds that ambiguous allegations of non-receipt of income do not amount to a clear averment of exclusion.

legal_question: Where a structure is built or land is used in breach of a statutory restriction (environmental, forest or planning) and without the required permission or approval, may the authorities order its removal, and will the court uphold that order?

predicates.challenge_to_removal_or_demolition_order: The case is an appeal or challenge against an order of an authority or tribunal directing removal or demolition of a structure or restoration of land.
predicates.structure_or_land_use_within_statutorily: The structure or land use is in an area where a statute or notification restricts construction or change of use (for example a coastal no-development zone, a restricted zone beside a scheduled road or in a controlled area, or forest land).
predicates.required_permission_or_approval_for_that: The structure or use had the permission or approval the statute requires, or falls within a permitted exception such as repair of an existing authorized structure or a use specifically approved for that land.
predicates.removal_or_demolition_of_unauthorized_st: The court affirms the order that the unauthorized structure be removed or demolished.

definition: A structure built or a land use made inside a statutorily restricted area (coastal no-development zone, scheduled-road or controlled area, forest land) without the permission or approval the statute requires, or beyond what was approved, is unauthorized. Courts uphold orders for its removal or demolition and do not let technical pleas or delay defeat the statutory purpose.
exceptions_or_limits: No removal where the structure is a permitted repair of an existing authorized structure within the stated limits, or is otherwise within a statutory exception.
In the coastal case, the earlier structure was authorized, but a materially different new structure (different shape, size, location) is not protected by it.
Approval for one specified use of forest land does not cover a different use.

The members rest on different statutes (CRZ Notification 1991, Punjab Act of 1963, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980), so the rule is stated at the level of unauthorized construction in restricted areas.

common_material_facts: Construction or change of use occurred in an area subject to a statutory restriction.
The required permission or approval was absent, or the structure exceeded or differed from what was approved or authorized.
Authorities or a tribunal had ordered removal or demolition, and the order was challenged in appeal.
statutes_and_provisions: CRZ Notification, 1991 (CRZ-III No Development Zone within 200 metres of the High Tide Line)
Punjab Scheduled Roads and Controlled Areas Restriction of Unregulated Development Act, 1963, ss. 3(1), 6, 7(1), 8, 12
Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, s. 2
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members uphold removal or demolition of the unauthorized structure.
variations: The coastal case turns on whether a pre-existing authorized structure was materially altered or replaced.
The road and controlled-area case also covers unpermitted non-agricultural use of agricultural land and stresses public interest over private interest.
The forest case turns on a use differing from the specific approved use and adds directions on who carries out demolition and cost recovery.
Authorities cited differ: Goa Foundation for the coastal case, and environmental rule-of-law cases for the forest case.

legal_question: Can a transferee who has taken possession under a written contract for the sale of immovable property rely on the part-performance defence in Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act to resist a suit for recovery of possession, notwithstanding a procedural or formal bar that would otherwise defeat a claim to the property (a registration requirement for completed sales, or the expiry of limitation for specific performance)?

rule.if: possession_recovery_suit_by_transferor_or_successor and written_contract_signed_by_transferor_for_consideration and transferee_in_possession_in_part_performance and section_53a_requirements_satisfied and defence_rests_on_contract_not_completed_sale and (sale_registration_requirement_for_completed_sale_applies or specific_performance_suit_time_barred)

predicates.possession_recovery_suit_by_transferor_o: The transferor, or the transferor's successor, has sued to recover possession from the transferee.
predicates.written_contract_signed_by_transferor_fo: There is a written contract to transfer immovable property for consideration, signed by or on behalf of the transferor, with ascertainable terms.
predicates.transferee_in_possession_in_part_perform: The transferee took possession in part performance of the contract, or continued in possession and did some act in furtherance of it.
predicates.section_53a_requirements_satisfied: All the statutory conditions for protection are proved, including that the transferee has performed or is ready and willing to perform their part of the contract.
predicates.defence_rests_on_contract_not_completed_: The transferee relies on the contract and part performance as a shield, and does not claim title under a completed sale or conveyance.
predicates.sale_registration_requirement_for_comple: A statutory provision requires registration for a sale to be valid, but no sale has actually been completed.
predicates.specific_performance_suit_time_barred: The limitation period for a suit for specific performance has expired, or no such suit was brought within it.
predicates.part_performance_defence_available_despi: The transferee may defend possession under Section 53A, and neither the registration requirement nor the limitation expiry by itself defeats the defence.

definition: A transferee who meets every requirement of Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act may defend possession on the basis of a written contract and part performance. A registration requirement that governs completed sales, or the expiry of limitation for a specific performance suit, does not by itself defeat that defence.
exceptions_or_limits: The defence fails if any Section 53A requirement is not proved. In particular, readiness and willingness to perform must be established, and in one member the defence failed for want of that proof.
The defence is defensive only. It protects possession and does not confer title or amount to a completed sale.
The registration point applies where the defence rests on a contract and no sale has occurred. It does not treat an unregistered sale as valid.

common_material_facts: A written agreement to sell immovable property, signed by the transferor
The transferee took possession in part performance, often with part payment or other acts in furtherance
The transferor or the transferor's successor sued for possession and the transferee relied on Section 53A as a defence
No suit for specific performance was brought, or it was time-barred, or no sale was completed
statutes_and_provisions: Section 53A, Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Section 70(8), Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 1950
Section 16(c), Specific Relief Act
Shrimant Shamrao Suryavanshi v. Pralhad Bhairoba Suryavanshi
Mahadeo Nathuji Patil v. Surajbai Khushal Chand Lakkad
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the Court held that the formal obstacle (registration of sales, or limitation for specific performance) does not by itself bar the Section 53A defence. In 2 members the defence was available. In 1 member it failed because readiness and willingness were not proved.
variations: One member concerns a registration requirement for completed sales under a state land revenue statute, while two concern limitation for specific performance.

One member applied the rule and upheld the defence, one stated the rule but denied the defence on the facts for want of proved readiness and willingness, and one discussed legislative history to construe Section 53A.
The third member's rule is framed with readiness and willingness as a condition, whereas the first omits it from its stated rule.

legal_question: Must a court in a criminal appeal give the accused or appellant a reasonable opportunity to be heard before disposing of an application or imposing a consequential order (such as sentence) that affects them?

rule.if: criminal_appeal_proceeding and (application_by_accused_pending or accused_newly_convicted_on_appeal_awaiting_sentence) and not opportunity_to_be_heard_given

predicates.criminal_appeal_proceeding: The matter is a criminal appeal (including an appeal against conviction) before an appellate court.
predicates.application_by_accused_pending: The accused or appellant has filed an application seeking relief (for example, further examination or summoning of witnesses) in the appeal that has yet to be decided.
predicates.accused_newly_convicted_on_appeal_awaiti: The appellate court has convicted the accused for the first time on appeal and has not yet imposed sentence.
predicates.opportunity_to_be_heard_given: The accused's counsel was given a real opportunity to be heard on the application or on the question of sentence before the court decided it.
predicates.court_must_give_reasonable_opportunity_t: The court is required to hear the accused or counsel before disposing of the application or imposing sentence, and disposal or sentence without such a hearing is wrong and unjust.

definition: In a criminal appeal, the accused or appellant must be given a reasonable opportunity to be heard before the court disposes of their application or, if convicted for the first time on appeal, before sentence is imposed. Disposal without such a hearing, for example in chambers or after the appeal is decided, is unjust.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule concerns the procedural right to be heard, not the merits of the underlying relief (e.g. whether additional evidence should be allowed).

The sentence-hearing limb rests on section 235(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and applies where conviction is first recorded on appeal; the application-hearing limb rests on a general requirement of reasonable opportunity, with no cited authority.
The rule applies only where no hearing was in fact given.

common_material_facts: Criminal appeal before the High Court or Supreme Court
Accused's application for further examination or summoning of witnesses disposed of without hearing counsel
Accused convicted for the first time on appeal and sentence not yet imposed
statutes_and_provisions: Section 561-A, Code of Criminal Procedure (1898)
Section 235(2), Code of Criminal Procedure
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the court held that the accused had to be given an opportunity to be heard. In 2 the disposal of the application without a hearing was held wrong and unjust, and in 1 a hearing on sentence was ordered before sentencing.
variations: Two members concern applications for additional evidence disposed of without hearing counsel (one in chambers, one after the appeal was decided), while the third concerns a hearing on sentence after a first conviction on appeal.
The hearing right derives from a general fair-hearing principle in two members and from the express section 235(2) in the third.
No member cites earlier cases.

split_suggestion: If a narrower grouping is wanted, separate 1020504_3 and 71479_1 (hearing before disposal of an application in a criminal appeal) from 767522_6 (statutory hearing on sentence after a first conviction on appeal).

legal_question: Is a notice of termination ineffective to end a tenancy, so that an eviction suit founded on it fails, where it does not give the notice period or end date that the governing tenancy statute requires?

predicates.eviction_suit_based_on_termination_notic: The landlord has brought or is pursuing an eviction or ejectment suit that relies on a notice purporting to terminate the tenancy.
predicates.notice_does_not_comply_with_statutory_no: The notice gives less than the minimum period required by the applicable tenancy statute, does not expire at the date the statute requires, or purports to end the tenancy before a statutorily extended term has expired.
predicates.notice_ineffective_to_terminate_tenancy_: The notice does not terminate the tenancy, so the landlord can obtain no eviction relief on the strength of that notice.

definition: Where an eviction suit rests on a termination notice that falls short of the statutory requirements for the tenancy, whether in length of notice, the date of expiry, or the statutorily extended term, the notice is ineffective and the suit cannot succeed on it.
exceptions_or_limits: The notice's defect must concern the statutory minimum notice or the statutory term or date. Defects of a different kind, such as the description of the premises, were distinguished in one member and are not covered.
A notice that is ineffective to terminate the tenancy may still be valid for another statutory purpose, for example as a rent demand in a composite notice.
Landlords are not barred from other proceedings that the law allows; only relief based on the defective notice is denied.

The required period and its computation depend on the governing statute: fifteen clear days for a month-to-month tenancy under the Transfer of Property Act, six months expiring with the tenancy year under the Bengal Act, and the statutory minimum term under the 1939 Act as amended.

common_material_facts: The landlord served a notice to quit or terminate the tenancy and then sued for eviction or ejectment.
The notice was timed so that it gave less than the statutory period, or ended the tenancy before the statutory term or date.
The tenancy was periodic (monthly) or was statutorily protected or extended.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 106, Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Section 9(1)(iii), Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act
Section 23(1)(b), 1939 Act as amended in 1946 (with the 1948 Act)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the notice was held ineffective to terminate the tenancy, and the eviction claim based on it failed.
variations: One member turns on counting fifteen clear days, excluding the day of service, for a month-to-month tenancy.
One member turns on a statutorily extended minimum term that outlasted the notice date, so no remand was needed.
One member turns on six months' notice expiring with the end of a tenancy year, measured from the tenancy's commencement.
One member treats the notice as valid for the rent-demand purpose but not for termination.

legal_question: Can a mortgage decree be enforced, by execution or sale, against land or rights that the State owns or that have vested in the State, where the State was not a party to the mortgage suit or the land was later settled back with the former owner under new rights?

rule.if: mortgage_decree_enforcement_sought and (property_owned_by_or_vested_in_state_free_of_mortgage or state_not_party_to_mortgage_decree) and not enforcement_permitted_by_statute

predicates.mortgage_decree_enforcement_sought: A mortgagee or decree-holder seeks to execute a mortgage decree or to sell property under it.
predicates.property_owned_by_or_vested_in_state_fre: The property is owned by the State, or the mortgaged proprietary interest has vested in the State under a land-reform statute free of encumbrances. This includes cases where the former owner was later given new tenure or raiyat rights in some of the lands.
predicates.state_not_party_to_mortgage_decree: The State, as owner, was not joined as a party to the mortgage suit or decree.
predicates.enforcement_permitted_by_statute: The governing statute or grant terms allow the mortgage decree to be enforced against the property.
predicates.mortgage_decree_cannot_be_enforced_again: The decree cannot be executed or the property sold under it, and any remedy lies only in the statutory compensation or claim procedure, where one exists.

definition: A mortgage decree cannot be enforced against property that belongs to the State or has vested in it, including new rights later conferred on the former owner. This holds especially where the State was not a party to the decree. The mortgagee is left to any statutory claim or compensation procedure.
exceptions_or_limits: The members apply the rule within the terms of the governing statutes (Government Grants Act, Bihar Land Reforms Act, U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act). Under a different statute or grant terms, enforcement may be permitted.

The non-party point (101261125_2) rests on the State not being joined. The vesting point (1217538_2, 647351_1) rests on statutory vesting free of encumbrances. These are separate grounds with the same result.
Where the lands vested, the creditor is not left without a remedy: the compensation or claim route under the Act, or under section 73 of the Transfer of Property Act, remains open.

common_material_facts: A mortgage decree or mortgage claim is sought to be enforced against property in which the State holds the title.
In two members the mortgaged estate or proprietary interest vested in the State under a land-reform law, and the former owner was given new tenure or raiyat rights in some lands.
In one member the State, as owner of Nazul property, was never joined in the mortgage suit.
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 2 and 3, Government Grants Act, 1895
Sections 3, 4(d), 6, 14 and 24(5), Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950
Sections 6(a)(i), 6(h) and 18, U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950
Section 73, Transfer of Property Act, 1882
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the mortgage decree cannot be enforced against the property. In the two vesting cases the creditor is directed to the statutory compensation procedure.
variations: One member turns on non-joinder of the State and the decree's own saving of non-parties' interests. The other two turn on statutory vesting.
In the Bihar case the lands were deemed settled back with the former owner as raiyat. In the U.P. case the new tenure rights were separate rights created after vesting.
The Bihar member relies on and rejects contrary authority. The other two cite no earlier cases.

split_suggestion: If a tighter grouping is wanted, separate 101261125_2 (State not a party to the mortgage suit) from 1217538_2 and 647351_1 (statutory vesting free of encumbrances, with compensation as the remedy).

legal_question: Under section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, when may market value be determined by capitalising the land's net income, as opposed to comparable sales or other valuation methods?

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The dispute concerns determination of compensation or market value for land compulsorily acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
predicates.reliable_comparable_sales_or_other_adequ: The record contains reliable evidence of comparable bona fide sales, expert opinion, or another adequate basis for valuing the land at the notification date.
predicates.income_evidence_available: The record contains a finding or evidence of the actual or reasonably obtainable net income (agricultural net annual income or rental income) from the acquired property.
predicates.capitalisation_of_net_income_is_an_appro: Market value may be determined by capitalising the net annual or rental income of the acquired property.

definition: Capitalisation of actual or reasonably obtainable net income is a residual method of fixing market value under section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act. It may be used where comparable sales or other adequate valuation evidence is unavailable or difficult to obtain, and should not be preferred where such evidence exists.
exceptions_or_limits: Where comparable bona fide sales or other adequate valuation evidence is available, capitalisation should not be preferred (member 1032443_1).
Capitalisation requires a reliable basis for net income, i.e. gross income less outgoings such as cultivation expenses and land revenue, or net rental income.
Valuation is as of the date of the section 4(1) notification.

common_material_facts: Land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, with compensation under section 23 in dispute
Reliable comparable-sale or other valuation evidence was absent or hard to obtain
Income evidence (agricultural net annual income or rental income) was available
Lower courts had used capitalisation
statutes_and_provisions: Section 23, Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Section 4(1) notification as the valuation date
Vyricherla Narayana Gajapatiraju v. Revenue Divisional Officer, Vizagapatnam
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Capitalisation is treated as a residual or fallback method and was accepted where other evidence was lacking (3 of 3). One member states the converse: it is not to be used when other adequate evidence exists.
variations: Two members involve agricultural or uncultivable land valued on net annual income; one involves land with a business building valued on rental income.
Member 1032443_1 states the rule negatively (capitalisation is not used when alternatives exist), while the others state it positively (capitalisation is used when alternatives are lacking).
Member 1726823_3 refers to the method as generally used for business property with buildings.

legal_question: Does a rent-control exemption (by notification or amendment) for a category of buildings operate only prospectively, so that it does not remove the Act's protection from buildings or tenancies that existed or qualified before it took effect, unless its language or circumstances show clear retroactive intent?

predicates.challenge_to_retroactive_application_of_: A party seeks to apply an exemption from rent-control law to buildings or tenancies that came into being or qualified before the exemption took effect.
predicates.exemption_instrument_affects_existing_re: The exemption (a notification or amending Act) would take away rent-control protection that already applied to existing buildings or tenancies.
predicates.instrument_clearly_indicates_retroactive: The wording of the instrument, expressly or by necessary implication, or the surrounding circumstances, shows a clear intention that the exemption apply to pre-existing buildings or tenancies.
predicates.exemption_operates_only_prospectively_an: The exemption applies only to buildings or tenancies arising on or after its effective date, and earlier ones remain subject to the rent-control law.

definition: Exemptions from rent-control legislation for new or described categories of buildings are presumed to operate prospectively. Absent clear words or circumstances showing retroactive intent, they do not strip protection from buildings or tenancies that existed or qualified before the exemption took effect.
exceptions_or_limits: The presumption yields where the language expressly or by necessary implication shows retroactive intent, or where surrounding circumstances establish that intent.
Where the language is unclear, the instrument must be read on its own wording and circumstances, including its purpose, such as encouraging new construction.
A date used merely to describe the category of covered properties does not by itself fix the period during which the exemption operates.
In one member, the petitioner was held unable to obtain relief on this point in the particular proceeding, although the law was held prospective.

common_material_facts: An exemption from rent-control law, by notification or amending Act, was invoked for a category of buildings.
The buildings or tenancies in issue pre-dated the exemption or had qualified before it.
The exemption text had no clear indication of retroactive effect.
statutes_and_provisions: Exemption notification under rent-control law
Clause 30 of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949
Amending Act 13 of 1972 (exemption for new buildings)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the exemption prospective only, so pre-existing buildings or tenancies stay under the rent-control law.
variations: One member discusses the presumption against retrospectivity at length, with case law and the purpose of encouraging new construction.
One member applies the presumption briefly, without citing cases.
One member holds that a cutoff date describing the property category does not make the exemption retroactive.
One member was decided on the notification's own language and circumstances, while the others rely on the general presumption.

legal_question: Can a court exercising supervisory or writ jurisdiction disturb or decline to give effect to a final eviction decree or order because of events after the decree (execution, a change in circumstances, or the landlord's death), where no jurisdictional defect or material change in the established need is shown?

rule.if: final_eviction_decree_or_order and challenge_in_supervisory_or_later_proceedings and (decree_executed_and_possession_delivered or subsequent_event_after_decree) and not prima_facie_jurisdictional_defect and not subsequent_event_materially_defeats_established_need

predicates.final_eviction_decree_or_order: An eviction decree or order has attained finality, whether from the statutory appellate authority or a civil court, or through a final qualifying permission.
predicates.challenge_in_supervisory_or_later_procee: The tenant seeks to challenge or undo the final eviction decree or order in supervisory or writ proceedings (Articles 226/227) or in later proceedings.
predicates.decree_executed_and_possession_delivered: The decree has been executed, possession has been delivered to the landlord, and the execution court has recorded satisfaction and closed the execution.
predicates.subsequent_event_after_decree: An event has occurred after the decree or order, or while the challenge was pending, that the tenant relies on, such as the landlord's death or later sale agreements.
predicates.prima_facie_jurisdictional_defect: The tenant has shown a prima facie challenge to the jurisdiction of the court or authority to make the decree.
predicates.subsequent_event_materially_defeats_esta: The subsequent event materially alters the position so that the landlord's established need is shown to have been met or to have ceased.
predicates.final_eviction_decree_not_disturbed: The supervisory or reviewing court should decline to interfere with the final eviction decree or order.

definition: A final eviction decree or order is not to be disturbed in supervisory or writ jurisdiction on the basis of post-decree developments, such as completed execution, the landlord's death, or later sale agreements. The exceptions are a prima facie jurisdictional defect, or a later event that materially defeats the established need where the governing scheme permits such review.
exceptions_or_limits: Review is open where the tenant shows a prima facie challenge to the jurisdiction of the court or authority to make the decree.
Courts may ordinarily take cautious account of later events to mould relief, but not where finality has attached and a statutory provision bars fresh inquiry into the ground.
Later events may matter if they materially alter the landlord's need; in the member that considered this, the sale agreements were uncompleted or unproved and the need persisted.
The members are decided on their own statutory schemes (Order 21 Rule 35 CPC; section 43(2)(rr) of the transitional rent law), so the outcome depends on the finality those schemes give.

common_material_facts: A final eviction decree or order existed, based on the landlord's need or requirement.
The tenant sought to unsettle the decree by relying on post-decree developments: execution, delivery of possession, the landlord's death, or later sale agreements.
No jurisdictional defect or material change in the landlord's need was shown.
statutes_and_provisions: Order 21 Rule 35 CPC
Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution
Section 43(2)(rr) of the transitional rent control provision
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members leave the final eviction decree undisturbed: the High Court should have declined review, supervisory interference was barred, and the appeal was dismissed.
variations: One member rests on completed execution and the absence of a jurisdictional issue.
One member rests on the bar on supervisory interference based on a subsequent event, namely the landlord's death.
One member engages with the doctrine of moulding relief for later events and finds the later events did not materially alter the need, under a statutory bar on fresh inquiry.
Only one member cites earlier cases (Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu, Hasmat Rai, Syed Asadullah Kazmi, Bansilal Sahu).

split_suggestion: Optionally separate the execution-completed supervisory-review member (103193047_3) from the two subsequent-event members (231653_1, 529151_2). The unifying point is the finality of eviction decrees against supervisory or later challenge.

legal_question: Is a gift of agricultural land, made without valuable consideration (only love and affection), a transfer for consideration within the statutory exception that protects transfers from land-ceiling and surplus-land provisions?

rule.if: land_ceiling_proceeding and land_transferred_by_gift and not valuable_consideration_given and statute_exception_requires_consideration

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: The case concerns determination of surplus land or ceiling-limit holdings under a state land-ceiling or tenancy statute.
predicates.land_transferred_by_gift: The landholder transferred the land by a gift, i.e. a voluntary transfer without consideration within the meaning of section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act.
predicates.valuable_consideration_given: The transferee gave valuable consideration capable of assessment in monetary terms, beyond natural love and affection.
predicates.statute_exception_requires_consideration: The statutory exception protects only transfers made for consideration (for example, for adequate consideration and in good faith).
predicates.gift_not_protected_by_consideration_base: The gift falls outside the statutory exception, so the transferred land is not protected and is ignored or treated as part of the holding when computing surplus land.

definition: A gift is by definition a voluntary transfer without consideration, and natural love and affection is not legal consideration. A gift therefore cannot come within a land-ceiling exception that protects only transfers for (adequate) consideration, and the land is counted in determining surplus area.
exceptions_or_limits: Applies where the exception depends on the transfer being for consideration; a bona fide gift does not become protected merely because it was made in good faith.
The claimant bears the burden of proving the exception's conditions, including adequate consideration (Explanation II, U.P. Act).
Transfers actually made for valuable consideration, and in good faith where required, may still qualify for the exception.

A conveyance on natural love and affection between close family members treated as good consideration in English authority (James Newton v. Hargreaves) was distinguished and does not displace the rule.

common_material_facts: A landholder gifted agricultural land to a relative or other person.
The gift was motivated by love and affection, with no valuable consideration.
The land-ceiling or surplus-land authorities refused to treat the gift as protected when computing surplus land.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 5(6) and its proviso (clause (b)) and Explanation II of the U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960
Section 32FF and Chapter IV-A of the PEPSU Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1955
Section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Section 2(d) of the Contract Act, 1872
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the gift is not a transfer for (adequate) consideration, so the exception does not apply; the appeals were dismissed or the gift was ignored in computing surplus land.
variations: Two members arise under the U.P. Act and concern post-cutoff transfers; one arises under the PEPSU Act and concerns a pre-cutoff gift to unrelated persons.
One member stresses that the gift was bona fide, an unchallenged finding, yet still unprotected for want of consideration.
The U.P. members rely on the 'adequate consideration' wording and the claimant's burden; the PEPSU member relies on the purpose of the ceiling chapter.
One member overruled an earlier decision (Fateh Singh) on the point.

legal_question: At what point does a purchaser at a court or statutory auction acquire title: on confirmation of the sale (with the price paid), or only when the sale certificate is issued, and does the Code of Civil Procedure's relation-back rule apply?

predicates.auction_sale_of_property: Property was sold at a public auction in execution of a decree or under a statutory recovery or rehabilitation scheme.
predicates.sale_confirmed_or_finalised: The sale was confirmed or approved by the competent authority or court, and, where the statutory scheme requires it, the full purchase price was paid.
predicates.governing_procedure_makes_certificate_th: The applicable statute or rules provide that the sale certificate itself effects the transfer, and so displace the general Code of Civil Procedure rule on title.
predicates.title_passes_to_purchaser_on_confirmatio: The purchaser's title vests on confirmation of the sale (in one member relating back to the sale date), and issuing the certificate later is a ministerial step that does not delay the transfer.

definition: Where an auction sale has been confirmed (and the price paid), title ordinarily passes to the purchaser on confirmation, and later issue of the sale certificate is only ministerial. This does not hold where the special statutory recovery procedure makes the certificate the operative transfer, in which case the sale occurs when the certificate is issued.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the special recovery statute or rules make the sale certificate the valid transfer and are inconsistent with section 65 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the sale occurs on issue of the certificate (as in the land-revenue recovery and tax-timing member).

The relation-back fiction in section 65 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to execution sales under the Code, but not to special schemes whose rules contain no such provision or are inconsistent with it.
In the rehabilitation rules member, title passes on confirmation with price paid, not at the auction date, and it was not held to relate back.

common_material_facts: Property sold at public auction, either in execution of a decree or under a statutory recovery or rehabilitation scheme
Sale certificate issued after the auction or confirmation
Dispute over the date on which title passed or the sale occurred
Question whether section 65 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies
statutes_and_provisions: Section 65 and Order XXI Rules 92 and 94, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Rules 90 and 92, Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Rules, 1955
Sections 279, 286 and 341, U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, and rules 281 and 285-M
Section 12B, Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Two of the three members hold that title passes on confirmation, with the certificate merely ministerial: one under the Code and one under the rehabilitation rules. The third holds that the sale occurs on issue of the certificate, because the special recovery procedure makes the certificate the transfer and displaces the general rule.
variations: The Code member treats title as relating back to the date of sale under section 65, while the rehabilitation rules member rejects the section 65 fiction and dates title from confirmation.
The recovery statute member turns the date of sale on the certificate, not on the auction or confirmation.
The context differs across the members: eviction and rent, execution confirmation, and capital-gains timing.

split_suggestion: If narrower rules are wanted, separate the members that apply the Code or a scheme silent on the certificate (title on confirmation) from the member whose special statute makes the certificate the operative transfer (1037719_2).

legal_question: When is a person claiming a statutory right to purchase land from the landowner or landlord ineligible because they fall outside the class of tenants on whom the statute confers that right?

predicates.claimant_seeks_statutory_purchase_right: The claimant applies to buy land from the landowner or landlord under a statutory purchase privilege given to tenants.
predicates.claimant_not_qualifying_tenant_of_land_u: On the statute's definitions, the claimant is not a tenant of the landowner holding land, for example because the claimant is only a sub-tenant of a tenant, or because the tenancy is of a building with appurtenant land rather than of land alone.
predicates.tenant_has_no_need_or_occupation_for_con: The tenant does not occupy the land and buildings for residence or business and does not need any of the land for their convenient enjoyment.
predicates.statutory_purchase_right_refused: The court or authority rejects the application to purchase, because the statutory right is unavailable or may be refused.

definition: A statutory right to compel the landowner to sell land is a limited, equitable privilege. It is available only to a claimant who is a tenant of land within the statute's definitions, and, where the court must fix the extent of land, only to one who actually needs the land. Sub-tenants, tenants of buildings with appurtenant land, and tenants with no occupation or need cannot claim it.
exceptions_or_limits: The 'no need' ground (1037405_2) is discretionary: the court 'may' refuse. The status-based grounds (appurtenant land, sub-tenancy) are categorical bars.
Whether land is appurtenant to a building is a question of fact, decided on extent, nature, situation and use. The lease's description of the property does not decide it.
The sub-tenant bar rests on the Punjab statute's text. The provisos on subletting do not extend the purchase right to sub-tenants.
Each member construes a different statute (Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act), so the rule applies only where a statute is similarly worded.

common_material_facts: The claimant applies to purchase land from the landlord or landowner under a statutory tenant's right.
The claimant's status or use of the property is inconsistent with the statutory class: sub-tenants, a building with appurtenant land, or a tenant not in occupation.
Lower courts and the High Court had already rejected the claim.
statutes_and_provisions: Tamil Nadu City Tenants' Protection Act, 1921, ss. 2(1), 2(2), 3, 9
Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, ss. 2(1), 2(6), 18
Punjab Land Revenue Act, s. 3(2)
Maharaja Singh v. State of U.P. [1977] 7 SCC 155
S.M. Transport (P) Ltd. v. Sankaraswamingal Mutt [1963] Supp. 1 SCR 282
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the purchase claim is refused and the refusal upheld.
variations: 1037405_2 turns on lack of occupation and need, and on equity.
1532816_1 turns on classification: the land is appurtenant to a building, so the tenancy is not of 'land'.
906386_1 turns on the claimant's status: a sub-tenant is not a tenant of the landowner.
Two members arise under the Tamil Nadu Act in ejectment suits, and one under the Punjab tenancy statute.

split_suggestion: The shared point is that the purchase right is limited to qualifying tenants. If a finer split is wanted, separate (a) eligibility by status or type of tenancy (1532816_1, 906386_1) from (b) discretionary refusal for lack of need or occupation (1037405_2).

legal_question: When mining in an ecologically sensitive or forest area is found to harm the environment, can the Court permit it to continue for a limited transitional period, and on what conditions, before it must end?

predicates.court_finds_mining_in_forest_or_ecologic: The court finds that the mining is in forest land or a sensitive forest area, and that it harms, or threatens, ecology, forests or environmental balance.
predicates.transition_period_supported_by_expert_as: The limited continuation is supported by expert committee assessments or by the practical effects of an abrupt closure, such as the effect on industry, investment and employment.
predicates.continuation_confined_to_existing_operat: The continuation is limited to mines already operating under unexpired original leases, or to the already broken-up or disturbed area.
predicates.ecological_safeguards_imposed: The court makes continuation subject to environmental or ecological safeguards, such as conditions, undertakings, monitoring and implementation of committee recommendations.
predicates.mining_may_continue_only_for_limited_tra: Mining may continue only until a fixed endpoint, namely lease expiry or exhaustion of the ore or the time period set. It carries no right to renewal or to permanent continuation, and must stop afterwards.

definition: Where mining harms a forest or sensitive ecological area, the Court gives priority to forest and ecological protection over continued exploitation. It may allow only a time-bound, phased continuation of existing operations or of already disturbed areas, subject to safeguards and without any right to renewal, after which mining must end.
exceptions_or_limits: Continuation is not permanent and gives no right to renewal; forest-conservation requirements continue to apply.
Continuation is limited to mines under unexpired original leases or to the already disturbed area; it does not extend to new mining or new areas.
Continuation depends on compliance with the ecological safeguards and committee recommendations.
Where there is no expert or practical support for a transition, the general priority of ecological protection would favour closure (inferred from the members' reasoning, not separately decided).

common_material_facts: Mining in forest or ecologically sensitive land that expert committees found harmful or sensitive
Existing operations, whether mines under unexpired leases or an already broken-up area, rather than new mining
Practical considerations or expert committee recommendations favouring phased rather than abrupt closure
Court-imposed ecological conditions and monitoring
statutes_and_provisions: Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980
Constitution Articles 48A and 51A(g)
Constitution Article 21
Convention on Biological Diversity
Sustainable development and precautionary principle
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members allow limited, time-bound continuation of existing mining under safeguards (2 in one judgment, 1 in the other), with no renewal and an end to mining at the set endpoint.
variations: The endpoint differs: expiry of the original leases (104313664_4, 104313664_6) versus a fixed date or exhaustion of the ore in the disturbed area (282585_3).
104313664_4 states the broader principle that mining must end as a continuing activity, while 104313664_6 focuses on the no-renewal limit for unexpired leases.
282585_3 rests on the sustainable development and precautionary principle and the committee reports; the others rest mainly on the Forest (Conservation) Act and expert findings of harm.

legal_question: Can a person who claims a deceased statutory tenant's protected occupancy only through a will, or through a right or defence personal to that tenant, succeed to the tenancy or continue the tenant's protection, where the governing rent statute does not confer that right on such a person?

rule.if: statutory_tenancy_protected_under_rent_act and original_tenant_deceased_or_bequeathing and claimant_claims_through_will_or_as_heir_of_personal_protection and not claimant_qualifies_under_statutory_succession_provision and not statute_extends_protection_to_claimant

predicates.statutory_tenancy_protected_under_rent_a: The occupation rests on a statutory tenancy or protected tenancy under a rent control statute, including a tenancy continuing after the contractual lease ended.
predicates.original_tenant_deceased_or_bequeathing: The tenant has died, or has made a will purporting to bequeath the tenancy right to take effect on death.
predicates.claimant_claims_through_will_or_as_heir_: The claimant relies on a testamentary bequest of the tenancy, or on being an heir seeking to continue a right or defence that was personal to the deceased statutory tenant.
predicates.claimant_qualifies_under_statutory_succe: The claimant fits the category the rent statute names for succession, for example a family member residing with or carrying on business with the tenant at death, or an heir selected under the statute.
predicates.statute_extends_protection_to_claimant: The rent statute contains a provision extending the deceased tenant's protection or defence to the claimant.
predicates.claimant_cannot_acquire_or_continue_stat: The claimant does not become a tenant and cannot continue the deceased tenant's statutory protection or personal defences against eviction.

definition: Statutory tenancy protection is personal to the tenant and passes on death only as the rent statute provides. A legatee under a will, or an heir who does not fit the statutory succession category, cannot become a tenant or invoke the deceased tenant's personal defences unless the statute extends the protection to them.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the claimant falls within the statutory succession category, such as a qualifying family member residing or carrying on business with the tenant at death.
The rule does not apply where the statute expressly extends the protection to heirs or representatives.
The Court left open whether a statutory tenancy personal to a tenant can ever be bequeathed.
Representatives may still raise defences appropriate to their representative character, as opposed to defences personal to the deceased.
The reasoning on 'heir' and on bequests comes from the Bombay Rent Act; for other statutes the result depends on their own wording.

common_material_facts: A tenant whose contractual tenancy had ended, or a tenant under a protected tenancy, has died or made a will.
The claimant is a legatee or heir who seeks to retain possession against the landlord.
The claimant is not within the statutory class of successors.
The landlord seeks possession or eviction.
statutes_and_provisions: Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, s. 5(11)(c)(i) and (ii)
Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, s. 15(1)
Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, s. 13
Code of Civil Procedure, Order 22 Rules 4 and 11
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All three members (3 of 3) deny the claimant the tenancy or the personal defence: two reject legatees' claims to tenancy, and one bars heirs from a defence personal to the deceased statutory tenant.
variations: Two members concern bequests under the Bombay Act, one for business premises under s. 5(11)(c)(ii) and one for residential premises under s. 5(11)(c)(i). The third concerns heirs' procedural and defence rights under the Rajasthan Act, with no will involved.
The business-premises member also relies on the s. 15(1) bar on transfer, whereas the residential member relies on the meaning of 'heir' and the priority of resident family members.
The Rajasthan member rests on the personal nature of statutory protection and Order 22, not on a statutory succession category.

split_suggestion: If a tighter grouping is wanted, separate the two Bombay Act legatee cases (1042662_1, 495691_1) from the Rajasthan heirs' personal-defence case (1205820_2).

legal_question: Does the right of private defence cover force used after the threat has ended, for example because the attackers have fled or the accused has reached safety?

rule.if: private_defence_claimed and (threat_to_accused_ceased_before_force_used or accused_pursued_fleeing_party) and force_used_after_threat_ceased

predicates.private_defence_claimed: The accused invokes the right of private defence of person or property, or in the alternative the exceeding of that right, as a defence to a criminal charge.
predicates.threat_to_accused_ceased_before_force_us: On the court's findings, the danger or reasonable apprehension of danger to the accused or their property had ended before the force in question was used. For example, the attackers fled, no further attack came, or the accused had reached a safe distance.
predicates.accused_pursued_fleeing_party: The accused chased and attacked persons who were running away after the immediate threat had passed.
predicates.force_used_after_threat_ceased: The accused inflicted injury or death by force applied after the threat had ended.
predicates.private_defence_not_available_for_force_: The right of private defence does not protect the later force, and the claim is rejected for that force, even if a right existed at the outset.

definition: The right of private defence lasts only while the danger or reasonable apprehension of danger lasts. Once the attackers have fled or the accused has reached safety, later force such as pursuing and attacking, or firing on distant or retreating persons, is not protected, even if a right existed at the outset.
exceptions_or_limits: The right must have existed at the outset for the question of its ending to arise. Where the accused was the aggressor, no right arose at all.
Courts allow for the excitement and confusion of a person facing an assault and do not judge the force with detached hindsight, as long as the threat is continuing.

The rule depends on a factual finding that the threat had actually ceased. While the attack or reasonable apprehension continues, the person is not required to measure the defensive force blow by blow.

common_material_facts: An initial confrontation in which the accused may have faced a threat or claimed to have done so.
The opposing party fled, or the accused moved away to a safe distance, so that the immediate danger was over.
The accused then used force, such as firing or chasing and assaulting, against persons at a distance or on the run.
Serious injuries or deaths resulted, leading to murder or related convictions.
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Penal Code sections 99, 100, 102 and 105, relied on in one member (1046645_1).
The other two members applied the principle without citing specific provisions.
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members reject the private defence claim for the force used after the threat ended, and the convictions stand.
variations: 1046645_1 accepted that a right existed initially and analysed proportionality and the temporal limit under the IPC sections.
1807187_2 rested on concurrent findings that the accused were the aggressors, and also rejected the alternative plea of exceeding the right.
31903_2 assumed a right arose and held that it ended when the accused reached a safe distance, with no further attack on him.

legal_question: Does a person or company that is allotted or leased land by the State or a development board after the land has been acquired for a public or industrial-development purpose become a beneficiary or interested person entitled to participate in, or challenge, the landowners' compensation proceedings, even if the allotment terms make it liable for additional compensation?

predicates.land_acquired_for_public_or_development_: The land was acquired for a public purpose, or for an industrial development board under an industrial-development statute, and not as an acquisition for a company.
predicates.acquisition_not_made_for_or_at_instance_: The acquisition notifications and record do not identify the allottee as the beneficiary, and do not show the land was acquired for the allottee or at its instance.
predicates.allotment_made_after_acquisition: The land vested in the State, and was transferred to the board where applicable, before it was allotted or leased to the claimant.
predicates.allottee_seeks_to_participate_in_or_chal: The allottee seeks to be heard in, appeals against, or files a writ petition against the compensation reference or award.
predicates.allottee_not_beneficiary_or_interested_p: The allottee is not a beneficiary or person interested under Section 3(b) of the Land Acquisition Act or the relevant industrial-development statute, and has no right to be heard in or challenge the compensation proceedings. A remand to hear it is unjustified.

definition: A subsequent allottee or lessee of land that was acquired for a public purpose or for a development board is not a beneficiary or interested person in the acquisition. It therefore has no right to participate in or challenge the compensation proceedings, even where its allotment terms make it liable to pay any enhanced compensation.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not cover acquisitions made directly for a company, or at its instance, under Part VII of the Land Acquisition Act, or for a statutory beneficiary. The members distinguish Himalayan Tiles, Gyan Devi and similar cases on that basis.
The rule applies where allotment follows completed acquisition and vesting in the State. It does not apply where the claimant was identified as the beneficiary in the acquisition.
A contractual liability to pay additional price or compensation does not by itself confer a right to participate.

common_material_facts: Land was acquired for a public purpose or for an industrial development board and vested in the State before any allotment.
The land was later allotted or leased to a company.
The allotment terms made the company liable for additional price or compensation if compensation was enhanced.
The company was not named as beneficiary in the acquisition notifications.
The company claimed a right to be heard on the ground that it would bear the financial burden.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 3(b) and 50
Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 9, 11, 18, 20 and 54
Code of Civil Procedure, Order I Rule 10
Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966, Sections 2(11), 28, 29, 30 and 32
Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board Regulations 4, 5, 7 and 10
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the post-acquisition allottee has no right to participate in or challenge the compensation proceedings. In two members the High Court's remand or setting aside of the award is reversed.
variations: One member is decided under the general Land Acquisition Act and Order I Rule 10 CPC. Two are decided under the Karnataka industrial-development statutory scheme.
The procedural route differs: a request to be impleaded, a writ petition against the award, and an appeal against the enhanced award.
The members distinguish Himalayan Tiles and Gyan Devi as concerning acquisitions for a company or statutory beneficiary.

legal_question: Does the absence of ballistic or recovery evidence (no expert report, no recovered firearm or cartridge, or recovered cartridges of an unspecified caliber) undermine an otherwise credible prosecution case of a shooting that rests on direct or eyewitness evidence?

predicates.criminal_shooting_case: The prosecution alleges that the victim(s) were killed or injured by firearm shots fired by the accused.
predicates.credible_direct_or_eyewitness_evidence_o: The prosecution relies on acceptable, consistent direct or eyewitness evidence of the shooting, including a consistent description of the weapons used, possibly corroborated by other witnesses or medical evidence.
predicates.firearm_or_cartridge_not_recovered: The alleged firearm or a spent cartridge was not recovered.
predicates.ballistic_expert_not_examined_on_unavail: No ballistic expert was examined, because the alleged firearms were unavailable for examination and any recovered firearm was not alleged by the prosecution to be the weapon that caused the deaths.
predicates.recovered_cartridge_caliber_not_specifie: Cartridges were recovered whose caliber the eyewitnesses did not specify, and which cannot readily be inferred from their description of the weapons.
predicates.gap_in_ballistic_or_recovery_evidence_do: The missing ballistic expert evidence, the non-recovery of the weapon or cartridge, or the unmatched cartridge caliber does not discredit or weaken the prosecution case.

definition: Where the prosecution case of a shooting rests on credible direct or eyewitness evidence, the absence of a ballistic expert, the non-recovery of the firearm or cartridge, or the recovery of cartridges of a caliber the witnesses did not specify does not by itself undermine that case.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule depends on the direct or eyewitness evidence being credible, consistent and acceptable; it does not cover cases where that evidence is doubtful.
Expert evidence may still be required where the prosecution alleges that a specific recovered weapon caused the injuries (the Mohinder Singh principle was distinguished, not rejected).
The cartridge-caliber point holds only where the witnesses' account makes the ammunition type hard to determine; it is not a general bar on using recoveries to contradict witnesses.

common_material_facts: Prosecution case of firearm killings or shootings supported by eyewitness or direct evidence
Alleged firearms or cartridges not recovered, or recovery that did not match the witnesses' account
Defence argued that the missing or mismatched ballistic or recovery evidence weakened the prosecution case
statutes_and_provisions: Mohinder Singh v. The State (distinguished in one member)
No statutory provision was relied on in the members
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the gap in ballistic or recovery evidence did not undermine the prosecution case.
variations: One member concerns the absence of a ballistic expert where the alleged rifles were unrecovered and the recovered revolver was not the prosecution's weapon.
One member concerns recovered cartridges of a caliber the witnesses did not specify.
One member concerns plain non-recovery of the firearm and spent cartridge where direct evidence was corroborated by medical evidence.

legal_question: Can an agency that was created for valuable consideration, and in which the agent has an interest in the subject matter of the agency, be terminated or revoked to the prejudice of that interest, absent an express contract to the contrary?

predicates.agent_has_interest_in_subject_matter_of_: The agent has a real interest in the property or fund that forms the subject matter of the agency (for example, a creditor-agent entitled to the proceeds, or a transferee with a registered transfer).
predicates.agency_created_for_value_or_to_secure_ag: The agency was created for valuable consideration, or the authority was given to effectuate a security or protect the agent's interest (for example, a debt owed to the agent).
predicates.express_contract_permitting_termination: The parties expressly contracted that the agency may be terminated despite the agent's interest.
predicates.agency_not_revocable_to_prejudice_of_age: The agency, and the authority under it, cannot be terminated or revoked in a way that prejudices the agent's interest, and it remains effective.

definition: Under Section 202 of the Indian Contract Act, where an agent has an interest in the property that is the subject matter of the agency, and the agency was created for consideration or to secure that interest, the principal cannot terminate it to the agent's prejudice unless there is an express contract allowing it. Steps such as complaints or a later power of attorney that preserves the earlier authority do not revoke it.
exceptions_or_limits: Does not apply where there is an express contract permitting termination.
Protection extends only to the extent of the agent's interest; revocation that does not prejudice that interest is not barred.
The agent's interest in the subject matter must be shown, not merely the authority to act.
Calling the power of attorney 'irrevocable' is supportive, but the members rest on the existence of the agent's interest.

common_material_facts: The agency was created for valuable consideration or to secure a debt or interest of the agent.
The power of attorney was described as irrevocable, or the instruments were registered.
The principal tried to avoid or undo the authority (complaints, a later power of attorney, or a challenge to execution).
statutes_and_provisions: Section 202, Indian Contract Act, 1872
Loonkaran v. State Bank, Jaipur (cited in one member)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the agency coupled with the agent's interest was not revoked and could not be revoked to the prejudice of that interest.
variations: Two members involve a bank as creditor-attorney authorised to execute a decree and credit the proceeds to the debtor's account.
One member involves registered transfer and powers of attorney, where the heirs' complaints and a later power of attorney did not revoke the earlier authority.
Procedural contexts differ: a challenge to a consent decree and execution proceedings.

legal_question: Does a tax applied uniformly to a defined class of agricultural taxpayers or landholdings violate Article 14 merely because incidental differences in practical effect (such as crop timing, produce quality, yield or profitability) arise, where hostile or unequal treatment is not established?

rule.if: equality_challenge_to_tax and uniform_tax_treatment_within_class and incidental_difference_in_effect_among_class_members and not hostile_unequal_treatment_proved

predicates.equality_challenge_to_tax: The tax law or levy is challenged as discriminatory or violating the equality guarantee under Article 14.
predicates.uniform_tax_treatment_within_class: The same tax, method of levy or rate applies to all members of the defined class of taxpayers or landholdings.
predicates.incidental_difference_in_effect_among_cl: Members of the class experience different practical effects (for example in timing of income, quality of produce, yield or profit) that arise incidentally from their varying circumstances rather than from the law singling them out.
