Authenticity and voice identification were in issue.
The recording was relied on to prove admissions or corroborate testimony.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 3 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (definitions of evidence and document)
Sections 7 and 8 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (relevant facts, conduct, res gestae)
Section 2(t) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (electronic record)
R.M. Malkani v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 1973 SC 157
Ziyauddin Barhanuddin Bukhari v. Brijmohan Ramdass Mehra
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members treat recorded conversations as receivable evidence or documents: 2 hold them admissible once the conditions are met, and 1 holds that a compact disc is a document.
variations: One member is a civil suit and one is a criminal bribery case. The third is a criminal trial that addresses only the document status of the recording.
The standard of proof for integrity differs. The civil member asks for proof eliminating manipulation, while the criminal member requires proof beyond reasonable doubt.
The members rely on different bases for relevance: section 8 conduct, res gestae, or the definition of document.

legal_question: What evidentiary weight should be given to an entry in an inam register (or alienation register) that classifies the nature or character of an inam grant, and is such an entry conclusive when read in isolation?

rule.if: inam_classification_is_disputed and register_entry_describes_grant_character and (other_relevant_evidence_or_register_context_exists or entry_is_amendable_under_governing_law)

predicates.inam_classification_is_disputed: The nature or character of the inam grant (for example religious or personal, permanent or not, or who the grantee was) is in dispute.
predicates.register_entry_describes_grant_character: An inam register or alienation register entry records a classification or description of the grant, such as religious, permanent or personal.
predicates.other_relevant_evidence_or_register_cont: There is other evidence about the grant (such as grant documents, title deeds, survey or settlement records, chronology, earlier proceedings) or other details in the same register that bear on the entry.
predicates.entry_is_amendable_under_governing_law: The governing statute contemplates that the register entry is deemed amended if the competent authority decides the classification differently.
predicates.register_entry_is_significant_evidence_b: The register entry carries real evidentiary value but is not conclusive on its own and must be read with the rest of the register and the other evidence.

definition: Inam or alienation register entries are official records with substantial evidentiary value, but an entry describing a grant's character is not conclusive when taken in isolation. It must be read as a whole with the other register details, the surrounding evidence and, where applicable, the statutory scheme allowing amendment.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the original grant documents are unavailable, the register has particular evidentiary importance, though it still does not displace authentic evidence.
Where the statute provides that the entry is deemed amended on a government decision, the entry yields to that decision.
The rule concerns evidentiary weight; it does not say that register entries may be ignored.

common_material_facts: A register entry classified the grant (religious, permanent, personal, or as supporting a shrine).
Other evidence or other details in the register bore on the true nature of the grant.
The original grant documents were sometimes unavailable.
statutes_and_provisions: Explanation I to section 2(1)(e), Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act, 1952
Section 53, Bombay Land Revenue Code
Rule 3(1) of the inam-settlement rules (continuation of inams for religious or charitable objects)

Arunachellam Chetty v. Venkatachalapathi Guruswamigal; Poohari Fakir Sadavarthy v. Commissioner, HR&CE; Vatticherukuru Village Panchayat v. Nori Venkatarama Deekshitulu; Jammi Raja Rao v. Sri Anjaneyaswami Temple
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that register entries are significant but not conclusive and must be assessed in context with other evidence.
variations: Two members (1140636_2, 1864792_2) rest on the evidentiary value of the Inam Register and the need to read it with other evidence or other columns.
One member (1696411_3) rests on statutory text showing the alienation register entry is amendable and descriptive, serving land-revenue purposes.
1864792_2 stresses internal inconsistency within the register and chronology; 1140636_2 stresses unavailability of the title deed.

legal_question: Does a Hindu widow's limited estate in inherited property enlarge into absolute ownership under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 when the Act commences, depending on whether an earlier transfer or mutation validly divested her and whether she still possessed the property with a right to possess it?

predicates.widow_held_limited_interest_in_property: The Hindu widow held only a limited (widow's) estate in the property, acquired by inheritance from her husband, before the Act came into force.
predicates.widow_possessed_property_with_right_to_p: When the Hindu Succession Act came into force the widow was in actual or constructive possession of the property and had a legal right to that possession, not merely possession as a trespasser.
predicates.earlier_transaction_validly_divested_wid: A prior mutation, gift or other transaction effectively transferred title or possession away from the widow, so that she was no longer the owner or rightful possessor.
predicates.widow_acquires_absolute_ownership_under_: The widow's limited estate is enlarged into absolute ownership, and she can validly dispose of the property by gift, will or otherwise.

definition: A Hindu widow's limited estate becomes absolute under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act if she was in possession with a right to possess when the Act commenced. An earlier mutation without transfer of title, or a gift that was ineffective, does not defeat this. A valid earlier transfer followed by wrongful re-entry gives her no such right.
exceptions_or_limits: Possession for Section 14(1) requires both a right to possess and actual or constructive possession; wrongful re-entry after a valid transfer, which makes her a trespasser, does not enlarge her estate.
A mutation entry does not itself create or extinguish title, so it does not divest the widow unless an effective transfer of title accompanies it.
A valid, effective gift or other transfer completed before the Act removes the property from her ownership, so Section 14 does not apply to it.

common_material_facts: A Hindu widow inherited property from her husband with a limited estate.
An earlier mutation or gift was alleged to have taken the property out of her hands.
The widow's possession at the commencement of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 was decisive.
A later dealing (gift, will, or retaking possession) was challenged by reversioners or other claimants.
statutes_and_provisions: Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 14(1)
Hindu Succession Act, 1956, Section 14(2)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 2 of 3 members the widow became absolute owner because the earlier mutation or gift had not divested her, and her later gift or will stood. In 1 of 3 she did not, because she had validly transferred the property and later regained possession wrongfully.
variations: One member turns on a mutation entry that conveys no title.
One member turns on a gift declared legally ineffective by a compromise decree.
One member turns on a valid gift followed by wrongful re-entry, which gives possession without a right to possess.
The outcome is for the widow in two members and against her in the third, depending on whether she had a right to possess.

legal_question: Is a suit relating to a mortgage (redemption or enforcement by sale) timely where it was instituted within the limitation period that the Limitation Act prescribes for that remedy, including any applicable transitional period?

predicates.mortgage_suit: The suit is brought on a mortgage, either by the mortgagor to redeem or recover possession, or by the mortgagee to enforce the mortgage by sale.
predicates.applicable_limitation_period_identified: The limitation period for the particular mortgage remedy is identified under the Limitation Act, including its starting point (such as accrual of the right to redeem, or execution of the mortgage) or any transitional provision that applies.
predicates.instituted_within_that_period: On the record, the suit was instituted within that period, or within the transitional period or old period, whichever expires earlier, where the transitional rule applies.
predicates.mortgage_suit_is_within_limitation: The suit is held to be filed in time and not barred by limitation.

definition: A mortgage suit, whether for redemption or for enforcement by sale, is timely if the record shows it was instituted within the limitation period the Limitation Act prescribes for that remedy, or within the transitional period where the shorter new period applies. The remedy and the starting point of time must be correctly identified, and an unchallenged institution date accepted by the courts below may be taken as the basis.
exceptions_or_limits: The period differs by remedy: Article 61(a) of the 1963 Act (thirty years from accrual of the right to redeem) for redemption, and Article 138 of the 1908 Act (twelve years) for enforcement by sale.
A claim for personal liability on the borrowers is a different remedy from enforcement by sale and is not governed by the mortgage-sale period.
Where the transitional rule applies, the suit must be instituted within the transitional period or the old period, whichever expires earlier.
Reliance on an earlier institution date depends on the record supporting it and on no specific challenge to it in the courts below.

common_material_facts: A mortgage suit, either for redemption or for sale, was filed and its timeliness was questioned.
The filing date was compared with the limitation period applicable to the remedy.
The courts below had found, or the record showed, that the suit was within time.
statutes_and_provisions: Limitation Act, 1963, Article 61(a)
Limitation Act, 1908, Article 138
Limitation Act, 1963, Section 30 (transitional provision)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members held the mortgage suit to be within limitation.
variations: Two members concern redemption suits, one by a mortgagor under a conditional sale and one under the transitional rule, and one concerns a mortgagee's suit for sale.

One member turns on the statutory period running from accrual of the right to redeem, another on execution of the mortgage, and the third on a transitional period and the record on the institution date.
The transitional member depends on an unchallenged factual record, while the other two are decided by simple computation against the statutory period.

split_suggestion: Optionally split into (a) suits within the main limitation article (114028626_2, 1496427_2) and (b) the transitional-period case turning on the record of the institution date (433804_2).

legal_question: When a tenant dies, do the heirs take the tenancy as joint tenants under a single undivided tenancy as against the landlord, or as tenants-in-common holding separate tenancies?

rule.if: original_tenant_died and heirs_succeeded_to_tenancy and no_succession_exclusion_or_limit and tenancy_remained_undivided

predicates.original_tenant_died: The tenant in whose favour the tenancy was created has died.
predicates.heirs_succeeded_to_tenancy: The deceased tenant's heirs inherited the tenancy and continued to hold the premises.
predicates.no_succession_exclusion_or_limit: No applicable statute or contract excludes or limits the devolution of the tenancy on heirs.
predicates.tenancy_remained_undivided: The tenancy remained a single tenancy, with no division of the premises or of the rent payable to the landlord.
predicates.heirs_hold_single_joint_tenancy_as_again: The heirs hold the tenancy as joint tenants with the same incidents as the original tenancy, as one tenancy and not as separate tenancies or tenancies-in-common.

definition: Absent a provision excluding or limiting succession, on a tenant's death the tenancy devolves on the heirs as one undivided joint tenancy with the same incidents as the original tenancy. Section 19 of the Hindu Succession Act (tenants-in-common) governs only the heirs' rights among themselves, not their relationship with the landlord.
exceptions_or_limits: Applies only where no provision of the governing rent legislation or contract excludes or limits succession by heirs.
Consequences of succession depend on the governing rent legislation (Gian Devi Anand).
Joint tenancy is as against the landlord; the heirs' inter se rights may follow succession law, such as tenancy-in-common under Section 19 of the Hindu Succession Act.
Because the tenancy is single, a breach by one heir may have consequences for the whole tenancy (890110_2).

common_material_facts: The original tenant died leaving one or more heirs who succeeded to the tenancy.
The tenancy remained single, with no division of premises or rent.
The dispute arose in rent control or eviction proceedings.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 19 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
Sections 12, 20 and 25 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
H.C. Pandey v. G.C. Paul
Smt. Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar
Mst. Surayya Begum v. Mohd. Usman
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the heirs succeed as joint tenants under a single tenancy, not as tenants-in-common.
variations: 115795579_1 stresses that Section 19 of the Hindu Succession Act governs only the heirs' rights inter se, and involves a jointly let tenancy with another surviving tenant.
1910531_1 states the general rule and overrules a contrary Allahabad High Court decision.
890110_2 applies the rule to a breach (sub-letting or admitting an outsider as partner) by one heir, which affects the whole tenancy.

legal_question: Where a statute gives a landlord connected with public service a special summary procedure to recover possession, does the landlord's retirement affect eligibility, and at what point must the statutory conditions be satisfied?

predicates.special_summary_eviction_application: The landlord has applied for possession of let premises under a special summary or immediate-possession procedure created for landlords connected with public service or government accommodation.
predicates.landlord_met_statutory_conditions_at_sta: The landlord satisfied the conditions the statute prescribes (for example, a landlord-tenant relationship at retirement, or an ownership-based vacate order served on an allottee) at the point of time the statute treats as decisive.
predicates.retirement_alone_is_made_disqualifying_b: The statute's wording itself makes retirement, or retirement before the application or demand, a bar to using the procedure.
predicates.special_summary_procedure_available: The landlord may maintain the special summary eviction application and seek possession under it.

definition: Eligibility for a special summary eviction procedure depends on whether the landlord met the statute's own conditions at the time the statute fixes. Retirement does not by itself disqualify a landlord whose right accrued under the statute before retirement. Where the statute fixes the time of retirement, as the Punjab provision does, the landlord must then have had the required landlord-tenant relationship.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the statute requires the landlord to have been entitled to receive rent from the tenant at retirement, a landlord whose tenancy began after retirement cannot use the procedure. A later filing window does not cure this.

The eligibility of a retired allottee depends on the precise wording of the statute. Under the Delhi provision, 'person' is read plainly and is not confined to serving employees, and the right accrues when the ownership-based vacate order is served.
The Delhi-type members involved an allottee who owned a residence and was required to vacate because of that ownership. Different facts may not attract the same result.

common_material_facts: The landlord was a public servant or government accommodation allottee who had retired.
The landlord sought possession of let premises through a special summary or immediate-possession procedure.
Retirement came before the application and, in one case, before the demand to vacate.
statutes_and_provisions: East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1985, ss. 2(hh) and 13-A
Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, s. 14A(1) and s. 25B
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Two of three members hold that retirement does not defeat the landlord's right under the Delhi provisions. One holds the special procedure unavailable because the landlord-tenant relationship did not exist at retirement under the Punjab provisions.
variations: The Punjab provision makes the position at retirement the test. The Delhi provision keys the right to the ownership-based vacate order and has no retirement-based limit.
One Delhi member stresses the plain meaning of 'person'. The other stresses that the right accrues on service of the order and that s. 25B only supplies the procedure.
The outcomes are opposite, and the difference lies in the statutory wording.

split_suggestion: If a tighter grouping is needed, put the two Delhi s. 14A members (1187427_1, 867163_1) together on the point that retirement does not defeat an accrued right. Treat the East Punjab s. 13-A member (115022_1) separately as a case where the statute makes the position at retirement a condition.

legal_question: Where the Transfer of Property Act (or its redemption provision) does not apply to a mortgage, may a civil court still apply the equitable principles of justice, equity and good conscience to protect the mortgagor's right of redemption, so that a restrictive term does not bar redemption?

predicates.mortgage_redemption_proceeding: The suit or proceeding seeks redemption of a transaction treated as a mortgage.
predicates.transfer_of_property_act_provision_inapp: The Transfer of Property Act, or its redemption provision (section 60), did not apply in the territory when the mortgage was made or the repayment period expired.
predicates.redemption_principle_consistent_with_jus: The redemption principle, including the protection against a clog or unreasonable restriction on the right to redeem, accords with justice, equity and good conscience and with the established practice of Indian courts.
predicates.no_contrary_local_law_established: No material shows that local law required enforcement of the restrictive term or excluded equitable principles in the territory.
predicates.civil_court_applies_equitable_redemption: The civil court applies the equitable principles underlying the statutory redemption rule, refuses to enforce a restrictive term (such as automatic ownership on default) as a bar, and may decree redemption, subject to limitation.

definition: Where the statutory mortgage-redemption provisions do not apply by their own force, civil courts still apply justice, equity and good conscience, and so uphold the mortgagor's right to redeem. Terms that unreasonably restrict redemption, such as forfeiture or ownership vesting on default within a fixed period, cannot defeat redemption unless a contrary local rule is shown.
exceptions_or_limits: The right to redeem remains subject to the general law of limitation.
Does not apply where material establishes that local law requires enforcement of the term or excludes equitable principles.
The members rely on an established judicial practice of applying equity to redemption; the principle is not unlimited where a binding statutory or customary rule is shown to the contrary.

common_material_facts: Suit for redemption of a mortgage in a territory where the Transfer of Property Act did not apply at the relevant time
In two members, the deed provided that the mortgagee would become owner if the debt was not repaid within a fixed period
No material was produced to show that equitable principles were inapplicable locally
Reliance on consistent High Court practice applying equity to redemption
statutes_and_provisions: Section 60, Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (right of redemption, as an underlying principle)
Principle of justice, equity and good conscience
Namdeo Lokman Lodhi v. Narmadabai (cited in 1155281_2 and 1531467_2)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the equitable principle applies despite the Act's non-application: redemption is allowed and the restrictive term cannot bar it, subject to limitation.
variations: Two members concern a clog on the equity of redemption, while one concerns the general power of the civil court to decree redemption.
The cited precedents differ: Madras, Bombay and Rajasthan decisions in two members, Punjab and Lahore decisions in the third.
Two members distinguish the Privy Council decisions that took a strict approach.

legal_question: Does Section 21-A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 bar a court from reopening a bank loan transaction merely because the interest charged is excessive, and does the bar remain subject to relief where the bank has charged interest contrary to Reserve Bank directions?

predicates.loan_granted_by_banking_company: The loan or advance was granted by a banking company to its debtor, whether the borrower is an agriculturist or a non-agriculturist.
predicates.court_asked_to_reopen_for_excessive_inte: The borrower asks the court to reopen or interfere with the bank-debtor transaction on the ground that the interest rate charged is excessive.
predicates.bank_charged_interest_contrary_to_regula: The bank charged interest (for example, at a higher rate or with rests not permitted) in breach of an applicable Reserve Bank direction governing interest on loans and advances.
predicates.court_cannot_reopen_transaction_for_exce: The court is barred by Section 21-A from reopening the transaction merely on the ground that the interest charged is excessive.

definition: Section 21-A bars courts from reopening a bank-debtor loan transaction merely because the interest is excessive, regardless of whether the borrower is an agriculturist. The bar does not protect interest charged contrary to binding Reserve Bank directions, which a court may disallow.
exceptions_or_limits: The bar does not prevent a court from disallowing interest charged contrary to an applicable Reserve Bank direction (Sections 21 and 35-A directions having statutory flavour).
Where the Reserve Bank has fixed a maximum rate, the bar applies when the bank has stayed within that maximum and permitted rests.
No opinion is expressed on cases where Reserve Bank directions fix only a minimum rate and leave the bank discretion to charge more.
The challenge must be to excessiveness of interest as such; it is not a bar to a challenge based on breach of regulatory directions.

common_material_facts: Bank loan or recovery dispute where the borrower complains of excessive interest
Reference to Reserve Bank directions on interest rates or rests
Section 21-A relied on as a bar to reopening transactions
statutes_and_provisions: Banking Regulation Act, 1949, Section 21-A
Banking Regulation Act, 1949, Sections 21, 35-A and 47-A
Usurious Loans Act, 1918
Entry 30, List II (agricultural indebtedness)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Section 21-A is applied broadly to bar reopening for excessive interest (2 of 3 members), with one member permitting disallowance of interest charged contrary to Reserve Bank directions.
variations: One member addresses the scope of Section 21-A (all borrowers, rejecting the State-competence reasoning).
One member confirms the bar where the bank complied with a maximum rate fixed by the Reserve Bank.
One member allows relief because the bank violated Reserve Bank directions, creating a limit on the bar.

legal_question: Must a plaintiff suing in respect of immovable property (for specific performance or possession) describe and identify the property sufficiently for the court to decree relief and for the decree to be executed, and what follows where the plaint or evidence does not do so?

predicates.suit_concerns_immovable_property: The suit seeks relief such as specific performance or recovery of possession in respect of immovable property.
predicates.relief_sought_requires_decree_over_speci: The relief claimed would result in a decree that must operate on, or be executed by delivery of, a particular identified property.
predicates.property_not_sufficiently_identified_in_: The plaint, title documents, maps or other evidence do not allow the property to be identified, for example because boundaries, numbers or descriptions do not correspond to survey or revenue records or to each other, and no adequate map or description is supplied.
predicates.court_must_require_sufficient_identifica: The court must insist on an adequate description or identification (such as a map or corroborating evidence) before decreeing, and a decree without it is not sustainable.

definition: A plaintiff claiming specific performance or possession of immovable property must describe the property so that it can be identified, in line with Order 7 Rule 3 CPC, and must show that the property in the title document is the property identified by the evidence. Where this is lacking, the court must require adequate identification before decreeing, since otherwise the decree cannot properly be passed or executed.
exceptions_or_limits: Applies only where identification is actually in doubt; where boundaries or survey numbers in the records identify the property, no further description is needed.

The members rest on the duty to identify the property (Order 7 Rule 3 and Order 20 Rule 3 CPC in one; general possession-claim requirements in another); none lays down a fixed form such as a map in every case.
Member 143742501_2 is on a different point (consequential relief under Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act), so this rule does not cover it.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns the bar on a bare declaration of title where possession could be claimed (proviso to Section 34 Specific Relief Act), not identification of the property.

common_material_facts: Suit over immovable property based on a sale deed or agreement
Descriptions of the property in title documents, plans or records did not correspond or could not be matched to survey or revenue records
Plaintiff did not supply, or relied only on a sketch instead of, a clear map or identification
statutes_and_provisions: Order 7 Rule 3 CPC
Order 20 Rule 3 CPC
Proviso to Section 34 Specific Relief Act, 1963 (outlier member only)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In the two covered members, the property had to be adequately identified; the plaintiff had to supply a map or show correspondence between the deed and the identified land, and the trial court should have required it. The third member (outlier) held a declaration-only suit not maintainable.
variations: One member is a pleading and procedural duty of the trial court under Order 7 Rule 3; the other concerns the plaintiff's burden of proof on identification in a possession claim.
The cluster also contains a Section 34 consequential-relief issue that does not turn on identification.

split_suggestion: Keep 1161674_1 and 1978591_2 together as property identification in suits over immovable property. Move 143742501_2 to a separate cluster on omission of consequential relief (possession) in declaratory suits under Section 34 Specific Relief Act.

legal_question: Does a challenge alleging that a statutory body or tribunal failed to follow prescribed procedure fail where the record shows compliance, or where the alleged breach is not established by evidence?

predicates.challenge_alleges_procedural_non_complia: The petitioner or appellant challenges a decision or levy on the ground that the deciding body (a village tribunal, local court or municipality) did not follow the procedure prescribed by statute or rules.
predicates.procedural_breach_established_on_record: The record or material before the court affirmatively shows that the prescribed procedure was violated. This is not satisfied where the record shows compliance, such as required signatures and a recorded dissent, or where the alleged breach is unsupported by evidence.
predicates.procedural_challenge_is_rejected: The court rejects the challenge based on alleged procedural non-compliance because no violation of the prescribed procedure has been established.

definition: A challenge based on alleged breach of prescribed procedure fails where the record shows the procedural requirements were met, or where no material establishes the breach. The burden lies on the challenger, and the decision is presumed to have followed the prescribed procedure.
exceptions_or_limits: Where an illegality or departure from statutory procedure is actually established, it is not cured by long acquiescence or passage of time (1631255_4).
The rule rests on a failure of proof or on shown compliance. It does not hold that procedural requirements may be disregarded.
In the municipal tax context the court also noted that the challenger had not specifically alleged any other procedural failure.

common_material_facts: The challenger alleged non-compliance with statutory or rule-based procedure.
The record showed compliance, or the material needed to prove breach was absent.
In two members the full-bench decision was signed by its members and the dissenting minute was signed by the dissenters under the Bihar Gram Cutcherry Rules.
No material was shown establishing a violation.
statutes_and_provisions: Rules 60 and 61 of the Bihar Gram Cutcherry Rules, 1949 (rule 60(2) on signatures and dissent)
Sections 131–136 of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act
Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members reject the procedural challenge because no violation was established: 2 on the Bihar Gram Cutcherry Rules and 1 on the municipal tax procedure.
variations: Two members concern village tribunal decision-recording rules and one concerns the procedure for imposing a municipal tax.

The tribunal cases turn on shown compliance, such as signatures and a recorded dissent. The municipal case turns on a failure of proof, where the draft proposals were not before the court and the allegation was denied.
Only the municipal case ties the procedural challenge to Article 19(1)(f), and it addresses delay and acquiescence.

legal_question: What does Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC require for a compromise to be recorded and decreed in a suit or appeal, and does it permit separate or staged agreements and decrees where the compromise is in writing and signed by the relevant parties?

predicates.order_xxiii_rule_3_compromise_proceeding: A suit or appeal in which a claim is said to have been adjusted wholly or partly by lawful agreement or compromise under Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC.
predicates.written_agreement_signed_by_parties_to_t: The compromise terms were reduced to writing and signed by the parties to that agreement, not merely stated orally before the court.
predicates.court_recorded_agreement_and_decreed_acc: The court, being satisfied of the lawful agreement, recorded it and passed a decree in accordance with it, whether for the whole or part of the subject matter.
predicates.compromise_or_part_compromise_decree_is_: The compromise decree is valid and not a nullity, and separate agreements recorded or separate decrees passed at different stages in the same suit do not invalidate it.

definition: Under Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC, a compromise must be a lawful agreement in writing signed by the parties, which the court records and decrees. Where that is satisfied, the compromise may cover only part of the suit, and agreements or decrees may come at different stages without invalidity. An oral compromise made in court and not reduced to signed writing cannot be acted on.
exceptions_or_limits: An oral compromise or offer stated before the court but not reduced to writing and signed by the parties cannot be recorded as an adjustment, and the proceeding must be decided on merits (1574511_1).
Agreements that are void or voidable under the Contract Act are not lawful compromises under the Explanation to the rule.
Staged recording of agreements is valid only if every party's settlement is completed before the final decree (386828_2).
The agreement must be capable of being embodied in a decree.

common_material_facts: A suit or appeal involving multiple parties in which some or all parties compromise
Challenge to the validity of a compromise or the decree based on it
Dispute over whether the compromise was recorded in the manner Order XXIII Rule 3 requires
statutes_and_provisions: Order XXIII Rule 3 CPC
Order XII Rule 6 CPC
Order XX Rules 1 and 12 CPC
Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Explanation to Order XXIII Rule 3)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Two of the three members uphold the compromise decrees (staged or partial decrees valid). One refuses to give effect to an oral, unsigned compromise.
variations: 1183935_3 concerns the validity of multiple decrees at different stages in one suit, resting also on Order XII Rule 6.
386828_2 concerns whether separately signed agreements and later decree satisfy the writing and signature requirement, and distinguishes Ajad Singh v. Chatra.
1574511_1 concerns an oral compromise made in an appeal hearing, which fails for want of signed writing, and overrules Manohar Lal v. Surjan Singh.

split_suggestion: Optionally split into (a) the writing and signature requirement for compromises (1574511_1, 386828_2) and (b) the validity of part or staged decrees in one suit (1183935_3, 386828_2).

legal_question: Can an administrative or statutory order that is challenged in court be defended or validated by reasons that were not stated in the order when it was made, but were supplied later in affidavits or pleadings?

predicates.administrative_order_challenged: An order made by a public authority under statutory or administrative power (for example a direction, a decision to re-auction, or a cancellation) is under judicial challenge.
predicates.order_records_contemporaneous_reasons: The order, or the notice or record leading to it, states the grounds or reasons on which it was made at the time of making.
predicates.authority_relies_on_additional_reasons_a: In court proceedings (for example in affidavits or a response to a petition) the authority seeks to defend the order on grounds not stated in the order or its contemporaneous record.
predicates.order_validity_judged_only_on_reasons_re: The court assesses the validity of the order only on the reasons stated when it was made and does not accept later-supplied reasons to supplement or validate it.

definition: A public order must be judged by the grounds stated in it when it was made; the authority cannot improve or validate it by adding fresh reasons through later affidavits or pleadings (Gordhandas Bhanji; Mohinder Singh Gill).
exceptions_or_limits: The rule concerns reasons not stated in the order or contemporaneous record; reasons actually recorded at the time remain open for examination.
The members do not address whether later material may be used for purposes other than justifying the order, so the rule is confined to attempts to supplement or substitute reasons.

common_material_facts: A public authority made an order (direction, re-auction decision, cancellation) stating particular reasons.
In court the authority advanced additional grounds not found in the order or the contemporaneous record (policy, delay, commercial interest, cartelization, other grounds).
The challenge was by way of judicial review or writ proceedings.
statutes_and_provisions: Commissioner of Police, Bombay v. Gordhandas Bhanji (1952) 1 SCR 135
Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief Election Commissioner (1978) 1 SCC 405 / (1978) 2 SCR 272
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members, the later-added reasons were not allowed to support the order, and validity was judged on the reasons recorded at the time.
variations: The orders differ in type: a government direction on a transaction, a re-auction decision, and a cancellation order.
The later reasons were raised in different forms: State affidavits in two members and a response to writ petitions in one.
One member relied on both Gordhandas Bhanji and Mohinder Singh Gill, one applied Mohinder Singh Gill applying Gordhandas, and one cited Mohinder Singh Gill alone.

legal_question: When may a court allow a review petition and correct or recall its earlier judgment because of an error in that judgment, including an error arising from overlooking a later or retrospective legal change?

rule.if: review_proceeding and (clear_error_apparent_on_record_shown or (later_or_retrospective_law_governs_matter and law_not_considered_in_original_decision and error_evident_from_record_without_rehearing))

predicates.review_proceeding: The matter is a review application or petition seeking reconsideration of an earlier decision of the court.
predicates.clear_error_apparent_on_record_shown: It is shown that the earlier judgment contains a clear, manifest error (such as a factual misdescription or an error apparent on the face of the record).
predicates.later_or_retrospective_law_governs_matte: A subsequent or retrospectively operative amendment applies to the transaction or to a proceeding that had not attained finality, and could change the result.
predicates.law_not_considered_in_original_decision: The amendment was unavailable at the time of the original decision or was not brought to the court's attention and was overlooked.
predicates.error_evident_from_record_without_rehear: The error can be seen from the record and the law itself, without a fresh investigation or a rehearing of the same issue.
predicates.earlier_judgment_may_be_reviewed_and_cor: The court may allow the review and correct, clarify or recall the earlier judgment.

definition: A court may allow review and correct its earlier judgment where a clear error apparent on the record is shown. This includes the case where a retrospective or intervening amendment governing the matter was unavailable or overlooked and the error is evident without rehearing the issue.
exceptions_or_limits: Review is not a rehearing of the same issue; the error must be manifest and not one that must be established by further investigation or long-drawn reasoning.
A later change in law supports review only if it applies to the matter, for example retrospectively or to a proceeding that had not reached finality, and could affect the result.
The grounds in Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC (new evidence, mistake, error apparent, other sufficient reason) frame the power; one member relied on no statutory provision.

common_material_facts: An earlier judgment contained an error that was revealed on review.
In two members, an amendment with retrospective or pending-proceeding effect was unavailable or overlooked when the original decision was made.
The error could be identified from the record without a fresh inquiry.
statutes_and_provisions: Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC
State amendment to sales tax law on standing timber (retrospective)
Statutory amendment exempting qualifying religious institutions in a tenant land-purchase context
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the review was allowed and the earlier judgment was corrected or reviewed.
variations: One member concerned a factual misdescription of an institution, with no authority cited.
Two members concerned a legal change (retrospective amendment) that was overlooked or unavailable.
Only one member expressly cited Order XLVII Rule 1 CPC and the Kunhayammed principles; another stated the general 'error apparent on the face of the record' test.

legal_question: When a mortgagee purchases the mortgaged property at a rent sale, does the mortgagor keep the right of redemption (under section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act), and if the sale extinguished it, can the mortgagor still redeem part of the property?

predicates.redemption_claim: The mortgagor seeks to redeem the mortgaged property.
predicates.mortgagee_or_beneficiary_purchased_at_re: The mortgagee, or a person buying for the mortgagee's benefit, purchased the mortgaged property at a rent or execution sale.
predicates.mortgagee_default_on_own_rent_liability_: The mortgagee defaulted on rent for which the mortgage terms made the mortgagee liable, and that default contributed to bringing about the sale.
predicates.mortgagee_default_trifling_or_ineffectiv: The mortgagee's default was trifling or not a real contributory cause, so the mortgagor's default alone effectively caused the sale, and no improper motive was shown.
predicates.mortgagor_retains_right_to_redeem: The mortgagor keeps the right of redemption because the mortgagee holds the purchase advantage for the benefit of the mortgagor.

definition: Under section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act, a mortgagee who contributes to a rent sale by defaulting on rent for which the mortgagee is liable, and then buys the property, holds the purchase for the mortgagor's benefit, so redemption survives even if the mortgagor also defaulted. If the mortgagee's default was trifling and not an effective cause of the sale, the purchase extinguishes redemption. Where the sale has extinguished the equity of redemption over the whole property, partial redemption is not available.
exceptions_or_limits: If the mortgagee's default was trifling and not an effective cause of the sale, the mortgagor's default alone caused it, and no improper motive was shown, section 90 does not apply and the sale extinguishes redemption.
The Court left open the case where the mortgagee's rent liability is so small that the property would not ordinarily be sold for it.

Once a rent sale of the whole mortgaged property has extinguished the equity of redemption, the last paragraph of section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act does not allow partial redemption on payment of a proportionate part of the mortgage money.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns partial redemption under section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act after the equity of redemption was already extinguished. It does not concern whether section 90 of the Trusts Act makes the mortgagee's purchase enure for the mortgagor. It is consequential to the extinction finding in 237664_1.

common_material_facts: The mortgaged land was part of a larger holding, and rent was apportioned between mortgagee and mortgagor.
Both mortgagor and mortgagee had defaulted, or at least the mortgagor had.
A rent or execution sale followed the arrears, and the mortgagee or someone for the mortgagee bought the property.
The mortgagor then claimed redemption.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 90, Indian Trusts Act, 1882, and Illustration (c)
Section 60, Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (last paragraph)
Basmat Devi v. Chamru Sao, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1707
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of the 3 members, 1 upholds redemption because the mortgagee's default contributed to the sale. 1 denies it because the mortgagee's default was trifling and the mortgagor's default was the effective cause. 1 denies partial redemption after extinction.
variations: The outcomes turn on whether the mortgagee's own rent default was a real contributory cause of the sale, as against a trifling default.
The mortgagor's concurrent default does not defeat redemption where the mortgagee's default also contributed.
One member deals only with the derivative question of partial redemption under the Transfer of Property Act.

split_suggestion: Keep 1181948_1 and 237664_1 together as the section 90 Trusts Act question on the mortgagee's contributory default. Treat 237664_2, on partial redemption under section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act after extinction, as a separate issue.

legal_question: Where property is bought in a wife's (or mother's) name with money supplied by her husband, does the husband's funding alone make the transaction benami, or make the property a gift of that property, or must the character of the transaction be determined from the intention shown by the evidence and the applicable classification rules?

rule.if: property_purchased_in_womans_name and husband_provided_purchase_money and (benami_or_gift_characterisation_sought_solely_from_source_of_funds or personal_law_gift_rule_invoked)

predicates.property_purchased_in_womans_name: The sale deed or conveyance for the property was executed in the name of the wife (or mother).
predicates.husband_provided_purchase_money: The husband supplied the purchase money or consideration, or the court proceeds on the assumption that he did.
predicates.benami_or_gift_characterisation_sought_s: A party asks the court to treat the property as benami or as a gift of the property itself merely because the husband paid the price.
predicates.personal_law_gift_rule_invoked: A personal-law or statutory rule on gifts to women (for example, the Dayabhaga stridhan rule on gifts of immovable property, or the in specie gift category in a succession statute) is relied on to characterise the transaction.
predicates.source_of_funds_alone_does_not_establish: The husband's payment of the price does not by itself make the transaction benami or the property a gift. Benami character requires proof of intention from the totality of the evidence, and a gift of money followed by a purchase does not make the purchased property a gift in specie.

definition: A husband's payment of the price for property bought in his wife's name does not by itself make the purchase benami, nor make the property a gift of that property. Benami character depends on intention proved by the party alleging it from the whole evidence, and personal-law rules on gifts to women do not show benami character or convert a purchase into a gift.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the party alleging benami proves from the totality of the evidence (source of funds, possession, motive, custody of title deeds, subsequent conduct, relationship) that the wife was meant to hold title only nominally, the transaction is benami.
The source of funds is relevant and important but not conclusive.

The succession classification (purchase versus gift) turns on how the property was acquired, not on who supplied the funds, and applies under the statute concerned (the Mysore Hindu Law Women's Rights Act, 1933).
The Dayabhaga stridhan limitation concerns succession and inheritance, not whether a transaction is benami.

common_material_facts: Property conveyed in the name of a wife or mother
Husband or father supplied the purchase money, or the court assumed he did
A party sought to recharacterise the transaction as benami or as a gift based on the source of funds or a personal-law rule
Gift of money is distinguished from gift of the property itself
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 10(2)(b) and 10(2)(d), Mysore Hindu Law Women's Rights Act, 1933
Dayabhaga law on stridhan and gifts of immovable property
Transfer of Property Act (restrictions on transfer; registered deed for gifts of immovable property)
Kanakarathanammal v. V.S. Loganatha Mudaliar, AIR 1965 SC 271
Jaydayal Poddar v. Bibi Hazira, (1974) 1 SCC 3
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the husband's funding did not establish that the purchase was benami or a gift of the property. Two members rejected the benami finding and one rejected gift classification.
variations: One member is a fact-intensive benami inquiry in which the burden on the alleger was not discharged.
One member is a legal point that the Dayabhaga stridhan rule is irrelevant to benami character.
One member is a succession classification under a statute, where the issue is gift versus purchase rather than benami.

split_suggestion: If a tighter split is preferred, separate the two benami members (1199737_1 on intention and burden of proof, 1199737_3 on the irrelevance of the Dayabhaga rule) from the succession-classification member (1386996_1 on gift versus purchase under the Mysore Act).

legal_question: Must a statutory notice proposing to alter an assessment or plan state the actual reasons or specific grounds, so that the affected person can effectively object, and what follows if it does not?

predicates.statutory_notice_of_proposed_change_requ: The governing statute requires notice to affected persons before an assessment, plan or similar entry is altered.
predicates.affected_persons_have_right_to_object: The statute, or natural justice, gives affected persons the right to object and be heard on the proposed change.
predicates.notice_omits_actual_reason_or_specific_g: The notice does not state the real reason for the proposed change or the specific statutory ground relied on. It uses a vague or printed formula listing alternative grounds.
predicates.notice_gives_no_basis_for_proposed_chang: The notice does not disclose the material facts or the error relied on, so the person cannot meaningfully respond.
predicates.notice_is_deficient_and_proposed_change_: The notice fails the statutory requirement, and the change made or proposed on it cannot stand.

definition: Where a statute requires notice and an opportunity to object before a proposed change, the notice must disclose the actual reasons or specific grounds, with enough particulars for an effective objection. A vague or formulaic notice defeats the condition precedent and invalidates the change. In the planning context, the same duty of reasons and meaningful public hearing applies to modifications that affect public amenities.
exceptions_or_limits: The invalidity consequence is stated in the two municipal assessment cases under section 67 of the Punjab Municipal Act. The planning case instead lays down affirmative procedural safeguards for future modifications.
The planning member adds specific directions (newspaper publication, public inquiry) that do not arise in the assessment cases.
The rule presupposes a statutory notice requirement. It does not address cases where notice is not required.

common_material_facts: A statutory notice proposing a change (assessment alteration or plan modification) was issued or bypassed.
The notice was vague, formulaic or silent on the actual reason or ground.
Affected persons were denied a reasonable opportunity to respond or object.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 67(1) of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911
Section 67 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911 (one month to object and a hearing)
Sections 22A, 28, 29 and 37 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Notices lacking stated reasons or specific grounds fail, and the resulting change is invalid (2 assessment cases). The planning case requires reasons, wide publication and a public inquiry (1 case).
variations: The assessment cases rest on natural justice and strict construction of taxing provisions, and treat notice as a condition precedent.
The planning case rests on public participation and scientific planning, and issues prospective directions rather than invalidating a particular notice.
In the assessment cases the notice was defective in content (a printed formula or alternative grounds). In the planning case the process was bypassed.

split_suggestion: Optionally separate the two Punjab Municipal Act assessment-notice cases (1202267_1, 274459_1), which are closely aligned, from the town-planning public-participation case (132334_9).

legal_question: Is a requirement in agrarian reform legislation that a landholder (or a family member) reside in the locality of the land for most of the year, and that agriculture be the principal source of income, constitutionally valid against challenges under Articles 14, 19 and 31?

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_agrarian_ref: The residence or income condition in agrarian reform legislation is challenged as violating fundamental rights (Articles 14, 19 or 31).
predicates.condition_requires_landholder_or_family_: The law requires the landholder or a member of the family to reside in the locality of the land for the greater part of the year (and, in some cases, to derive the principal income from the land).
predicates.condition_supports_personal_cultivation_: The condition is linked to personal cultivation, ensuring the cultivator gives the land attention, and discouraging absentee landholding.
predicates.condition_is_partial_reasonable_restrict: The condition only partially restricts residence and occupation (e.g. other occupations allowed, part-year absence allowed, family member may satisfy it) and serves agrarian reform and public interest, so it is a reasonable restriction under Articles 19(4) and 19(5).
predicates.legislation_has_close_nexus_to_article_3: The legislation has a close nexus to distributing material resources for the common good under Article 39(b), so Article 31C bars challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31.
predicates.residence_condition_is_constitutionally_: The residence (and income) condition is upheld as not violating the challenged fundamental rights.

definition: A condition in agrarian reform law that the landholder or a family member reside near the land for most of the year, tied to personal cultivation and prevention of absentee holding, is upheld. It is valid either as a reasonable, non-disproportionate restriction under Article 19 or because the law is shielded by Article 31C through its nexus with Article 39(b).
exceptions_or_limits: Reasonableness under Article 19 was found because the restriction was partial: the tenant could pursue other occupations, reside elsewhere for part of the year, and a family member could satisfy the residence condition.
The Article 31C route depends on a close nexus between the legislation and Article 39(b) objectives.
The members do not address a residence condition unconnected to cultivation or agrarian reform.

common_material_facts: The law required the landholder or a family member to reside in the locality of the land for the greater part of the year.
The condition was linked to personal cultivation and preventing absentee landholding.
Some members also required agriculture to be the principal source of income.
The condition formed part of agrarian reform legislation.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 39(b)
Article 31C
Articles 14 and 31
State of Madras v. V.G. Row
Sri Sri Kalimata Thakurani v. Union of India
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members uphold the residence condition as valid, one as a reasonable restriction under Article 19 and two on the basis of Article 39(b) and Article 31C, with beneficial or reasonableness observations.
variations: 1205156_4 decides on Article 19 reasonableness using the V.G. Row contextual test, with no reliance on Article 31C.
151597034_2 and 1736660_2 rely mainly on Article 39(b) and Article 31C, reading the condition as beneficial to cultivation.
151597034_2 and 1205156_4 address the principal-income requirement, while 1736660_2 addresses only residence.

legal_question: Do allegations of fraud in a private civil or commercial dispute, covered by an arbitration agreement, make the dispute non-arbitrable so that a court must refuse to refer it to arbitration?

rule.if: arbitration_agreement_covers_dispute and fraud_is_alleged and dispute_is_private_civil_or_contractual and not fraud_vitiates_arbitration_agreement_itself and not dispute_raises_public_law_or_public_overtones

predicates.arbitration_agreement_covers_dispute: A valid, executed arbitration agreement or clause exists and its scope covers the dispute that is the subject of the proceedings.
predicates.fraud_is_alleged: A party alleges fraud, misrepresentation or concealment in connection with the transactions or agreements between the parties.
predicates.dispute_is_private_civil_or_contractual: The dispute is a civil or contractual dispute between private parties concerning their dealings, and the fraud alleged is fraud of that kind (including fraud in inducement or performance amounting to civil deceit).
predicates.fraud_vitiates_arbitration_agreement_its: The alleged fraud goes to the arbitration agreement itself, for example by denying that the agreement was ever executed, so that the arbitration clause is invalid or non-existent.
predicates.dispute_raises_public_law_or_public_over: The allegations raise a public-law controversy, for example against the State or its instrumentalities, or have public overtones that require adjudication by a public court.
predicates.fraud_allegations_do_not_bar_arbitration: The fraud allegations do not make the dispute non-arbitrable, and the court should refer the parties to arbitration so the arbitrator can examine them.

definition: Allegations of fraud in a private civil or contractual dispute do not make it non-arbitrable. Seriousness, complexity or possible criminal overtones are not enough on their own. A court refuses reference only where the fraud vitiates the arbitration agreement itself or the dispute raises public-law or public-overtone issues.
exceptions_or_limits: Arbitration may be refused where the fraud vitiates the arbitration agreement itself, for example where the agreement is denied to have been executed.
Arbitration may be refused where the allegations raise a public-law controversy or have public overtones that require a public court to adjudicate.

The earlier 'serious and complicated fraud' test, under which a court could refuse reference where allegations amount to a virtual criminal offence, is displaced by the later cases (Avitel line). N. Radhakrishnan v. Maestro Engineers is stated to be overruled or no longer of precedential value on this point.

common_material_facts: Commercial or contractual agreements contain arbitration clauses.
One party alleges fraud, misrepresentation or concealment in the underlying transactions.
Criminal proceedings or criminal overtones are present or possible but are not treated as decisive.
The dispute is between private parties, with no public-law element.
statutes_and_provisions: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 8
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 16 (competence-competence and separability)
Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 17
A. Ayyasamy v. A. Paramasivam (2016) 10 SCC 386
Avitel Post Studioz Ltd. v. HSBC PI Holdings (Mauritius) Ltd.
Rashid Raza v. Sadaf Akhthar
N. Radhakrishnan v. Maestro Engineers
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the fraud allegations do not bar arbitration and that the arbitrator can examine them, so the dispute is referred to arbitration or held arbitrable.
variations: One member applies the Ayyasamy 'serious and complicated' threshold and finds it not met. The other two rely on the Avitel approach, which treats civil fraud as arbitrable regardless of seriousness, and say Radhakrishnan is overruled or no longer good law.

The members differ in how they frame the exceptions. One refers to fraud vitiating the arbitration agreement itself and public-law allegations, another to non-execution of the agreement and public overtones, and the first to seriousness and complexity.
One member arises under Section 8 in a suit. Another is an arbitration referral proceeding. The third is a general statement of principle.

legal_question: Is a statutory scheme or power that affects property or fiscal liability (assessment, valuation, or takeover of land management) arbitrary and invalid under Article 14 when it rests on uncontrolled or subjective official discretion, with no objective standards, rational method, or adequate procedure for determining the relevant matters?

predicates.challenge_to_property_related_fiscal_or_: The case challenges a statute or official action that assesses, values, or takes over management of land or property, affecting a person's property or tax liability.
predicates.power_exercised_on_uncontrolled_or_subje: The power is left to an officer's subjective view or uncontrolled discretion, with no specified officer, process, or criteria guiding the decision.
predicates.method_is_unscientific_or_uncontrolled_t: The valuation or assessment relies on a haphazard, non-expert method, such as untrained personnel, with the responsible authority having delegated the work without control or supervision.
predicates.no_objective_standards_or_rational_metho: The law or practice supplies no objective criteria or rational, scientific method for making the determination, so results can vary arbitrarily.
predicates.no_adequate_procedure_or_effective_oppor: The affected person has no adequate procedure for determination and no effective notice or opportunity to challenge or correct the decision.
predicates.scheme_or_action_is_arbitrary_and_violat: The scheme, power, or action is held arbitrary and unreasonable, violating Article 14 and invalid, with consequent orders quashed where applicable.

definition: A law or official action affecting property or fiscal liability is arbitrary and invalid under Article 14 if it leaves the decision to uncontrolled or subjective discretion or an unscientific, uncontrolled method, without objective standards or a fair procedure to determine and contest the outcome.
exceptions_or_limits: Members differ on which element carries the arbitrariness: absent procedure to contest (1213194_2), absent objective standards and determination process (782593_3), or an unscientific, uncontrolled method (890111_2). The rule's conditions are a combined, flexible formulation, and not every member shows all of them.

Where the statute or its incorporated instruments supply objective criteria, a workable procedure and a rational method, the rule would not apply. In 1213194_2 administrative standing orders did not count because the statute did not incorporate them.
The rule is limited to arbitrariness under Article 14 and does not state a general invalidity of discretionary powers.

common_material_facts: Property or fiscal burdens determined by officials without objective criteria or controlled method
No effective procedure or opportunity for the affected holder to contest or correct the decision
State defended the scheme by pointing to administrative practice or the authority's own view, which the Court did not accept as supplying standards
statutes_and_provisions: Article 14 of the Constitution
Sections 2(1), 2(5) and 65 of the agricultural tenancy statute
Section 106 of the West Bengal Municipal Act, 1993 and section 9 of the West Bengal Central Valuation Board Act, 1978
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the scheme, power, or method arbitrary and invalid under Article 14; in one, the takeover orders were also quashed.
variations: One member concerns the lack of any assessment procedure or means of challenge in a land assessment scheme.
One concerns a power to take over land management based on subjective views of inefficient cultivation, with no objective standards.
One concerns a valuation method using untrained survey workers under an uncontrolled delegation, with extreme variation in demands.
The remedy differs: a scheme was struck down, a statutory amendment was held ultra vires with orders quashed, and a valuation method was held unconstitutional.

legal_question: Can a court, in the exercise of its discretion, permit a procedural defect (such as a court-fee deficiency or a misdescription) to be corrected, with the correction treated as relating back to the original timely filing, despite the opposing party's plea that limitation or a statutory bar defeats the proceeding?

rule.if: proceeding_timely_instituted and curable_procedural_defect and court_permits_correction_in_discretion and no_gross_injustice_or_violation_of_legal_principle

predicates.proceeding_timely_instituted: The appeal, memorandum or suit was originally presented or filed within the limitation period or before the statutory bar took effect.
predicates.curable_procedural_defect: The defect is a curable procedural one, such as a deficient court fee or a misdescription in the pleading, and does not change the substantive relief sought.
predicates.court_permits_correction_in_discretion: The court, exercising its judicial discretion (for example under section 149 of the Code of Civil Procedure or under its power to permit amendment), allows the defect to be corrected and the correction is actually made within the time allowed.
predicates.no_gross_injustice_or_violation_of_legal: The exercise of discretion does not violate recognised principles of law or cause gross injustice to the opposing party.
predicates.correction_allowed_and_relates_back_to_o: The correction is upheld and the proceeding is treated as validly instituted from its original filing, so the limitation or statutory-bar objection does not defeat it.

definition: Where a proceeding was timely instituted and suffers only from a curable procedural defect, a court may in its discretion permit correction, and the corrected proceeding is treated as having been validly filed from the outset. A limitation or statutory-bar objection by the opposing party does not automatically prevent this.
exceptions_or_limits: Discretion must be exercised judicially; interference is warranted if the exercise violates recognised principles of law or causes gross injustice.
The rule presupposes original filing within limitation or before the bar; it does not cover proceedings that were themselves out of time.
Relation back is supported where the correction leaves the substantive relief unchanged; an amendment adding genuinely new or time-barred relief is not automatically barred but depends on the facts.
The deficiency must actually be made good within the time allowed, and the document must not have been rejected.

common_material_facts: The original proceeding was filed in time or before a bar took effect.
The defect was curable and procedural (insufficient court fee or misdescription of property).
The opposing party invoked limitation or a statutory bar to resist the correction.
The court permitted correction and the substantive claim remained unchanged.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 149, Code of Civil Procedure
Order 41 rule 1, Code of Civil Procedure
Section 4, Court Fees Act
Section 3(1) and 3(2), U.P. High Court (Abolition of Letters Patent Appeals) Act, 1962
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the limitation or bar objection failed and the correction was upheld, with the proceeding continuing or being treated as pending from the original filing.
variations: Two members concern court-fee deficiency under section 149 CPC (one with a limitation defence, one with a statutory bar on appeals), while one concerns amendment of a plaint for misdescription.

One member rests on harmonising section 149 CPC with section 4 of the Court Fees Act and a saving clause for pending appeals; another rests on appellate non-interference with discretion; the third relies on the general discretion to allow amendment and relation back.
Only some members cite authorities by name; one names none.

split_suggestion: If a tighter grouping is needed, separate the two court-fee deficiency cases under section 149 CPC (121106_3, 423307_1) from the amendment-of-pleading case (541289_3).

legal_question: Is a landlord-tenant or lease dispute arbitrable where the tenancy is governed by general property law (the Transfer of Property Act) and not by a special rent-control statute that gives a specified court or forum exclusive jurisdiction?

predicates.landlord_tenant_dispute: The dispute is between a landlord and tenant (or lessor and lessee or sub-lessee) arising from a lease or tenancy, such as eviction, possession, rent arrears or determination of the lease.
predicates.governed_by_general_property_law: The lease or tenancy is governed by the general law of property (the Transfer of Property Act, 1882) and not by a special rent-control or tenant-protection statute.
predicates.special_statute_with_exclusive_forum_app: A special rent-control or tenant-protection statute applies to the tenancy, gives the tenant statutory protection against eviction, and confers exclusive jurisdiction on a specified court or forum.
predicates.dispute_is_arbitrable: The dispute can be referred to arbitration and the arbitration clause can be invoked, if the parties have a valid arbitration agreement covering it.

definition: Landlord-tenant disputes under ordinary property law are arbitrable, because the Transfer of Property Act neither expressly nor by necessary implication bars arbitration. The exception is for tenancies under special rent statutes that protect tenants and give a specified court or forum exclusive jurisdiction.
exceptions_or_limits: Disputes under rent-control legislation that gives a specified court or forum exclusive jurisdiction over the special rights and obligations are not arbitrable (Booz Allen exception; Natraj Studios).
A valid arbitration agreement covering the dispute is still required, as the two members applying the clause stress.

The tenant-protective provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, including relief against forfeiture, continue to apply and the arbitrator must apply them. They do not make the dispute non-arbitrable.
The contrary view in Himangni Enterprises is overruled (Vidya Drolia), although 28390841_1 only referred it for reconsideration.

common_material_facts: Landlord-tenant or lease dispute with eviction, possession or lease-determination claims
Tenancy governed by the Transfer of Property Act and not by a special rent statute
Arbitration clause in the lease or sub-lease (in two of the three members)
Reliance on Booz Allen and Natraj Studios as concerning special-statute tenancies only
statutes_and_provisions: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, including sections 111, 114 and 114A
Rent-control legislation conferring exclusive jurisdiction on a specified court or forum
Booz Allen four-fold test of non-arbitrability
Vidya Drolia v. Durga Trading Corporation (overruling Himangni Enterprises)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the dispute arbitrable where the tenancy is governed by general property law and no special statute with an exclusive forum applies.
variations: 121987320_2 is the authoritative larger-Bench holding that overrules Himangni Enterprises, applying the four-fold test to subordinate rights in personam.
28390841_1 is an earlier decision that referred Himangni for reconsideration and focused on relief against forfeiture and the Act's silence on arbitrability.
62126347_1 applies Vidya Drolia to a sub-lease and notes that special rent statutes make disputes non-arbitrable.

legal_question: Does the absence of blood, bullets or a visible blood trail at the alleged scene of occurrence, without more, discredit the prosecution's account of the time and place of the offence where the evidence and surrounding circumstances reasonably explain the absence?

predicates.criminal_appeal: The matter is an appeal arising from a criminal trial, whether against conviction or against acquittal.
predicates.prosecution_account_of_place_or_occurren: The prosecution's version of where and when the offence occurred is supported by other evidence such as eyewitness, medical or recovery evidence.
predicates.expected_physical_traces_absent_at_alleg: Physical traces such as blood, bullets or a visible blood trail that might be expected were not found, or were found only in small quantity, at the alleged scene.
predicates.circumstances_reasonably_explain_absence: The evidence or surrounding circumstances (for example rain or mud, dust or passers-by, internal bleeding, movement of the injured person, dragging of the body, or blood-stained earth recovered nearby or elsewhere) reasonably account for the absence of those traces.
predicates.absence_of_physical_traces_does_not_disc: The missing physical traces do not by themselves show that the prosecution misstated the place or time of occurrence or undermine its case.

definition: Where the prosecution's account of the occurrence is otherwise supported by evidence, the absence of blood, bullets or a blood trail at the alleged scene does not by itself defeat that account if the circumstances reasonably explain the absence. The physical evidence must be assessed in light of those explanations and the evidence as a whole.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where no reasonable explanation for the absence of traces is shown or found on the evidence.
Absence of traces is not decisive either way; the court must still assess the evidence as a whole, and the rule does not displace other grounds for doubting the prosecution case.
Where blood or traces are absent both at the occurrence site and nearby, the reasoning (as noted in one member) may not be available.

common_material_facts: Blood, bullets or a blood trail was missing at the alleged place of occurrence.
Courts identified circumstances explaining the absence, such as rain and mud, an unpaved dusty road, internal bleeding, the injured person moving, or dragging of the body.
Blood or related traces were found elsewhere or nearby (courtyard, bullets in the body, blood-stained earth).
statutes_and_provisions: No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on in the members that state this.
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the absence of physical traces was held not to undermine the prosecution account of the place or occurrence.
variations: One member is an appeal against conviction, one is a state appeal against acquittal, and one is a general criminal appeal.
One member concerns a claimed change of the place of occurrence, one concerns proof of time and place, and one concerns a missing blood trail.
The explanations differ: weather and movement of the victim, road conditions and internal bleeding, or dragging of the body with blood-stained earth recovered.
In the acquittal-appeal member the High Court's contrary treatment was held unsustainable.

legal_question: Does a mineral concession rule or royalty levy imposed under central law or delegated authority, regulating extraction of government-owned minerals, violate the constitutional guarantees of free trade and movement of trade (Articles 301 and 304(b))?

predicates.mineral_regulation_challenge_under_trade: The challenge is to a mineral concession rule or royalty levy on the ground that it violates the constitutional freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse (Articles 301 to 304).
predicates.measure_made_under_central_or_parliament: The rule or levy was made under a central or parliamentary enactment, or under authority delegated by it, and is not a State legislative imposition.
predicates.measure_is_regulatory_or_royalty_for_exc: The measure regulates mines and mineral development in the public interest, or is a royalty payable for the right to extract government-owned minerals for profit.
predicates.measure_does_not_directly_impede_interst: The measure does not directly and immediately impede the flow of trade between States, because quarrying does not itself move goods across States and any later outbound movement is not its direct consequence.
predicates.measure_does_not_violate_constitutional_: The measure does not violate the constitutional guarantee of free trade, commerce and intercourse, and the challenge fails.

definition: A mineral concession rule or royalty made under central or parliamentary authority to regulate mines or charge for the right to extract government-owned minerals does not offend the freedom of trade provisions. It is regulatory, is not a State-law restriction, and does not directly impede inter-State movement of trade.
exceptions_or_limits: The Article 304(b) reasoning applies only where the levy comes from central law; a State legislative imposition would fall within that provision.
The Article 301 reasoning depends on the measure being regulatory and not directly and immediately impeding trade movement.
A rule treated as law must be properly made under the delegating enactment.
The movement-of-trade reasoning depends on the finding that inter-State movement is not a direct consequence of quarrying.

common_material_facts: Challenge to a mining rule or royalty on quarrying or extraction of minerals
The measure was made under a central or parliamentary law, including delegated rules
Minerals were government-owned and extraction was regulated or paid for
Challenge based on constitutional freedom of trade and movement
statutes_and_provisions: Article 301
Article 302
Article 304(b)
Parliamentary mines and minerals regulation and development enactment and rules made under it
Atiabari Tea Co. v. State of Assam
Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All three members (3 of 3) reject the trade-freedom challenge to the mineral rule or royalty.
variations: One member relies on Articles 301 and 302 (regulatory measure, public interest).
One relies on Article 304(b) applying only to State legislation, plus the paid exclusive right to exploit government minerals.
One relies on the absence of a direct inter-State movement consequence from quarrying.

split_suggestion: Could be split into (a) regulatory rules under Articles 301/302 and central-law versus State-law under Article 304(b), and (b) the direct-movement-of-trade reasoning for quarrying royalties.

legal_question: Is an alienation of joint family or coparcenary property by its manager (father or karta) binding on the sons or other coparceners when it is not supported by legal necessity, benefit to the estate, or payment of an antecedent debt?

predicates.coparcenary_or_joint_family_property_ali: The father or karta sold or otherwise transferred property that was joint family or coparcenary property.
predicates.coparcener_son_has_interest_in_property_: The challenging son held an interest in the property, by birth, before the alienation was made.
predicates.alienation_supported_by_legal_necessity_: The alienation was made for legal necessity, for the benefit of the estate, or to discharge an antecedent debt.
predicates.alienee_proved_bona_fide_inquiry_into_ne: The alienee proved that he or she made proper and bona fide inquiries and took reasonable steps to satisfy himself or herself that legal necessity or benefit to the estate existed.
predicates.alienation_not_binding_on_son_and_invali: The alienation does not bind the son and is invalid, null and void, as to the coparcenary property, so that possession or cancellation may be granted.

definition: A manager of joint family or coparcenary property may alienate it only for legal necessity, benefit to the estate, or discharge of an antecedent debt. Otherwise, the alienation does not bind a son who holds an interest in the property, and it is invalid as to the coparcenary property, unless the alienee proves bona fide inquiry into necessity.
exceptions_or_limits: An alienation made before the son's birth cannot be challenged by the son on this basis.
The alienee bears the burden of proving necessity or benefit, or of showing proper bona fide inquiry into it.
Where the father was the sole surviving coparcener, the restriction applies only from the son's birth. The parties may pursue separate remedies for the share that would have fallen to the father.
The cluster does not state that a transfer is invalid where necessity, estate benefit or an antecedent debt is shown.
