common_material_facts: The father, as manager or karta, sold coparcenary or joint family property.
The son's interest in the property pre-dated the alienation.
No legal necessity, estate benefit or antecedent debt was established.
The alienee failed to prove necessity or bona fide inquiry, or no consideration was paid.
statutes_and_provisions: Mulla, Principles of Hindu Law (para 295 on antecedent debt, and general discussion)
Raja Brij Narain v. Mangala Prasad, AIR 1924 PC 50
Rani v. Santa Bala Debnath
Vijay A. Mittal v. Kulwant Rai
M. Yogendra v. Leelamma, (2009) 15 SCC 184
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members held the unsupported alienation not binding on the son or invalid. The remedies were possession decreed, sale deeds cancelled, or the deeds declared null and void as to the coparcenary property.
variations: One member turns on the absence of an antecedent debt and the sale being unconnected to the earlier loan.
One member stresses the alienee's burden of proving necessity or bona fide inquiry, and the payment of no consideration.
One member turns on the timing of the son's birth relative to the alienation, and reserves remedies for the father's notional share.

legal_question: Where a decree has been obtained against a Hindu father (as manager or ancestor) for a debt, how far can it be enforced against, or must it be challenged by the sons in respect of, their interests in joint family or partition property, and by what procedure?

predicates.decree_obtained_against_father_or_his_es: A money or mortgage decree has been passed against the father (as manager or ancestor) or against his estate in the hands of his legal representatives.
predicates.decree_is_executable_against_sons_intere: The decree can be executed against the sons' interest in joint family or partition property unless it is set aside or the sons successfully resist liability.
predicates.sons_dispute_binding_effect_or_liability: The sons contend that the decree or the debt does not bind their interest in the family property.
predicates.sons_dispute_must_be_raised_through_the_: The sons' objection must be dealt with in a procedure that addresses the decree's executability: within execution proceedings where they are representatives (no separate suit needed; court may marshal assets), or, if they sue for a declaration, as a suit with consequential relief attracting ad valorem court fee.

definition: Because a decree against a Hindu father can be executed against sons' interest in family property if the debt binds them, the sons' challenge is treated according to its substance: as representatives they contest liability in execution (and the court may order the father's property to be exhausted first), while a suit declaring the decree non-binding is in substance a suit for consequential relief and attracts ad valorem court fee.
exceptions_or_limits: Execution procedure does not create or enlarge the substantive Hindu-law liability of sons; property is reachable only if actually liable.
Execution against partition property without separate suit applies where sons were brought on record as legal representatives of the deceased father.
Marshalling (father's property first, then sons' ancestral property for balance) applies only if the sons are found liable and the father's property is insufficient.
Ad valorem fee for consequential relief applies where the decree remains executable against the claimants' interests unless set aside.

common_material_facts: Decree obtained against a Hindu father or his estate for a debt
Sons claim their share in joint family or partition property is not liable
Creditor seeks to execute the decree against property in which sons have interests
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 47, 52(1), 53 Code of Civil Procedure
Section 7(iv)(c) Court Fees Act
Sections 8 and 9 Suits Valuation Act
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All three members resolve the dispute by tying the sons' challenge to the decree's executability: two (1252014_3, 1252014_4) allow execution against sons' property with objections heard in execution and ordering of assets; one (431146_2) requires ad valorem fee for a declaration suit.
variations: Two members concern execution procedure against legal representatives; one concerns court fee on a declaratory suit.
1252014_4 addresses the order of resort to assets rather than whether a separate suit is needed.
431146_2 involves sons as plaintiffs challenging a decree, whereas the others involve sons as judgment-debtor representatives.

split_suggestion: Could be split into (a) execution against sons' property as legal representatives, including order of assets (1252014_3, 1252014_4) and (b) court fee for declaratory suits against decrees binding joint family property (431146_2).

legal_question: Is a land acquisition made for a specific beneficiary or company's project, whose cost is not met from public revenues or a local-authority fund, an acquisition for a company (requiring the company-acquisition procedure) even if the notification describes the purpose as public?

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The case concerns a compulsory acquisition of land under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
predicates.acquisition_for_identified_beneficiary_p: The acquisition is made for the specific project of an identified company or society, which sought or selected the land, as shown by the notification, the agreement or the official records, whatever public-purpose label the notification uses.
predicates.cost_not_met_from_qualifying_public_fund: The compensation is paid wholly by the beneficiary, or by funds that are not public revenues or a fund controlled or managed by a local authority, so the public-funding condition for a public-purpose acquisition is not met.
predicates.acquisition_is_for_a_company_and_company: The acquisition is classified as one for a company, and the statutory procedure for company acquisitions (agreement, inquiry and related rules) must be followed.

definition: Courts classify an acquisition by its substance, reading the notification fairly together with the agreement and the records. If it is made for an identified beneficiary's project and the cost is borne by the beneficiary rather than met from public revenues or a local-authority fund, it is an acquisition for a company. The company-acquisition procedure is then mandatory, whatever the notification calls the purpose.
exceptions_or_limits: An acquisition primarily for a company can still be for a public purpose where the statutory public-funding condition is met, wholly or partly from public revenues or a local-authority fund.
State contribution is not required in every company acquisition (291475_1).

The Supreme Court judges split in 168057026_1: one held the acquisition was for a company and invalid, the other held it was for a public purpose. That member therefore supports the rule only as the view of one judge, and the point was left without a common conclusion.
Pre-amendment authorities that treated company acquisitions as public purpose were distinguished in light of the 1984 amendment to Section 3(f).

common_material_facts: The notification or preliminary notice described the purpose as public, but the project was that of a specific society or company.
The beneficiary sought the land or selected the site, and an agreement or records tied the acquisition to its project.
The beneficiary bore the cost, or the cost was not met from public revenues or a local-authority fund.
The company-acquisition procedure was in issue, and in one case was not followed.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Section 3(e) and 3(f) (as amended in 1984)
Section 6(1), its proviso and Explanation 2
Sections 39–41 and Part VII
Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963, Rules 3–5
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 2 of 3 members (1252016_1, 291475_1) the acquisition was held to be for a company despite the public-purpose label. The third (168057026_1) was split between the judges, with Gowda J. holding it was for a company and Mishra J. holding it was for a public purpose.
variations: 1252016_1 and 291475_1 turned on the beneficiary paying all compensation under an agreement.
168057026_1 involved a State-owned corporation that raised the funds by loans, and the question was whether this counted as qualifying public funding.
The authorities relied on differ: Jhandu Lal and Somawanti were used as pre-amendment cases, and Pratibha Nema was treated as turning on the source of funds.

legal_question: Where a landlord's eviction claims under rent control legislation are affected by another eviction proceeding or another house (concurrent or separate proceedings, or a prior purchase and sale), does that circumstance bar or prejudice the landlord's bona fide need claim?

predicates.residential_eviction_proceeding_on_landl: The landlord seeks eviction of a tenant from a residential building under a rent control statute on the ground of the landlord's own need or another statutory ground tied to the landlord's residential position.
predicates.landlord_has_other_proceeding_or_prior_t: The tenant or the circumstances point to a concurrent eviction case against another tenant, a separate pending need-based petition, or a prior purchase and sale of another house, as a ground to bar or prejudice the claim.
predicates.bar_condition_actually_established: The statutory disqualification is actually made out on the facts, for example a true repeat application on the same ground, actual occupation or vacation of another suitable residence, or a sale intended to defeat the tenant's claim.
predicates.landlord_bona_fide_need_claim_not_barred: The landlord's need-based eviction claim is not barred, disqualified or prejudiced by the other proceeding or prior transaction, and may continue to be pursued on its merits.

definition: A landlord's need-based eviction claim is not barred or prejudiced by a concurrent or separate proceeding, or by a prior purchase and sale of another house, unless the statutory disqualification is actually established on the facts. Concurrent cases against separate tenants, dismissal of a different ground, or a sale of a non-vacant house without intent to defeat the tenant do not disqualify the landlord.
exceptions_or_limits: The outcome differs if the statutory disqualification is genuinely made out, for example a real fresh application on the same ground after failure, or the landlord actually occupies or has vacated another residential building.
A sale made with intent to defeat the tenant's claim or evade the statutory restriction would not be protected.
Preservation of the separate need-based claim only leaves the parties' rights open; it does not decide the merits of that claim.

common_material_facts: Landlord seeks eviction of a residential tenant on a need-based ground under a state rent control Act
Another proceeding or transaction (concurrent case, separate petition, other house) is invoked against or alongside the claim
No finding that the statutory disqualifying condition is actually met
statutes_and_provisions: Second proviso to section 13(3)(a), East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949
Section 13(3)(a)(i), Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the landlord's need-based claim survives: it is not barred as a repeat application (1), not disqualified by the prior sale (1), and not prejudiced by dismissal of a different ground (1).
variations: 1249629_4 concerns the repeat-application proviso and concurrent cases against separate tenants.
15535_6 concerns disqualification through the purchase and sale of another house and reads the statute reasonably.
1642416_2 is procedural: it preserves a separate pending need-based petition when only the other-residence ground is dismissed.

split_suggestion: If a tighter grouping is needed, separate 1249629_4 (repeat-application bar) and 15535_6 (other-house disqualification), which are substantive statutory-bar questions, from 1642416_2 (preservation of rights in a separate pending proceeding).

legal_question: Is an appeal maintainable under the Code of Civil Procedure where it is directed against an order or decree passed by consent of the parties, or otherwise against something that is not an appealable decree or order (such as a mere finding)?

rule.if: appeal_proceeding and (appeal_challenges_consent_order_or_decree or appeal_targets_only_a_finding) and not appeal_expressly_provided_by_statute

predicates.appeal_proceeding: A party has filed an appeal under the civil procedure code (or a writ appeal) to challenge a decision of a court.
predicates.appeal_challenges_consent_order_or_decre: The appeal is directed against an order or decree passed with the consent of the parties, with the court having recorded that consent or compromise.
predicates.appeal_targets_only_a_finding: The appeal is directed only against a finding recorded in the judgment and not against any decree or order for which an appeal is provided.
predicates.appeal_expressly_provided_by_statute: The Code or another statute expressly provides a right of appeal against the decree or order challenged (for example, an appeal from a contested decree under Section 96 or an appealable order under Order 43 Rule 1).
predicates.appeal_not_maintainable: The appeal cannot be entertained because it is barred or no right of appeal exists, and the court should dismiss it.

definition: The right of appeal exists only where a statute confers it. An appeal does not lie against a decree or order passed by consent (Section 96(3) CPC), where the recorded consent is not shown to be invalid, or against a mere finding that is not a decree or appealable order.
exceptions_or_limits: For a consent order, a party who says there was no valid compromise must show a proven basis to set aside the consent. Bare, late allegations that the compromise was unauthorised or that the court's record is false will not do, because a court's record of what happened before it cannot be contradicted on appeal.

The remedy against a consent decree lies before the court that recorded the compromise (proviso to Order 23 Rule 3), not by appeal. Order 23 Rule 3A also bars a separate suit to set aside a compromise decree on the ground that the compromise was unlawful.
The bar on appeal against a consent decree may be raised for the first time at the appellate stage because it goes to jurisdiction.
Where an appeal is also directed against a decree or an appealable order, it is not defeated merely because it also challenges a finding.

common_material_facts: The appellant used the appellate route to attack something that is not appealable under the Code.
In two members the order or decree was passed on the parties' recorded compromise or statements.
In one member the appeal was aimed only at a finding (that a partition was sham) and not at the preliminary decree.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 96(3) CPC
Sections 96, 100, 104(1) and 105(1) CPC
Order 43 Rule 1 CPC (including the deleted clause (m))
Order 23 Rules 3 and 3A CPC
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the appeal not maintainable. Two do so because of the Section 96(3) bar on appeals against consent decrees, and one because no appeal lies against a mere finding.
variations: Two members rest on the consent-decree bar and one on the absence of any decree or appealable order under challenged.
One member turns on a writ appeal and the court's recorded consent, with the contrary allegation raised late. Another sends the party to the court that recorded the compromise.
The finding-only member concerns the statutory nature of the right of appeal and does not involve consent.

split_suggestion: The cluster could be split into (a) appeals against consent orders or decrees (127110_2, 363952_1), governed by Section 96(3) and Order 23 Rule 3, and (b) appeals directed only at a finding (1350326_1), governed by the rule that an appeal lies only from a decree or an expressly appealable order.

legal_question: Does delay and laches bar a constitutional court (Article 226 or Article 32) from granting relief to a person whose property the State took without lawful process or compensation, where the deprivation is continuing and justice compellingly demands relief?

predicates.constitutional_relief_proceeding: The claimant seeks relief from a constitutional court under its writ or extraordinary jurisdiction (for example Article 226 or an appeal from a writ disposal).
predicates.state_took_private_property_without_lawf: The State or its authorities took or kept possession of private land without acquisition proceedings or any other process known to law, and the State admitted this or could not show consent or valid acquisition.
predicates.compensation_unpaid_and_deprivation_cont: The owner has not been compensated and the unlawful deprivation continues, so the cause of action is treated as continuing.
predicates.compelling_demand_for_justice: The circumstances make refusal of relief unjust, for example the owner is illiterate or vulnerable, the State's conduct perpetuated the injustice, and no third-party interest is affected.
predicates.delay_and_laches_do_not_bar_relief: The court should not reject the claim on the ground of delay or laches and may grant constitutional relief.

definition: Where the State has taken private property without authority of law and without compensation, the deprivation is continuing, and the demand for justice is compelling, a constitutional court will not refuse relief for delay and laches. Laches is an equitable doctrine applied by balancing the circumstances, not a rigid limitation bar.
exceptions_or_limits: Delay is not irrelevant. The court weighs the length of delay, the reason for it, the conduct of the parties in the interval and the nature of the right breached.
The members stress that no third-party interest was identified; intervening third-party rights could weigh against relief.
The relief is discretionary and equitable; the rule applies where the claim is legally sustainable and the cause of action is continuing.
The rule does not remove the State's ability to show lawful acquisition, valid consent or compensation.

common_material_facts: State took land without acquisition proceedings or payment of compensation
Owners approached the court after a long delay
Owners were illiterate or vulnerable and remained uncompensated
State admitted the taking or could not substantiate its claim of consent or acquisition
High Court or State relied on delay or disputed facts to refuse relief
statutes_and_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution
Article 300-A of the Constitution
Article 31 of the Constitution (as applicable at the time)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the court rejected the delay-and-laches objection and allowed constitutional relief.
variations: One member stresses the shock to the judicial conscience and the absence of any prescribed limitation period.
One member emphasises that the State compensated some similarly placed owners only after they sued, and that its alleged consent was unproved.
One member stresses the owners' repeated efforts, the lapsed later acquisition, and the absence of third-party interest.
The members cite different supporting authorities, but all rely on Sadasivaswamy-type reasoning.

legal_question: Does a statutory scheme regulating public charitable and religious institutions and endowments apply to private endowments, trusts or gifts, or only to public ones?

predicates.statute_regulates_religious_or_charitabl: The enactment relied on is a scheme for regulating, supervising or administering religious or charitable endowments or trusts, whose scope turns on whether they are public.
predicates.property_or_trust_is_private_not_public: The property, endowment or trust is found to be private, for example an absolute gift to an individual, a private temple, a family-idol endowment, or a trust with definite and ascertainable beneficiaries.
predicates.private_gift_or_definite_ascertainable_b: The private character rests on an absolute private gift, on beneficiaries who are definite individuals, or on worship of a family idol in which the public has no interest.
predicates.public_dedication_or_public_interest_est: It is established that the property or trust was dedicated to the public, or that an uncertain and fluctuating body of people (the public or a section of it) has a beneficial interest. Long public use alone, such as use as a dharamshala, does not establish this.
predicates.regulatory_statute_not_applicable_to_pro: The regulatory statute does not apply to the property or trust, and its provisions cannot be invoked against it.

definition: Statutes regulating religious and charitable endowments and trusts apply only to public endowments and trusts, and do not reach private endowments, private trusts or absolute private gifts. Private character is shown by definite beneficiaries or an absolute gift, and mere long public use does not establish public dedication.
exceptions_or_limits: The exclusion applies only if the endowment is in fact private. Where the endowment is found to be public, as in one member, the exclusion does not prevent proceedings under the Act.
Public character is not established merely by long use of the premises by the public, for example as a dharamshala; dedication to the public must be shown.
A religious group or sect may itself constitute the relevant public, so a trust for it may be public.
The scope of each statute depends on its own definitions and provisions, as construed in light of its purpose and legislative history.

common_material_facts: A statute regulating religious or charitable trusts or endowments is invoked against property said to be private.
The dispute turns on classifying the endowment or trust as public or private.
Features indicating a private character include an absolute gift deed, a private temple, a family idol and definite beneficiaries.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 1(3), Andhra Pradesh Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987

Sections 2(1), 4(5), 29, 30, 32 and 48 of the religious trusts Act, together with the Religious Endowments Act 1863, the Charitable Endowments Act 1890, the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act 1920 and section 92 CPC
The Act regulating Hindu religious trusts, as applied in Mahant Ram Saroop Dasji v. S. P. Sahi, which excludes private endowments
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the regulatory Act is held to apply only to public endowments or trusts. In 2 members it is held inapplicable because the property or trust was private. In 1 member the endowment was found public, so the private-endowment exclusion did not help the respondent.
variations: One member rests on a finding of an absolute private gift and a private temple, and rejects dharamshala use as proof of dedication.
One member decides by interpreting the statutory definition and structure against Hindu-law concepts of public and private trusts.
One member states the rule that private endowments are excluded but finds on the facts that the endowment was public.

legal_question: Will a court reviewing a disciplinary punishment direct or refer it for upward revision or further enhancement where the penalty has already been imposed by the disciplinary authority?

predicates.disciplinary_punishment_review: The court is examining the quantum or adequacy of a punishment imposed in disciplinary proceedings.
predicates.penalty_already_imposed_by_disciplinary_: The disciplinary authority has already found misconduct and imposed a penalty, whether minor (such as censure) or major.
predicates.no_wednesbury_violation_shown: The choice of penalty is not shown to be arbitrary, irrational or shockingly disproportionate under Wednesbury principles, including where the authority weighed mitigating circumstances or a mixed record of reports and advice.
predicates.reduction_challenge_pending_before_tribu: The officer's challenge seeking reduction of an already imposed major penalty is pending before the competent administrative tribunal.
predicates.court_declines_upward_revision_or_enhanc: The court declines to refer the punishment for upward revision or to enhance it further, leaving any pending challenge to be decided by the tribunal in accordance with law.

definition: A court reviewing disciplinary punishment applies only a secondary Wednesbury review and will not substitute a harsher penalty for the one the disciplinary authority chose unless a reviewable defect is shown. It also will not further enhance an already major penalty while the officer's challenge to it is pending before the tribunal.
exceptions_or_limits: Upward revision may be warranted if the penalty chosen is shown to be arbitrary or shockingly disproportionate, i.e. to violate Wednesbury principles.
The pending-tribunal ground applies where the penalty is already major and the officer's challenge to it is pending; the court then leaves the matter to the tribunal.
Where an earlier direction limited the permissible punishment to a minor one, the choice is confined to that range.

common_material_facts: Misconduct had been found and a penalty (minor or major) imposed by the disciplinary authority in the same proceedings.
The authority considered a mixed record of inquiry or commission reports and public service commission advice.
The court was asked to refer the punishment for upward revision or enhancement.
statutes_and_provisions: Wednesbury principles of unreasonableness
Union of India v. Ganayutham
B.C. Chaturvedi v. Union of India
Ranjit Thakur v. Union of India
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the court declined upward revision or further enhancement. Two did so because no Wednesbury violation was shown, and one because a challenge to the major penalty was pending before the tribunal.
variations: One member involves a minor penalty (censure) and the other two involve major penalties.
Two members rest on Wednesbury review of the authority's decision; one rests on deference to the pending tribunal proceeding without a merits analysis.
The minor-penalty member also relied on mitigating circumstances and an earlier direction limiting the penalty to a minor one.

legal_question: Does a State infringe a fundamental right (so as to support a petition under Article 32) when it refuses to honour or stops performance of a private contract, licence or grant, where the claimant holds no enforceable property interest against the State and the State has not acquired or taken possession of the contractual right?

predicates.fundamental_rights_enforcement_petition: The claimant seeks to enforce fundamental rights (e.g., under Articles 19(1)(f), 19(1)(g) or 31) by a petition under Article 32.
predicates.claimant_right_is_only_contractual_or_li: The claimant's right rests only on a personal contract, a licence, or a transfer or grant that is legally ineffective (e.g., oral or unregistered) so that no proprietary interest passed.
predicates.state_did_not_acquire_or_take_possession: The State merely declined to recognise or be bound by the contract or licence and did not acquire it, take possession of it, or claim its benefits or payments.
predicates.no_enforceable_property_interest_survive: Under any available construction of the instrument, the claimant has no property interest enforceable against the State, because it was ineffective for want of formality or registration, vested in the State, or ended with the grantor's title.
predicates.no_fundamental_right_infringement_suppor: The State's action does not infringe any fundamental right of the claimant in a way that supports relief under Article 32, so the petition fails and any remedy lies in an ordinary civil suit, if available.

definition: A State's mere refusal to recognise or be bound by a private contract, licence or ineffective grant, without acquiring or taking possession of it or claiming its benefits, does not infringe a fundamental right. Where no enforceable property interest exists against the State, Article 32 relief is unavailable and the claimant's remedy, if any, is an ordinary suit.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule depends on the right being merely contractual, licence-based or ineffectively transferred; a valid proprietary interest that the State actually takes or interferes with could support a fundamental-rights claim.
If the State acquires, takes possession of or claims the benefit of the contract or licence, the conclusion may differ.
The dismissal does not bar a civil suit for breach of contract, where such a remedy is available.
In the abolition-of-proprietary-rights context, a licence ends when the licensor's title is extinguished.

common_material_facts: Claimants relied on private agreements, licences or grants made by former proprietors or by the earlier holders of the rights.
The State refused to recognise the arrangement or stopped its performance after its own legislation or action.
The instruments were oral, unregistered, or only contractual or licence-based.
The State did not take over the contracts or claim their benefits.
The petition was brought directly under Article 32.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 32
Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(1)(g)
Article 31(1)
Registration Act (unregistered instruments do not transfer interests in immovable property)
Section 3, Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950
Ananda Behera v. State of Orissa
Shrimathi Shantabai v. State of Bombay
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that there is no fundamental-rights infringement and dismiss or deny Article 32 relief. The claimant is left to any civil remedy.
variations: One member (12663_5) rests on the State's non-acquisition of merely contractual or licence rights under abolition legislation.
Another (148933_3) adds that oral transfers conferred no title, and assumes arguendo that a contract is property.

The third (963790_1) analyses alternative constructions of an unregistered forest grant (proprietary interest, profit à prendre, licence, personal contract) and reaches the same result on each. It declines to follow Chhotabai Jethabai Patel.

legal_question: Does Article 31A(1)(e) protect a law that terminates, modifies, restricts or curtails rights under a mining lease from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31?

predicates.law_affects_rights_under_mining_lease_or: The challenged law, rule or notice operates on rights held under a mining lease, agreement or licence.
predicates.lease_concerns_searching_for_or_winning_: The lease or licence is for searching for or winning minerals, with 'winning' read broadly as getting or extracting minerals and purposes incidental to that, not narrowly as preparing a mine for working.
predicates.law_terminates_or_modifies_or_restricts_: The law provides for premature termination, or modification (including alteration, limitation or restriction, even if temporary) of the lease rights.
predicates.law_protected_from_challenge_under_artic: The law cannot be challenged as invalid on the ground that it infringes the rights conferred by Articles 14, 19 or 31.

definition: Article 31A(1)(e) shields a law that terminates or modifies (including by altering, limiting or temporarily restricting) rights under a lease or licence for searching for or winning minerals from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31. 'Winning' is read in its broad popular sense of extracting minerals and acts incidental to extraction.
exceptions_or_limits: Protection applies only where the lease or licence is for searching for or winning minerals.
Protection is against challenge on the specified fundamental rights grounds (Articles 14, 19, 31), not on every ground.
Statutory definitions of 'win' in other enactments or rules do not control the meaning of the constitutional expression.
The point on premature termination (1291977_3) was decided only in the dissent; the majority left it undecided.

common_material_facts: Challenge to a mining statute, rule or notice affecting mineral lease rights
Lease authorised extraction or removal of minerals (e.g. mine, white clay)
Law terminated, modified or temporarily restricted lease rights
Challenge based on Articles 14, 19 or 31
statutes_and_provisions: Article 31A(1)(e), Constitution of India
Articles 14, 19, 31 and 31(2)
Section 3(d), Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957
Lewis v. Fothergill and Lord Rokeby v. Elliot (distinguished)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the law was held protected by Article 31A(1)(e) and the fundamental-rights challenge failed or was barred; in one (1291977_3) this was the dissent's view, with the majority not deciding the point.
variations: 1291977_3 concerns premature termination, 1690233_2 modification of duration and royalty, and 516439_5 a temporary restriction.
1690233_2 and 1291977_3 turn on the meaning of 'winning', while 516439_5 turns on the meaning of 'modification'.
1291977_3 is a dissent, the other two are holdings of the court.

legal_question: Does an internal file notation or inter-departmental or departmental communication count as a binding government order or decision affecting rights when it has not been finalised, communicated, or expressed and authenticated as the Constitution requires for executive action?

predicates.internal_or_departmental_communication_r: A file notation, inter-departmental communication or departmental letter is relied on as if it were a decision, order or policy of the Government.
predicates.formally_expressed_and_authenticated_as_: The communication was expressed in the name of the President or Governor and authenticated in the prescribed manner as required for executive action (Arts. 77 and 166).
predicates.finalised_and_communicated_to_affected_p: The decision was finally taken and communicated to the person affected by it.
predicates.communication_is_not_a_binding_governmen: The communication is not a government order or decision and cannot be relied on to affect rights, support a finding of deficiency, or be treated as government policy.

definition: A file noting, inter-departmental communication or departmental letter records only an official's opinion or part of the decision-making process. It is not a binding government order or policy unless it is finalised and communicated, or expressed and authenticated as required by Articles 77 and 166. Without these features it cannot affect rights or be treated as a government decision.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule concerns whether a document counts as a government order. It does not decide the merits of the underlying claim.
A communication that is properly expressed in the name of the President or Governor and authenticated, or that is finally decided and communicated, may be treated as a government order.

Members differ on the test: one relies on lack of finalisation and communication, the others on non-compliance with Articles 77 and 166. The rule is stated disjunctively on the negative conditions as a simplification.
Article 166(3) concerns rules for the transaction of government business and is not itself the source of the authentication requirement.

common_material_facts: A lower forum or High Court treated an internal note or departmental communication as a government decision.
The communication recorded a recommendation, opinion or committee proposal, not a final government order.
There was no showing of formal expression, authentication, approval or communication to the affected party.
statutes_and_provisions: Constitution of India, Articles 77(1) and 77(2)
Constitution of India, Articles 166(1), 166(2) and 166(3)
State of Punjab v. Sodhi Sukhdev Singh
Bachhittar Singh v. State of Punjab
State of Bihar v. Kripalu Shankar (1987) 3 SCC 34
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the communication or notation is not a binding government order or policy decision.
variations: One member (consumer dispute) rests on an internal notation that was never finalised or communicated, without invoking the Articles.
Two members rest on the constitutional requirement of expression in the Governor's or President's name and authentication.
The contexts differ: deficiency in service, a compensation recommendation rejected by the Government, and a policy on regularising constructions on acquired land.

legal_question: Does an appeal against an award or order determining compensation for compulsorily acquired or requisitioned property attract ad valorem court fee, computed by comparing the amount awarded with the amount claimed, rather than a fixed residuary fee?

predicates.appeal_concerns_compensation_award_for_a: The appeal challenges an arbitrator's or similar statutory authority's award or order determining compensation for property acquired or requisitioned for a public purpose.
predicates.compensation_claimed_differs_from_amount: The appellant claims a higher or different amount of compensation than the amount awarded, so that a difference is in dispute in the appeal.
predicates.court_fee_law_computes_fee_on_difference: The applicable court-fee statute provides that the fee on an appeal against an order relating to acquisition compensation is computed by comparing the amount awarded with the amount claimed.
predicates.ad_valorem_court_fee_applies_and_fixed_r: Court fee is payable ad valorem under the general schedule on the disputed difference, and the fixed-fee residuary provision is not attracted.

definition: Where an appeal challenges a statutory award or order fixing compensation for acquired or requisitioned property and the court-fee statute computes the fee by comparing the amount awarded with the amount claimed, the fee is ad valorem on the difference and not a fixed residuary fee. The order under appeal need not have the force of a decree.
exceptions_or_limits: Applies only where the applicable court-fee statute contains a computation provision comparing the amount awarded with the amount claimed.
The computation provision is not itself a charging provision; the ad valorem charge comes from the general schedule.
The rule rests on the award being an order under the statute; no additional requirement that it have the force of a decree is imposed.

outlier_members.reason: It does not concern court fees. It is a fact-specific disposition upholding acquisitions on public-interest grounds, subject to revised compensation and payment conditions, without deciding the legality of the findings under appeal.

common_material_facts: Appeal against an arbitrator's or statutory authority's compensation award for acquired or requisitioned property
The claimant sought more than the amount awarded
The court-fee statute compared the amount awarded with the amount claimed
statutes_and_provisions: Section 7(1) of the Bombay Court-fee Act, 1959, with Schedules I and II
Section 51 of the Tamil Nadu Court Fees and Suits Valuation Act, 1955, with Article 1 of Schedule I and Article 3(iii)(A)(1)(a) of Schedule II
Section 11 of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Ad valorem court fee was held payable in both court-fee members (2 of 2), and the fixed residuary fee was rejected. The third member is unrelated.
variations: One member stresses that the provision is a computation provision and that the order need not have the force of a decree, relying on Anandalal Chakrabarti.
The other member relies on the broad meaning of acquisition and on the arbitrator's award being an order, following Sahadu Gangaram Bhagade.
The Bombay-based member involved a cross-objection, while the Tamil Nadu-based member involved requisitioning under the 1952 Act.

split_suggestion: Separate 1581873_1, which is a discretionary, fact-specific disposition of land-acquisition appeals, from the two court-fee members, 1293751_2 and 1896732_3, which form a coherent group.

legal_question: When property is sold at a compulsory (execution or revenue) sale, does the purchaser acquire only the interest actually put up for sale, as defined by the sale and its notification, and not the wider rights or interests that were not sold?

predicates.compulsory_sale_purchase: The claimant bought property or an interest in it at an execution sale or a revenue sale.
predicates.purchaser_acquires_only_the_interest_act: The interest that passed is limited to what was actually put up for sale, as fixed by the judgment-debtors' interests sold, the nature of the undivided interest, or the statutory sale notification.
predicates.claimed_right_or_interest_exceeds_intere: The purchaser claims something beyond the interest sold, such as the share of a coparcener whose interest was not sold, income or possession of a specific portion before partition allots it, or the privileges of a purchaser of an entire estate when only separate shares were sold.
predicates.purchaser_cannot_claim_the_additional_ri: The court rejects the claim to the excess right, share, possession or privilege, and the purchaser is confined to what was actually sold and to the remedies that go with it.

definition: A purchaser at an execution or revenue sale takes only what was actually sold, as defined by the sale proceedings, the nature of the interest or the statutory notification. The purchaser cannot claim the share of a coparcener whose interest was not sold, possession or profits of an undivided interest before partition allots a specific portion, or the privileges of a purchaser of an entire estate when only separate shares were sold.
exceptions_or_limits: In the revenue-sale context, the purchaser obtains entire-estate privileges only if the separate accounts were closed or merged into one demand and a fresh notification for the entire estate was issued.
An undivided-interest purchaser may work out his rights through a partition suit, and possession begins only when a specific allotment is made.
The members rest on different statutory and doctrinal grounds: general sale law and coparcenary rights for the execution sales, and the Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act, 1859 for the revenue sale.

common_material_facts: The property or interest was sold in a compulsory sale (execution or revenue).
The purchaser claimed more than what was actually sold: an additional coparcener's share, a share of income or possession before partition, or entire-estate privileges.
The sold interest was either partial, undivided or separately notified.
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 6, 13, 14 and 37 of the Bengal Land Revenue Sales Act, 1859 (971934_1)
Execution-sale and partition principles for coparcenary interests (1297847_3, 94289_2), with no specific provision cited
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the purchaser's expanded claim was rejected and he was confined to the interest actually sold.
variations: 1297847_3 concerns the quantum of the share, which was two-thirds rather than four-fifths because a coparcener's interest was not sold.
94289_2 concerns the timing of possession and profits before partition.
971934_1 concerns the character of a revenue sale (separate shares versus the entire estate) and the resulting privilege to annul under-tenures.
Only 971934_1 relies on earlier decisions and statutory sections; the other two cite no earlier case.

split_suggestion: If a tighter grouping is wanted, separate the two execution-sale coparcenary members (1297847_3, 94289_2) from the revenue-sale entire-estate member (971934_1), which turns on statutory notification.

legal_question: Where a Hindu widow holds her husband's property only as a limited (life) estate holder, what are the reversioners' rights on her death, and can her will, her negligence or possession adverse to her limited estate defeat or diminish those rights?

rule.if: property_inherited_by_widow_as_limited_estate and reversioner_claims_after_widow_death and not wilful_waste_established and not alienation_for_necessity_or_power_of_disposal_established

predicates.property_inherited_by_widow_as_limited_e: The disputed property was inherited by a Hindu widow from her husband and held only as a limited (life) estate, without absolute ownership.
predicates.reversioner_claims_after_widow_death: The claim is made by the reversioners (the persons entitled to succeed to the husband's estate) after the limited estate holder has died.
predicates.wilful_waste_established: The facts pleaded and proved show wilful waste of the estate by the widow, as distinct from mere negligence or loss.
predicates.alienation_for_necessity_or_power_of_dis: It is shown that the widow had power to devise or dispose of the property, or that a legal necessity supported the alienation.
predicates.reversioners_entitled_to_property_left_a: The reversioners succeed to whatever remains of the husband's estate at the widow's death. Her will, her negligence, and possession adverse during her lifetime do not defeat that right, and no compensation is recoverable from her separate property.

definition: A Hindu widow with a limited estate in her husband's property cannot pass it by will, and her negligence or sufferance does not prejudice the reversioners. The reversioners, whose interest is a mere spes successionis during her life, take the property left at her death. Their claim is not defeated by adverse possession attributable to the widow's conduct if brought within limitation after her death. They cannot obtain compensation from her separate property for loss absent wilful waste.
exceptions_or_limits: If the widow had power to devise or alienate, or a legal necessity for the alienation is proved, the outcome may differ.
If the beneficiary of the will had been proved to be an adopted son and so the sole reversioner, he would succeed as reversioner (noted in 1301243_4).
A claim based on wilful waste needs specific allegations and is a separate matter, such as a suit to prevent waste during the widow's lifetime.
The reversioner's claim must be brought within the limitation period (twelve years after the widow's death under Article 141 of the Limitation Act, 1908).
The reversioner's right is only a spes successionis during the widow's lifetime. It gives no right to compensation for loss from her separate property.

common_material_facts: Property inherited by a Hindu widow from her husband as a limited estate holder
Dispute between the widow's transferee, devisee or successor and the reversioners
Claim arising after or in view of the widow's death
No proof of necessity, wilful waste or adoption supporting the opposing claim
statutes_and_provisions: Article 141 of the Limitation Act, 1908
Hindu law of the widow's limited estate and reversioners (spes successionis)
Kalipada Chakraborti v. Palani Bala Devi
Mulla's Hindu Law
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the reversioners' position is protected: they take the husband's estate or what remains at the widow's death. The widow's will (1301243_4) and adverse possession (998380_4) do not defeat their claim. Compensation for loss is limited absent wilful waste (456049_2).
variations: 1301243_4 concerns a will by the widow and the failure to prove an adoption.
456049_2 concerns a reversioner's claim for compensation for loss from the widow's negligence (revenue sale), which is denied.
998380_4 concerns limitation and adverse possession against the reversioners.
In 1301243_4 and 998380_4 the reversioners recover the property. In 456049_2 they are limited to what remains and receive no compensation.

legal_question: Where a preliminary mortgage decree for sale has been passed, what is the effect of a later event (confirmation of the decree on appeal, or expiry of the time to apply for a final decree) on the time fixed for payment, the mortgagee's underlying rights, and independent rights such as a rent-note right to possession?

rule.if: preliminary_mortgage_decree_passed and procedural_event_after_preliminary_decree and not express_extension_or_merger_of_rights

predicates.preliminary_mortgage_decree_passed: A preliminary decree has been passed in a mortgage suit under Order XXXIV of the Code of Civil Procedure.
predicates.procedural_event_after_preliminary_decre: A later procedural event has occurred, such as appellate confirmation of the preliminary decree after a final decree was passed, or expiry of the time to apply for a final decree for sale.
predicates.express_extension_or_merger_of_rights: The appellate court expressly extended the payment time, or the law provides that the mortgagee's rights merge into or are extinguished by the decree or by limitation.
predicates.existing_decree_terms_and_independent_ri: The time originally fixed for payment is not restarted, and the mortgage security, the mortgagor's right to redeem and any independent right (e.g. under a rent note) continue. Only the specific remedy barred by limitation, namely recovery by sale, is lost.

definition: A later procedural event after a preliminary mortgage decree does not by itself change the decree's terms or destroy the mortgagee's other rights. Confirmation on appeal does not extend the payment time without an indication to that effect. Expiry of the time for a final decree bars only the sale remedy, leaving the security, the right to redeem and independent possession rights under a rent note intact.
exceptions_or_limits: If the appellate court expressly extends the time for payment, the original deadline does not remain in force.
Loss of the time to apply for a final decree still bars recovery of the mortgage money by sale.

An independent right to possession survives only if it is genuinely continuing and independent of the mortgage; Section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908 extinguishes a right to property when the period for a possession suit on that right has expired.
The first member concerns a final decree already passed before the appeal was decided; the other two concern the time-barred final decree application.

common_material_facts: A preliminary decree for sale in a mortgage suit had been passed
A subsequent procedural or limitation event occurred (appellate confirmation, or expiry of time for a final decree)
The question was whether that event altered the decree's terms or extinguished the mortgagee's rights
statutes_and_provisions: Order XXXIV, Code of Civil Procedure
Section 28, Limitation Act, 1908
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the preliminary decree's terms and the mortgagee's rights are not altered or extinguished by the later event, except that the sale remedy is lost on limitation.
variations: One member concerns the payment deadline after appellate confirmation.
One concerns merger of the mortgage rights into the preliminary decree and the loss of the sale remedy.
One concerns survival of a separate rent-note possession right under Section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908.

split_suggestion: If a tighter grouping is needed, separate the appellate-confirmation and payment-time issue (1305048_3) from the two members on the effect of the time-barred final decree application (1447819_2 and 1447819_3). Those two could be split further into mortgage-security survival and independent rent-note possession rights.

legal_question: Does Union legislative control or regulation of an industry or mining activity (or a central levy on its product) displace a State's separate power to tax land, buildings or mineral rights, absent a parliamentary limitation on State taxation or a shown conflict with the central scheme?

rule.if: challenge_to_state_levy_on_land_or_mineral_rights and state_levy_falls_within_state_taxation_entry and central_law_controls_or_regulates_industry and not central_law_limits_state_taxation and not levy_impedes_central_scheme

predicates.challenge_to_state_levy_on_land_or_miner: The validity of a State or local levy on land, buildings, or mineral rights is challenged on the ground that the Union has legislated on or controls the industry or activity concerned.
predicates.state_levy_falls_within_state_taxation_e: On a pith-and-substance analysis, the true subject of the levy is land, buildings or mineral rights, a head assigned to the States (for example Entries 49 or 50 of List II), even if the burden is measured by produce or falls on an industry.
predicates.central_law_controls_or_regulates_indust: Parliament has enacted a law controlling or regulating the industry or activity (and possibly imposing its own central levy), with or without a declaration of Union control in the public interest.
predicates.central_law_limits_state_taxation: The central law, or a parliamentary limitation on State taxation, actually restricts or bars the State from imposing the levy in question.
predicates.levy_impedes_central_scheme: The levy is shown to interfere with or defeat the objectives of the central regulatory scheme, or it is in substance a levy on the central subject.
predicates.state_taxing_power_not_displaced: The State (or authorised local body) retains competence to impose the levy, and the central control or central levy does not invalidate it.

definition: Union control or regulation of an industry, or a distinct central levy on its product, does not by itself oust a State's power to tax land, buildings or mineral rights. The power to regulate is distinct from the power to tax, so the State levy stands unless Parliament has limited State taxation or the levy is shown to impede the central scheme.
exceptions_or_limits: The State levy is displaced if Parliament has, by a law within its competence, expressly limited State taxation in the field, as the Union may do to the extent provided by a declaration such as that in section 2 of the mining statute.
The levy is not protected if, in pith and substance, it is a tax on the central subject (for example a general tax on minerals or on the product itself) rather than on land or mineral rights.
The levy is not protected if it is shown to impede or defeat the objectives of the central legislation; the members note that no such impediment was shown.

common_material_facts: A State or local levy was imposed on land, buildings or mineral-bearing land and was challenged as encroaching on a central field.
Central legislation controlled or regulated the industry concerned (tea or mining) and in some cases itself imposed a central levy or made a declaration of Union control.
No parliamentary limitation on State taxation, and no impediment to the central scheme, was shown.
statutes_and_provisions: Entries 49 and 50 of List II (and Entry 5 of List II for municipal functions)
Entries 52 and 54 of List I and other relevant Union entries
Articles 245, 246 and 248
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (Sections 2, 13, 18, 25)
Coal Mines Nationalisation Act, 1973
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members uphold the State's or local authority's taxing power against the claim of displacement by central control.
variations: One member concerns a central excise cess on tea and a State land cess measured by green-leaf yield.
One member concerns a municipal tax on lands and buildings used for coal mines and relies on the absence of any shown impediment to the central scheme.

One member concerns State levies on mineral rights and mineral-bearing land and relies on the absence of a parliamentary tax limitation, and distinguishes cases such as India Cement and Orissa Cement.

legal_question: Can an agriculturist debtor obtain scaling down, under the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act 1938 as amended in 1948, of a decree (including a compromise decree) that had not been executed or satisfied in full when the amending law commenced?

rule.if: debt_scaling_application and decree_not_executed_or_fully_satisfied_when_amending_law_commenced and debtor_is_eligible_agriculturist and not legal_bar_to_scaling

predicates.debt_scaling_application: The debtor has applied to the court to scale down a decretal debt under the debt-relief law as amended.
predicates.decree_not_executed_or_fully_satisfied_w: The decree, whether passed after contest or by compromise, had not been executed or satisfied in full when the amending law came into force.
predicates.debtor_is_eligible_agriculturist: The debtor qualifies as an agriculturist under the Act, for example because the assessment attributable to the debtor is below the disqualifying limit, and has established this.
predicates.legal_bar_to_scaling: A legally sufficient bar, such as res judicata from a prior judicial determination of the debtor's entitlement or a pleaded and proved estoppel, prevents the claim.
predicates.decree_is_subject_to_scaling_down_and_de: The decree falls within the amended law and the debtor is entitled to have it scaled down, without refunding sums already paid or realised.

definition: Under sections 19(2) and 16(iii) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938 as amended in 1948, a decree (contested or by compromise) that remained unexecuted or not fully satisfied when the amendment commenced can be scaled down at the instance of a debtor who proves he is an agriculturist, unless a legal bar applies. Amounts already paid or realised are not refundable.
exceptions_or_limits: The debtor must prove agriculturist status; the court must determine eligibility before relief is granted.
Relief is unavailable where a legal bar exists, such as res judicata or a properly pleaded and tried estoppel; a compromise by itself is not such a bar.
Sums already paid or realised under the decree are protected by the proviso and need not be refunded.
Decrees fully satisfied before the amending law commenced are outside the rule.

common_material_facts: Decree not executed or satisfied in full when the amending law commenced
Debtor applied to scale down the decretal debt
Agriculturist status of the debtor was in issue or established
Decree passed by compromise or after contest
statutes_and_provisions: Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, s. 19(2)
s. 16(iii) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief (Amendment) Act, 1948 (Madras Act 23 of 1948)
s. 3(ii) of the 1938 Act (agriculturist definition)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members allow scaling down or consideration of it for a qualifying agriculturist; 1 remits eligibility for determination, 2 uphold scaling down.
variations: One member concerns a decree passed after the principal Act and treats decretal debt as 'debt', leaving agriculturist status to be proved.
One member concerns whether a compromise decree is treated differently from a contested decree, holding it is not.
One member addresses agriculturist status by share-wise assessment and rejects res judicata or estoppel bars.

legal_question: Can a conviction for forgery or for abetting forgery of a property document be sustained where the evidence shows that the accused assisted in procuring, executing, identifying or using the forged document, even if the person who physically forged it is not identified or the accused claims an innocent mistake?

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_forgery_related_: The matter is an appeal against a conviction for forgery or abetment of forgery (with or without cheating) in relation to a document.
predicates.evidence_establishes_document_was_forged: The evidence shows that the document was forged, for example executed by someone impersonating the real owner or a dead person, or bearing a thumb impression that was not the purported executant's.
predicates.evidence_establishes_accused_participate: The evidence shows that the accused executed the forged document, or assisted, arranged, identified the impersonator, procured or used the document, so that the accused's role as principal or abettor is made out.
predicates.accused_innocent_explanation_supported_b: The accused's claim of honest mistake or genuine execution is backed by evidence that raises a reasonable doubt.
predicates.forgery_or_abetment_conviction_sustained: The conviction for forgery or abetment of forgery is upheld, or an acquittal on the abetment charge is set aside and a conviction entered, and the appeal fails to that extent.

definition: A conviction for forgery or abetment of forgery stands where the evidence shows the document was forged by impersonation and the accused took part in or assisted the forgery, for example by executing, arranging, identifying the impostor or procuring or using the deed. The physical forger need not be identified, and an unsupported claim of innocent mistake does not defeat the conviction.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply if the accused's innocent explanation is supported by evidence that raises a reasonable doubt.
The accused's own role must be established by the evidence; mere presence or a connection to the document is not enough.
In one member the first accused had been acquitted by the High Court on a procedural ground, and the Supreme Court set that aside on the evidence.
Where the appellate court agrees with the trial court's appreciation of the evidence, it need not repeat the reasons already given.

common_material_facts: A property document (sale deed or mortgage deed) was executed through impersonation of the real owner or a dead person.
The accused identified the impostor, arranged the transaction, or obtained and used the deed.
The accused's defence of genuine execution or honest mistake was unsupported by evidence.
The convictions were concurrent or were affirmed on appeal.
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Penal Code Sections 467, 465, 114, 109, 417
Registration Act Sections 34(3) and 35(1)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members sustain the convictions for forgery or abetment of forgery. One also sets aside an acquittal and convicts the first accused of abetment, and one dismisses the appeal against concurrent findings.
variations: One member convicts the executing impersonator as principal and the arranging accused as abettor; the other two concern abettors only.
One member relies on the registering officer's duty to verify identity under the Registration Act.
One member relies on fingerprint expert evidence and the complainant's denial, and notes that the physical forger was not identified.
Only one member invokes the doctrine that an appellate court need not repeat the trial court's reasons.
The offences charged differ: Sections 467 with 114, Sections 467 and 417 with 109, and Sections 465 with 109.

legal_question: When may an appellate court (including the Supreme Court in its discretionary jurisdiction) decline to disturb a lower court's discretionary reduction of a sentence or an interest rate, because the reduction is reasonable on the circumstances of the case?

predicates.appeal_challenges_lower_court_reduction: The appeal is brought by a party (e.g. the State or a creditor) seeking to undo or lessen a reduction of a sentence or interest rate made by the lower court.
predicates.reduction_was_in_exercise_of_judicial_di: The lower court reduced the sentence or interest rate in the exercise of a discretion that the law left open to it, and not contrary to a mandatory provision.
predicates.circumstances_of_case_support_reduction: The facts of the case, such as the offender's role and personal circumstances, long delay, prolonged litigation, changed interest rates or the size of the interest compared with the principal, make the reduction reasonable and justify leaving it in place.
predicates.appellate_court_leaves_reduction_undistu: The appellate court declines to interfere with and upholds the lower court's reduced sentence or interest rate.

definition: An appellate court will ordinarily not interfere with a lower court's discretionary reduction of a sentence or an interest rate where the circumstances of the case reasonably support the reduction. The decision rests on the facts of the case and does not set a precedent that overrides a governing rule.
exceptions_or_limits: In the sentencing member, the court relied on the lower court having given sufficient reasons for leniency. In the interest members, the reduction was left in place even though the High Court gave no reasons (one member) or on the basis of the court's own assessment of reasonableness.

The interest member decided under Article 136 expressly confined itself to its own facts and parties and did not override the governing statutory rule (Rule 64A of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960). It is not authority for departing from a mandatory rule.
The rule does not apply where the reduction was outside the lower court's discretion or was unreasonable on the facts.
The sentencing member requires that the conviction remain in force.

common_material_facts: A lower court had reduced a sentence or an interest rate in the exercise of discretion.
The appellant (the State, or a creditor or State authority seeking the higher interest) sought to undo or lessen the reduction.

Case-specific circumstances made the reduction appear reasonable, such as the offender's illiteracy and subordinate role, long delay before suit, large accumulated interest, prolonged litigation or changed market rates.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 467 of the Indian Penal Code
Article 136 of the Constitution of India
Rule 64A of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 (not overridden)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members leave the lower court's reduction undisturbed.
variations: One member concerns criminal sentencing; two concern interest rates (pendente lite interest, and interest on amounts due from mining lessees).
The lower court's reasons were found sufficient in the sentencing member and were absent in one interest member, where the appellate court still found no reason to interfere.
One member expressly limits its decision to its own facts and disclaims precedential effect over a governing rule.

split_suggestion: The shared point is non-interference with a discretionary reduction. If a narrower grouping is wanted, separate the sentencing member (131360_4) from the two interest members (1429485_2, 79780222_4), and treat the Article 136 and Rule 64A member separately from the pendente lite interest member.

legal_question: Under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, when is a notice terminating a month-to-month tenancy valid, in particular whether it must expire with the end of the correctly identified tenancy month and how it is to be construed?

predicates.monthly_tenancy_termination_notice_chall: The validity of a notice terminating a month-to-month tenancy (including one created by holding over) is disputed.
predicates.statutory_notice_period_given: The notice gives the minimum period required under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act for the type of lease.
predicates.notice_construed_as_whole_in_context_fix: Read as a whole, in a common-sense manner and in light of the facts known to the parties, the notice makes clear that the tenancy ends on the last day of a tenancy month, with the tenant entitled to remain until then.
predicates.notice_validly_terminates_tenancy: The notice is held effective to terminate the tenancy.

definition: A notice terminating a monthly tenancy under section 106 must give the required notice period and expire with the end of a tenancy month, with the month computed according to the tenancy's actual start. The notice is read as a whole, in a common-sense way and in context, so as to make it effective, and it is valid if it clearly ends the tenancy at month's end; a notice that purports to terminate before the tenancy month ends is invalid.
exceptions_or_limits: If the notice on its terms expires before the end of the correctly computed tenancy month, it does not validly terminate the tenancy, and liberal construction cannot cure that (131693_2).
Liberal construction applies only to ambiguity or form. It does not dispense with the statutory notice period (278584_2 distinguishes a case where the notice did not give a clear notice period).
The tenancy month must be computed correctly: the commencement date of the lease is excluded under section 110, and the holding-over monthly tenancy runs from the following day.

common_material_facts: A month-to-month tenancy, either created by holding over after a fixed term or originally monthly
A landlord's written notice terminating the tenancy that is challenged as defective
The dispute turns on the date or timing of termination relative to the end of the tenancy month
statutes_and_provisions: Section 106, Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Section 110, Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (computation of lease term)
Section 116, Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (holding over)
Harihar Banerji v. Ramsashi Roy (construction of notices)
Sidebotham v. Holland
Benoy Krishna Das v. Salsiccioni
Mangilal v. Suganchand Rathi
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: The notice is upheld in 2 of 3 members (278584_2, 752533_1), where it is read as a whole to end the tenancy at the proper time. It is held invalid in 1 of 3 (131693_2), where it expired before the end of the tenancy month.
variations: 131693_2 turns on arithmetic: the tenancy month is computed under section 110 and the notice, which terminated on the eighth day, expired too early.
278584_2 and 752533_1 turn on construction: apparently inconsistent or loosely worded notices are read in context to find a clear termination date.
278584_2 also involves a notice sent to the lessee and not to the sublessee.
752533_1 relies on a notice requiring vacation within the month and treating the tenants as trespassers from the next month.

legal_question: Can a court direct or refer a matter for investigation against a public official where the legal preconditions for that step, namely a prima facie finding of an offence or the prior sanction required by statute, have not been met?

predicates.court_directs_or_refers_investigation_ag: A court directs, or a magistrate refers a complaint for, investigation into the conduct of a public official or public servant.
predicates.no_prima_facie_offence_finding: The court has not found prima facie that an offence was committed or that the person was involved in one, and the direction is meant only to discover whether an offence occurred.
predicates.corruption_offence_covered_by_sanction_r: The alleged offence is one for which the corruption statute requires prior sanction before a court takes cognizance against a public servant, and it relates to the exercise of official functions.
predicates.valid_prior_sanction_obtained: A valid prior sanction from the competent authority was obtained before the court directed or referred the investigation.
predicates.investigation_direction_or_referral_is_i: The direction or referral for investigation cannot lawfully be made and is liable to be set aside or deleted.

definition: A court may not order or refer an investigation against a public official as a fishing inquiry to see whether an offence exists, without a prima facie finding of an offence. Where the alleged offence is a protected corruption offence against a public servant, a referral for investigation, including under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C., also requires valid prior sanction under Section 19(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
exceptions_or_limits: The members rest on two distinct bases, which are the absence of a prima facie finding (Article 21) and the absence of statutory sanction (Section 19 PC Act). Either alone suffices on its own terms.
The sanction requirement applies only to offences covered by Section 19 PC Act and to acts alleged to be done in an official capacity.
Section 19(3) does not make prior sanction directory, but it limits reversal of findings, sentences or orders for a sanction defect absent a failure of justice.
The prima facie requirement is stated only for directions to investigate whether an offence has been committed. It does not bar investigation where a prima facie offence is found.

common_material_facts: A court or magistrate directed or referred an investigation into the conduct of public officials or public servants.
The conduct concerned the exercise of official functions, such as land-related decisions or ministerial or administrative conduct.
The precondition for the investigation, a prima facie finding or sanction, was missing.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 21 of the Constitution
Section 19(1) and 19(3) of the Prevention of Corruption Act
Section 156(3) Cr.P.C.
Section 190 Cr.P.C.
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members held the investigation direction or referral impermissible. One deleted the direction, one held that sanction is required, and one upheld the quashing of the referral.
variations: One member rests on the Article 21 principle that an investigation cannot be ordered to discover whether an offence occurred, without any statutory sanction analysis.
Two members rest on mandatory prior sanction under Section 19 PC Act, applying a broad meaning of cognizance to pre-cognizance referral under Section 156(3).
One member concerns a constitutional-court direction against senior political functionaries, and the other two concern magistrate referrals of private complaints.

split_suggestion: If a tighter rule is needed, split into (a) investigation directions without a prima facie finding (132334_8) and (b) Section 156(3) referrals against public servants without Section 19 PC Act sanction (187807399_1, 60804618_1).

legal_question: When may a court disregard a company's separate legal personality and lift the corporate veil because the corporate form is being used for fraud, a dishonest design or other improper conduct?

predicates.corporate_form_used_by_controllers_for_f: Those controlling or dealing through a company, or through related corporate entities and share transactions, used its separate personality to commit fraud, evade obligations, conceal assets or transactions, or advance a dishonest or improper purpose.
predicates.court_finds_on_evidence_that_separate_pe: On the material before it (affidavits, unexplained changes in directorship or shareholding, withheld disclosure, or the conduct of the controllers), the court finds that the corporate personality is being abused as a cloak or device.
predicates.court_may_lift_corporate_veil_and_look_a: The court may disregard the separate corporate personality, treat the assets or transaction according to their real character, and bind the persons behind the company.

definition: Separate corporate personality is not a shield for fraud or improper conduct. Where the persons controlling a company, or related entities, use the corporate form to perpetrate fraud, screen or conceal assets or transactions, or further a dishonest design, the court may lift the veil and deal with the assets or transaction as they really are.
exceptions_or_limits: The ordinary rule of separate corporate personality applies unless the corporate form is shown to be used for illegality, fraud, evasion of obligations or other improper or inequitable purposes.
The power is discretionary ('may') and depends on evidence of abuse; the members do not lift the veil merely because of common control or relationship.

common_material_facts: Persons or family members controlled the company or group of companies concerned.
The corporate form or share and directorship arrangements were used to screen assets, conceal a transaction or further a personal dishonest design.
Lack of satisfactory explanation, or withholding or inconsistency of disclosure, supported the inference of abuse.
statutes_and_provisions: No statutory provisions are cited; the members rely on case law: Salomon v. Salomon; Tata Engineering v. State of Bihar; DHN Food Distributors; Kapila Hingorani; Renusagar Power; Playworld Electronics; Yukong Line; Juggilal Kamlapat; Jai Narain Parasrampuria; LIC v. Escorts.
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the court lifted or disregarded the corporate veil and looked at the true character of the property or transaction.
variations: One member concerned screening of property from creditors or defrauded purchasers (recovery and contempt context).
One concerned promoters who abused the company's personality and could not take a position inconsistent with the company's interests.
One concerned concealed sale of subsidiaries and a suppressed transaction, together with a breach of a disclosure direction.

legal_question: For the purpose of deemed lapse of a land acquisition under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act, when is compensation treated as paid under an award made under the 1894 Act: only when it is tendered or delivered to the interested person or, where a Section 31(2) contingency prevents payment, deposited in the reference court, rather than being retained by the authority or deposited in a treasury?

rule.if: acquisition_lapse_payment_assessment and (compensation_tendered_and_received_by_interested_person or (compensation_tendered_or_offered and statutory_contingency_prevented_payment and compensation_deposited_in_reference_court))

predicates.acquisition_lapse_payment_assessment: The court must decide whether compensation under an award made under the 1894 Act counts as paid for the purpose of deemed lapse under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act.
predicates.compensation_tendered_and_received_by_in: The compensation was tendered to the interested person entitled to it and was actually delivered to or received by that person.
predicates.compensation_tendered_or_offered: The Collector or authority tendered or offered the compensation to the interested person entitled to it.
predicates.statutory_contingency_prevented_payment: Payment was prevented by one of the contingencies listed in Section 31(2) of the 1894 Act, such as refusal to receive, absence of authority to receive, or disputed title.
predicates.compensation_deposited_in_reference_cour: The compensation was deposited in the court to which a reference under Section 18 of the 1894 Act may be made, and not merely in a treasury, revenue account or with the authority.
predicates.compensation_treated_as_paid: The compensation is regarded as paid for the purpose of deciding deemed lapse under Section 24(2).

definition: Under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act read with Section 31 of the 1894 Act, compensation counts as paid only if it is tendered and delivered to the interested person or, where a Section 31(2) contingency prevents payment, tendered and deposited in the reference court. Retention by the authority, or a deposit in a treasury or the State's revenue account, is not payment.
exceptions_or_limits: A treasury deposit, retention by the authority pending the claimant's application, or a deposit under a local standing order does not substitute for a reference-court deposit where a Section 31(2) contingency applies.
The court deposit route applies only where a recognized statutory contingency actually prevented payment; absent such a contingency, tender and payment to the interested person is required.
The rule concerns whether compensation was paid for deemed lapse; the other conditions of Section 24(2) are not addressed by the members.

common_material_facts: An award was made under the 1894 Act and the matter was later tested under Section 24(2) of the 2013 Act.
Compensation was not paid to the landowners and was either retained by the authority or placed in a government treasury.
No deposit was made in the court to which a reference could be made.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 24(2) of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013
Sections 31(1) and 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Sections 32, 33 and 34 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Pune Municipal Corporation v. Harakchand Misirimal Solanki
