Nazir Ahmad v. King Emperor
Agnelo Santimano Fernandes v. State of Goa
Prem Nath Kapur v. National Fertilizers Corporation
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members, retention by the authority or a treasury deposit was held not to amount to payment; payment requires tender and delivery or a reference-court deposit where a contingency applies.
variations: One member involved the authority withholding compensation until the claimants applied and furnished title documents and a surety bond.
One member involved a local standing order permitting treasury deposits, which the court held did not override Section 31(2).
One member involved a notice to landowners to collect compensation followed by a treasury deposit.
The rules differ in framing: two state when compensation is treated as paid, while one states when it is not paid as required.

legal_question: Is a civil suit barred from challenging the correctness, computation or extent of a tax or statutory-levy assessment where the governing statute provides its own remedies and finality, unless the plaint alleges a fundamental statutory breach or a breach of fundamental principles of judicial procedure?

rule.if: assessment_challenge_suit and assessment_made_under_special_statutory_scheme and statutory_scheme_provides_remedies_or_finality and challenge_is_to_correctness_or_extent_of_assessment and not alleged_fundamental_statutory_noncompliance_or_procedural_breach

predicates.assessment_challenge_suit: The plaintiff has filed a civil suit seeking to set aside, modify, or question the assessment of a tax or statutory levy.
predicates.assessment_made_under_special_statutory_: The assessment was made under a special statute (for example an income-tax, cess or municipal tax enactment) that creates the liability and prescribes the assessment procedure.
predicates.statutory_scheme_provides_remedies_or_fi: The statute provides its own remedies against the assessment (such as objections or appeals) and/or makes the assessment or the appellate decision final, or expressly bars civil suits.
predicates.challenge_is_to_correctness_or_extent_of: The grievance is only that the assessment was wrong, excessive, arbitrary, unreasonable or wrongly computed or interpreted, or that the officer failed to inquire into a claim, which are matters for the statutory authorities.
predicates.alleged_fundamental_statutory_noncomplia: The plaint alleges that a fundamental provision of the statute was not complied with, that fundamental principles of judicial procedure were not followed, or that the law is invalid.
predicates.civil_suit_barred_or_not_maintainable: The civil court has no jurisdiction, and the suit is barred or not maintainable to that extent, so the taxpayer must use the remedies within the statute.

definition: Where a special taxing or levy statute prescribes the assessment procedure and provides remedies or finality, a civil suit cannot be used to challenge the correctness, computation or extent of the assessment. The taxpayer must use the statutory remedies, unless the plaint shows a fundamental statutory non-compliance or a breach of fundamental principles of judicial procedure.
exceptions_or_limits: Civil court jurisdiction remains where the plaint alleges non-compliance with fundamental provisions of the statute or failure to follow fundamental principles of judicial procedure (Dhulabhai; Mask & Co.).
Civil court jurisdiction may remain where the statute or the levy is invalid, as recognised in the municipal tax member.
Exclusion of civil jurisdiction is not readily inferred; it depends on the statute providing an adequate remedy and finality.
In the income-tax member, the bar applies only so far as the suit seeks to set aside or modify the assessment.

common_material_facts: The plaintiff filed a civil suit instead of using the statutory objection or appeal route.
The grievance concerned the correctness, computation or extent of an assessment.
The statute prescribed an assessment procedure with appeals and finality.
No fundamental statutory breach or procedural breach was alleged.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 67 and section 30, Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922
Sections 75 and 102, Bengal Cess Act, 1880
Rule 25 of Part I of Schedule III, and sections 108, 109, 117, 147 and 148, Karnataka Municipal Corporations Act, 1976
Dhulabhai v. State of M.P.; Collector of South Arcot v. Mask & Co.; Commissioner of Income-tax v. Tribune Trust; Shiv Kumar Chadha v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the civil suit is barred or not maintainable, and the taxpayer is left to the statutory remedies.
variations: The income-tax member rests on an express statutory bar (section 67) and does not discuss the Dhulabhai exceptions.
The cess and municipal members apply the Dhulabhai/Mask & Co. framework of implied exclusion and its exceptions.
The cess member also stresses that the company did not pursue the statutory remedies on that issue.
The municipal member rejects allegations of excessiveness or arbitrariness as insufficient to bring the case within an exception.

legal_question: Does a wakf or deed that provides substantially for the settlor's own family or descendants (with only incidental or deferred charitable or religious application) qualify as a religious or charitable purpose or use under a statute that requires such a purpose, merely because Muslim law treats family provision as pious or permits a family wakf?

predicates.statute_requires_religious_or_charitable: The claim depends on a statutory provision (an exemption or a special procedure) that applies only to holdings or gifts for a religious or charitable purpose or use.
predicates.wakf_or_deed_provides_substantial_benefi: The wakf or deed gives substantial and continuing benefits (maintenance, allowances or income) to the settlor, the settlor's family or descendants, with any charitable or religious application being limited or postponed.
predicates.family_provision_not_religious_rite_or_s: The family provision involves no religious worship, teaching, service or rites, is not directed to poor or needy persons, and serves no general public utility object.
predicates.family_provision_is_not_religious_or_cha: The family provision is not a religious or charitable purpose or use under the statute, so the wakf or deed is not exclusively or wholly religious or charitable and does not get the statutory benefit.

definition: Provision for the settlor's family or descendants is not a religious or charitable purpose or use under a statute that requires one. This holds even if Muslim law regards it as pious or permits a family wakf, or if charity is incidental or comes only after the family line ends, unless the provision is itself a religious rite or service, relief of the poor, or a public benefit.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule may not apply where the family provision has ended or become inoperative, or is directed only to poor or needy relatives, or otherwise falls within a statutory head of charity such as relief of the poor or public utility.
The Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913 and the Shariat Act, 1937 validate family wakfs but do not recharacterise family support as religious or charitable.

The meaning of 'religious or charitable' depends on the statute's own definitions (for example, sections 2(c) and 2(n) of the West Bengal Act) and context (for example, the Oudh Estates Act applying to talukdars of all religions).

common_material_facts: Wakf deeds gave continuing benefits to the settlor's family or descendants alongside some charitable or religious expenditure
Charitable or religious application was minor or postponed until the family line became extinct
The family provisions were not shown to be for poor or needy relatives or to involve religious rites
statutes_and_provisions: West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act, 1953, sections 2(c), 2(n) and 6(1)(i)
Oudh Estates Act, sections 11, 12 and 18
Mussalman Wakf Validating Act, 1913, sections 3 and 4
Shariat Act, 1937
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 issues hold that family or descendant provision is not a religious or charitable purpose or use, so the statutory exemption or special treatment is denied.
variations: Two members arise under the West Bengal Estates Acquisition Act (religious purpose via section 2(n); charitable purpose via section 2(c)); the third concerns the Oudh Estates Act's procedure for gifts to religious or charitable uses.

The reasoning differs: one member turns on the absence of religious worship or rites; one on the lack of public benefit or relief of the poor; one on statutory construction and the postponement of charity.
The exclusivity requirement in section 6(1)(i) applies in the West Bengal members but not in the Oudh member.

legal_question: When a State law and a Parliamentary (Central) law both operate on a Concurrent List subject and are repugnant, does the State law yield to the Parliamentary law under Article 254, and on what conditions?

rule.if: state_and_central_laws_on_concurrent_subject and central_law_applicable_in_state and repugnancy_exists and not state_law_saved_by_presidential_assent

predicates.state_and_central_laws_on_concurrent_sub: A State law and a Central/Parliamentary law both legislate on a matter in the Concurrent List.
predicates.central_law_applicable_in_state: The Central/Parliamentary law is in force and applicable in the State concerned.
predicates.repugnancy_exists: The two laws are repugnant: there is a direct irreconcilable conflict, or the Central law is an exhaustive code occupying the field, or both laws regulate the same subject matter in an overlapping way, and the laws cannot be harmonised.
predicates.state_law_saved_by_presidential_assent: The State law received Presidential assent under Article 254(2) in a way that would preserve it against an earlier Central law.
predicates.state_law_yields_to_central_law_to_exten: The State law is displaced, being inoperative or void to the extent of the repugnancy, and the Central law prevails, without any express repeal being necessary.

definition: Under Article 254, where a State law and an applicable Parliamentary law on a Concurrent List subject are repugnant, whether by direct conflict, occupation of the field by an exhaustive code, or regulation of the same subject, the State law yields to the Parliamentary law to the extent of the repugnancy. This operates automatically, including by necessary implication, unless the State law is saved by Presidential assent under Article 254(2).
exceptions_or_limits: Article 254(2): a State law that has received Presidential assent may prevail in that State, but the proviso allows Parliament to enact a later law on the same matter, which prevails.
Repugnancy is not the first choice: if the two laws can be harmonised, no repugnancy arises.
The State law is displaced only to the extent of the repugnancy, according to the text and context of the Central law.
The rule applies only to Concurrent List subjects.

common_material_facts: State and Central laws both regulated the same Concurrent List subject (land acquisition, eviction from public premises, promoter-purchaser relations).
The Central law was applicable or later in time, and its provisions differed from or overlapped with the State law.
The State law lacked Presidential assent or any saving under Article 254(2).
statutes_and_provisions: Constitution of India, Article 254(1)
Constitution of India, Article 254(2) and its proviso
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the Parliamentary/Central law prevailed and the State law was displaced to the extent of repugnancy, with no express repeal needed.
variations: One member treats the displacement as an accepted, automatic repeal by implication.
One member emphasises that the later Parliamentary law prevails under the proviso to Article 254(2).
One member sets out the tests for repugnancy (direct conflict, exhaustive code, identical subject) and the harmonisation caution, and notes the absence of Presidential assent.

legal_question: Does a finding or observation that was unnecessary to the decision of the earlier case (and not directly and substantially in issue) bind the parties, by way of res judicata or otherwise, in the same or later proceedings?

predicates.finding_or_observation_made_in_earlier_p: A court in an earlier suit or appeal recorded a finding, observation or conclusion on an issue, and a party seeks to rely on it or challenge it in a later or related proceeding.
predicates.finding_unnecessary_to_decision: The finding was not necessary to the decree or disposal of the matter, because the case was decided on another ground, or the issue was not directly and substantially in issue.
predicates.finding_not_binding_or_not_to_be_relied_: The finding does not operate as res judicata, cannot found an appeal on that basis alone, and is not to be taken into account in pending or future proceedings between the parties.

definition: A finding or observation that was unnecessary to the decision, because the matter was resolved on another or threshold ground or the issue was not directly and substantially in issue, does not operate as res judicata and is not to be relied on in other proceedings. This applies with added force where the affected party could not appeal it or where no pleadings or evidence raised the dispute.
exceptions_or_limits: Applies only to findings that were unnecessary to the decree or disposal; findings on issues directly and substantially in issue and necessary to the decision may operate as res judicata.
In the appellate-observation scenario, non-binding effect is supported where the affected parties could not appeal the decree, or where there were no inter-party pleadings or evidence.

The direction to disregard findings in pending or future proceedings rested on the Court's own reasoning in the case, without a cited statute or precedent, and may be specific to threshold-ground disposals.
The Court did not decide whether a finding's appealability generally depends on whether it would operate as res judicata.

common_material_facts: An earlier court made a finding or observation that the decision did not require.
The earlier matter was disposed of on another ground, such as a restricted decree, a threshold lack of authority, or dismissal of an appeal.
A party tried to rely on the finding, or to challenge it, in an appeal or in later or pending proceedings.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 11, Code of Civil Procedure (res judicata), cited in 542852_1 and implicit in 1350326_3
Harchandra Das v. Bholanath Day (considered but not decided on) in 1350326_3
Keshardeo Chamria v. Radha Kissen Chamria [1953] SCR 154 (distinguished) in 542852_1
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the unnecessary finding is not binding, or is not to be considered, in other proceedings. One dismisses an appeal against the finding as not maintainable, one directs that the finding be disregarded, and one rejects its res judicata effect in a later suit.
variations: 1350326_3 concerns the maintainability of an appeal against a finding alone.
19689_2 concerns a Supreme Court direction that the lower court's findings not be considered in pending or future proceedings, without a res judicata analysis.
542852_1 concerns the binding effect of an appellate observation in a later suit, and adds that the parties could not appeal and that no pleadings or evidence raised the dispute.

legal_question: Does a judgment or direction lose its binding or enforceable force when the legal ruling on which it rests is overruled, or conflicts with a later decision of a larger bench or the Supreme Court?

predicates.earlier_judgment_or_direction_rests_on_l: An earlier judgment, or a direction issued under it, depends on a particular legal ruling or interpretation of a point of law.
predicates.later_decision_of_larger_bench_or_suprem: A later decision of a larger bench of the same court, or of the Supreme Court, decides the same legal point in a way that conflicts with or reverses the earlier ruling.
predicates.later_decision_binds_the_court_or_partie: The later decision is binding on the court or parties before it, because of the hierarchy of benches or Article 141.
predicates.earlier_judgment_or_direction_is_not_gov: The earlier judgment is no longer treated as law to be followed. Conflicting judgments are set aside or disposed of in line with the later ruling, and directions resting solely on the displaced ruling are unenforceable.

definition: Where an earlier judgment or direction depends on a legal ruling that a later binding decision of a larger bench or the Supreme Court overrules or contradicts, the earlier judgment ceases to be governing law. Courts must follow the later ruling, and directions resting solely on the displaced ruling cannot be enforced, even if they were not appealed.
exceptions_or_limits: The earlier judgment remains effective until it is set aside or overruled, or its correctness is doubted by a higher court.

The unenforceability of an unappealed direction applies where the direction depended solely on the displaced legal basis. Finality and res judicata principles were distinguished, not generally displaced.
The later ruling must be on the same legal issue and must actually conflict with the earlier one.

common_material_facts: An earlier judgment took a legal position on a point.
A later larger-bench (Full Bench) or Supreme Court decision resolved the same point differently.
Someone sought to rely on, comply with or enforce the earlier judgment or direction after the later decision.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 141 of the Constitution (binding effect of Supreme Court law)
Territorial-jurisdiction provision interpreted in the first member
Precedents on mandamus and finality (Shenoy; Satyadhyan Ghosal; Hemant Kumar Bhattacharjee; Krishnamurthy Chetty)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the earlier or conflicting judgment yields to the later larger-bench or Supreme Court ruling. It is treated as non-est, set aside, or unenforceable.
variations: One member concerns an intra-court overruling by a Full Bench, with an administrative registry asked to comply.
One concerns reconciling conflicting equal-strength benches via a Full Bench, with the conflicting judgment set aside in appeal.
One concerns a Supreme Court reversal that defeats an unappealed, final mandamus between the parties.

legal_question: When is a suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure not maintainable, because the property is not shown to be a public trust, or because no breach of trust is proved and no genuine need for administrative directions is shown?

rule.if: section_92_suit and (not public_trust_established or (alleged_breach_not_proved and not genuine_need_for_directions_shown))

predicates.section_92_suit: The suit is brought under the special procedure of Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure for relief concerning a public religious or charitable trust.
predicates.public_trust_established: The evidence shows that the property was fully dedicated to the public as a public trust, as opposed to a private trust.
predicates.alleged_breach_not_proved: The alleged breach of trust was not substantiated by evidence, as found by the courts.
predicates.genuine_need_for_directions_shown: The plaint and evidence give a factual and reasoned foundation showing that directions are necessary for the administration of the trust, and such directions are actually sought.
predicates.suit_not_maintainable_under_section_92: The suit cannot proceed under Section 92 and fails, because there is no cause of action or foundation under that section.

definition: A Section 92 suit presupposes a public trust and either an alleged and proved breach of trust or a genuine, factually grounded need for directions for its administration, together with a claim for the reliefs specified in the section. If the public trust is not shown, or the breach is unproved and no genuine need for directions is shown, the suit is not maintainable.
exceptions_or_limits: The plaint is examined first to see whether the suit falls within Section 92. Failure on the evidence leads to dismissal only if the breach is not made out and the request for directions is vague or without factual basis.
The Court in one member did not decide the broader meaning of 'directions necessary for the administration of the trust'.
The rule applies only to public trusts. Private trusts fall outside Section 92.
The first member turns on the absence of public dedication. The other two turn on failure of the breach and directions limbs.

common_material_facts: Plaintiffs sued under Section 92 CPC for relief in respect of a trust.
The foundation of the suit failed on the evidence, found by the courts.
In two members, alleged breach of trust by the person managing the institution was not proved concurrently by the courts.
In two members, no real foundation was shown for directions for administration.
In one member, public dedication was not established and the owners retained control.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 92, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All three members hold the Section 92 suit not maintainable or without cause of action (3 of 3).
variations: One member rests on the absence of a public trust, since Section 92 does not cover private trusts.
Two members rest on the absence of a proved breach and of a factual basis for administrative directions.
One member says that directions sought only to bring the suit within Section 92 are insufficient.
In one member, the High Court's contrary finding of a public trust was reversed.

legal_question: Can an accused's absconding, or failure to surrender or appear, after an offence by itself establish guilt or supply a determining link in a circumstantial chain of evidence?

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The case is a criminal trial or appeal in which guilt of the accused is in issue, including where the prosecution relies on circumstantial evidence.
predicates.accused_absconded_or_failed_to_surrender: The accused was untraceable, did not promptly appear before the authorities, or did not surrender for some period after the offence.
predicates.other_credible_evidence_establishing_gui: The prosecution relies solely on the absconding, with no other credible evidence that independently establishes guilt. This is a limit-style predicate, true only when other proven evidence is available for the absconding to corroborate.
predicates.absconding_alone_does_not_establish_guil: The accused's absconding or failure to surrender, taken by itself, is not proof of guilt and cannot be a determining link in a circumstantial chain. At most it is a circumstance that may add weight to other proved evidence.

definition: Absconding or failure to surrender after an offence is relevant only as a circumstance to be weighed with other evidence. It cannot by itself establish guilt, complete a circumstantial chain, or make up for unreliable prosecution evidence.
exceptions_or_limits: Absconding may still lend weight to other evidence that independently points to guilt; it is relevant, but not conclusive.
Its probative value depends on the circumstances of each case.
Non-recovery of a vehicle has no evidentiary value unless there is evidence that it would have contained incriminating traces.

common_material_facts: The accused was untraceable, did not appear, or did not surrender for a period after the offence.
The prosecution's other evidence was weak, unreliable, or circumstantial.
Lower courts or the prosecution treated the absence as an incriminating circumstance.
statutes_and_provisions: No statutory provisions are cited.
Cited precedents: Prakash Mahadeo Godse v. State of Maharashtra; Matru v. State of U.P.; Rahman v. State of U.P.; State of M.P. v. Paltan Mallah; Bipin Kumar Mondal v. State of West Bengal.
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that absconding or failure to surrender alone does not establish guilt. It may only add weight to other evidence.
variations: One member also addresses non-recovery of the accused's vehicle, which had no evidentiary value without evidence of incriminating traces.
One member also considers the relatives' lack of effort to obstruct the prosecution, which could not cure the weak evidence.
In one member the absence was not put to the accused, and the omission was held inconsequential because absence alone could not establish guilt.
The duration of absence varies, from a short period to nearly a year.
One member cites no earlier authority; the others rely on precedent.

legal_question: Does a rent-control provision that differentiates between residential and non-residential premises (in eviction grounds or in tenant protection) violate Article 14 when the distinction lacks a rational nexus to the statute's objects, including where changed circumstances have removed its original rationale?

rule.if: rent_control_classification_challenged_under_article_14 and law_treats_residential_and_nonresidential_premises_differently_on_eviction_or_protection and objects_of_law_apply_equally_to_both_premises_types and (no_rational_nexus_between_premises_use_distinction_and_objects or original_rationale_lost_through_changed_circumstances) and state_has_not_justified_the_distinction

predicates.rent_control_classification_challenged_u: The challenge is to a rent-control law's classification on the ground that it violates the constitutional guarantee of equality.
predicates.law_treats_residential_and_nonresidentia: The law grants or withholds an eviction ground or a protection (such as bona fide need eviction or tenant protection from the law) differently depending on whether the premises are residential or non-residential.
predicates.objects_of_law_apply_equally_to_both_pre: The law's stated objects (regulating tenancy, controlling rents, preventing unreasonable or mala fide eviction) and its general scheme apply alike to residential and non-residential premises.
predicates.no_rational_nexus_between_premises_use_d: The differentia of premises use (or use combined with rent) bears no rational relation to the law's objects; for example, a landlord's bona fide need or a tenant's need for protection is not different between the types.
predicates.original_rationale_lost_through_changed_: A rationale that may have justified the classification when enacted has disappeared or become artificial because circumstances changed (for example, housing availability or rent levels).
predicates.state_has_not_justified_the_distinction: No material is shown to support the claim that the excluded or differently treated class stands on a different footing relevant to the law's objects.
predicates.premises_use_based_distinction_is_violat: The discriminatory provision or limitation is held unconstitutional and struck down, with any remedy confined to the discriminatory part.

definition: A rent-control classification between residential and non-residential premises is invalid under Article 14 where the distinction has no rational nexus to the statute's objects, including where a once-valid rationale has lapsed with changed circumstances, and the State shows no justification for it.
exceptions_or_limits: A classification with an intelligible differentia that has a rational relation to the law's object remains valid.
A classification valid when enacted is invalidated only if circumstances have since removed its rationale.
The invalidation can be confined to the discriminatory limitation rather than the whole provision.
Observations on the validity of classifications made in a context other than an Article 14 challenge do not govern.

common_material_facts: Rent-control statute distinguishes between residential and non-residential premises
The general object of the statute (tenant protection, rent control, preventing unreasonable eviction) applies equally to both types
No convincing justification shown for the distinction, or the historical justification has faded
Challenge brought under Article 14
statutes_and_provisions: Article 14 of the Constitution
State rent-control legislation (eviction for bona fide need; rent-threshold exemption)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the premises-use-based distinction violates Article 14 and strike down the discriminatory provision or limitation (2 on eviction for personal need, 1 on rent-based exemption).
variations: Two members concern eviction for bona fide need (one striking an amendment that removed the ground for non-residential premises, one striking the exclusion of non-residential premises); one concerns exclusion of higher-rent residential tenants from protection.
Two members expressly rely on changed circumstances making a once-valid classification arbitrary; the first rests mainly on absence of a rational nexus with the statute's objects.
Direction of discrimination differs: non-residential tenants disadvantaged in two members, residential tenants disadvantaged in one.
Remedy: the first restores the original provisions, the second strikes only the discriminatory limitation, the third strikes the exemption.

legal_question: Are persons interested in a public trust (including trustees and beneficiaries), even if not named parties to the proceeding, entitled to sue or to apply in court to protect or recover trust property under the statutory scheme governing the trust?

predicates.claimant_is_person_interested_in_public_: The claimant is a trustee, beneficiary or other person with an interest in the public trust (the inclusive definition covers trustees as well as beneficiaries).
predicates.proceeding_is_for_protection_or_administ: The suit or application seeks to protect, recover or administer property of a public trust, for example a declaration of trust ownership, recovery of possession, or directions under a scheme decree.
predicates.statutory_or_decree_conditions_for_invok: Any procedural precondition of the governing regime is met, such as the written consent of the Charity Commissioner and the minimum number of plaintiffs under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, or a liberty-to-apply clause in the scheme decree in a representative suit.
predicates.claimant_has_standing_to_invoke_trust_re: The claimant has standing, and the suit or application is maintainable, to invoke the trust remedy; the claimant may not be excluded for being a trustee or for not being named in the original suit title.

definition: Persons interested in a public trust are read broadly. This includes trustees and beneficiaries, and persons bound as represented in a representative suit. They may sue under the trust statute, or apply under a scheme decree, to protect or recover trust property, provided the procedural conditions of the relevant regime are met.
exceptions_or_limits: Under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, a suit under section 50 needs the written consent required by section 51 and the Charity Commissioner or two or more interested persons as plaintiffs.
Section 92 CPC does not apply to trusts governed by the Bombay Act (section 52(1)); section 50 is wider than section 92.
The right to apply under a scheme decree depends on the decree permitting parties to apply for further directions.
The restrictive reading of 'person having an interest' in Ganapathi Ram Naik is overruled; the contrary Karnataka Full Bench decision was reversed.

common_material_facts: Public trust or temple property is in dispute, with non-trustee or adverse claimants.
The claimants are trustees or beneficiaries who are interested in the trust.
A statutory or decree-based procedure for protecting the trust is invoked.
statutes_and_provisions: Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, ss. 2(10), 50(ii), 50(ii)(a), 51, 52(1)
Code of Civil Procedure, s. 92, s. 93, s. 11 Explanation VI, Order I Rule 8
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 issues favour the interested persons: they are held to have standing or the suit is held maintainable, and the restrictive lower-court or High Court views are reversed.
variations: Two members concern the Bombay Public Trusts Act (a definitional point and maintainability under s. 50), while one concerns s. 92 CPC representative suits and a scheme decree.
The standing arises in different ways: inclusive statutory definition, statutory suit with Commissioner's consent, and representative-suit binding effect.

split_suggestion: If a finer division is wanted, separate the two Bombay Public Trusts Act members (1368304_1 and 1368304_2, on the definition of an interested person and the maintainability of a s. 50 suit) from the s. 92 CPC representative-suit and scheme-decree member (1681806_1).

legal_question: Can the recovery, production or possession of a weapon be used against an accused in a criminal case when the prosecution has not shown a reliable link between that weapon and the offence?

predicates.criminal_proceeding: The matter is a criminal prosecution, trial or appeal from conviction.
predicates.weapon_recovered_produced_or_possessed: A weapon or ammunition was recovered, produced to the police, or found in the accused's possession.
predicates.no_reliable_evidentiary_link_between_wea: The prosecution has not established a reliable link between the weapon and the offence. Examples are no forensic or blood evidence, no proof of recent firing, no admissible statement leading to discovery, no proof the weapon was concealed at a place known only to the accused, or a disbelieved account of production.
predicates.weapon_evidence_does_not_connect_accused: The weapon evidence cannot be treated as connecting the accused to the crime and cannot by itself sustain a conviction.

definition: The prosecution must prove the link on which it relies. Mere recovery, production or possession of a weapon does not connect the accused to the offence unless evidence such as forensic results, proof of recent use, or an admissible discovery statement with exclusive knowledge ties the weapon to the crime. Withholding vital forensic evidence can also lead to an adverse inference against the prosecution.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule applies where the link is absent or unreliable. A proved forensic, ballistic or Section 27 discovery link can make the weapon evidence relevant.

The Section 27 Evidence Act point (a statement by the accused relating to the discovery, and concealment at a place known only to the accused) is specific to the discovery-based recovery and was stated in only one member.
The adverse inference for withholding vital forensic evidence was stated in only one member and applies only where such evidence was in fact withheld.
Insufficiency of the weapon evidence does not itself decide guilt, because other independent evidence may still support a conviction.

common_material_facts: Weapons were recovered from, produced by or possessed by the accused.
No forensic, chemical or firing evidence tied the weapons to the offence.
The prosecution's account of recovery or production was unreliable or not backed by an admissible statement.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 27 of the Evidence Act (discovery statement)
Section 8 of the Evidence Act (referred to by the High Court, not relied on by the Supreme Court)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the weapon evidence was held insufficient to connect the accused to the offence. In 1 member an adverse inference was also drawn against the prosecution.
variations: One member rests on missing or withheld forensic evidence and an adverse inference.
One member rests on mere possession of licensed guns with no proof of recent firing and a disbelieved production account.
One member rests on Section 27 and the absence of a discovery statement or exclusive knowledge.

legal_question: Can a conviction or finding of rape under Section 376 IPC be sustained where the evidence does not establish the offence, in particular the absence of consent, or leaves a reasonable view of consensual intercourse?

predicates.appeal_against_rape_conviction_or_findin: The matter is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction for rape, or a finding that the accused committed rape.
predicates.evidence_establishing_rape_including_lac: The evidence, beyond reasonable doubt, establishes the ingredients of rape, including that intercourse took place without the woman's consent or against her will (or that she was below the age at which consent is legally relevant), and a charge for the offence was framed where required. This is false where the evidence shows at most intercourse or a mere possibility of rape, or where a consensual view is reasonably possible.
predicates.rape_conviction_or_finding_cannot_be_sus: The conviction or finding of rape must be set aside, with the accused getting the benefit of doubt or acquittal on that charge.

definition: A conviction or finding of rape cannot stand unless the evidence proves the ingredients of the offence, notably intercourse without consent or against the woman's will. Evidence of mere intercourse, a mere possibility of rape, or a reasonable view of consensual intercourse (for a woman above the age of consent), and the absence of a charge, are not enough.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where there is evidence of lack of consent or the woman is below the age at which consent is legally relevant.
The absence-of-charge ground (1385297_1) is specific to a finding of rape made without a Section 376 charge; the benefit-of-doubt ground (413943_1) depends on two reasonable views being possible.
The members rest on the facts and evidence before the court and cite no earlier cases.

common_material_facts: Evidence was inconclusive on rape: medical evidence showing only possibility, or semen showing only intercourse.
No evidence that intercourse was against the woman's will or without consent.
The appellate court set aside a rape finding or conviction for want of proof.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 376 IPC
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the rape finding or conviction unsustainable: one for no charge and no evidence, one for no evidence of lack of consent, one for benefit of doubt on a reasonably possible consensual view.
variations: 1385297_1 turns on the absence of a rape charge and evidence.
186059_1 turns on proof of the lack-of-consent element beyond semen evidence.
413943_1 involves a High Court reversal of an acquittal and applies the benefit of doubt where the complainant was above the age of consent and the complaint was delayed.

legal_question: Can a conviction safely rest on the identification of the accused by a single (often child) eyewitness, in court or otherwise, where the witness's prior familiarity with the accused is not established and the identification was not properly tested (no identification parade, a prompted first identification, or an unexplained delay in recording the statement)?

rule.if: criminal_case_turns_on_identification and identification_rests_on_single_eyewitness and not prior_familiarity_or_opportunity_to_identify_established and identification_not_adequately_tested_or_assured

predicates.criminal_case_turns_on_identification: The prosecution case depends on proving the identity of the accused through eyewitness identification, and identity is disputed.
predicates.identification_rests_on_single_eyewitnes: The only identification evidence the court finds reliable enough to assess is that of one eyewitness, or of a young witness whose identification is the key evidence.
predicates.prior_familiarity_or_opportunity_to_iden: The evidence reliably shows that the witness knew the accused beforehand or otherwise had an adequate opportunity to see and identify him.
predicates.identification_not_adequately_tested_or_: The circumstances give no adequate assurance against mistake, for example because no identification parade was held, the first identification was prompted by a leading suggestion, the statement was recorded after an unexplained delay, or a parade the accused requested did not test that witness.
predicates.identification_unsafe_and_benefit_of_dou: The court holds the identification unsafe to rely on for conviction and gives the accused the benefit of doubt, which leads to acquittal where no other reliable evidence exists.

definition: Where identity is disputed and the case rests on a single eyewitness, including a child, whose prior familiarity with or opportunity to identify the accused is not established, the identification is unsafe if the circumstances do not adequately guard against mistake. Examples are no identification parade, a prompted first identification, an unexplained delay in recording the statement, or an untested requested parade. The accused then gets the benefit of doubt.
exceptions_or_limits: A sole eyewitness's testimony can support a conviction where there is reliable evidence that the witness had an opportunity to see and identify the accused.
Where prior familiarity with the accused is established, or the circumstances justify dispensing with an identification parade, dock identification need not be discounted.
Other reliable corroborative evidence connecting the accused to the offence may displace the rule; the members found none.

common_material_facts: Identification of the accused by a single eyewitness, in two of three cases a child, was the core of the prosecution case.
Prior acquaintance of the witness with the accused was unproved or only limited.
The identification process was flawed: no parade, a leading-question prompt, a delayed statement, or a requested parade that did not test the witness.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 161 CrPC (delay in recording the statement), in one member
Japal Singh v. State of Punjab, 1996(4) Crimes 74 (SC) on dock identification without a parade, in one member
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All three members found the identification unreliable or unsafe. Two gave the accused the benefit of doubt and acquitted. One held the court could not safely rely on the dock identification.
variations: The reasons for unreliability differ: a prompted first identification and unexplained delay (1385297_2), no parade and unestablished familiarity (1462333_2), and a requested parade that did not test the sole witness (1922173_9).
One member concerns an appeal from conviction ending in acquittal, one is a finding on reliability of dock identification, and one set aside a conviction.
The child-witness element is present in two members and absent in the third.

legal_question: At a preliminary stage (anticipatory bail or the magistrate's decision whether to issue process), should the court confine itself to a prima facie assessment of whether the complaint or evidence discloses the offence, rather than critically weighing the evidence as at trial?

predicates.preliminary_stage_proceeding: The court is deciding a preliminary question (such as anticipatory bail, or whether to issue process on a complaint) and not conducting a trial.
predicates.accusation_of_serious_offence_with_speci: The complaint or preliminary evidence makes specific allegations of an offence that carries a statutory consequence at the threshold (a statutory bar on anticipatory bail, or exclusive triability by the Court of Session).
predicates.prima_facie_offence_disclosed: On a cursory reading, the complaint averments or preliminary evidence prima facie disclose the alleged offence.
predicates.court_must_act_on_prima_facie_disclosure: The court must give effect to the prima facie disclosure (refuse anticipatory bail under the statutory bar, or issue process and commit the case) and must not critically or meticulously weigh the evidence at this stage.

definition: At a preliminary stage, the court only checks whether the complaint or preliminary evidence prima facie discloses the offence. If it does, the court must apply the consequence the statute attaches (the bar on anticipatory bail, or issue of process and commitment to the Sessions Court), and must not appraise the evidence as if at trial.
exceptions_or_limits: Anticipatory bail is available under the special Act's bar only if the court prima facie finds that no offence under that Act is made out.
The outcome depends on the specific averments of the complaint; the mere invocation of the special Act does not suffice.
For offences exclusively triable by the Court of Session, the Sessions Judge may still discharge the accused under Section 227 if sufficient ground to proceed is absent.
The magistrate-stage member concerns issue of process and commitment, not bail; the common point is the limited, prima facie scope of inquiry.

common_material_facts: A complaint with specific allegations of serious offences (caste-based abuse and assault; shooting causing death).
A preliminary-stage decision was made, either on anticipatory bail or on issue of process.
A court or magistrate was told or tempted to weigh the evidence in detail.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 18 of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
Sections 200, 202, 203, 204, 209 and 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the inquiry is limited to a prima facie assessment. Two (the anticipatory bail issues) hold that bail is barred or scrutiny is confined to the complaint's prima facie disclosure. One holds that the magistrate erred by meticulously weighing evidence and should have issued process and committed the case.
variations: Two members arise under the SC/ST Act bar on anticipatory bail, while one arises under the magistrate's powers in a complaint case.
One member (138839044_2) states only the scope of the inquiry. The others also state a concrete outcome (bail unavailable; process to issue and commit).
The SC/ST members reject High Court decisions as precedent against the statutory bar. The magistrate member relies on State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh.

split_suggestion: To get tighter rules, split into (a) the two SC/ST Act anticipatory bail issues (Section 18 bar and limited prima facie scrutiny) and (b) the magistrate's threshold under Sections 200-204 for offences exclusively triable by the Court of Session.

legal_question: Is a sale of secured property by a secured creditor or statutory financial corporation invalid where it was conducted in breach of the mandatory or fair sale procedure (inadequate notice, no written terms for a private treaty, or an unexplained unfair process), absent a waiver by the borrower?

rule.if: secured_asset_sale_by_creditor_or_statutory_corporation and (sale_notice_period_inadequate or private_treaty_without_written_terms or (sale_process_unfair_and_unexplained)) and not borrower_waived_protection

predicates.secured_asset_sale_by_creditor_or_statut: A secured creditor (under the SARFAESI Act and Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules) or a statutory financial corporation sold or tried to sell a secured asset in exercise of its statutory recovery powers.
predicates.sale_notice_period_inadequate: The sale notice gave less time than the law requires (e.g. under 30 days) or an unreasonably short period for prospective buyers to inspect and make offers.
predicates.private_treaty_without_written_terms: The asset was sold by a method other than public auction or tender (private treaty) without terms settled in writing between the relevant parties.
predicates.sale_process_unfair_and_unexplained: The sale process had irregularities (such as extreme haste, widely differing valuations, or the buyer paying before the offer deadline) that prevented fair participation and the best price, and the seller gave no credible explanation.
predicates.borrower_waived_protection: The borrower validly waived the procedural protection (e.g. the notice requirement) that was breached.
predicates.sale_is_invalid_and_liable_to_be_set_asi: The sale is null and void or otherwise invalid and cannot be sustained.

definition: A sale of secured property that does not comply with the mandatory statutory sale procedure (adequate notice, written terms for a private treaty) or that is conducted unreasonably and without credible explanation, so that fair participation and the best price are not secured, is invalid and may be set aside, unless the borrower validly waived the protection breached.
exceptions_or_limits: Waiver by the borrower of a protection that exists for the borrower's benefit may validate a non-compliant sale; no waiver was found in the member that discussed it.

For statutory financial corporations not governed by the SARFAESI Rules, invalidity rests on unfairness or unreasonableness judged against the best-price standard and on unexplained irregularities, not on breach of the Rules.
The unfair-process limb needs circumstances indicating abuse or unfairness plus the seller's failure to explain them; a mere short notice or a valuation difference alone may not suffice.

common_material_facts: A secured asset was sold by a bank or statutory financial corporation to enforce a security interest.
The sale departed from the prescribed or ordinary procedure (short notice, no written private-treaty terms, or hasty and irregular process).
The borrower or the challenger had not consented to the departure.
statutes_and_provisions: SARFAESI Act 2002, ss. 13(1) and 13(8)
Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules 2002, rr. 8(5), 8(6), 8(8) and 9(1)
Article 300A of the Constitution
State Financial Corporations Act 1951, s. 29
Article 226 of the Constitution
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members held the sale invalid, null and void or unsustainable, and set it aside or upheld the order setting it aside.
variations: Two members rest on breach of mandatory SARFAESI Rules (Mathew Varghese); one rests on the fairness and best-price standard under the State Financial Corporations Act and Article 226 review.
The trigger differs: short notice (139101201_2), no written private-treaty terms (53236279_1), or unexplained haste and irregularities with valuation differences and early payment (1770523_2).
Only one member discusses waiver (Ikbal).

legal_question: Does the doctrine of merger cause a lower court's reasoning to merge into, or become a declaration of law by, a superior court where the superior court disposes of an appeal without considering the merits or adopting that reasoning?

predicates.appeal_against_lower_court_order: The superior court was seised of an appeal against a decision of a lower court or tribunal.
predicates.superior_court_considered_merits_or_adop: The superior court examined the merits of the issues decided below and recorded a finding on them, or adopted, reiterated or expressly approved the lower court's reasoning.
predicates.lower_court_reasoning_does_not_merge_and: The lower court's reasoning does not merge into the superior court's order and is not a declaration of law binding under Article 141. At most the operative part is affected, and the lower court's decision otherwise continues to hold the field.

definition: Merger attaches to the operative part of the order. The lower court's reasoning merges, and becomes a declaration of law, only if the superior court considers the merits and records findings, or adopts or approves that reasoning. Where the superior court disposes of the appeal on a procedural or limited basis without doing so, the reasoning does not merge and no law is declared.
exceptions_or_limits: Merger applies to the reasoning where the superior court considers the merits and records findings, or adopts, reiterates or expressly approves the lower court's reasoning.
Merger is not universal. It depends on the nature and scope of the superior court's jurisdiction and the subject matter it considered.
Even where the reasoning does not merge, the operative part of the order may merge (as in the dismissal for non-joinder), or the superior court's limited alteration governs the operative result.
A declaration of law under Article 141 requires a decision that expressly or necessarily considers the point.

common_material_facts: A High Court decision was taken in appeal to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal on a limited or non-merits basis (a government undertaking to proceed by other means, modification of a time-limit direction only, or dismissal for non-impleadment of a necessary party).
The Supreme Court did not examine or approve the High Court's reasoning on the substantive issue.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 141 of the Constitution
Doctrine of merger
Shanmugaval Nadar v. State of Tamil Nadu, (1989) 4 SCC 187
Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the lower court's reasoning did not merge and was not treated as law declared by the Supreme Court. The High Court judgment continued to hold the field, or only the operative part was affected.
variations: One member concerns total non-merger of the High Court judgment, where the appeal was disposed of on a government statement.
One member concerns limited alteration of the order, so only the resulting operative order governs.
One member concerns dismissal for a party defect, where the operative part merged but the reasoning did not.

legal_question: Is an administrative export-canalisation or export-control policy an unreasonable restriction on the right to carry on trade under Article 19(1)(g) when it excludes producers from direct export and leaves them with no viable domestic market, no assured purchaser and no definite safeguards for fair allocation or prices?

rule.if: export_control_challenge_under_article_19_1_g and negligible_domestic_market and producers_excluded_from_direct_export and no_buyer_bound_to_purchase_producers_output and no_definite_safeguards_for_fair_allocation_or_price

predicates.export_control_challenge_under_article_1: The case challenges an administrative export-control or canalisation policy as infringing the right to carry on trade or business under Article 19(1)(g).
predicates.negligible_domestic_market: The commodity has practically no domestic market, so producers depend on export sales.
predicates.producers_excluded_from_direct_export: The affected producers, such as mine owners without prior export performance, cannot export directly and must sell through established exporters or a state trading corporation.
predicates.no_buyer_bound_to_purchase_producers_out: Neither the established exporters nor the state trading corporation is obliged to buy any quantity of the excluded producers' output.
predicates.no_definite_safeguards_for_fair_allocati: The policy lays down no definite rules guaranteeing excluded producers quotas, purchases, fair prices or fair treatment.
predicates.export_policy_is_unreasonable_restrictio: The policy is an unreasonable restriction on the right to carry on trade that fails the general reasonableness standard of Article 19(6).

definition: On the dissenting view of Subba Rao J., an administrative export-canalisation policy fails the reasonableness test of Article 19(6) if it shuts producers out of direct export, where there is no domestic market, and leaves them dependent on buyers who need not purchase and on no definite rules for fair allocation or prices. Article 19(6)(ii) does not itself authorise a monopoly created by administrative action, though such action may still be tested under the general reasonableness standard.
exceptions_or_limits: The conclusion is from a dissenting opinion. The majority rejected it in the case that is the source of these issues.
Even on the dissenting view, the appeal was dismissed as infructuous because the licensing period had expired.

The rule depends on the combination of facts: negligible domestic market, no obligation on buyers to purchase, and no safeguards. Where definite rules protect producers, or producers have a viable alternative market, the conclusion may differ.
Article 19(6)(ii) protects a monopoly created by a valid law, not one created by administrative action.

common_material_facts: Practically no domestic market for the ore.
Producers without export history could not export directly and depended on established exporters or the state trading corporation.
Buyers were not bound to purchase, so producers could be left without a market or forced to accept dictated terms.
Private export quotas were progressively reduced, leaving the state trading corporation as the virtual sole buyer.
No definite rules guaranteed quotas, purchases or fair prices.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 19(1)(g), Constitution of India
Article 19(6) (general reasonableness standard)
Article 19(6)(ii) (state monopoly; does not authorise a monopoly by administrative action)
Saghir Ahmad v. State of U.P., [1955] 1 SCR 707
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members record Subba Rao J.'s dissenting conclusion that the policy was an unreasonable restriction. The appeal was nonetheless dismissed or treated as infructuous because the licence period had expired, and the majority disagreed on the merits.
variations: One member stresses that the corporation's virtual monopoly resulted from the progressive reduction of private quotas.
One member states that the dissent concluded the restrictions destroyed or crippled the trade of the affected mine owners.
Members differ slightly in how they frame the Saghir Ahmad discussion: as general protection of business rights, or as the treatment of state monopolies.

legal_question: Does an unpaid final money judgment, decree or recovery certificate give a creditor a fresh cause of action to apply for corporate insolvency resolution, so that the application is within limitation if filed within three years of the judgment, decree or certificate (and is that rule good law)?

predicates.insolvency_application_by_creditor: A creditor has applied to commence corporate insolvency resolution under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.
predicates.unpaid_final_money_judgment_decree_or_re: A tribunal has finally adjudicated the debt by a money judgment or decree, or has issued a recovery certificate, and the amount due remains unpaid.
predicates.application_filed_within_three_years_of_: The insolvency application was filed within three years of the date of the judgment, decree or recovery certificate.
predicates.fresh_cause_of_action_arises_and_applica: The unpaid adjudicated debt gives a fresh cause of action, and limitation under Article 137 is measured from the judgment, decree or certificate rather than only from the earlier default, so the application is timely.

definition: Under Sections 7 and 238A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code read with Article 137 of the Limitation Act, a final money judgment, decree or recovery certificate that remains unpaid gives the creditor a fresh cause of action. An insolvency application filed within three years of it is within limitation, and the Dena Bank rule to this effect is not per incuriam.
exceptions_or_limits: Ordinarily limitation runs from the date of default; the fresh cause of action arises only where there is a final adjudication, decree or recovery certificate for the unpaid dues.
The application must be filed within three years of the judgment, decree or certificate.
Earlier decisions on limitation from default (such as Jignesh Shah and Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave) do not displace the rule because they did not decide the effect of a decree or recovery certificate.
The dues must remain unpaid when the application is filed.

common_material_facts: A final money judgment, decree or recovery certificate was issued in favour of the creditor.
The adjudicated or certified dues remained unpaid.
The Section 7 application was filed within three years of the judgment or certificate, though possibly later than three years from the original default.
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 3(6), 3(10), 3(11), 3(12) and 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code
Section 238A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code
Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members uphold the fresh cause of action: 2 hold the application timely because it was filed within three years of the judgment or certificate, and 1 affirms the underlying Dena Bank precedent as not per incuriam.
variations: Two members apply the rule to the facts of timeliness, while one addresses the precedential validity of the rule.
One member concerns a recovery certificate specifically, while another covers judgments, decrees and certificates generally.
One member reverses an appellate tribunal that had run limitation from the earlier default.

legal_question: Is a child born during the continuance of a valid marriage conclusively presumed to be legitimate under Section 112 of the Evidence Act, where the party denying legitimacy has not proved that the spouses had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten?

rule.if: legitimacy_disputed and child_born_during_valid_marriage and not nonaccess_proved

predicates.legitimacy_disputed: The legitimacy or paternity of the child is put in issue, for example in an inheritance, property or other proceeding, usually by the husband or someone claiming through him.
predicates.child_born_during_valid_marriage: The child was born while a valid marriage between the mother and the alleged father was subsisting.
predicates.nonaccess_proved: The party denying legitimacy has established by clear and satisfactory evidence, direct or circumstantial, that the spouses had no opportunity for marital intercourse at any time when the child could have been begotten.
predicates.child_presumed_legitimate: The child is held to be the legitimate child of the husband under the Section 112 presumption, which is not displaced.

definition: Under Section 112 of the Evidence Act, birth during a valid marriage is conclusive proof of legitimacy. It can be displaced only by clear and satisfactory proof that the spouses had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten. Mere denial of paternity, disputes between the spouses, or living apart, without proof of no opportunity for intercourse, does not rebut it.
exceptions_or_limits: The presumption is displaced if non-access is proved at the time when the child could have been begotten.
The burden of proving non-access lies on the person denying legitimacy, and the proof must be clear and satisfactory.
Access means the existence of opportunities for marital intercourse, not actual intercourse. Spouses living apart in the same village or nearby houses does not establish non-access.
The rule requires a valid marriage at the time of birth.

common_material_facts: The child was born during the subsistence of a valid marriage.
The husband or his side denied paternity or legitimacy.
The spouses were estranged or living separately but close by, and no evidence showed lack of opportunity for intercourse.
Courts below made concurrent findings of legitimacy.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 112, Indian Evidence Act, 1872
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the presumption of legitimacy stood because non-access was not proved.
variations: The context differs: a family property claim, an inheritance claim by the child, and a general legitimacy dispute.
One member relies on Chilukuri Venkateswarlu, Karapaya and Ammathayee, one relies on Karapaya for the meaning of access, and one cites no earlier case.
One member states the test as when the husband could, in the ordinary course of nature, have fathered the child, while the others refer to any time when the child could have been begotten.

legal_question: Is a later civil suit barred where it raises, or seeks to reopen, a question about rights in land that could or ought to have been raised and was (or could have been) decided by the competent consolidation or revenue authorities in earlier proceedings that have become final?

rule.if: later_civil_suit_concerning_land_rights and competent_consolidation_or_revenue_authority_had_jurisdiction_over_the_matter and matter_was_or_could_or_ought_to_have_been_raised_in_earlier_proceedings and earlier_proceedings_became_final and not later_suit_challenges_legality_of_earlier_proceedings_on_a_ground_open_to_civil_court

predicates.later_civil_suit_concerning_land_rights: A civil (or revenue) suit is brought later and concerns title, possession or other rights or interests in land.
predicates.competent_consolidation_or_revenue_autho: The consolidation authorities (for land in a notified consolidation area) or the revenue authorities had jurisdiction to adjudicate the question now raised.
predicates.matter_was_or_could_or_ought_to_have_bee: The question in the later suit was actually decided, or could or ought to have been raised, in the earlier consolidation or revenue proceedings.
predicates.earlier_proceedings_became_final: The earlier consolidation or revenue decision or allotment attained finality, for example through completion of the proceedings, dismissal of review, or non-challenge.
predicates.later_suit_challenges_legality_of_earlie: The later suit validly challenges the legality or validity of the earlier proceedings on a ground a civil court can examine, such as a jurisdictional defect.
predicates.later_civil_suit_is_barred: The civil court cannot entertain the suit, or the omitted issue cannot be raised in it, because of a statutory bar or constructive res judicata.

definition: A civil suit on rights in land is barred where the issue was, or could and ought to have been, decided by the competent consolidation or revenue authorities in proceedings that became final. The bar rests on the statutory exclusion of civil courts under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, or on constructive res judicata for revenue proceedings.
exceptions_or_limits: The bar applies only where the consolidation or revenue authority had jurisdiction over the matter; a suit that properly challenges the legality or validity of the earlier proceedings may lie, as one member notes.

The statutory bar (Section 49 of the Consolidation Act) depends on the land being in a notified consolidation area. Outside that setting, as in the revenue-proceedings member, the bar rests on constructive res judicata.
A mutation entry alone does not confer title; the bar arises from the final adjudication, not from the mutation entry as such.
Disputes arising after consolidation operations had been completed under the earlier statutory scheme were distinguished in one member.

common_material_facts: Earlier consolidation or revenue authorities had adjudicated or could have adjudicated the competing claims to the land.
The earlier decision or allotment had become final.
A later civil suit sought to reopen or contest the land rights or an underlying question.
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 4(2), 5(2) and 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953
Section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 (bar on civil and revenue courts)
Principle of constructive res judicata
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the later suit, or the omitted issue, barred: 2 under the statutory bar of the Consolidation Act and 1 under constructive res judicata.
variations: Two members rest on the statutory jurisdictional bar in a notified consolidation area; the third rests on constructive res judicata for revenue proceedings.

One member involves a suit seeking a declaration that the consolidation order was without jurisdiction; another involves a possession suit after denotification; the third involves a challenge to a claimed relationship to the original allottee.
The revenue-proceedings member reserves review of the legality of the earlier proceedings in an appropriate civil suit, which the suit before it did not pursue.

legal_question: Does a tenant who has lost, or failed to preserve, the status or step on which a statutory tenant-based right depends (holding the tenancy through the decree for pre-emption, or delivering possession by the decreed date for reoccupation) lose entitlement to the statutory remedy?

predicates.statutory_tenant_remedy_claim: The tenant claims a remedy conferred by statute on tenants, such as pre-emption on the basis of tenancy or reoccupation after an eviction for rebuilding.
predicates.remedy_conditioned_on_tenant_status_or_c: The statute makes the remedy depend on the claimant holding the qualifying tenancy or on complying with a specified condition, such as delivering possession by a date fixed in the decree.
predicates.tenancy_ended_before_decree: The claimant's tenancy ended, by eviction order, eviction decree or dispossession, after the sale and before the pre-emption decree, even if physical dispossession had not occurred.
predicates.required_step_not_performed_by_stipulate: The tenant did not perform the step the statute requires, such as delivering possession on or before the date specified in the decree, within the stipulated time.
predicates.tenant_not_entitled_to_statutory_remedy: The tenant cannot obtain the statutory remedy, whether a pre-emption decree or restoration of possession.

definition: Where a statute gives a tenant a remedy only if the tenant keeps the qualifying tenancy status or complies with a stipulated condition, the tenant loses the remedy if the tenancy ends before the decree (an eviction order suffices, without physical dispossession) or if the tenant misses the stipulated time for the required step.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule applies only where the statute makes the right depend on continuing tenant status or on timely compliance; it does not extend to remedies without such conditions.
For pre-emption, the claimant must have been a tenant at the time of sale and must hold that status up to the decree.

The members rest on different statutes. The two pre-emption members apply the Punjab Pre-emption Act and the reoccupation member applies the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, so the shared point is a general one about strict conditions on tenant remedies.

common_material_facts: The claimant was a tenant when the triggering event occurred (sale of the land or a rebuilding eviction decree).
The tenant's position changed adversely before the final relief: an eviction order or decree, dispossession, or late delivery of possession.
The tenant sought a statutory tenant-based remedy: pre-emption or reoccupation.
statutes_and_provisions: Punjab Pre-emption Act, 1913, s. 15(1)(a) Fourthly
Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, ss. 13(1) proviso (g), 15 and 15(3)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All three members deny the tenant the statutory remedy: two pre-emption claims fail because the tenancy ended before the decree, and one reoccupation claim fails because possession was delivered late.
variations: Two members concern pre-emption and require the tenancy to continue to the decree; one concerns reoccupation after rebuilding and turns on a deadline in the decree.
In one pre-emption case the claimant was actually dispossessed. In the other the eviction order alone ended the tenancy.
The pre-emption members rely on precedent (the Court overruled some earlier decisions and approved others). The reoccupation member cites no earlier cases.

split_suggestion: Optionally split into (a) pre-emption cases where the tenant must keep tenancy status through the decree (1413134_1, 580610_1) and (b) the reoccupation case turning on timely delivery of possession under s. 15(3) (1854410_1).

legal_question: What is the scope of an executing court's power under section 47 CPC to construe a decree and consider objections in execution, given that it must execute the decree as it stands and cannot vary it or go behind it?

predicates.execution_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding to execute a decree, including a question arising between the parties under section 47 CPC.
predicates.executing_court_asked_to_construe_decree: The executing court is asked to interpret the decree in light of applicable law, or to consider an objection to execution based on law that does not attack the decree's validity or correctness.
predicates.outcome_requires_altering_express_decree: Granting the request would change, contradict or substitute the clear operative terms of the decree, for example by treating an expressly stated liability as discharged.
predicates.executing_court_may_construe_decree_and_: The executing court may interpret the decree in light of applicable law and entertain the objection, and acting on that basis is not a variation of the decree.

definition: An executing court must execute a decree as passed and cannot modify it or go behind it. It may still construe the decree in light of applicable law, or consider an objection that a law, including a later change in law, affects compliance or enforceability, because doing so does not vary the decree. It may not use interpretation to contradict the decree's clear terms.
exceptions_or_limits: The executing court cannot use interpretation to make a new decree or contradict clear terms fixing a party's liability.
The objection must go to enforceability or compliance, not to the validity or correctness of the decree.
Consideration of an objection based on later law permits refusal of execution only if the later law actually removed the decree-holder's right to enforce the decree.

Treating an act as compliant under a legal rule, such as performance at the first practicable opportunity after court closure, depends on the decree's deadline falling on a day when the court was closed.

common_material_facts: A decree was sought to be executed and a party raised a dispute in execution under section 47 CPC.
The dispute turned on the effect of the law or the decree's terms on enforcement, not on the decree's validity.
The executing court was asked to construe or give effect to the decree.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Order XXI, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: The executing court's power to construe the decree in light of law and to hear enforceability objections was upheld in 2 of 3 members. In 1 of 3 the executing court was held to have exceeded its power by recording satisfaction contrary to the decree's express terms.
variations: One member concerns construing a deposit deadline in light of the rule permitting an act at the first practicable opportunity after court closure.
One concerns a later change in law divesting the decree-holder of the proprietary right underlying the decree.
One concerns an attempt to record full satisfaction contrary to the decree's stated liability, which was refused.

split_suggestion: Optionally split into (a) permissible construction or consideration of objections in light of law (1422366_2, 437793_1) and (b) the bar on altering express decree terms (811397_2).

legal_question: Can a death sentence imposed for murder be maintained where the accused personally inflicted fatal injuries in a brutal, deliberate killing and a motive is shown?

predicates.sentencing_appeal_against_death_sentence: The case is an appeal or review in which a death sentence imposed or confirmed by the courts below is challenged.
predicates.accused_personally_inflicted_fatal_injur: The evidence establishes that the accused himself inflicted the fatal injury or injuries on the victim, rather than being liable only constructively.
predicates.killing_brutal_and_deliberate: The Court finds the killing brutal, callous or determined, showing a deliberate intention to kill, including an attack on a helpless victim or repeated or severe blows.
predicates.death_sentence_maintained: The Court declines to interfere with the death sentence and upholds it as justified.

definition: The Court will uphold a death sentence where the accused is shown to have personally inflicted fatal injuries in a brutal and deliberate killing. A motive such as pre-existing enmity or property gain, or a helpless victim, reinforces this finding but is not stated as indispensable by every member.
exceptions_or_limits: The members give little reasoning and cite no structured sentencing test; they rest on the brutality and deliberateness of the killing and, in two members, a motive.

In one member, death sentences were confined to the accused who personally inflicted the fatal injuries, while co-participants did not receive the extreme penalty. Section 34 was not used to justify the death sentence.
The rule rests on the Court finding no reason to interfere with the sentence below. It does not state when a death sentence would be commuted.

common_material_facts: The accused personally inflicted fatal injuries on the victim or victims.
The Court described the killing as brutal, callous or determined.
A motive was shown in two of the three members: pre-existing enmity in one, property gain in another.
A death sentence had already been imposed or confirmed by the courts below.
statutes_and_provisions: Indian Penal Code Section 302
Indian Penal Code Section 34 (noted as not needed to justify the sentence)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members maintain the death sentence and decline to interfere.
variations: One member stresses the helplessness of the victim and pre-existing enmity.
One member stresses medical evidence of necessarily fatal injuries and the individual attribution of those injuries.
One member stresses a property-related motive and two killings, and refers to Dalbir Singh v. State of Punjab on reasons weighing toward death.
Only one member cites an earlier case; the others cite no authority for the sentencing conclusion.

legal_question: Can a later judicial decision that determines rights affecting taxable income constitute definite information for reopening an assessment under section 34 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, and, once validly reopened, may the reassessment cover all income that escaped assessment for the year?

predicates.reassessment_proceeding: The tax authority has issued a notice to reopen a completed assessment under section 34 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
predicates.later_judicial_decision_determines_tax_r: A judicial decision given after the original assessment determines ownership or entitlement rights that bear on who is taxable on the income, and it is relied on as the information for reopening.
predicates.income_escaped_assessment: Assessable income was omitted or left untaxed in the original assessment, even though a return was filed.
predicates.reassessment_valid_and_may_cover_all_esc: The reopening is valid because the decision is definite information, the earlier under-assessment is set aside, the assessment begins afresh, and the authority may and must assess the entire escaped income for that year.

definition: A later judicial decision that settles rights affecting taxable income is definite information under section 34(1)(b) of the 1922 Act. If it shows that assessable income escaped assessment, the reopening is valid, and the authority may reassess the whole income that escaped for the year, not merely the part that first justified reopening.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule depends on income having actually escaped assessment; a filed return does not by itself prevent this.
It is stated under section 34 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, and the members do not address later statutes.
The decision must be relevant to the taxpayer's liability. The members rely on non-disclosure of the compromise, but do not make non-disclosure a separate condition.

common_material_facts: Ownership of a mill and its income was in litigation when the original returns were filed.
