The taxpayer did not disclose the compromise under which he obtained the mill's income.
A later Privy Council decision held that the vendor was the absolute owner and the vendor's sons had no interest.
The tax officer reopened the assessment after that decision.
The taxpayer argued that reassessment should be confined to part of the income.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 34(1)(b), Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Section 34 read with section 22(2), Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Maharaj Kumar Kamal Singh v. Commissioner of Income-tax
Kamakhya Narain Singh's case
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members uphold the reassessment. Two hold the later judicial decision to be definite information, and two hold that valid reopening allows assessment of the entire escaped income. One member decides both points.
variations: 1429523_1 deals only with whether the decision is definite information.
1429523_2 deals only with the scope of reassessment after valid reopening.
754385_1 decides both points and also cites section 22(2) and Kamakhya Narain Singh's case.

legal_question: Under Sections 5A and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, is a landowner who has been heard in the objection inquiry entitled to a further hearing by the government after the collector's report is submitted and before the final acquisition declaration?

rule.if: land_acquisition_proceeding and objector_heard_in_section_5A_inquiry and report_and_objection_record_submitted_to_government and government_considered_report

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The matter concerns a land acquisition proceeding under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, in which objections are inquired into under Section 5A and a declaration is made under Section 6.
predicates.objector_heard_in_section_5A_inquiry: The landowner or objector filed objections and was given a real opportunity to be heard in the inquiry conducted by the collector or other officer.
predicates.report_and_objection_record_submitted_to: The inquiring officer submitted a report, with the objections and record of the inquiry, to the government.
predicates.government_considered_report: The government considered the officer's report and the material before it before deciding whether to issue the declaration.
predicates.no_further_hearing_required_before_final: The statute does not require the government to give the objector a second hearing after the report is submitted and before the final declaration.

definition: Where a landowner has been heard in the Section 5A objection inquiry and the officer's report and record go to the government, which considers them, no second hearing by the government is required before the Section 6 declaration. The report is recommendatory, and the government forms its own satisfaction on the record.
exceptions_or_limits: Applies only where the objector actually received a full opportunity to be heard in the Section 5A inquiry; the members stress that natural justice must be satisfied in that inquiry.
Does not decide whether other statutory or constitutional requirements apply, or whether the government's decision is otherwise open to challenge.

common_material_facts: Objectors filed objections and were heard in the Section 5A inquiry
The collector or inquiring officer submitted a report to the government
The government considered the report and proceeded to the acquisition declaration
The objectors argued that they were entitled to a further hearing
statutes_and_provisions: Section 5A, Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Section 6, Land Acquisition Act, 1894
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that no further or second hearing is required after the report is submitted to the government.
variations: One member relies on State of Gujarat v. Ambalal Haiderbhai on natural justice in inquiries
One member follows Abdul Husein Tayabali v. State of Gujarat
One member stresses that the report is merely recommendatory and the government forms its own satisfaction
The members differ in how much they say about the Section 6 declaration, but all reach the same outcome

legal_question: Can a sale be treated as a mortgage by conditional sale under Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, when the condition for repurchase or reconveyance is contained in a separate document and not in the document that effects or purports to effect the sale?

predicates.transaction_is_sale_with_condition_of_re: The property was transferred by an ostensible sale and the transferee agreed that the property would be transferred back on certain terms, such as repayment of the price.
predicates.repurchase_condition_not_embodied_in_doc: The sale deed or other document that effects or purports to effect the sale does not itself contain the condition for transfer back.
predicates.repurchase_condition_contained_in_separa: The covenant or agreement to repurchase or reconvey appears in a distinct document from the sale deed, even if executed or registered around the same time.
predicates.transaction_not_mortgage_by_conditional_: The transaction cannot be characterised as a mortgage by conditional sale; it is a sale with a personal right of repurchase enforceable according to the agreement, and a claim of mortgage or redemption on that footing fails.

definition: Under Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, a sale is a mortgage by conditional sale only if the condition for repurchase or reconveyance is embodied in the document that effects or purports to effect the sale. Where the condition is in a separate document, the transaction is a sale with a repurchase right and not a mortgage, so a claim of mortgage or redemption fails.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule turns on the statutory proviso to Section 58(c); where the condition is embodied in the sale document itself, the intention of the parties is assessed from the language of the document and surrounding circumstances to decide whether it is a mortgage.
Separate execution or registration on the same day does not by itself bring the condition within the sale document.
The consequence is that the transferor has only a personal right to repurchase enforceable according to the agreement, not a right of redemption.

common_material_facts: A sale deed conveyed the property outright.
The covenant or agreement to reconvey was in a separate document, sometimes executed or registered on the same day.
The claimant sought to characterise the transaction as a mortgage, by conditional sale or securing a loan, and in one case sought redemption.
statutes_and_provisions: Transfer of Property Act, 1882, Section 58(c) and its proviso
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the mortgage-by-conditional-sale characterisation was rejected; the transaction was treated as a sale with a condition of repurchase.
variations: One member frames the point as inadmissibility of proof of the mortgage characterisation, in a specific performance proceeding.
Another member adds the distinction that a mortgage leaves a debt and a right to redeem, while a sale with repurchase creates only a personal right.
A third member arose in a redemption suit appeal and notes that intention is read from the documents and surrounding circumstances, but the proviso still applies.
The members cite different supporting precedents, but all apply the same statutory requirement.

legal_question: Does joining, or the presence of, a person claiming through or succeeding to a tenant (a subtenant, invalid subtenant or legal representative) in a landlord's rent eviction proceeding against the tenant change its character, for example into a proceeding against a trespasser, so as to oust the rent forum's jurisdiction or defeat the proceeding?

predicates.landlord_tenant_eviction_proceeding_unde: The proceeding is a landlord's eviction or ejectment action concerning tenanted premises that falls within a rent-control statute or rent forum's jurisdiction.
predicates.person_claiming_through_or_succeeding_te: A subtenant, invalid subtenant, other person claiming under the tenant, or the deceased tenant's legal representative has been joined or substituted as a party.
predicates.proceeding_remains_one_for_eviction_of_t: The proceeding continues as a landlord-tenant matter, with relief sought against the tenant or the tenant's estate and not only against the joined person as a stranger or trespasser.
predicates.person_claims_trespasser_status_or_indep: The joined person asserts that they are a trespasser, hold independent title, or that their own tenancy or subtenancy is invalid, in order to argue that the rent forum lacks jurisdiction.
predicates.proceeding_retains_character_and_rent_fo: The proceeding keeps its landlord-tenant character, the rent forum retains jurisdiction, and the joined person cannot defeat the proceeding on that basis.

definition: Joining or substituting a person who claims through a tenant, or who succeeds the tenant, does not turn a landlord-tenant eviction proceeding into one against a trespasser or take it outside the rent forum's jurisdiction. The joined person cannot defeat the proceeding by pleading trespasser status, invalid subtenancy, or independent title that the rent forum cannot decide.
exceptions_or_limits: Where eviction is ordered against the subtenant alone as a trespasser and no eviction order is made against the tenants-in-chief, the proceeding becomes one between an owner and a trespasser and falls outside the rent statute (the Hiralal Vallabhram distinction).
A legal representative may be joined in a personal capacity to assert independent title only where the forum has jurisdiction to determine that title, which a rent authority lacks.
A person claiming through a tenant is a proper party, not a necessary party, because a possession decree against the tenant binds those claiming under the tenant.

common_material_facts: A landlord's eviction or ejectment proceeding against a tenant is pending before a rent forum.
A person deriving rights from the tenant (subtenant, invalid subtenant, or heir/legal representative) is added as a party.
The added person argues that they are a trespasser or that the forum lacks jurisdiction.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
Order XXII Rule 4(1) and 4(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Importers and Manufacturers Ltd. v. Pheroz Framroze Taraporewala
Hiralal Vallabhram v. Kastorbhai Lalbhai (distinguished)
Jagdish Chander Chatterjee v. Sri Kishan
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the proceeding keeps its landlord-tenant character and the rent forum retains jurisdiction, so the trespasser or jurisdictional objection fails.
variations: One member concerns a legal representative substituted after the tenant's death under Order XXII Rule 4, and two concern subtenants joined under Section 28 of the Bombay Rent Act.
One member emphasises that the forum lacks jurisdiction to decide independent title; the others emphasise that joinder does not alter the suit's character.
One member treats the joined person as a proper but not necessary party; another treats the joined person as an invalid subtenant.

legal_question: Can the age of a document (more than thirty years old) alone, under Section 90 of the Evidence Act, be used to presume due execution and attestation of a will, particularly where only a copy is produced, or must the will and its execution be proved by the ordinary rules for wills and secondary evidence?

rule.if: will_or_old_document_relied_on and document_more_than_thirty_years_old and (document_is_a_will_requiring_statutory_proof or only_copy_produced_instead_of_original)

predicates.will_or_old_document_relied_on: A party relies on a will, or on an alleged copy of a will or other old document, to establish rights in a civil dispute.
predicates.document_more_than_thirty_years_old: The document, or the copy relied on, is more than thirty years old, and the party invokes that age to seek a presumption.
predicates.document_is_a_will_requiring_statutory_p: The document is a will, whose execution and attestation must be proved under the Succession Act (s. 63(c)) read with s. 68 of the Evidence Act.
predicates.only_copy_produced_instead_of_original: The original document is not produced and only a copy (whether or not admitted as secondary evidence) is relied on.
predicates.section_90_presumption_of_due_execution_: The court does not presume due execution and attestation of the will or original from age (and proper custody) alone; at most the signatures authenticating an admissible copy may be presumed genuine, and execution must be proved by the legally required evidence.

definition: Age of more than thirty years does not by itself give rise to a presumption that a will was duly executed and attested; a will must be proved under the Succession Act and Evidence Act requirements. Where only a copy is produced, Section 90 does not extend to the original's execution even if the copy is admitted as secondary evidence, and a copy not admissible as secondary evidence cannot be used at all.
exceptions_or_limits: A copy must first qualify as secondary evidence under sections 63 and 65 of the Evidence Act; otherwise it is excluded altogether.
Where an admissible copy is produced from proper custody, the signatures authenticating the copy may be presumed genuine, but this does not extend to due execution or attestation of the original.
Admission of a copy as secondary evidence only proves its contents; execution of the original must still be proved by other legally required evidence.

common_material_facts: A will or alleged copy of a will more than thirty years old was relied on
The party sought a presumption of due execution and attestation based on age
In two members the original was not produced and only a copy or translation was available
statutes_and_provisions: Section 90, Indian Evidence Act
Section 68, Indian Evidence Act
Sections 63 and 65, Indian Evidence Act
Section 63(c), Indian Succession Act
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members refuse to apply the Section 90 presumption of due execution and attestation: 1 for a will generally, 1 where the copy was inadmissible as secondary evidence, and 1 where the copy was admitted but gave no presumption for the original.
variations: One member concerns an original will and holds Section 90 inapplicable to wills as such.
One member concerns an inadmissible copy/translation with no foundation for secondary evidence, so it was excluded.
One member concerns a certified copy validly admitted as secondary evidence from proper custody, where only authenticating signatures could be presumed.

legal_question: Does a purported partition deed or expression of intention to separate sever joint family status where it is a sham, made to defeat family members' rights and not acted upon?

predicates.purported_partition_or_separation_expres: A partition deed or other expression of an intention to separate was relied upon as severing the joint family status.
predicates.expression_was_sham_not_genuinely_intend: The deed or expression was found to be a pretence, made to defeat the claims of family members or avoid legal consequences, and was not intended to be effective.
predicates.family_continued_joint_possession_and_li: After the deed the family members continued in joint possession of the property and lived (and messed) together as before.
predicates.joint_family_status_not_severed: The joint family status continues because the purported deed did not effect severance.

definition: A definite, unequivocal and communicated intention by a coparcener to separate can sever joint status. A purported partition deed or expression of intention that is a mere pretence, made to defeat family claims and not acted upon, does not sever joint status. Concurrent findings of sham, supported by evidence such as unequal division and continued joint living and possession, are ordinarily accepted.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the expression of intention to separate is genuine, definite, unequivocal and clearly communicated to the other coparceners; such an expression can sever status without their assent.
In a special leave appeal, concurrent findings that the deed is a sham are accepted unless they lack evidentiary support.
Continued joint living and possession are evidence supporting the finding of sham, not by themselves a separate condition stated by the Court as necessary.

common_material_facts: A partition deed between brothers divided the lands unequally and made no provision for the family house.
The brothers continued in joint possession and lived and dined together after the deed.
Courts found the deed was intended to limit or defeat the widows' claims and avoid the consequences of a possible adoption.
statutes_and_provisions: Merla Ramanna v. Chelikani Jagannadha Rao, A.I.R. 1941 P.C. 48 (severance by unequivocal intention; a sham does not suffice)
Anant v. Shankar, A.I.R. 1943 P.C. 196 (uncertainty about the effect of a widow's adoption)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 issues hold that the deed was sham (1 issue on the factual finding) and so did not sever joint family status (2 issues).
variations: 1457288_1 deals with the factual characterisation of the deed as sham and the acceptance of concurrent findings, while 1457288_2 and 270552_2 deal with the legal consequence for severance.
270552_2 appears to be the same dispute as 1457288 (same facts, same authority), phrased with slightly different predicates.

legal_question: When is a sale of property to or of a minor, made through a guardian or parent without consideration, genuineness, authority or court permission, ineffective against the claimant who challenges it?

rule.if: minor_involved_in_impugned_sale and sale_made_through_guardian_or_parent and (sale_without_consideration_and_not_genuine or (guardian_lacked_authority and court_permission_absent))

predicates.minor_involved_in_impugned_sale: The impugned sale was made to a minor as buyer, or concerned a minor's immovable property as seller.
predicates.sale_made_through_guardian_or_parent: The sale was effected by a person acting as the minor's guardian or parent.
predicates.sale_without_consideration_and_not_genui: The court found, on the circumstances, that the sale was not supported by consideration and was not a genuine transaction.
predicates.guardian_lacked_authority: The parent who executed the sale of the minor's property was not the person with authority to act as natural guardian, for example because the other parent remained present and involved.
predicates.court_permission_absent: The prior permission of the court required for alienating a minor's immovable property was not obtained.
predicates.sale_not_binding_on_claimant: The sale does not bind the claimant, either because it is ineffective against that claimant or because it is void.

definition: A sale involving a minor and made through a guardian or parent does not bind the claimant who challenges it, where it is found to be without consideration and not genuine. It is likewise ineffective, and void rather than merely voidable, where the parent lacked authority as guardian and the court's prior permission was not obtained.
exceptions_or_limits: The two limbs rest on different grounds: a factual finding of no consideration or genuineness (two members), and want of guardian authority plus absence of court permission under Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 (one member).

Voidness rather than voidability was held only where the mother sold while the father remained present and involved. Where the father is effectively absent from the minor's affairs, the distinguished earlier decision suggests a different result.
Whether a general challenge to alienations in the pleadings covers the sale depends on the disputed property being included in the schedule to the plaint.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns a sale of a minor's own property by a mother without authority and without court permission under Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, and decides void versus voidable and limitation. The other two members concern a sale to a minor that was without consideration and not genuine.

common_material_facts: A minor is a party to the impugned sale, with a guardian or parent acting for the minor.
The sale was challenged by a family member or the minor, as claimant, in a property suit.
Findings of fact were made that the sale lacked consideration, genuineness or justification, such as legal necessity.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 8, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 (in 80881_2 only)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members held the sale not binding on the claimant: 2 for want of consideration and genuineness, and 1 because the sale was void for lack of guardian authority and court permission.
variations: Two members turn on factual findings (minor buyer with no property of her own, seller as guardian, no consideration), while one turns on statutory guardianship authority.
One member also addresses whether the pleadings encompassed the sale, and another addresses limitation.
The members differ on the sale's position: a sale to a minor versus a sale of a minor's property.

split_suggestion: Group 1457288_4 and 270552_5, which concern a sale to a minor without consideration that is not genuine. Treat 80881_2 separately as a guardian's authority and court permission issue under Section 8 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956.

legal_question: Can an executive or planning authority permit a land use that conflicts with the use designated in the statutory development plan or master plan without following the statutory procedure for amending or changing the plan?

predicates.development_plan_designates_use: A statutory development plan, master plan or zoning regulation designates the land or sector for a specified use (for example residential, or public and semi-public use).
predicates.proposed_use_conflicts_with_designated_u: The use proposed or actually made of the land (for example commercial, industrial or restaurant use) is different from, or prohibited under, the designated use.
predicates.statutory_plan_change_process_followed: The plan was lawfully amended or changed through the route the governing statute prescribes, including any required basis, public interest finding, consistency with other laws and publication or objections procedure.
predicates.conflicting_land_use_cannot_be_validly_a: An executive direction, policy decision, ordinary permission or approval cannot validly authorize the conflicting use, and any such authorization or conversion is invalid.

definition: Where a statutory plan designates a land use, the State or planning authority cannot permit a conflicting use by executive direction, policy decision or ordinary permission. The use can be changed only by lawfully amending or changing the plan through the prescribed statutory process.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the statute supplies a power and procedure for changing the use and that procedure is actually followed, with its conditions met (for example a stated basis, public interest, and publication inviting objections).
Ordinary permission provisions that govern changes conforming to the plan and zoning regulations cannot authorize a use that those regulations prohibit.
A public notice inviting suggestions on a possible change does not amount to a lawful amendment unless the statutory process is finalized.

common_material_facts: Land was designated in a development plan, master plan or zoning regulation for a specific use (residential, or auditorium/cinema for public and semi-public purposes).
A different use (industrial, commercial, restaurant) was allowed or sought by executive direction, authority action or ordinary permission.
No lawful plan-amendment or change-of-use process was shown to have been completed.
statutes_and_provisions: Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973
U.P. Industrial Area Development Act, 1976, ss. 6(2)(b), 6(2)(h), 7, 8, 14, 18, 19; NOIDA plan regulations 1991 and Building Regulations 2006
Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, ss. 13(3), 14(1), 14(2), 14-A, 15
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All three members (3 of 3) hold that the conflicting use cannot be authorized through executive action or ordinary permission, and the authorization or conversion fails absent a lawful plan-change process.
variations: One member concerns an executive allotment for a printing press on land reserved for public use.
One concerns unauthorized commercial use of residential plots in an industrial development area.
One concerns the interplay between ordinary permission provisions and the provision for changes from the development plan, which operate in different fields.

legal_question: In a pending or remanded rent-control eviction proceeding where the originally pleaded ground has been defeated, superseded or is uncertain, may the landlord be allowed to amend or file fresh pleadings on another statutory ground, with the other side given a fair opportunity to respond, instead of the proceeding being ended and the parties sent to fresh litigation?

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding_pending: An eviction proceeding under a rent-control statute is pending (at trial or appeal/revision stage) or has been remitted for fresh disposal.
predicates.original_ground_unavailable_superseded_o: The ground originally pleaded has been defeated by a later event, superseded by statutory amendment, or is otherwise uncertain, so that the landlord may not succeed on it.
predicates.another_statutory_ground_available_to_la: The statute permits another legally permissible ground for eviction on which the landlord may rely.
predicates.landlord_seeks_to_plead_that_ground: The landlord applies or is willing to amend or file fresh pleadings setting out the other ground, whether as a substitute or alternative.
predicates.fair_opportunity_to_respond_and_lead_evi: The opposing party can file a response and both sides can lead additional evidence on the new ground.
predicates.landlord_may_be_permitted_to_amend_or_fi: The court may allow the amended or fresh pleading on the other ground and continue the existing proceeding rather than terminating it and requiring new litigation.

definition: To avoid needless fresh litigation and delay, a court dealing with a pending or remitted rent-control eviction case may allow the landlord to plead another legally permissible ground, by amendment or fresh pleading, and let the case go on, giving both sides a fair chance to plead and lead evidence. Findings already settled, and statutory conditions on the new ground, remain binding.
exceptions_or_limits: Findings already finally established against the landlord (e.g. a statutory disability) cannot be reopened.

The new ground must be one the statute permits, and any statutory conditions on it (waiting period, permission requirements) must be met; where the statute defines institution, the suit is treated as instituted on the new ground when the fresh pleading is filed.
Permission is generally conditional on the landlord applying and on fairness to the tenant, including an opportunity to respond and lead evidence.
One member treats the permission as discretionary, with no specific provision cited.

common_material_facts: Eviction proceeding already pending, on appeal or revision, or remitted
The originally pleaded ground was defeated, superseded or uncertain
Another statutory ground was available to the landlord
Court allowed further pleadings and evidence to avoid prolonged litigation
statutes_and_provisions: Section 10(3)(iii), Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960
Amended eviction grounds for transferee-landlords, with a post-transfer waiting period and a safety-related permission exception
General statutory grounds for eviction under the Rent Control Act (alternative pleading on remand; no specific provision cited)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members allow the landlord to plead another statutory ground in the existing proceeding, with opportunity for responsive pleadings and evidence, rather than ending the proceeding.
variations: One member rests on a later event defeating the original ground, with a preserved finding of disability.
One member rests on statutory amendment, treating the fresh pleading as the date of institution, subject to the waiting period or safety permission.
One member concerns remand, permitting alternative pleading on application, with a personal-requirement ground suggested.

legal_question: When may the Supreme Court enhance a custodial sentence on the ground that the sentence imposed is grossly or manifestly inadequate in light of the gravity and circumstances of the offence?

predicates.criminal_appeal: The matter is before the appellate court in a criminal appeal, whether against conviction or against the adequacy of the sentence.
predicates.grave_offence: The offence is serious or brutal, such as culpable homicide or an attack causing permanent grievous injury.
predicates.custodial_sentence_imposed_is_very_short: The court below imposed only a brief term of imprisonment, or reduced the sentence to the short period already undergone.
predicates.sentence_grossly_inadequate_to_gravity_a: Considering the nature of the offence, the manner of its commission and its consequences, the sentence is grossly or manifestly inadequate, with no adequate reasons for leniency and a fine alone not meeting the gravity of the offence.
predicates.custodial_sentence_enhanced_to_proportio: The appellate court increases the custodial sentence to a term proportionate to the gravity of the offence.

definition: Where an offence is grave and the custodial sentence imposed is very short or limited to time already served, so that it is grossly or manifestly inadequate given the offence's nature and consequences, the Supreme Court may enhance it to a proportionate term of imprisonment.
exceptions_or_limits: Enhancement depends on the sentence being grossly or manifestly inadequate, not merely lenient.
Where the court below gave genuine, relevant reasons for a lower sentence, the case for enhancement is weaker; the members involved unexplained or unreasoned leniency.
A fine or compensation alone does not cure an inadequate custodial sentence for a grave offence (stated in one member).
The sentence must remain proportionate; the enhanced terms differ by offence (five years, six years).

common_material_facts: A grave offence (culpable homicide, a sword attack severing a hand, or another grave crime).
The custodial sentence was very short, often reduced to the period already undergone (less than six months or a few days).
The court below gave no particular reasons for the leniency (two members).
The Supreme Court found the sentence grossly or manifestly inadequate and substituted a longer rigorous imprisonment.
statutes_and_provisions: No specific statutory provision is relied on in the sentencing decisions; reliance is on general sentencing principles and, in one member, a line of sentencing precedents.
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All three members (3 of 3) enhanced the custodial sentence, to five years' rigorous imprisonment, six years' rigorous imprisonment with fine, and a proportionate rigorous term in addition to the fine respectively.
variations: One member rests only on the bare finding of gross inadequacy with no precedent cited.
One member lays out detailed sentencing principles (proportionality, deterrence, protection of society, victim impact, discretion exercised on reasons rather than whim) and rejects a fine alone.
In one member the original sentence was a trial-court sentence of two years, while in the others the High Court had reduced the sentence to time served.

legal_question: Does the statutory suspension of proceedings against a sick industrial company (Section 22 of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985) bar or suspend a landlord's proceeding to evict the company from leased premises?

predicates.landlord_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding is brought by a landlord to evict a tenant and recover possession of leased premises.
predicates.tenant_is_sick_industrial_company: The tenant is a company treated or declared as a sick industrial company, with rehabilitation-related proceedings pending or a scheme under way, under the 1985 Act.
predicates.proceeding_seeks_possession_not_recovery: The proceeding seeks only recovery of possession of the premises and is not execution, distress or a similar process for recovering dues against the company's property.
predicates.sick_company_suspension_does_not_bar_evi: Section 22 of the 1985 Act does not bar or automatically suspend the eviction proceeding, which may continue without the consent of the statutory authority.

definition: A landlord's proceeding to evict a sick industrial company from leased premises is not a proceeding for execution, distress or the like against the company's property. Section 22(1) of the 1985 Act therefore does not bar or automatically suspend it, even while rehabilitation proceedings are pending.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule concerns the eviction and possession claim only. Money claims such as mesne profits may still need permission from the competent authority (the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction), as the trial court held in one member.
Section 22(1) continues to suspend true recovery processes (execution, distress or the like) against the company's property unless the authority consents.
The rule rests on the 'or the like' words being read with 'execution' and 'distress'; it does not extend to proceedings that are in substance recovery against company property.

common_material_facts: The tenant was a sick industrial company with proceedings before the statutory body pending.
The landlord sought eviction and possession of the premises, in rent-control or similar proceedings.
The tenant argued that Section 22 of the 1985 Act barred or suspended the eviction.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 22(1) of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985
Shree Chamundi Mopeds Ltd. v. Church of South India Trust Association, (1992) 3 SCC 1, relied on in two members
Gujarat Steel Tube Co. Ltd. v. Virchandbhai B. Shah and Carona Ltd. v. Parvathy Swaminathan and Sons, relied on in one member
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that Section 22 does not bar the eviction proceeding. Eviction petitions or orders stand.
variations: One member separately held that recovery of mesne profits needed the Board's permission.
One member reasons from the purpose of the Act: a tenant company should not keep incurring rent liabilities while the landlord must keep providing premises.
One member concerns a statutory tenant under rent control, and the eviction was for default in paying rent.
One member states the conclusion shortly, relying on precedent.

legal_question: When municipal annual value is fixed by reference to the rent lawfully obtainable, how does the applicable rent-control law supply the fair-rent measure for the assessment period (the agreed rent during an initial deeming window, and the statutory formula after it)?

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment: The dispute concerns the determination of annual value or rental valuation of a building for municipal tax under a municipal statute that ties valuation to fair rent or the rent lawfully obtainable.
predicates.rent_control_law_in_force_for_assessment: A rent-control statute in force during the period for which the assessment is made lays down how fair rent is measured for the premises, for example by deeming the agreed rent to be fair rent for an initial period, or by a cost-based formula afterwards.
predicates.annual_value_is_determined_by_fair_rent_: The assessing authority must fix annual value using the fair-rent measure the rent-control law in force for the assessment period prescribes. That measure is the agreed rent if the initial deeming window applies, and the statutory cost-based formula once that window has ended.

definition: Where a municipal statute bases annual value on fair rent or the rent lawfully obtainable, the fair rent must be determined under the rent-control law in force for the assessment period. Under the West Bengal tenancy law, the agreed rent applies during the initial deeming window and the cost-based formula applies once it has ended, so the assessing authority must first establish when the premises were first let.
exceptions_or_limits: Whether the agreed rent or the cost-based formula applies depends on whether the initial agreed-rent window applies or has ended, which turns on the date of first letting. The assessing authority must determine that date.
The cost-based formula in the West Bengal tenancy law covers premises constructed and let after that law commenced.
Assessment books are ordinarily revised periodically, but the rules also provide a procedure for changing an assessment when a case for change is made out.

common_material_facts: Municipal annual value or rental valuation is tied by the municipal statute to fair rent or the rent lawfully obtainable.
A rent-control statute supplies the fair-rent measure.
The assessing authority or lower courts had not applied the correct rent-control provision or period.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 8(1)(d) and its proviso, West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956
Section 168, Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951
Section 82(2), Madras District Municipalities Act, 1920, and the Fourth Schedule rules
Corporation of Calcutta v. Sm. Padma Debi [1962] 3 S.C.R. 49
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the Court required annual value to be fixed under the applicable rent-control measure: the agreed rent in the initial window (1), the cost-based formula after it (1), and the law in force during the assessment period (1). Fresh determination was needed.
variations: Two members concern the West Bengal and Calcutta statutes and split the agreed-rent window from the cost-based formula after it.
The Madras member concerns which rent-control Act applies in time, not the content of the measure.
The West Bengal members require a factual finding on the date of first letting.

legal_question: Where an entire estate is acquired and compensation is provided for the estate as a whole (for example, by reference to its net income), does the absence of separate compensation for some component properties, such as non-income-producing property, make the compensation illusory, confiscatory or otherwise invalid?

predicates.entire_estate_acquired: The law acquires the estate (or inam) as a whole, including both income-producing and non-income-producing property, rather than acquiring separate pieces of property.
predicates.compensation_provided_for_estate_as_a_wh: The law provides for compensation to be determined and paid for the estate as a whole, for example by reference to its net income or net assets, and not item by item.
predicates.no_separate_compensation_for_some_compon: Some property within the acquired estate, such as non-income-producing property or waste land, receives no separate compensation.
predicates.absence_of_separate_compensation_does_no: The lack of separate compensation for components is not alone a ground to hold the compensation illusory, confiscatory or in violation of the compensation requirement.

definition: When a law acquires an entire estate and fixes compensation for the estate as a whole, for example on net income, the lack of separate compensation for some parts, such as non-income-producing property, does not by itself make the compensation illusory or confiscatory or breach the compensation requirement. One member also relies on Article 31A or 31(4) to bar such challenges.
exceptions_or_limits: The reasoning applies to acquisition of an estate as a whole; it is contrasted with acquisition of separate pieces of property, where separate compensation may be required.

Compensation must be legally due and determinable, for example by an assessing officer with an appeal; rules fixing an unreasonably remote time for payment may be challenged separately as an abuse of power.
In some members the challenge is barred by constitutional protections (Article 31A or 31(4)) for estate acquisitions, not decided purely on the merits of adequacy.

common_material_facts: Statute acquires whole estates (or inams) including income-producing and non-income-producing property
Compensation is computed for the estate as a whole, by net income or net assets
Appellants complain that some components, such as waste land, receive no separate compensation
statutes_and_provisions: Article 31(2)
Article 31A
Article 31(4)
Legislative entries on acquisition and compensation
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members reject the challenge: lack of separate compensation for parts of an acquired estate does not make the scheme illusory, confiscatory or unconstitutional.
variations: 1500251_3 relies mainly on Article 31A barring an Article 31(2) challenge, and assumes without deciding that some properties got no separate compensation.
511375_3 relies on Article 31(4) and the statutory payment mechanism (assessment officer, appeal, cash or bonds), and notes that unreasonably remote payment rules could be challenged.
629631_9 reasons on the merits that estate-wide net-income compensation is not confiscatory, contrasting it with acquisition of separate pieces of property.

legal_question: Under Section 2(11) of the Code of Civil Procedure, does a person who takes or claims only a share or part of a deceased person's estate (such as a partial legatee, a heir with a share, or a legatee intending to represent the estate) qualify as that person's legal representative?

rule.if: person_claims_or_holds_interest_in_deceased_estate and (holds_only_part_or_share_of_estate or is_legatee_intending_to_represent_estate) and not claim_is_wholly_foreign_to_estate

predicates.person_claims_or_holds_interest_in_decea: The person holds, or asserts under a will, inheritance or settlement, an interest in the property or estate of the deceased party.
predicates.holds_only_part_or_share_of_estate: The person holds only a separate portion or a share of the estate, not the whole estate, and need not be the head or administrator of the family or heirs.
predicates.is_legatee_intending_to_represent_estate: The person is a legatee under a will who seeks to come on record to represent the deceased testator's estate, and so intermeddles with it.
predicates.claim_is_wholly_foreign_to_estate: The person's claim has no connection with the deceased's estate, so the person does not represent the estate in any sense.
predicates.person_qualifies_as_legal_representative: The person falls within the inclusive definition of legal representative in Section 2(11) CPC and may be brought on record or treated as representing the estate, subject to the court deciding any competing claims.

definition: Section 2(11) CPC is inclusive and broad. A person who represents the deceased's estate, or who intermeddles with it, is a legal representative even if he holds only a share or separate portion of the estate, is not the head or administrator, or is a legatee intending to represent the estate.
exceptions_or_limits: Where several persons compete to represent the estate, the court must still decide who is to represent it; qualifying as a legal representative does not settle the competing claims.
For a legatee who merely intends to represent the estate, the status is only that he may qualify, and it is subject to the court's determination.

common_material_facts: A party to a suit or proceeding died and the question was who could represent the estate.
The proposed representative held only a share or part of the estate, or claimed as a legatee.
There was an argument that the person was not the sole holder, the head of the family, or the administrator.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 2(11), Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members read Section 2(11) broadly and treat the partial holder, the share-holding heir or the intending legatee as a legal representative, one of them expressly subject to the court's determination.
variations: 1508646_2 concerns legatees of separate portions under a will, and disapproves a contrary observation in an earlier case.
1528864_1 concerns a widow with an inheritance share, and the reasoning rests on representing the estate rather than on intermeddling.
785816_3 rests on intermeddling by a legatee and leaves the final decision on representation to the court.

legal_question: Does natural justice require an individual hearing (or recorded reasons) before delegated or subordinate legislative action is taken, where the governing statute does not require one?

predicates.action_is_legislative_or_delegated_legis: The impugned act is the exercise of plenary, subordinate or conditional legislative power of general application (for example a notification, a rule, a planning modification, or the formation of a municipal corporation), and not an individualised adjudicatory or administrative decision.
predicates.governing_law_does_not_require_hearing_o: The statute or enactment under which the action is taken does not expressly prescribe a hearing, notice or recorded reasons at the relevant stage. A general enabling power to make such inquiry as is considered necessary does not count as a requirement.
predicates.no_implied_duty_of_individual_hearing_or: Natural justice does not imply a duty to give affected persons an individual hearing or to record reasons, and the action is not invalid for the lack of either.

definition: Delegated or subordinate legislation is legislative in character, so natural justice does not imply a right to an individual hearing or recorded reasons before it is made, unless the governing statute expressly requires them. Hearings that were given voluntarily, or a general power to make inquiry, do not create an enforceable hearing right at a later stage.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the governing statute expressly requires notice, a hearing or reasons.
It applies to legislative or conditional legislative action and not to individualised, adjudicatory or quasi-judicial decisions.
A hearing or objection process that was given voluntarily or because the statute required it at an earlier stage does not create a further hearing requirement at the final stage.

common_material_facts: The impugned act was a notification, a government decision or a sanction made under delegated statutory power.
The governing statute was silent on a hearing or reasons, or required none at the stage challenged.
Affected persons claimed a hearing or reasons based on natural justice.
In some cases a limited objection or hearing process had been offered earlier, or only to some parties.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 3 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949 (formation of a corporation)
Delegated notification power withdrawing an exemption
Planning enactment providing for government inquiry as considered necessary before sanction
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that no hearing or reasons were required, because the action was legislative and the statute did not require them. One of the three reverses a High Court direction to hold hearings.
variations: Member 1524072_3 also addresses reasons, in addition to a hearing.
Member 1931795_1 arises from a High Court direction to hear objectors, and a hearing had been given to one party under an assurance.
Member 758867_2 concerns a final sanction stage after an earlier hearing, and treats an enabling inquiry power as not creating a hearing right.
The measures differ: exemption withdrawal, formation of a municipal corporation, and a planning modification.

legal_question: Under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, must a tenant challenge the validity of a limited-term tenancy permission promptly during the tenancy, and may a challenge first raised after expiry (in response to the landlord's application for possession or execution) be entertained?

predicates.limited_tenancy_permission_under_section: The tenancy is a fixed-term limited tenancy created on the Rent Controller's permission under Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.
predicates.tenant_knew_or_with_diligence_could_have: The tenant knew, or with due diligence could have discovered, during the tenancy the facts said to vitiate the permission (such as fraud, collusion, suppression, misrepresentation or lack of vacancy).
predicates.challenge_not_brought_to_controller_duri: The tenant did not seek adjudication of the alleged defect from the Rent Controller during the currency of the limited tenancy, and first raised it after expiry, in response to the application for possession or in execution.
predicates.tenant_shows_no_earlier_opportunity_or_e: The tenant establishes that there was no opportunity to learn the facts earlier and that awareness arose only later, or otherwise shows an exceptional circumstance justifying the delay.
predicates.belated_post_expiry_challenge_to_permiss: The Controller or court should reject the belated challenge to the permission, or treat it as an afterthought, and the landlord is entitled to possession.

definition: A tenant who discovers, or with diligence could discover, facts said to vitiate a Section 21 limited-tenancy permission must seek adjudication from the Rent Controller during the tenancy. A challenge first raised after expiry is ordinarily not entertained, because the permission is presumed valid, unless the tenant shows no earlier opportunity to know the facts or an exceptional circumstance.
exceptions_or_limits: A narrow exception applies where the tenant satisfies the Controller that there was no earlier opportunity to learn the facts and that awareness came only later, or where exceptional circumstances exist (Shrisht Dhawan).

A fraud or collusion plea raised at the possession stage may still be considered by the Controller, as in S.B. Noronah, but the tenant risks its rejection as an afterthought. The initial permission is presumed regular, and the Controller need not invite such pleas in every case.
In one member the High Court's remand for the Controller to consider the tenant's objections was left undisturbed.
S.B. Noronah was confined to its facts in one member, and remarks in Vohra and Shiv Chander Kapoor that post-expiry objections might be examined were treated as obiter.

common_material_facts: The Rent Controller granted permission for a fixed-term limited tenancy under Section 21.
The tenant raised the challenge only after the tenancy expired, in response to the landlord's application for possession or in execution.
The tenant had not approached the Controller during the tenancy despite the ability to learn the relevant facts.
The tenant alleged fraud, suppression, misrepresentation or non-vacancy of the premises.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 21, Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958
Section 14, Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 (ordinary protection against eviction, distinguished)
S.B. Noronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna
J.R. Vohra v. India Export House
Shrisht Dhawan v. Shaw Brothers
Pankaj Bhargava v. Mohinder Nath
Inder Mohan Lal v. Ramesh Khanna
Shiv Chander Kapoor v. Amar Bose
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In 2 of 3 members the belated challenge was rejected and possession was ordered for the landlord. In the third the Court advised prompt recourse but left undisturbed a remand to consider the plea, warning that delay risks the plea being rejected as an afterthought.
variations: One member (1516172_2) is softer: a plea raised at the possession stage may still be considered, whereas the other two bar it unless an exception is shown.
One member (1553975_2) also found no concealment on the facts, and one (933165_1) narrowed the earlier Noronah decision.
The members differ in the exact wording of the exception (exceptional circumstances versus no earlier opportunity to know the facts).

legal_question: Can compensation for loss, injury or damage be fixed by a uniform formula or rate (such as a fixed interest rate or a fixed rate of return) without assessing the facts and the loss actually shown in each case?

predicates.compensation_claim_before_forum: A court, commission or other statutory forum is deciding the amount of compensation for loss, injury or damage (for example under the Telegraph Act or the Consumer Protection Act).
predicates.loss_or_damage_varies_with_case_circumst: The nature and extent of the loss, injury or damage depend on the particular facts of each case, such as location, extent of interference, delay, who was responsible, or harassment suffered.
predicates.compensation_fixed_by_uniform_formula_or: The compensation was set by applying a fixed formula, rate of return, or blanket interest rate to every case, without examining the individual facts or relating the award to the loss or injury shown.
predicates.uniform_formula_or_rate_unsustainable_an: The uniform formula or rate cannot be sustained, and compensation must be reassessed according to the circumstances of the case and the loss or injury established.

definition: Compensation is recompense for the loss or injury actually established, so it cannot be fixed by a universal formula or blanket rate (such as 18% interest or a fixed rate of return) irrespective of the facts. It must be assessed case by case, with the award correlated to the loss shown.
exceptions_or_limits: Established methods (such as yield or annuity calculation, or interest awarded on the facts of a particular case) may still be used as aids where suited to the facts; they do not form a universal formula.
A particular rate, such as 18%, may be upheld where it is justified by the facts of that case; the rule bars only its mechanical, blanket application.
The rule requires reassessment on the merits; it does not itself fix the amount of compensation.

common_material_facts: A tribunal or authority had applied a uniform method or rate (annuity rate of return, or 18% interest) across differing cases.
The cases varied in the nature and degree of loss or injury.
The apex court set aside or refused to sustain the blanket approach and called for case-specific assessment.
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 10(d) and 16(3), Indian Telegraph Act, 1885
Section 51, Indian Electricity Act, 1910
Consumer Protection Act (compensation for deficiency in service)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that a uniform formula or rate is unsustainable and compensation must be assessed on the circumstances and loss shown in each case (1 overhead-line compensation case, 2 consumer interest cases).
variations: One member concerns property damage from overhead electric lines, while two concern consumer compensation, awarded as interest on housing and development delays.
The overhead-line member recognises yield and annuity-type methods as possible aids, whereas the consumer members rely on correlating the award to the loss or injury and to responsibility for delay.
One consumer member notes that the record was not before the Court, and another notes that some awards were enhanced on the authority's own appeal.

legal_question: When may a suit or complaint be maintained in a representative capacity under Order I Rule 8 CPC (or its consumer-law equivalent), and what does the court look at to decide whether the represented persons have the same interest?

rule.if: representative_proceeding_sought and represented_persons_numerous and (shared_interest_established_on_pleadings_and_reliefs or common_grievance_established) and not reliefs_depend_on_individual_circumstances

predicates.representative_proceeding_sought: The suit or complaint is brought by one or more persons on behalf of others under Order I Rule 8 CPC or an equivalent provision such as the Consumer Protection Act provisions applying it.
predicates.represented_persons_numerous: The persons sought to be represented are numerous.
predicates.shared_interest_established_on_pleadings: The pleadings and the reliefs claimed show that the represented persons have the same interest, for example because they hold materially identical terms and the challenged demand or conduct is uniform.
predicates.common_grievance_established: The represented persons share a common grievance arising from the same basis, and the plaintiff's plea is available to all of them.
predicates.reliefs_depend_on_individual_circumstanc: The relief claimed varies with each represented person's own circumstances, for example differing delays, differing acceptance of compensation, or separate individual grievances.
predicates.representative_proceeding_maintainable: The court holds that the suit or complaint may proceed in a representative capacity on behalf of the persons sought to be represented, notwithstanding any separate causes of action.

definition: A representative proceeding is maintainable where the pleadings and reliefs show that the represented persons share a sufficient community of interest or grievance. Separate causes of action do not defeat it, but a shared cause of action alone does not establish shared interest, and individualised reliefs or unpleaded commonality defeat it.
exceptions_or_limits: Sameness of cause of action is not required (Explanation to Order I Rule 8), but it is also not sufficient on its own to show sameness of interest.

Where the pleadings do not specifically establish shared interest, or the reliefs depend on each person's circumstances, representative permission is refused and the complaint may be treated as a joint complaint of the named complainants only.

For suits against the Government, the representative suit is not defective under section 80 CPC merely because another person who served the notice did not join, provided the suing person served the notice, the cause of action and relief are the same, and the court permitted the representative suit (795303_1). This is a notice-compliance point rather than the test for sameness of interest.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns whether a representative suit against the Government is defective under the section 80 CPC notice requirement when only one of two notice-givers sues. It does not decide whether the represented persons share the same interest.

common_material_facts: A group of numerous persons (allottees, purchasers, inamdars) is sought to be represented by one or a few of them.
The dispute turns on whether the group's interest is sufficiently uniform.
Permission to sue representatively under Order I Rule 8 CPC was granted or sought.
statutes_and_provisions: Order I Rule 8 CPC and its Explanation (added by the 1976 Amendment)
Section 35(1)(c) and Section 38(11), Consumer Protection Act, 2019
Section 80 CPC
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Of 3 members, 2 uphold the representative form (the housing allottees suit and the Government suit, which is not defective on the notice point) and 1 denies representative permission (the consumer complaint). The result turns on uniformity of interest as shown in the pleadings and reliefs.
variations: 150513_2 and 45257695_1 apply the same-interest test and reach opposite results because of uniform versus individualised demands and reliefs.
45257695_1 arises under consumer law, which incorporates Order I Rule 8, while 150513_2 arises in a civil suit.
795303_1 addresses notice compliance under section 80 CPC rather than sameness of interest.

split_suggestion: Keep 150513_2 and 45257695_1 together as the 'sameness of interest under Order I Rule 8' group. Move 795303_1 to a separate group on section 80 CPC notice requirements in representative suits against the Government.

legal_question: Does failure to lay a published notification or order before the legislature, where the laying requirement does not make its effectiveness depend on prior legislative approval, invalidate the notification or order?

rule.if: delegated_instrument_validity_challenge and instrument_not_laid_before_legislature and laying_requirement_is_simple_or_directory and not effectiveness_conditional_on_legislative_approval

predicates.delegated_instrument_validity_challenge: The validity or enforceability of a notification, rule or exemption order issued under delegated statutory power is challenged.
predicates.instrument_not_laid_before_legislature: The notification or order was not laid or placed before the legislature as the statute required, at least initially.
predicates.laying_requirement_is_simple_or_director: The laying provision is read as a simple laying requirement or as directory: it requires placement, and may allow the legislature to modify or annul the instrument after it is laid, but it does not make the instrument depend on legislative approval.
predicates.effectiveness_conditional_on_legislative: The statute makes the instrument's coming into effect or continued effect depend on prior approval by the legislature, or on its being laid.
predicates.non_laying_does_not_invalidate_instrumen: The omission to lay does not by itself invalidate the notification or order or the action taken under it; the defect is curable by later laying.

definition: Where a statute requires a delegated notification or order to be laid before the legislature but does not make its effect depend on legislative approval, the requirement is treated as directory. Failure to lay it does not invalidate it, and the Court may direct that it be laid and that the requirement be complied with in future.
exceptions_or_limits: The effect of a laying clause depends on its wording and the degree of legislative control it creates; a clause requiring prior approval or making effectiveness conditional on laying may lead to a different result.
The laying requirement is not futile; it operates as a check, and the authority may be directed to lay the instrument at the earliest and comply in future.

common_material_facts: A notification or exemption order was issued under a statute containing a laying requirement.
The instrument was not laid before the legislature.
The laying clause did not require prior legislative approval for the instrument to take effect.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 28(3), Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 (contrasted with Section 28(1))
State statutory laying clauses for exemption orders and notifications
Atlas Cycle Industries Ltd. v. State of Haryana
Jan Mohammad Noor Mohammad Bagban v. State of Gujarat
Quarry Owners' Association v. State of Bihar
D.K. Krishnan v. Secretary, Regional Transport Authority, Chittoor
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members, non-laying did not invalidate the instrument. In 2 members (1524072_2 and 281568_3) the Court expressly directed that the instrument be placed before the legislature.
variations: One member frames the clause as simple laying, one as directory, and one by its wording permitting later modification or annulment.
The Court directed later placement in two members but not expressly in the simple-laying exemption order member.
One member notes the notification was referred to in administrative reports but was not actually placed before the legislature.

legal_question: When can a family co-sharer invoke the statutory right under Section 4 of the Partition Act, 1893 (read with Section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882) to buy an outsider transferee's share in an undivided family dwelling house, and when is that right not available because the transferee has not sought partition or the decree has been fully executed?

rule.if: undivided_family_dwelling_house and share_transferred_to_outsider and family_shareholder_seeks_to_purchase and outsider_transferee_seeks_partition_or_separate_possession and not partition_decree_fully_executed

predicates.undivided_family_dwelling_house: The property is a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family and still held in common.
predicates.share_transferred_to_outsider: A share in the dwelling house has been transferred to a person who is not a member of the family.
predicates.family_shareholder_seeks_to_purchase: A family shareholder applies to buy the outsider transferee's share.
predicates.outsider_transferee_seeks_partition_or_s: The outsider transferee sues for partition, including by pursuing execution of a partition decree, to obtain separation and possession of the share. Merely asserting a share does not satisfy this.
predicates.partition_decree_fully_executed: The partition decree has been fully executed and satisfied by division by metes and bounds and delivery of possession to the respective shareholders.
predicates.statutory_preemption_right_available: The family shareholder's application to purchase the outsider's share under Section 4 of the Partition Act is maintainable.

definition: A family shareholder may buy an outsider transferee's share in an undivided family dwelling house under Section 4 of the Partition Act once the transferee sues for partition, which includes seeking execution of a partition decree. The right is not available if the transferee has not sought partition and separate possession (the application is premature), nor after the decree has been fully executed and possession delivered.
exceptions_or_limits: If the transferee only asserts a share and does not seek partition or separation and possession, the application is premature and fails. It may be renewed if the transferee later seeks partition.

Once the decree is fully executed by division by metes and bounds and delivery of possession, the dwelling house no longer belongs to an undivided family as to the separated portion, and the remedy ends.
The right depends on the property being a dwelling house of an undivided family and the transferee being a stranger to the family.

common_material_facts: A dwelling house belonging to an undivided family
A share transferred to a non-member (stranger) transferee
A family co-sharer seeking to buy the transferee's share
The stage of the partition proceedings (not yet sought, pending execution, or fully executed) determines the outcome
statutes_and_provisions: Section 4, Partition Act, 1893
Section 44, Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Section 38 and Order 21 Rule 16, Order 22 Rules 10 and 12, Explanation VII to Section 11, CPC
Explanation to Section 52, Transfer of Property Act (as relied on in 155465_1)
Ghantesher Ghosh v. Madan Mohan Ghosh
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: The three members delimit the temporal scope of the right. One (155465_1) holds the application maintainable while execution is incomplete. One (155465_2) holds the remedy unavailable after full execution. One (240013_2) holds the application premature because the transferee has not sought partition.
variations: 155465_1 and 155465_2 arise from the same decision and address opposite sides of the full-satisfaction boundary.
240013_2 concerns the earlier threshold: the transferee must actually seek partition and separate possession.
155465_1 treats pursuit of execution of a decree as 'suing for partition', while 240013_2 treats a mere assertion of a share in the pleadings as insufficient.

legal_question: When a deed of transfer states an absolute transfer and contains no term making the transfer conditional, temporary or security-based, is it construed as an outright, unconditional transfer of title, so that a party asserting a condition or a nominal character fails?

rule.if: transfer_deed_in_dispute and deed_terms_express_absolute_or_unconditional_transfer and no_condition_or_return_term_in_deed and not surrounding_circumstances_show_contrary_intention

predicates.transfer_deed_in_dispute: The dispute concerns the legal effect or character of a deed transferring immovable property (sale, exchange or allocation).
predicates.deed_terms_express_absolute_or_unconditi: On its plain terms the deed transfers the property absolutely, for consideration or in exchange for other rights, and relinquishes the transferor's remaining interest or claims.
predicates.no_condition_or_return_term_in_deed: The deed contains no term making the transfer conditional on payment or further performance, no term making it provisional or temporary, and no term for return of the property. A separate same-day agreement to reconvey does not by itself supply such a term.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_show_contrary_: Evidence outside the deed, such as conduct, possession or contemporaneous documents, establishes that the parties intended the transfer to be conditional, provisional or only a security.
predicates.deed_operates_as_outright_unconditional_: The deed is held to pass title or ownership outright and unconditionally. A claim that it was conditional, nominal, provisional or security only is rejected.

definition: A deed that on its terms transfers property absolutely, and contains no condition, return clause or security character, is construed according to its plain terms as an outright transfer. The party asserting a condition, nominal character or provisional transfer must show it from the deed or from surrounding circumstances, and cannot read a condition into the deed contrary to its terms.
exceptions_or_limits: If the deed expressly makes passage of title conditional on payment or performance, the condition governs (the Panchoo Sahu illustration in the sale-deed member).
If the deed is ambiguous, surrounding circumstances may be used to find a different intention, subject to Section 92 of the Evidence Act.

Under Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, a sale and an agreement to reconvey embodied in the same document may amount to a mortgage by conditional sale. Separate documents executed the same day do not.
Under Sections 8 and 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, title passes on a registered sale unless a different intention is expressed or necessarily implied.

common_material_facts: A written deed with clear terms of absolute transfer or allocation.
The party challenging the deed alleges it was conditional, nominal, provisional or security only.
The deed has no express condition or return term.
Possession was delivered to or held by the transferee.
Collateral circumstances such as a mortgage, a retained receipt or a reconveyance agreement did not displace the deed's terms.
statutes_and_provisions: Transfer of Property Act 1882, Sections 8, 54 and 58(c)
Evidence Act, Section 92
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the deed to be an outright, unconditional transfer and reject the challenge, based on the deed's plain terms.
variations: One member concerns a registered sale deed and the passage of title (Sections 8 and 54).
One member concerns a sale with a same-day reconveyance agreement and the sale-versus-mortgage characterisation (Section 58(c)).
One member concerns a family allocation or exchange deed, construed on its plain terms without a statutory test.
Only the first member expressly discusses burden and surrounding circumstances.

legal_question: When is an owner whose land is partly acquired entitled to compensation for severance or for injurious effect on the remaining property?

rule.if: land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding and part_of_property_acquired and remainder_left_with_owner and claimant_seeks_compensation_for_remainder_damage and acquisition_caused_damage_to_remainder

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_proceeding: The matter is a compulsory acquisition compensation proceeding, including a reference to the court for determining compensation.
predicates.part_of_property_acquired: Only part of the owner's land or property was acquired.
predicates.remainder_left_with_owner: A portion of the property remains with the owner after acquisition.
predicates.claimant_seeks_compensation_for_remainde: The claimant claims compensation for severance or for the acquisition injuriously affecting the remaining property or earnings.
predicates.acquisition_caused_damage_to_remainder: The claimant has established, by evidence or reasonable inference, that the acquisition itself diminished the value or usefulness of the remaining property. Pre-existing conditions or unproved expenditure do not satisfy this.
predicates.severance_or_injurious_effect_compensati: The claimant is entitled to compensation for severance or injurious effect on the remainder, and the claim may be considered in the compensation reference.

definition: Where part of a property is acquired, the owner may claim, in a compensation reference, additional compensation for severance or injurious effect on the remainder. The claim succeeds if the acquisition caused damage to the remainder, such as diminished value. It fails if the damage is unproved or pre-existed the acquisition.
exceptions_or_limits: Compensation is denied where the claimed expenditure on protective works is not substantiated by accounts or other material.
Compensation is denied where the alleged impairment, such as water stagnation, existed before the acquisition or is otherwise unsubstantiated.
Retention of an entrance or access to the remainder does not by itself defeat a severance claim, but continued usability of access may show that no damage was caused.
A claim for additional compensation for injury to remaining property is distinct from a request to acquire the whole building under the separate provision.

common_material_facts: Only part of the claimant's property was acquired and a remainder was left with the owner.
The claimant sought additional compensation for severance or injurious effect on the remainder.
The existence of access or an entrance to the remainder featured in the reasoning.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 23(1), including its third and fourth clauses (severance and injurious affection)
Section 18 (reference to court)
Section 49 (acquisition of the whole building, distinguished)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Two of the three members allow or permit consideration of compensation for damage to the remainder (1690721_3, 444729_3). One denies it for failure of proof (1559215_4).
variations: 1559215_4 stresses the claimant's burden to prove acquisition-caused damage and denies the claim.
1690721_3 decides only that such a claim may be entertained in a section 18 reference.
444729_3 holds that diminution in value is enough and that an entrance does not negate it, restoring the award despite the lack of quantified depreciation evidence.

legal_question: When a judgment-debtor applies under Order XXI Rule 89 CPC to set aside an execution sale, must the required deposit be made within 30 days of the sale (Order XXI Rule 92(2)), or is a deposit made within the longer 60-day application period under Article 127 of the Limitation Act sufficient?

predicates.execution_sale_set_aside_application: The judgment-debtor or another eligible person has applied to set aside a sale of property held in execution of a decree, with a deposit under Order XXI Rule 89 CPC.
predicates.application_filed_within_article_127_per: The application to set aside the sale was filed within the 60-day period prescribed by Article 127 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
predicates.required_deposit_made_within_article_127: The full amounts required under Order XXI Rule 89 (decretal amount and the percentage of the purchase price) were deposited within 60 days of the sale, even if after the first 30 days.
predicates.rule_92_2_thirty_day_period_treated_as_m: The court reads Order XXI Rule 92(2) as fixing 30 days from the sale as a strict outer limit for the deposit, independent of the application period.
predicates.late_deposit_within_application_period_i: A deposit made after 30 days but within the 60-day application period does not bar the application; the sale is liable to be set aside, or the court has discretion to set it aside, on the merits.

definition: On the view taken by two of the three members, Order XXI Rule 92(2) is harmonised with Article 127 of the Limitation Act. An application and the required deposit made within the 60-day application period are not defeated because the deposit came after 30 days, and the sale may be set aside. One member (1672592_1 treated as discretionary) frames the outcome as the court's discretion rather than an entitlement. The third member takes the opposite view.
exceptions_or_limits: Under the contrary line (1544426_1), the deposit is a condition precedent to the application and must be made within 30 days of the sale under Rule 92(2). The 60-day period under Article 127 governs only the application, so a deposit after 30 days is out of time.
Where the deposit or application falls outside the 60-day Article 127 period, even the more lenient view gives no relief.

Under 672592_1, a deposit made after the first 30 days but within 60 days leaves the court with discretion whether to allow the application. The set-aside is not automatic, whereas a deposit within 30 days removes that discretion.
Courts must apply clear statutory text without adding words. The members differ on whether Rule 92(2) is clear enough to bar a later deposit.

outlier_members.reason: It reaches the opposite conclusion: the deposit must be made within 30 days of the sale, separately from the 60-day application period. It rejects the harmonising approach of Basavantappa and treats Rule 92(2) and Article 127 as consistent, with separate periods for separate steps.

common_material_facts: Immovable property was sold in execution of a decree.
An application to set aside the sale was made with a deposit under Order XXI Rule 89.
The deposit was made after 30 days but within 60 days of the sale, and the auction-purchaser objected that it was late.
The Article 127 period was extended from 30 to 60 days by the 1976 amendment.
statutes_and_provisions: Order XXI Rules 89, 90 and 92(2), Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Article 127, Limitation Act, 1963 (60 days, as amended by Act 104 of 1976)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Two of the three members (1689577_1, 672592_1) hold that a deposit within the 60-day application period suffices; one of these makes the grant discretionary. One member (1544426_1) holds that the deposit must be made within 30 days, and it allowed the auction-purchaser's appeal.
variations: 1689577_1 finds Rule 92(2) inconsistent with Article 127 and harmonises them, noting that legislative amendment is needed.
672592_1 finds no inconsistency. It reads Rule 92(2) only as removing discretion where the deposit is within 30 days, and leaves the court discretion for a later deposit within 60 days.
1544426_1 treats the deposit as a condition precedent with its own 30-day limit, and refuses to supply words or to repair the provision where the text is clear.
The members rely on conflicting authorities: Basavantappa and Thangammal on one side, P.K. Unni and Nalinakhya Bysack on the other.

split_suggestion: The members share one legal question but give conflicting answers. Treat 1689577_1 and 672592_1 (deposit allowed within 60 days, the latter with discretion) as one line and 1544426_1 (strict 30-day deposit) as the opposing line. 672592_1 could be separated further as the discretion variant.

legal_question: When compensating for acquired land that bears fruit-bearing trees, may the claimant receive a separate award for the trees' potential or income value on top of the land's market value, or does that double-count the same value?

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_case: The dispute concerns determining compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
