It may not do so merely by reweighing the evidence and substituting its own view.
exceptions_or_limits: In revision, mere reappraisal of evidence, a wrong view of law or a misapprehension of evidence does not justify setting aside an acquittal; the High Court must not act as an appellate court.

The categories of qualifying defects are illustrative, not exhaustive (e.g. lack of jurisdiction, exclusion of admissible evidence, consideration of inadmissible evidence, overlooking evidence, invalid compounding).
The power must be exercised sparingly and only where justice clearly requires it.
If the High Court reweighs the evidence and identifies no manifest illegality, gross miscarriage or analogous glaring defect, a retrial order is revoked and the acquittal restored.

common_material_facts: An accused had been acquitted by a subordinate criminal court (magistrate or Sessions Court).
A complainant or private party invoked the High Court's appellate or revisional power against the acquittal.
The outcome turned on whether the acquittal had a legal or jurisdictional defect rather than just a disputed assessment of evidence.
statutes_and_provisions: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, section 417(3)
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, section 423
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, section 439
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, section 345(7)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Two of three members (1727403_2, 380704_1) uphold High Court interference, setting aside the acquittal and ordering retrial or continuation of the trial. One (1835803_1) reverses the High Court's interference because it only reweighed the evidence.
variations: 1727403_2 arises on appeal against acquittal under sections 417 and 423, with a broad discretion and an omitted serious offence beyond the magistrate's jurisdiction.
1835803_1 arises in private revision under section 439 and stresses strict limits on revisional interference with acquittals.
380704_1 is a revision where the acquittal rested on compounding a non-compoundable offence under section 345(7).
The qualifying defect differs: omitted serious offence and jurisdiction, invalid compounding, or absence of any defect.

split_suggestion: Optionally split into (a) appeals against acquittal under sections 417 and 423 (1727403_2) and (b) revisions against acquittal under section 439, with 1835803_1 (limits on interference) and 380704_1 (invalid compounding) as contrasting applications of the same test.

legal_question: Under the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, do heirs who normally resided with a deceased residential tenant become tenants in their own right, so that one heir's construction or acquisition of another residence in the same city does not end the tenancies of the other heirs or make the premises deemed vacant?

predicates.residential_rent_control_tenancy_proceed: The dispute concerns a tenancy of a residential building governed by the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972.
predicates.tenant_died: The original tenant of the residential building has died.
predicates.heirs_normally_resided_with_tenant_at_de: The heirs (such as the widow and children) normally resided with the tenant in the building at the time of the tenant's death and so fall within the statutory definition of tenant after death.
predicates.one_heir_acquired_another_residence_in_s: One heir built or acquired another residential building in the same city, and moved into it.
predicates.other_heirs_continued_occupying_tenanted: The remaining qualifying heirs continued to occupy the original tenanted premises.
predicates.resident_heirs_are_individual_tenants_an: Each qualifying heir is a tenant in his or her own right, not a joint tenant, and the tenancies of the other heirs do not cease and the premises are not deemed vacant because of one heir's acquisition.

definition: Heirs who normally resided with a deceased residential tenant at the time of death become tenants individually under Section 3(a), not as joint tenants. Section 12(3)'s deemed cessation of occupancy, triggered by the tenant or a member of the tenant's family acquiring another residence, therefore applies only to the heir who acquired it and that heir's family. It does not end the tenancies of the other heirs or make the premises vacant.
exceptions_or_limits: Only heirs who normally resided with the tenant in the building at the time of death qualify as tenants; non-resident heirs do not.
Section 12(3) can still operate against the heir who built or acquired the other residence and against that heir's statutory family.
The rule rests on the statutory definitions in Sections 3(a) and 3(g); personal law and joint tenancy concepts do not govern.

common_material_facts: A residential tenant died leaving a widow and children who normally lived with him in the premises.
The heirs continued to live in the premises and rent was paid.
One heir built or acquired a separate house and moved into it.
The authorities treated the whole premises as vacant because of that acquisition.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 3(a), U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
Section 3(g), U.P. Act 13 of 1972 (definition of family)
Section 12(3), U.P. Act 13 of 1972 (deemed cessation of occupation)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that qualifying heirs are tenants in their own right and that one heir's acquisition of another residence does not end the other heirs' tenancies. The Allahabad Full Bench decision in Smt. Rama Devi Shakya was rejected or overruled.
variations: 175590800_1 states the foundational point that heirs become individual tenants.
175590800_2 and 816036_1 apply that point to Section 12(3) deemed vacancy.
816036_1 adds that personal law and joint tenancy do not govern, and records the overruling of Rama Devi Shakya and the allowing of the appeal.

legal_question: Can a court supervising a liquidation or court-ordered sale reopen or set aside a sale, even one already confirmed or paid for, and direct fresh bidding, when a higher bona fide offer shows that the price obtained is inadequate and renewed competition may secure a better price?

predicates.court_supervised_sale: The sale of the property or asset is conducted under the supervision of a court, such as a sale in winding-up or liquidation or an auction ordered in an appeal.
predicates.sale_not_finally_concluded_or_court_reta: The sale is still subject to court confirmation, or the sale terms or appellate directions reserve the court's power to alter or set it aside even after confirmation or payment, and the transfer is not yet completed in a way that defeats that power.
predicates.bona_fide_higher_offer_made: A genuine higher offer, supported where appropriate by a deposit or demand drafts, is made before the sale is finally concluded.
predicates.renewed_bidding_likely_to_secure_better_: The higher offer, a grossly inadequate price, or a restricted earlier auction indicates that fresh competitive bidding is likely to yield a better price benefiting the company, creditors, workmen or other interested persons.
predicates.court_may_reopen_or_set_aside_sale_and_d: The court has discretion to reopen the sale, or set it aside, and order further or fresh competitive bidding.

definition: A court supervising a liquidation or similar sale must act judicially in the interests of the company, creditors and others. A highest bidder has no vested right to confirmation, and where the court retains power over the sale and a bona fide higher offer shows that fresh competition is likely to give a better price, the court may reopen or set aside the sale and order fresh bidding, without proof of fraud or irregularity.
exceptions_or_limits: The discretion must be exercised judicially, not arbitrarily; repeated disturbance of court auctions may discourage bidders and must be weighed.
Where a sale is confirmed, the members stress grossly inadequate price, a bona fide higher offer and no completed transfer of possession or title.
Where a conveyance was executed, the power rested on sale conditions and appellate directions reserving the court's power to set the sale aside.
A mere higher offer is not enough; the court must be satisfied that the offer is genuine and that fresh bidding is likely to benefit those interested in the estate.
The fraud or material irregularity requirement of Order 21 Rule 90 CPC concerns setting aside under that rule and is not a precondition for the court's discretion over a liquidation sale.

common_material_facts: A court-supervised auction or liquidation sale produced a highest bidder, who was then followed by a higher offer.
The higher offer came before final conclusion of the sale, and in some cases after confirmation or payment.
The sale proceeds would benefit the company, its creditors and others interested.
Sale conditions or appellate directions reserved the court's power to alter or set aside the sale.
statutes_and_provisions: Companies Act (court's sanction of liquidation sale)
Rule 273 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959
Order 21 Rule 90 CPC (distinguished)
Navalkha and Sons v. Ramanuja Das
Kayjay Industries v. Asnew Drums
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the court upheld its power to reopen or set aside the sale and ordered further or fresh bidding.
variations: One member concerns a sale still subject to confirmation, another a confirmed sale with a conveyance executed but subject to the appeal, and the third a confirmed sale with no transfer.
One member relies on the grossly inadequate price, another on the earlier auction being limited to two bidders.
Two members expressly rely on sale conditions reserving the power to set aside, while the first rests on the court's discretion before confirmation.

legal_question: Does the constitutional protection under Article 31A(1)(a) for laws modifying rights in an estate extend to land-reform laws that affect interests, shares or portions of land treated as an estate (or restructure a landlord's rights in it) under the applicable land-tenure law?

predicates.land_reform_law_challenged_as_violating_: The validity of an agrarian or land-reform law is challenged in court on constitutional grounds.
predicates.law_modifies_or_restructures_rights_in_l: The law modifies the rights of landowners, landlords or tenants in the land, including by resumption, transfer to tenants, or extinguishment of others' rights, even where the right is transferred rather than extinguished.
predicates.land_is_an_estate_or_share_or_portion_of: Under the existing land-tenure law of the area, the land or interest affected is an estate, or a share or portion of an estate (such as a holding), or an interest in land that the tenure law's definition of estate covers, including where occupancy rights are recognised.
predicates.law_is_protected_under_article_31A_as_la: The law falls within Article 31A(1)(a) and receives the constitutional protection it gives to laws modifying rights in an estate.

definition: Article 31A(1)(a) is read broadly in light of its agrarian-reform purpose. A land-reform law that modifies or restructures rights in land protected as an estate is covered. An estate is determined by the local land-tenure law and includes shares, portions, holdings and interests in land, not only whole estates.
exceptions_or_limits: Whether the land is an estate depends on the definition in the existing land-tenure law of the relevant area (Article 31A(2)(a)); where that law does not treat the interest as an estate, the protection may not apply.
The law must actually modify or extinguish rights in the land; the members do not extend protection to laws that do not alter those rights.
Member 919121_2 rests on the interpretation of a specific tenure statute's definition and recognition of occupancy rights; this limits how far it generalises.

common_material_facts: Agrarian or land-reform legislation altering rights of landowners, landlords and tenants
Land held as a share, portion, holding or interest within a land-tenure system
Challenge to the law's validity on constitutional grounds, met by invoking Article 31A
statutes_and_provisions: Article 31A(1)(a)
Article 31A(2)(a)
Article 31A(2)
Sections 3(1) and 3(3) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 issues were resolved in favour of extending Article 31A protection to the impugned land-reform provisions or interests.
variations: 1764620_2 concerns shares or portions of estates (holdings) and applies the principle that the greater includes the less.
1976172_1 concerns restructuring of a landlord's rights by resumption and transfer to tenants, and treats a transfer of rights as a modification.
919121_2 concerns whether interests in land, including unalienated land under an occupancy tenure, are an estate under the local tenure law.

legal_question: Does the recovery of a deceased person's body, belongings or blood-stained presence at a particular house or residence, without proof of the accused's exclusive control of the place or other evidence linking the accused to the crime, support an inference of guilt or shift the burden of explanation to the accused?

predicates.circumstantial_criminal_case: The prosecution case against the accused rests on circumstantial evidence rather than direct evidence.
predicates.recovery_or_presence_connected_to_a_plac: The circumstance relied on is the recovery of the deceased's body or belongings from, or the alleged taking or presence of the deceased at, a house or residence.
predicates.accused_exclusive_possession_or_knowledg: The prosecution has proved that the accused exclusively owned or possessed the place, or knew of the body or items being there.
predicates.independent_incriminating_evidence_linki: There is other evidence, apart from the recovery or presence at the place, that connects the accused to the crime.
predicates.no_inference_of_guilt_and_no_burden_shif: The recovery or presence at the place supports no inference against the accused, the accused is not required to explain the death, and a conviction resting on it cannot stand.

definition: Where the prosecution relies on circumstantial evidence, the recovery of a body or belongings from a residence, or the alleged presence of the deceased there, does not by itself incriminate the accused. Without proof of the accused's exclusive possession or knowledge, or other independent evidence of involvement, no inference of guilt arises, no burden to explain shifts to the accused, and a conviction cannot rest on it.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply where the prosecution proves the accused's exclusive ownership or possession of the place, or the accused's knowledge of the body or items.
The rule does not apply where independent evidence connects the accused to the crime.
Ordinary belongings found where they would normally be kept carry no incriminating significance; items out of place or otherwise significant may be treated differently.
The members cite no earlier cases for this point. They rest on the general circumstantial-evidence standard and the principle that conviction cannot rest on conjecture.

common_material_facts: The only link to the accused was a connection with a house or residence: belongings found where the deceased lived, the deceased allegedly taken to a house, or a body found in the accused's home.
The prosecution did not prove exclusive possession, knowledge or other independent incriminating circumstances.
The case was wholly circumstantial.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (accused's statement considered)
Indian Penal Code Sections 120B and 302 read with Section 149 (offences of conviction in one member)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members find the place-based circumstance insufficient: one draws no inference from the belongings, one refuses to shift the burden to the accused, and one sets aside the convictions and acquits.
variations: One member concerns ordinary belongings at the deceased's own residence, one an alleged taking of the deceased to a disputed house, and one a body found in the accused's home.
The outcome differs in form: no inference drawn, no burden shifted, or acquittal on appeal.
Only one member expressly sets out the circumstantial-evidence standard and the penal provisions.

legal_question: Does the availability of an alternative statutory remedy bar a High Court from entertaining a writ petition under Article 226, and will an appellate court interfere with the High Court's discretionary decision to grant relief despite that remedy?

rule.if: constitutional_writ_petition and alternative_statutory_remedy_exists and high_court_exercised_discretion_to_entertain_or_grant_relief and not arbitrary_or_unreasonable_exercise_shown

predicates.constitutional_writ_petition: The proceeding is a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before a High Court.
predicates.alternative_statutory_remedy_exists: An alternative statutory remedy (such as an appeal, rectification or supervisory revision) was available to the petitioner.
predicates.high_court_exercised_discretion_to_enter: The High Court chose to hear the writ petition and granted relief despite the alternative remedy.
predicates.arbitrary_or_unreasonable_exercise_shown: It has been shown that the High Court's exercise of discretion was arbitrary or unreasonable.
predicates.alternative_remedy_is_not_a_jurisdiction: The alternative remedy does not remove the High Court's jurisdiction or discretion under Article 226, and the appellate court will ordinarily not interfere with the High Court's decision to grant relief.

definition: An alternative statutory remedy does not oust the High Court's Article 226 jurisdiction; whether to entertain the petition is a matter of discretion. Where the High Court has exercised that discretion to grant relief, the appellate court ordinarily will not interfere unless the exercise was arbitrary or unreasonable.
exceptions_or_limits: High Courts ordinarily decline to exercise Article 226 jurisdiction where an adequate and efficacious alternative remedy exists; relief despite such a remedy is for appropriate cases.
Appellate interference is possible if the exercise of discretion is shown to be arbitrary or unreasonable.
An objection based on an alternative remedy that was not pressed before the High Court may not be entertained at a later stage (one member).

common_material_facts: Tax or revenue dispute in which a statutory remedy (appeal, rectification, Board of Revenue supervisory powers) was available
Petitioners nonetheless approached the High Court under Article 226
High Court exercised its discretion and granted relief
The State or revenue authority objected on the basis of the alternative remedy
statutes_and_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution of India
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the alternative remedy was held not to bar the writ; the High Court's discretionary decision was left undisturbed (2 on appellate non-interference, 1 by declining to entertain the unpressed objection).
variations: One member stresses the discretion/jurisdiction distinction and non-interference by the Supreme Court.
One member rests on the objection not having been pressed before the High Court.
One member expressly adds the arbitrary-or-unreasonable standard for appellate interference.

legal_question: When land acquisition compensation is assessed on comparable sales of smaller developed plots, what level of deduction for development and size differences is appropriate where the acquired land is developed, partially developed or ready for construction, and when must an excessive or flat deduction be replaced?

predicates.land_acquisition_compensation_appeal: The case is an appeal or reference concerning the market value or compensation for land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
predicates.acquired_land_is_developed_or_ready_for_: The acquired land is wholly or partly developed, lies within or near developed municipal or built-up areas, or has lost its agricultural character and is more or less ready for construction.
predicates.comparable_sales_are_of_smaller_plots_or: The valuation relies on sale exemplars of smaller plots than the acquired land, or the lower court applied a fixed percentage deduction uniformly.
predicates.existing_deduction_is_excessive_or_not_m: The deduction applied (such as 40, 50 or 60 percent) is too high, or does not reflect the land's location, development potential, degree of development and condition.
predicates.deduction_reassessed_to_reasonable_level: The court replaces the deduction with a reasonable one, here one-third, and recomputes compensation, rejecting devices such as belting where they do not reflect the land's value.

definition: No rigid percentage applies to development or size deductions. Where acquired land is developed, partly developed or ready for construction and the comparables are smaller plots, an excessive or flat deduction (40–60 percent) is replaced by a reasonable deduction, here one-third, based on location, development and potential, and compensation is recomputed.
exceptions_or_limits: There is no fixed percentage; the deduction depends on location, development potential, development required and the land's condition, so one-third is not a universal figure.
Anticipated value from the future use for which the land is acquired is not to be taken into account (Section 24).
Where the court has expressly directed a different deduction in a particular case, the one-third reduction does not apply.
Belting was rejected only where it did not reflect the land's value; the member does not bar it in all cases.

common_material_facts: The High Court or trial court applied a high deduction (40, 50 or 60 percent) to sale-exemplar prices.
The acquired land was developed, partly developed, within municipal limits or ready for construction.
Comparable sale plots were smaller than the acquired land.
The Supreme Court substituted a one-third deduction.
statutes_and_provisions: Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Sections 23(1-A), 23(2), 28
Land Acquisition Act, 1894, Section 24
Charan Dass v. HUDA; Haridwar Development Authority v. Raghubir Singh; Kasturi v. State of Haryana; Saibanna v. Assistant Commissioner and LAO; Subh Ram; Kanta Devi
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members reduce the deduction to one-third and direct compensation to be reassessed or recomputed; one also rejects belting and fixes a rate.
variations: One member addresses a 60 percent deduction for municipal land, one a uniform 40 percent deduction across cases, and one a 50 percent deduction combined with belting.
One member also applies an annual escalation to arrive at a per-square-yard rate.
One member emphasises loss of agricultural character, passage of time and the Section 24 bar on anticipated value.

legal_question: Is income from the sale of spontaneously grown forest trees agricultural income when the owner only maintains the forest, assists tree growth or spends heavily on upkeep, without any basic agricultural operations such as planting or cultivation?

predicates.forest_tree_income_claimed_as_agricultur: The assessee claims that income from selling forest trees is agricultural income exempt from tax.
predicates.trees_grew_spontaneously: The fact-finding authority found that the trees producing the income grew on their own, without being planted.
predicates.basic_agricultural_operations_raised_the: The trees were raised by basic agricultural operations such as cultivation or substantial plantation, to which any later operations are connected.
predicates.income_is_not_agricultural_income: The income from the sale of the trees is not agricultural income under the Income-tax Act.

definition: Income from selling trees that grew spontaneously is not agricultural income unless basic agricultural operations such as planting or cultivation raised the trees. Later maintenance, assistance of growth or substantial upkeep expenditure does not supply the missing basic operations. Such expenditure alone does not prove plantation and cannot override a finding of spontaneous growth.
exceptions_or_limits: Where a considerable portion of the forest is found to have been planted, substantial expenditure may support an inference that the income comes from planted trees; the inference depends on all the facts found.
Subsequent operations such as pruning or watering have an agricultural character only when connected with basic operations such as planting or cultivation.
The rule rests on the Tribunal's factual finding of spontaneous growth and does not decide whether sale receipts are capital or revenue.

outlier_members.reason: It asks whether receipts from selling spontaneously grown tree trunks are capital or revenue, turning on the owner's object in felling and on whether stumps were left to regenerate or to protect land for cultivation. It does not ask whether the income is agricultural income, and it reaches a non-taxable capital-receipt result.

common_material_facts: Income arose from the sale of forest or spontaneously grown trees.
The trees were found to be of spontaneous growth.
The owner or estate carried out maintenance or protective measures, or left stumps and roots in place, and relied on these to change the character of the receipts.
statutes_and_provisions: Sections 2(1) and 4(3)(viii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922
Commissioner of Income-tax v. Raja Benoy Kumar Sahas Roy
V. Venugopala Varma Rajah v. CIT, 76 ITR 460
A. K. T. K. M. Vishnudatta Antharjanam v. CAIT, 78 ITR 58
CIT v. Shaw, Wallace and Co., 6 I.T.C. 178
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Collectively the members hold that maintenance, upkeep expenditure or the mere retention of stumps does not alter the character of the receipts. In 2 of 3 members the claim of agricultural income fails. In 1 of 3 the receipts are held to be capital and not taxable.
variations: Two members concern the agricultural-income exemption; one concerns the capital versus revenue character of tree-sale receipts.

One member turns on the absence of basic operations such as planting; another on the insufficiency of maintenance expenditure as evidence of plantation; the third on the owner's object in leaving stumps and roots, with the burden on the department to show that regeneration was intended.
The outcomes differ: the claim to agricultural income fails in two members, while in the third the assessee succeeds because the receipts are capital.

split_suggestion: Keep 1766505_3 and 1766505_4 together as the agricultural-income question for spontaneously grown trees. Move 389334_1 to a separate cluster on the capital versus revenue character of tree-sale receipts, which depends on the intention behind felling and on retention of stumps and roots.

legal_question: Can an agent or partner be taken to have authority to sell or transfer the principal's or firm's immovable property from general authority to negotiate, manage, or do other acts, when the authority to sell or conclude the transfer is not clearly or expressly conferred?

predicates.authority_conferred_is_limited_to_negoti: The agent or partner was given authority only to negotiate or find a buyer, to manage affairs generally, or to do other specified acts (such as leasing, borrowing or registering documents), and not to sell.
predicates.instrument_expressly_or_clearly_confers_: The written instructions, power of attorney or partnership deed expressly or in clear words authorise the agent or partner to sell or transfer the immovable property or to conclude a binding sale contract.
predicates.contrary_usage_or_custom_established: A usage or custom is shown that permits the agent or partner to transfer immovable property without express authority.
predicates.agent_lacks_authority_to_bind_principal_: The agent or partner has no authority to bind the principal or firm to the sale or transfer, so the purported sale or contract does not bind the principal and, where the agent actually transferred the property, conveys no valid title.

definition: Authority to sell or transfer immovable property must be expressly or clearly conferred. Authority to negotiate, to manage generally, or to do other acts such as leasing or borrowing is construed strictly and does not include authority to conclude a sale or transfer, so the principal or firm is not bound.
exceptions_or_limits: Under Section 19(2)(g) of the Partnership Act, a contrary usage or custom may permit a partner to transfer firm immovable property without express authority.
The partnership conclusion was prima facie, reached at the interlocutory injunction stage.
If the instrument clearly confers authority to sell or conclude a binding contract, the rule does not apply.
The no-valid-title consequence follows where the agent actually executed a transfer without authority (nemo dat quod non habet). It was not stated for the agent's contract in the estate agency case.

common_material_facts: The written instrument gave some authority (negotiation, management, leasing or borrowing) but said nothing express about selling or transferring immovable property.
The agent or partner nonetheless purported to conclude or execute a sale or transfer.
The counterparty or purchaser relied on the general authority to argue that the principal was bound.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 19(1) and 19(2)(g) of the Partnership Act
Principle nemo dat quod non habet
Strict construction of powers of attorney (Church of Christ Charitable Trust v. Ponniamman Educational Trust)
Chadburn v. Moore; Rosenbaum v. Belson; Durga Charan Mitra v. Rajendra Narayan Sinha
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 of 3 members, the agent or partner was held to lack authority to sell or transfer the immovable property, and the principal or firm was not bound.
variations: The sources of authority differ: an estate agent's commission note, a partnership deed with a management clause, and a power of attorney.
The partnership issue rests on statute (Section 19(2)(g)), while the other two rest on case law and strict construction.
The estate agent case also relies on the absence of detailed sale terms in the instructions.
Only the power of attorney case expressly holds that the sale conveyed no valid title to a subsequent purchaser.
The partnership holding was prima facie, at the interlocutory stage.

legal_question: In an inquiry or dispute over whether a religious institution or endowment is a public trust, on whom does the burden of proof lie, and what follows if that party fails to prove the status or the other side fails to produce title documents?

predicates.public_trust_status_inquiry: The proceeding is an inquiry or dispute about whether a religious or charitable institution, endowment or property is a public trust (as opposed to private).
predicates.public_character_asserted_by_a_party: A party, whether the charity authority or a private claimant, asserts that the institution or property is a public trust.
predicates.asserting_party_bears_burden_of_proving_: The burden of proving the public character rests on the party asserting it. It may be discharged by reliable evidence from which dedication to public use can be inferred. It is not shifted to the opposing party, and the opposing party's failure to produce unavailable title documents does not by itself justify an adverse inference.

definition: The party asserting that a religious institution or endowment is a public trust bears the burden of proving it. That burden can be met with reliable evidence of dedication, such as long public worship, public funding and management. It cannot be shifted onto the party denying public character, and that party's inability to produce title documents does not by itself justify an adverse inference.
exceptions_or_limits: The burden is discharged where reliable evidence, such as long uninterrupted public use, public funding and management records, supports an inference of dedication to the public.
Failure to produce title or founding documents does not justify an adverse inference, at least where the documents are untraceable and the asserting party made no effort to obtain available records.
The members do not identify a separate statutory source for the burden rule. It is applied within the Bombay Public Trusts Act and Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act frameworks.

common_material_facts: A dispute or inquiry over whether a temple, religious institution or religious head's property is public or private.
One side asserts public character and the other relies on possession, management or private character.
Title or founding documents are missing, or are demanded from the party denying public character.
Evidence of public worship and public access is central.
statutes_and_provisions: Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, sections 2(17), 2(13), 18 and 72
Bihar Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1951, section 2(1)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all three members the burden is placed on the party asserting public trust character. In one the charity authority discharged it, in one the burden was wrongly shifted to the private claimant, and in one no adverse inference could be drawn from missing grants.
variations: The asserting party is a charity authority in one member and a private or other claimant in the others.
One member finds the burden discharged on the evidence, one finds an error in shifting the burden, and one rejects an adverse inference from non-production of documents.
One member turns on possession by a religious head and the claimant's failure to seek available estate records.

legal_question: Does a procedural shortfall in a disciplinary enquiry, such as refusing legal representation or not supplying document copies, invalidate the enquiry or punishment where the rules do not give an absolute right and the employee shows no prejudice to his defence?

rule.if: disciplinary_enquiry and procedural_shortfall_alleged and (governing_rules_confer_no_absolute_right_or_only_discretionary_permission or substantial_compliance_or_access_given) and employee_had_fair_opportunity_to_defend and no_prejudice_to_defence_shown

predicates.disciplinary_enquiry: The proceeding challenged is a departmental or disciplinary enquiry against an employee.
predicates.procedural_shortfall_alleged: The employee alleges a procedural defect, such as refusal of legal representation or non-supply of copies of statements or documents.
predicates.governing_rules_confer_no_absolute_right: The applicable rules either do not provide for the facility claimed or make it a matter of the authority's discretion in light of the circumstances.
predicates.substantial_compliance_or_access_given: Although the literal requirement was not met, the employee was given substantially equivalent access, such as inspecting the materials and taking notes before the relevant testimony.
predicates.employee_had_fair_opportunity_to_defend: Considering the circumstances as a whole, including the simplicity of the charge, the nature of the evidence, the employee's own qualifications and his participation in the enquiry, the employee had a reasonable opportunity to defend himself.
predicates.no_prejudice_to_defence_shown: The employee did not object during the enquiry and did not establish any specific way in which his defence was impaired.
predicates.enquiry_and_punishment_not_invalidated_f: The procedural shortfall does not vitiate the enquiry, violate natural justice or invalidate the punishment.

definition: A procedural shortfall in a disciplinary enquiry, such as refusal of an advocate or non-supply of copies, does not invalidate the enquiry where the rules give no absolute right or only discretionary permission, or there was substantial compliance. The employee must also have had a fair hearing and shown no specific prejudice.
exceptions_or_limits: The approach applies to procedural breaches. Breaches of substantive requirements, or procedural requirements fundamental in nature, may not be assessed on a prejudice basis.
Cases of no notice, no opportunity or no hearing are not governed by the prejudice test.
Where the enquiry is legally complex, or the presenting officer is legally trained or experienced so that the circumstances show unfairness, refusal of legal representation may be unfair.
Where the rules confer discretion, the refusal must be a proper exercise of that discretion having regard to the circumstances.

common_material_facts: Employee challenged a disciplinary enquiry on a procedural ground.
The employee made no contemporaneous objection, or the charge or enquiry was simple or record-based.
The employee did not identify concrete prejudice to his defence.
The employee had some alternative means of assistance or access, such as inspecting documents or seeking help from another officer.
statutes_and_provisions: Rule 14(8), Madhya Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1966
Section 2(i), Advocates Act, 1961
Regulation 68(b)(i) and (iii), State Bank of Patiala (Officers') Service Regulations, 1979
Section 99 CPC and section 465 CrPC (as illustrations)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the procedural shortfall did not invalidate the enquiry or punishment: 2 on refusal of legal representation and 1 on non-supply of copies.
variations: Two members concern the right to legal representation, and one concerns non-supply of witness statement copies.

One member rests on the discretionary 'may' in the rule and on the presenting officer being a serving judge; another rests on the rules giving no entitlement and the enquiry's simplicity; the third rests on substantial compliance and absence of prejudice.
The non-supply of copies member expressly distinguishes substantive from procedural breaches and mentions waiver.

legal_question: Can a reasoned, non-arbitrary change in government policy adopted in the general public interest prevail over inconsistent contractual rights or expectations (including legitimate expectation or promissory estoppel) held by private parties dealing with a public authority?

rule.if: government_policy_changed_affecting_private_contractual_position and policy_serves_general_public_interest and policy_is_reasoned_and_non_arbitrary and not policy_amounts_to_abuse_of_power

predicates.government_policy_changed_affecting_priv: The government or a public authority adopted or changed a policy that conflicts with the contractual rights, terms or expectations of a private party (for example, a right to bid in future tenders or the payment terms of an allotment or lease).
predicates.policy_serves_general_public_interest: The policy was adopted to serve the general public interest, such as preventing monopolisation, promoting competition or funding compensation for affected landowners, rather than a private or extraneous purpose.
predicates.policy_is_reasoned_and_non_arbitrary: The policy is guided by reason and is free from arbitrariness, irrationality, bias and malice, and satisfies Wednesbury reasonableness.
predicates.policy_amounts_to_abuse_of_power: The government action amounts to an abuse of power, so that it is not a bona fide exercise of policy-making authority.
predicates.public_policy_prevails_over_conflicting_: The policy is valid and enforceable against the private party, and the party's contractual right, legitimate expectation or estoppel claim does not prevent its implementation, without any need for separate legislation.

definition: Courts will not interfere with a government policy change that is reasoned, non-arbitrary and made in the general public interest, even if it overrides contractual terms, bid rights or legitimate expectations of private parties. Public interest prevails over private contractual interest unless the policy is arbitrary or amounts to an abuse of power.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule does not apply if the policy is arbitrary, irrational, biased, malicious or fails Wednesbury reasonableness.
A legitimate expectation may prevail where the state action amounts to an abuse of power.
Promissory estoppel is equitable and yields only where equity and the public good require; it is not an absolute bar on the policy change.
The policy must in fact serve the general public interest, and not merely be asserted to do so.

common_material_facts: A private party held contractual rights or expectations (a right to bid in future tenders, or fixed lease or allotment terms) with a public authority.
The government later changed policy in a way that conflicted with those rights.
The policy was justified by a public-interest objective, such as preventing monopolisation and promoting competition, or funding compensation for landowners.
The private party challenged the policy-based exclusion or demand as unfair or in breach of contract.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 14 of the Constitution (arbitrariness and Wednesbury reasonableness)
Doctrine of legitimate expectation (Sethi Auto Service Station v. Delhi Development Authority)
Doctrine of promissory estoppel (Kasinka Trading; Indo-Afghan Agencies; Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills; Godfrey Philips)
APM Terminals B.V. v. Union of India (policy may override private treaties)
Shimnit Utsch India v. West Bengal Transport Infrastructure Development Corporation
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the government policy prevailed over the private contractual right or expectation, and the challenge failed.
variations: Two members arise from port tender exclusion; one arises from additional payment demands on land allottees.

The framing differs: the first treats the policy as overriding a contractual bid right without legislation, the second treats legitimate expectation as defeated by public-interest policy, and the third relies on public interest and limits on promissory estoppel.
The competition rationale appears only in the port cases, whereas the third rests on funding compensation for landowners.
The third member also notes that the allottees had expressed willingness to cooperate, which is a factual feature the other members lack.

legal_question: Must a land acquisition Collector keep a timely redetermination application (under Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894) pending while the court award relied on is under appeal, and decide it on the final appellate judgment? If the Collector decides prematurely, how is that cured?

predicates.is_redetermination_application_case: The proceeding concerns an application to a land acquisition Collector to redetermine compensation on the basis of a court award given to other claimants (Section 28A type).
predicates.timely_redetermination_application: The redetermination application was made within the time allowed by the statute.
predicates.award_relied_on_is_under_appeal: An appeal challenging the court award on which the redetermination application relies is pending when the Collector would decide the application.
predicates.collector_must_defer_decision_until_appe: The Collector must keep the application pending until the appeal is finally decided and then determine compensation by reference to the final appellate judgment and decree.

definition: Where a timely redetermination application relies on a court award that is under appeal, the Collector must keep it pending and decide it on the final appellate judgment, because the appellate decree is the executable decree. If the Collector decides prematurely, the original application is reconsidered on the final appellate judgment instead of the applicant being left to file a successive application.
exceptions_or_limits: The deferral duty applies to timely applications relying on an award that is actually under appeal.

Where the Collector has already decided prematurely, a further application based on the appellate judgment is not maintainable under the one-application rule. The remedy is to set aside the premature award and reconsider the original application, adjusting amounts already paid (22209155_3).

common_material_facts: A redetermination application was filed on the basis of an enhanced court award.
The relied-on award was under appeal when the Collector acted or decided.
The appellate outcome could affirm, vary or set aside the award, and in one case it altered the compensation.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 28A, Land Acquisition Act, 1894
Babua Ram v. State of U.P.
U.P. State Industrial Development Corporation v. State of U.P.
Union of India v. Munshi Ram
Kendriya Karamchari Sehkari Grah Nirman Samiti Ltd. v. State of U.P.
Union of India v. Pradeep Kumari (one-application rule)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the Collector must defer to the final appellate decision. In 1 of them, where the Collector decided prematurely, the original application is reconsidered on the appellate judgment.
variations: 1806862_6 and 22209155_1 state the duty to defer. 22209155_3 addresses the remedy after a premature decision.
22209155_3 reconciles the duty with the one-application rule and the beneficial nature of Section 28A.

legal_question: Under section 171 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, can a previously assessed Hindu undivided family be treated as partitioned for income-tax purposes where the property has not been divided in the manner its nature permits (physical division if it admits of it), even though there is a severance of status, an agreement or decree, or a division of income?

predicates.income_tax_assessment_with_partition_cla: In an income-tax assessment, a partition (total or partial) of the Hindu undivided family's property is claimed so that the family is treated as divided.
predicates.previously_assessed_undivided_family: The family had earlier been assessed to income tax as a Hindu undivided family.
predicates.required_property_division_proved: The claimant has proved that the property was divided as section 171 requires: physical division (by metes and bounds, including equitable apportionment of multiple assets with equalising payments) where the property admits of it, or division to the extent the property admits where it does not. Mere severance of status, an agreement, a preliminary decree, allocation of undivided shares, or division of income does not suffice.
predicates.partition_not_recognized_for_tax_purpose: The family is not treated as partitioned for income-tax purposes, and its status and the income from the property continue as those of an undivided family.

definition: For income-tax purposes a previously assessed Hindu undivided family is treated as partitioned only if the claimant proves the division of property that section 171 and its Explanation require, namely physical division where the property admits of it, or the fullest division it admits otherwise. Severance of status under Hindu law, an agreement or preliminary decree, allocation of undivided shares and division of income are not enough.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the property genuinely cannot be physically divided, the family must still divide it to the extent it admits, as in the Charandas Haridas situation where the fullest possible measure was taken; physical division is then not required.
Hindu law may recognise partition without division by metes and bounds, but section 171 imposes additional conditions for tax purposes.
Section 171 requires the Income-tax Officer to record a finding of partition; the burden of proving the required division lies on the claimant.
Decisions under different statutory schemes, such as agricultural income tax cases, do not govern.

common_material_facts: The family had previously been assessed as a Hindu undivided family.
A partition (often partial) was claimed for the first time in the assessment proceedings.
There was no physical division of the properties by metes and bounds.
Reliance was placed on division of income, defined or undivided shares, or an agreement or decree instead of actual division.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 171 and the Explanation to section 171 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, especially clauses (a)(i), (a)(ii) and (b)
Appovier v. Rama Subba Aiyan (Hindu law partition without physical division)
Charandas Haridas v. Commissioner of Income-tax (distinguished)
Kaloomal Tapeshwar Prasad v. C.I.T., Kanpur, 133 I.T.R. 690
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the claim of partition was rejected for tax purposes and the family continued to be treated as undivided.
variations: Two members concern the same eighteen immovable properties, where division with cash equalisation was feasible; the third involves a partition agreement and preliminary civil decree.
One member stresses the burden of proof on the claimant.
One member stresses that the properties could be apportioned as lots with equalising payments, which counts as physical division.
The members differ in how they distinguish Charandas Haridas and the agricultural income tax cases.

legal_question: In a consumer housing dispute where the purchaser seeks possession rather than a refund, from what date does compensation (interest) for delayed possession run, and does the start date differ for a transferee?

predicates.possession_claim_in_housing_project: The purchaser or allottee seeks delivery of possession of a unit in a housing project, not a refund, and claims compensation for delay.
predicates.contractual_possession_period_expired: The developer's contractual period for making possession available (including any agreed extension) has ended without possession being delivered.
predicates.parties_agreed_or_settlement_framework_a: The parties have agreed to, or the Court has adopted, a settlement or earlier-decision framework for calculating delay compensation in possession cases (for example, interest at 9%).
predicates.delay_compensation_interest_runs_only_af: Delay compensation is calculated only for the period after the contractual possession period expires. For a transferee it starts on the later of the transfer date and that expiry. Where possession is offered, it may continue for a fixed period after the offer.

definition: Where a purchaser seeks possession and the parties have agreed to, or the Court has adopted, a settlement framework, delay compensation (interest at 9%) is counted only after the contractual possession period expires. For a transferee it starts on the later of the transfer date and that expiry, and in one member it continues for two months after the offer of possession.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule rests on agreed or settlement frameworks adopted by the Court, not on an independently identified statutory provision.
It applies to possession claims, not refund claims.
The two-month continuation after the offer of possession was directed in the one project-specific order and is not stated in the other members.
The 9% rate and the three-year period are those of the framework in these cases and may differ where the parties have agreed otherwise.

common_material_facts: Purchasers sought possession of units in a housing project rather than a refund.
The agreement gave the developer a contractual possession period of about three years, including an extension.
Compensation was fixed at 9% interest under a settlement or agreed framework, following earlier decisions in the Himanshu Arora line.
Some purchasers were transferees who had stepped into the original allottee's position.
statutes_and_provisions: DLF Homes Panchkula Pvt. Ltd. v. Himanshu Arora (settlement terms)
DLF Homes Panchkula (P.) Ltd. v. Sushila Devi (settlement terms)
No statutory provision identified by the members
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that delay compensation starts only after the contractual possession period expires, or for a transferee on the later of the transfer date and that expiry. One also continues interest for two months after the offer of possession.
variations: One member also addresses the post-offer period and the occupation certificate, and the others address only the start date.
One member states the general start-date rule and another states the transferee rule.
The members rely on party agreement or settlement terms rather than independent statutory reasoning.

legal_question: Does a public servant commit criminal misconduct under the corruption statute (Section 13(1)(d) of the 1988 Act, or Section 5(1)(d) of the 1947 Act) by abusing his or her official position to obtain a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage for himself, herself or another person?

predicates.public_servant_case: The accused was a public servant who held the office or power through which the impugned act was done.
predicates.official_position_abused_dishonestly_or_: The public servant used his or her office or power dishonestly, by corrupt or illegal means, or contrary to the governing rules and the purpose for which the power was conferred, and not in an innocuous or good-faith way.
predicates.valuable_thing_or_pecuniary_advantage_ob: As a result of the abuse, the public servant, or another person for whom he or she acted, obtained a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, such as property, an allotment or a price benefit, without any public interest.
predicates.criminal_misconduct_established: The conduct amounts to criminal misconduct under the statute, and a conviction for it can be sustained if the facts are proved.

definition: A public servant who dishonestly or illegally abuses his or her official position to obtain a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage for self or another person, without public interest, commits criminal misconduct. The statutory alternatives are independent, so any one suffices. The advantage need not come from a third party, and the abuse may involve bypassing allotment rules or misstating facts.
exceptions_or_limits: The penal provision is construed strictly: dishonest intent is required, and innocuous acts or ordinary administrative lapses are not covered (35536_1).
The abuse and the advantage must be proved on the evidence. Concurrent findings of fact are not readily disturbed on appeal (32843746_1).
35536_1 concerns the 1947 Act (Section 5(1)(d)), while the other two concern the 1988 Act (Section 13(1)(d)). The reasoning is parallel but the provisions differ in text.

common_material_facts: A public servant in charge of allotting or assigning government or authority land or plots.
Allotments, conversions or assignments made in breach of the governing rules or by manipulating facts.
The benefit went to the public servant or to a relative (daughters, brother-in-law).
The authority or government suffered a loss, or the advantage was a valuable property or a price concession.
statutes_and_provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, Section 13(1)(d)(i)–(iii)
Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, Section 13(2)
Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, Section 5(1)(d)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members find criminal misconduct established or the conviction upheld (2 upheld convictions, 1 held that the conduct, if proved, falls within the provision).
variations: Two members apply the 1988 Act's three independent, disjunctive limbs. One applies the older Section 5(1)(d) and stresses dishonest intent and strict construction.
The advantage went to the public servant himself or herself in one case, to the public servant and relatives in another, and to a relative only in the third.
The abuse took different forms: bypassing scheme limits and preferential pricing, defective applications and layout changes, or understating the value of trees.

legal_question: Should judges or judicial officers who decided a matter in their judicial capacity be joined as parties to a writ petition, special leave petition or appeal challenging that decision when no relief is claimed against them?

predicates.challenge_to_judicial_decision: The proceeding (writ petition, special leave petition, or appeal, including an appeal from a contempt decision) challenges a decision given by a judge or judicial officer acting in a judicial capacity.
predicates.judges_named_as_parties_only_because_the: The judges or judicial officers are impleaded as parties solely because they decided the matter under challenge, and not because they have a separate interest in the outcome.
predicates.no_relief_claimed_against_judges: The petitioner or appellant seeks no relief against the judges or judicial officers personally.
predicates.judges_should_not_be_joined_as_parties: The practice of impleading the deciding judges or judicial officers should be discontinued; they are not proper parties, and in contempt matters the proceeding is titled in the name of the alleged contemnor.

definition: Judges or judicial officers who decide a case in their judicial capacity have no litigant's interest in its outcome. They should not be impleaded in a writ petition, special leave petition or appeal challenging their decision when no relief is claimed against them. In contempt matters the proceeding should be titled in the name of the alleged contemnor.
exceptions_or_limits: Applies only where no relief is claimed against the judges; persons against whom relief is sought, or who have an interest in the result, remain proper parties.
The in re / alleged-contemnor title is stated only for contempt proceedings and appeals from them.
The members describe this as a practice to be deprecated or discontinued, not as a statutory bar.
Ambard v. Attorney-General for Trinidad & Tobago is noted as an example of different party practice and was not relied on as the basis of the rule.

common_material_facts: Judges or judicial officers who decided the matter below were named as respondents in the higher-forum challenge.
No relief was claimed against them and they had acted only in their judicial capacity.
The court considered the joinder unnecessary and unjustified.
statutes_and_provisions: Articles 226 and 138 of the Constitution of India (writ petitions and special leave petitions), as cited in the civil-proceedings member
Ambard v. Attorney-General for Trinidad & Tobago, noted as an example of different party practice
No statutory provision was applied in the contempt members
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the deciding judges should not be impleaded and the practice should be discontinued. Two of the three (contempt) add that the title should name the alleged contemnor.
variations: One member concerns civil proceedings and judicial officers in writ petitions and special leave petitions; two concern contempt convictions and appeals.
The contempt members rely on the general test of who is a proper party (claiming relief, relief sought against them, or an interest in the result); the civil member states the point more briefly.
Only one contempt member refers to the English in re title practice.

legal_question: Is an individual governmental exemption from a regulatory protection (building controls or tenant/rent-control protections) invalid where it rests on irrelevant grounds, or where the government has not applied its mind to considerations germane to the purpose of the governing legislation?

predicates.individual_exemption_granted_under_statu: The government granted an exemption to a particular person, building or institution from the operation of a regulatory statute (building controls or rent/tenant protection) under a statutory exemption power.
predicates.exemption_grounds_not_germane_to_statuto: The reasons relied on for the exemption are irrelevant to, or inconsistent with, the policy and purpose of the legislation (for example, land cost, mere expiry of a tenancy, a tenant's exercise of statutory protection, or mere qualifying status and use of income).
predicates.relevant_considerations_not_applied_or_i: The decision-maker did not apply its mind to, or ignored, considerations relevant to the statute's purpose (for example, expert committee findings, the master plan, environmental requirements, availability of alternative accommodation, or a relevant ground for exemption).
predicates.exemption_order_invalid: The exemption order or notification is ultra vires, illegal or void and liable to be quashed or held unenforceable.

definition: A statutory power to exempt must be exercised consistently with the policy and purpose of the Act. An individual exemption is open to challenge and is invalid if it rests on irrelevant grounds or the government did not apply its mind to the relevant considerations, even where the exemption power itself is valid or validated.
exceptions_or_limits: The exemption power itself is not invalid; the challenge is to the individual order (a validation clause protects the power, not an individual order from review).
Qualifying status or use of income merely entitles an applicant to apply; it does not itself justify an exemption.
In the tenant-protection case two judges dissented and would have upheld the order on the circumstances, so the application of the germane-grounds test to the facts can be contested.
Review is limited to discrimination, irrelevant grounds, non-application of mind or mala fides, not a general merits review.

common_material_facts: The government granted an individual exemption from a protective regulatory statute.
The stated or recorded reasons were unrelated to the statutory purpose or were absent.
Relevant considerations were not examined (expert recommendation and environment; alternative accommodation; a policy-relevant ground).
statutes_and_provisions: Tamil Nadu District Municipalities Act 1920, Chapter X-A (ss. 217-B, 217-C, 217-D, 217-K, 217-Q) and Hill Stations Building Rules 1993, rr. 26-27
Section 3 of Tamil Nadu Act 52 of 1994 (validation)
Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act 1961, s. 3(2)
Madras Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act 1949, s. 13 (via P. J. Irani)
Article 14; Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Tendolkar; Sardar Inder Singh v. State of Rajasthan
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the exemption order invalid or quashed (one by majority, with two dissenters).
variations: The building case turned on ignored expert and environmental requirements and irrelevant factors, with a validation clause argument rejected.
The tenancy case turned on reasons not germane to preventing unreasonable eviction and on failure to consider alternative accommodation, with a dissent.
The institutional-owner case turned on absence of any recorded relevant ground and non-application of mind.

legal_question: Does mere presence at the scene of an unlawful assembly establish membership under Section 149 IPC, or must the prosecution show participation or other circumstances that distinguish a member from a mere spectator?

rule.if: unlawful_assembly_prosecution and accused_presence_at_assembly_shown and not (individual_conduct_or_participation_proved or surrounding_circumstances_exclude_spectator_status)

predicates.unlawful_assembly_prosecution: The accused are prosecuted for offences allegedly committed by an unlawful assembly, with liability sought under Section 149 IPC.
predicates.accused_presence_at_assembly_shown: The evidence shows that the accused was present at the scene or in the crowd.
predicates.individual_conduct_or_participation_prov: Credible evidence shows the accused did an act or omission, such as attacking, inciting, concealing the crime or disposing of bodies, that joined them to the assembly and furthered its common object, or the case falls within Section 142 IPC.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_exclude_specta: Proved circumstances, such as injuries at the scene, the accused's relationship to the parties and their stake in the dispute, make it inconsistent with the accused being a curious onlooker.
predicates.mere_presence_does_not_establish_members: Presence alone is insufficient to hold the accused a member of the unlawful assembly, and liability under Section 149 cannot rest on it.

definition: Under Section 149 IPC, being present at or in a crowd at an unlawful assembly does not by itself make a person a member, since the person may be a mere spectator. Membership must be shown by individual conduct, a Section 142 basis, or proved circumstances that exclude spectator status. Where such material exists, membership and common object are questions of fact and can be established.
exceptions_or_limits: Membership can be established where credible evidence of participation, or circumstances such as injuries at the scene combined with a stake in the dispute and relationships to the parties, make spectator status implausible (as in 960347_3).
General-term evidence that people were present and armed must be closely scrutinised, and each accused's case considered individually.
Absence of recovery of weapons from the accused does not prevent a finding of membership if other evidence of participation is accepted.
Conduct furthering the common object, such as disposing of the victims' bodies, can support membership.

common_material_facts: A large crowd or mob at the scene of a violent incident, in a village setting
The possibility that some of those present were curious onlookers
Differing evidence against individual accused: some with no specific act, others with specific conduct or connecting circumstances
statutes_and_provisions: Section 149 IPC
Section 142 IPC
Section 148 IPC
Masalti v. State of U.P. (cited)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Two of three members (1879133_3, 808611_4) hold that mere presence does not establish membership, with those lacking individual conduct given the benefit of doubt or acquitted. One (960347_3) upholds membership because evidence of participation and surrounding circumstances negated spectator status.
variations: 960347_3 applies the principle on the opposite side: membership was found because evidence went beyond bare presence.
808611_4 sets out the fullest test: conduct, omission or Section 142, with individual scrutiny of each accused.
1879133_3 is brief and relies on Masalti.
960347_3 treats membership and common object as questions of fact assessed on all circumstances.

legal_question: May polluting industries be required to maintain functional effluent treatment systems and hold operating consent from the Pollution Control Board, and be restrained or closed if they do not, with operation resuming only after the plant is restored and fresh consent is obtained?

rule.if: environmental_public_interest_proceeding and industry_requires_operating_consent and (effluent_treatment_not_functional_or_inadequate or operating_consent_not_obtained)

predicates.environmental_public_interest_proceeding: The matter is a public interest proceeding before the Court seeking to control industrial pollution.
predicates.industry_requires_operating_consent: The industry is of a kind that needs operating consent from the Pollution Control Board to operate.
predicates.effluent_treatment_not_functional_or_ina: The industry's effluent treatment plant or pollution-control system is not functional, not fully operational, or inadequate, including after notice and inspection.
predicates.operating_consent_not_obtained: The industry has failed to obtain, or does not hold, the Board's operating consent (including fresh consent after restraint).
predicates.industry_must_be_restrained_or_closed_un: The industry must be restrained from operating, or closed, and may resume only once its treatment plant is functional to the required capacity and operating consent is obtained.

definition: An industry needing operating consent may operate only with a functional effluent treatment or pollution-control system and the Board's consent. If it defaults, it may be restrained (including by electricity disconnection) or closed, and may resume only after restoring the plant and obtaining fresh consent.
exceptions_or_limits: Restraint follows notice and inspection by the Pollution Control Board in the first member's directions.
Resumption requires both a plant functional to the required capacity and fresh operating consent; restoring the plant alone is not enough.
Members 190799178_1 and 190799178_2 cite no statutory provision; the statutory basis (Water Act 1974; Environment (Protection) Act 1986, ss. 5 and 7) appears only in 1934103_7.

common_material_facts: Environmental public interest proceedings concerning industrial effluent
Industries with absent, non-functional or inadequate treatment plants
Operating consent from the Pollution Control Board as a condition for operation
Court-issued directions with restraint or closure as the consequence of default
statutes_and_provisions: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 (consent for outlets and discharges)
Environment (Protection) Act 1986, sections 5 and 7
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members result in compliance directions: restraint or closure of defaulting industries (2 members) and resumption only after restoration and fresh consent (1 member).
variations: One member concerns tanneries with a statutory basis and closure; two concern restraint of industries generally, without citing a provision.
One member addresses the conditions for resumption rather than the initial restraint.
Enforcement mechanisms differ: electricity disconnection on Board recommendation versus closure for failure to obtain consent.

legal_question: Will a higher court (revisional or reviewing) interfere with an appellate court's discretionary decision, under Order XLI Rule 27 CPC, to receive or refuse additional evidence?

rule.if: appellate_court_decided_additional_evidence_application_in_exercise_of_discretion and appellate_court_acted_within_jurisdiction and (decision_rests_on_grounds_supported_by_record or application_very_belated or appeal_still_pending_with_remedy_after_decree) and not decision_shown_to_be_beyond_jurisdiction_or_unsupported

predicates.appellate_court_decided_additional_evide: The appellate court allowed or refused an application to receive additional evidence under Order XLI Rule 27 CPC in exercise of its discretion.
predicates.appellate_court_acted_within_jurisdictio: The appellate court's order on the additional-evidence application was within its jurisdiction.
predicates.decision_rests_on_grounds_supported_by_r: The appellate court's decision rests on grounds supported by the record, such as materiality of the evidence and its unavailability despite due diligence or its later creation.
predicates.application_very_belated: The application for additional evidence was made very late, many years after the suit began and after the appeal was filed.
predicates.appeal_still_pending_with_remedy_after_d: The appeal is still pending, so the interim order can be challenged in accordance with law after the appellate decree.
predicates.decision_shown_to_be_beyond_jurisdiction: It is shown that the appellate court's decision was outside its jurisdiction or lacked support in the record.
predicates.higher_court_should_not_interfere_with_a: The revisional or reviewing court should leave the appellate court's discretionary decision on additional evidence undisturbed, and any interference is unwarranted.

definition: A revisional or reviewing court should not disturb an appellate court's discretionary order allowing or refusing additional evidence where the order is within jurisdiction and is supported by the record, or the application was very belated, or the appeal is pending and the order can be challenged after the appellate decree.
exceptions_or_limits: Does not apply where the appellate court acted outside its jurisdiction or without grounds supported by the record.
The members rest on different grounds, namely belated application, support in the record, and interim interference in a pending appeal, so the rule is framed as alternatives.
The pending-appeal ground leaves the challenge open after the appellate decree.
The belated-application member is a Supreme Court decision declining to interfere with a High Court refusal, rather than a revision under Section 115 CPC.

common_material_facts: An application for additional evidence was made in a civil appeal, which was decided at the appellate stage under Order XLI Rule 27 CPC.
A higher court was asked to interfere, or did interfere, with the appellate court's discretionary decision.
The evidence sought was a document or expert examination, such as a bank letter, a will's signature, or landlord-tenant documents.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 115 CPC
Order XLI Rule 27 CPC
Mahavir Singh v. Naresh Chandra (2001) 1 SCC 309
Gurdev Singh v. Mehnga Ram (1997) 6 SCC 507
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the higher court's interference was held unwarranted or was declined. In 2, the High Court's revisional order was set aside and the appellate order restored or the application remanded. In 1, the High Court's refusal was left undisturbed.
variations: One member involves a refusal of additional evidence, while two involve grants of it.
The grounds differ: very belated application, interim interference in a pending appeal, and discretion exercised on supported grounds (materiality and due diligence).
Remedies differ: the application was remanded for fresh decision in one, the appellate order was restored in another, and the refusal was left undisturbed in the third.

legal_question: Is a petition under Article 32 maintainable where no infringement of a fundamental right is established, whether because the action is merely alleged to be illegal or because the claimed right depends on an entitlement finally negated by a competent authority?

predicates.article_32_petition: The proceeding is a petition invoking the Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 32 for enforcement of fundamental rights.
predicates.fundamental_right_infringement_establish: The petitioner has shown an actual infringement of a fundamental right. This is not shown where the action is merely illegal, where no fundamental right to the claimed benefit exists, or where the claimed right depends on an underlying entitlement that a competent authority has finally decided against the petitioner and that decision is neither void nor set aside.
predicates.article_32_petition_not_maintainable: The Article 32 petition cannot be maintained and relief under Article 32 is unavailable.

definition: Relief under Article 32 requires a demonstrated infringement of a fundamental right. Illegality of government action alone is not enough, and a right that depends on an entitlement finally negated by a competent authority is not established while that determination stands.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the claimed right depends on an underlying status or entitlement, a final determination by a competent authority defeats the claim unless it is shown to be a nullity (for example, for want of jurisdiction) or has otherwise been set aside.
A challenge to the merits of a final determination must be brought through an appropriate proceeding, not an Article 32 petition.

A statutory bar on other courts' jurisdiction (such as section 28 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950) does not oust Article 32. The lack of an established infringement still defeats the petition.

common_material_facts: The petitioner invoked Article 32 against government or administrative action.
No fundamental right was shown to be infringed.
Two members concern the grant of a mineral lease to a third party, where the petitioners alleged illegality but showed no fundamental right to the lease.
One member concerns land declared evacuee property by a final determination, on which the claimed rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 depended.
statutes_and_provisions: Article 32 of the Constitution
Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution
Articles 136, 226 and 227 of the Constitution
Sections 2(d), 2(f) and 28 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950
Mining legislation and rules (lease grant)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the Article 32 petition not maintainable for want of an established fundamental-right infringement. Two do so even assuming the government action was illegal, and one because a final determination negated the underlying entitlement.
variations: Two members rest on the simple proposition that illegality without a fundamental-right violation is insufficient.

One member (323060_1) turns on the finality of a competent authority's determination, which negates the entitlement on which the right depends, subject to nullity or setting aside. It relies on Sahibzada Saiyed Muhammed Amirabbas Abbasi v. State of Madhya Bharat.
The mining-lease members cite no earlier authority.

legal_question: Is expenditure on the upkeep and maintenance of immature, non-bearing plantation (rubber) trees deductible in computing agricultural income under a plantation agricultural income-tax statute, where it is not capital or personal expenditure and is laid out wholly and exclusively for the plantation or for deriving agricultural income, even though the trees yield no income in that year?

rule.if: agricultural_income_tax_deduction_claim and immature_nonbearing_tree_upkeep_expense and wholly_and_exclusively_for_plantation_or_agricultural_income and not capital_or_personal_expense

predicates.agricultural_income_tax_deduction_claim: The assessee claims a deduction in computing agricultural income under a plantation or agricultural income-tax statute whose deduction provision excludes capital and personal expenditure and requires the expense to be laid out wholly and exclusively for the plantation or for deriving agricultural income.
predicates.immature_nonbearing_tree_upkeep_expense: The expense was incurred for upkeep or maintenance (such as forking and manuring) of immature plantation trees, such as rubber trees, that are not yet bearing or yielding.
predicates.wholly_and_exclusively_for_plantation_or: The expenditure was laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the plantation or for deriving agricultural income.
predicates.capital_or_personal_expense: The expenditure is of a capital nature (for example, acquiring an income-earning asset) or is a personal expense of the assessee.
predicates.upkeep_expense_deductible: The upkeep expenditure on the immature trees is an allowable deduction in computing agricultural income.

definition: Expenditure on maintaining immature, non-yielding plantation trees is deductible if it is not capital or personal expenditure and is laid out wholly and exclusively for the plantation or for deriving agricultural income. The deduction does not depend on the trees producing income in the same accounting year.
exceptions_or_limits: Capital expenditure incurred to acquire or create an income-earning asset is not covered; the Assam Bengal Cement distinction was treated as inapplicable only because it concerned capital expenditure.
Personal expenses are not deductible.
Where the governing provision is worded differently, the precedent applies directly only if its test is the same as or more favourable to the assessee than the test in the controlling decision.
The quantum of deductible expenses may still need to be ascertained, as the tribunal directed for forking and manuring.

common_material_facts: Rubber plantation with immature, non-bearing trees
Expenses claimed for upkeep and maintenance, such as forking and manuring
Expenditure not disputed to be non-capital and non-personal and incurred for the plantation
Tribunal and High Court generally allowed the deduction
statutes_and_provisions: Section 5(e) of the Madras Plantations Agricultural Income Tax Act, 1955
Section 5(j) and section 5 of the Travancore-Cochin Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1950
Travancore Rubber & Tea Co. Ltd. v. CAIT Kerala, [1961] 3 S.C.R. 279
