predicates.family_custom_or_other_sufficient_eviden: Clear and unambiguous evidence, such as family consensus, traditional belief, statements, documents and consistent conduct, shows an ancient and invariable family custom treating the identified movables (for example ceremonial regalia) as impartible, or other sufficient evidence shows they form part of the estate.
predicates.movable_property_is_impartible_and_exclu: The identified movable property is held to be impartible estate property and is not available for partition.

definition: The doctrine of incorporation applies to immovable property and does not by itself make movables part of an impartible estate. Movables, such as ceremonial regalia, are excluded from partition only if a family custom of impartibility (ancient, invariable and clearly proved by family consensus, belief, statements and conduct) or other sufficient evidence is established. Without it, the movables are ordinary property and may be partible or personal.
exceptions_or_limits: Where no custom or other sufficient evidence of incorporation is found, movables are not treated as estate property; in one member they were held to be personal property and not partible.
The custom must be ancient and invariable and proved by clear and unambiguous evidence; a family custom needs fewer instances of proof than a territorial or community custom.
Exclusion extends only to the identified items or category proved to be regalia or impartible.
A proved custom may continue after the circumstances that gave rise to it have changed, such as abolition of the estate.
Findings of fact on identification of the items are generally not disturbed by the Supreme Court.

common_material_facts: Partition dispute over movable property such as jewels, jewellery or utensils claimed to be part of an impartible estate
Claim that the items are regalia or estate property rather than partible property
Reliance on family documents, wills, lists of jewels used at an installation ceremony, and family conduct as evidence of custom
statutes_and_provisions: Doctrine of incorporation, which applies to immovable and not movable property
Family custom modifying the ordinary law of partition
Ramalakhmi Ammal v. Sivanantha Perumal Sethurayar (ancient, invariable custom proved clearly)
Abdul Hussein Khan v. Bibi Sona (proof of family custom)
Shiba Prasad Singh v. Rani Prayag Kumari Debi (impartible estates)
Rai Kishore Singh v. Mst. Gahenabai (custom may outlive its originating conditions)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Incorporation is rejected for movables in all 3 members. Where a family custom was proved (2 of 3), the identified jewels were held impartible regalia, with 38 jewels upheld. Where no custom or evidence was found (1 of 3), the movables were personal and not partible.
variations: Two members found a custom proved from evidence of regalia treatment, while one found no custom and held the movables personal property.
One member addresses continuation of the custom after the estate was abolished and the circumstances changed.
One member addresses movables acquired from estate income and jewellery received at marriage.

legal_question: Is standing timber (trees or bamboos) that is agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale 'goods' under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, so that its sale or purchase can be taxed under sales or purchase tax laws, whatever the label the contract carries?

predicates.sales_or_purchase_tax_dispute: The case concerns the liability to, or the validity of, a sales tax or purchase tax levied on a transaction in standing timber, trees or bamboos.
predicates.timber_or_trees_attached_to_land: The subject matter is timber, trees or bamboos standing on or attached to land at the time of the contract.
predicates.contract_provides_for_severance_before_s: The contract, or the agreement between the parties, requires or contemplates that the timber be severed before sale or under the contract of sale, as in section 2(7) of the Sale of Goods Act.
predicates.transaction_in_substance_transfers_timbe: Looking at substance rather than description, the transaction transfers the timber (not an interest in the land) for a price or consideration, so that it is a completed sale or purchase of goods and not a mere agreement to sever.
predicates.timber_is_goods_and_transaction_is_taxab: The timber counts as goods within the Sale of Goods Act, and the State may tax the transaction as a sale or purchase of goods under Entry 54 of List II and the applicable state Act.

definition: Trees, timber or bamboos attached to land are goods under section 2(7) of the Sale of Goods Act when they are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale. A transaction that in substance transfers such timber for consideration is therefore a taxable sale or purchase of goods, even if styled a lease. A state law or notification taxing it is valid if it taxes a completed sale or purchase and not merely an agreement to sever.
exceptions_or_limits: A State cannot extend 'sale of goods' beyond the meaning in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930; transactions that are not sales of goods under that Act cannot be taxed.
A notification or levy is valid only if it taxes a completed sale or purchase and not a mere agreement to sever.
Where the buyer takes an interest in the land as land, or the contract does not provide for severance, the timber may not be treated as goods (implied by the focus on substance and on severance).
Property may pass before severance only if the goods are specific or ascertained, the contract is unconditional, the goods are in a deliverable state, and no contrary intention appears.

common_material_facts: Standing timber, trees or bamboos attached to land were the subject of the contract.
The contract or the statutory definition contemplated severance before sale or under the contract of sale.
The dispute concerned liability to or validity of sales tax or purchase tax under a state Act.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 2(7), Sale of Goods Act, 1930
Sections 4 and 18–23, Sale of Goods Act, 1930
Entry 54, List II, Seventh Schedule
Section 2(g) and sections 2(n), 2(o), 2(t), Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act
Sections 3B and 5(1), Orissa Sales Tax Act, 1947
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the timber to be goods and the transaction or notification taxable or valid: the Forest Department was liable (1), the appeal was allowed with the amendment held valid as applied (1), and the purchase tax notifications were upheld (1).
variations: One member looked through the 'lease' label to the substance of the contract.
One member tested the validity of a retrospective state amendment to the definition of goods against the Sale of Goods Act.
One member addressed when property passes before severance, in order to uphold a purchase tax on a completed purchase.
The taxes differ: sales tax in two members and purchase tax in one.

legal_question: Does the right to life under Article 21 include the right to livelihood, so that State action (eviction or acquisition) that deprives a person of the means of livelihood must satisfy constitutional requirements, such as a just, fair and reasonable procedure, and compensation or rehabilitation?

rule.if: article_21_claim and livelihood_depends_on_property_or_place and state_action_deprives_that_livelihood and not livelihood_based_on_illegal_or_immoral_occupation

predicates.article_21_claim: The petitioner invokes the constitutional right to life as a ground to challenge State action.
predicates.livelihood_depends_on_property_or_place: The person's means of living depends on particular property or on a place (such as land held or a dwelling near the workplace).
predicates.state_action_deprives_that_livelihood: State action, such as land taking or eviction, removes or puts in jeopardy that means of livelihood.
predicates.livelihood_based_on_illegal_or_immoral_o: The livelihood claimed comes from an occupation that is illegal or immoral.
predicates.deprivation_engages_article_21_and_is_un: The deprivation falls within Article 21 (the right to livelihood is part of the right to life). It is invalid unless it follows a just, fair and reasonable procedure established by law, and where persons are uprooted the State must give adequate compensation and rehabilitation.

definition: The right to life under Article 21 includes the right to livelihood, because a person cannot live without the means of living. State action such as eviction or land taking that deprives a person of that livelihood therefore violates the Constitution unless done by a just, fair and reasonable procedure. Where people are uprooted, the State must provide adequate compensation and rehabilitation.
exceptions_or_limits: The protection was not extended to livelihood from an illegal or immoral occupation (In Re: Sant Ram was distinguished on this ground).
Deprivation is permissible if it follows a just, fair and reasonable procedure established by law.

The compensation and rehabilitation duty was stated for persons actually uprooted by State action whose livelihood depended on the property; eviction cases stated the violation but members do not uniformly require alternative accommodation.

common_material_facts: Petitioners were economically weak persons (farmers, pavement or slum dwellers) whose livelihood depended on the land or place at stake.
State action, such as land taking or eviction, threatened or removed that livelihood.
No compensation, alternative accommodation or rehabilitation was provided.
statutes_and_provisions: Constitution Article 21
Articles 37, 39(a) and 41 (directive principles used to interpret Article 21)
Article 19(1)(e) and (g)
Tamil Nadu Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1971, including s.11(a)
Tamil Nadu Land Encroachment Act, 1905
Madras City Municipal Corporation Act, 1919
Tamil Nadu Town and Country Planning Act, 1971
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold that the right to livelihood is part of Article 21. Deprivation without fair procedure (2 members) or without compensation and rehabilitation (1 member) is unconstitutional.
variations: One member is a land-taking case centred on compensation and rehabilitation, citing K. Krishna Reddy on prompt compensation.
Two members are pavement or slum eviction cases; one states the principle and the other applies Olga Tellis to Tamil Nadu statutes and adds Articles 19(1)(e) and (g).
Only one member expressly distinguishes illegal or immoral occupations.

legal_question: In a land ceiling proceeding, must a voluntary transfer made after the statutory cutoff date be disregarded when determining the land to be surrendered or the ceiling area, so that the holder or successor stays liable for the excess?

rule.if: ceiling_proceeding and land_would_exceed_ceiling_without_transfer and transfer_made_after_statutory_cutoff and not transfer_within_exception_that_applies_after_cutoff

predicates.ceiling_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding to determine a landholder's ceiling area or the excess land to be surrendered under a land ceiling statute.
predicates.land_would_exceed_ceiling_without_transf: The land held on the relevant date would exceed the ceiling limit (be surplus) if the impugned transfer were not taken into account.
predicates.transfer_made_after_statutory_cutoff: The transfer, such as a gift, was made after the date on which the ceiling or surrender obligation became operative or was fixed by statute.
predicates.transfer_within_exception_that_applies_a: The transfer falls within a statutory exception that actually protects transfers made after the cutoff. Under the Kerala members, an excepted category does not protect a post-cutoff transfer. Under the U.P. member, the proviso exceptions are applied to the transfer.
predicates.transfer_disregarded_and_land_counted_in: The transfer is ignored, and the transferred land is treated as still held by the transferor (or by the successor who inherited it) when determining the surplus land to be surrendered.

definition: A voluntary transfer made after the statutory cutoff date that fixes the ceiling or surrender obligation is ignored in the ceiling determination, so the land stays in the computation and the holder remains liable to surrender the excess. In the Kerala cases, even a transfer of a type excepted from invalidation does not help if made after the cutoff. In the U.P. case, the rule also covers a predecessor's transfer where the successor inherited the land before the assessment date.
exceptions_or_limits: Under the U.P. Act, a transfer within the proviso's exceptions is not ignored.

Under the Kerala Act, transfers between the publication of the Bill and the notified date are considered unless within an enumerated exception. Only transfers after the notified date are ignored regardless of exception.
For a predecessor's transfer to be ignored in a successor's determination, the successor must have inherited the land before the assessment date.
The rule applies only where the land would otherwise be surplus.

common_material_facts: Gifts of land were made after the statutory cutoff date.
Without the gifts the holding would exceed the ceiling.
The gifts were claimed to be protected, either as excepted transfers or as outside the provision's reach.
statutes_and_provisions: Kerala Land Reforms Act, sections 82-87, especially section 84
U.P. Imposition of Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1960, section 5(6) and its proviso
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members, the post-cutoff transfer is disregarded and the land counts toward the ceiling or surrender determination. Two are Kerala cases that treat excepted transfers as ineffective after the cutoff, and one is a U.P. case that extends the rule to a predecessor's transfer.
variations: The Kerala members concern the holder's own transfers, including gifts to children who were minors on the notified date.
The U.P. member concerns a predecessor's transfer and a successor who inherited before the assessment date.
The Kerala members hold that excepted-category transfers do not save post-cutoff transfers, while the U.P. member depends on the proviso exceptions not applying.
The Kerala members rely on State of Kerala v. Philomina and State of Kerala v. K. A. Gangadharan. The U.P. member distinguishes Arjan Singh v. State of Punjab.

legal_question: After severance of joint family status and pending final partition, must a family member who possesses or manages joint family property account to the other co-sharers for the rents, income, profits or dividends received from it?

predicates.joint_status_severed_and_partition_pendi: The joint family status has been severed (or partition demanded) and final partition of the family property has not yet been effected.
predicates.member_possessed_or_managed_joint_family: The family member had possession, control or management of joint family property after severance.
predicates.member_received_income_from_that_propert: The member received rents, income, profits or dividends from the joint family property after severance and before final partition.
predicates.member_must_account_to_other_co_sharers_: The member is liable to render an account of those receipts to the other co-sharers, to be adjusted in the final accounts.

definition: Once joint family status is severed, the members hold the property as tenants in common, and any member who possesses or manages it must account to the other co-sharers for the rents, income, profits and dividends received from the date of severance (or demand) until final partition. A co-sharer's own receipt of income from some property does not release the managers from accounting, but is taken into account when the accounts are finally adjusted.
exceptions_or_limits: Liability runs from severance or the demand for partition, not for earlier dealings, where the claim is so limited.
Money in the accounting member's hands is not thereby impressed with a trust, and separate acquisitions are not automatically family property.
The income the claimant received from other family property, and the claimant's possession of part of it, is set off in the final adjustment of accounts rather than extinguishing the duty to account.

common_material_facts: Joint family status was severed and the members held the property as tenants in common.
Members in possession or management received rents, income, profits or dividends before final partition.
The decree or direction required accounts of such receipts.
statutes_and_provisions: Gulabrao Fakirrao v. Baburao Fakirrao (relied on in 516830_5 and referred to in 78061201_5)
John Kennedy v. Mary Annette De Trafford (relied on in 516830_5 and 78061201_5)
M.N. Aryamurthy v. M.D. Subbaraya Setty (applied in 78061201_5)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the member in possession or management was held liable to account for post-severance income, with set-off of what the claimant received.
variations: 516830_5 and 78061201_5 concern a possessing co-sharer's duty to account for income until final partition; 582191_6 concerns whether the claimant's own receipt of some income releases the managers from accounting.
In 582191_6 accounting is limited to dealings after the demand for partition and excludes earlier dealings.
78061201_5 applies a binding earlier decision, while 516830_5 states the principle directly.

legal_question: Does a litigant have a vested right to have an appeal heard by a particular number of judges (e.g., a Division Bench) as prescribed when the suit or appeal was instituted, or may the appeal be validly heard by the bench composition prescribed by competent law in force at the time of hearing?

predicates.appeal_available_in_high_court: The substantive right of appeal to the High Court continues to exist and was exercised, so the appeal is actually heard by the High Court.
predicates.bench_composition_changed_by_competent_l: A competent legislature changed the number of judges required or permitted to hear the appeal (including through repeal of a provision or reorganisation of the court) before the appeal was heard.
predicates.bench_composition_is_procedural_not_subs: The number of judges hearing an appeal is a matter of procedure and not part of the substantive right of appeal, and the challenged provision is not shown to be unconstitutional.
predicates.no_vested_right_to_specific_bench_and_he: The appellant has no vested right to a bench of the size prescribed at institution, and a hearing by the bench constituted under the law in force at the time of hearing is valid.

definition: The right of appeal is substantive, but the number of judges who hear it is procedural. A party therefore has no vested right to the bench strength prevailing when the suit or appeal was filed, and an appeal heard by the bench prescribed by competent law at the time of hearing is valid. A related consequence is that losing a Division Bench hearing creates no vested further appeal to the Supreme Court where the Constitution requires Parliament to authorise appeals from a single Judge.
exceptions_or_limits: The rule presupposes that the change in bench composition was made by competent legislation; the appellant did not challenge the repeal or change as unconstitutional.
The substantive right of appeal itself remains protected; only the bench composition is treated as procedural.
Further appeal to the Supreme Court from a single High Court Judge's judgment is unavailable under Article 133(3) unless Parliament has provided for it.

common_material_facts: Appeal was instituted when law required a larger bench (Division Bench or three-judge bench).
Subsequent legislation or court reorganisation reduced the required bench strength before hearing.
Appeal was heard by a smaller bench (single Judge or two judges).
Appellant claimed a vested right to the larger bench.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 96, Code of Civil Procedure
Article 133(3), Constitution of India
Travancore-Cochin High Court Act
Legislation governing the successor High Court after state merger
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members reject the claim of a vested right to a specified bench strength; the hearing by the bench under the law in force is upheld (2 directly on bench composition, 1 on the consequential Article 133 appeal).
variations: 460659_1 and 861817_6 decide the bench-composition point directly, while 460659_2 deals with the derivative claim of a vested appeal to the Supreme Court.
460659_1 turns on a later statute expanding single-Judge jurisdiction; 861817_6 turns on abolition of the former High Court and repeal of the full-bench provision.
460659_1 relies on precedent (Garikapati Veeraya, Ittavira Mathai, Mahendra v. Darsan) and rejects Radhakrishan v. Shridhar; 861817_6 relies on the successor High Court's governing legislation.

legal_question: For the purposes of section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, when is property 'possessed by' a female Hindu so that her limited estate is enlarged into full ownership, and does this require actual physical possession?

rule.if: section_14_1_conversion_claim and female_hindu_acquired_property_lawfully and (actual_possession or constructive_or_legal_possession or retained_ownership_with_enforceable_right_to_recover) and not rights_completely_parted_with_or_mere_trespasser

predicates.section_14_1_conversion_claim: The dispute is whether a Hindu female's limited interest in property became full ownership under section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
predicates.female_hindu_acquired_property_lawfully: The female Hindu acquired the property by a lawful title (for example inheritance, or reconveyance of the property to her), not by trespass without title.
predicates.actual_possession: The female Hindu was in actual physical possession of the property.
predicates.constructive_or_legal_possession: The female Hindu had constructive possession or possession in any form recognised by law, for example through a permissive holder or by holding a legal interest when her title was challenged.
predicates.retained_ownership_with_enforceable_righ: The female Hindu kept her ownership rights and could enforce a right to recover the property from a trespasser or dispossessor, for example through a pending recovery suit.
predicates.rights_completely_parted_with_or_mere_tr: The female Hindu had parted with her rights so completely that she can no longer exercise them, or she had no title and was merely a trespasser.
predicates.property_is_possessed_by_female_hindu_an: The property counts as possessed by the female Hindu under section 14(1) and she holds it as full owner.

definition: The word 'possessed' in section 14(1) is read broadly. It covers actual possession, constructive possession, possession in any form recognised by law, and retained ownership with a right to recover the property. The female Hindu must have acquired the property lawfully and must not have completely parted with her rights or be a mere trespasser. If so, her limited estate enlarges into full ownership.
exceptions_or_limits: The provision does not apply where the female Hindu has alienated or parted with her rights so completely that she can no longer exercise them.
The provision does not apply where she has no title and is merely a trespasser, or where she acquired possession by trespass without title.

Physical or constructive possession at the commencement of the Act is not itself a prerequisite where she holds a legal interest in lawfully acquired property when her title is challenged (977945_2); this reflects that member's reasoning and is not stated by the others.

common_material_facts: A Hindu widow acquired property from her husband or otherwise lawfully.
She was not in actual physical possession, or her possession was disputed, when her title was questioned.
Someone else held the property by dispossession, permission or an earlier transfer.
statutes_and_provisions: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members, 'possessed' was read broadly and the female Hindu was held to be full owner.
variations: 502707_3 relies on retained ownership and an enforceable right to recover from a dispossessor, through a pending suit.
977945_2 relies on reacquisition of the property after an earlier transfer, so that she held a legal interest when her title was challenged.
990120_1 relies on constructive possession through a permissive holder, on the assumption that the adoption was invalid.
The members differ on whether possession is assessed at commencement of the Act or when title is challenged.

legal_question: Where a rent-control statute prescribes its own hierarchy of remedies (appeal and a designated revision), can a party seek a further or different revision, whether under the general civil procedure code or the statute's own revision provision, against the appellate or revisional decision?

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The dispute is an eviction or recovery-of-possession proceeding governed by a state rent-control statute.
predicates.statute_provides_own_appeal_and_designat: The rent-control statute itself sets out a hierarchy of remedies, namely an initial decision, an appeal, and a designated revision limited to specified orders or courts.
predicates.statute_makes_decision_final_except_thro: The statute provides that the decision is final and cannot be questioned in any court except through the designated statutory revision (or, for a trial court order, that the revision provision covers only that order and further remedy lies elsewhere).
predicates.party_seeks_revision_outside_designated_: The party invokes a revision that the statutory scheme does not authorise. Examples are a second revision under the general civil procedure code after the statutory revision was decided, or a statutory revision against an order (such as an appellate decree) that the revision provision does not cover.
predicates.further_or_alternative_revision_not_main: The attempted revision is not maintainable, and the court lacks jurisdiction to interfere through it.

definition: Where a rent-control statute provides its own tiers of appeal and revision and makes the decision final except through that revision, a party cannot bring a further revision under the general civil procedure code after the statutory revision, nor use the statutory revision against an order it does not cover. Any further remedy must be one the statute or ordinary procedural law (for example a second appeal under Section 100 CPC after an appeal) actually allows.
exceptions_or_limits: The result depends on the wording of the particular state statute. A materially different statute (for example the Karnataka provisions) may permit a further revision.

Where an appellate decree is challenged and the revision provision covers only trial court orders, the proper remedy is a second appeal under Section 100 CPC, subject to its restrictions. In 500073_2 the Court treated the revision as a second appeal because the objection was not raised earlier.
The finality-based exclusion of a second revision is drawn from the Kerala statute (sections 18(5), 20 and 20A). Its application elsewhere requires a similar finality and revision structure.

common_material_facts: Eviction or recovery of possession sought under a state rent-control statute
The statute provides a trial, an appeal and a designated revision
A party sought a revision that the statutory scheme did not contemplate (a High Court revision after the statutory revision, or a revision against an appellate decree)
The High Court had entertained the challenge
statutes_and_provisions: Section 14(8), Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent & Eviction) Control Act, 1982
Section 100, Code of Civil Procedure
Sections 18(5), 20 and 20A, Kerala Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1965
Section 115, Code of Civil Procedure
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members the further or alternative revision was held not maintainable. In 2 Kerala cases the High Court orders were set aside. In the Bihar case the revision was treated as a second appeal under Section 100 CPC.
variations: 500073_2 concerns the scope of the statutory revision (trial court orders only) and the remedy under Section 100 CPC. The Kerala cases concern exclusion of a second revision under Section 115 CPC after the statutory revision.
In 500073_2 the Court saved the proceeding by treating it as a second appeal. In the Kerala cases the High Court orders were set aside.
570358_1 relies on the breadth of the statutory revisional power and the power to remand, and distinguishes a different state's statute.

split_suggestion: If a tighter grouping is wanted, separate 52016_1 and 570358_1 (no second revision under Section 115 CPC after the Kerala statutory revision) from 500073_2 (the Bihar revision provision does not cover appellate decrees, so the remedy is Section 100 CPC).

legal_question: Where a joint decree has been passed against several defendants, can a defendant (or surviving co-appellant) who has an independent interest pursue an appeal from that decree despite another defendant's failure to appeal or death during the appeal, and when can survivors instead rely on survival of the right to sue?

rule.if: joint_decree_against_several_defendants and decree_rests_on_ground_common_to_them and appealing_defendant_has_independent_interest_in_decree and (coparty_did_not_appeal or coappellant_died_during_appeal)

predicates.joint_decree_against_several_defendants: A single decree (e.g., for eviction) was passed against more than one defendant together.
predicates.decree_rests_on_ground_common_to_them: The decree is based on a ground that applies to all the defendants, so it is joint and not severable.
predicates.appealing_defendant_has_independent_inte: The defendant who appeals (or survives as appellant) has his own substantial interest in the decree and an independent right of appeal, not derived merely from the other party.
predicates.coparty_did_not_appeal: Another defendant bound by the joint decree chose not to appeal.
predicates.coappellant_died_during_appeal: Another appellant died while the appeal was pending.
predicates.appeal_maintainable_at_instance_of_appea: The appeal by the defendant with independent interest is not defeated by the co-party's omission to appeal or death, and the appellate court must hear it and may grant relief on the merits.

definition: A defendant against whom a joint decree resting on a common ground has been passed has an independent right to appeal and to obtain relief. The other defendant's failure to appeal, or death during the appeal, does not by itself defeat the appeal. Survivors cannot, however, rely on Order XXII Rule 2 survival of the right to sue unless they establish that the right survives to them alone.
exceptions_or_limits: Where survivors rely on Order XXII Rule 2 (right to sue surviving to them alone), they must prove the basis, such as a joint Hindu family. Failing that, Order XXII Rules 3 and 11 apply and abatement follows if legal representatives are not substituted in time.
The rule protects only a party with a real, independent interest in the decree. It does not cover a deceased appellant's own interest where no substitution is made.
The decree must be joint or rest on a ground common to the defendants. Where the decree rests on a ground personal to the deceased or non-appealing party, the result may differ.

outlier_members.reason: It concerns abatement and whether survivors can continue under Order XXII Rule 2 when the joint-family basis is unproved. The appellants had no independent-interest or common-ground finding, and the outcome went against continuation. It is the counterpoint limit rather than the same holding.

common_material_facts: Eviction decree passed jointly against several tenants, subtenants or occupants
Only some defendants appealed, or an appellant died mid-appeal
Question whether the remaining party could still maintain the appeal
statutes_and_provisions: Section 34 of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952
Order XLI Rule 4 CPC
Order XXII Rules 2, 3 and 11 CPC
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: Two of three members (569555_3, 760518_1) allow the appeal to proceed and be decided on the merits for the defendant with independent interest. One (72077064_1) refuses continuation because the survival-of-right basis was not proved.
variations: Non-appeal by a co-defendant (569555_3) versus death of a co-appellant (760518_1 and 72077064_1)
Order XLI Rule 4 and independent right of appeal versus Order XXII Rule 2 survival of right
Success depends on showing an independent interest or common ground; the unproved joint-family claim failed

split_suggestion: Separate the appeal-from-joint-decree members (569555_3, 760518_1) from the abatement and substitution member (72077064_1), which turns on Order XXII Rule 2 and proof of joint-family survivorship.

legal_question: Can an agricultural income-tax assessment be validly made on the strength of a general public notice calling for returns, where no valid individual or special notice was issued by the competent assessing authority and no return was validly made to that authority?

rule.if: is_tax_assessment_proceeding and general_return_notice_was_issued and not valid_individual_or_special_notice_from_competent_authority_initiated_proceeding and not return_validly_filed_with_assessing_authority_in_response_to_notice

predicates.is_tax_assessment_proceeding: The matter concerns an assessment (including best-judgment or fresh assessment) under an agricultural income-tax statute.
predicates.general_return_notice_was_issued: A general notice calling for returns was published or issued, or is assumed to have been issued, to taxpayers generally.
predicates.valid_individual_or_special_notice_from_: An individual or special notice requiring a return was served on the taxpayer by the authority competent to assess (or a timely escaped-assessment notice was served), thereby validly initiating proceedings.
predicates.return_validly_filed_with_assessing_auth: The taxpayer filed a return with the competent assessing authority in response to a valid notice, so that the return can found the assessment.
predicates.general_notice_cannot_support_assessment: The general notice alone cannot validly initiate or sustain the assessment, which is invalid or cannot proceed on that basis.

definition: A general notice calling for returns does not by itself initiate assessment against an individual taxpayer. Assessment requires a valid individual or special notice from the competent authority (or timely escaped-assessment proceedings), and a return made to another authority under an invalid notice cannot be relied on.
exceptions_or_limits: Where the taxpayer files a return in response to the general notice, proceedings may be initiated against that taxpayer (implied in 588334_1).
Where a timely notice for escaped assessment is served within the limitation period, assessment may be validly made.
The conclusions rest on the specific provisions of the Assam and U.P. agricultural income-tax statutes and the absence of any transfer procedure in the U.P. scheme.

common_material_facts: A general notice calling for returns was issued or assumed.
No valid individual or special notice by the competent authority initiated proceedings against the assessee.
The assessment was made or sought to be made without a return validly made to the assessing authority.
statutes_and_provisions: Assam Agricultural Income-tax Act ss. 19(1)-(3), 20(4), 30, 43(2)(a)
U.P. Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1948 ss. 2(6), 14, 15(1), 15(3)
Income-tax Act ss. 22, 23, 34 (analogy)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members hold the assessment invalid or unsupported: assessments quashed in 1 and the Collector barred from assessing on the return in 2.
variations: 588334_1 concerns taxpayers who filed no return and limitation for escaped assessment; the U.P. members concern a return filed to an unauthorized officer.
876169_3 focuses on vacation of the proceeding for want of jurisdiction; 876169_4 focuses on the distinct routes of ss. 15(1) and 15(3).
Only 588334_1 relies on precedents; the U.P. members rely on none.

split_suggestion: Optionally split into (a) general notice and no return or individual notice, with limitation for escaped assessment (588334_1), and (b) invalid special notice by an unauthorized officer and no reliance by another authority on that return (876169_3 and 876169_4).

legal_question: Under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, can a woman who has lived in a domestic relationship and a shared household obtain relief even though she has no ownership or beneficial interest in the household, is not residing there at the time of the violence or filing, or the relationship no longer subsists?

predicates.domestic_violence_application: The woman seeks protection, residence or other relief under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.
predicates.aggrieved_person_has_lived_in_domestic_r: The woman is or was in a qualifying domestic relationship (such as marriage or in-law relationship) and lived, or has the right to reside, in the household as a settled arrangement rather than a merely casual or fleeting stay.
predicates.alleged_violence_related_to_domestic_rel: The alleged domestic violence arose during the domestic relationship or was later inflicted on account of that relationship.
predicates.aggrieved_woman_may_seek_relief_under_th: The woman is entitled to maintain the application and seek relief; the absence of ownership or a beneficial interest of her or her husband in the household, her not residing there when the violence occurred or when she applied, or the end of the relationship by filing does not by itself bar her.

definition: A woman who has lived in a domestic relationship in a household with some degree of permanence, and whose alleged violence relates to that relationship, may seek relief under the Act. Neither the husband's ownership or tenancy of the household, nor her actual residence there at the time of violence or filing, nor the continued existence of the relationship is a precondition.
exceptions_or_limits: Merely casual or fleeting residence does not make a place a shared household; the nature and permanence of the living arrangement and the parties' intention are considered.
The alleged violence must relate to the domestic relationship, either during it or later inflicted on account of it.
The woman must fall within the statutory definitions of aggrieved person and domestic relationship (Sections 2(a), 2(f)); past relationships are included.
For non-residence, the woman must have a right to reside in the shared household under Section 17(1).

common_material_facts: Daughter-in-law or widowed wife claims relief against in-laws under the domestic-violence statute
Lower authorities or the respondent denied relief on a technical ground: no ownership by husband, no current co-residence, or no subsisting relationship
Allegations of harassment or violence by the husband's family
statutes_and_provisions: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 2(a)
Section 2(f)
Section 2(s)
Section 17
Section 19
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All 3 members read the Act's definitions broadly and in favour of the aggrieved woman, rejecting narrow preconditions (ownership, current residence, subsisting relationship).
variations: One member concerns the meaning of shared household and property interest, overruling S.R. Batra v. Taruna Batra, with a permanence qualifier
One member concerns non-residence at the time of violence or filing, based on the right to reside under Section 17(1)
One member concerns termination of the domestic relationship before filing, requiring that violence relate to the relationship

legal_question: When an aggrieved woman asserts a shared-household residence right in a civil suit, may and must the civil court consider that claim under Section 26 of the Domestic Violence Act, and how does a parallel domestic-violence proceeding or order affect the civil court's decision?

predicates.civil_proceeding_concerns_residence_in_p: A civil suit or other civil proceeding is pending that concerns possession of, or removal of a person from, a residential property.
predicates.person_resisting_or_claiming_is_aggrieve: The woman affected by the civil proceeding has pleaded that the property is her shared household and that she has a right to reside in it under the Domestic Violence Act.
predicates.civil_court_must_consider_residence_clai: The civil court must itself decide the pleaded residence claim under Sections 17, 19 and 26, on the evidence led before it. Relief requires the statutory conditions to be proved, including domestic violence. Any pending domestic-violence proceeding or order (interim or final) is relevant evidence but is neither a bar nor binding.

definition: A civil court hearing a suit about residence in a property must consider a woman's pleaded shared-household residence claim under Section 26 of the Domestic Violence Act, rather than leave it to a separate proceeding. It decides the claim independently on the evidence before it, treating any domestic-violence order as relevant but not conclusive. Residence relief depends on the claimant pleading and proving the statutory requirements, including domestic violence by the person against whom relief is sought.
exceptions_or_limits: Residence relief is not automatic: the claimant must plead and prove the statutory conditions, including an act of domestic violence by the person treated as respondent.
A prima facie interim order from the domestic-violence court does not itself establish those conditions in the civil suit.
An owner who is in a domestic relationship with the claimant may be treated as a respondent, since the words 'adult male' in Section 2(q) were struck down.
The domestic-violence court's orders are relevant evidence under Section 43 of the Evidence Act but do not bind the civil court.

common_material_facts: Owner (father-in-law) sued in a civil court to remove the daughter-in-law from the house.
The daughter-in-law pleaded in her written statement that the house was a shared household and that she had a right to reside there.
A separate application under the Domestic Violence Act was pending, with an interim order against dispossession except by a competent court.
statutes_and_provisions: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Sections 2(a), 2(q), 12, 17, 18-22, 19, 25, 26, 28, 36
Indian Evidence Act, 1872, Section 43
Vaishali Abhimanyu Joshi v. Nanasaheb Gopal Joshi
Hiral P. Harsora v. Kusum Narottamdas Harsora
Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah
Shanti Kumar Panda v. Shakuntala Devi
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: All three members hold that the civil court can and must consider the residence claim under Section 26, and that the domestic-violence proceeding is no bar. Its orders are only relevant evidence, and relief depends on proof of the statutory conditions (3 of 3 consistent).
variations: Member 3 focuses on the duty to consider the claim and avoid multiplicity of proceedings.
Member 4 focuses on who may be a respondent and on the requirement to plead and prove domestic violence.
Member 7 focuses on the relationship between parallel proceedings and the evidentiary weight of the domestic-violence order.

legal_question: Does a mining leaseholder who has made a timely application for renewal, or for continuation of the lease, that the State Government has not decided before the lease would expire or lapse get the benefit of a deemed extension of the lease, and within what limits?

rule.if: lease_extension_or_lapse_dispute and timely_statutory_application_made and application_undecided_when_lease_would_expire_or_lapse and not (lease_rejected_determined_or_lapsed_within_statutory_exclusion) and extension_conditions_satisfied

predicates.lease_extension_or_lapse_dispute: The dispute is whether a mining lease has expired or lapsed or instead continues by statutory extension.
predicates.timely_statutory_application_made: The leaseholder made, within the time the governing rule or statute requires, an application for renewal or for continuation of the lease.
predicates.application_undecided_when_lease_would_e: The State Government had not decided that application by the date the lease would otherwise have expired or lapsed.
predicates.lease_rejected_determined_or_lapsed_with: The renewal was rejected, the lease was determined, or the lease lapsed in the sense the statute excludes. Mere expiry of the grant or renewal term is not enough.
predicates.extension_conditions_satisfied: Any condition the regime attaches to the extension is met, such as compliance with lease terms and conditions, including required clearances and approvals.
predicates.lease_deemed_extended_pending_decision_w: The lease is treated as continuing until the application is decided or the outer limit the applicable provision prescribes is reached, whichever comes first.

definition: Where a leaseholder made a timely renewal or continuation application that remained undecided when the lease would expire or lapse, the governing rules or statute deem the lease extended while the application is pending. The extension is subject to the limits and conditions of the applicable provision and does not apply where the lease was rejected, determined or lapsed in the statutory sense.
exceptions_or_limits: The extension is not unlimited. It lasts only until the application is decided or the prescribed outer limit is reached, whichever comes first.
Under the amended statutory regime, entitlement depends on compliance with all lease terms and conditions, including required clearances and approvals.
Leases whose renewal was rejected, which were determined, or which lapsed are excluded from the amended extension regime. Mere expiry of the lease or renewal term is not such an exclusion.
The application must be timely under the governing rule, for example a renewal application made at least twelve months before expiry.

common_material_facts: The leaseholder made a timely application (for renewal or for continuation) that the State Government had not decided when the lease would expire or lapse.
A rule or statutory provision deemed the lease extended while the application was pending.
The extension was bounded by an outer limit or by other conditions of the provision.
The Court rejected the argument that expiry or lapse operated automatically.
statutes_and_provisions: Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, Rule 24A(1) and Rule 24A(6), before and after amendment
Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, Rule 28(2) and Rule 28(4)
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, Sections 8A(5), 8A(6) and 8A(9)
recurring_patterns.typical_outcome: In all 3 members, the leaseholder with a timely, undecided application got the benefit of a deemed extension, limited by the terms of the applicable provision.
variations: One member concerns first renewals under Rule 24A(6) and its amended, limited extension.

One member concerns the statutory regime for pre-amendment leases that expired before the amendment, and makes entitlement conditional on compliance with lease terms and on the lease not being rejected, determined or lapsed.
One member concerns Rule 28 applications for continuation where mining operations could not be conducted, with the extension capped by a prescribed outer limit.
